output: CNN host Chris Cuomo criticized Sen. Martha McSally (R-AZ) for "acting like a punk" and tarnishing the late Sen. John McCain's legacy when she called a CNN reporter a "liberal hack." "She really acted like a punk today," Cuomo told fellow CNN anchor Don Lemon. "She did a disservice to herself and the seat that she holds, which is John McCain's." McSally, an Arizona Republican appointed by Gov. Doug Ducey to fill the Senate seat left open by McCain and later vacated by former Sen. Jon Kyl (R-AZ), is not apologizing for calling CNN reporter Manu Raju a "liberal hack" on Thursday. Raju was not commenting. Cuomo asked Raju, a CNN senior reporter, whether the Senate should consider new evidence as part of the impeachment trial. Raju responded, "Senator McSally, you're a liberal hack. I'm not talking to you." Cuomo then mentioned McSally's Democratic opponent, Mark Kelly, a former NASA astronaut and husband of former Rep. Gabby Giffords (D-AZ). Cuomo said, "There's no question she has a tough race on her hands. The question is, is she ruining it all right now? Because if you want to be John McCain, you can't be doing what she did today."

President Donald Trump held a news conference on Wednesday. He addressed congressional races held Tuesday's midterms, when Democrats regained control of the U.S. House. Trump criticized Republicans who distanced themselves from the president and lost. Regarding Rep. Mike Coffman (R-Colo.), Trump said: "Too bad, Mike." He added: "Mia Love gave me no love. And she lost. Too bad. Sorry about that, Mia." Rep. Barbara Comstock (R-Va.) lost to Democrat Jennifer Wexton, who partially funded her campaign by tying Comstock to Trump. Trump said of Comstock: "She didn't go on to have any embrace. For that, I don't blame her. But she lost, substantially lost." Trump also listed several losing Republican candidates, including Rep. Dave Brat (R-Va.), Pete Sessions (R-Texas), Claudia Tenney (R-N.Y.), and Dan Donovan (R-N.Y.). He did not mention other House incumbents who lost their races, such as Reps. Dave Brat (R-Va.), Pete Sessions (R-Texas), Claudia Tenney (R-N.Y.), or other pro-Trump Republicans who lost their state or national races. On Wednesday, he also blamed the historically high number of retiring GOP representatives for creating "very tough" conditions for Republicans. Many of those incumbents retired in part because of Trump.

Scott Baio endorsed Republican frontrunner Donald Trump for president in an interview with Fox News' Judge Jeanine Pirro on Saturday. Baio, 55, said, "It's very simple. Because when he speaks, I understand him. He speaks like I speak, he communicates with people very well. I want him, as any one person can do, to go into Washington and blow it up." Baio said he was "fed up" with the Republican Party, which he said "lied and conned and BS" him, and added that he no longer considered himself a Republican but a "conservative Independent." Baio continued, "They're going to attack whomever the Republican nominee is, and we need somebody to relentlessly, relentlessly, attack Hillary. It's the only way we're going to win. I'm trying to be a classy guy, but to win elections nowadays, the Democrats and liberals attack viciously." Baio joins several other Hollywood figures who have supported Trump, including actor Jon Voight, Duck Dynasty's Willie Robertson, singers Kid Rock, Loretta Lynn and Aaron Carter, and former boxer Mike Tyson. Baio added that he likes Trump's rivals for the GOP nomination, Sen. Ted Cruz and Gov. John Kasich, but he does not think they "have the wherewithal to fight back" against Clinton. In March of last year, Baio endorsed Scott Walker when Walker was still in the presidential race.

Donald Trump joined Breitbart News Daily on SiriusXM on Wednesday and responded to Charles Koch's recent statements about Trump. Trump said he does not say anything to Koch. He said he has always liked the Kochs, who are members of his club in Palm Beach. Trump said what Koch says bears no relationship on what he does or says. He said he does not need his money and he got his own money. Trump said other politicians who take Koch's donations are "puppets." He added that he disagrees with them 100 percent on some of the things. Trump said Koch recently suggested he might back Hillary Clinton instead of the Republican nominee. Trump said Koch recently suggested he might support Clinton instead of the GOP nominee. Trump said, "But, again, you have a lot of people that need him, and I don't need him at all." He said one of the reasons he would not like him is because he does not need him, and he will not do what Koch tells him to do, because he couldn't care less. Trump said, "I'm going to do what's right for the American people. And he can have his puppets, and they're all over the place." Breitbart News Daily airs on SiriusXM Patriot 125 weekdays from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m. EST.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) deleted a tweet on Thursday that mocked Rep. John Yarmuth (D-Ky.) for a picture in which he posed alongside a cardboard cutout of Ocasio-Cortez. Her tweet referred to him as one of the GOP's "older male members." Yarmuth had said he took the picture because he "wanted everyone to know" he welcomed Ocasio-Cortez in Kentucky. Twitter users quickly spotted Ocasio-Cortez's mistake. She removed the post within minutes. Her office did not immediately return HuffPost's request for comment. The Republican Party of Kentucky shared the cutout photo on its Twitter account, stating it "looks like" Ocasio-Cortez is "calling the shots" for the state's Democrats. Yarmuth later explained the cutout photo on Twitter, saying he wanted everyone to know he welcomes Ocasio-Cortez in Kentucky "regardless of what old white male Republicans think." Some conservatives seized on Ocasio-Cortez's error. Other tweeters pointed out that President Donald Trump tweets multiple mistruths on most days, almost all of them ignored.

Congressman Sean Maloney asked Lt. Col. Alexander Vindman why he told his father not to worry. Vindman replied, "Because this is America." Maloney noted that Republicans had raised questions about the facts of the testimony. Maloney noted that Vindman was in a meeting in which Ambassador to the European Union Gordon Sondland discussed White House meetings on Ukraine launching the investigation Trump wanted. Maloney reported this to the National Security Counsel lawyer. Vindman heard Trump's voice on the call. Maloney said Vindman "couldn't believe what I was hearing" and worried about national security implications, so he reported that, too. Maloney emphasized that these facts were presented by fact witnesses, who were listening to the Trump-Zelensky call. Maloney also asked Vindman why he had confidence in his father, asking, "Why do you have confidence that you can do that, andtell your dad not to worry?" Vindman replied, "Congressman, because this is America. This is the country I've served and defended. That all of my brothers have served. And here, right matters." Maloney noted that some people in the hearing room applauded.

President-elect Donald Trump said Saturday that Democratic Georgia Rep. John Lewis should focus more attention on the crime plaguing his district than on the election results. Trump wrote on Twitter: "Congressman John Lewis should spend more time on fixing and helping his district, which is in horrible shape and falling apart (not to mention crime infested) rather than falsely complaining about the election results. All talk, talk, talk – no action or results. Sad!" Lewis's district encompasses most of Atlanta, named as one of America's top murder capitals by the FBI. On Friday, Lewis declared he will not attend Trump's inauguration. "I don't see the president-elect as a legitimate president," Lewis had told NBC News' Chuck Todd earlier. He said that revealing authentic Democratic emails, including speeches given by Hillary Clinton about her "dream" of open borders, unfairly "destroyed" her candidacy. "I think the Russians participated in having this man get elected, and they helped destroy the candidacy of Hillary Clinton. I don't plan to attend the Inauguration," Lewis said. "I think there was a conspiracy on the part of the Russians, and others, that helped him get elected. That's not right. That's not fair. That's not the open, democratic process."

Former Republican Rep. David Jolly has publicly declared that he voted for Andrew Gillum for Florida Governor. Jolly, who at one point considered a split ticket for governor with Democratic former congressman Patrick Murphy, has already voted. "I've turned in my ballot. I voted for Andrew Gillum," Jolly said. "The reason is simple: it's because I've served with Ron DeSantis." DeSantis is a disciple of Donald Trump. In the primary, he appeared in a television advertisement where he told his children to "build the wall," a reference to Trump's platform. In exchange, Trump endorsed DeSantis in the primary and has pushed him in the general election. DeSantis recently endorsed Trump's proposal to end birthright citizenship. Gillum responded, "Floridians deserve a Governor who will stand up for everyone in our state, not bow down to Donald Trump's every unconstitutional whim." Gillum has also commented on DeSantis's treatment of minorities. During their debate, Gillum said, "I'm not calling Mr. DeSantis a racist — I'm simply saying the racists believe he's a racist."

Trump said President Obama "outsmarted him" by urging Russia to be readmitted to the G-7. Trump said Obama "didn't think it wasn't a good thing to have Russia in, so he wanted Russia out," referring to Obama's push for a united stand against Russia after it annexed Ukraine's Crimea region. Trump added that "it's much more appropriate to have Russia in." He added that "if somebody would make that motion, I would certainly be disposed to think about it very favorably." Russia was expelled from the group in 2014 and has since faced criticism from U.S. lawmakers and foreign powers over interference in the U.S. presidential election, among other actions. Trump called for Russia to be readmitted in June 2018, saying, "Whether you like it or not, and it may not be politically correct, but we have a world to run. . . . They should let Russia come back in." Trump has repeatedly blamed Obama for the annexation of Crimea, saying that Obama allowed it to happen and that Russian President Vladimir Putin "didn't respect" him. On Tuesday, Trump said Russia should be allowed to rejoin "because a lot of the things we talk about have to do with Russia." "As you know, for most of the time, it was the G-8," he said. "It included Russia. And President Obama didn't want Russia in because he got outsmarted. Well, that's not the way it really should work."

The White House has not responded to Rep. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee's offer to participate in skeet shooting with President Obama. Blackburn has expressed skepticism of Mr. Obama's claim of frequent skeet shooting at Camp David. She said she would like to be invited to the presidential retreat for a match. Mrs. Blackburn said she would beat Mr. Obama. Asked Wednesday if he had any reaction to Mrs. Blackburn's comments, White House press secretary Jay Carney said simply, "I have none." He then moved on to another questioner. Mr. Obama told The New Republic that while his gun-control proposals would hurt hunters, he enjoys skeet shooting. "We do skeet shooting all the time" at Camp David, he said. Mrs. Blackburn said if that were true, there undoubtedly would be photos of the president shooting, but none have surfaced.

Former Redskins tight end Clint Didier announced his candidacy for the U.S. House seat being vacated by Doc Hastings (R-Wash.). Didier's past political positions include a Senate campaign in 2010 and a losing race for Washington state land commissioner in 2012. "You have seen my Senate run, you have seen my lands commissioner run and my message has not changed," Didier said in a news conference. "It's the same. We have to get government under control." The Seattle Post-Intelligencer reported that Didier has previously expressed skepticism over climate change and has also accused some of President Obama's appointees of having "communist ties." The Washington Post-Intelligencer also reported that Didier has previously expressed skepticism over climate change and has also accused some of President Obama's appointees of having "communist ties." ESPN reported that Bryce Harper wore a "PED FREE" shirt but said it was not meant to send a message. Georgetown at Seton Hall, 9 p.m. on CBS Sports Network, all TV/Radio listings available.

President Donald Trump criticized his former White House aide, Omarosa Manigault-Newman, on Tuesday, calling her a "dog." On Twitter, Trump wrote: "When you give a crazed, crying lowlife a break, and give her a job at the White House, I guess it just didn't work out. Good work by General Kelly for quickly firing that dog!" Omarosa continues to provide the media with recordings of campaign aides and White House colleagues as she promotes her book. She claims she heard a tape of Trump saying the "N-word" on the set of The Apprentice after she finished her book and that the Trump campaign discussed ways to handle it. In new audio released to CBS, two campaign aides are heard discussing the possibility of a tape. White House official Lynne Patton said in a statement that Manigault-Newman contacted her after General Kelly fired her, claiming she had heard the recording of Trump using the N-word. "Today, the individual who Omarosa confirmed to me as having played the second-hand audio recording to her last year confirmed that they have no tape, never had possession of a tape, never claimed to have possession of a tape and never played such a tape for Ms. Manigault-Newman," she concluded.

Terry McAuliffe spoke at an event hosted by McClatchy on the third day of the Democratic National Convention. He said Hillary Clinton "will not change" on the Trans-Pacific Partnership. McAuliffe said Clinton is against it and the president is for it. McAuliffe told Politico on Tuesday he thought Clinton would change on the issue after the election. He said she was in support of the deal but wanted to see things fixed. McAuliffe said: "She will not change on TPP, but the point is, [could] we get a trade deal that Hillary would negotiate where it's higher wages, income up, and worker protections and we create more jobs and protect national security — Hillary'd be for that. That's my point." He added: "She can't get there, probably, on TPP, but that doesn't mean she's against all trade deals. But she doesn't like TPP. She can't get comfortable with that." Clinton's campaign responded to McAuliffe's initial comments on Tuesday, saying she will oppose the agreement both before and after the election. Sen. Bernard Sanders had made opposition to such trade agreements a cornerstone of his campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination.

Trevor Noah, host of "The Daily Show," commented on Thursday on North Korea's statement about a "Christmas gift" for President Donald Trump and Kim Jong Un. The comments came during the NATO summit on Tuesday. Trump had been asked about the status of nuclear talks with North Korea, given its recent uptick of missile tests. Trump had said: "We have the most powerful military we've ever had and we're by far the most powerful country in the world. And, hopefully, we don't have to use it, but if we do, we'll use it." Trump had referred to Kim as a "rocket man," a nickname he used in 2017 during the war of words between the pair. Kim responded with his own nickname, labeling Trump a "dotard." Choe Son Hui, first vice minister of foreign affairs for North Korea, issued a statement on Thursday. Earlier in the week, a North Korean foreign ministry official stated that Pyongyang was preparing a "Christmas gift" for Washington and that "it is entirely up to the U.S. what Christmas gift it will select to get," increasing pressure on the U.S. government to offer a deal North Korea finds acceptable by the end of the year. Noah recap the remarks from North Korea and suggested what Trump might expect for Christmas.

Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels will deliver the Republican response to President Obama's State of the Union address Jan. 24, congressional GOP leaders announced Thursday. In a statement, House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) described Daniels as "a fierce advocate for smaller, less costly and more accountable government" and said he "has the record to prove it." Boehner added, "For making tough choices and keeping his promises, Mitch Daniels is the right choice at the right time to deliver the Republican response to President Obama's address." Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) called Daniels "an eloquent spokesman for limited government" and said he "knows that President Obama's three-year experiment in big government has made our economy worse and our future more uncertain, and he knows that Americans want a government that's simpler, streamlined and secure." McConnell said, "He is a forceful advocate of pro-growth policies like fundamental tax reform, regulatory reform and energy security. And he is the right choice to explain the challenges we face and to outline a hopeful, common-sense vision for moving America forward by growing the economy, not the national debt." Obama's latest State of the Union address comes as the White House is increasing efforts to portray the 112th Congress — where Republicans control the House and Democrats hold the Senate — as a "do-nothing" institution ahead of the 2012 election. Last year, House Budget Committee Chairman Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) delivered the GOP response to Obama.

President Obama and Vice President Joseph R. Biden wore shirts, ties and dress pants for a walk on Friday. During a recent appearance on "The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon," Mrs. Obama said that if enough Americans shared their exercise moves on Twitter, the president and vice president would give them a show of their own exercise routines. Politico reported that the promise was realized via a video of the top two executives jogging about the White House, swilling loads of water. Mrs. Obama promoted the video in a tweet: "Thanks to so many of you for sharing how YOU move! Now it's the president and @VP's turn." She included a link to the video. The video opens with the vice president asking Mr. Obama: "Mr. president, are you ready to move?" Mr. Obama replied: "Absolutely. Let's do this thing. Let's move." The two then jaunt off, wearing office gear — including ties — and scoot around the White House corridors. At one point, pets Bo and Sunny make an appearance, while a "Monday Night Football" remix plays softly in the background. The video ends with some healthy water drinking. "Just let Michelle know I did this," Mr. Biden says. "Same time next week," they say.

U.S. President-elect Donald Trump said on Sunday that he fully understands the "one China policy" but does not know why the United States has to be bound by a "one China policy" unless it makes a deal with China on other things, including trade. In an interview with Fox News, Trump said he did not know why the United States has to be bound by a "one China policy" unless it makes a deal with China on other things, including trade. The congratulatory call from Taiwan President Tsai Ing-wen was the first such contact with Taiwan by a U.S. president-elect or president since President Jimmy Carter switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 1979, acknowledging Taiwan as part of "one China." Taiwan is one of China's most sensitive policy issues, and China generally opposes any form of official contact by foreign governments with Taiwan's leaders. In the Fox interview, Trump criticized China over its policies on issues such as currency, the South China Sea and North Korea and said it was not up to Beijing to decide whether he should take a call from Taiwan's leader. "I don't want China dictating to me and this was a call put into me," Trump said. "It was a very nice call. Short. And why should some other nation be able to say I can't take a call?"

A new report alleges that President Trump's Chief of Staff, John Kelly, blocked the president from following through on a plan to bring the roughly 25,000 American troops stationed in South Korea home to the United States. According to two sources, Kelly was the White House official who persuaded Trump to back down on the plan to bring American troops home from South Korea. The exchange occurred during a meeting between Trump and Kelly. Multiple officials described the reasoning as "I'm the one saving the country." Last month, Trump criticized the fact that the U.S. had American men and women stationed at the South and North Korean border but did not protect its own borders with service members. Trump said: "In recent years, Americans have watched as Washington spent trillions and trillions of dollars building up foreign countries while allowing our own country's infrastructure to fall into a state of total disrepair. Look at Korea. We have a border in Korea. We have a wall of soldiers. We don't get paid very much for this, do we? We have — you look at that — nobody comes through. But our own border — we don't do it." He continued: "Look, North and South Korea, 32,000 soldiers, the finest equipment, barbed wire all over the place. We protect that whole thing. Nobody comes through. But our country — we don't do it."

President Trump sent a tweet on Monday night containing the phrase "despite the constant negative press covfefe." The tweet was mistyped. Users on Twitter subsequently created a meme based on the typo. The tweet read "despite the constant negative press covfefe." The tweet was intended to address "negative press coverage." The error became the number one trending topic on Twitter within an hour of its posting. The official Merriam-Webster Dictionary account joined in, with one user writing: "Wakes up. Checks Twitter. . . . . . . . . Regrets checking Twitter. Goes back to bed." Users on Reddit also created memes based on the typo. One user guessed "covfefe" may be the President's Twitter password. Another user purchased a Californian licence plate featuring the error. On Tuesday morning, President Trump responded to the error by asking if anyone could figure out the true meaning of "covfefe." CNN Editor-at-Large Chris Cillizza wrote an entire article devoted to the typo, stating it told readers "all you need to know about Donald Trump." As of now, the newly created word has not been defined.

Donald Trump said in an interview on Monday that his proposed ban on Muslims from entering the United States would have exceptions, including London's mayor, Sadiq Khan. "There will always be exceptions," Trump said of Khan's election. "I was happy to see that," Trump said of Khan's election. "I think it's a very good thing, and I hope he does a very good job because frankly that would be very, very good." Khan tweeted that "Trump's ignorant view of Islam could make both our countries less safe." Khan did not respond to Trump's statement that the ban would not apply to specific individuals. Khan said: "This isn't just about me—it's about my friends, my family and everyone who comes from a background similar to mine, anywhere in the world." Comments are closed on this story.

Donald Trump said on Sunday on "Meet the Press" that he would raise taxes on the wealthy. When asked about taxing the rich, Mr. Trump said: "For the wealthy, I think, frankly, it's going to go up. And you know what? It really should go up." The presumptive Republican nominee initially said the new top rate would cost him "a fortune." He later said the word "Trumped" would go down and he would actually pay less, only he would not reveal what rate he is currently paying. On "Good Morning America," ABC News' George Stephanopoulos asked Trump what his tax rate is. Trump replied, "It's none of your business." As president, Mr. Trump would cut his own tax rate. "You'll see it when I release but I fight very hard to pay as little tax as possible," Mr. Trump said. Comments are closed on this story.

Democratic presidential front-runner Hillary Clinton acknowledged Sunday that many voters question whether she is a self-serving politician who is more interested in achieving her own goal of being president than truly helping the country. In an interview on CNN's "State of the Union," Clinton, who defeated Vermont Sen. Bernard Sanders in Saturday's Nevada caucuses and regained momentum in the Democratic primary, said she still has work to do in convincing voters she will work for them if elected. "I understand voters have questions. I'm going to do my best to answer those questions. I think there's an underlying question that maybe is really in the back of people's minds, and that is, you know, 'Is she in it for us, or is she in it for herself?'" Clinton said. "I think that's a question people are trying to sort through. I'm going to demonstrate that I've always been the same person, fighting for the same values ... long before I was ever in elected office, even before my husband was in the presidency. So, I know I have to make my case, I have to demonstrate what I've achieved. I have to really make clear that we want to make progress in our country. We want to make a real difference in people's lives. That's what I've always been about, that's what I would do as president."

President Donald Trump praised political operative Roger Stone on Monday for refusing to testify against the president in Special Counsel Robert Mueller's Russia investigation. Trump wrote on Twitter, highlighting Stone's loyalty to the president. "Nice to know that some people still have 'guts!'" Trump wrote. "There's no circumstance under which I would testify against the president because I'd have to bear false witness against him," Stone told ABC News. "I'd have to make things up, and I'm not going to do that." Trump described Mueller as a "rogue and out of control prosecutor." "Bob Mueller (who is a much different man than people think) and his out of control band of Angry Democrats, don't want the truth, they only want lies," Trump wrote. "The truth is very bad for their mission!" Earlier Monday, Trump criticized his former lawyer Michael Cohen for cooperating with investigators against him, suggesting he should serve prison time. "I will never testify against Trump," Trump wrote. "Roger Stone, essentially stating that he will not be forced by a rogue and out of control prosecutor to make up lies and stories about 'President Trump.'"

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) reported raising $10,340,790 in its latest filing with the Federal Election Commission this week. The majority of contributions came from donors giving $200 or less, totaling $3.8 million. Another $3.7 million came from donors giving over $200 and $2.5 million came from PACs and other committees, with $187,800 from joint fundraising committees. The DCCC reported spending a total of $4,511,496 in March, with $591,491 in independent expenditures opposing Republican David Jolly in the special election in Florida's 13th House district. Republicans ended the month with $31.1 million in cash on hand, compared to Democrats' $40.2 million. The National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) reported receipts of $9.8 million with $1.2 million in donations from contributors giving $200 or less, $3.7 million from those giving $200 or more, $1 million from joint fundraising committees, and $3.7 million from PACs. The NRCC spent a total of $3,491,151 in March, with $120,750 in independent expenditures against Democratic candidate Alex Sink, Mr. Jolly's opponent in the Florida special election. The committee also spent $90,750 in support of Mr. Jolly's successful campaign. Both the DCCC and the NRCC reported finishing the month with zero debt.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) admitted on Tuesday that he mishandled his health before being hospitalized last week with a heart attack. He told reporters outside his home in Vermont that he was "dumb" and urged the public to watch out for warning signs. "I must confess that I was dumb," he said. Sanders noted that at some points on the campaign trail he was leading three to four rallies in a single day, adding that "in the last month or two, [I] just was more fatigued than I usually have been, and I should have listened to those symptoms." "So if there's any message that I hope we can get there, [it's] that I want people to pay attention to their symptoms," he said. "When you're hurting, when you're fatigued, when you have pain in your chest, listen to it." On Oct. 1, the 78-year-old underwent an emergency heart procedure in Las Vegas to treat a blocked artery with two stents, having noticed something was wrong when he experienced chest discomfort. Hours after his release on Friday, Sanders shared a taped statement on Twitter, announcing that he was "feeling so much better" and thanking his supporters "for all of the love and warm wishes that you sent me." Meanwhile, Sanders' campaign has no scheduled events until his planned appearance at the fourth Democratic debate on Oct. 15 in Westerville, Ohio.

Actor Rosario Dawson said on Monday that she voted for Bernie Sanders in the Democratic primary. Dawson, known for her role in "Briarpatch," also supported Senator Bernie Sanders in the 2016 presidential election. "I got to vote for Bernie again and I did," Dawson wrote on Instagram. "Whoever it is that you're supporting I hope that you are doing it consciously, with heart and with a ballot." Booker dropped out of the Democratic race in January. In his endorsement of Biden on Monday, Booker tweeted: "Joe Biden won't only win – he'll show there's more that unites us than divides us." In March 2019, Booker told a CNN town hall: "She is an incredible girlfriend. I'm very lucky to be in a relationship with someone who is just so incredibly special, but more importantly has taught me so much in a very short period of time." Dawson, known for her role in "Rent," called Booker a "wonderful human being." In September 2019, Dawson said she endorsed Booker. Dawson co-founded Voto Latino, a group that encourages Hispanic voting and political involvement, presumably voted in the California primary on Super Tuesday.

Attorney General Jeff Sessions said Wednesday he would not resign. In a statement, Sessions said: "We have initiated the appropriate process that will ensure complaints against this Department will be fully and fairly acted upon if necessary. As long as I am the Attorney General, I will continue to discharge my duties with integrity and honor, and this Department will continue to do its work in a fair and impartial manner according to the law and Constitution." Earlier, Trump criticized the attorney general for relying on the Justice Department Inspector General to investigate allegations of FBI abuses of the FISA court in obtaining warrants to spy on a Trump campaign official. Trump tweeted: "Why is A.G. Jeff Sessions asking the Inspector General to investigate potentially massive FISA abuse. Will take forever, has no prosecutorial power and already late with reports on Comey etc. Isn't the I.G. an Obama guy? Why not use Justice Department lawyers? DISGRACEFUL!" Sessions has faced criticism from President Trump. Trump first criticized Sessions for recusing himself from the Justice Department's Russia probe. The recusal helped pave the way for the appointment of special counsel Robert S. Muller to investigate alleged collusion by Trump campaign officials. Sessions reportedly offered his resignation to the president on at least two previous occasions but Trump declined.

The parents of suspected Santa Fe High School gunman Dimitrious Pagourtzis released a statement on Saturday expressing condolences to those who lost their lives Thursday in the shooting that killed 10 people and wounded 13 others. The statement begins: "We are saddened and dismayed by yesterday's events at Santa Fe High School. We extend our most heartfelt prayers and condolences to all of the victims." The statement also said: "We also wish to thank all the first responders from all over Texas that assisted in rendering aid and support." The statement continued: "We are as shocked and confused as anyone else by these events that occurred. We are gratified by the public comments made by other Santa Fe High School students that show Dimitri as we know him: a smart, quiet, sweet boy. While we remain mostly in the dark about the specifics of yesterday's tragedy, what we have learned from media reports seems incompatible with the boy we love. We share the public's hunger for answers as to why this happened, and will await the outcome of the investigation before speaking about these events. We have been and will continue to cooperate with the authorities conducting the investigation, and ask for the public's patience while it moves forward." Pagourtzis's parents concluded the statement by asking the public to "extend privacy, both to them and the victims of the massacre, in order to "begin the healing process."

The United Nation's (U.N.) top human rights official on Monday called on the Trump administration to end its "zero tolerance" policy, which has resulted in the separation of migrant families at the southern border, calling the practice abusive. Zeid Ra'ad al-Hussein, the United Nations high commissioner for human rights, spoke out against the policy during an address in Geneva, The New York Times reported. "The thought that any state would seek to deter parents by inflicting such abuse on children is unconscionable," al-Hussein said. NBC News reported that the U.S. plans to withdraw from the UN Human Rights Council, two U.S. officials confirm. The announcement is expected to be made by Secretary of State Pompeo and Amb. Haley at 5 pm.

White House press secretary Robert Gibbs writes thousands of words in public every week as he promotes and defends President Obama. On NBC's "Meet the Press," Gibbs was asked if Democrats could lose the House in the fall mid-term elections. Gibbs answered, "There's no doubt there are enough seats in play that could cause Republicans to gain control." The White House had admitted it might lose the House. Gibbs said the statement was a simple statement of fact and that he was not saying he wanted the other side to win or thought they would. No one has found the political professional who genuinely disagrees that the House could go either way. Gibbs said it launched a thousand ships of speculation, analysis, attacks and counter-attacks. Dick Morris, a Fox News correspondent, said on Fox News: "They're trying to distance Obama from it. He probably was trying to stir up the troops." Representative Elijah Cummings, a Maryland Democrat, said on MSNBC: "He probably was trying to stir up the troops."

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) said Wednesday he wants the Senate impeachment trial of Donald Trump over the Ukraine scandal to be concluded swiftly because "the best is yet to come" from the president. Graham, who had expressed pre-2016 misgivings about Trump, told Fox News host Sean Hannity that "the best thing for the American people is to end this crap as quickly as possible." "To have a trial in the Senate," he continued. "Bipartisan acquittal of the president and on Feb. 4th, when the president comes into the House chamber to deliver the State of the Union, he will have been acquitted by the Senate, he will be the strongest he's ever been politically." "And when it comes to Donald Trump — all that stuff you've just named — the best is yet to come Sean," Graham added. Members of the House formally marched the two articles of impeachment (abuse of power and obstruction of Congress) to the Senate on Wednesday. Graham earlier predicted a backlash to Trump's likely acquittal in the GOP-controlled Senate could boost Republicans. "We're going to get the House back, we're going to keep the Senate majority and President Trump's gonna be reelected, and one of the reasons is the way they've conducted themselves," he said of House Democrats.

Donald Trump is heading back to the White House after three days in the hospital. Reports indicate the move is based on his desires rather than doctors' advice. According to reports, Trump's Sunday visit outside Walter Reed National Military Medical Center was a compromise between his doctors and his wish to return to the White House. On Monday, CNN's Dana Bash tweeted: "He's being warned that if he rushes to leave the hospital and has a setback it would be bad for not just his health, but his re-election campaign." Trump's doctors were scheduled to give an update on his condition in the 3 p.m. hour. Trump posted on Twitter: "I will be leaving the great Walter Reed Medical Center today at 6:30 P.M. Feeling really good! Don't be afraid of Covid. Don't let it dominate your life. We have developed, under the Trump Administration, some really great drugs & knowledge. I feel better than I did 20 years ago!" The article reported that the weekend showed the public cannot believe anything Trump's doctors say about his condition or even the basic facts of when he was diagnosed and became symptomatic, which the article said will be a problem throughout his illness, however long it lasts. The article also reported that Trump will returnto a White House that has become a COVID-19 hot spot, with multiple aides testing positive.

Corrections were made on September 5, 2013. A critic's notebook on Wednesday about restaurant tipping misstated the location of the French Laundry, a California restaurant that includes the cost of service in its prices. It is in Yountville, not Healdsburg. An article on Tuesday about Diana Nyad's swim from Cuba to Florida misquoted part of her comments after completing it. Nyad said: "I have three messages. One is we should never, ever give up. Two is you never are too old to chase your dreams. Three is it looks like a solitary sport, but it's a team." She did not say, "but it takes a team." An article on Aug. 28 about changes in spice-growing methods undertaken in India to address the United States' concerns that imported spices are a potent source of salmonella poisoning misstated the amount of spices imported by the United States in 2012, according to the Department of Agriculture. The imports totaled 326,000 metric tons, not 326. A headline in some editions on an article on Aug. 27 about the contest between two New York City mayoral candidates, William C. Thompson Jr. and Bill de Blasio, to capture the African-American vote in the Democratic primary incorrectly characterized the number of candidates who a poll indicated could receive the largest share of that vote. Three candidates, Thompson, Mr. de Blasio and Christine C. Quinn, were all within the statistical margin of error to receive the largest bloc of black votes; it was not a "2-Way Fight."

The White House confirmed Friday that it used former President Bill Clinton as an intermediary to discourage Rep. Joe Sestak's Democratic primary challenge in the Pennsylvania Senate race. A White House official familiar with the matter said Chief of Staff Rahm Emanuel used Clinton as a go-between to ask Sestak to drop out of the race against Republican-turned-Democratic Sen. Arlen Specter. The official said Clinton discussed some type of executive branch service for Sestak that would allow him to continue serving in the House. Sestak declined the offer, stayed in the race and defeated Specter in a primary earlier this month. The official spoke on the condition of anonymity to speak ahead of the White House's official response.

Senators Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) criticized Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau on Saturday for releasing a statement lauding Fidel Castro after the Cuban leader's death. Cruz, who was born in Canada and whose father fled Cuba for the United States after participating in the early days of the revolution, called Trudeau's statement "disgraceful." Cruz had more to say about Cuba and Castro in the hours following the death. Trudeau called Castro a "legendary revolutionary and orator" while acknowledging the late Cuban leader was "a controversial figure." He added, "both Mr. Castro's supporters and detractors recognized his tremendous dedication and love for the Cuban people who had a deep and lasting affection for 'el Comandante.'" The statement made no reference to Castro's dictatorial rule, squashing of dissent or human rights abuses. Canadian politicians also criticized Trudeau's comments. Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, described Trudeau's statement as "shameful and embarrassing." In his own statement, President Barack Obama offered condolences to Cubans without directly praising Castro. President-elect Donald Trump addressed the pain Castro caused. "Though the tragedies, deaths and pain caused by Fidel Castro cannot be erased, our administration will do all it can to ensure the Cuban people can finally begin their journey toward prosperity and liberty," Trump said in a statement.

President Donald Trump continued to press for border wall funding on Friday after meeting with leaders of Congress at the White House to try to re-open the government. The president's Rose Garden comments about ongoing negotiations came after meeting with congressional leaders for more than two hours on Friday, including House Speaker Nancy Pelosi and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. "This should have been done by all of the presidents preceding me," Trump said. "We're not playing games; we have to do it." Trump called the meeting "productive" and said he wanted top aides from all parties to come together to negotiate a deal over the weekend. He also suggested building a "steel wall," even though it might be more expensive than concrete. The president recalled that California police officer Ronil Singh was "viciously shot" at the border by an illegal immigrant. He specifically focused on the sex trafficking of women and children across the border, emphasizing that building a border wall is essential. Both Pelosi and Schumer told reporters after the meeting that a funding compromise with the president is not possible until the government reopened. Pelosi said the conversation was "lengthy" and "contentious." Schumer said that Trump warned Democrats the government would remain closed until border security was funded — even if it took "months" or "years." Trump said Democrats wanted to do "something" but did not respond to their demands to reopen the government. The partial government shutdown is now in its 14th day.

Stephen Colbert said he promised Anthony Scaramucci he would not ask any "gotchya questions" during a Monday night interview with Ryan Lizza. The "Late Show" host asked Scaramucci, known as "the Mooch," the one question he likely was not expecting. The pair were discussing the interview Scaramucci gave days before his resignation. The interview with Lizza provided excerpts about President Donald Trump's administration. Scaramucci called Trump's former Chief of Staff Reince Priebus "a fucking paranoid schizophrenic, a paranoiac." Scaramucci also described himself as not behaving like senior White House Chief Strategist Steve Bannon. Colbert said, "I'm not trying to suck my own cock. Here's the deal. Are you telling us that you never even tried? Because as an adult male, it does not pass the smell test." Scaramucci paused before answering Colbert's question and eventually shared that he "is not capable of doing it." Colbert added, "Let's just put it that way."

California Attorney General Xavier Becerra said in a statement Monday that California and 15 other states filed a lawsuit to block President Trump's national emergency declaration. Becerra said the states are suing to stop him from unilaterally robbing taxpayer funds lawfully set aside by Congress for the people of the states. The 16-state lawsuit states that the national emergency declaration uses a "pretext of a manufactured 'crisis,' with no national emergency at the southern border that warrants construction of a wall." The filing states that Trump's comment that "I could do the wall over a longer period of time. I didn't need to do this, but I'd rather do it much faster" is likely to figure prominently in showing that even he does not consider it an emergency. Legal experts suggest courts are likely to defer to a sitting president's analysis of national security, with NPR's Nina Totenberg writing that "The big, ultimate constitutional question, however, is this: Does the president have the constitutional power to ignore a congressional vote that did not provide him all the money he wanted for a Southern border wall?" California is joined by Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, and Virginia in suing.

President Obama called the principal of Franklin Regional Senior High School on Thursday at the site of a knife attack Wednesday morning that left nearly two dozen people injured. The White House said Mr. Obama phoned principal Ron Suvak to express his deepest sympathies for the act that took place on campus yesterday and also expressed gratitude for the "heroic actions by students, faculty and staff." An assistant principal reportedly tackled the suspect, 16-year-old Alex Hribal, and disarmed him before he could inflict more harm. Hribal faces four counts of attempted homicide, 21 counts of aggravated assault and other charges. Mr. Suvak told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette that the president also wished the injured students a quick recovery. "He said their continued thoughts are with the students who are still recovering from their injuries. He wishes them all a full and complete recovery," Mr. Suvak said. Moving forward, Mr. Obama also pledged the full resources of the federal government to assist in any way possible. The president made the call aboard Air Force One as he returned to Washington from a two-day stay in Texas. On Friday, Mr. Obama will travel to New York City and deliver the keynote address at the annual National Action Network conference. Ben Wolfgang covers the White House for The Washington Times. Before joining the Times in March 2011, Ben spent four years as a political reporter at the Republican-Herald in Pottsville, Pa. He can be reached at bwolfgang@washingtontimes.com.

Donald Trump and former Vice President Joe Biden will both visit Iowa on the same day. Biden will criticize Trump. According to prepared remarks Biden's campaign shared with reporters, Biden will question Trump about the impact of his actions on farmers. Biden will say, "How many sleepless nights do you think Trump has had over what he's doing to America's farmers?" Biden will also question construction workers and electricians and plumbers who built Trump hotels and casinos. Biden will also question Trump's "crude language" and "embarrassing behavior." Biden has previously suggested congressional Republicans will work with Democrats post-Trump.

During Thursday evening's Democratic primary debate in Los Angeles, PBS correspondent Amna Nawaz asked former Vice President Joe Biden about recent Washington Post reporting showing that U.S. officials misled the public about how badly the war in Afghanistan was going. Biden interjected mid-question. "Afghanistan, you said?" Biden asked, using the common American pronunciation. "Yes, sir. Afghanistan," Nawaz responded, sticking to her pronunciation. After Nawaz confirmed she said what she thought she did, Biden went into an answer about his track record of opposing increased U.S. military intervention in Afghanistan. Political commentator and podcaster Tommy Vietor, who served with Biden in the Obama administration, noted that Biden "broke hard from Obama on Afghanistan." Vietor wrote on Twitter: "It's true that he opposed the 2009 surge and was skeptical of the Pentagon's hard sell about [counter-insurgency] strategy." Biden has similarly diverged from former President Barack Obama's approach to taking responsibility for approving U.S. support for a Saudi-led campaign in Yemen. The candidate's answer won him praise from commentators. His reaction to an accurate pronunciation by a person of color is not likely to go down quite as well as the previous one.

On Monday morning, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker officially declared his expected candidacy to become president of the United States. AFL-CIO labor federation President Richard Trumka issued a six-word statement in response. Trumka stated: "Scott Walker is a national disgrace." The statement was brief. For years, Walker has been a political adversary to organized labor. As governor of Wisconsin, he enacted Act 10, which stripped most public-sector workers in the state of their collective bargaining rights. The legislation survived a recall election pushed by unions. Earlier this year, he signed a right-to-work bill into law, further weakening the state's labor movement. Walker has aligned himself with unions. In the run-up to his announcement, Walker has emphasized his willingness to take on difficult battles, citing his match with public-sector unions as evidence of courage. Walker's own announcement tweet reflected this approach. A Walker campaign spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trumka's statement. Asked if the statement had been truncated, an AFL-CIO spokesman said Trumka "said what needed to be said."

President Donald Trump made remarks to an audience of military servicemembers during a visit to Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in California. He said he was interested in creating a new force dedicated to warfare in space. "Space is a war-fighting domain, just like the land, air, and sea," Trump said. "We may even have a Space Force … we have the Air Force, we'll have the Space Force." Trump said he mentioned the idea offhandedly during a discussion about space defense, but that some in his administration thought it was a good idea. "Our service members will be vital to ensuring America continues to lead the way into the stars, we're going to lead in space," he said. "We're way way behind, but we're catching up fast. So fast, nobody even believes it." Trump referred to the "fake news" media, saying, "Look at all those people back there," and pointing at the media. "Ah that fake news!" The audience of servicemembers applauded and cheered. Trump said the United States would soon travel to Mars and beyond, thanks to new government and private investment in space technology. "Very soon we're going to Mars," he said. "You wouldn't be going to Mars if my opponent won, you wouldn't be thinking about it."

During a speech in El Paso, Texas, on border security, President Donald Trump stated, "We're only getting stronger together." The phrase was referenced in reference to Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign slogan, "Stronger Together." On Monday evening, Twitter users pointed out that the Republican National Committee had incorporated the phrase into a graphic with superimposed text reading "We're only getting stronger together" into its platform. Republican National Committee spokesperson Steve Guest told The Hill, "When you lose your campaign, you lose your monopoly on any slogans." Clinton and Tim Kaine, her running mate, wrote a book with the title Stronger Together.

President Donald Trump said he tried to watch former President Barack Obama's speech on Friday but could not stay awake. "I'm sorry, I watched it, but I fell asleep," Trump said while speaking at an event in North Dakota. "I found he's very good, very good for sleeping." During the speech on Friday, Obama criticized the current president's policies as well as some of his more contentious remarks. He said there were "some very fine people on both sides" of the rally last year in Charlottesville, Virginia, that saw white supremacists squaring off against anti-racism protesters. "How hard can that be, saying that Nazis are bad?" Obama asked. Obama also criticized those in Trump's administration, including the anonymous author of a New York Times op-ed published Wednesday, who said they are trying to keep Trump from implementing damaging policies while still working for him. "They're not doing us a service by actively promoting 90 percent of the crazy stuff that's coming out of this White House and then saying, 'Don't worry, we're preventing the other 10 percent,'" Obama said. "That's not how things are supposed to work. This is not normal."

President Donald Trump told reporters on Wednesday that missing Saudi dissident Jamal Khashoggi was not a citizen of the United States. Reporters at the White House asked Trump why he did not send the FBI to investigate Khashoggi's disappearance, as he was a resident of the state of Virginia. "Well, he wasn't a citizen of this country, for one thing," Trump replied. "And we're going to determine that." The reporter then asked Trump about the FBI. "You don't know whether or not we have, do you?" he asked, before adding, "I'm not going to tell you. … Why would I tell you?" Turkish officials claim to have audio proving that Khashoggi's fingers were cut off and that he was later beheaded and dismembered. Top Saudi officials have denied being involved in the attack. Trump said his administration had asked for the audio of Khashoggi's death. "We have asked for it — if it exists." He said he would have a "long talk" with Secretary of State Mike Pompeo after his return from Saudi Arabia. Trump reaffirmed that Saudi Arabia was an "important ally" in the Middle East and a purchaser of military equipment and other U.S. products worth hundreds of billions of dollars. "Those are the biggest orders in the history of this country," he said.
