Steele said, "We are seeing the opening of every newscast, every show with Donald Trump. Leading into this debate in two weeks' time—if this is the continual motion—the level of the frustration on that stage is going to be so high, you will cut it with a knife. And anything could happen, the explosion could be monumental." Steele was commenting on the latest incident from Trump after South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham called him a "jackass" several times during a Tuesday morning interview. Graham said, "I don't care if he drops out. Stay in the race, just stop being a jackass." Trump responded later that day at a rally on Graham's home turf in South Carolina. After hurling insults at Graham, including suggesting he could not so much as "get a job" in the private sector, Trump pulled out a sheet of paper with Graham's personal cell number on it and read it aloud to the crowd. "Give it a shot," Trump said, urging the audience to call the number, which had a Washington, D.C. area code. "Your local politician, you know? He won't fix anything but at least he'll talk to you."

Publisher Simon & Schuster released an image Friday depicting Hillary Clinton's new memoir "Hard Choices." The image shows a black-and-white portrait of the former first lady wearing business attire and smiling. The book, which comes out June 10, is billed as Mrs. Clinton's "inside account of the crises, choices, and challenges she faced during her four years as America's 67th Secretary of State, and how those experiences drive her view of the future." The publisher noted that Mrs. Clinton expected to serve out her term as a senator from New York after the 2008 presidential campaign. "To her surprise, her former rival for the Democratic Party nomination, newly elected President Barack Obama, asked her to serve in his administration as Secretary of State," the publisher says on a webpage devoted to the book. "This memoir is the story of the four extraordinary and historic years that followed, and the hard choices that she and her colleagues confronted." The publisher also noted that the book's release and subsequent promotion are expected to draw interest in whether Mrs. Clinton, the presumptive Democratic front-runner, plans to run for president in 2016. Republicans have begun to criticize her record, particularly by focusing on her response to the deadly 2012 attacks in Benghazi, Libya, while she led the State Department.

The Trump administration is using the military to house migrant families it detains and prosecuting at great expense and is currently under court order to reunite. The plan calls for 2,000 people to be held at military facilities within 45 days and for more capacity to be added going forward. The Defense Department said it was asked to identify any of its facilities that could house 12,000 people, and if those spaces are not available it has been asked to build "semi-separate, soft-sided camp facilities" capable of housing 4,000 people each at three separate locations. A retired Air Force colonel said recently that the whole plan "smacks of totalitarianism," while other observers have pointed to the likelihood of abuses. The article states that the whole plan originated with the act of ripping children out of their parents' arms in order to prosecute the parents overwhelmingly for misdemeanors, and that the government resists accepting legitimate asylum applications. It also states that abuse is hard-wired into the process. It says that Hiding it away on military bases and resisting efforts by even members of Congress to conduct oversight is a sign that the Trump administration intends abuse to continue.

On Tuesday afternoon, MSNBC released a clip of an upcoming interview with former White House advisor Valerie Jarrett. Jarrett, an attorney who worked with President Obama, was the main target of actress Roseanne Barr's tweet. Barr made the comment Tuesday morning. By Tuesday afternoon, Barr was fired and the hit comeback show "Roseanne" was cancelled. ABC issued a statement early Tuesday afternoon. Jarrett responded via an MSNBC video and transcript. She said she was worried about people who do not have a circle of friends and followers who come to their defense. She said she was worried about people walking down the street minding their own business and seeing somebody cling to their purse or run across the street, or every black parent she knows who has a boy who has to sit down and have a conversation, the "talk" as we call it. When asked if ABC made the right call in canceling the sitcom "Roseanne," Jarrett said that the network did and that Bob Iger, the chief executive officer of Disney, had called her before the announcement. Disney is the corporate owner of ABC. Iger apologized, Jarrett said, adding that he told her there would be zero tolerance for that type of comment. "He wanted me to know before he made it public that he was canceling the show," she said.

On Monday, Fox News personalities Sean Hannity and Jeanine Pirro joined President Donald Trump on stage at a campaign rally in Missouri. Hannity had criticized the media as "fake news" at the event. Hours before the event, he denied reports that he would join Trump on stage. "To be clear, I will not be on stage campaigning with the president," he said. "I am covering the final rally for my show." Hannity had faced criticism from his network in 2016 for appearing in a video endorsing Trump. Twitter users expressed opinions about the latest move by the two Fox News hosts. Fox News labeled its hosts' actions an "unfortunate distraction" in an emailed statement to HuffPost on Tuesday. "FOX News does not condone any talent participating in campaign events. We have an extraordinary team of journalists helming our coverage tonight and we are extremely proud of their work. This was an unfortunate distraction and has been addressed," the statement said. Hannity responded on Tuesday, arguing that getting on stage to praise the president during a campaign rally was not a problem because it "was NOT planned." He clarified that he did not mean to include his Fox News colleagues.

Former Vice President Joe Biden won four states on a night six states voted. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) won two states. Biden was declared the winner in Missouri and Mississippi immediately after polls closed. Shortly after, he was declared the winner in Michigan, a state Sanders won in 2016 and the state with the most delegates up for grabs this week. He later went on to take Idaho. Biden thanked Sanders and his supporters in a speech Tuesday to a small group of reporters in Philadelphia after both candidates canceled campaign events due to growing concerns over coronavirus. "To all those who have been knocked down, to all those who have been counted out, left behind, this is your campaign," Biden said. "Just over a week ago many of the pundits declared that this candidacy was dead. Now we're very much alive." Rep. Tulsi Gabbard (Hawaii) is still campaigning despite having won only two delegates so far. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) and former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg dropped out last week after poor showings in the Super Tuesday primaries. Former South Bend, Indiana, Mayor Pete Buttigieg and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (Minn.) exited the race just before Super Tuesday, throwing their support behind Biden. The states with primary elections Tuesday included: Follow results here as they come in. Live updates on the March 10 primaries are available.

President Obama had promised on his 2009 inauguration to close the facility opened by his predecessor and once housing around 700 inmates accused of terrorism charges. Congress prevented the transfer of any inmates to U.S. soil, forcing the search for countries abroad to take them. Under Obama, 179 prisoners were resettled. The Omani Foreign Ministry said that the men released from Guantanamo would "temporarily reside" in the country. The move was in response to a request by the U.S. government and "out of consideration for their humanitarian situation." The statement did not identify the prisoners names or nationalities. There has been no official announcement by the U.S. government, but a U.S. defense official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the transfer of the 10 detainees. An estimated 40 inmates will remain in the facility, which President-elect Donald Trump has pledged he would keep open and "load it up with some bad dudes." The detention facility operates outside the U.S. legal framework. Prisoners first arrived in Guantanamo in January 2002 and it became a depository for those accused of plotting terrorism against the United States. 16 years later, even the main suspects in the 9/11 attack, including mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, have yet to be tried. Additional reporting by Missy Ryan and Julie Tate from Washington, D.C.

President Obama spoke at the Cybersecurity and Consumer Protection Summit held at Stanford University on Friday. He made jokes about the university. "I've got to admit, like, I kind of want to go here," Obama said to the crowd. "I was trying to figure out why it is that a really nice place like this is wasted on young people who don't fully appreciate what you got. It's really nice." "This is the place that made 'nerd' cool," he said. "I was thinking about wearing some black-rimmed glasses, some tape in the middle, but I guess that's not what you do anymore. Ambassador McFaul told me if I came to Stanford, you'd 'talk nerdy to me.'" President Obama said he was pleased to be joined by members of his team who bleed Cardinal red. "We're infiltrated with Stanford people," he said. He pointed out his Senior Advisor Valerie Jarrett, National Security Advisor Susan Rice, and Secretary of Commerce Penny Pritzker are Stanford alumni. Last June, Obama's oldest daughter Malia toured the campus, according to a San Francisco Chronicle report. The article cited a source who said, "She came with a couple of friends (and) they did the regular tour, and probably some extra stuff."

Former President Bill Clinton appeared on CBS' "The Late Show" on Tuesday and addressed comments he made about the Monica Lewinsky scandal and the #MeToo movement during his book tour. Clinton said the interview aired Monday on NBC's "Today Show" and that he considered it "not my finest hour." When asked about his relationship with Lewinsky, a former White House intern with whom he had a sexual affair, Clinton said he would not have resigned if his tryst in the Oval Office had occurred at the height of the #MeToo movement. Clinton said: "When I saw the interview, I thought that, because they had to distill it, and it looked like I was saying I didn't apologize and I had no intention to. I was mad at me — not for the first time." He said: "that was a very painful thing, that happened 20 years ago, and I apologize to my family, to Monica Lewinsky and her family, and to the American people — I meant it then, I meant it now." Clinton added that he has had to "live with the consequences" of his affair "everyday since." Clinton reiterated that he believes the anti-sexual harassment awakening seen throughout the country is "long overdue, necessary and should be supported."

Fred Eshelman sued Houston-based True the Vote Inc. for $2.5 million, the sum of a number of donations made to the organization, over what he described as "vague responses, platitudes, and empty promises" regarding the Trump election lawsuits. Eshelman said in the lawsuit that True the Vote promised to investigate, litigate, and expose suspected illegal balloting and fraud in the 2020 general election. The group filed lawsuits in several battleground states and collected statements from whistleblowers claiming they witnessed attempts to impede legal vote tallies. The efforts were described as an attempt to bolster unsubstantiated allegations amid ongoing legal battles by President Trump, who has claimed widespread voter fraud cost him the race against Democratic challenger Joe Biden. According to reports by Bloomberg, Eshelman's lawsuit, filed Wednesday in Houston federal court, claims his donations were for naught and that True the Vote failed to update him on the status of the election, so he asked for his money back. Eshelman said in the complaint that True the Vote offered him $1 million if he would not sue. Eshelman is the former CEO of Pharmaceutical Product Development and founding chairman of Furiex Pharmaceuticals.

Civil rights figure Myrlie Evers-Williams has been chosen to deliver the invocation at President Obama's inauguration on Jan. 21, the Presidential Inaugural Committee announced Tuesday. Mrs. Evers-Williams is the widow of Medgar Evers, the NAACP official who in 1963 was murdered at his home in Jackson, Miss. She fought for 30 years to bring his killer to justice and is a distinguished scholar at Alcorn University in Lorman, Miss. She has won numerous civil rights awards. "I am humbled to have been asked to deliver the invocation for the 57th inauguration of the president of the United States — especially in light of this historical time in America when we will celebrate the 50th Anniversary of the civil rights movement," she said in a statement. "It is indeed an exhilarating experience to have the distinct honor of representing that era." The committee said Mr. Obama had a role in selecting Mrs. Evers-Williams and in choosing Rev. Louie Giglio, pastor of Passion City Church in Atlanta, to deliver the benediction. "Their voices have inspired many people across this great nation within the faith community and beyond," Mr. Obama said. "Their careers reflect the ideals that the vice president and I continue to pursue for all Americans — justice, equality and opportunity." Rev. Giglio is founder of Passion Conferences, a movement that brings together college-aged people in events such as worship and raising awareness about human trafficking.

Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin announced at the daily White House coronavirus briefing on Tuesday that the April 15 deadline for Americans to file their income taxes will now allow individuals who owe money to the Internal Revenue Service to defer payment up to one million dollars with no interest or penalty fee for 90 days. "We previously talked about deferring IRS payments," Mnuchin said. "The president earlier this morning authorized me to announce this program." "I announced we would defer to one hundred billion dollars and the president suggested we increase that to $300 billion," Mnuchin said. Mnuchin also encouraged people to file their taxes by the usual April 15 deadline. "We encourage the American who can file their taxes [by April 15] to continue to file their taxes because you will get tax refunds and we don't want you to lose out," Mnuchin said. "Many people do this electronically, which is easy for them and the IRS," Mnuchin said. "If you owe a payment to the IRS, you can defer up to a million dollars as an individual and the reason we are doing a million dollars is because that covers pass-throughs and businesses, and $10 million for corporations, interest free and penalty free for 90 days." "All you have to do is file your taxes," Mnuchin said. "Any American has the right to extend their taxes."

Harley-Davidson motorcycles have been affected by tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump. The company announced it is shifting some production out of the United States. The move was made in response to European Union tariffs on motorcycles imposed in retaliation for Trump's tariffs on the EU. In prepared remarks, the company said: "Harley-Davidson maintains a strong commitment to U.S.-based manufacturing which is valued by riders globally. Increasingasing international production to alleviate the EU tariff burden is not the company's preference, but represents the only sustainable option to make its motorcycles accessible to customers in the EU and maintain a viable business in Europe. Europe is a critical market for Harley-Davidson." The company also said in prepared remarks: "Harley-Davidson maintains a strong commitment to U.S.-based manufacturing which is valued by riders globally.Increasing international production to alleviate the EU tariff burden is not the company's preference, but represents the only sustainable option to make its motorcycles accessible to customers in the EU and maintain a viable business in Europe. Europe is a critical market for Harley-Davidson." The announcement comes months after an announcement that Harley-Davidson would consolidate two U.S. plants due to falling motorcycle sales. The announcement comes at the same time as aMissouri nail company announced it had laid off 60 temporary workers due to Trump's tariffs, with more jobs on the line.

The Senate will take up Donald Trump's impeachment next week, bringing a halt to the body's business. Majority Mitch McConnell has shut down legislating. Democratic Sen. Kamala Harris's intervention will not be a factor. The trial will involve more court-packing by McConnell and Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Lindsey Graham. There will not be committee hearings during the trial. The three-day MLK holiday weekend will be a busy one for the prosecution and defense. As of Thursday afternoon, McConnell had not shared the text of the trial procedures with Senate Democrats. Democratic leader Chuck Schumer plans to force votes for calling witnesses at the outset on Tuesday. They want a minimum of four witnesses, including former national security adviser John Bolton and acting White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney. McConnell has a plan, aided by Sen. Susan Collins, to delay that vote by postponing any votes on witnesses or documents until after the presentation of the case by the House and the rebuttal by Trump's lawyers. Republicans are expected to say they have heard enough to vote to acquit. It is possible there could be enough new bombshells in the case, a la Lev Parnas, to weigh on the necessary four Republican senators to flip that scenario, but it is not very probable.

Iranian President Hassan Rouhani's English Twitter account used the hashtag #RouhaniCare on Wednesday to refer to a new health care initiative that will extend medical insurance to all Iranians. The hashtag is a reference to the Affordable Care Act, commonly dubbed "Obamacare." According to Your Middle East, the website's Iran correspondent Alborz Habibi first used the hashtag in connection with the health care announcement. Habibi said on the website: "Rouhani hinted at an insurance and health care program. Then I joked and used RouhaniCare hashtag on Twitter." According to Bloomberg News, Rouhani announced the new health care plans in a televised address to the nation on Wednesday night. The speech also covered topics such as the Geneva accords on Iran's nuclear program and the country's economy. Experts and pundits responded to the #RouhaniCare tweet, with many referring to the obstacles the Affordable Care Act has faced in the U.S. The Iranian president told reporters at the World Economic Forum in Davos last January that he does not run his English Twitter account himself but trusts "friends" to post frequent updates. The headline on the story was changed to highlight that Iranian President Rouhani does not manage his English twitter account personally, and did not originate the phrase "Rouhani care."

Rumors and conspiracies have proliferated in the aftermath of the Sunday night shooting at a Las Vegas music festival that left at least 59 dead. The falsehoods include false allegations about the gunman, a person of interest, and Nevada's gun control laws. Before police named Stephen Paddock as the gunman, some bloggers and social media users incorrectly identified a man named Geary Danley as the "murderer." In a now deleted post, the right-wing blog The Gateway Pundit called Mr. Danley "a far left loon" and noted that he had followed several pages dedicated to liberal politics on Facebook. All of these claims are untrue. The unfounded rumors appear to have originated on the anonymous messaging board 4chan. ISIS claimed responsibility for the attack and said the gunman had recently converted to Islam. An FBI spokesman said there is no proof so far that Mr. Paddock had any ties to international terrorist groups. Some social media accounts spread the unfounded claims that Mr. Paddock has been radicalized. New York Times reporter Rukmini Callimachi, who has covered ISIS for several years, noted on Twitter that the organization has incorrectly claimed responsibility for two recent attacks, casting further down on any assertion of an ISIS connection. Additionally, Graeme Wood, who has reported on ISIS for The Atlantic, noted that Mr. Paddock was a gambler and had committed suicide, actions that are at odds with ISIS' ideology.

President Obama has sometimes watched events around the White House, including ones he helped create, only on television. Throughout his presidency, Mr. Obama and his wife, Michelle, have complained to friends about how isolated their lives have become: no trick-or-treating, quick shopping trips or date-nights out. The two have mostly refrained from publicly complaining publicly about how security concerns have hurt their freedom and friendships, for fear that they would be seen as ungrateful for the extraordinary opportunities they have been given as the first family. On Tuesday, President Obama expressed regret that he was not able to celebrate with crowds outside the White House that had gathered on Friday hours after the Supreme Court struck down limits on same-sex marriage. The administration lit the White House in rainbow colors that evening in celebration of the ruling. "To see people gathered in an evening outside on a beautiful summer night and to feel whole and to feel accepted and to feel that they had a right to love, that was pretty cool. That was a good thing," Mr. Obama said when asked about the extraordinary week. "And the only bad part about it was I couldn't go out and peek at it myself, because then I would have had to clear out all the people, or the Secret Service would have. So I — I could only reflect on it from a television screen. That's a moment worth savoring."

House Armed Service Committee Chairman Buck McKeon is set to announce his retirement on Thursday. A source close to the California congressman told The Hill that McKeon will be making his announcement Thursday morning. Politico and the Huffington Post published headlines and stories about McKeon's soon-to-be-announced retirement. Office spokeswoman Alissa Curley said in a statement to The Washington Post: "The congressman will make an announcement when he is ready to make the announcement." McKeon's retirement leaves an influential role overseeing military policy and Pentagon budgets. Defense industry insiders say Rep. Mac Thornberry from Texas is the front-runner, The Hill reported. Two other members have strong support: Reps. Randy Forbes from Virginia and Michael Turner from Ohio. Industry insiders say Thornberry will likely be McKeon's choice. One defense lobbyist in The Hill said: "Thornberry does all the right things. He does what he needs to for the party. He's well thought of on the committee and Buck wants him to be his heir apparent. There's no reason to pass him over."

Former House Speaker Gordon Fox announced Monday he had stepped down. Frank Anzeveno Jr., chief of staff to Fox, said in a statement that he had planned to leave at the end of the General Assembly's session in June because he had known for a while that Fox would not run again. Anzeveno said: "In light of recent events at the Statehouse, time has accelerated. I cleaned out my office over the weekend in anticipation that a new speaker needs to bring in his own staff." Fox, a Providence Democrat, resigned Saturday after raids by state and federal authorities, including the IRS. Officials have not provided details on what the investigation is about or whom it is targeting. Fox had said publicly as recently as December that he planned to run for re-election this fall and seek another term as speaker in 2015. Anzeveno is a former state representative who also was chief of staff to Fox's predecessor, Bill Murphy. He said Fox did not want to announce his decision not to run again "so that the focus would be on the many challenging issues before the House of Representatives." He added: "I will always respect the House of Representatives and wish them the best in tackling the difficult issues before them."

During an interview broadcast on Thursday's edition of CNN's "AC360," former Republican presidential candidate Carly Fiorina responded to President Trump's "horseface" tweet about Stormy Daniels. Fiorina said such insults diminish the presidency and that Daniels, her attorney Michael Avenatti, and Trump are "all birds of a feather. They're all in show business." Fiorina said, "There's no doubt that the office of the presidency is diminished when the occupant engages in this kind of insult over Twitter. On the other hand, when I think about the people involved here, Stormy Daniels, her lawyer, Donald Trump, I honestly think they're all birds of a feather. They're all in show business. And so, while she's talking about his private parts, he's talking about her face, and they're all getting a lot of publicity." Fiorina added that while rhetoric is important, "we also need to focus on the startling reality that we're not making much progress in terms of toxic work cultures or the abuse of women or the underrepresentation of women and people of color in positions of impact and influence." She concluded that it is unfortunate that women's issues have become politicized and that female conservatives should not be criticized for failing to fall in line with Democratic policies.

On Friday's "Late Night with Jimmy Fallon" the former Republican presidential candidate and former governor of Massachusetts, Mitt Romney, appeared on the program. The documentary "Mitt" is available on Netflix. Fallon presented a running gag featuring a guest, either Brian Williams or Barack Obama, and ad-libbed Barry White-style. Romney was referred to as "Roma lama ding dong" by the "Late Night" crew. The segment covered Tuesday's State of the Union speech. The menu included unemployment, debt, immigration reform and "wide spread wire tapping." Fallon responded, "Ah yeah. President Obama looked at the American people up and down and said, 'I'd tap that.'" Romney remained composed for the remainder of the program. On his way out of New York, Romney ran into "Scrubs" star Zach Braff at JFK airport. A selfie ensued. The segment included the phrase "The Hunger Games" reference.

Stephen K. Bannon, former Executive Chairman to Breitbart News, told the New York Times' Michael Grynbaum during a telephone call on Wednesday evening that the "elite media" has "no authority" to report on what the American people want from newly-inaugurated President Donald Trump. Bannon said the American press had been "humiliated" by an election outcome few anticipated, and repeatedly described the media as "the opposition party" of the current administration. "The media should be embarrassed and humiliated and keep its mouth shut and just listen for awhile," Bannon said. "I want you to quote this," Bannon added. "The media here is the opposition party. They don't understand this country. They still do not understand why Donald Trump is the president of the United States." "The elite media got it dead wrong, 100 percent dead wrong," Bannon said of the election, calling it "a humiliating defeat that they will never wash away, that will always be there." "That's why you have no power," Bannon added. "You were humiliated."

The Democratic Party is holding a debate in South Carolina tonight. Candidates are seeking to gain votes toward Super Tuesday. Mike Bloomberg has faced criticism for his history of bad work practices and his standing as a billionaire in an era of extraordinary income inequality. Senator Elizabeth Warren criticized Bloomberg for his financial support of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham. Bloomberg responded by stating he also spent lots of money on Democratic campaigns. Bloomberg made the remarks on the record. He said: "Let's just go on the record. They talk about 40 democrats. 21 of those were people they spent $100 million to help elect. All of the new Democrats that came in, put Nancy Pelosi in charge, and gave the congress the ability to control this president, I bought--Igot them."

An NBC/WSJ/Marist survey released Thursday found 58 percent of likely Democratic voters in New Hampshire back Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, while 38 percent support Mrs. Clinton. That result is virtually unchanged from a poll the group released last week before the caucuses. Lee Miringoff, director of the Marist College Institute for Public Opinion, said Mrs. Clinton continued to face an "uphill fight" in New Hampshire as Mr. Sanders remained popular in his neighboring state. Mr. Sanders is leading by a large margin with independents, men and younger voters. He is also doing better with women. Mrs. Clinton, meanwhile, has an edge with voters older than 60. There is still hope for Mrs. Clinton heading into the primary on Tuesday, as she overcame a polling deficit in 2008 and defeated Senator Barack Obama in New Hampshire. Mrs. Clinton and Mr. Sanders will also face off for their first one-on-one debate on Thursday night in Durham, N.H., giving voters a last chance to judge them against each other in person. The poll released Thursday, which was conducted after the Iowa caucuses, had a margin of error of plus or minus four percentage points.

White House Staff Secretary Rob Porter resigned on Wednesday amid allegations that he abused two of his ex-wives, Colbie Holderness and Jennifer Willoughby. The Daily Mail reported on the allegations on Wednesday. According to Axios, Porter shared stories and photo evidence of repeated physical abuse. According to Axios, Porter had been urged by some White House staff including Gen. John Kelly to "stay and fight" for his position. Porter is currently in a relationship with White House Communications Director Hope Hicks and was a close ally of Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner. Porter denied the allegations in a statement on Wednesday, describing them as "false" and "vile claims." He said: "These outrageous allegations are simply false. I took the photos given to the media nearly 15 years ago and the reality behind them is nowhere close to what is being described. I have been transparent and truthful about these vile claims, but I will not further engage publicly with a coordinated smear campaign. My commitment to public service speaks for itself. I have always put duty to country first and treated others with respect. I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to have served in the Trump Administration and will seek to ensure a smooth transition when I leave the White House." Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT), who employed Porter as his chief of staff, said he was "heatbroken" by the allegations.

Vice President Joe Biden delivered a speech Tuesday at Philadelphia's city hall to respond to President Donald Trump's nationwide crackdown on violent protest and looting. Biden spoke on the morning after protests over the killing of George Floyd by police in Minneapolis, Minnesota, had again erupted into violence and looting in many cities. Biden criticized violent protest but also blamed police: "There's no place for violence, no place for looting or destroying property or burning churches or destroying businesses, many of them built by the very people of color who are [for] the first time in their lives are beginning to realize their dreams and build wealth for their families. Nor is it acceptable for our police, sworn to protect and serve all people, to escalate tension, resort to excessive violence. We need to distinguish between legitimate, peaceful protests and opportunistic violent destruction." It was not immediately clear what Biden meant. On Sunday, the New York Times reported that police responded to protests with greater force. In many cities, many residents complained that police had retreated in the face of widespread looting and destruction in Santa Monica, Philadelphia, and other cities. The Trump campaign responded to Biden's speech by accusing him of "stand[ing] with the rioters," noting that Biden's staff had paid bail for several people arrested by police during the clashes.

Iran's interior minister Mostafa Mohammad Najjar said at a press conference Saturday in Tehran that moderate candidate Hasan Rowhani won the presidential vote. Rowhani obtained more than 50 percent of more than 36 million votes cast in Friday's election. He was the lone moderate candidate in the race supported by reformists. Rowhani's conservative and hard-line opponents were far behind him. Rowhani has vowed to follow a policy of detente and interaction with the outside world.

President Donald Trump denied knowledge of any attempt to hide the guided-missile destroyer USS John S. McCain during his visit to the Pacific. He said the attempt was "well-meaning." "I would never do a thing like that," he said. "Now, somebody did it because they thought I didn't like him. Okay? They were well-meaning, I will say. I didn't know anything about it. I would never have done that." The president commented on the story as he left the White House for a commencement speech at the Air Force Academy. Trump again confirmed that he never liked McCain, citing his vote to kill the Republican effort to repeal Obamacare and his effort to get America to go to war in Iraq. "I wasn't a fan of John McCain. I never will be, but certainly, I couldn't care less if there is a boat named after his father," Trump said. The Wall Street Journal reported an email from the White House Military Office to the U.S. Navy Seventh Fleet directing the guided-missile destroyer to be out of sight during Trump's visit. Trump did not deny the story. "I don't know who did it. We will probably be able to find out who did it," he said. "They thought they were doing me a favor because they know I am not a fan of John McCain."

Donald Trump, the 2012 Republican nominee, posted on Twitter on Thursday criticizing Mitt Romney. Romney had earlier stated on Fox News that there was "a bombshell in Donald Trump's taxes." Romney had earlier stated on Fox News that there was "good reason to believe that there's a bombshell in Donald Trump's taxes." Romney also called on Sen. Marco Rubio (R-FL) and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) to release their tax information. Romney said either Rubio is not anywhere near as wealthy as he says he is, or he hasn't been paying taxes as expected, or perhaps he hasn't been giving money to vets or to the disabled like he has been telling us he has been doing. Trump posted on Twitter: "Mitt Romney, who was one of the dumbest and worst candidates in the history of Republican politics, is now pushing me on tax returns. Dope! Why doesn't @MittRomney just endorse @marcorubio already. now! Just for your info, tax returns have 0 to do w/ someone's net worth. I have already filed my financial statements w/ FEC. They are great! I'm going to do what @MittRomney was totally unable to do- WIN!"

The government said it expects to receive $750 million more from the latest sale of stock held in American International Group. The sales are part of an effort to recoup taxpayer money from the largest bailout of the 2008 financial crisis. The Treasury Department said the banks underwriting the sale exercised their option to buy 24.6 million AIG shares at the offering price of $30.50 each, bringing the total from the fourth round of sales in AIG stock to $5.75 billion. Treasury announced last week that it sold $5 billion in AIG stock. Treasury says it has received $23.3 billion from four sales of AIG stock. Treasury and the Federal Reserve provided $182 billion to rescue New York-based AIG from collapse in September 2008. Treasury's portion of the bailout was $47.5 billion. With the latest sale, AIG still owes taxpayers about $24 billion on the original investment, according to Treasury estimates.

Nearly three weeks after the shooting of Michael Brown prompted widespread protests in a St. Louis suburb and a national examination of race and police tactics, Hillary Rodham Clinton on Thursday praised President Obama's response to the episode and called for a swift investigation into the circumstances that led to the unarmed black teenager's death. In a paid speech at a technology conference in San Francisco, Clinton said she watched the funeral of Mr. Brown, the 18-year-old who was shot by a white police officer in Ferguson, Mo. "As a mother, as a human being, my heart just broke for his family," she said. "But I also grieve for that community and for many like it across our country," she said. "Behind the dramatic, terrible pictures on television are deep challenges that will be with them and with us long after the cameras move on." On Sunday, as Mrs. Clinton finished up a book signing for her memoir "Hard Choices" in the beach community of Westhampton, N.Y., she declined to respond to news media inquiries about Ferguson. Mrs. Clinton had been criticized for not speaking out on the subject. On Thursday, she weighed in with extended remarks that included praise of Mr. Obama for deciding to send Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. to Ferguson, and for having demanded a swift investigation into the circumstances that led to Mr. Brown's death.

President Donald Trump commented on Monday after former Vice President Joe Biden's son, Hunter Biden, stepped down from his role at a Chinese-backed investment firm. Trump wrote on Twitter: "Wow! Hunter Biden is being forced to leave a Chinese Company." Hunter Biden's attorney confirmed Sunday that he would step down from the board. Trump warned followers that the media would continue to protect Hunter, as ABC News conducted an interview with the former vice president's son late last week. The interview airs Monday. Trump also wrote: "Now watch the Fake News wrap their greasy and very protective arms around him. Only softball questions of him please!" Trump made similar statements at two rallies last week. "Whatever happened to Hunter? Where the hell is he?" Trump asked last Thursday in Minneapolis. "Where's Hunter?" Trump also criticized establishment news broadcasts for repeatedly saying that Trump's claims of corruption were "totally unsubstantiated." "It's not unsubstantiated; he took a fortune out of Ukraine, knew nothing, took a fortune out of China," Trump said on Friday. On Sunday, Trump posted on Twitter: "Now looks like he has raided and scammed even more countries!" and "Media is AWOL."

Since the publication of her book Unhinged last month, former White House aide Omarosa Manigault Newman has been releasing audio clips that she argues are damning to President Donald Trump and his administration. On Monday's "The View," Manigault Newman said she thinks a rumored "racial slur" tape, featuring Trump using the n-word during the making of "The Apprentice," not only exists but will be released before the midterm elections. "I don't hold the tape," Manigault Newman said. "I've heard the tape." Several people associated with the "Apprentice" and "Celebrity Apprentice" series have said they heard Trump use racist or other offensive language, but no one has provided concrete evidence. Former "Apprentice" producer Bill Pruitt tweeted in 2016 that such tapes exist, but in subsequent posts admitted he does not know where. In Monday's interview, Manigault Newman also introduced new audio she recorded while sitting in on meetings with the president and other White House staff last year. In this tape, Trump rants that Hillary Clinton is "getting killed now with Russia" and that the "real Russia story is Hillary and collusion."

A federal judge on Friday allowed Lev Parnas, an associate of Rudy Giuliani, to turn over documents to Congress as part of the impeachment proceeding against President Donald Trump. U.S. District Court Judge Paul Oetken granted Parnas' request to turn over to the House intelligence committee documents and data seized by federal investigators when Parnas was arrested in October. Parnas' attorney, Joseph Bondy, said in a court filing he expected to receive the materials from the U.S. Justice Department this week. Parnas and another man, Igor Fruman, played key roles in efforts by Giuliani, Trump's personal lawyer, to launch a Ukrainian corruption investigation against Democratic presidential contender Joe Biden and his son Hunter. Parnas and Fruman were indicted in October on federal campaign finance violations related to a $325,000 donation to a group supporting Trump's reelection. They have pleaded not guilty. Parnas has provided documents to the intelligence committee in response to a congressional subpoena. His attorney says he wants to provide more information that falls "within the scope" of the subpoena, including two batches of documents seized from his home and the contents of one of his iPhones, according to court filings. "Review of these materials is essential to the Committee's ability to corroborate the strength of Mr. Parnas's potential testimony," Parnas' attorney, Joseph Bondy wrote in a filing.

Vice President Joseph R. Biden addressed the White House weekly address on Saturday. He asked his representatives to ask why they oppose raising the federal minimum wage. Biden said, "Ask your representatives who oppose raising the federal minimum wage—why do they oppose it. There's no reason in the world why an American working 40 hours a week has to live in poverty." President Obama is pursuing an election-year push with congressional Democrats to raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 to $10.10 per hour. Many Republican lawmakers oppose the action, pointing to a study that the move would eliminate about 500,000 jobs nationwide. Biden, who filled in during the trip while traveling overseas, said there is evidence that raising the minimum wage is good for the economy. "There's clear data that shows fair wages generate loyalty of workers to their employers, which has the benefit of increasing productivity and leading to less turn over," Biden said. "It's really good for the economy as a whole because raising the minimum wage would generate an additional $19 billion in additional income for people who need it the most." Biden also said it would help to close the gap in pay between men and women, because women make up the majority of minimum-wage employees. "The president and I think they deserve it," Biden said. "And we think a lot of you do too. So, folks, it's time to act. It's time to give America a raise."

Rep. Michele Bachmann (Minn.) faced criticism this past week after it came to light that she and four other House Republicans had sent letters to the inspectors general of the departments of Homeland Security, State and Justice asking them to examine whether the Muslim Brotherhood has tentacles within the U.S. government. The focus on Abedin angered Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.), who spoke on the Senate floor and called the attacks "sinister" and described Abedin as "an intelligent, upstanding, hard-working and loyal servant of our country and our government." House Speaker John A. Boehner (R-Ohio) also criticized his colleagues, saying Thursday that "accusations like this being thrown around are pretty dangerous." CNN's Wolf Blitzer described the allegation against Abedin as "an outrageous McCarthy-like charge." Bachmann, who is typically ubiquitous on the cable chat circuit, did not comment on the criticism.

Sen. Jeff Sessions, R-Ala., the top Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee, plans to vote against Supreme Court nominee Sonia Sotomayor, citing concerns about her record of "judicial activism." In a USA Today column Monday, Sessions wrote that Sotomayor "renounced the pillars of activist thinking" during her testimony before the committee, but he does not believe she will follow through. "I don't believe that Judge Sotomayor has the deep-rooted convictions necessary to resist the siren call of judicial activism. She has evoked its mantra too often," he wrote. Sessions aide Andrew Logan confirmed that Sessions will oppose Sotomayor. Sessions' decision comes the day before the Judiciary panel is to vote on President Obama's first high court nominee. Sen. Charles Grassley, R-Iowa, another Republican on the Judiciary Committee, also announced Monday afternoon that he would oppose Sotomayor. South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham is the only Republican on the committee to come out in favor of the justice. Sotomayor is virtually certain to be confirmed by a vote of the full Senate by the end of next week, becoming the first Hispanic justice. Sessions acknowledged she probably had the votes in his column. He cited several decisions she has joined that were "contrary to the Constitution." He said each was "consistent with liberal political thought" and led him to doubt her "repudiation of judicial activism." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Eric Trump criticized George Conway, Kellyanne Conway's husband, on Twitter. Trump wrote: "Of all the ugliness in politics, the utter disrespect George Conway shows toward his wife, her career, place of work, and everything she has fought SO hard to achieve, might top them all. @KellyannePolls is great person and frankly his actions are horrible." The article noted that the Conways have been known to differ from each other for their entire married life. Earlier Monday, Trump criticized the president, accusing him of jury- and witness-tampering. Trump had praised former campaign adviser Roger Stone for resisting to work with the special counsel's team. Trump tweeted: "'I will never testify against Trump.' This statement was recently made by Roger Stone, essentially stating that he will not be forced by a rogue and out of control prosecutor to make up lies and stories about 'President Trump,'" and added: "Nice to know that some people still have 'guts!'"

Turkey's leading press organization and two experts in Internet law filed a complaint in a local Ankara court on Monday to try to overturn a government ban on Twitter. The organization, which represents 3,300 journalists, filed the complaint arguing that the ban violated freedom of information protected by the Constitution and the European Convention on Human Rights. Using a similar argument to challenge the ban's legality, two lawyers specializing in Internet regulation filed a case at the Constitutional Court of Turkey, which has the authority to revoke the ban. Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan moved to ban Twitter on Thursday after a series of leaks on social media helped fuel a corruption scandal involving his government. The scandal is one of the biggest challenges to Mr. Erdogan's authority since he came to power 11 years ago. Despite international outcry over the ban, the government has remained undeterred. Over the weekend, The Hurriyet Daily News, a Turkish newspaper, reported that the government had moved to make it more difficult for Twitter users to try to circumvent the ban. Thousands of users have been altering the Domain Name System settings on their devices to allow them to use Twitter. The United States has criticized the ban. On Friday, Douglas Frantz, the assistant secretary of public affairs at the State Department, described it as "21st-century book burning."

On Sunday, White House aide Kellyanne Conway and CNN host Jake Tapper exchanged heated exchanges during an appearance on CNN's "State of the Union." Tapper suggested Conway had a credibility problem. During the exchange, Tapper questioned Conway about a $130,000 payment to adult film actress Stormy Daniels. Conway pointed out that CNN had Daniels' attorney Michael Avenatti on the network over 65 times in less than two months. Conway said she did not see this on CNN, citing the economy and immigration, health care, ISIS, historic talks on North Korea, and the precipice of ending decades of war between North Korea and South Korea in large part due to this presidents leadership. Tapper asked Conway whether he thought Trump's job includes lying to the American people, and Conway responded, "You just want that to go viral. And you want to say President Trump and lie in the same sentence."

Before leaving for New York for a series of fundraisers, President Obama held a press conference at the White House to discuss his lack of strategy on Syria. Obama told reporters that his strategy was still developing and that he would continue to consult with congress and the American people about any action in Syria. "I don't want to put the cart before the horse," he said. "We don't have a strategy yet." Obama criticized the news media for "getting a little further ahead of where we're at than we currently are" on confronting ISIL in Syria. "I think that's not just my assessment but the assessment of our military, as well," he said. Obama said that to solution to the situation in Syria was not simply a military issue but also a political issue. He suggested that the United States would support a "moderate opposition" inside of Syrian to give the country's citizens a choice. "We have to give people inside of Syria a choice other than ISIL or Assad," he said, "And I don't see any scenario in which Assad somehow is able to bring peace and stability to a region that is majority Sunni." Obama also explained that he had no intention of taking military action against Russia, even though it was clear that Vladamir Putin was acting aggressively in Ukraine. "We are not taking military action to solve the Ukrainian problem," he explained.

Senate Republican leaders said Tuesday that there would be no confirmation hearings, no vote, not even a courtesy meeting with President Obama's nominee to replace Justice Antonin Scalia. The statement came alongside a written vow from Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee that they would not hold any confirmation hearings. The pledge was the clearest statement yet from the Senate's majority party that it would do everything it can to prevent Mr. Obama from shifting the ideological balance of the nation's high court. Senator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, the majority leader, urged Mr. Obama to reconsider even submitting a name. "This nomination will be determined by whoever wins the presidency in the polls," Mr. McConnell said. "I agree with the Judiciary Committee's recommendation that we not have hearings. In short, there will not be action taken." Their first full day back at the Capitol since Justice Scalia's death afforded Senate Republicans the opportunity to unite around a message and strategy to thwart Mr. Obama. Huddles in Mr. McConnell's Capitol suite and a lunchtime conclave appeared to stem any wavering and push Republican troops into line. They had the ammunition they needed in a June 1992 floor speech by Joseph R. Biden Jr., then a senator, urging President George Bush against any nomination to the Supreme Court until after that year's presidential election.

President Trump criticized Nordstrom department store chain on Wednesday for dropping his daughter Ivanka's accessories and clothing line. The criticism raised ethical questions about the relationship between his presidency and his family's business interests. Trump has previously criticized companies such as Boeing, Lockheed Martin, automakers and news organizations, sometimes causing stock prices to spike and prompting debates about whether corporations would tailor their conduct to suit a president. In those cases, his criticism targeted government contracts, departing American jobs or news coverage. Six days after Nordstrom announced that, based on sales, it would no longer carry Ivanka Trump's products, a decision that prompted some Trump supporters to call for a boycott of the stores. Trump posted on Twitter that "Ivanka has been treated so unfairly" by the company. He first posted the message from his personal account and then re-sent it from his official White House account. The complaint also raised questions about how he might handle the moves of numerous other companies as their relationships with Trump brands change. The large national discount retailers T. J. Maxx and Marshalls, and Neiman Marcus, the luxury department store, have recently taken steps to give less prominence to Ms. Trump's products.

President Obama addressed gun violence on Friday at a White House press conference, urging Americans to pressure Congress to pass tougher gun-control legislation after nine people were killed a day earlier at an Oregon community college. "Our inaction is a political decision that we are making," Obama said. "Every couple of months we have a mass shooting. This will not change until the politics change." On Thursday, 26-year-old Christopher Harper Mercer opened fire in a classroom at Umpqua Community College in Roseburg, Ore., killing nine people before being shot down by responding officers. The president tried unsuccessfully to get comprehensive gun-control legislation through Congress in 2012, after a gunman killed 26 people inside the Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newton, Conn. "The shootings will not go away until policies, elected officials change," Obama said Friday. "This is happening every single day in forgotten neighborhoods around the country." Obama called on Americans to "vote against" members of Congress who do not support efforts to control gun violence and to let them know "precisely why" they cast such votes. He also called on voters, gun-control groups and others to take on the National Rifle Association, which was influential in blocking the Capitol Hill legislation several years ago. "The NRA is very effective," he said. Obama said the group knows how to "stir up fear" and raise money.

On Monday, Rep. Ben Ray Luján became the first major Democrat to announce a bid to succeed New Mexico Sen. Tom Udall, a Democrat who announced last week that he would retire. Luján served as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee during the last two election cycles, including during the party's 2018 year. He has represented the northern third of New Mexico in the House since his 2008 win. Luján also hails from a prominent local family. In 1989, then-GOP Sen. Pete Domenici joked that New Mexico may as well have three parties: The Democrats, the Republican, and The Lujáns. Ben Ray Luján's late father served as speaker of the state House from 2002 until his death in 2012. Democratic Gov. Michelle Luján Grisham and the congressman are distant cousins by marriage. Luján will face a formidable opponent in the primary in this Democratic-leaning state. Secretary of State Maggie Toulouse Oliver is considering the race. She reportedly told Luján last week that she would be willing to run against him. Freshman Rep. Deb Haaland and Valerie Plame, the CIA agent whose identity was leaked by the Bush administration, are also considering running in the Democratic primary.

Senate Republicans will add the repeal of Obamacare's individual mandate to the tax bill, Senate leaders said Tuesday afternoon. President Donald Trump urged the Senate in a tweet Monday to add the repeal. Sen. Rand Paul said Tuesday morning that he would push for the move. Sen. Tom Cotton also indicated that he supported putting the repeal in the bill. Republican leaders confirmed the repeal will be part of the bill and that they have enough votes for it to pass through the Senate. "We're optimistic that inserting the individual mandate will be helpful," Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell told reporters Tuesday. Senate Majority Whip John Cornyn and Sen. John Thune also told reporters that the repeal would be included. The savings from the repeal would "be distributed in the form of middle-income tax relief," Thune said. Thune also said that the bill had 50 votes in the Senate, enough to pass with a tie-breaking vote by Vice President Mike Pence if done under rules that allow for the passage of certain bills by a bare majority. A repeal of the individual mandate would save $338 billion over the next decade, according to the Congressional Budget Office's analysis. "Repealing the mandate pays for more tax cuts for working families and protects them from being fined by the IRS for not being able to afford insurance that Obamacare made unaffordable in the first place," Sen. Cotton said in a statement, according to the Hill.

The Senate returns to work Monday at 4 PM. Majority Leader Mitch McConnell is scheduled to vote on a motion to proceed to an Obamacare repeal motion. The floor is not yet open to senators who will have to vote on the repeal bill, and the bill is not yet known. The bill could not be voted on. It appears McConnell is still trying to patch together some kind of replacement bill, which would take weeks rather than hours. The bill could still require a commitment from 50 senators to vote on repeal and delay, a vague promise to figure out all the provisions to replace Obamacare in the next two years. The next 24 hours are key. The article urges readers to call their Republican senators' offices to demand they vote against repealing Obamacare and to demand they oppose repealing it.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) said in a statement in Allen, S.C., that Donald Trump would appoint liberal justices to the Supreme Court, like his sister, Maryanne Trump Barry. Trump said last year that his sister would be a "phenomenal" Supreme Court justice, but he has now said he was kidding. Cruz said, "Now it's good to stand with your sister, but Donald's sister was a Bill Clinton-appointed federal appellate judge who is a radical pro-abortion extremist." In July 2000, Barry wrote the majority opinion on a panel that ruled that New Jersey's ban on late-term abortions was "constitutionally vague" and "unduly burdened a woman's constitutional right to obtain an abortion." One of the other judges on the panel was now-Supreme Court Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr. The case involved Planned Parenthood, which Trump said in Saturday night's debate is doing "wonderful things" for women's health. Cruz said, "Even among liberal judges that position is extreme and Donald said his extreme abortion-supporting sister would make a terrific Supreme Court justice." Cruz said, "A vote for Donald Trump is a vote to write the Second Amendment out of the Bill of Rights."

Multiple media outlets reported that Russians accessed a single laptop computer belonging to the Burlington Electric Department (BED), a municipal-owned electrical utility company serving Burlington, Vermont. The Burlington Electric Department issued a statement: "Last night, U.S. utilities were alerted by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) of a malware code used in Grizzly Steppe, the name DHS has applied to a Russian campaign linked to recent hacks. We acted quickly to scan all computers in our system for the malware signature. We detected the malware in a single Burlington Electric Department laptop not connected to our organization's grid systems. We took immediate action to isolate the laptop and alerted federal officials of this finding. Our team is working with federal officials to trace this malware and prevent any other attempts to infiltrate utility systems. We have briefed state officials and will support the investigation fully." Comments are closed on this story.

Former White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders apologized Thursday after a tweet mocking Joe Biden's stuttering during Thursday's Democratic debate. Biden responded: "It's called empathy. Look it up." Sanders' first tweet received responses. In a subsequent tweet, she stated she "was not trying to make fun of anyone with a speech impediment." She deleted the tweet. Biden later apologized. Biden has battled to overcome stuttering. He said he keeps in touch with people who have reached out to him for help. "The little kid who said, 'I-I-I can't talk. Wh-wh-what do I do?' I have scores of these young women and men who I keep in contact with," he said. Sanders initially posted a tweet reading: "I I I I I I I I I I I I I I I hhhave absolutely no idea what Biden is talking about." She later tweeted that she was not "trying to make fun of anyone with a speech impediment." Biden responded that she was not "trying to make fun of anyone with a speech impediment."

Iranian news service Fars News Agency, described as "Iran's leading independent news agency," ran a story about a poll finding that the "overwhelming majority of rural white Americans said they would rather vote for Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad than U.S. President Barack Obama." The Fars story is a word-for-word reprint of an Onion piece. The article notes that the agency's description of the poll was described as deadpan. The article also references an Onion piece describing the same poll finding that 77 percent of rural white Americans said they would rather go to a baseball game or have a beer with Ahmadinejad, who has repeatedly denied the Holocaust and has had numerous political prisoners executed. The article also references a Gallup poll finding that 60 percent of rural whites said they at least respected Ahmadinejad, who does not try to hide the fact that he is Muslim.

President Trump said Thursday that he did not forewarn the Russians and Syrians of an upcoming missile strike in a Wednesday tweet. "Never said when an attack on Syria would take place. Could be very soon or not so soon at all! In any event, the United States, under my Administration, has done a great job of ridding the region of ISIS. Where is our 'Thank you America?'" Trump tweeted. On Wednesday, the president sent another tweet warning Russia that missiles "will be coming," earning criticism for tipping off the Russian-backed Assad regime. After new reports of chemical weapons by Syrian President Bashar Assad, the U.S. and other world leaders are trying to decide what to do next about the situation in Syria. Last spring, Mr. Trump ordered missile strikes after photos of children killed or severely injured by gas agents surfaced. The Assad regime and Russians both deny any use of chemical weapons. Russia vows to shoot down any and all missiles fired at Syria.
