Mike Allen reported in Axios that President Trump considers his 2020 re-election strategy. The "America First" agenda championed by former White House chief strategist Steve Bannon is in conflict with the "Economy First" agenda supported by most of Trump's current White House advisers on trade policy and the importance (or lack thereof) of the promised border wall. Allen reported that in conversations at Mar-a-Lago and back in Washington, friends and advisers have begun giving President Trump advice about how to win reelection in 2020. The report stated that Trump is receiving conflicting advice. The Bannon purists want America First, and most of his friends want Economy First. The report said Trump has governed like a fairly conventional Republican, so the Economy First camp is winning. The next month, with pending decisions on immigration and trade wars, will show whether he reverts to his campaign norm in action, not just words. The Bannon-Breitbart-Stephen Miller wing believes Trump has to deliver on building a wall, curtailing immigration and cracking down on China. Moderating forces such as Gary Cohn, Steven Mnuchin, James Mattis and Rex Tillerson are counseling against moves that could alienate allies and roil global markets. The report predicted a hot war this next month in conservative media on this front.

Democratic Sen. Ed Markey responded on Twitter to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz's coronavirus relief proposal, which would give "every person" in the country $2,000 a month for a sustained period of time. Markey, of Massachusetts, tweeted Monday afternoon: "Give every person in our country $2000/month for the duration of the pandemic, $2000/month for 3 months after that, and $2000/month retroactive to March." He asked: "Why be so cheap? Give everyone $1 million a day, every day, forever. And three soy lattes a day. And a foot massage. We have a magic money tree — we should use it!" Cruz responded: "It's not a god–- joke Ted. Millions of families are facing hunger, the threat of eviction, and the loss of their health care during a pandemic that is worsening every day. Get real." The exchange followed President Trump's announcement over the weekend of four executive actions to provide Americans financial relief from the pandemic after talks failed in Congress on Friday.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie and David Letterman laughed about jokes made by Letterman about the lawmaker's ample girth. Christie has termed his plumpness "fair game" for comedians. During his first appearance on "Late Show with David Letterman" on Monday, the Republican and potential 2016 presidential contender read two of Letterman's jokes that he said were "some of my personal favorites." The governor also drew laughs when he pulled out a doughnut and started eating it while Letterman asked him if he was bothered by the digs that have been made about his weight. Christie said he wasn't, noting that he laughs at the jokes if he finds them funny. "Late Show" airs on CBS at 11:35 p.m. Eastern time.

Lawyers for President Donald Trump invoked the government shutdown to seek a delay in a court case over claims that Trump is illegally profiting from business his Washington hotel does with foreign countries. The article reported that lawyers for Trump are invoking the shutdown to seek a delay in a court case over claims that Trump is illegally profiting from business his Washington hotel does with foreign countries. The article also noted speculation about his decision to cause a partial government shutdown. The article speculated that Trump made the decision after watching right-wing media, which it described as possible. It also speculated that he saw an opportunity to personally benefit from the situation. The article stated that Trump is not adverse to a little—or a lot—of obstruction of justice. The article suggested the most likely scenario is a combination of all three: he is stupid, he is weak, and he is a crook. The only thing the article knows for sure is that his actions, again, are causing a lot of people a lot of pain.

Iran summoned Denmark's ambassador to Tehran on Tuesday to protest a decision by the European Union to impose sanctions on Iran's oil imports, according to the semiofficial Fars News Agency. Iran said it protested because Denmark holds the rotating presidency of the European Union, the agency reported. Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Ali Asqar Khaji said at the meeting, according to Fars: "There are forces in the EU that seek to create tension in the relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran by following the U.S. policies and adopting a hostile approach." The European Union announced Monday it would cut off oil imports from Iran and freeze assets in an effort to starve the country's nuclear program of funding. The sanctions freeze the assets of Iran's central bank in European Union nations and ban the importation of Iranian oil to those countries. The measures also block European Union countries from exporting petrochemical equipment and technology to Iran, or trading diamonds and precious metals with the Middle Eastern state. The European Union will allow contracts that are already in place to be fulfilled until July 1, it said. The U.S. Treasury Department on Monday targeted the nation's third-largest bank, the state-owned Bank Tejarat, for allegedly working with other Iranian banks and firms subject to sanctions tied to Iran's nuclear program.

Potential jurors in the William Beavers tax evasion trial are expected to field questions about IRS audits and their feelings about gambling as the selection process begins with a U.S. District judge Monday. The Cook County Commissioner, who has referred to himself as "The Hog With The Big Nuts," faces allegations that he siphoned off thousands of dollars in campaign money to pay for gambling debts racked up at the Horseshoe Casino and other personal expenses, according to Fox Chicago. In all, Beavers, 77, allegedly diverted $226,000 in campaign funds then failed to report it as income on his tax returns, according to Fox. Beavers has called the tax dodging "an oversight," according to NBC Chicago, and implied he was asked by the feds to participate in a bigger investigation into activities by fellow commissioner John Daley and then-board president Todd Stroger. According to the Tribune, Beavers can tell the jury he repaid the campaign money and amended his taxes upon learning of the investigation if called to take the stand. If convicted, NBC reports Beavers faces a fine of $250,000 and maximum penalty of three years in federal prison for each count against him. Opening statements could begin as soon as Tuesday in what is expected to be a two-week trial.

Michael R. Bloomberg, the billionaire former mayor of New York, announced Wednesday that he has registered as a Democrat. Bloomberg, a former Republican and more recently declared political independent, announced his decision in an early morning Instagram post. He referenced his speech at the 2016 Democratic National Convention. "At key points in U.S. history, one of the two parties has served as a bulwark against those who threaten our Constitution," he wrote. "Two years ago at the Democratic Convention, I warned of those threats. Today, I have re-registered as a Democrat — I had been a member for most of my life — because we need Democrats to provide the checks and balance our nation so badly needs." Bloomberg has said he will "take a look" at a presidential campaign after the midterm elections. He has been working in recent months to solidify his ties to the Democratic Party. Last week, Bloomberg announced he would give $20 million to the main Democratic Senate super PAC. The sum brings Bloomberg — who has already pledged to spend $80 million to support Democratic congressional candidates — up to $100 million in spending commitments for the 2018 election cycle.

On Monday, a winner emerged in the Senate race between former "Saturday Night Live" star Democrat Al Franken and incumbent Republican Norm Coleman. After seven weeks of ballot contests and extensive litigation, the Minnesota State Canvassing Board certified election results declaring Franken the winner. The recount process involved two months of hand-inspection of several million ballots, with Franken emerging as the winner despite a narrow margin of victory. The recount was subsequently endorsed by Minnesota's highest court. The article reported that prolonged litigation undermines the integrity and validity of Minnesota's electoral system and adds to the controversy surrounding the U.S. Senate as Congress returns to work. The article stated that while all factors are significant, their prevalence does not diminish the importance of ensuring a fair election in which every eligible voter can cast a ballot and all ballots are counted. The article reported that Coleman's campaign claims that some ballots were mishandled and others wrongly excluded from the recount, which gave Franken an edge in the process. The article also noted that the appearance of impropriety and the Board's refusal to consider several hundred additional votes warrant another look, especially given the narrow lead held by Franken. The article called for ensuring every vote was counted and counted accurately.

Thousands of Albanian opposition supporters clashed with police at an anti-government rally on Saturday. They called for the resignation of what they describe as a corrupt and inefficient cabinet and for early elections. Supporters of the center-right Democratic Party broke police ranks as they tried to enter the building of the Socialist Party prime minister, Edi Rama. Protesters threw petrol bombs, flares and other objects and tried to destroy scaffolding that protects the main door, which they broke. They did not make it inside. A security officer appealed for calm as some protesters tried to dismantle a piece of artwork. The police offered little resistance. Officers fired tear gas and water cannons and called through loudspeakers for protesters to disperse. Demonstrators affected by the tear gas were taken away in ambulances and cars. In an interview with The Associated Press before the rally, the Democrats' leader, Lulzim Basha, said the protesters wanted the resignation of the government, a transitional cabinet and early elections "in order to restore democracy through a Parliament that is elected by the will of people and not the money or the threats of the criminals." The United States, the European Union and international institutions had called on the opposition to hold a peaceful rally. Albania has been hoping to enter full European Union membership negotiations this year. Fighting corruption and organized crime remain the nation's top priorities.

Republican incumbent Norm Coleman is seeking a total recount of all ballots in Minnesota's U.S. Senate race, which he narrowly lost to Democrat Al Franken, the Minneapolis Star-Tribune reported. Coleman had argued that about 12,000 ballots be rejected when he was leading during the initial recount. He now wants those ballots to be counted in a new recount. Franken, who won by 225 votes, responded to the suggestion of a total recount. Franken said the total recount was not an Arnold Schwarzenegger movie. Bryant said the first recount took half a lifetime and that the next one should be done by the time his 17-year-old son is eligible for Social Security. Bryant also wrote that it would be almost ironic if Coleman's margin of victory lies among the 12,000 ballots he initially said should be rejected. Bryant also wrote a humor blog and weekly humor column, both titled "Out of Context."

In the closing days of a U.S. Senate race in Kansas, Independent Greg Orman criticized Republican candidate Bob Dole for referring to Dole as a "clown." According to the Washington Examiner, when asked about the long line of Republican candidates who had campaigned for incumbent Senator Pat Roberts, including Dole, Orman replied: "It sort of seems like a Washington establishment clown car to me." The Roberts campaign responded: "In the final days of this campaign, Democrat Greg Orman is finally showing Kansans his true colors and revealing his arrogant disdain for Republicans. His liberal personal views aside, for Greg Orman to attack Senator Dole as a 'Washington establishment clown' is an outrage. Few leaders have done more for Kansas and this country than Senator Bob Dole, and Greg Orman should immediately apologize for his slimy attack on Senator Dole and other Republican leaders." Dole also released a short statement: "I don't think I've ever been called a 'clown' before. I'm disappointed by Mr. Orman's statement." According to the Real Clear Politics poll of polls, Orman leads by a single point with 4 days to go.

A U.S. solider was killed in combat in eastern Afghanistan on New Year's Day, the first such death in 2018 the military announced. Four other U.S. service members were wounded during a "combat engagement" in Achin, Nangarhar province, officials said Tuesday. Two were in stable condition and the two others returned to duty. General John Nicholson, commander of U.S. Forces-Afghanistan, said in a news release: "We are deeply saddened by the loss of one of our own. At this very difficult time our heartfelt sympathies go out to the families and friends of our fallen and wounded brothers." The name of the soldier has not been released pending family notification. The United States formally concluded its combat mission in Afghanistan at the end of 2014 but still carries out operations against the Taliban and an ISIS affiliate, both of which are active in Nangarhar. Vice President Pence made an unannounced trip to Afghanistan just before the Christmas holiday and thanked troops for their service while reiterating the "real progress" the U.S. is making in the country to "put the Taliban on the offensive." "I believe victory is closer than ever before," Pence said. "I believe with all my heart that Afghanistan will be free." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

President Obama told radio host Tom Joyner on Wednesday that he was "too polite" in last week's presidential debate. Obama said, "I think it's fair to say I was just too polite." He said Romney changed his past positions and would be more aggressive in the next two debates, scheduled for Oct. 16 and 22. Obama said, "Because, you know, it's hard to sometimes just keep on saying 'and what you're saying isn't true,' because it gets repetitive." The president and his aides said he wanted to have "a conversation" with voters. After the debate, Obama said Romney was hard to pin down because he was two-faced. Obama told Joyner, "The good news is, is that's just the first one. Gov. Romney put forward a whole bunch of stuff that either involved him running away from positions that he had taken, or doubling down on things like Medicare vouchers that are going to hurt him long term. ... And, you know, I think it's fair to say that we will see a little more activity at the next one."

President Obama is set to announce San Antonio Mayor Julian Castro will be the new head of the housing administration. Castro gave a keynote address at the 2012 Democratic Convention. He has a twin brother who is also in politics. The current housing secretary, Shaun Donovan, will now run the budget office. Republican Senator Bob Corker described a meeting between top White House aides and republicans in Congress as "bizarre." The meeting was supposed to answer questions on President Obama's foreign policy, but republicans say they did not get answers they wanted. New home sales are expected today. Wall Street reaction is expected. Doug McKelway is reporting on train travel from Union Station. Laura Ingle is watching traffic on the road from the Port Authority bus station in NYC. Adam Housley is keeping an eye on the roads from the 405 freeway in L.A. Mike Tobin is reporting on the dramatic changes to air travel thanks to technology. He is at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport. Jonathan Serrie is reporting today on the disgusting amounts of bacteria on airplane seats and door handles. The U.S. military commander in the Pacific warned that the Pacific is a tinderbox right now and there is a high risk of "miscalculation" in a standoff between Vietnam and China over fishing rights in the ocean.

The New York Times published a front-page headline that suggested President Donald Trump was attempting to unify the country. The headline was changed for the second edition to "Assailing Hate but Not Guns." At least 31 people were killed in separate shootings in El Paso, Texas, and Dayton, Ohio. Trump on Monday denounced hate and white supremacy. He did not acknowledge his own history of hateful and racist rhetoric. Trump has referred to immigration as an invasion, and last month he told four women of color in Congress to "go back" to their ancestral countries. He also made a joke when someone at a rally in Florida suggested shooting immigrants. The alleged gunman in Texas reportedly shared a manifesto online that used similar language to Trump's, referring to immigrants as "invaders" and using the phrase "Send them back." The first edition carried a front-page headline suggesting the president was attempting to unify the country: "Trump Urges Unity vs. Racism." Critics attacked the paper on Twitter, and the headline was changed for the second edition to "Assailing Hate but Not Guns." It is not clear if the change was the result of the criticism. Twitter users criticized the paper, and some said they were canceling their subscriptions and urging others to do the same.

Florida Sen. Marco Rubio's 12-year-old daughter, Amanda Rubio, was injured in a car accident Saturday afternoon in South Florida, according to a statement by his office. The statement said Amanda Rubio was the oldest daughter of Senator Marco Rubio. While visiting with classmates, she was a passenger on a golf cart involved in a collision in a private gated community. She was airlifted to Miami Children's Hospital with a head injury. She has been admitted to the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit. She is in fair condition. Senator Rubio and Mrs. Rubio are grateful for all the outpouring of support and prayers. The Rubio's are touched and grateful for calls from President Obama and Vice President Biden, and Governor Romney's personal message earlier today. The Senator was alerted to the accident after leaving a campaign rally in Kissimmee with Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney. At 6:44 p.m., the Romney motorcade pulled over to the side of Interstate 4. Rubio was seen talking on a cell phone outside the campaign bus for several minutes, before shaking hands with a few people and driving away in a Florida State Trooper's vehicle. Rubio appeared at two events for Romney today and was scheduled to appear at a third tonight in Land O' Lakes, near Tampa.

President Obama visited Roseburg, Oregon, on Friday to meet with the families of the victims of last week's massacre at Umpqua Community College. The shooting prompted the president to renew his call for gun-safety measures. Protesters in the small Oregon town held signs reading "Gun free zones for sitting ducks," "Obama is wrong," "Nothing trumps our liberty," and other anti gun-control slogans. Reporters traveling with the president said several hundred people greeted Obama at the airport, and roughly half of them were protesting his calls for more gun legislation. The meeting with victims' families was closed to the press, and details of their discussions are not expected to be released. Following the meeting with the families, the president said he will continue pushing for new gun-safety measures. "We're going to have to come together as a country, but today is about the families," he said.

Police in San Bernardino, California held a press conference about Wednesday's mass shooting. Police confirmed 14 dead and 17 wounded. Status of wounded was not known at this time. Two suspects were killed: Syed Rizwan Farook, a male, age 28, apparently "U.S. born," and Tashfeen Malik, female, 27. Police did not have a definitive answer on the relationship between Farook and Malik. They may have been married or engaged. Police said they believe they are "pretty comfortable" with the idea that there were only two shooters, who are both deceased, and not three or more as had previously been reported. They said they do not have a motive at this point. Police also said that bombs were discovered at the site of the shooting and have been disposed of by the bomb squad. Police believe there "had to have been some degree of planning" based on how the attackers were equipped. Police said they will not speculate on motive, including whether or not there was a connection to ISIS. One police officer was wounded in the response. The press conference concluded. Police are not sure if they will conduct another one tonight but said they expect to speak with the media again early Thursday morning.

President Barack Obama danced and took in baseball games while the Western world reels from the terror attacks in Brussels, Belgium. Hours after the attacks that killed over 30 people, including some Americans, Obama gave a speech that lasted 50 seconds. The speech was intended to praise Cuba and condemn the U.S. An hour later, Obama participated in a day's event planned by his communist hosts. The same president who had only 50 seconds of his time to discuss the attacks in Brussels was seen doing a wave at a Cuban baseball park. Not long afterward, the press was treated to scenes of the president doing the tango with a Cuban woman. Obama stated that defeating ISIS was his "number one priority." Obama said on the presidency: "It's not promotion, not marketing. It's hard." ABC's The View reported that the "optics" of seeing Obama do the wave at a Cuban ballpark were a bad sight for the American people and for the world.

Mitt Romney will announce his running mate at 8:45 a.m. ET Saturday in Norfolk, Virginia, according to an official press release from the Romney campaign. The announcement comes roughly two weeks before the start of the Republican National Convention in Tampa. The campaign has not yet confirmed who the running mate is. Speculation has centered lately on Rep. Paul Ryan of Wisconsin, but Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, Ohio Sen. Rob Portman and former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty have all been mentioned as possibilities in recent days. The Romney campaign could also decide to announce an outside-the-box selection Saturday morning. The announcement comes as some polls, including a recent Fox News survey, show the Republican presidential candidate losing some ground to President Obama. In a statement issued Friday night, the Romney campaign said the running mate would be revealed at 9 a.m. EDT at the Nauticus Museum. Romney is beginning a four-day bus tour through swing states. The vice presidential selection will dominate headlines, and Romney's team has been teasing the announcement for weeks.

The White House is refusing to confirm whether President Barack Obama followed up on his pledge to take a 5 percent pay cut due to sequestration last year. Obama promised last April to take a 5 percent pay cut in solidarity with federal employees furloughed as a result of the automatic budget cuts, known as the sequester. The cut was meant to equate to the level of spending cuts imposed on nondefense federal agencies. "The president has decided that to share in the sacrifice being made by public servants across the federal government that are affected by the sequester, he will contribute a portion of his salary back to the Treasury," a White House official said at the time. According to his tax returns, Obama is still receiving the presidential salary of $400,000 per year. Last year, he earned $394,796 in wages from the Defense Financing and Accounting Service (DFAS-CIVPAY), which handles the salaries for civilian members of the Defense Department. Obama's income was commensurate to his salaries in recent years. He took in $395,188 in 2010, $394,821 in 2011, and $394,840 in 2012. The salary is also comparable to what former President George W. Bush received in 2007, when he earned $397,839.

A delegation of congressional Democrats began a three-day visit to Cuba on Saturday to discuss expectations for the normalization of relations between the United States and the island nation, while New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo added his name to other high-ranking politicians planning a trip to the island. The delegation's leader, Sen. Patrick Leahy of Vermont, said in a statement Saturday that the lawmakers want to explore opportunities for greater cooperation and to encourage Cuban officials to address issues of concern to Americans and their representatives in Congress. Traveling with Leahy were Sens. Dick Durbin of Illinois, Debbie Stabenow of Michigan and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and congressmen Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Peter Welch of Vermont. New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo is planning a trade mission to Cuba to promote the state, spokeswoman Melissa DeRosa said Saturday. She did not say when the Democratic governor would travel, adding that details would be announced later. DeRosa says the trip to Cuba would be part of a "Global NY" initiative. Cuomo has previously announced that he plans trips to Israel, China, Mexico and elsewhere during his new second term as governor. Last month, President Barack Obama announced plans for renewed economic ties and other administration-led initiatives aimed at re-establishing relations with Cuba. Many congressional Republicans have been supportive of the effort.

James B. Comey, the former FBI director, has been conducting a book-tour campaign against President Trump. Former aides and advisers have criticized Comey. In interviews, Twitter posts, television appearances, and private conversations, they have used Comey's book to re-litigate their grievances. These critics describe them as card-carrying members of what they describe as "the Resistance." They argue that they are still too angry at Comey, the former F.B.I. director, to see past what they view as egregious actions that handed the White House to Mr. Trump. Jared Bernstein, who served as one of Mrs. Clinton's senior economic advisers during the campaign, said: "The damage Comey did to the country by the role he played in the election far, far surpasses any credit he now gets for calling Trump out." Bernstein added: "History will remember and judge him for the former, not the latter."

Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday that accusations of Russia meddling in the 2016 United States presidential election were "simply rumors." U.S. intelligence officials said they have definitive evidence linking Moscow to the Democratic Party email hacks. Putin made the comment during a news conference with German Chancellor Angela Merkel, who was visiting Russia for the first time in two years. The Russian president added that the claim was being used as part of the political fight in Washington. "We never interfere in the political life and the political processes of other countries and we don't want anybody interfering in our political life and foreign policy processes," Putin said. U.S. intelligence agencies claim Russia hacked email account with the aim of benefiting Donald Trump's campaign and harming his Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. On Tuesday, Clinton also blamed part of her loss on Russia's role in hacking into her campaign's internal emails and subsequently coordinating their release on WikiLeaks. "He [Putin] certainly interfered in our election," Clinton said during the Women for Women International's annual luncheon in New York. "And it's clear he interfered to hurt me and help his opponent." Merkel said Germany would take "decisive measures" if it believed there was foreign meddling in its upcoming election. Relations between Germany and Russia remain strained, mostly over the unresolved conflict in eastern Ukraine.

Erik Prince, the founder of the security contractor Blackwater, is seriously considering a Republican primary challenge for a Senate seat in Wyoming, according to people who have spoken to him in recent days. Prince appears increasingly likely to challenge John Barrasso, a senior member of the Senate Republican leadership, according to people who have spoken to him in recent days. He has been urged to run next year by Stephen K. Bannon, who is leading the effort to shake up the Republican leadership with financial backing from the New York hedge fund billionaire Robert Mercer and his daughter Rebekah. Over the weekend, Prince traveled to Wyoming with his family to explore ways to establish residency there, said one person who had spoken to him. If he runs, Prince would face obstacles in seeking to unseat Barrasso, a popular and genial but low-profile senator who will have the full backing of Senator Mitch McConnell, the majority leader, and the well-funded political committees loyal to him. Prince has never run for public office. He has been a prominent figure in the security contractor community for years, as Blackwater faced ethical and legal problems over its work for the military in Iraq, including an episode in 2007 in which its employees killed 17 civilians in Baghdad.

A senior White House adviser on Sunday said President Obama's forthcoming budget would not resemble the House Republican proposal, which the adviser said was a rehash of the Romney plan that Americans had already rejected. "The American people rejected it," Obama adviser Dan Pfeiffer said on "Fox News Sunday." "And (Republicans) shouldn't be doubling down on it." The president is scheduled to release a budget Wednesday that is expected to include tax increases and cuts to Social Security and Medicare. "You can do both," Pfeiffer said. "That's what you'll see." Pfeiffer also told ABC's "This Week" that Obama will not "enact a Romney economic plan," which he said was essentially drastic cuts to entitlement programs with tax breaks for the wealthiest Americans. "What we won't do is cut our way to prosperity," he said. On Saturday, the president said his budget was not his "ideal plan," but it was a compromise he would be willing to accept. House Speaker John Boehner said last week that the Obama budget blueprint holds reforms "hostage" to tax increases.

A Quinnipiac University poll released Monday showed former Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Ridge at 43 percent and Sen. Arlen Specter at 46 percent in a hypothetical general election matchup. The poll was conducted in a hypothetical general election. Specter is not a declared candidate. Reports indicated over the weekend that the former homeland security secretary is considering a bid to be the Republican nominee after Specter switched from Republican to Democrat last week. The current front-running Republican candidate in the race, former Rep. Pat Toomey, is trailing Specter by a wide margin. The latest poll showed Specter beating Toomey 53-to-33 percent in a Pennsylvania general election. Polls recently showed Toomey trouncing Specter in the GOP primary, which may have contributed to Specter's decision to switch parties. In a statement, Quinnipiac pollster Clay Richards said Ridge is probably the only figure in Pennsylvania who could pose a significant challenge to Specter. The poll also found that Ridge would lead 47-to-37 percent among independents if he enters the race. If the GOP nominee is Toomey, the poll showed independents backing Specter 45-to-36 percent.

President Trump announced Saturday afternoon that he will hold a rally on April 29 in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, the same night as the White House Correspondents' Dinner. Trump wrote on Twitter: "Next Saturday night I will be holding a BIG rally in Pennsylvania. Look forward to it!" The announcement followed his decision to skip the annual dinner in February, following a tradition presidents in recent years have followed by attending the event. Politico reported that the rally will be held on April 29 in Harrisburg, the same day as Trump marks the 100th day of his presidency. A senior White House official said the decision to hold the rally that day had more to do with how Trump planned to spend the hours of the 100th day than the correspondents' dinner. The official said: "The media is trying to make this about them when — respectfully it has nothing to do with you guys. It's about focusing on the people." No White House staff will attend the dinner. Vanity Fair, TIME, People, Bloomberg, and the New Yorker have canceled their parties. Washington Post reporters Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein will headline the event in Trump's place to present journalism awards.

The Senate passed a bill reshaping parts of the new health care overhaul law and sent it back to the House for final congressional approval. Democrats had hoped the Senate's 56-43 vote Thursday would finish lawmakers' work on the measure. Republicans managed to kill a provision on grants for low-income students that violated Congress' budget rules. The House now must approve an identical bill before President Barack Obama can sign it. House leaders predicted their chamber will complete the bill by day's end. The measure boosts health care subsidies for low-income people and reduces new taxes on high-cost health insurance policies. George W. Huguely V lied to friends about his whereabouts the night Yeardley Love was reported. Reston-based LightSquared Inc. vowed Wednesday to continue its fight to establish a national wireless broadband. Defense Secretary Leon Panetta engaged in a dispute with Rep. J. Randy Forbes over the issue. The article also included a section titled "How does our 50th state view D.C. politics? Thinking a little deeper about our lives, our country and our values. Reflections on raising families in a holistic way -- with a focus on nutrition and alternative health." D.C. officials advocate for statehood in New Hampshire.

Rep. Dave Camp (R-Mich.) will not run for reelection in 2014. In a statement Monday, Camp announced he will not seek re-election. He said the decision was reached after much consideration and discussion with his family. Camp said serving in Congress is the great honor of his professional life. He said he is deeply grateful to the people of the 4th Congressional District for placing their trust in him. He said over the years, their unwavering support has been a source of strength, purpose and inspiration. During the next nine months, Camp said he will redouble his efforts to grow the economy and expand opportunity for every American by fixing the tax code, permanently solving physician payments for seniors, strengthening the social safety net and finding new markets for U.S. goods and services. Rep. Dave Camp (R-Mich.) said in a statement Monday that he will not seek another term. The Michigan Republican said in a statement Monday that he will retire after 12 terms in the House. He was term-limited as chairman of the committee. His district is strongly Republican and the GOP is expected to hold the seat. Camp is the second senior Michigan Republican to announce his retirement. Rep. Mike Rogers said Friday he would retire.

Sen. Martha McSally (R-Ariz.) tweeted footage of Raju asking her whether she thought the Senate should consider new evidence in President Donald Trump's impeachment trial. Raju replied: "You're a liberal hack. I'm not talking to you." McSally said: "You're not to going to comment about this?" Raju continued: "You're a liberal hack." As a result of the encounter, Raju's tweet trended on Twitter. Fellow media professionals noted that Raju was doing his job. McSally responded by tweeting a video of the encounter from her angle. The video shows Raju politely but firmly asking a question that all senators, regardless of party, were being asked. Raju's fellow CNN journalists defended him. McSally's reaction to the question may have unintended consequences for her reelection campaign. Hours after the tweet, the name of her Democratic opponent, former NASA astronaut Mark Kelly, became a trending term on Twitter, with many users citing McSally as the reason.
