President Barack Obama is planning an online town hall-style meeting on the White House website this Thursday. The White House says Obama will answer questions about the economy and other topics at WhiteHouse.gov. Visitors to the website can determine what questions the president will answer. During his campaign, Obama used the Internet to connect with voters, mobilize supporters and raise a record amount of money. He has used that online approach during the first months of his presidency. President George W. Bush's administration also took questions online at the White House's website. As the clock winds down before the payroll-tax holiday expires at the end of the month, a Northwest resident has obtained petitions to begin recalling Mayor. A coroner's official says some prescription medicines were found in the hotel room where Whitney died.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) will not try to block the Senate from moving ahead on a House-passed bill that would keep the government running and defund Obamacare, according to McConnell spokesman Don Stewart on Monday afternoon. McConnell supports the House Republicans' bill and will not vote to block it, since it defunds Obamacare and funds the government without increasing spending by a penny. Cruz has been calling for the House-passed plan. Cruz wants his colleagues to join him to prevent the Senate from moving ahead on the measure. Because once the bill clears a procedural vote requiring the support of 60 senators, Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) intends to strip out the portion that would defund Obamcare. Because of Senate rules, the new measure could pass the Democratic-controlled Senate with a simple majority. Stewart said McConnell would vote against any amendments that add funding for Obamacare back into the House-passed bill. Stewart said: "If and when the Majority Leader goes down that path, Washington Democrats will have to decide — without hiding behind a procedural vote — whether or not to split with their leadership and join Republicans and their constituents in opposing the re-insertion of Obamacare funding into the House-passed bill."

Voters in San Diego will elect their next mayor today, months after Democrat Bob Filner resigned amid mounting sexual harassment allegations. The outcome of the race will carry implications that will resonate well beyond San Diego's city limits. After a fall election whittled the field, the contest comes down to two city councilmen: Republican Kevin Faulconer and Democrat David Alvarez. The returns come in tonight. The White House does not involve itself in any race. On Saturday, President Obama endorsed Alvarez. Obama said he was watching the campaign and believes it is winnable. Obama said he would not hand over an endorsement at the eleventh hour for a candidate destined to lose. If Alvarez wins, he will trigger an alliance between the White House and the new head of one of the nation's largest cities. One of the main reasons Alvarez has been able to compete is the strong backing of organized labor. The news Web site inewsource.org has a rundown of the seven-figure investment unions have put behind Alvarez. Polling shows the two candidates are running neck and neck.

President Trump criticized his own secretary of state on Sunday, calling his effort to open lines of communication with North Korea a waste of time and seeming to rule out a diplomatic resolution to the nuclear-edged confrontation with Pyongyang. A day earlier, Secretary of State Rex W. Tillerson said he was reaching out to Pyongyang in hopes of starting a new dialogue. Trump criticized the idea and left the impression that he was focused mainly on military options. Adviser advisers described Trump as furious at Tillerson for contradicting the president's public position that now is not the time for talks. Trump wrote on Twitter: "I told Rex Tillerson, our wonderful Secretary of State, that he is wasting his time trying to negotiate with Little Rocket Man," using the nickname he has assigned to Kim Jong-un, the North Korean leader. "Save your energy Rex," he added, "we'll do what has to be done!" Some analysts wondered if the president was intentionally playing bad cop to the secretary of state. Veteran diplomats said they could not remember a time when a president undermined his secretary of state so brazenly in the midst of a tense situation. The episode raised questions about how long Tillerson would remain in his job.

State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert has been chosen as the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, President Donald Trump confirmed Friday. Nauert had been Trump's top pick for the position since mid-October, shortly after Nikki Haley announced her departure by the end of the year. CNN reported that Trump was looking for a candidate who had a willingness to defend him. Trump called his U.N. pick "very talented, very smart and very quick" as he spoke to reporters in front of the White House, praising her work at the State Department. "I think she's going to be respected by all," he said. Haley had insisted that her ambassadorship be a Cabinet-level role, but Secretary of State Mike Pompeo reportedly asked that Nauert's position not be so high-level. Nauert was criticized over an Instagram photo she shared in October depicting her smiling in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh shortly after Pompeo arrived there to discuss the disappearance of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi, a U.S. resident. The Saudi government later acknowledged that Khashoggi had been murdered.

Georgia's Rep. John Lewis spoke on the House floor Tuesday. He declared it time to bring impeachment proceedings against Donald Trump. Lewis said he was "deeply concerned about the future of our democracy, and I'm not alone." He continued, "We cannot delay. We must not wait. Now is the time to act. I have been patient while we tried every other path and used every other tool. We will never find the truth unless we use the power given to the House of Representatives and the House alone." He said they took an oath to protect and defend the Constitution, and, he said, "I am afraid to go to sleep for fear I wake up and our democracy will be gone." He spoke of Trump's "disdain and disregard for the law and the constitution," concluding, "I truly believe the time to begin impeachment proceedings against this president has come. To delay or to do otherwise would betray the foundation of our democracy." The outcome of the Democratic caucus meeting on whether to move forward with impeachment proceedings is less in doubt. However, a delay on making it official until Thursday, when acting Director of National Intelligence Joseph Maguire appears before Congress, with or without the Ukraine whistleblower's complaint.

Anderson Cooper criticized President Donald Trump for failing as a dealmaker, stating that "the one thing he says he does better than anyone else." Trump is expected to sign a new border security deal that would avoid another partial government shutdown. Trump has made it known that he is not "thrilled" with the deal. Under the deal, $1.375 billion would be allocated to border barriers, less than a quarter of the $5.7 billion Trump has been demanding. Cooper said it came as no surprise that Trump was unable to secure a better agreement, especially given that "the president's record in the private sector is riddled with ill-fated deals." Cooper said the president is said to be angry, he's said to be upset, and he has complained publicly about where things have ended up, but the reality is he could've had a better deal than this one. Cooper said whatever the lessons he preached in The Art of the Deal, they did not work out for him this time. Cooper said this may not have been the legacy that he wanted, but it's hard to deny that it is the legacy he's earned in this case.

A new Quinnipiac University poll shows Hillary Clinton trails all leading Republican contenders in Colorado by 11 percentage points. Florida Sen. Marco Rubio leads Clinton 52% to 36%, the biggest gap. Ben Carson wins a potential head-to-head matchup as well, with a 52% to 38% advantage. Donald Trump leads 48% to 37%. Tim Malloy, the assistant director of the Quinnipiac University Poll, described it as a "chilly if not frigid reception" in Colorado for Clinton. In the nominating contest, Colorado's Republican voters' preference does not count because it violates Republican National Committee rules requiring states to bind their delegates to the winners of their votes. Carson is Republican voters' preference at 25%, followed by Rubio at 19%, Trump at 17%, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz at 14%, Carly Fiorina at 5%, Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul at 3% and former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush at 2%. Among Democrats, Clinton leads with 55% support to Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' 27% and former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley's 2%. President Barack Obama won the Centennial State in both 2008 and 2012.

Donald Trump will hold his first rally as President of the United States this weekend at Orlando-Melbourne International Airport. The rally comes after a week in which the resignation of National Security Advisor Mike Flynn and bilateral press conferences with Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In a tweet, Trump urged supporters to "join me this Saturday at 5pm for a rally at the Orlando-Melbourne International Airport," accompanied by an image pledging to "put America back to work" and to put "people before government." Volusia County Republican Party Chairman Tony Ledbetter told USA Today Trump is "likely to talk about his early accomplishments as president and his plans for the future." The event will be Trump's first individual rally since his inauguration, after having held a "Thank You Tour" in the states that put him over the top. In the November election, Trump defeated Hillary Clinton by over 100,000 votes and by a margin of 1.2 per cent.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un oversaw Tuesday's firing of a super-large multiple rocket launcher, state propaganda organ KCNA said late Tuesday. Two short-range projectiles were fired hours after the North indicated a willingness to resume denuclearization talks with the United States later this month. The projectiles were fired from South Pyongan Province, which surrounds the capital city of Pyongyang, and landed in the waters off North Korea's east coast, South Korean officials said. Kim was accompanied by senior military personnel and officials with the Workers' Party of Korea during the tests, KCNA said. He said the weapons system "has been finally verified in terms of combat operation" and "running fire test" is what remains to be done. It was not clear what such a test would entail. KCNA reported that Kim said future tasks and steadily attaining goals to cutting-edge national defense were also needed. President Trump has downplayed a slew of recent weapons tests by the North this year. The latest was the tenth such launch since May. He has said the short-range firings do not violate any agreements. Before Tuesday's launchings, North Korean officials said they would be willing to restart denuclearization negotiations with American officials. Talks between Trump and Kim fell apart in February when Trump rejected Kim's demand for sanctions relief in exchange for partial denuclearization.

Several protesters disrupted the opening-night speeches Monday at the Republican National Convention. A Code Pink demonstrator unfurled a banner near the VIP box of vice-presidential nominee Indiana Gov. Mike Pence that read "Yes We Can End War." Nearby convention-goers surrounded the woman and shouted "arrest her" until Secret Service agents and other law-enforcement officials arrived and removed her. A man wearing a "Bikers for Trump" shirt attempted to rip the sign out of her hands and help police. Another Code Pink protester also attempted to disrupt the speeches. A third protester, in the second deck of the Quicken Loans Area, where the four-day convention is being held, put up a sign that read "Refugees Welcome," which brought on loud cheers of "USA, USA, USA." The expected protests outside the convention's security perimeter took place through the day and night, but there were no reports of clashes or other violence. Cleveland Mayor Frank Jackson told reporters in the early evening that the protests have so far been "peaceful" and that just one arrest was made and that a small knife, gas masks and a sling shot has been confiscated.

Attorney General William Barr wrote in a letter to Congress on Friday that the Justice Department has "no plans" to submit Robert Mueller's nearly 400-page special counsel report to the White House for an executive privilege review before its mid-April public release. Barr wrote that although the President would have the right to assert privilege over certain parts of the report, he has stated publicly that he intends to defer to me and, accordingly, there are no plans to submit the report to the White House for a privilege review. Barr released a four-page letter on Sunday that reflected the "principal conclusions" of Mueller's report. He also wrote that it is inaccurate to describe that letter as a "summary" of the Mueller report. "The Special Counsel's report is nearly 400 pages long (exclusive of tables and appendices) and sets for the Special Counsel's findings, his analysis, and the reasons for his conclusions," Barr wrote. "Everyone will soon be able to read it on their own. I do not believe it would be in the public's interest for me to attempt to summarize the full report or release it in serial of piecemeal fashion."

The North Carolina Republican Party issued a press release in response to an apparent arson attack this weekend at a party office in Hillsborough, North Carolina. The office in Hillsborough, located in Orange County, was firebombed overnight, causing major damage and destruction. No one was reported injured. An explosive device was thrown through the window of the office, and the words "Nazi Republicans, leave town or else" were painted on a nearby building. The news came less than 25 days before Election Day. NCGOP volunteers and activists are canvassing the state and spending long hours getting out the vote and exercising their rights in a free and open democratic society. Dallas Woodhouse, executive director of the North Carolina Republican Party, said, "Whether you are Republican, Democrat, or Independent, all Americans should be outraged by this hate-filled and violent attack against our democracy." Woodhouse added, "Whether the bomb was meant to kill, destroy property, or intimidate voters, everyone in this country should be free to express their political viewpoints without fear for their own safety. We will be requesting additional security at all Republican Party offices and events between now and Election Day to ensure the safety of our activists, volunteers, and supporters." Woodhouse added, "We will not be deterred by this hate crime."

President Obama held a news conference today. He made a statement and took no questions. He was flanked by first responders. The news conference concerned the impending sequester, which would make cuts to several social programs and arbitrary cuts to the military. The President issued a statement to Republicans. He said: "The Republicans in Congress face a simple choice. Are they willing to compromise to protect vital investments in education, healthcare, national security, and all the jobs that depend on them. - Or would they rather put hundreds of thousands of jobs and our entire economy at risk just to protect a few special interest tax loopholes that benefit only the wealthiest Americans and biggest corporations." The President's message was short and succinct: "If the sequester goes into effect in March, $85 million will go into effect immediately. Cuts will be a self inflicting wound that depresses the economy." Cuts will include furloughed FBI agents and reduction in funds for police and fire personnel. Cuts will include the lay off of thousands of teachers. Head Start will be cut. Homeland Security cuts will cause severe delays at airports. A carrier group scheduled for the Persian Gulf will not be deployed.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell on Thursday evening introduced a coronavirus economic rescue legislative package. The plan largely reflects the proposal outlined earlier by Breitbart news. Direct cash payments go to taxpayers based on 2018 tax returns. Individuals will receive up to $1,200, with the amount scaling down for individuals earning $75,000 or more. Those earning more than $99,000 will be ineligible. Married couples will get up to $2,400 and an additional $500 for every child. Payments decline after $150,000 of income, with the cap placed at $200,000. Small Business Support. $300 billion for loan guarantees for small businesses. Loan Guarantees for Airlines. $50 billion in loan guarantees for passenger airlines and $8 billion for air cargo shippers. $150 billion for other businesses in areas or sectors affected by the coronavirus, which affects pretty much everyone and everywhere. The bill will be negotiated with Democrats, who want to attach conditions on the aid to businesses. Some Republicans may also try to change the income caps, pointing out that these are based on 2018's reported income, which would not reflect the negative impact of the pandemic.

On Tuesday, ahead of Lt. Col. Alex Vindman's testimony as part of the House Democrats' impeachment inquiry into President Donald Trump, Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-CA) criticized GOP House members questioning Vindman's political motives for testifying against the president. CNN "New Day" host Alisyn Camerota asked Maloney about Sen. Ron Johnson (R-WI) suggesting in a letter that Vindman never accepted Trump as a legitimate president. Maloney said to question Vindman's patriotism is "disgusting." He added that anybody lying about the "war hero" should question their life choices. Maloney told Camerota, "Here's a pro tip: If you find yourself lying about a war hero, you should probably question your choices in life." He continued, "I don't know what he was doing when Lieutenant Colonel Vindman earned the Purple Heart in Iraq in an IED attack, but to question Lieutenant Colonel Vindman's patriotism is disgusting." Maloney also said House Republicans cannot "deal with the facts, so they're lying about a war hero."

President Obama said Wednesday he did not hand the election to Republican Mitt Romney with his debate performance last week. "Governor Romney had a good night. I had a bad night," Obama told ABC News' Diane Sawyer. "It's not the first time I've had a bad night." Obama said the "fundamentals of what this race is about haven't changed." "Maybe this is because I played a lot of sports when I was a kid, and still do," he said. "If you have a bad game, you just move on. You look forward to the next one. And it makes you that much more determined. The difference between this and sports is that the stakes are so high." The two candidates will debate next at Hofstra University in Hempstead, N.Y., on Tuesday.

Federal law requires that Medicaid beneficiaries may obtain services, including family-planning care, from any qualified provider. Terminating Planned Parenthood's Medicaid provider agreements restricts access by not permitting them to get services from providers of their choice, according to the Department of Health and Human Services. Planned Parenthood has not committed fraud or a criminal act. In fact, in Louisiana Planned Parenthood does not even provide abortions. In some previous attempts by states to cut off funding, Planned Parenthood has prevailed in court. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, a unit of HHS, has notified Louisiana and Alabama, which have taken action to terminate their Medicaid provider agreements with Planned Parenthood, that they may be in conflict with federal law, according to HHS. CMS said that by restricting which provider a woman could choose to receive care from, women could lose access to critical preventive care, such as cancer screenings. The agency reached out to Louisiana's Medicaid director on Aug. 5 and spoke with Alabama's Medicaid agency on Aug. 7. CMS said it provided both states with guidance it released in 2011 on this issue. The June 2011 memo says states are not permitted to exclude providers from Medicaid solely on the basis of the range of medical services they provide. The memo says states may exclude providers under certain circumstances, such as when providers commit fraud or certain criminal acts.

Khizr Khan, a prominent Democratic spokesman for the 2020 Democratic National Convention, appeared on the second night of the 2020 DNC to present Virginia's delegate votes and claimed that President Donald Trump "praised those racists" in Charlottesville. Khan, a former Vice President Joe Biden, made the claim central to his campaign message. Trump repeatedly condemned the neo-Nazis in Charlottesville in August 2017. The neo-Nazis were not the only violent group in Charlottesville. The "clash" occurred peacefully with Antifa extremists. Trump had been referring to peaceful protests both for and against the removal of a statue of Confederate General Robert E. Lee. Khan lost a son fighting for the U.S. in Iraq and emerged as a prominent Democratic spokesman after the 2016 DNC.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) on Wednesday told Republican colleagues he is undecided on whether to vote to convict President Donald Trump in the Senate's impeachment trial following last week's riots at the U.S. Capitol. "While the press has been full of speculation, I have not made a final decision on how I will vote and I intend to listen to the legal arguments when they are presented to the Senate," McConnell wrote in a letter obtained by The Hill. The House of Representatives voted Wednesday to impeach President Donald Trump on charges he incited an "insurrection" at the U.S. Capitol a week ago. The chamber voted 232-197 in favor of impeachment, making Trump the first U.S. president in history to be impeached twice. Ten Republicans voted along with Democrats, including Rep. Liz Cheney, R-Wyo. Despite the House vote, McConnell declined to convene an emergency session beginning Friday to open an impeachment trial in the upper chamber. "Given the rules, procedures, and Senate precedents that govern presidential impeachment trials, there is simply no chance that a fair or serious trial could conclude before President-elect Biden is sworn in next week," the Republican lawmaker said in a statement. The UPI contributed to this report.

White House Press Secretary Robert Gibbs stepped down from the post Friday after two years as President Barack Obama's top spokesman. Jay Carney, the current communications director for Vice President Joe Biden, will succeed him at the podium. Gibbs announced his decision to leave in January. Gibbs called it a "remarkable privilege" to serve the president. He said he wants to "step back a little bit and recharge some" after four years of campaigning and a hard-fought first half of the Obama administration, which he described as "probably the busiest years that Washington and the White House have seen in a couple of decades." Gibbs said he will remain in the Washington area as a pundit, supporting White House positions on cable television and in speeches. "It's a remarkable privilege. It is in many ways the opportunity of a lifetime," he told reporters at the White House briefing announcing his decision. But he added, "We've been going at this pace for four years." In a written statement, Obama described Gibbs as "a close friend, one of my closest advisers and an effective advocate from the podium." He said it was "natural" for his longtime aide "to want to step back, reflect and retool." Gibbs was Obama's spokesman during the 2008 presidential campaign, having joined the future president's team when Obama ran for U.S. Senate in 2004.

A letter to the editor responded to a front-page article titled "A 'New Day' of Openness, Taxed by Old Grievances" dated March 22. The letter stated that President Obama referred to the First Amendment, free speech, freedom of assembly and religious freedom. The letter also referenced President Raúl Castro's comments at a news conference in Cuba on Monday. The letter writer wrote that they welcome President Castro commenting on areas where he feels the country is falling short, and that the country should not be immune or afraid of criticism or discussion. The writer stated that they cannot be the only person who recognizes the maturity, honesty and statesmanlike nature of that remark. The writer stated that the country desperately needs this kind of grown-up behavior in elected officials. The writer stated that the "we're No. 1!" attitude does nothing to help at home or improve the country's standing in the world. The writer stated that the country is not faultless and it is not weakness to acknowledge mistakes. The writer asked whether the country will mature to the point at which it welcomes and praises a leader willing to voice awareness of error and pledge to do better. The writer was from Santa Fe, N.M.

A Suffolk University/7News poll conducted Jan. 11-13 of 500 registered voters in the state showed Republican candidate Scott Brown leading Democrat Martha Coakley by 4 percentage points. Brown had 50 percent support, Coakley had 46 percent, and independent candidate Joseph Kennedy, who is not related to the late senator, had 3 percent. The race is within the 4.4-point margin of error. David Paleologos, the university's political research center director, said in a statement that the survey shows Brown has "surged dramatically." Polls of the Massachusetts race have shown the race tightening over the past several weeks, but most have shown Coakley in the lead. With the election set for Tuesday, both candidates have brought out heavy hitters to campaign for them. A Brown win would break the Democrats' 60-vote, filibuster-proof majority in the Senate. Former President Bill Clinton and Sen. John Kerry, D-Mass., are headlining a rally for Coakley Friday afternoon in Boston. Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani is campaigning with Brown in Boston Friday.

President Barack Obama's State of the Union address and Representative Paul Ryan's Republican response on Tuesday night offer competing visions of the country. For Mr. Obama, it is business as usual. A year ago the euphemism was "stimulus." Now it is "investment." Most of his hour-long speech was a paean to liberal activism, as the president called for redoubling outlays on high-speed rail and "countless" green energy jobs. His single concrete proposal about cutting spending was a five-year freeze on nondefense discretionary outlays. This follows last year's call for a three-year freeze that was never enacted. The president's proposal would save $400 billion over 10 years. But that is on a federal budget that has increased 25% in two years, raising government's share of GDP to 25% from roughly 20%. Freezing government at the current record levels is insufficient. Republicans have proposed cutting $100 billion from this year's budget. This would save $1.5 trillion over the next 10 years. The GOP already made a $42 billion down payment on their $100 billion in cuts from the president's budget by deep-sixing the Democratic omnibus bill during the lame-duck session.

President Obama will not re-nominate former Georgia legislator Michael Boggs to a lifetime position on the federal bench. Boggs was nominated last December as part of a deal with Georgia's two Republican senators. He did not receive a confirmation vote in the Senate before it adjourned. During his time in Georgia's House of Representatives, Boggs compiled a conservative voting record. Though nominally a Democrat, he campaigned on his "quality conservative Christian values," including opposing marriage equality, opposing "homosexual Boy Scout leaders," and supporting school prayer. Boggs drew opposition from civil rights figures including Georgia Rep. John Lewis (D), a member of the Congressional Black Caucus, for his record, including a vote to keep the Confederate battle emblem as part of the Georgia state flag. Boggs said, "My parents would expect nothing less."

Former Rep. Bob Beauprez won the Colorado Republican Primary for Governor. Former Rep. Tom Tancredo, Secretary of State Scott Gessler, and former State Senate Minority Leader Mike Kopp were among the candidates. Tancredo called Beauprez to concede the race, which showed him trailing by about four points with more than 60 percent of votes counted. Gessler placed third, while Kopp placed fourth. Beauprez entered the race late, announcing his candidacy in March, but quickly received support from many in the Denver business community. He was also endorsed by former Massachusetts governor Mitt Romney and Texas Governor Rick Perry. Republican Governors Association Chairman Chris Christie called to congratulate Beauprez on his victory. Colorado Republicans have been seeking a rematch against Democratic Governor John Hickelooper in the Fall. Hickenlooper won in 2010 after Republican candidate Dan Maes was challenged by Tancredo, who ran as a candidate for the Constitution party. Beauprez has a history of losing to Democrats. In 2006, a year for Republicans, Beauprez lost by 17 points in the race for governor against Democratic candidate Bill Ritter. Republicans believe Hickenlooper is vulnerable after enacting a liberal agenda in Colorado including a series of controversial gun control laws.

General Motors chief executive Mary T. Barra spoke at an investor conference on the sidelines of the Detroit auto show on Tuesday. She urged the Trump administration not to scrap the North American Free Trade Agreement. Barra said any changes in the pact should account for the effect on American automakers and workers. "There could be unintended consequences, changes made, that would directly impact jobs in the United States," she said. "Nafta needs to be modified," she added, but she rejected the idea that "we need to walk away from it." President Trump has said that Nafta should be renegotiated and has at times suggested that the United States could withdraw from the agreement or tax vehicles imported from Mexico, where G.M. makes certain small cars, sport-utility vehicles and pickup trucks. Barra said she favored steps to modernize the agreement and added, "We are completely aligned with the administration on job preservation." She said G.M. had had discussions with officials from the United States, Mexico and Canada "to make sure everybody understands the complexity" of how the pact affects automakers and the flow of parts and vehicles across borders within North America.

Russia's victory came three days after Victory Day, in the form of Secretary of State John Kerry's visit this week to the Black Sea resort city of Sochi. The visit was widely interpreted by the Americans as a signal of surrender by President Obama and an acknowledgment that Russia and its leader are too important to ignore. Since the seizure of Crimea more than a year ago, Mr. Obama has worked to isolate Russia and its president, Vladimir V. Putin, portraying him as a lawless bully atop an economically failing, increasingly irrelevant petrostate. Mr. Obama led the charge by the West to punish Mr. Putin for his intervention in Ukraine, booting Russia from the Group of 8 economic powers, imposing sanctions on some of Mr. Putin's closest confidants, and delivering financial and military assistance to the new Ukrainian government. In recent months, however, Russia has not only weathered those attacks and levied painful countersanctions on America's European allies, but has also proved stubbornly important on the world stage. That has been true especially in regard to Syria, where its proposal to confiscate chemical weapons has kept President Bashar al-Assad, a Kremlin ally, in power, and in the negotiations that secured a tentative deal on Iran's nuclear program.

Former first daughter Jenna Bush Hager announced Wednesday that she is pregnant with her first child, due in the spring. The 31-year-old made the announcement on NBC's "Today" show, where she is a contributing correspondent. Hager is the twin daughter of former President George W. Bush and her husband, Henry. They have been married for four years. During a phone call on the show, former President Bush said he is "fired up" about becoming a grandfather, and former first lady Laura Bush said she is "thrilled." It will be the couple's first grandchild.

John McCain said Hillary Clinton vs. Rand Paul in 2016 would be a "tough choice." McCain made the comment in response to a Yahoo headline stating: "John McCain to Endorse Hillary Rodham Clinton in 2016." McCain said Clinton did a fine job as secretary of state. He said she has, maybe not glamour, but certainly the aura of someone widely regarded throughout the world. McCain said it is interesting that the issues where John Kerry is engaging are where Hillary Clinton did not engage in, that those decisions were left to the White House and the National Security Council. McCain said when Clinton versus Paul occurs in 2016, he would have to decide who to vote for. McCain added: "It's gonna be a tough choice [laughs]." McCain then clarified: "Let me just clarify that. I think that Rand Paul represents a segment of the GOP, just like his father. And I think he is trying to expand that, intelligently, to make it larger." McCain then asked: "Am I happy? I'd like to be president of the United States."

Former President Bill Clinton said in an interview with Town & Country magazine that he is less angry now that he has a granddaughter, Charlotte Clinton Mezvinsky, born in September 2014. Clinton said Charlotte keeps him from harboring bad feelings. "I've told Hillary that I don't think I'm good [at campaigning] anymore because I'm not mad at anybody," Clinton said. "I'm a grandfather, and I got to see my grand daughter last night, and I can't be mad." Clinton also noted he will likely be a "backstage adviser" to his wife, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, in her potential 2016 presidential run. Hillary Clinton is expected to make an announcement on her 2016 plans in the coming weeks. "I think it's important, and Hillary does too, that she go out there as if she's never run for anything before and establish her connection with the voters," Bill Clinton told T&C. In the interview, Clinton also defended work done by the Clinton Foundation, which he said is, "by a good long stretch, the most transparent of all the presidential foundations and more transparent than a lot of other major foundations in the country."

North Korea neared completion of the transition to its new leader, Kim Jong-un, on Thursday as a confrontation with the United States continued over the North's intent to launch a long-range rocket. The governing Workers' Party declared Mr. Kim "supreme leader" on Wednesday and awarded him the title of first secretary. On Thursday, North Korea also said that Mr. Kim had been elevated to chairman of the party's central military commission and granted membership in the Politburo and its presidium. The elevation of Mr. Kim later this week to the top defense commission post will cap his rise to the pinnacle of party, military and state leadership. Analysts in the region said the speed of his elevation reflected the insecurity of the young leader's status as much as the leadership's need to have a solid power center in place immediately. The country's Unha, or Galaxy, rocket is expected to blast off within days. The North says the rocket's purpose is peaceful — to put a satellite in orbit — but the United States and other countries see the event as a test of long-range missile technology.

President Obama called Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko on Tuesday and expressed optimism that a settlement can be reached. Obama is weighing whether to provide the Ukrainian military with lethal arms to help the fight against pro-Russian rebels. The president will not make a final decision until Poroshenko and Russian President Vladimir Putin meet with German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Francois Hollande in Belarus on Wednesday. The German and French leaders have said diplomacy must be given another chance before the United States takes additional steps, such as sending arms to Ukraine. In his call with Putin, the president urged the Russian leader to embrace diplomacy and call off the pro-Russian fighters still wreaking havoc in eastern Ukraine. "President Obama reiterated America's support for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine. President Obama underscored the rising human toll of the fighting and underscored the importance of President Putin seizing the opportunity presented by the ongoing discussions between Russia, France, Germany, and Ukraine to reach a peaceful resolution," the White House said in a readout of the call. The president also warned Putin that Moscow will face additional costs if it does not change course.

The Republican-led House of Representatives voted Wednesday to extend expiring George W. Bush-era tax cuts at all income levels for another year. With Congress leaving Washington on Friday for a month-long recess, the vote was a pre-election statement of the GOP's opposition to raising taxes for any taxpayer. It also earned support from a handful of Democrats facing difficult reelection campaigns this fall. The final vote count was 256-171, according to The Washington Post Congressional Votes Databse. 19 Democrats voted with Republicans to approve the bill. Collectively, these 19 Democrats vote with their party 72 percent of the time. Donnelly, who is running for the U.S. Senate and has touted his moderate record, votes with Democrats 67 percent of the time, according to the votes database. Of these 19 Democrats, several have consistently abandoned the party on high-profile votes, including Boren, Kissell, McIntyre and Matheson, who face difficult reelection bids, and Ross, who is retiring but many one day run for statewide office.

At CBS's Republican presidential primary debate on Saturday, moderator John Dickerson exchanged remarks with Senator Ted Cruz (R-TX). The exchange resulted in the audience booing Dickerson after he said, "Sorry, I want to get the facts straight for the audience. I apologize." Dickerson then asked Cruz where the president should appoint a successor, stating that the Constitution states the president shall appoint with advice and concept from the Senate to clear that up. Cruz responded that he did not think the president should. Dickerson asked where the appointment would begin, stating it would begin in election year, December, November, September, and that once set the date, the president would abide by that date. Cruz referenced the 80 years of not confirming presidents. Dickerson referenced LBJ's nomination of Abe Fortas, noting Fortas did not get confirmed and was defeated. Dickerson said Kennedy was confirmed in 1987. Dickerson said no Kennedy was confirmed in 1987. Dickerson asked whether appointing or confirming was the issue, and Cruz responded, "In this case it's both. If i could finish."

Montana election results indicate a contest between incumbent Democrats and Republican state auditor Matt Rosendale. President Trump visited Montana in 2016. The White House has made a series of visits to Montana, including visits to the White House. The visits are intended to defeat incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Tester and replace him with Republican state auditor Matt Rosendale. Tester is described as a "pro-gun, anti-big-business prairie pragmatist." He is seeking to keep the race local, while Rosendale is banking on his association with the president. Tester is a former rancher and teacher. He is one of two Democrats in Montana who have held statewide office. The other is Gov. Steve Bullock, who won in 2016 on a platform that included expanding Medicaid, raising the minimum wage and opposing the Citizens United decision. Taxes would be increased on all tobacco products, including electronic cigarettes, with the revenue used to expand eligibility for Medicaid coverage under the Affordable Care Act. This measure would ban people from collecting election ballots filled out by others, unless they are relatives, members of the same household as the voter, election officials, postal workers, or the like.

President Obama and ABC News' George Stephanopoulos exchanged questions Sunday over whether the president's health care plan includes a tax increase. Stephanopoulos asked Obama to look up the Merriam-Webster dictionary definition of taxes. In the interview airing Sunday, Stephanopoulos pressed the president on his plan to require people to purchase health insurance. Obama responded: "Under this mandate, the government is forcing people to spend money, fining you if you don't. How is that not a tax?" Stephanopoulos then asked: "No, but -- but, George, you -- you can't just make up that language and decide that that's called a tax increase." Stephanopoulos then offered the dictionary definition. Obama said: "I don't think I'm making it up. Merriam-Webster's dictionary: 'Tax, a charge, usually of money, imposed by authority on persons or property for public purposes.'" Obama rejected the notion it was a tax increase and said pulling the dictionary out was a sign the host was "stretching" a little. "No. That -- that's not true, George. The -- for us to say that you've got to take a responsibility to get health insurance is absolutely not a tax increase," Obama said.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi lost 19 Democrats on Wednesday's vote to be House speaker. The vote was the worst for a party's nominee in more than 80 years. Mrs. Pelosi won the support of 173 Democrats, but 18 others voted for someone else and one voted "present." Rep. John A. Boehner, Ohio Republican, won the vote with the support of all 241 Republicans who voted. According to figures from the House historian's office and the Congressional Research Service, the last time a party's nominee for speaker lost that much support was in 1923. On the first ballot that year, the GOP's nominee Frederick H. Gillett saw 23 lawmakers support other Republicans. Mr. Gillett still won the speakership on the ninth ballot. Rep. Heath Shuler, North Carolina Democrat, garnered 11 votes on Wednesday. Shuler afterward said it was an effort to forge a middle ground between Mrs. Pelosi and Mr. Boehner. Speaker's elections have historically pitted the leaders of the House Republican Conference against the House Democratic Caucus, and from 1945 through 1995 those were the only two candidates to receive any votes. In four of the seven speaker's elections since then, other candidates have received votes from conservative Democrats seeking to register disapproval with their party's direction.

Top White House aide Dan Pfeiffer said Sunday that President Obama is not threatening Congress by promising to take more actions on his own in 2014. Obama's use of "a pen and a phone" -- the pen being the use of so-called executive actions, a.k.a. generally limited policy declarations that a president takes unilaterally -- is expected to be a major theme of his State of the Union address Tuesday. The White House has been telegraphing this strategy for weeks. Some observers have interpreted this strategy as threatening Congress that, if it does not act, Obama will. "I don't think it's confrontational," Pfeiffer said on CNN's "State of the Union." "Let's find some areas we can work together." Pfeiffer said Obama "is not going to tell the American people that he's going to wait for Congress." Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), appearing on the same program, said the White House's comments do indeed sound like a threat. "It sounds vaguely like a threat, and I think it also has a certain amount of arrogance in the sense that one of the fundamental principles of our country were the checks and balances -- that it wasn't supposed to be easy to pass legislation, that you have to convince people," Paul said.

President Obama will cut short his European trip to visit Dallas early next week after a sniper killed five police officers Thursday night in that city, according to the White House. The president will visit on the invitation of Dallas Mayor Mike Rawlings, also said the White House, which stated it will release more details about the trip as soon as they are available. Police have identified the shooter as Micah Johnson, a black Army veteran, who is reportedly upset about two recent incidents in which a police officer fatally shot a black male. In all, 12 officers were shot in the sniper attack. Obama condemned the shooting of the black males in Minnesota and Louisiana, and the police shootings, saying Friday from Poland: "There is no possible justification for these kinds of attacks or any violence against law enforcement. … Anyone involved in the senseless murders will be held fully accountable. Justice will be done." Obama will return on Sunday to Washington, one day earlier than planned. He will travel on Saturday from Warsaw, Poland to Madrid, Spain, then participate Sunday in meetings with his Spanish counterpart and other government officials and later go to the Northern Mariana Island of Rota, as previously scheduled, to speak with U.S. military personnel serving there. However, his visit to Seville, Spain, was cancelled for the early departure.

A House panel voted Wednesday to place a five-year moratorium on bonuses to senior executives at the Department of Veterans Affairs. The sponsor, Rep. Jeff Miller, Republican chairman of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, said the legislation was in response to media reports about various executives who received performance bonuses despite significant problems at the VA during their watch, such as the increase in the number of disability claims pending longer than 125 days. The VA had already halted bonuses for those executives overseeing disability claims, but Miller's legislation extends the ban to other divisions within the government's second-largest department. The VA did not respond to a request for comment, but has stated previously that bonuses have been reduced in recent years. In 2009, the department awarded executives $3.3 million in bonuses. Last year, the amount of bonuses fell to $2.3 million. The bonuses go to career professionals and not to political appointees. The Florida lawmaker's amendment was part of a larger bill requiring states to charge in-state tuition rates for veterans using their Post 911 GI Bill benefits. No lawmakers spoke in opposition to the amendment. Miller said in a prepared statement sent out after the vote: "Until we have complete confidence that VA is holding executives accountable rather than rewarding them for their mistakes, no one should get a performance bonus. Period."

The House on Thursday rejected a measure that would have withdrawn funding for U.S. military operations in Libya. The amendment was offered as an amendment to a defense appropriations bill. It failed on a 199 to 229 vote. The measure was sponsored by Reps. Dennis J. Kucinich (D-Ohio) and Justin Amash (R-Mich.) and co-sponsored by a bipartisan group of 13 other critics of U.S. involvement in Libya. The measure states that "none of the funds made available by this Act may be used for the use of military force against Libya." The vote occurred two weeks after the House rejected a measure authorizing the U.S. mission in Libya and a bill that would have limited funding of U.S. operations in that country. On Thursday, another Libya-related amendment, sponsored by Rep. Tom Cole (R-Okla.), passed on a 225 to 201 vote. That measure would prevent funds from being used for equipment and training related to the Libyan operation.

Secretary of State John Kerry addressed critics of a potential nuclear deal with Iran on Capitol Hill on Tuesday, a week before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel is scheduled to deliver an address to Congress criticizing the emerging accord. Kerry said: "Anybody running around right now, jumping in to say, 'Well, we don't like the deal,' or this or that, doesn't know what the deal is. There is no deal yet. And I caution people to wait and see what these negotiations produce." At another point, Kerry said Netanyahu had been wrong about the Obama administration's policy toward Iran in the past. Kerry said Netanyahu had denounced a 2013 interim accord to freeze much of Iran's nuclear program, only to acknowledge it was in Israel's interest. Kerry said: "I don't know anybody who looks at the interim agreement and doesn't say, 'Wow, this has really worked' — including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who would like to see it extended, having opposed it vehemently in the beginning, calling it the deal of the century for Iran."

Senator Rob Portman will not be running for re-election in 2022. The announcement came via the Columbus Dispatch. Portman cited "partisan gridlock" as the reason for his retirement. The article states that on the Republican side, this could set up a primary between the Trumpist wing of the party and more moderate Republicons. Former congressman Jim Renacci ran against incumbent senator Sherrod Brown in 2018. Other Trumpist tools, like Rep. Jim Jordan, might also enter the race. It could also see more mainstream GOP politicians enter the race, such as Lt. Gov. John Husted. On the Democratic side, there is a lack of statewide officeholders who have the same kind of name recognition as Brown. Maybe it will be a congressman or congresswoman instead, such as Rep. Tim Ryan. The Democratic candidate may have a better shot at this seat than one might expect, given the division in the GOP right now and the likelihood that they will be more divided by the election. The article also raises the possibility that Portman may use this announcement to distance himself from the Trumpists and possibly break with the Trumpist line on impeachment and votes on Biden's legislative agenda.

The president will visit on the invitation of Dallas Mayor Mike Rawlings, also said the White House, which stated it will release more details about the trip as soon as they are available. However, his visit to Seville, Spain, was cancelled for the early departure.

President Donald Trump posted a video on Independence Day weekend that appeared to endorse violence against the press, particularly CNN. CNN commentator Ana Navarro appeared on ABC News' "This Week" and said the president took things too far and his tweet was inciting violence. "He is going to get somebody killed in the media," she said. "Maybe that will stop him." Days earlier, Deputy White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the president has never incited violence. CNN posted its official response to Trump's tweet by quoting the comments Sanders made two days prior. Navarro, a Republican strategist, has criticized the president since he launched his candidacy for the nation's highest office. Last week, she called Trump a "lunatic man baby" for attacking MSNBC's Mika Brzezinski. The Wall Street Journal reported that the president's son-in-law and top advisor, Jared Kushner, complained about Navarro's coverage to a senior executive at CNN's parent company, Time Warner. Navarro has not stopped criticizing the president and his administration.

Democratic Rep. Chaka Fattah of Pennsylvania offered Wednesday his resignation from the House effective Oct. 3. House Speaker Paul Ryan called on Fattah to resign immediately because Fattah is slated to be sentenced Oct. 4. Ryan said in a statement the veteran Pennsylvania lawmaker had betrayed the trust of the House and his constituents. Ryan said he hoped Democratic leaders would join him in calling for Fattah's immediate resignation. Fattah was convicted on charges of racketeering, fraud and money laundering. The case was largely centered on efforts to repay an illegal $1 million campaign loan. His lawyers had argued that the schemes were engineered without Fattah's knowledge by two political consultants who pleaded guilty in the case. The 59-year-old Democrat had been in Congress since 1995. He lost his April primary and his bid for another term. In a letter to Ryan, Fattah outlined accomplishments he produced in the House and wrote: "I'm very sad about the verdict the jury rendered yesterday and because of that, my resignation is effective Oct. 3, 2016. Despite my resignation I am working to clear my name of these charges and plan to mount an appeal." Fox News' Chad Pergram and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

House Budget Committee Chairman Paul Ryan (R-Wisc.) appeared on CNN's State of the Union on Sunday to discuss his federal budget proposal and whether he would run for Senate. When asked if the Bush administration bore some responsibility for the nation's fiscal woes, Ryan said both parties messed this up. Ryan said President Obama had offered some ideas regarding how to cut spending and deal with entitlements, but that a formal plan, in writing, had not been released by either the president or Senate Democrats. "My townhall meetings went phenomenally well," Ryan said when asked to address the line he and other Republicans were attempting to walk — specifically, calling for the preservation of oil industry tax breaks at a time of rising gas prices, while asking seniors-to-be to accept cuts in Medicare benefits. Asked if he would run for the Senate to replace retiring Senator Herb Kohl (D-Wisc.), Ryan said, "We just started digesting this. I plan on making an announcement very quickly." He said he would announce his intentions this week.

Secretary of State John Kerry toured miles of roofless homes and damaged shantytowns destroyed by Typhoon Haiyan on Nov. 8. Kerry said additional American humanitarian aid would be sent to the Philippines. He called the storm a warning of extreme weather in a warming world. "No words can do justice to the level of destruction we've seen in this entire community," he said. For the most part, severe shortages of food and clean water in the two weeks after the typhoon ended have ended. Four million people lost their homes to storm surges or gusts that reached 200 miles an hour, and the effort to rebuild has barely begun. The Philippine government raised the official death toll to 6,092 on Thursday, with 27,665 injured and 1,779 missing. Local officials said the number of dead will continue to rise as more bodies are found. Running water has been restored in some central areas of Tacloban, but large areas of Leyte and Samar Islands still have none. "Looking around here," Kerry said, "you see an unmistakable example of what an extreme weather event looks like, and a reminder of our responsibility to act to protect the future."

President Obama on Wednesday nominated Sharon Block, a former Democratic Labor Department official, and Richard Griffin, a Democratic union lawyer, to serve on the National Labor Relations Board. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia ruled on Jan. 25 that their appointments to the NLRB were invalid because Mr. Obama installed them in the posts in January 2012 through an unconstitutional exercise of his appointment powers. The court said the president did not have the authority to make the "recess appointments," a means of circumventing the Senate confirmation process, because the Senate was not in recess at the time. The ruling meant that the NLRB does not have a quorum to make decisions, which has raised questions about its actions for the past year. Forty U.S. senators led by Republican Orrin G. Hatch of Utah signed a letter calling on Mr. Griffin and Ms. Block to step aside. The letter read in part: "We write to insist that you immediately leave the National Labor Relations Board, withdraw from all Board activities and stop drawing salaries and other benefits associated with the positions you purport to hold, as your purported appointments have been found constitutionally invalid."

President Donald Trump posted a video on Independence Day weekend that appeared to endorse violence against the press, particularly CNN. CNN commentator Ana Navarro appeared on ABC News' "This Week" and said the president took things too far and his tweet was inciting violence. "He is going to get somebody killed in the media," she said. "Maybe that will stop him." Days earlier, Deputy White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the president has never incited violence. CNN posted its official response to Trump's tweet by quoting the comments Sanders made two days prior. Navarro, a Republican strategist, has criticized the president since he launched his candidacy for the nation's highest office. Last week, she called Trump a "lunatic man baby" for attacking MSNBC's Mika Brzezinski. The Wall Street Journal reported that the president's son-in-law and top advisor, Jared Kushner, complained about Navarro's coverage to a senior executive at CNN's parent company, Time Warner. Navarro has not stopped criticizing the president and his administration.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.) told MSNBC's Rachel Maddow on Wednesday that he would end the Republican Party if he did not care more about the country. "If I didn't care so much about our country, I would hope that [Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas)] would get the Republican nomination for president, because that would be the end of the Republican Party," Reid told Maddow. "He stands for everything America doesn't." Reid criticized the right for what he described as offending women, the gay community, the poor and just about every other minority group through recent legislation, such as food stamp cuts and the Employment Non-Discrimination Act, known as ENDA. "The Republican Party is staggering right now," Reid said. Reid said he is "comfortable" the bill will get enough support from the right to pass the Senate. "Why in the world should someone in modern day America be allowed to be fired or have their employment in any way discriminated against because their sexual orientation? They shouldnt be," Reid said. "We are calling for fairness."

President Barack Obama signed into law a final bill authored by former Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, who was wounded in an Arizona shooting a year ago. Giffords participated in the signing ceremony at the White House. She resigned from Congress last month as she continues to recover from a gunshot wound to the head. The legislation increases the penalties for using ultra-light aircraft when smuggling drugs into the country. The small, single-seat planes are an increasingly favored tool that smugglers use to fly at night and then release their haul without detection. Giffords stepped down on the day the House passed her bill by a vote of 428-0. She has focused on her recovery and said she will eventually return to public service.

Sen. Jack Reed said Tuesday that special counsel Robert Mueller should testify before Congress to offer transparency into the almost two-year investigation into alleged collusion between Russia and President Trump's 2016 election campaign. Reed told CNN that he thought it would be appropriate after the report was released to have Mueller come before the Congress. He said Mueller should be available to answer questions that the American public will have, not just members of Congress. Reed also expressed concern he may not get the chance to view the report and expressed hope Attorney General William P. Barr would make the findings public. Rep. Steve Cohen echoed Reed's sentiment, saying the White House "waived their right to executive privilege when they cooperated with the investigation." Cohen said the White House is the subject of the investigation and possible target of impeachment. Cohen said the idea that they should be able to go back after they waived privilege and redact or edit the report before Congress sees it and the public sees it is "just totally wrong." Cohen also said he does "not have faith" in Barr preventing the White House from doctoring the report.

A comparison of the Federal Reserve's statements from its two-day meeting that ended Wednesday and its meeting Nov. 1-2 shows the Fed raising its target range for the federal funds rate to 1/2 to 3/4 percent. The statement now states: "In view of realized and expected labor market conditions and inflation, the (Fed) decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 1/2 to 3/4 percent. The stance of monetary policy remains accommodative." The statement then states: "Against this backdrop, the (Fed) decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 1/4 to 1/2 percent." In December, the Fed sees growth picking up, to a "moderate" pace, which is faster than "modest." In November, the Fed indicates that the labor market has continued to strengthen and that economic activity has been expanding at a moderate pace since mid-year. In November, the Fed says the labor market has continued to strengthen and growth of economic activity has picked up from the modest pace seen in the first half of this year. In December, the Fed sees some mild improvement in the job market as well: "Job gains have been solid in recent months and the unemployment rate has declined." November: "Although the unemployment rate is little changed in recent months, job gains have been solid."
