Thousands of people are expected to visit Capitol Hill to pay respects to congressman and civil rights leader John Lewis, but President Donald Trump will not be among them. "No, I won't be going," the president told reporters Monday. "No." The president made the comment as he was leaving the White House for North Carolina. Lewis' American flag-draped casket was arriving at the Capitol and being carried into the building by a military honor guard. Lewis, who died July 17 at the age of 80, will be lying in state at the U.S. Capitol until Thursday's funeral at Atlanta's historic Ebenezer Baptist Church, which the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. once led. Trump did not say why he was declining to visit Lewis. Lewis was critical of Trump during his time in office. A week before the 2017 inauguration, Lewis said he did not consider Trump a legitimate president. Vice President Mike Pence and presumptive Democratic nominee Joe Biden are expected to pay their respects. One Twitter user said the president's decision was just another sign he's a racist. Others considered his presence inappropriate.

Trump tweeted an anti-Semitic photograph. Paul Ryan, the Republican candidate, responded: "Look, anti-Semitic images - they've got no place in a presidential campaign. Candidates should know that." Ryan then said: "I don't know what flunky put this up there - they've obviously got to fix that." The article reported that Ryan and other Republicans have been actively working to help Trump for the past year. Comments on the story were closed.

Former New York City Mayor Ed Koch has been placed in the intensive care unit at New York-Presbyterian Hospital, his spokesman George Arzt said Thursday. Koch spokesman George Arzt spoke to CNN affiliate WCBS and said the mayor "was in obvious discomfort." Arzt said after speaking to him that his lead doctor and cardiologist decided he should be put into the intensive care unit. Koch, 88, was hospitalized last September for anemia and underwent a blood transfusion at the same hospital. The lawyer-turned-public-servant was a U.S. congressman from 1968 until he ran for mayor of the city in 1977. He served three terms from 1978 to 1989 until he was defeated in a Democratic primary by David Dinkins. After leaving office, Koch practiced law, hosted a radio show, was a newspaper columnist and made numerous appearances on TV series as himself. His cameos included "Sex and the City," "Spin City," and "Picket Fences." For two years starting in 1997, he was the judge on the syndicated show "The People's Court."

President-elect Donald Trump on Saturday wished a "Happy New Year" to friends and enemies on Twitter. "Happy New Year to all, including to my many enemies and those who have fought me," Trump began on Twitter. He ended the tweet by wishing everybody "Love," but not before making sure that all those who "lost so badly" to him knew the New Year's message was also intended for them. "They just don't know what to do," he wrote. To whom Trump was speaking is unclear. He and supporters have since Election Day argued that backers of defeated Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton and others continue to search for excuses and others to blame for her defeat. Trump tweeted again at midnight, wishing all Americans a "Happy New Year." Trump has roughly 18 million Twitter followers and continues to use the social media site to bypass conventional media outlets such as television and newspapers to send messages to Americans. Trump spent New Year's Eve at his private Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that President Obama plans to give back 5% of his salary to the Treasury, retroactive to March 1. The president's salary is $400,000 per year, so the 5% reduction will amount to $20,000 annually. The official said the move was taken "in solidarity with federal workers who are going to be furloughed as part of the automatic budget cuts known as the sequester," and added that "the president has decided that to share in the sacrifice being made by public servants across the federal government that are affected by the sequester." The administration official noted the president's support for federal workers, but did not mention taxpayers. Starting in April, the president will write a monthly check to the Treasury for $1,667.67, according to the unnamed official. This payment will be in addition to the amount withheld from the President's monthly salary for federal income taxes. It was unclear if President Obama plans to continue this practice for the remaining three and a half years of his term or only for the next twelve months.

Jon Stewart released a race card for President Barack Obama's re-election campaign. The article states that Stewart and fellow humorists often set entertainment criteria aside to promote their agendas and will have to perform additional footwork to keep Obama in office for four more years. The article questions whether Republicans will try every chocolate in the box, and references the phrase "White Man's Sampler" and references the phrase "White Man's Sampler." Stewart encountered difficulty locating the race card after an overwhelmingly white Occupy Wall Street crowd blocked public space for weeks. The article notes that Republicans were eager to cast their vote for Herman Cain before a series of sexually-charged allegations shut down Cain's campaign. The article concludes that Stewart must play the full race card deck before the final vote is tallied in November.

Hillary Clinton addressed an audience in San Diego on Thursday. She said Donald J. Trump was hopelessly unprepared and temperamentally unfit to be commander in chief. Clinton said Electing him would be a "historic mistake." She described Trump as reckless, childish and uninformed, describing him as a reckless, childish and uninformed amateur who was playing at the game of global statecraft. "This is not someone who should ever have the nuclear codes," she said, "because it's not hard to imagine Donald Trump leading us into a war just because somebody got under his very thin skin." Clinton's campaign had been grappling for weeks over how to handle Trump. She addressed an audience that laughed and cheered as she deconstructed Trump's foreign policy pronouncements. She said they were "not really ideas, just a series of bizarre rants, personal feuds and outright lies."

President-elect Donald Trump continued his dispute with Democratic Congressman John Lewis after Lewis said he does not believe Trump is a "legitimate president" and that this is the first inauguration he will not attend. After his comment, a Washington Post report surfaced reporting that Lewis skipped Bush's inauguration because he did not believe Bush was the true elected president. Trump wrote on Twitter: "John Lewis said about my inauguration, 'It will be the first one that I've missed.' WRONG (or lie)! He boycotted Bush 43 also because he 'thought it would be hypocritical to attend Bush's swearing-in....he doesn't believe Bush is the true elected president.' Sound familiar!" Lewis said he will skip Trump's inauguration because the President-elect is "wrong" for America. "I don't plan to attend the inauguration," Lewis said, adding, "It will be the first one that I miss since I've been in Congress. You cannot be at home with something that you feel that is wrong."

Senior U.S. intelligence officials told NBC News that they believe with "a high level of confidence" that Russian President Vladimir Putin became personally involved in the covert Russian campaign to interfere in the U.S. presidential election. Two senior officials with direct access to the information said new intelligence shows that Putin personally directed how hacked material from Democrats was leaked and otherwise used. The intelligence came from diplomatic sources and spies working for U.S. allies, the officials said. A high-level intelligence source told NBC News that Putin's objectives were multifaceted. The official said what began as a "vendetta" against Hillary Clinton morphed into an effort to show corruption in American politics and to "split off key American allies by creating the image that [other countries] couldn't depend on the U.S. to be a credible global leader anymore." All 538 members of the Electoral College must be presented with an intelligence briefing detailing connections between the Russian Government and the Trump Campaign. The briefing must also cover the extent of Russian interference in the election and aid to the Trump campaign. Comments are closed on this story.

Eagle Forum President Phyllis Schlafly said she never urged Rep. Todd Akin (R-Mo.) to end his bid against Sen. Claire McCaskill (D), contrary to a BuzzFeed report. Schlafly has been a vocal supporter of Akin since he mused about "legitimate rape," even as most prominent Republicans abandoned the congressman. She told The Post that it would be significant if she had private doubts about his electability. "I criticized his campaign, but in no way was that meant to urge him to get out," she told The Post. "I was very critical of the staff and it was a strong statement to urge him to hire good people." She added that she believed Akin was following her advice; he recently hired Rick Tyler, a long-time aide to Newt Gingrich. The meeting in question happened in Tampa, shortly before the Republican National Convention, during a conference held by the conservative Center for National Policy. Schlafly said that anyone who claimed she wanted Akin to drop out must have misunderstood. She noted that at the same event, she held a fundraiser for Akin's campaign.

Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) said Wednesday that he supports Barack Obama's nomination of Samantha Power as the new U.N. ambassador. McCain stated, "I believe she is well-qualified for this important position and hope the Senate will move forward on her nomination as soon as possible." Obama said, "To ensure that we have the principled leadership we need at the United Nations. I would strongly urge the Senate to confirm her without delay." In 2002, Power called for an invasion of the Jewish state. She said that "external intervention" using a "mammoth protection force" was necessary to keep Israelis and the Palestinians apart. She said such a move would be "unfortunate," asserting, "Unfortunately, imposition of a solution on unwilling parties is dreadful. I mean, It's a terrible thing to do, it's fundamentally undemocratic."

President Obama said on Wednesday that he believed the United States had "a credible way forward" in its nuclear negotiations with Iran. He suggested that after consultations with Congress, which has been threatening additional sanctions, he would seek an extension of the talks beyond Sunday's deadline. "There are still some significant gaps between the international community and Iran," he said in the White House press room, before announcing additional sanctions on Russia, "and we have more work to do." Iran has signaled it wants more time to negotiate. Obama is almost certain to face opposition on Capitol Hill if he agrees to it. Republicans and even some Democrats have argued that Tehran is stalling. It is unclear whether Iran will demand more sanctions relief in return for an extension. In Vienna over the past two weeks, as Iran and the West began to define what a deal might look like, Obama's aides debated a question that no longer seems theoretical: How much risk is the United States willing to take to reach a deal that will almost certainly leave Iran with some potential, over the long term, to make a nuclear weapon?

Mitt Romney criticized Donald Trump on Tuesday, saying "we have a good reason to believe that there's a bombshell in Donald Trump's taxes." Romney had delayed releasing his own tax returns as the 2012 Republican nominee. Trump responded: "It's my honor, real honor, to endorse Mitt Romney," with Romney and his wife standing nearby. Trump called Romney "tough" and "smart" and said, "he's not going to continue to allow bad things to happen to this country." Comments are closed on this story.

Outgoing Vice President Joe Biden spoke with PBS NewsHour's Judy Woodruff on Thursday. Biden said, "Grow up, Donald." Woodruff asked about Trump's tweets, including one this week calling Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) the "head clown." Biden urged Trump to focus on the issues instead. "Time to be an adult, you're president," Biden said. "You gotta do something, show us what you have." Biden said it is time for Trump to propose legislation, let the public decide and allow lawmakers to vote. "It's going to be much clearer what he's for and against, and what we're for and against now that it's going to get down to actually discussing in detail the issues that affect people's lives," Biden said. Biden also spoke about Trump's criticism of the U.S. intelligence community, the Affordable Care Act and his plans after leaving office.

Indiana Gov. Mike Pence accepted the nomination to serve as Republican nominee Donald Trump's vice president. Pence told the Republican National Convention the 2016 general election is about "change versus status quo." "I'm a Christian, a conservative and a Republican in that order," Pence said as he introduced himself. "I thought I'd be spending this evening with all my friends from the great state of Indiana, yet there I was a few days ago in New York City with a man who won 37 states." Pence was officially announced Trump's running mate last weekend in New York City. The Indiana governor introduced his family and spoke about his conservative record. "We will always stand with those who stand on the thin blue line of law enforcement in America," Pence stated. "Hillary Clinton will never become President of the United States of America," he said, adding she "essentially offers a third Obama term." "Conservative principles work every time you put them in to practice," he said.

President Trump said he would nominate Rep. John Ratcliffe as Director of National Intelligence. Trump had sought Ratcliffe's nomination last August. Ratcliffe's resume for the position was a lie. Trump withdrew the offer. Trump tweeted that Ratcliffe was out of the running. Trump tweeted that he would have completed the process earlier but wanted to wait until after the IG Report was finished. Trump wrote that Ratcliffe is an outstanding man of great talent. Trump tweeted that Ratcliffe is his nominee. Trump said he would have completed the process earlier but wanted to wait until after the IG Report was finished. Trump also tweeted that Ratcliffe is an outstanding man of great talent. The nomination was withdrawn last time because Republican senators opposed it, including Richard Burr, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee. Burr had warned Trump not to nominate Ratcliffe for the nomination because he was partisan.

President Barack Obama attributed the election results to Donald Trump's successful personality. "I think it's fair to say that I was surprised by the election results," Obama said when asked by NBC's Chris Jansing during a press conference in Greece about whether he felt responsible for his party's loss of the presidency. "Presidential elections always turn on personalities. They turn on how campaigns are run," Obama said, hinting that Clinton lacked both. Obama acknowledged that some in America might want change after eight years of his presidency, but noted that he still has high approval ratings. "Last I checked, a pretty healthy majority of the American people agree with my world view on a whole bunch of things," Obama said. Obama said that Americans probably just wanted to "shake things up" after eight years of his presidency and try something new. "I do think, as I've said before, that history doesn't move in a straight line, it zigs and zags, and sometimes goes forward, sometimes moves back and sideways," he said.

A gun discharged inside a 5-year-old kindergartener's backpack at a Tennessee elementary school cafeteria on Thursday, though no one was hurt, officials said. A statement from the Shelby County school district said the gun went off inside a kindergarten student's backpack as students were waiting for the opening bell in the cafeteria of Westside Elementary School. There were no injuries. School staffers took control of the backpack. School security officers and the Memphis Police Department responded quickly, the district said. The child was detained and was still being questioned by officers Thursday afternoon, with the child's mother present. Police spokeswoman Karen Rudolph said investigators were trying to determine how the gun ended up in the backpack. Students were kept safe and calm while the matter was handled, the district said. There was no evidence of harmful intent, the district said. "However, weapons of any kind are prohibited on campuses, and this student will be disciplined in accordance with the state's zero tolerance policy," the statement said. The zero-tolerance policy calls for "certain, swift and reasoned punishment" for students who bring drugs or guns to school. It could include expulsion.

President-elect Donald Trump wished a happy new year to all on Saturday morning, including his "many enemies." Trump tweeted: "Happy New Year to all, including to my many enemies and those who have fought me and lost so badly they just don't know what to do. Love." The tweet referenced a 2013 tweet from Trump extending wishes to "the haters and losers" on September 11, 2013. Trump wrote: "@realDonaldTrump: I would like to extend my best wishes to all, even the haters and losers, on this special date, September 11th." During his transition, Trump criticized opponents and the media. The Obama administration disagreed with the administration over its belief that Russia meddled in the 2016 election to aid his campaign. Trump spent the holidays at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. Later Saturday, Vice president-elect Mike Pence posted on Twitter: "Happy New Year! 2017 will be the year we Make America Great Again! We wish you every blessing for healthy & prosperous New Year! The Pences."

Some of the most powerful names in television media arrived at Trump Tower in New York City Monday afternoon to meet with President-elect Donald Trump. NBC's Lester Holt, Chuck Todd, and president Debora Turness were seen. CNN's Jeff Zucker, Erin Burnett, and Wolf Blitzer were also seen. Fox News executives Bill Shine, Jack Abernethy, Jay Wallace and Suzanne Scott, CBS's John Dickerson Norah O'Donnell, Gayle King and Charlie Rose were also seen entering the building. ABC's George Stephanopoulos, Martha Raddatz and David Muir were also reported to have been in attendance. The meeting was reported as "Off the Record." Some reporters and executives did not attend, with some stationed outside elevators or waved awkwardly. Very little was reported about the meeting. When a reporter asked Chuck Todd what he was doing there, he shrugged his shoulders and said, "I wish I knew!" He added, "Here's what I'm going to fight for," motioning to the press. "A protective pool."

President Donald Trump on Friday blamed Iran for attacks on two oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman. "Iran did do it, and you know they did it because you saw the boat, I guess one of the mines didn't explode and it's probably got essentially Iran written all over it," Trump said during a phone interview on Fox and Friends on Friday morning. He said it was obvious Iran was covering up their role in attacking the tankers by trying to secretly remove the unexploded mine. "They're a nation of terror," Trump said. "They've changed a lot since I've been president, they were unstoppable and now they're in deep, deep trouble." Trump said Iran was flourishing in the Obama administration, actively involved in 14 different conflicts in the Middle East, but they were "pulling back." "I'm not looking to hurt that country, but they can't have a nuclear weapon, it's very simple," he said.

CNN reported that CNN correspondent Sanjay Gupta has withdrawn his name from consideration as the nation's next surgeon general. Gupta will discuss his decision and the president's health care agenda on CNN's Larry King Live tonight. Fox News reported earlier Thursday that Gupta might be out. Jerry Farrell, who heads the Commissioned Officers Association, told FOXNews.com Thursday that CNN's chief medical correspondent is known to have taken himself out of consideration. "The general consensus from everybody is Gupta is no longer in contention ... it's more he's withdrawing himself," Farrell said, citing conversations he has had with "well-placed" individuals. According to Farrell, Gupta had misgivings about both the pay cut he would have to take and the fact that he could be reporting to two high-level bosses: both the health secretary and health reform office director. When Gupta's name surfaced, President Obama had planned to have former Sen. Tom Daschle fill both of those roles. After Daschle withdrew from consideration, the president named two separate nominees for the posts.

British officials voiced suspicions that a bomb destroyed a Russian plane over the Sinai Peninsula, killing 224 people. An American official said U.S. intelligence also has "a definite feeling it was an explosive device planted in luggage or somewhere on the plane." CNN reported that other U.S. officials also said their analysis pointed toward a bomb attack. Based on this intelligence, CNN's source said ISIS, or a group affiliated with them, is most likely responsible for the attack. As with U.K. intelligence, the American officials noted their conclusions were tentative and a formal consensus had not been reached. The British government held an emergency meeting Wednesday afternoon on the plane crash and the safety of aviation in Egypt. The Russians believe there was an explosion aboard the plane, although they have so far been reluctant to declare it a terrorist attack or name ISIS as the likely perpetrator. The UK Telegraph reported that Russian president Vladimir Putin's political situation could be delicate, with the possibility that he may gain more public support for action in Syria due to public outrage, or his government might be criticized for allowing the destruction of the plane.

Former CIA Director John Brennan appeared Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press." Brennan, whose security clearance has been revoked by President Donald Trump, said he believed Trump's behavior was "treasonous." Brennan said, "I called his behavior treasonous which is to betray one's trust and to aiding and abet the enemy and I stand very much by that claim." He continued, "I think these are abnormal times and I think a lot of people have spoken out against what Mr. Trump has done. And maybe it's my warning, training as an intelligence professional. I have seen the lights blinking red in terms of what Mr. Trump has done and is doing and is bringing this country down on the global stage and fueling and feeding divisiveness in our country." He added, "He continually lies to the American people. The type of things he is doing, I need to speak out. I don't believe I'm being political at all. I am not a Republican. I am not a Democrat."

All three judges that will hear Tuesday's arguments on the constitutionality of President Obama's health care law were appointed by Democratic presidents, including Obama himself. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit made the announcement shortly before the trial started, even though the case has been scheduled for months. Judges Diana Motz, the senior member of the panel, was appointed to the bench by President Bill Clinton in 1994. Andre Davis and James Wynn were appointed by Obama. The hearing in Richmond is the first appellate review of Obama's signature legislation passed last year and combines two cases. The first case was brought by Liberty University, and the second case was brought by the government after losing to Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinell. The judges were randomly selected by computer a couple of months ago. They have presumably been reading briefs in the case ever since. The full 14 member Fourth Circuit is evenly split between Republican and Democratic judges, but only three judges hear any given case. The fact that the judges are Democratic appointees does not mean they will decide to uphold the law in the end, but this has been one of the most bitterly partisan issues around the country in recent memory.

Donald Trump has named former World Wrestling Entertainment CEO Linda McMahon as his nominee to head the Small Business Association. McMahon is the co-founder of the professional wrestling franchise WWE along with her husband, Vince McMahon, and twice a former Republican Senate candidate from Connecticut. She stepped down from her duties at WWE in 2009 and ran two failed bids for the Senate in 2010 and 2012. She donated $6 million in August and September to Rebuilding America Now, a super PAC that supported Trump's presidential bid. McMahon is the single largest donor to the Trump Foundation, having given nearly as much as the total amount Trump and his companies have donated to the foundation.

White House Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said on Tuesday's broadcast of the Fox News Channel's "Hannity" that President Trump accepted House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's (D-CA) earlier invitation to give the State of the Union in front of the House. Sanders said, "We're moving forward until something changes on that front." She said Pelosi invited the president and he accepted, citing security concerns as a potential reason to delay the speech. Sanders said the United States Secret Service and DHS have addressed those concerns and that the department is moving forward until something changes. Sanders also discussed the possibility of having the speech take place elsewhere, saying, "I don't know if there would be a place that all of those members would attend, but the president's focus is on speaking to the American people. ... And if Nancy Pelosi chooses to go in that direction, the president will continue to speak to the American people, and I'm sure that he'll do that on that evening as well."

The article reports that Donald Trump said, "we're sending an armada," and that the aircraft carrier Carl Vinson and its strike group were heading in the opposite direction toward the Korean Peninsula, a few thousand miles to the south. The article also reports that a misinformation campaign has been deployed by the Trump White House in other areas, including ethics. On the day that Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner were dining with Chinese President Xi Jinping and other Chinese dignitaries, Ivanka Trump received the go-ahead to promote her products in China. The article describes Trump as a coal-mine-loving "populist" and describes him as having the wealthiest billionaire-filled administration in the history of the United States. The article states that Wall Street bankers and hedge fund managers are helping run the show because of populism. The article notes that the author would not have thought Trump was not really a populist. The article recommends readers keep an eye on the blog for navigational misdirection and on Patreon. Comments are closed on the story.

Sarah Palin appeared on Sean Hannity's Fox News program this week to discuss her 2008 predictions that Russia's Vladimir Putin would take advantage of President Obama's weak overseas policies. Palin said the Russian invasion of Crimea shows her prediction to be true. "Anybody who carries the common-sense gene knows that Putin doesn't change his stripes," she said. She then said that a weak United States opens the door for other nations, like Russia, to take the international stage, a scenario that leads to bold foreign strikes, such as the one going forth in the Ukraine. Palin said that Putin is seen as a leader who "wrestles bears and drills for oil," while Obama is perceived as one with serious "weakness," and as a man who "wears mom jeans and equivocates and bloviates," Mediaite reported. Palin also said that Obama's main foreign policy is "leading from behind," and that other nations will soon be "taking advantage of that weakness in America at this point," Mediaite reported.

Georgia voters have one final chance to cast their ballots this week in two Senate races. Congress will take the final step to certify Joe Biden's victory over President Donald Trump by counting Electoral College votes. Control of the U.S. Senate will be determined by runoff elections in Georgia on Tuesday. Republican David Perdue is running for reelection against Democrat Jon Ossoff, and Sen. Kelly Loeffler (R) is facing off against Democrat Raphael Warnock. Trump and Biden have both campaigned with their party's candidates ahead of the election. Trump has also repeatedly criticized the state's GOP election officials. He threatened Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger (R) with criminal prosecution unless he could find 11,780 votes in Trump's favor. On Wednesday, Congress will formally count the Electoral College votes from the 2020 presidential election, certifying Biden's win. At least 12 Republican senators have pledged to object to the vote certification, delaying the process but not changing the result of the race.

Former FBI deputy Director Andrew McCabe will likely face federal criminal charges for allegedly misleading Justice Department investigators who were probing the leak of an investigation into the Clinton Foundation during the 2016 campaign. McCabe's legal team received notice from a top Justice Department official indicating that the office had rejected their appeal of the decision by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia to move forward with the case, according to a person familiar with the matter. McCabe's team had asked the D.C. office to veto the D.C. office's decision to indict. USA Today first reported the news Thursday. An investigation found that McCabe lacked candor about whether he authorized media disclosures about the Clinton investigation during the 2016 campaign. McCabe filed suit last month over his 2018 dismissal, which came hours before his planned retirement. President Donald Trump had targeted McCabe, a Republican, in part due to his wife's run for office as a Democratic candidate. McCabe went on to write a book about his experiences in the FBI, and recently joined CNN as a commentator.

Defense Secretary Ashton B. Carter will convene a meeting in Brussels on Thursday to urge about two dozen of his counterparts to contribute more to the American-led campaign against the Islamic State. The meeting is one of his biggest leadership challenges since he took office a year ago. President Obama told Carter in December that as the administration intensifies its efforts against the Islamic State, other countries — particularly Arab ones — need to do more. Carter said Tuesday that he was confident he would leave the meeting this week with pledges of aid like air support, special forces, trainers and money. Foreign policy analysts and former American diplomats say that while the administration may gain some help from European allies, it continues to miscalculate what the Arab countries are willing to do. Ryan C. Crocker, a former United States ambassador to Iraq, said: "The thing is, the Islamic State is nobody's top enemy. For the Turks, the enemy is the Kurds, and for the Sunni Arabs, it's Iran, followed by Assad," referring to President Bashar al-Assad of Syria.

The midday bulletin arrived as another moment in the presidential campaign of Donald Trump. Trump admitted Obama was born in the United States. The headline read "Trump Finds the Earth No Longer Flat." Trump then changed the campaign slogan to "Trump Finds the Earth No Longer Flat." The article reported that Trump had previously insisted that President Obama was not born a legitimate American citizen. The article did not report whether Trump apologized to Obama and the American people for what it called political poison spread for so long. The article characterized Trump's statements as substituting a lie for a lie. It reported that Trump accused Hillary Clinton of starting the birther myth and further claimed he had nobly "finished" it off by badgering the White House for proof that Obama was born in Hawaii, not Africa. The article characterized campaign mishaps as "flip-flop," "retreat," and "walk-back." The article stated that standard words for campaign mishaps — "flip-flop," "retreat," "walk-back" — do not apply to this candidate's spirals through unreality.

President Donald Trump said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal that he felt betrayed by his former campaign strategist Steve Bannon. The comments about the president's family were published in a book about the presidency. "I feel betrayed because you're not supposed to do that," Trump said. When asked if the relationship was over permanently, Trump replied, "We'll see what happens. I don't know what the word permanent means." Trump made the comments about Bannon after news broke that his former campaign chief would testify to Congress about the Russian collusion investigation. Trump criticized Bannon, accusing him of unfairly taking credit for his election win. "Steve's greatest asset is that he was able to convince a corrupt media that he was responsible for my win," Trump said. He asserted that his former campaign manager Corey Lewandowski and his deputy campaign manager David Bossie deserve more credit than Bannon. "Steve had nothing to do with my win, or certainly very little," he said.

The White House continued its full-court press on Syria. A previous version of the post misspelled the White House chief of staff's first name as Denis. The congressional debate over whether to intervene militarily in Syria dominated the discussion on Sunday morning political talk shows. White House Chief of Staff Denis McDonough argued on each of the major shows that Syria's alleged use of chemical weapons on its own citizens necessitates a U.S. military response. He said it was "too early" to count votes when asked about Washington Post reports that a majority of the House is committed to or leaning toward voting against authorizing force. Republicans attempted to attach military funding to the debate. Charlie Rose previewed a Sunday morning interview with Syria's President Bashar al-Assad to air on PBS on Monday night. The president will continue his full-court press on courting support for a military strike, with plans to sit down for Monday interviews with PBS, CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News Channel. On Tuesday, he will make his case to the nation. Administration officials estimated Saturday they had contacted 85 senators and more than 165 House members.

A letter to the editor asked whether Hillary Rodham Clinton was the best Democratic presidential candidate. The writer stated they were tired of wordsmithing and hair-splitting regarding her emails and the issue of classification. The writer described information being fed by her campaign and its supporting pedants as nonsense. The writer cited two points that the writer considered germane. First, the writer said it was unimportant to learn whether Clinton's email communications were marked with some classification. The writer noted that Clinton was the secretary of state at the time and that she should have known that virtually all her official communications had some classification, including her schedule. The writer also said mixing personal and official communications is not a very smart thing to do, and that mixing them on a personal server located in a private, non-governmental residence is just plain dumb. The writer also said that when listening to what Clinton says about anything, her explanations are akin to a ball in a pin-ball machine: they never seem to be consistent or true. The writer noted that at least Bernie Sanders is consistent and truthful. The writer asked why the writer was ignoring a fine person like Martin O'Malley.

Freedom Industries, a West Virginia company at the center of a chemical spill that left 300,000 residents without water for days, and an unsure future for their families, has won a $4 million bankruptcy deal with a lender that will help it continue operations. The terms of the arrangement allow that Freedom Industries' 51 employees will continue to get paid and so will vendors. The company will start concerted clean-up efforts at the site of the Elk River spill, said Freedom Industries attorney Mark Freelander to The Associated Press. Freedom Industries President Gary Southern testified in bankruptcy court that the Jan. 9 chemical spill has left his company and the community "completely chaotic," AP said. He also said his company has already spent $800,000 to fix environmental damages in the past week. The chemical company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protections, a move that immediately halted dozens of lawsuits that were filed by businesses and residents. Meanwhile, state and federal investigators are still trying to determine what led to the spill of the coal-cleaning chemical into the water. The company's biweekly payroll amounts to about $172,000, AP reported.

US President Donald Trump said Friday following his summit with Kim Jong Un that he has "largely solved" the North Korean nuclear problem. Speaking to reporters outside the White House, Trump said that former President Barack Obama told him before he took office that the "most dangerous problem" for the United States was North Korea's nuclear weapons program. "I have solved that problem," Trump said. "Now we're getting it memorialized and all but that problem is largely solved." "We signed a very good document," he said. "But more importantly than the document I have a good relationship with Kim Jong Un. That's a very important thing. I can now call him," he said. "I gave him a very direct number. He can now call me if he has any difficulty. We have communication." "People are shocked," the president continued. "They thought Trump was going to get in, he's going to start throwing bombs all over the place. It's actually the opposite."

Hillary Clinton's campaign raised $63 million in July, its most successful month to date, her campaign announced on Tuesday. Clinton officials also said the campaign received $8.7 million in the 24 hours after Clinton's speech Thursday accepting the nomination, with $8.7 million raised. Clinton also raised $26 million in July for the Democratic National Committee, money she is certain to benefit from now that she is formally the Democratic nominee. Clinton began August with $58 million in the bank. At a rally on Monday, Trump said his campaign had "raised with small donors $35.8 million. I believe it's 517K donors." Trump did not specify whether that figure applied only to his campaign or to his joint fund-raising operation with the Republican National Committee. His campaign did not respond to a request for more information.

The article reported that the nine Supreme Court justices heard testimony from two cases involving same-sex marriage. The article stated that the nine justices were "very uncomfortable striking down" the case and suggested dismissing it, which would leave in place a 9th Circuit ruling favoring same-sex marriage. The article reported that arguments were concluded and that the Supreme Court would not uphold or strike down Proposition 8, citing Kennedy's view that it was too soon to rule on the issue. The article reported that the outcome was expected to be reached in 30 minutes. The article noted that the Supreme Court has been quoted favorably in mainstream media. The article stated that the unbiased, objective, not-at-all-liberal media should stop criticizing the site. The article concluded that there is nothing the unbiased, objective, not-at-all-liberal media hates more than a buzz-killing party pooper.

On June 5, the U.S. Senate voted 78 to 17 to confirm Sylvia Burwell, an appointee of President Obama, as secretary of Health and Human Services. The confirmation process proceeded with bipartisan support. All likely Republican presidential contenders voted "no" on her confirmation. With Senate approval, Burwell will replace the retiring Kathleen Sebelius as head of HHS. Her most difficult responsibility will be to push regulations for President Obama's Obamacare law. Burwell's confirmation was swift and devoid of any protracted debate over her suitability. All the no votes were cast by Republicans. Each of the three senators thought to be vying for the GOP nomination for president in 2016 were included. Her biggest experience in government was as an economic adviser to Bill Clinton. She led his economic transition team in 1992 and went on to stints at agencies including the National Economic Council and the Office of Management and Budget during the Clinton years. After Clinton left office, one of Burwell's longest-held jobs was at the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation.

The husband-and-wife team of Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump, now both senior federal government officials, has been alongside President Trump as the White House has hosted dozens of chief executives and a handful of world leaders in recent weeks. The crowd has included the top executives of some of the world's largest automobile, airline, chemical, pharmaceutical and tech companies. Mr. Kushner will continue to keep such select company now that he has helped create a new office that Mr. Trump is calling the White House Office of American Innovation. The financial disclosure report released late Friday for Mr. Kushner shows that he and his wife still benefit financially from a real estate and investment empire worth as much as $740 million. Several prominent experts on the subject said the couple is walking on perilous legal and ethical ground. Unlike Mr. Trump, who is exempt from conflict of interest laws, both Mr. Kushner and Ms. Trump — who took a formal White House position this past week — are forbidden under federal criminal and civil law to take any action that might benefit their particular financial holdings.

North Korea's leader Kim Jong-un proposed direct talks with South Korea on New Year's Day. The proposal came as sanctions appeared to be affecting the North, with reports of shortages in the North and pressure by Washington to intercept ships engaged in fuel smuggling. South Korea's president, Moon Jae-in, embraced the initiative. Moon sees his first concrete chance to carry out his campaign agenda of engaging with the North, while also easing tensions as Mr. Trump's threats have rattled his country. In a telephone message delivered through the restored cross-border hotline on Friday, North Korea accepted the South's proposal that the two sides begin talks on Tuesday, South Korean officials said. The talks, to be held in the border village Panmunjom, will be the first high-level inter-Korean dialogue in two years. Skepticism abounds in Washington and South Koreans.

Roger Stone, a longtime confidant of President Trump, apologized late Monday for posting a picture on Instagram of U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson with what appeared to be crosshairs next to her face. Stone's attorneys filed a court filing saying in the filing: "Roger J. Stone hereby apologizes to the Court for the improper photograph and comment posted on Instagram today." Earlier in the day, Stone posted a picture of U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson with what appeared to be crosshairs in the background. The photo was deleted. A caption below the photo depicted Judge Jackson as a partisan judge who has targeted conservatives. Stone was arrested last month during an FBI raid of his Florida home. He is charged with obstruction of justice and lying to Congress. He posted a statement on Instagram later Monday saying that "any inference that this was meant to threaten the judge or disrespect the court is categorically false." The statement also said the image next to Judge Jackson's head was not crosshairs, but the "logo of the organization that originally posted it."

Political pundits expressed disapproval over the resignation of Mozilla CEO Brendan Eich after news of his support of a 2008 anti-gay marriage campaign came to light. Last week, Bill Maher suggested that Eich's resignation was the result of pressure from within the LGBT movement. The remarks prompted social media debate. Some lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) rights advocates said his words are ripe for misinterpretation. Freedom to Marry's John Becker said the situation was not as a result of pressure from within the LGBT movement. Becker noted that Maher has been an ally to the LGBT community in the past and added, "This is all about internal pressure from within the Mozilla community itself." Activist and political consultant Scott Wooledge said Eich's resignation was partly due to pre-existing opposition from within the Mozilla group, as evidenced by the fact that three board members stepped down ahead of the CEO's appointment.

President-elect Donald J. Trump invited the leading anchors and executives of television news to join him on Monday for a private meeting of minds. On-air stars including Lester Holt, Charlie Rose, George Stephanopoulos and Wolf Blitzer headed to Trump Tower for the off-the-record gathering, typically the kind where journalists and politicians clear the air after a hard-fought campaign. Trump said the television networks were dishonest in their reporting and shortsighted in missing the signs of his upset victory. He criticized some in the room by name, including CNN's president, Jeffrey A. Zucker, according to multiple people briefed on the meeting who were granted anonymity to describe confidential discussions. It is not unusual for journalists to agree to off-the-record sessions with prominent politicians, including President Obama, as a way to gain insights and develop relationships.

The Republican presidential debate took place this week. The event was scheduled for the last week until December. Donald Trump proposed boycotting Starbucks for changing its holiday coffee cup design. Trump also promised a crowd recently that when he becomes president, "we're all going to be saying 'Merry Christmas' again." Jeb Bush sent a mass email before the event began asking friends to send a dollar so he would "know you're at home cheering me on." The debate was described as more issue-oriented than the previous one. The subject was expected to be the economy. Tax plans were not discussed.

Among the 36 states in which same-sex couples can marry, 20 have invoked the Constitution to strike down marriage bans. The Supreme Court declined to hear a same-sex marriage case even though three federal appeals courts had struck down marriage bans. The 6th Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a ban. The Supreme Court decided to intervene. Those rulings would conflict with the nation's highest court if the justices uphold the power of states to limit marriage to heterosexual couples. A decision is expected by late June in cases from Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and Tennessee. Top officials in some states, including California, appear determined to allow gay and lesbian couples to continue to marry regardless of the court decision. Some county clerks, who issue marriage licenses, might not go along, experts said. In other states, a high court ruling in favor of state bans would prohibit any more such unions but could give rise to new efforts to repeal marriage bans through the legislature or the ballot.

A Pew Research Center survey found that as the Supreme Court prepares to hear arguments on two same-sex marriage cases and with several other high-profile cases on its docket, the court's favorability rating remains close to an all-time low. The survey also found that 9 percent of Republican conservatives say the court steered by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. is actually conservative. Among Americans overall, 52 percent view the court favorably, 31 percent unfavorably. Forty-seven percent of Republicans have a favorable opinion, up from 38 percent in July, following discussions about health care reform. By contrast, favorable sentiment among Democrats slipped from 64 percent to 56 percent. The survey also found that about as many conservative Republicans say the Supreme Court is liberal as middle of the road (39 percent). Very few conservative Republicans, 9 percent, say the court is conservative. Nearly half of liberal Democrats (48 percent) say the Supreme Court is conservative; 31 percent say it is middle of the road and 15 percent view the court's ideology as liberal.

Michelle Obama discussed her daughters' White House chores during an appearance on "The View." She said she told them, "They will not live in the White House forever. And if they're 17, 18 and can't make a bed, they will be pretty pathetic." She said Malia will have to start doing laundry soon, and First Granny Marian Robinson apparently still does her own. Michelle Obama said, "They've had pooty duty before, but actually Bo, like, goes in a private place. He's really good about that." Michelle Obama also said Sasha and Malia have to take Bo out after dinner, and they have to take him out during the weekends when they are not in school. Michelle Obama said, "They've had pooty duty before, but actually Bo, like, goes in a private place. He's really good about that."

President Obama sent a plan on Tuesday to close the United States military prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. The plan faces near-certain rejection by Congress. The prison has come to symbolize the darker side of the nation's antiterrorism efforts. Obama outlined a series of steps at the White House. The steps were an acknowledgment of the constraints binding him during his final year in office as a practical blueprint for transferring prisoners. In presenting them, the president made little secret of his frustration that his quest to close Guantánamo, once regarded as a bipartisan moral imperative, had become a divisive political issue. "I am very cleareyed about the hurdles to finally closing Guantánamo: The politics of this are tough," Mr. Obama said during a 17-minute address. "I don't want to pass this problem on to the next president, whoever it is. And if, as a nation, we don't deal with this now, when will we deal with it?"

New York Democrats flipped a Republican-held New York State Assembly seat on Tuesday that had been in Republican control for nearly 40 years. Steve Stern, a former Suffolk County legislator who ran as the Democrat candidate, defeated Republican candidate Janet Smitelli in the race to represent the 10th Assembly District in Long Island. Stern won with 59 percent of the vote, while Smitelli had 42 percent of the vote in the special election to fill a seat vacated by Republican Chad Lupinacci. The district had been in Republican hands since 1978. Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton and former President Barack Obama carried the district in the 2016 and 2012 elections. Voter registration in the state shows more Democrats are registered to vote in the district than Republicans. The Albany Times Union reported that Democrats had 6,000 more registered voters in the district than Republicans. In 2016, the Democrat candidate for New York Assembly in the 10th Assembly District lost by 9,000 votes. Two labor unions, the New York AFL-CIO and New York State United Teachers (NYSUT), supported Stern's candidacy. Stern's campaign claimed higher turnout in the special election.

Hillary Clinton answered a question about Bill Clinton's alleged sexual impropriety on Thursday at a campaign stop in Hooksett, New Hampshire. A woman asked Clinton: "Secretary Clinton, you recently came out to say that all rape victims should be believed. But would you say that Juanita Broaddrick, Kathleen Willey and Paula Jones be believed as well?" Clinton responded: "Well, I would say that everyone should be believed at first until they are disbelieved based on evidence." She then moved on to the next question. Broaddrick in 1999 said on NBC's "Dateline" that Bill Clinton had raped her two decades earlier, during his campaign for the Arkansas governor's office. Willey was a Democratic activist and White House volunteer who said that in 1993, Bill Clinton had grabbed and kissed her in the Oval Office's private study. Jones was an Arkansas state worker who sued Bill Clinton for sexual harassment, saying he had propositioned her for sex and exposed himself during a 1991 meeting in a hotel room. Bill Clinton's office declined CNN's request for comment.

North Korea's state-run newspaper Rodong Sinmun reported that Kim Jong-un has been taking tours of meteorological buildings and complaining that weather forecasters are giving "too many incorrect" predictions, CNN reported. The news agency did not explicitly state that Kim threatened to take action against those responsible for the faulty forecasts. The report included photographs of Kim appearing to criticize and chastise some officials cast by the newspaper as meteorological experts. Kim said outdated weather equipment was partly to blame. He also said forecasters' scientific method could stand some improvement, CNN reported. He relayed the importance of providing accurate weather reports to protect citizens' lives and property from "abnormal climatic phenomenon," and to help agricultural and fisheries industries stabilize their production, the state-run news outlet reported, CNN said.

Rep. Elijah Cummings, chair of the House Oversight and Reform Committee, is scheduled to spend Wednesday in a hearing with Michael Cohen, Donald Trump's longtime personal lawyer and fixer. Hours before the hearing, Cummings sent letters to two additional Trump lawyers seeking information about Trump's legally mandated financial disclosures and hush money payments. Cummings is seeking to depose Sheri Dillon, Trump's tax lawyer who conducted a January 2017 photo opportunity with Trump to settle concerns about conflicts of interest between his businesses and his official role. Cummings's questions for Dillon and for Stefan Passantino center on Trump's financial disclosure forms from June 2017 and May 2018. The former does not mention a debt to Cohen, while the latter covers a payment to him. Michael Cohen is providing a barrage of bombshells. The investigation into Trump's finances will not end on Wednesday.

President Obama will issue an executive order on Thursday reversing the Bush administration policy that bans the use of federal dollars by non-govermental organizations that discuss or provide abortions outside of the United States. The order will be signed on the 36th anniversary of the Roe v. Wade Supreme Court ruling that legalized abortion in all 50 states. The policy, known in governmental circles as the "Mexico City policy," requires any non-governmental organization to agree before receiving U.S. funds that they will "neither perform nor actively promote abortion as a method of family planning in other nations." The language was announced at the United Nations International Conference on Population in 1984, and was approved by President Reagan and originally drafted by his assistant secretary of state, Alan Keyes. Keyes ran unsuccessfully as the GOP nominee against Obama for the U.S. Senate in 2004. President George Herbert Walker Bush continued Reagan's Mexico City policy. President Bill Clinton issued an executive order lifting the ban on Jan. 22, 1993. President George W. Bush issued an executive order re-instating the ban on federal dollars for NGOs that discuss or provide abortions on Jan. 22, 2001.

Ukraine is in the middle of a political crisis. Dozens of people died this week and hundreds more were injured as protesters fought police in the capital, Kiev. Lethal violence has been spreading to the rest of the country, and a truce announced early Thursday fell apart as the death toll kept growing. What began in November as peaceful protests in favor of closer ties with the European Union and greater autonomy from the influence of Russia has escalated into a conflagration. To save Ukraine, the government and opposition alike must make the difficult but necessary choice to compromise and reconcile. European leaders should immediately schedule direct talks with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and his top officials to find a temporary solution to stop the bloodshed and a longer-term plan that would allow Ukrainians to determine their political destiny in a peaceful and democratic fashion. The West must make clear to Moscow that Ukraine — a bridge between East and West — should not be the object of geopolitical games. European leaders should back down from their threats of sanctions against Ukraine and its embattled president, Viktor F. Yanukovych, which would only prolong the suffering of the Ukrainian people. Russian interference in Ukraine's internal affairs must not be tolerated.

President Trump posted a video Friday afternoon on Twitter that was based on a TIME Magazine cover from October 2018. The cover showed a series of "Trump" election signs, with the years extending until 2044. The cover read "How Trumpism outlasts Trump." In the president's version of the video, it zoomed in on one of the signs and projected a picture of himself hovering over it. Instead of stopping at 2044, the years continued to climb at a rapid rate until the sign read "Trump 4EVA." The video was created by Twitter user Carpe Donktum. The president's comments received wide-ranging reviews, many from journalists and his most ardent supporters. Some critics speculated whether Trump would leave office voluntarily after an election defeat. "Real Time" host Bill Maher said he is convinced he will not leave the White House if he loses in 2020.

The author wrote that Democrats can adopt what the author called an extremist position, which the author described as trying to end all of the New Deal, removing obstacles to corporations doing whatever they want, and making sure the rich pay little in taxes. NBC Universal said in a statement that after further review it recognized the insensitive nature of the advertisement and decided to cease airing it across its properties as soon as possible. NBC Universal had previously responded when Donald Trump Jr. criticized the network for not running it. The network's public relations account posted on Twitter: "CNN has made it abundantly clear in its editorial coverage that this ad is racist. When presented with an opportunity to be paid to take a version of this ad, we declined." The advertisement was paid for by Donald Trump for President. The article reported that the advertisement demonizes immigrants and gaslighted his followers into believing the country is under threat of imminent invasion. The article also reported that Fox News pulled the same advertisement. The article concluded that the intended damage had been done and that the network was happy to pull the advertisement with less than 24 hours to the vote.

The United States is threatening to cut aid, withholding some $800 million, nearly a third of the $2 billion that the country gives to the country every year. Pakistan has responded by declaring it rejects conditional aid from the United States. Corps Commanders in the Pakistani Army say they will rely on their own resources instead. They also say they will pull troops from the Afghan border if the U.S. cuts aid, which they say will mean the Taliban will have free reign in the border region. "If Americans refuse to give us money, they okay. I think the next step is that the government or the armed forces will be moving from the border areas. We cannot afford to keep military out in the mountains for such a long period," said Pakistan's Defense Minister. The White House announced cutting aid. China declared it pledged to continue its support for Pakistan, describing it as "a close ally."

Former Gov. Charlie Crist of Florida announced Monday that he would run for the office again, this time as a Democrat. Crist, 57, a former Republican, spoke to a crowd of about 250 supporters in a bayfront park in St. Petersburg. He described himself as the "People's Governor" and urged them to trust him with the stewardship of the state in 2014. "The voice of the people has been silenced by the financial bullies and the special interests," Crist told the crowd as his wife, Carole, stood behind him. "So today I announce that I am running for governor of Florida, and the reason is to put you back in charge." Crist also criticized Gov. Rick Scott, who was elected in 2010 on a wave of Tea Party support, as an extremist who cares more about big business than the lives of ordinary Floridians.

President Obama on Monday will take executive actions to ease the burden of college loan debt for potentially millions of Americans, in a White House event coinciding with Senate Democrats' plans for legislation addressing the issue. Before an East Room audience, Mr. Obama is scheduled to announce "new steps to further lift the burden of crushing student loan debt," said a White House official, who declined to be identified describing the actions in advance of the president's event. Despite past actions by the administration, borrowers' debt load is growing and retarding the ability to buy homes, start businesses or otherwise spend to spur the economy, economists say. Mr. Obama's main action will be to expand on a 2010 law that capped borrowers' repayments at 10 percent of their monthly income. The intent is to extend such relief to an estimated five million people with older loans who are currently ineligible — those who got loans before October 2007 or stopped borrowing by October 2011. But the relief would not be available until December 2015, officials said, given the time needed for the Education Department to propose and put new regulations into effect.

On Thursday night, the two presidential candidates held town halls on rival networks — Trump on NBC and Biden on ABC — but the events after their events were over received less attention. After the president's town hall, which lasted an hour, Trump stayed for a few photos but did not answer voter questions, according to USA Today. After the 90-minute broadcast ended, Biden stayed on at least 30 additional minutes to answer questions to voters who did not speak during the ABC broadcast. Topics ranged from whether the National Guard should quell protests to the Trump administration's Muslim travel ban. Mediaite noted that Biden received lots of praise for answering voter questions off-camera. ABC News did not show the interactions in the background while pundits speculated on what it meant. Some social media viewers are asking ABC News to make the footage with sound available for viewing, according to Newsweek.

In November, Bob Filner became the first Democrat in two decades to be elected mayor of San Diego. He celebrated with his fiancée at his side in Old Trolley Barn Park, where he thanked hundreds of supporters who had showed up. After a week in which seven women publicly accused him of sexual harassment, it was all but impossible to find any Filner supporters in Old Trolley Barn Park. Democrats and Republicans have been united on an issue: their insistence that the mayor resign. On Friday, the mayor announced he would take two weeks away from City Hall to seek what he described as intensive behavior therapy. Many residents complained that he was dragging the city through the mud in hopes of salvaging his own career. Mona Mukherjea-Gehrig, 46, said: "I'm bummed. I voted for him. Can you change in two weeks? That's a joke. What are you going to do in two weeks?"

Kathleen Sebelius, the woman who oversaw the Obamacare rollout, said she will not run for the Senate seat held by Senator Pat Roberts. Roberts is a former friend of Sebelius's. Sebelius said she is not considering a run. A spokeswoman said: "Secretary Sebelius is continuing her important work at H.H.S. and is not considering a run for the Senate." Some Democrats had told The Times' Jeremy Peters that they wanted to see her run. The health care website opened with a crash. Fox News reported that it has a new variation on "The Bachelor" in which 12 American women believe they are competing for the hand of England's Prince Harry.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate on Wednesday for the second time since the 2008 financial crisis. Economists discussed the impact the decision will have on markets. The Fed's decision can affect the cost of housing, cars, student loans and even the interest on credit card, though not necessarily right away. When the Fed raises rates, all other expenses eventually tick up. The move is part of what will be a slow, upward climb for what is known as the federal funds rate. Banks are ordered by law to have a certain amount of money in reserve, so they typically make overnight loans to each other to keep those balances up. The federal funds rate is the level of interest that applies to those short-term loans. Because the rate has been close to zero since 2008, as part of the Fed's strategy to bring the nation out of a recession, there is hardly anywhere for it to go but up. As the economy improves and President-elect Donald J. Trump unveils his stimulus package, economists expect rates to rise steadily over a period of years.

A deal-book Briefing was scheduled for Tuesday. The briefing covered the Memo to Qualcomm, the president's response to Broadcom's bid for Qualcomm, and the companies planning to spend tax savings. It also covered Larry Page's flying taxi start-up, and the presumptive heir to Goldman Sachs, Goldman Sachs' presumptive heir. President Trump intervened to protect Qualcomm from Broadcom, a foreign company that wanted to purchase the San Diego-based chip maker. The administration had concerns about national security. In a March 5 letter, the administration stated that Broadcom would reduce Qualcomm's spending on research and development, which would cause Qualcomm to lose ground in the race to develop new technologies such as 5G, which is designed to make wireless networks faster and more reliable. The briefing noted that Chinese companies may gain an advantage in 5G.

Donna Brazile, the Democrat strategist who ran Al Gore's campaign, said Republican candidates who ignore the Tea Party do so at their peril. "The Tea Party is still highly caffeinated," she said on ABC's This Week, acknowledging that the "Tea Party is the energy inside the Republican Party." Brazile said that Cantor ignored Tea Party conservatives who also rose up in part to protest George W. Bush's expansion of the federal government and paid for it with his political career. "You ignore them, you ignore the base and that's a problem," Brazile said. "And he ignored the base." Breitbart News reported that only after Brat started criticizing Cantor on amnesty did his broader message tying Cantor to crony capitalism resonate. The pro-free markets and anti-crony capitalism message resonates with voters fed up with Washington's bipartisan permanent political class is one that former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin has been hammering for years and throughout her political career, as she did in a 2011 speech in Iowa.

In a preview clip of an interview set to air on Fox News Channel's Tuesday broadcast of "Fox & Friends," President Donald Trump said Presidents Bill Clinton and Barack Obama were "outplayed" by North Korea. Trump said, "I don't want to telegraph what I'm doing or what I'm thinking. I'm not like other administrations, where they say we're going to do this in four weeks. It doesn't work that way. We'll see what happens. I hope things work out well. I hope there's going to be peace, but they've been talking with this gentleman for a long time. You read Clinton's book and he said, 'Oh, we made such a great peace deal' and it was a joke. You look at different things over the years with President Obama. Everybody has been outplayed. They've all been outplayed by this gentleman and we'll see what happens. I just don't telegraph my moves."

Former Gov. Bob McDonnell of Virginia and his wife Maureen McDonnell, on trial for conspiring to use his office for personal enrichment, outlined a defense on Tuesday in federal court in Richmond, Virginia. Their lawyers made clear they planned to rely on the details of their union as the basis of their legal defense. It was the first time the McDonnells' version of events had been heard in the case. The case has been widely publicized for months. The indictment charges the couple with accepting more than $165,000 in cash and luxury gifts from a Virginia businessman. Maureen McDonnell's lawyer said she had a "crush" on the businessman, Jonnie R. Williams Sr., the prosecutors' star witness. The government said Williams would detail the designer clothing, vacations, golf rounds and cash he provided in exchange for the governor's help in promoting his company, which made a dietary supplement.

Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson (R) was turned away from the polls because he did not have proper ID as required under Arkansas's Voter ID Law. The Arkansas Democratic Party pointed out the irony of the voter ID laws. Hutchinson was turned away from the polls because he did not have proper ID at the polls. The Arkansas Democratic Party noted that Hutchinson's support for making it harder for Arkansans to cast a ballot was noted. The Arkansas Democratic Party expressed hope that Hutchinson's experience at the polls yesterday would cause him to reconsider the burden the Voter ID law places on senior citizens, students, and those serving in the military. Arkansas's Voter ID law was ruled unconstitutional and is still under review.

While Democratic and Republican members of Congress sat together for President Obama's State of the Union speech Tuesday night, Rep. Paul Broun posted on Twitter about the president and his speech. In a tweet at the end of Obama's address to the nation, Broun wrote: "Mr. President, you don't believe in the Constitution. You believe in socialism." Other Broun tweets included: " Corporate tax rates should be zero." These were only a sampling of Broun's State of the Union tweets. Broun, a medical doctor by profession, has previously criticized the administration. In 2009, he criticized the president and Democrats for their health care reform proposal, warning that if it became law — which it did — then "when mama falls and breaks her hip, she'll just lie in her bed in pain until she dies with pneumonia because her needed surgery is not cost efficient."

19 Democrats voted against Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) to continue as Speaker of the House on Wednesday. Pelosi lost the election to John Boehner. The vote followed a Democratic caucus vote in which 11 Democrats voted against her. Rep. Heath Shuler (D-N.C.), who had challenged Pelosi in a Democratic caucus vote, received 11 votes. Shuler voted for himself. Other Democrats received protest votes, including Reps. Dennis Cardoza (Calif.), Jim Costa (Calif.), Jim Cooper (Tenn.), John Lewis (Ga.), Marcy Kaptur (Ohio). Rep. Sanford Bishop (Ga.) voted "present," while Rep. Peter DeFazio (Ore.), a Pelosi dissenter, missed the vote entirely. Under House rules, each party puts up a candidate to be the next speaker. All 241 Democrats in the new Republican majority voted for Boehner on Wednesday, except for Boehner, who did not vote, while 173 Democrats backed Pelosi. The full list, via The Hill, appears below.

U.S. Park police revealed that there was a shooting outside the White House complex, near West Executive Drive on 17th and Pennsylvania. According to CNN, a suspect brandished a firearm outside the White House complex before being shot by Secret Service agents and taken into custody. Further reports indicate the shooting took place at 3:15 pm and the shooter was a man. According to the DC Fire and Emergency Services, the man was transported with critical injuries to a local hospital. Reporters at the White House were told to seek shelter in the basement and remain in the building while Secret Service cleared the North Lawn. ABC News reported that Vice President Joe Biden was at the White House at the time but was immediately secured. President Barack Obama was out golfing at the time of the incident, having left earlier in the afternoon for the golf course at Andrews Air Force Base. A White House official said the situation was under control. "No one within or associated with the White House was injured, and everyone in the White House is safe and accounted for," the official said. "The president has been made aware of the situation."

Bill Gates, a Microsoft founder and philanthropist, visited Trump Tower on Tuesday afternoon for a visit. Earlier in the day, Gates appeared on CNBC and praised Trump for his message to make America a better place economically. Gates compared Trump to former President John F. Kennedy. Gates said: "In the same way President Kennedy talked about the space mission and got the country behind that, I think whether it's education or stopping epidemics, other health breakthroughs, finishing polio and in this energy space, there can be a very upbeat message that his administration is going to organize things, get rid of regulatory barriers, and have American leadership through innovation." Gates said he spoke with the president-elect on the phone after the election and appeared upbeat that he would pursue "the power of innovation." Gates spent most of his interview promoting his new initiative to move the world into a "green" clean energy future. "I think this administration likes a good deal," Gates said, signaling his hope that Washington D.C. would increase the research and development spending for cheap sources of clean energy.

Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) appeared Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" and said President Donald Trump has "parroted" the policies of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Warner said, "That's the defining question of our investigation and the Mueller investigation; was there collusion? I'm not going to talk about what we may have been briefed in the gang of eight when these investigations opened. But I do think it's curious that throughout that whole summer when these investigations started, you had Vladimir Putin policies almost being parroted by Donald Trump." He added, "You had Trump say only nice things about Putin. He never spoke ill about Russia. The Republican campaign doctrines softened on Russia. And decreased their willingness to defend Ukraine. There was a series of outside actions. We all remember when Trump and his bluster basically said to the Russians, 'if you've got more e-mails, bring them on.' These are not actions of a traditional president for the United States."

Anheuser-Busch proposes selling Corona rights in the U.S. A federal judge in Washington on Wednesday agreed to delay proceedings to allow Anheuser-Busch to revise its efforts to take over the Mexican brewers of Corona and Corona Light. Judge Richard Roberts put off any court proceedings until March 19. Last month Justice Department antitrust lawyers blocked Anheuser-Busch InBev from taking over Grupo Modelo of Mexico. The Justice officials argued that the merger of the nation's No. 1 brewer, makers of Budweiser and Bud Light, and the nation's third-largest brewer, Grupo Modelo, would be anticompetitive and harm consumers. The officials said beer prices would go up. Anheuser-Busch then agreed to sell the rights to Corona and other Grupo Modelo brands in the United States to an independent company, Constellation Brands, a large wine company. It is unclear whether that $3 billion deal to sell the Corona rights would be enough to satisfy the Justice Department. The Anheuser-Busch merger with Grupo Modelo is estimated to be worth $20 billion.

South Carolina's top cop, State Law Enforcement Division Chief Reggie Lloyd, said Thursday that Gov. Mark Sanford did not improperly use state funds for visits with his Argentine mistress. Lloyd said Sanford did not break any laws. The governor's spokesman said he does not intend to resign. South Carolina's attorney general asked police to investigate the governor's travel after Sanford revealed to The Associated Press he had spent time with Maria Belen Chapur more often than previously disclosed. Sanford has given two personal checks totaling $3,300 to the state treasurer as reimbursement for part of a taxpayer-funded trip to South America last year. The money covered lodging, meals and airfare to Buenos Aires, where he saw Chapur. Top South Carolina Republicans have called for Sanford to step down.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu informed the Obama administration that he will not attend President Obama's nuclear security summit in Washington next week, according to a senior U.S. official familiar with the situation. The Israeli government is sending Deputy Prime Minister Dan Meridor in Netanyahu's place, U.S. National Security Council spokesman Mike Hammer announced Thursday. Hammer said Thursday that Israel is a close ally and looks forward to continuing to work closely with it on issues related to nuclear security. Hammer said the summit is focused on addressing the security of nuclear materials and is geared toward having participants take practical measures to ensure that terrorists cannot get access to those materials. The announcement followed a meeting between Obama and Russian President Dmitry Medvedev in the Czech Republic earlier Thursday. The new Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, known as START, reduces the number of nuclear weapons held by the United States and Russia by about one-third, among other provisions.

A Quinnipiac University poll shows Cory Booker leading Republican nominee Steve Lonegan by 12 points among likely voters in the Oct. 16 New Jersey special election. Booker is at 53 percent, while Lonegan is at 41 percent. Before the primary, a pollster showed Booker led Lonegan by 25 points among registered voters, rather than likely voters. The poll shows Booker leading among registered voters by a 60-34 margin. Among men, the two candidates are split, with 48 percent choosing Lonegan and 46 percent choosing Booker. The poll shows Booker's favorable rating is 53 percent, compared to 30 percent unfavorable. Lonegan's unfavorable rating is 35 percent, compared to 22 percent for Booker. The two are running for the seat of the late Sen. Frank Lautenberg (D-N.J.). National Republicans have not yet endorsed Lonegan's candidacy.
