Republican Senate candidate Joni Ernst of Iowa, a former state senator and self-proclaimed "mother, soldier and conservative," appears in an advertisement for the 2014 election cycle. In the advertisement, Ernst says she knows how to cut pork in Washington because she grew up castrating pigs on her farm in Iowa. She adds, "Washington is full of big spenders. Let's make 'em squeal." The ad features Ernst in a vest and flannel shirt and shots of pigs in pens. Ernst will face a Republican primary field to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin. She is one of five GOP candidates competing against Rep. Bruce Braley, who is running unopposed on the Democratic side.

Republican vice presidential nominee Mike Pence said on "Fox News Sunday" that New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie will still lead Donald Trump's transition team despite the Bridgegate controversy. Pence said Christie has continued to state his position that he had no knowledge of the actions taken. Pence said Christie said late in the week that what the convictions proved was that he was right to immediately fire those people for the actions they had taken. Pence, the governor of Indiana, said he and Trump are "grateful for Chris Christie's role in the campaign." He said there are no plans to alter Christie's role, particularly on Election Day. "Look, there's no changes in personnel here in the waning days of the campaign," Pence said. "We're 100% focused in bringing home a great victory for the American people." Two former Christie aides were convicted last week of charges tied to the closure of the George Washington Bridge in what was described as political retribution. Testimony during their trial indicated Christie knew what was happening.

Secretary of State Mike Pompeo plans to travel to Israel to meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in his first international trip since coronavirus-related restrictions were put in place. The department said Friday that Pompeo will depart for Israel on Wednesday. He will meet with Netanyahu and Speaker of the Knesset Benny Gantz, who last month agreed on a unity government after three close elections. The three leaders will talk about efforts to fight the COVID-19 pandemic, security issues and threats from Iran. State Department spokeswoman Morgan Ortagus said: "The U.S. commitment to Israel has never been stronger than under President [Donald] Trump's leadership. The United States and Israel will face threats to the security and prosperity of our people together." Pompeo's trip will be his first since March 23, when he traveled to Afghanistan amid efforts by leaders there to form a new government. After discussions with President Ashraf Ghani and Chief Executive Abdullah Abdullah, Pompeo announced the United States' plan to cut $1 billion in assistance.

Rep. Tim Murphy, a Pennsylvania Republican, said Tuesday that both General Motors and the nation's highway safety body "messed up pretty bad" in failing to recall cars with an ignition-switch problem linked to more than a dozen deaths. Murphy, a Pennsylvania Republican, will hear from GM CEO Mary Barra on Tuesday when he chairs a hearing on the matter Tuesday before his Energy and Commerce Committee panel on oversight and investigations. "Something terrible went wrong within this company," Murphy told MSNBC's The Daily Rundown. He said the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration "also knew something was wrong" and will have to answer for its oversight. NHTSA acting administrator David Friedman is also set to testify to Murphy's subcommittee. GM is accused of knowing about the switch problem since 2005, but doing little to rectify the situation. Since then, relatives of motorists who died in car crashes linked to the problem have come forward and demanded answers from the company, which also received billions in bailout money from the U.S. government after the 2008 economic recession. GM has recalled millions of vehicles because of the revelations.

Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) won reelection against State Treasurer Josh Mandel on Tuesday, according to the Associated Press. Recent polls showed Brown with a consistent but narrow lead in his bid for a second term. Mandel received over $22 million in outside spending, according to the Center for Responsive Politics. His opponent, Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), has had over $14 million in outside help. The Karl Rove-linked Crossroads GPS has boosted Mandel by $6.3 million, in addition to his $4.3 million from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and over $1 million from the National Federation of Independent Business, none of which are required to disclose their donors. Brown had millions more spent against him in issue ads, which are not counted in Federal Election Commission data compiled by CRP. Mandel had also said he would have opposed the auto bailout, which hurt him in the state. Brown first won election to the Senate in 2006. He served in the U.S. House from 1993-2007.

More than six weeks after killing nine members of a black congregation in Charleston, South Carolina, in 2015, Dylann S. Roof wrote in a journal about his purpose. He wrote that he hoped to incite others to join him in fomenting a race war. "I did what I thought would make the biggest wave," the then 21-year-old white supremacist wrote, "and now the fate of our race is in the hands of my brothers who continue to live freely." Page after page from the journal was read aloud on Thursday afternoon in Federal District Court in Charleston, where jurors will decide, perhaps as early as next week, whether to sentence Roof to death. The journal provided an extension of the manifestoes Roof wrote before he opened fire in the fellowship hall of Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church on June 17, 2015. Seemingly aware that he faced the likelihood of at least a life term in prison, Roof wrote that he "would rather live in prison knowing I took action for my race than live with the torture of sitting idle."

Scott Pruitt received pay raises this week. The EPA administrator is allowed to hire thirty hires that do not require White House approval. The pay raises were paid for by two of his employees, who were not authorized to receive the raises. Pruitt also lived for the first part of last year in a condo provided by a lobbyist and his wife. The condo was rented for the first part of the year, but only for the nights Pruitt stayed in the Capitol Hill condo. The lobbyist and his wife provided the condo for the remaining nights. The condo was also provided for the nights Pruitt stayed in the Capitol Hill condo. The lobbyist and his wife held the condo open for the other nights. A lobbyist's client received EPA approval for a pipeline.

House Republicans said Friday they would agree to lift the federal government's statutory borrowing limit for three months, with a requirement that both chambers of Congress pass a budget in that time to clear the way for negotiations on long-term deficit reduction. The proposal came out of closed-door party negotiations at a retreat in Williamsburg, Va. The White House press secretary, Jay Carney, said he was encouraged by the offer. Senate Democrats, who had opposed the demand for a budget, were also reassured and viewed it as a de-escalation of the debt fight. The change in position represented a retreat for House Republicans, who had previously declined to lift the debt ceiling. Speaker John A. Boehner of Ohio had previously said he would raise the debt ceiling only if it were paired with immediate spending cuts of equivalent value. The new strategy is designed to start a more orderly negotiation with President Obama and Senate Democrats on ways to shrink the trillion-dollar deficit.

On Sunday, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), a 2020 presidential candidate, appeared on CBS's "Face the Nation." She said the anti-abortion laws being passed in several states were a result of President Donald Trump starting "a war" on women. Gillibrand said, "This is nothing short of all-out assault on women's reproductive freedoms. An effort to take away our human rights and civil rights make no mistake. Make no mistake, the 30 states that are trying to unwind abortion rights are trying to get rid of Roe v. Wade. It's nothing more complex than that. They do not believe that women should have the right to make the most intimate, personal, life, and death decision, and I think it's untenable. I hope American people are paying attention because President Trump has started a war on America's women if it's a fight he wants to have it's a fight he's going to have, and he's going to lose."

On Friday, Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-HI) appeared on CNN's "New Day" and responded to reports that President Donald Trump has his eyes on former Attorney General William Barr to serve as attorney general and State Department spokeswoman Heather Nauert to serve as United Nations ambassador to replace outgoing Nikki Haley. Hirono questioned Barr's appointment as Jeff Sessions' replacement, arguing that Trump is looking for people who will "protect him" and "cover for him." Barr has defended former FBI Director James Comey's firing and has been critical of FBI special counsel Robert Mueller's team. On Nauert's nomination, Hirono said she would have "difficulty" supporting her due to her lack of experience. "I do not know that being loyal to the president is the uppermost qualification. It is for the president, but it isn't for me," Hirono said. She added that Trump "very clearly" struggles to find experienced and qualified people for jobs within the administration.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ted Cruz exchanged Twitter posts on Thursday. The exchange began when Ocasio-Cortez tweeted a link to a story about a large number of ex-lawmakers working as lobbyists and suggested the laws be changed to stop it. Cruz responded to the tweet and said he agreed with the congresswoman and suggested some bipartisan cooperation might be in order. Ocasio-Cortez suggested that bipartisan cooperation might be needed to make a good bill with some teeth in it. Cruz responded: "You're on." The exchange occurred amid political differences between the two political parties. Some Twitter users expressed optimism about the potential partnership.

A Washington Post-ABC News poll conducted Sept. 29 to Oct. 2 found that Republicans are overwhelmingly confident about taking back the White House in 2012. Fifty-five percent of Americans expect a Republican victory next year. Thirty-seven percent predict President Obama will win reelection. Fifty-seven percent of independents say the GOP nominee will prevail. Fifty-eight percent of Republicans say the GOP nominee, whoever he or she may be, is likely to claim the presidency next year. Fifty-eight percent of Democrats expect a Republican win. Nineteen percent of Republicans say they sense a repeat for Obama. Among Republicans who strongly support the tea party movement, 91 percent say they think the GOP candidate will win the general election. The poll has a margin of sampling error of plus or minus four percentage points. More from the poll will be available in tomorrow's Washington Post.

The Wall Street Journal reported Monday that National Security Agency director Gen. Keith Alexander offered to resign earlier this year following leaks by former contractor Edward Snowden. The Journal reported that the Obama administration declined Alexander's offer because it did not want to hand Snowden a political victory and calculated that Alexander's resignation would not fix the NSA's problems. A former senior defense official said that when the leaks began, some top administration officials found their confidence in Gen. Alexander shaken because he presided over a grave security lapse. The officials also did not think his resignation would solve the security problem and were concerned that letting him leave would wrongly hand Mr. Snowden a win. There was speculation throughout the summer as to why the administration had not asked Alexander to resign. President Barack Obama had dismissed senior military leaders for less serious lapses, as in 2010, when he fired Gen. Stanley McChrystal, then the head of U.S. forces in Afghanistan, for negative comments about the President and Vice President attributed to his staff by a reporter for Rolling Stone magazine.

Jeb Bush's mother, Barbara Bush, has expressed support for a potential presidential campaign. In a Monday interview on Bloomberg's "Street Smart" program, Neil Bush, Jeb Bush's brother, said Barbara Bush has "come around now" because so many people have come up to her and said Jeb is the best qualified candidate. Neil Bush said he did not know if Barbara Bush will decide to enter the race but emphasized that Barbara Bush is "starting to swing a little bit" in favor of Jeb running. Neil Bush noted that Jeb Bush has to decide "whether he wants his family to go through this and enter the campaign fray with joy." Jeb Bush has said his support for amnesty legislation and Common Core will turn off conservatives. He has also said a candidate must be willing to lose the primary in order to win the general and said he would decide "in short order" whether to run for president.

On Thursday, former Florida Governor Jeb Bush appeared on Fox News Radio's "Kilmeade and Friends." Bush was asked whether former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton should voluntarily turn over her private server, which stored all her email from her tenure as secretary of state. Bush replied, "I don't know." When asked whether she should turn over her server, Bush said, "I don't know. I don't know what the laws are. I think being clear and transparent in a world of deep disaffection where people don't trust folks is the right thing to do. That's why we unveiled 200, and whatever it was, and 80 thousand emails." Former President George W. Bush jokingly referred to Hillary Clinton as his "sister-in-law." Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-SC) and House Speaker John Boehner (R-OH) have asked Clinton to turn over the server.

The Republican National Committee voted unanimously Friday at its summer meeting in Boston for a resolution banning CNN and NBC from hosting 2016 primary debates if they proceed with proposed programs about former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. The RNC tweeted the news Friday: "BREAKING: RNC resolution to stop CNN & NBC from hosting GOP primary debates in 2016 PASSES!" Republican National Committee Chairman Reince Priebus had said that if CNN and NBC did not scrap their Clinton programs, he would seek an RNC vote saying the Republican Party would not work with the two networks on its 2016 primary debates or sanction the debates sponsored by them. In preparation for the next presidential election, Priebus said the party would consider holding its 2016 nominating convention in June or July, rather than August, to reduce the amount of time Republican candidates spend competing against one another. An earlier convention also would allow the Republican nominee to focus on the Democratic opponent. "Our party should not be involved in setting up a system that encourages the slicing and dicing of candidates over a long period of time with moderators that are not in the business of being at all concerned about the future of our party," Priebus told reporters this week.

Scott Walker is expected to formally enter the race for the Republican presidential nomination on Monday. A social media message read "Scott is in. Are you? Join our team today." The tweet included a photo of the governor with "Scott Walker is running for president" superimposed on it. The tweet has since been deleted. A Twitter spokesman said in a statement to Fox News: "We're looking into today's issue, and we've determined the Walker team was not at fault." Throughout the day, Walker aides remained adamant about his upcoming announcement. Rick Wiley, another aide, replied to a message about Walker's announcement, saying: "Set your DVR for 5pm on Monday bro, it will be epic." Walker is expected to enter the race. Walker has spent months touring the country, trying to court voters on his way to entering the competition.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, and Sen. Ted Cruz, a conservative, discussed a potential lobbying ban on Thursday on Twitter. Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, wrote: "If you are a member of Congress + leave, you shouldn't be allowed to turn right around&leverage your service for a lobbyist check. I don't think it should be legal at ALL to become a corporate lobbyist if you've served in Congress." Cruz also expressed support for a lifetime ban, saying he would work across the aisle to get it done. "The Swamp would hate it," Cruz tweeted. Ocasio-Cortez said she wanted a "clean" bill deadline specifically addressing the lobbying issue. It is not clear what Cruz has in mind legislatively, but he sounded eager to try something.

President Donald Trump signed a measure Monday creating a new national historic park for Martin Luther King Jr. during a trip to the college football national championship game in Atlanta. The President performed the signing on Air Force One with Alveda King, the niece of the late civil rights leader, looking on. The law creates the first national historic park in the state of Georgia. It was sponsored by Democratic Rep. John Lewis, a vocal Trump critic who recently boycotted the opening of the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum because the President spoke at the event. The legislation expands the boundaries of the former Martin Luther King Jr. National Historic Site in Atlanta to include the Prince Hall Masonic Temple, a site that King used as the headquarters for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, according to a White House spokesman. White House deputy press secretary Hogan Gidley told reporters on Monday afternoon: "Through his life and work, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. made America more just and free. This important historical park tells his story, and this bill will help ensure that the park continues to tell Dr. King's story for generations to come."

A senior U.S. military official visiting Seoul warned Pyongyang over recent threats and reassured South Korea that military backing would not be affected by a U.S. budget debate. Deputy Secretary of Defense Ashton Carter told reporters Monday that Pyongyang's threats would only deepen Washington's defense commitment to Seoul. He said that includes a "nuclear umbrella" security guarantee for Seoul, which does not have atomic weapons. Ashton said deep U.S. budget cuts would not alter Pentagon efforts to make South Korean defense a priority. Pyongyang is angry over U.S.-South Korean war games and U.N. sanctions meant to punish it for its third nuclear test. It has threatened nuclear attacks on Washington, though it is not believed to have the weapons needed to do so. South Korean marines take a rest on their K-55 self-propelled howitzers during an exercise against possible attacks by North Korea near the border village of Panmunjom in Paju, South Korea, Thursday, March 14, 2013.

The Justice Department released a legal opinion Wednesday outlining why Matthew Whitaker can legally serve as the interim Attorney General. President Donald Trump appointed Whitaker following the resignation of Attorney General Jeff Sessions last Wednesday. The department argues Whitaker's appointment was lawful under a statute called the Vacancies Reform Act. The department's Office of Legal Counsel offers advice to the executive branch but its guidance does not carry the force of law. Department officials had previously advised the White House that Trump could designate Whitaker as acting attorney general, a senior Justice Department official said Wednesday. The department wrote in its opinion: "As all three branches of government have long recognized, the President may designate an acting official to perform the duties of a vacant principal office, including a Cabinet office, even when the acting official has not been confirmed by the Senate."

Mitt Romney will embrace public discussion of his Mormon faith on Thursday night when the Republican convention will stage a tableau of speakers who are expected to offer accounts of the candidate as a man of compassion, character and deep beliefs. For most of his political career, Romney has said his life in the church has nothing to do with politics, and he has offered only clipped discussions of his religious views, privately concerned about the impact of his faith on his electability. He has changed course because of an urgent problem: voters who find him distant and unlikable have become a greater threat to his political fortunes than those who may be biased against Mormonism. In his speech on the convention night, Romney will testify about how faith has guided his life, according to Eric Fehrnstrom, a campaign strategist. Other speakers are expected to relate stories that could pack emotional wallops: how Romney helped church members whose children were sick or dying — crouching by a disabled infant's crib to pray for her survival, helping a teenager with incurable cancer write his own will.

On Friday, NBC's "Meet the Press" host Chuck Todd criticized Fox News for not taking action against host Sean Hannity when he did not disclose he was a client of Trump's attorney Michael Cohen while commenting on the FBI raids on Cohen's office. Todd said, "Sean Hannity can do what he wants to do, but I'm surprised Fox isn't making him, at a minimum, disclose a conflict every time he talks about this." Todd also criticized a post on Hannity's website titled "The Utter Hypocrisy of Chuck Todd," which highlighted Todd's wife, who was a consultant for Democrats. Todd said, "What I take offense to on that is — that's my wife, that's not me. I think it's a ridiculous place that we're in society that it's guilt by association."

President Donald Trump announced on Wednesday the first rally since his inauguration. The President tweeted an announcement for the rally set for Saturday in Melbourne, Florida. "Join me in Florida this Saturday at 5pm for a rally at the Orlando-Melbourne International Airport!" Trump tweeted. An administration official said Trump would rally supporters at an airport hangar there, the same venue where he held a rally in September. Trump is slated to arrive at the rally by landing at the airport on Air Force One and disembarking in front of the crowd, just as he did during the campaign, the official said. White House press secretary Sean Spicer said on Wednesday the event was a campaign rally and directed questions about it to "the campaign." He said Trump's campaign was paying for it but did not offer further details. Trump indicated in a form sent to the Federal Election Commission on Inauguration Day that he intended to run for President again, but noted it did not constitute the formal announcement of his 2020 candidacy. Last week, the Office of Special Counsel issued guidance for federal bureaucrats regarding the re-election effort.

Mark Zuckerberg, the social network's chief executive, testified this week. He revealed limited understanding of Facebook's operations and how it works. Members of Congress raised concerns about Facebook's privacy and data collection policies. He made several points about how computers work. These questions did not produce a unified theory of Facebook's troubles or suggestions of how they might be solved. The article argues that technological illiteracy is the problem, and that some older and tech-phobic lawmakers are fundamentally incapable of regulating Facebook properly. The article argues that the biggest obstacle to regulating Facebook is not Congress's lack of computer literacy, which gave Zuckerberg the upper hand this week. It is a lack of political will and an unwillingness to identify the problems they are trying to fix.

Texas state Sen. Wendy Davis, a Democrat from Fort Worth, has decided to run for governor in 2014, according to sources who spoke to Fox News. Davis intends to file paperwork for the race Wednesday or Thursday. The 50-year-old mother of two, who participated in a filibuster at the Texas Capitol in June, blocked new statewide abortion restrictions from being passed in June. The abortion bill was eventually signed into law by Gov. Rick Perry. The bill requires doctors to have admitting privileges at nearby hospitals, allow abortions only in surgical centers, limits where and when women may take abortion-inducing pills and bans abortions after 20 weeks. Davis' filibuster drew hundreds of supporters to the Texas state capitol and drew a mention from President Obama's campaign Twitter account. No other Texas Democrats have entered the governor's race. Republican Attorney General Greg Abbott announced his candidacy this summer and is the early favorite to succeed Gov. Rick Perry. Perry is not seeking re-election after 14 years in office.

President Donald Trump placed his hands on the shoulders of former adviser Steve Bannon, whom White House Press Secretary Sarah Sanders said was not close to the president. White House Press Secretary Sarah Sanders said she could not give legal advice, but Ronald Klain was giving it away free. Klain stated that an ex-staffer's statement cannot both be an inappropriate disclosure of a confidence and wildly false. He said no one is violating a contractual non-disclosure provision if they are disclosing things that they say didn't happen. Former acting Solicitor General Neal Katyal expressed skepticism. Katyal said Trump's strategy is, well, only as sound as the mind behind it. Katyal also said the disclosure probably wouldn't qualify as a violation of an NDA. Katyal said ex-staffer's opinions that his former colleagues are idiots are not disclosure violations anyway. Trump is the most public of public figures, and Katyal said he was not sure any private NDA would apply in any case.

Gov. Sam Brownback of Kansas was confirmed to an ambassadorship on Wednesday after a six-month wait. The Senate split 49-49 along party lines on the nomination of Mr. Brownback, a Republican who has grown unpopular in Kansas, to be ambassador at large for international religious freedom. Vice President Mike Pence cast the tiebreaking vote. Many religious leaders praised Mr. Brownback's confirmation, and said he could use his political experience to help religious minorities, including Christian and Yazidi communities in the Middle East. "He has been a consistent, vocal, competent and impassioned advocate for these issues," said the Rev. Johnnie Moore, a Southern Baptist minister who served on the evangelical advisory board for President Trump's campaign. "It was all very logical to us that he would be the nominee, and we were thrilled by it." Many Democrats and gay rights advocates opposed the nomination of Mr. Brownback, who ended anti-discrimination protections for gay state workers in 2015.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman is "considering going to Singapore," his agent Darren Prince told CNN. Rodman's agent, Darren Prince, said that while he is considering making the trip, "no plans or flights have been made yet." The US President is expected to meet with the North Korean leader on June 12. White House press secretary Sarah Sanders announced on Tuesday that the exact location for the meeting will be the Capella Hotel on Singapore's Sentosa Island for a historic diplomatic meeting. The White House and State Department did not immediately respond to CNN requests for comment. A senior administration official told CNN that Rodman is not part of anything the White House team is doing at the summit. A State Department official told CNN: "We have no comment on Dennis Rodman's private travel. He's not a representative of the US government." Rodman has traveled to North Korea in the past and has struck up an unlikely friendship with the North Korean leader.

A Gallup poll released Monday shows Hillary Clinton's favorability rating below 60 percent for the first time since 2008. Fifty-eight percent of the public views Clinton favorably, while 39 percent see her unfavorably. That is down from 66 percent favorability in a mid-2012 Gallup poll, although still above her numbers during the 2008 primary. Gallup's Andrew Dugan writes that the poll shows only slight changes in the public's overall assessment of Clinton, with her unfavorable rating now marginally higher than at any time since 2008. Among self-described independents, 52 percent now view Clinton favorably, down 11 points from 63 percent in April. Clinton was also down 4 points among Republicans, although her numbers rose 2 points among Democrats. The Gallup survey is the latest of several polls to show Clinton taking a hit amid the continuing controversy on her handling of Benghazi, as well as speculation on her plans for 2016. HuffPost Pollster, which includes all publicly available polling, shows her numbers dropping about 4 points since January. The Gallup poll surveyed 1,529 voters by phone between June 1 and June 4.

On Monday, Broadway's Hamilton creator Lin-Manuel Miranda joined President Obama in the Rose Garden and performed a rap song about civic terminology. The two-minute freestyle session showed Obama holding up cards with the words "Constitution," "Obamacare," and "NASA" written on them. As Obama flipped the cards, Miranda rapped lyrics off the top of his head about the key words. "Constitution, the POTUS, I'm freestylin' You know this," he sang as seen in the video clip posted to the White House Facebook page. The Grammy-winning Hamilton cast also mingled with first lady Michelle Obama. The first lady had the cast perform for a group of high schoolers visiting the White House. Monday was not Miranda's first visit to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. Six years ago, Miranda performed the song "Alexander Hamilton" in the East Room of the White House.

Mitt Romney's campaign borrowed $20 million before the Republican convention to stay competitive until federal rules allowed it to tap general election campaign funds, according to a report by the National Review that was confirmed to Fox News by the campaign. The National Review article notes that Federal Election Commission rules barred the campaign from using general election funds until Romney was officially nominated, even though his nomination was a foregone conclusion leading up to the late-August convention in Tampa, Fla. A campaign aide told the National Review that borrowing money to improve cash flow in the meantime is permitted by the FEC, and that similar arrangements have been made by past campaigns. The aide said the campaign was able to "collateralize this debt with $20 million of general-election funds that were already sitting in our bank account." A senior campaign advisor told Fox News the campaign is not in debt because of the loan, and that its cash on hand exceeds its liability. The adviser said the campaign took advantage of the finance law to stay competitive during the primary. The campaign has paid back $9 million, the conservative magazine reported.

Montana Democrats need a U.S. Senate nominee. Actor Jeff Bridges has suggested that he run for the seat. Actor Jeff Bridges, known for his role in the "Big Lebowski" film "The Dude," would say, "Yeah, well, you know, that's just like your opinion, man." Bridges, who has a home in Paradise Valley, said in an interview on Howard Stern's radio show Monday that his wife opposes the idea of him running. "Don't even think about it," Bridges said. Pratt, who lives in Billings, started a petition on Change.org to encourage Bridges to run. It attracted more than 1,100 signatures. "I look down and see this thing, Jeff Bridges for senator, and I say what?" explained the actor. Sen. John Walsh (D-Mont.) dropped out of the race last week amid plagiarism allegations. Montana Democrats will gather at a Saturday convention to choose his replacement. Rep. Steve Daines (R) is favored to win the seat.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie responded to a former White House physician who said on national television earlier this week that his health could not handle the rigors of being president. Dr. Connie Mariano, an ex-Navy physician who headed the Medical Unit in the White House during President Bill Clinton's administration, said on CNN that Mr. Christie — who had appeared on "Late Show With David Letterman" on Monday — could die in office if elected president, United Press International reported. Mr. Christie responded at a Wednesday news conference, saying, "This is just another hack who wants five minutes on TV," and explaining that the doctor had never even examined him, according to UPI. Dr. Mariano had also addressed that argument in her CNN appearance, during which she said that in cases involving body types such as Mr. Christie's, up-close examinations were not necessary. "When I see someone who looks like him, you don't have to be a White House doctor to be concerned about health issues," she said during her CNN appearance, UPI reported.

President Donald Trump said federal authorities are making progress on discovering the motives of the Las Vegas shooter. "They're learning a lot more," Trump said. "And that'll be announced at the appropriate time." The president made the comments as he was leaving the White House for a trip to Las Vegas to visit with victims and first responders to the country music festival shooting that killed 59 people and wounded hundreds. "It's a very sad thing. We're going to pay our respects and to see the police who have done really a fantastic job in a very short time," Trump said. First Lady Melania Trump is also traveling with the president on the trip. "It's a very, very sad day for me, personally," President Trump told reporters. The president plans to meet with victims of the shooting and medical staff at a Las Vegas hospital later this afternoon as well as some of the law enforcement officials and first responders who responded to the shooting.

Speaker Paul Ryan appeared on "The Lead" with Jake Tapper on Thursday afternoon. Ryan said: "We do not always nominate a Lincoln and Reagan, but we hope that that person advances the principals of our party and appeals to a wide vase majority of Americans ... Saying that we're unified does not unify us, but actually taking the principles that we believe in and running a campaign that the Republicans can be proud about, and that can actually appeal to the majority of Americans. That's what takes it unify the party. ... I think conservatives want to know does he share the values and our principles and the government and the role of the executive. It's the constitution. There are a lot of questions that they're going to want answers to and myself included."

Republican Sen. Jeff Flake, who has opposed Republican Alabama Senate candidate Roy Moore, posted a photo Tuesday of a check with his signature on it addressed to Moore's Democratic rival, Doug Jones. Flake's Twitter account posted the image of the $100 check along with the caption, "Country over Party." Flake, who has announced he is not running for re-election, attended a meeting with President Donald Trump and other Republican senators at the White House earlier Tuesday, where he was seated next to the President. In that meeting, Trump again expressed support for Moore in the special election set for next week. Flake said later Tuesday the President was "wrong" for backing the GOP candidate, who faces multiple allegations of sexual assault from several decades ago. "I do think the President is wrong here. I think it will have negative impacts for the party in the long term," he told reporters. CNN's Kristin Wilson and Phil Mattingly contributed to this report.

Stormy Daniels has filed a lawsuit against President Trump alleging defamation. According to a document filed Monday with the U.S. District Court for Central California, Daniels, an adult-film star whose real name is Stephanie Clifford, claims that Michael Cohen insinuated, falsely, that she lied when claiming she had had a sexual affair in 2006-07 with Mr. Trump, then a reality-TV star and real-estate mogul. The document amends a lawsuit that sought to declare null and void a non-disclosure agreement that Ms. Clifford signed in 2006. The amended lawsuit also says the $130,000 that Mr. Cohen paid Ms. Clifford as "hush money" out of his own funds in October 2016 was a campaign contribution that, because of the amount and the fact it was not disclosed publicly, violated federal laws. Earlier on Monday, Mr. Cohen filed a cease-and-desist order against Ms. Clifford over her "60 Minutes" interview, in which she made explicit her longtime claims of an affair with Mr. Trump in 2006-07.

On Wednesday, NBC's "Megyn Kelly Today" featured Lanny Davis, the lawyer for Michael Cohen, who was seeking donations for his trial. Davis asked the audience to remind them that Cohen has suffered a tragic and difficult experience with his family and that he is without resources, and that they have established a website called michaelcohentruth.com hoping that he will get some help from the American people so he can continue to tell the truth. After the audience booed and laughed, host Megyn Kelly said, "The audience, they don't appear ready to donate Lanny." The audience booed again after Davis said, "I would say the reaction of your audience maybe they are not as interested in getting the truth out about Donald Trump as many other people in the country. Approximately 60 percent of the country would not have the reaction of your audience."

President Barack Obama canceled White House tours due to the sequester on Wednesday. The White House reported that Obama hosted a steak dinner for twelve Republican senators on Wednesday. The dinner included steak, salad, sautéed vegetables, and coconut sorbet. RNC chairman Reince Priebus said that since the president had been complaining loudly about the cutbacks they had had to make at the White House—including tours for schoolchildren—due to the sequester, it would be more appropriate if the country's leaders also dined on a budget. Priebus said he would like to order pizza for them and have it delivered to the White House. Priebus added that if the pizza was lucky, maybe the pizza would illuminate an important economic point for President Obama: instead of redistributing the slices, the best way to make everyone happy is to make the pie bigger. Priebus said this is as true for dinner as it is for economic growth and opportunity. The senators reportedly discussed gun control, immigration reform, and the debt with Obama.

President Trump on Sunday suggested that the thousands of Tax Day protesters in cities across the country over the weekend were paid, and he called for "someone" to investigate who funded the effort. The president tweeted about the rallies about 9 a.m. on Easter Sunday. Saturday's Tax Day protests included rallies in New York City; Chicago; Washington, D.C., and near his golf course in West Palm Beach, Florida, and elsewhere. The protests were aimed at pressuring Mr. Trump to release his federal income tax returns, which he has refused to do despite lingering questions about his financial ties around the world. In criticizing the protests, Mr. Trump questioned the motives of the demonstrators and said the question of his tax returns was settled in the November election. "I did what was an almost impossible thing to do for a Republican — easily won the Electoral College! Now Tax Returns are brought up again?" Mr. Trump tweeted before following up seven minutes later with accusations about the protests themselves. "Someone should look into who paid for the small organized rallies yesterday. The election is over!" he tweeted.

A South Carolina man, 24-year-old Michael Vines, was arrested over the weekend and charged with weapons possession after he slammed a Toyota Camry into a power pole on Saturday night. According to The Smoking Gun, firefighters saw him toss a handgun into the grass. Authorities charged Vines with driving under a suspended license, driving too fast for conditions, and unlawful carrying of a firearm. The handgun police accused Vines of carrying was a fully loaded Smith & Wesson .38-caliber revolver. Vines is prohibited from owning a gun because of a rap sheet that includes multiple narcotics convictions. Vines has a tattoo of a handgun prominently displayed on his forehead. Greenville police made a reference to the tattoo in a Facebook post, noting that "the real weapon was placed in property and evidence."

Donald J. Trump held his first of three rallies in Dubuque, Iowa, on Saturday. The airport hangar was cold and crowded. At the outset, Mr. Trump said he would let small children "run through the plane" as he talked. "Because the parents will damage it," he added. The aircraft moved low past the crowd as the theme from the movie "Air Force One" blared, prompting "ooohs!" from the crowd. The rally did not fill the area created for attendees, although hundreds were on hand.

President Donald Trump commented on the disqualification of Maximum Security at the Kentucky Derby on Saturday. The horse had led throughout the race before initially snaring victory. On Sunday, Trump wrote on Twitter: "The Kentucky Derby decision was not a good one. It was a rough and tumble race on a wet and sloppy track, actually, a beautiful thing to watch." The stewards ruled that Maximum Security interfered with other horses in the final turn, disqualifying the horse. The decision made Country House the winner, the first time it occurred in the history of the Derby. Trump wrote: "Only in these days of political correctness could such an overturn occur. The best horse did NOT win the Kentucky Derby – not even close!"

Mission Hospital released a statement to The Huffington Post stating that Billy Graham returned to his home in Montreat today following a two-day stay in the hospital, where he was admitted for pulmonary-related tests and observations. William R. Hathaway, Chief Medical Officer at Mission Hospital, said Graham was alert and in good spirits during his stay. Hathaway said the hospital was pleased with the results of Graham's evaluation. WCNC reported that Evangelist Billy Graham has been hospitalized in North Carolina for respiratory problems. The 95-year-old was taken to Mission Hospital in Asheville for treatment on Tuesday, but should return home in a couple of days, according to Mark DeMoss, a spokesperson for the Graham family. Graham was at Mission Hospital a month ago for pulmonary testing prior to his birthday party. DeMoss told WCNC: "Mr. Graham is in the hospital with a respiratory congestion issue, similar to what he had a few weeks ago. As was the case then, we expect he will be able to return home in a day or two."

Former GOP presidential candidate John McCain gave his support Monday to fellow party member Robert Ehrlich in his attempt to retake the Maryland governorship. McCain said after a meeting at the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis, Md., that Mr. Ehrlich is a "fine guy" and has his endorsement, according to the Associated Press. In the state's GOP primary Tuesday, Mr. Ehrlich faces business investor Brain Murphy, who has been endorsed by Sarah Palin, Mr. McCain's running mate in 2008. Mr. Ehrlich is expected to win the primary, then continue in what polls show is a tight race with incumbent Democratic Gov. Martin O'Malley, who defeated Mr. Ehrlich in 2006.

On Wednesday, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani tweeted for his own RouhaniCare. The tweet stated: "Gov will extend medical insurance to all Iranians. First step will be to cover 5mn uninsured Iranians by the social safety net #RouhaniCare." Twitter users asked: "Will the website work?" The Huffington Post's Mehdi Hasan wrote: "Obama must sue for trademark violation." The Daily Caller's Jim Antle wrote: "Now the Iranians are just trolling." MSNBC's Christopher Hayes wrote: "#RouhaniCare is the hashtag of the day. Not even close." Wall Street Journal columnist Sadanand Dhume tweeted: "In spirit of cooperation, feel free to copy US website." BuzzFeed's Andrew Kaczynski said: "If you like your plan you can keep it." Rouhani's account is not verified by Twitter and is thought to be run by his aides.

The Republican National Committee released a statement criticizing CNBC debate moderators. RNC Chairman Reince Priebus said the performance by the CNBC moderators was extremely disappointing and did a disservice to their network, the candidates, and voters. A source inside the RNC told The Daily Caller they are discussing options for the future, adding that "nobody in the building is happy with what happened right now." RNC insiders said there are limits to how much control the party can exert over topics and questioners. Priebus said he will fight to make future debates more about issues than the moderators. Priebus said he is proud of his team for standing up against what he called an improper and unprofessional display put on by CNBC. CNBC responded that a candidate should be able to handle such questions. CNBC responded to Republican criticism by stating: "People who want to be President of the United States should be able to answer tough questions."

The Supreme Court issued a unanimous rebuke on Thursday to President Obama, stating that he had overreached in issuing recess appointments during brief breaks in the Senate's work. The justices said Mr. Obama violated the Constitution in 2012 by appointing officials to the National Labor Relations Board during a break in the Senate's work when the chamber was convening every three days in short pro forma sessions in which no business was conducted. Those breaks were too short, Justice Stephen G. Breyer wrote in a majority opinion joined by the court's four other justices. At the same time, the court largely reinstated an arrangement between the executive branch and the Senate in which recess appointments were allowed during more substantial breaks. Justice Breyer said such appointments generally remained permissible so long as they were made during breaks of 10 or more days. Although there may be few immediate practical consequences of the ruling, given the recent overhaul of the Senate's filibuster rules, the decision was nonetheless momentous, involving a constitutional adjudication of the balance of power between the president and the Senate.

On Wednesday, Iranian President Hassan Rouhani tweeted for his own RouhaniCare. The tweet stated: "Gov will extend medical insurance to all Iranians. First step will be to cover 5mn uninsured Iranians by the social safety net #RouhaniCare." Twitter users asked: "Will the website work?" The Huffington Post's Mehdi Hasan wrote: "Obama must sue for trademark violation." The Daily Caller's Jim Antle wrote: "Now the Iranians are just trolling." MSNBC's Christopher Hayes wrote: "#RouhaniCare is the hashtag of the day. Not even close." Wall Street Journal columnist Sadanand Dhume tweeted: "In spirit of cooperation, feel free to copy US website." BuzzFeed's Andrew Kaczynski said: "If you like your plan you can keep it." Rouhani's account is not verified by Twitter and is thought to be run by his aides.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat, said Tuesday on the Senate floor that President Trump should thank his predecessor for the booming economy during Tuesday night's State of the Union address. Schumer said the president would be eager to defend the accomplishments of his nascent administration and take credit for a healthy American economy, pointing to low employment, job growth, and a soaring stock market. Schumer said these trends were present before Trump took office. Schumer said Trump was handed an already healthy economy by his predecessor and, like many things in his life, he inherited the healthy economy. Schumer said two words he would not hear Trump say about the economy: "Thanks, Obama." Schumer added that President Trump created more jobs in the last year of his term than in the first year of yours. Schumer said, "So if you're going to pat yourself on the back, give a shout out to Barack Obama."
