The New York Daily News posted its Friday cover on Twitter late Thursday. The headline referenced former FBI Director James Comey's memoir, A Higher Loyalty: Truth, Lies, and Leadership, in which Comey states that Trump asked him to look into reports that there is a "pee tape" in which he was filmed watching prostitutes urinate in a Moscow hotel suite. Comey said Trump denied the incident happened but wanted proof to assure first lady Melania Trump. The book is scheduled for release next week. The Daily News has previously used its front page to criticize the president. In February, it depicted Trump with an NRA-branded tape over his mouth on one cover and criticized him for golfing during the funerals of the Parkland, Florida, mass shooting victims in another. It has also depicted him as Dr. Evil, a clown, and a racist, and called his actions "treasonous."

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said during an interview with Yahoo News' Skullduggery podcast that a Joe Biden presidential run "doesn't particularly animate me." She said she understands why people would be excited by that idea, that there is an emotional element to it, but she does not want to go back. She said she wants to go forward. Ocasio-Cortez said she does not have a candidate in the 2020 election field. She mentioned her support for Sens. Bernard Sanders and Elizabeth Warren. "I'm very supportive of Bernie's run. I haven't endorsed anybody, but I'm very supportive of Bernie. I also think what Elizabeth Warren has been bringing to the table is truly remarkable, truly remarkable and transformational," she said. Biden has not announced his candidacy to face President Trump in the 2020 presidential election despite being the frontrunner in many polls.

Caitlyn Jenner used the women's restroom at the Trump International Hotel and Tower in Manhattan. The Republican presidential candidate said last week that he believes transgender people should be able to use whichever bathroom they choose. Trump said North Carolina's "bathroom law," which directs transgender people to use the bathroom that matches the gender on their birth certificates, has caused unnecessary strife. Trump said that if Jenner, who won an Olympic gold medal as Bruce Jenner, were to walk into Trump Tower, she could use whichever bathroom she wanted. Instead, Jenner used the women's room without incident. The Washington Times is switching its third-party commenting system from Disqus to Spot.IM. Users will need to either create an account with Spot.im or, if they wish to use a Disqus account, look under the Conversation for the link "Have a Disqus Account?" and read the Comment Policy before commenting.

President Obama is traveling to the Union Depot in St. Paul, Minn., on Wednesday to call for new spending on transportation infrastructure. The issue remains stalled in Congress. The president will call on lawmakers to pass a four-year, $302 billion surface transportation reauthorization bill that would help repair and modernize the nation's roads, bridges, railways and transit systems, according to a fact sheet provided by the White House. To help fund the initiative, Obama will propose dedicating $150 billion in "one-time transition revenue from pro-growth business tax reform," officials said. Funding for many transportation projects is due to expire later this year, according to the White House, putting more than 700,000 jobs in jeopardy. Obama will also launch a $600 million competition through the Transportation Department's existing TIGER grant program, which funds a range of infrastructure projects. TIGER stands for Transportation Investment Generating Economic Recovery. The grants, according to officials, will go to projects that will have a significant impact on a region, promote better job access and financial opportunity, save energy and fuel and spur economic development.

Former President Barack Obama had not finished his speech at the 2020 Democratic National Convention before President Donald Trump criticized him. In the speech, Obama said the current president "hasn't grown into the job because he can't." Obama said, "The consequences of that failure are severe. 170,000 Americans dead. Millions of jobs gone." Obama also said, "Our worst impulses unleashed, our proud reputation around the world badly diminished, and our democratic institutions threatened like never before." In response, Trump posted an all-caps tweet criticizing Obama. Trump had previously made similar statements about Obama, including that Obama "hasn't grown into the job because he can't." Several reports published during the Democratic primary cited sources close to Obama who said Obama purposefully stayed out of the race. In April, Biden told reporters he had asked Obama not to endorse him in the race, saying "whoever wins this nomination should win it on their own merits."

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) spoke Thursday about a hypothetical run for president by former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. When USA Today's Susan Page asked whether the Democratic party is coalescing behind Clinton, Pelosi responded, "I think so; I think so." She said there is a great deal of excitement about the prospect that she would run. She clarified that she was not making an endorsement but added, "But I am gauging, I'm gauging. I'm encouraging people to think about it, so in case she asks us, we have something to say to her." Pelosi has previously expressed support for the idea of Clinton running for president. She said in May that she is praying for Clinton to run, and in an interview with the San Francisco Chronicle last year she said Clinton was the Democrats' best "shot" for 2016. Clinton has not announced her plans for 2016. A super PAC supporting her candidacy has endorsed her. Sen. Claire McCaskill (D-Mo.) recently announced that Ready For Hillary has her support.

House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy (R-CA) said Thursday that he believes Alabama's latest move against abortion, which bans almost all abortions in the state, goes too far. "It goes further than I believe, yes," McCarthy stated during a press conference after being asked about the new abortion law. He continued by reaffirming his position on abortion, stating, "First of all, I believe the most precious gift God gives us is life. And I defended my pro-life position my whole political career." McCarthy also stated that he has believed in three exceptions to abortion, which include "rape, incest, and life of the mother." He added, "That's exactly what Republicans have voted on in this House. That's what our platform says." McCarthy also said he believes many of his Republican colleagues stand in agreement with him. Gov. Kay Ivey signed the bill, which does not include exceptions for rape and incest, into law Wednesday evening. The new law also seeks to criminally punish any doctor who performs an abortion.

West Virginia Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin said Friday he will vote for Republican Sen. Jeff Sessions to be confirmed as the nation's next Attorney General. Sessions needs a simple majority in the Senate to confirm him as the nation's next attorney general. Republicans will control 52 Senate seats by December if the GOP wins Louisiana's special election. Manchin may face a tough re-election in 2018. His state voted for President-Elect Donald Trump with every single county voting Republican and giving him 68.7 percent of the vote. Manchin is one of several Democrats in vulnerable seats, with Democratic seats in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Florida, and Ohio also up for grabs. All five states voted for Trump, with Pennsylvania turning red for the first Republican presidential candidate since 1988. Republicans could hold a filibuster-proof majority after mid-term elections if they win those 10 seats in the states which Trump won. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has also announced he supports Sessions for attorney general. Sessions was the first Senator to endorse Trump.

Caitlyn Jenner posted her first tweet at 12:17 p.m. on Monday. Four hours and three minutes later, she set a new Guinness World Record for the fastest time to gain 1 million followers on Twitter. In doing so, Jenner broke the previous record held by President Obama, who earned the title when he began his @POTUS account in May. It took Obama just under five hours to break the record, set in 2014 by Robert Downey Jr. Jenner's debut on Twitter drew congratulations from administration officials such as senior Obama advisor Valerie Jarrett, who tweeted "nice to meet you." As of this writing, Jenner's first tweet — a photo of the Vanity Fair cover showing her with the quote, "Call me Caitlyn" — has been re-tweeted more than 180,000 times. News of Jenner's new name, which she used to be known as Bruce, prompted 1.5 million tweets, according to Twitter, peaking at 11,000 tweets a minute.

Bob Dylan, the folk music legend and recipient of the 2016 Nobel Prize in literature, will not attend a Wednesday meeting with President Obama, a White House spokesman said Wednesday. The president is slated to meet with the other winners of the exclusive honor in a closed-to-press confab. Dylan did not initially return the Nobel committee's calls after the award was announced. He later proclaimed himself to be honored. A representative for Dylan did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Dylan did not receive Obama's praise in person. Obama tweeted last month: "Congratulations to one of my favorite poets, Bob Dylan, on a well-deserved Nobel."

Political analyst David Gergen made a critique of President Trump's campaign-style rally Saturday night in an appearance on CNN's "Newsroom." Gergen, who has been a White House adviser to four presidents, said: "To bring your campaign speech into the presidency is something presidents rarely do. This was the most divisive speech I've ever heard from a sitting American president." Trump delivered an address to a crowd of supporters in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, instead of attending the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in Washington. The nearly-hour-long speech began with attacks on the press and covered his tax plan, jobs, the yet-to-be-built wall, trade and other topics Trump had touted throughout his 2016 campaign. Gergen said: "He played to his base and he treated his other listeners, the rest of the people who have been disturbed about him or oppose him, he treated them basically as 'I don't care, I don't give a damn what you think, because you're frankly like the enemy.' I think it was a deeply disturbing speech."

White House counselor Kellyanne Conway accused CNN's Anderson Cooper of sexism on Thursday after an appearance on his show earlier in the week. Conway said on Fox News: "Let me tell you something, Hillary Clinton is in search of sexism as an excuse for why her disastrous candidacy and campaign lost six months ago. I face sexism a lot of times when I show up for interviews like that." Cooper rolled his eyes while interviewing Conway on Thursday. Conway was responding to a reel of past video clips of President Trump praising former FBI Director James B. Comey, who was recently fired by Trump. Conway was explaining that the clips were "conflating two things" but mentioned that she was grateful for "the trip down memory lane," and reminded Cooper that Trump won Michigan, which prompted his eye roll. Conway added: "Could you imagine having a male anchor on a network roll [his] eyes at Hillary Clinton or a female representative spokeswoman for President Obama or President Bill Clinton? I think not."

A letter to the editor responded to a front-page article titled "Obama to 'Put Everything I've Got' Into Gun Control'" dated Jan. 17. The letter writer stated that it has become fashionable of late to lament the unbridgeable divide over guns in the country. The writer said President Obama's critics charge that his recent action on gun control puts him at odds with all gun owners and enthusiasts. The writer stated that as a hunter, gun owner and gun control advocate, the reality is different. The writer stated that Americans are far from poles apart on the issue of gun control. The writer said all things entail some measure of risk as well as benefit, and that they legislate regulations accordingly. The writer said guns divide us because they fall in the gray area; the writer disagreed as to whether their utility outweighs their risk. The writer said this is largely because the gun lobby has done its best to suppress all research on firearms and their dangers. The writer also said President Obama said on Wednesday, "We don't benefit from not knowing the science of this epidemic of violence." The writer described the promise to back research into this area as encouraging.

A U.S. District Court judge in Bismarck issued a temporary block on Monday to North Dakota's new ban on abortions in cases where a heartbeat is detected in the fetus. The law could have an impact on those who are as early as six weeks pregnant. Judge Daniel Hovland called the law "clearly invalid and unconstitutional," The Associated Press reported. He issued the temporary injunction that prevents the law from taking effect until at least Aug. 1. "There is no question that [the law] is in direct contradiction to a litany of United States Supreme Court cases addressing restrains on abortion," the judge wrote, AP reported. "[It] is clearly an invalid and unconstitutional law based on the United States Supreme Court precedent in Roe v. Wade from 1973 … and the progeny of cases that have followed." The law cleared the Republican-controlled legislature and was signed into law by Gov. Jack Dalrymple earlier this year. The ban makes North Dakota one of the most restrictive in terms of abortion, AP reported.

Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel on Tuesday ordered the American military to review its policies concerning hairstyles popular with black women. He told critics of new Army regulations banning large cornrows, twists and dreadlocks that he takes "very seriously" concerns that military rules on hair have unfairly targeted black women. Responding to a complaint lodged by the 16 women of the Congressional Black Caucus, Hagel said he had given the secretaries and military leaders of the Army, Air Force, Navy and Marines three months to review comprehensive military regulations as they pertain to black women "to ensure standards are fair and respectful of our diverse force." Hagel's order raises the possibility that the Pentagon will go beyond the initial request of the black caucus that he overturn the Army's new hair rules. A Pentagon spokesman said that instead of looking only at the new Army regulations, Hagel is "opening the aperture" on all of the services, which black servicewomen have said for decades have forced them to conform to norms based on the hair of white women.

Former first lady Barbara Bush was admitted Saturday to Methodist Hospital in Houston, Texas, for routine tests, a spokeswoman said. Jim Appleby, spokesman for former President George H.W. Bush, said Bush is in for some routine tests, not an emergency of any kind. She had not been feeling well for about a week, said Jean Becker, chief of staff for Bush's husband. Bush, 84, is expected to stay at the hospital for a day or two, Becker said. Details on the testing were not immediately available. Becker said her hospitalization is "not serious at all." Last year, Bush underwent open-heart surgery during which doctors replaced her aortic valve with a biologic valve. She spent nine days in the hospital afterward. Becker said her recent hospitalization is "not related" to the surgery. In November 2008, Bush underwent surgery for a perforated ulcer.

Conservative billionaire Charles Koch, the Koch Industries CEO, criticized Donald Trump's proposed temporary ban on Muslims entering the country during an interview that aired on Sunday. Koch said Trump's support is antithetical to the approach and that he has a problem with Trump's support of using a database to track Muslims in the country. "That's reminiscent of Nazi Germany. I mean that's monstrous, as I said at the time," Koch told ABC News. Despite his strong feelings about Trump's stance, Koch said he and his brother David will still not "put a penny" toward the Never Trump" movement to stop the real estate mogul from securing the Republican nomination, even though they have been asked to contribute. The Koch brothers have not spent money for or against any particular GOP candidate in the primary. "That's not what we do," Koch said. "What we're trying to do is build alliances to make the country better. Like we have one with the White House on criminal justice reform. You do it by trying to find areas where you can work with everybody."

According to a Monday evening Washington Post report, Mark Zuckerberg, the company's co-founder and CEO, has told close colleagues that he would rather run Facebook than be president of the United States. The report states that Zuckerberg told close colleagues that he would rather run Facebook than be the president of the United States. When reporters recently questioned Zuckerberg during a conference call about whether someone else should lead Facebook, Zuckerberg was reportedly "adamant" that he was the right person to run the company. Zuckerberg fanned speculation about a potential presidential run last year when he appeared in Iowa for photo opportunities and delivered a Harvard commencement speech in which he called for universal basic income and teared up while speaking about so-called "Dreamers" and DACA recipients. He also said the fight against nationalism is the "struggle of our time." Zuckerberg will testify before the Senate Commerce and Judiciary Committees on Tuesday. On Wednesday, he will appear before the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

Two Democratic congressmen, Ted Lieu and Don Beyer, called on the Justice Department on Tuesday to criminally investigate Jared Kushner for omissions in his security clearance process. Lieu, a member of the Judiciary Committee, and Beyer urged Attorney General William Barr to investigate whether Kushner made false statements on his security applications. "Ultimately, the President and his son-in-law have made a mockery of the security clearance process," they wrote. "Their actions put U.S. national security at risk and offend the thousands of dedicated career officials who both grant and receive clearances the correct way." Recently, reports surfaced that President Trump granted security clearance for his son-in-law and senior advisor despite concerns from other top officials in the administration, including former White House Counsel Don McGahn and former chief of staff John Kelly. In previous interviews, the president, his daughter Ivanka Trump, and an attorney for Kushner have all denied that Trump intervened in the security clearance process.

President Obama extended his summer vacation on Martha's Vineyard to two weeks this year. The extension will interrupt the golfing, biking and beaching with two days back at work in Washington. Mr. Obama and his family depart Saturday for Martha's Vineyard and he will fly back to the White House a week later, on Sunday Aug. 17, for two days of meetings before jetting back to the island Tuesday, Aug. 19, CNN reported. The return trip could signal that Mr. Obama will make a policy announcement, such as his anticipated moves to ease immigration laws, that would benefit from a backdrop that is more stately than a summer resort. Mr. Obama and his family have vacationed on the Massachusetts island every summer since he became president, except during his 2012 re-election campaign. In the past, it was always a one-week stint at the affluent summer colony. Similar to past presidents, Mr. Obama has weathered criticism for taking vacations during crises at home and abroad. White House aides have insisted that the president is always on the job, keeping informed and issuing directives using secure communications equipment.

California Rep. Kevin McCarthy, the House minority leader, said Thursday that Alabama's new state law banning almost all abortions goes too far. McCarthy told reporters the law, which does not allow exceptions for abortions in cases of rape and incest, "goes further than I believe." McCarthy said he believes in "exceptions for rape, incest and life of the mother." McCarthy would not take a stand on whether the Supreme Court should strike down the measure, which the measure, the strictest abortion law in the nation, if a challenge were to reach the court. Opinion polls show widespread opposition to overturning the high court's Roe v. Wade decision, which could return the issue back to the states. Republicans struggled to win over suburban women in last year's midterm elections and the controversy over abortion restrictions could prove politically troublesome. Republicans have been on the offensive this year trying to link congressional Democrats to late-term abortion measures pushed by some of the party's most liberal forces in state legislatures such as New York's.

Margot Gerster, a Hillary Clinton voter, encountered her daughter Phoebe on a walk through woods near Clinton's New York home on Tuesday. Gerster wrote on Facebook that she was "heartbroken" about Clinton's defeat by Republican nominee Donald Trump in Tuesday's election and decided to take her daughter for a stroll to clear her head. "As we were leaving, I heard a bit of rustling coming towards me and as I stepped into the clearing there she was, Hillary Clinton and Bill with their dogs doing exactly the same thing as I was," Gerster said. "I got to hug her and talk to her and tell her that one of my most proudest moments as a mother was taking Phoebe with me to vote for her," the post continued. Clinton then posed for a picture, which Gerster confirmed to a Facebook commenter was taken by the 42nd President. "I do wish I'd asked [the Secret Service] to take one so he could be in it," she said.

President Donald Trump signed a bill to create a national historic park in Atlanta honoring Martin Luther King Jr. The new law expands an existing historic site commemorating King to include the Prince Hall Masonic Temple. The temple served as the headquarters of an organization once headed by King, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference. The site currently includes King's childhood home and a church where he was a pastor, Ebenezer Baptist Church. Trump signed the legislation aboard Air Force One on Monday after arriving in Georgia to attend the college football championship game. He is being joined by King's niece Alveda King. White House spokesman Hogan Gidley said King made America "more just and free."

The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll shows President Donald Trump with a job approval rating of 45 percent. In the same poll, at this same point in his presidency, former President Obama's approval rating was 45 percent. They also shared the exact same disapproval rating of 52 percent. The poll also includes coverage from the establishment media during Obama's presidency and compares it to two-year hate campaigns the media have launched against Trump. Among Republicans, Trump enjoys an 86 percent approval rating. Independents approve at 34 percent, and Democrats approve at 11 percent. In the generic ballot that looks at the 2018 midterm elections, the lead for Democrats over the GOP has dropped to just two points (41-39 percent). One week ago, in this same poll, Democrats enjoyed a six-point lead. This drop in support for Democrats is in keeping with other polls released this week, which average out to just a two-point lead, down from seven points three weeks ago.

Ukrainian Parliament voted to remove Viktor Yanukovich from office. He fled his office and opposition protesters took control of his residence. Parliament also voted to free jailed former prime minister Yulia Tymoshenko. The newly-installed interior minister declared that security police are to cease actions against protesters and police are rallying to the opposition. Events are moving quickly, much more so than was anticipated yesterday when Yanukovich's government and opposition groups agreed to cease fire and negotiations. Today's events suggest a much larger power shift and change in national direction, obviously, away from the influence of Yanukovich's pal Putin. Reports and details continue to emerge, and it is sure that there remains a great deal to be sorted out before it can realistically be said peace has come to Ukraine.

Hillary Rodham Clinton arrived in Vineyard Haven, Mass., on Wednesday. Hundreds of admirers waited hours in rain for a glimpse of the woman they hope will be the next president. Lily Richards, a 17-year-old high school senior from Greenfield, Mass., whose high school thesis paper argued for Mrs. Clinton's election as president, said: "When I heard Hillary was going to be here, I literally started crying. Oh my God, I have to go." President Obama is vacationing at a sprawling shingled home, where he is receiving friendly waves from locals when his motorcade passes. After six years, energy in the area appears to be shifting from Mr. Obama toward Mrs. Clinton, as the former secretary of state moves away from the president's orbit toward her own political future.

Florida Sen. Marco Rubio defended Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder on Thursday during a Fox News Republican debate held in Detroit. Rubio said the Republican governor took responsibility for the Flint water crisis. Rubio said, "I give the governor credit. He took responsibility for what happened and he's talked about being held responsible for it." Rubio criticized Democrats for the way they portrayed the situation in the media. Thursday's debate took place in Detroit, about 70 miles from Flint. The water crisis in Flint started after the city left the Detroit water system as part of a cost-saving measure in 2013. Despite warnings, officials did not treat the water from the Flint River, which caused lead to leach from pipes into the drinking water. Independent tests in August showed the water contained high levels of lead. In September, a pediatrician, Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha, compared blood tests and found a spike in lead poisonings in Flint.

White House physician Dr. Sean Conley said Tuesday that President Trump was reporting no symptoms after returning home on Monday night after receiving treatment for the coronavirus. Conley read a memo from the White House physician's office stating that the president's team of physicians met with him in the residence and that he had a restful first night at home and that he reports no symptoms. Conley said the president's vital signs and physical exam remained stable, with an ambulatory oxygen saturation level between 95 and 97 percent. Conley concluded that overall he continues to do extremely well and said he would provide updates as they learned more. The president returned home from Walter Reed hospital Monday night after spending the weekend being treated for the virus. Doctors will monitor his ongoing recovery for the next several days. Conley told reporters on Monday afternoon that if he could get through to Monday with him remaining the same or improving better, they would all take that final sigh of relief.

An anonymous senior official in Donald Trump's administration confirmed the existence of the "deep state" resistance in the presidency. The official told Axios, "I find the reaction to the NYT op-ed fascinating — that people seem so shocked that there is a resistance from the inside." The official said some of them wished they had written the piece. "I hope he knows — maybe he does? — that there are dozens and dozens of us," the source continued. On Thursday, Trump wrote on Twitter: "The Deep State and the Left, and their vehicle, the Fake News Media, are going Crazy – and they don't know what to do." Trump added that he would continue to "drain the swamp" despite their resistance to his important changes. "I'm draining the Swamp, and the Swamp is trying to fight back," he wrote on Wednesday night. "Don't worry, we will win!"

On Tuesday, Microsoft founder Bill Gates appeared on CNBC's "Squawk Box" and discussed a phone conversation with President-elect Donald Trump in recent days. Gates said part of the conversation dealt with Trump seeing areas where things could be improved. Gates compared Trump to former President John F. Kennedy, who he said had a similar "upbeat message" to that of Trump. Gates said: "[I]n the same way President Kennedy talked about the space mission and got the country behind that, I think whether it's education or stopping epidemics, other health breakthroughs, finishing polio and in this energy space, there can be a very upbeat message that his administration is going to organize things, get rid of regulatory barriers, and have American leadership through innovation be one of the things he gets behind." Gates added: "Of course, my whole career has been along those lines. And he was interested in listening to that. And I'm sure there will be further conversation."

The US supreme court justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg underwent an emergency heart procedure at a Washington hospital on Wednesday after reporting discomfort following routine exercise, a court statement said. Ginsburg, 81, was resting comfortably after having a stent placed in her right coronary artery and is expected to be discharged from MedStar Washington Hospital Center within 48 hours, the statement said. She reported discomfort after routine exercise on Tuesday night, according to the court statement. Ginsburg, the oldest member of the nine-justice court, has previously survived serious bouts with cancer in 1999 and 2009.

The United States has a new charge d'affairs in Libya to oversee diplomatic efforts following the killing of Ambassador Chris Stevens. Laurence Pope arrived Thursday in Tripoli to take on the role, the State Department announced. With no ambassador in the country, Pope will handle those duties. State Department spokeswoman Victoria Nuland said Pope looks forward to working with the Libyan government and the Libyan people during this historic and challenging time, as they build strong economic, social, political, and educational bridges between the two people. "We will continue to assist as Libya builds democratic institutions and broad respect for the rule of law -- the goals that Ambassador Stevens worked hard to achieve," Nuland said in a written statement. Pope, who was born in 1945, is coming out of retirement to take the job. A speaker of Arabic and French, he spent decades in the diplomatic ranks, beginning in 1969, before retiring in 2000. He held some senior posts, including director of Northern Gulf Affairs, associate director for counterterrorism, and political adviser to the commander of U.S. Central Command.

Sen. Ted Cruz made a statement opposing the prospect of President Barack Obama nominating a successor to Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, who died on Saturday of natural causes. "We have 80 years of precedent of not confirming justices in an election year," Cruz said at the CBS Republican presidential debate in South Carolina, arguing that the vacancy on the court should instead be filled by the next president in 2017. In fact, Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy was nominated by former President Ronald Reagan in 1987 and confirmed by the Senate in 1988, an election year. After debate moderator John Dickerson interjected to note the error, Cruz, a former Supreme Court clerk, paused and conceded he had gotten his history wrong. The audience booed. Sen. Marco Rubio had made a similar point prior to Cruz, but he correctly distinguished between the nomination and successful confirmation of a Supreme Court justice. "It's been over 80 years since a lame duck president has appointed a Supreme Court justice," he said.

FBI Director James B. Comey and the director of the National Security Agency, Adm. Michael S. Rogers, appeared before the House Intelligence Committee on Monday. The hearing was conducted by the Federal News Service. Comey testified before the committee. He thanked members of the committee for including him in the hearing. Comey said he was honored to represent the people of the FBI. He said he hoped the hearing showed them through actions and words how much the FBI valued their oversight of the work and how much they respect their responsibility to investigate those things. Comey said both are being taken very seriously. Comey said the practice is not to confirm the existence of ongoing investigations, especially those investigations that involve classified matters, but that in unusual circumstances where it is in the public interest, it may be appropriate to do so as Justice Department policies recognize. Comey said this is one of those circumstances.

President Obama on Thursday renewed his call for an immigration overhaul, telling an audience of activists at the White House that the fate of a bipartisan Senate bill now rests with Republicans in the House. "Anyone still standing in the way of this bipartisan reform should at least explain why," Mr. Obama said to repeated applause in the East Room. "If House Republicans have new and different additional ideas for how we should move forward, then we should hear them. I will be listening." The Senate passed legislation in June by a vote of 68-32. The vote was intended to improve border security, require employers to verify the immigration status of their workers, and provide a path to citizenship for 11 million undocumented immigrants. White House strategists hoped the vote would prompt action in the House, where Republicans had resisted similar calls for an overhaul of the system. The effort stalled this summer, with many House Republicans expressing dissatisfaction with the increases in border security and saying they do not support any plan that would allow people in the country illegally to eventually become citizens.

The Senate on Thursday voted 100-0 to approve the nomination of Charlotte mayor Anthony Foxx as Transportation Secretary. The unanimous vote was a rarity for a Cabinet appointee. Foxx's confirmation process was smooth. His city hosted the 2012 Democratic National Convention. Foxx, 42, will be the youngest member of the Obama Cabinet and will replace Ray LaHood at the helm of the DOT. Foxx's confirmation leaves two Cabinet nominees pending in the Senate: Tom Perez for Secretary of Labor and Gina McCarthy to head the Environmental Protection Agency. McCarthy's nomination was already meeting with Republican resistance in the Senate. The article reported that McCarthy might face a tougher time getting approved now that President Obama has revealed a climate-change agenda that is concerned Republicans. Juliet Eilperin reported that now that the president is proceeding with regulating greenhouse gas emissions from existing power plants, Senate Republicans are likely to be even tougher on McCarthy, who informed them in April the agency was not drafting such regulations.

Gen. Keith Alexander, the Director of the National Security Agency, offered to resign after former NSA contractor Edward Snowden revealed himself as the source of leaked agency documents, according to a Wall Street Journal report on Monday. The Obama administration declined the offer. One former defense official told the newspaper that officials were concerned that Alexander's resignation would give Snowden a win. The report comes about a month after the announcement that Alexander would leave the agency early next year. Reuters reported Oct. 16 that Alexander was expected to leave by March or April, citing anonymous officials. White House Press Secretary Jay Carney confirmed a day later that Alexander, who has led the agency for eight years, would leave his post in March. Snowden leaked classified documents to The Washington Post and The Guardian in June detailing the agency's telephone and Internet spying programs. He fled to Hong Kong and then Moscow, where he is currently residing. White House National Security Council spokeswoman Caitlin Hayden declined to comment on the report, pointing instead to Carney's Oct. 28 statement that President Barack Obama has "full confidence" in Alexander.

Dave Chappelle praised fellow comic Michelle Wolf for "speaking truth to power" during her performance Saturday night at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner. Wolf's routine drew criticism from President Donald Trump and his supporters who did not appreciate her cracks aimed at the administration, particularly her jokes about White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders. Chappelle said, "I don't know who those people think they are that she can't say that to them because they offend people all the time. For many people, it's cathartic to watch that woman speak truth to power like that." He said the routine was "grounded in her truth" and that he respected Wolf's artistry. "I know how hard it is to do what she did in front of that lame-ass crowd," he said.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad faced international condemnation at the United Nations on Thursday as Syrian forces blocked U.N. monitors from investigating a fresh massacre site in a village near the city of Hama. Special emissary Kofi Annan acknowledged that his six-point plan for a political transition in Syria has reached a dead end, with both sides refusing to implement it. He said a reinvigorated diplomatic push would be required to avert a full-fledged civil war, and he warned for the first time that any party blocking a political transition should face unspecified "consequences."

The Senate voted to move forward on the Violence Against Women Act. Nebraska Republican Deb Fischer voted yes. Wisconsin Republican Ron Johnson voted no. Ohio Republican Rob Portman voted no. Iowa Republican Chuck Grassley urged a yes vote on the motion to proceed. The bill passed the Senate without a vote. House Republicans objected to the bipartisan bill because they did not like its protections for immigrants, Native Americans, or LGBT people. They passed their own version of the law last year. Republican leadership refused to allow the bipartisan bill that had passed the Senate to come to a vote. The question remains whether John Boehner and Eric Cantor will continue blocking a bipartisan bill because it offers legal protections to groups they do not like. The author of the report urged Congress to reauthorize the expanded, bipartisan version of the Violence Against Women Act.

ABC canceled Roseanne Barr's top-rated "Roseanne" show after she tweeted an insult about Valerie Jarrett, a former aid to President Barack Obama. Barr said Jarrett, who is black, was from the movie franchise "Planet of the Apes." She tweeted: "muslim brotherhood & planet of the apes had a baby=vj." The president did not discuss Barr's tweet at a rally Tuesday in Tennessee. The White House declined to address it when asked repeatedly by reporters. Some news outlets, including CNN and MSNBC, have blamed Mr. Trump for fueling racism in the U.S. Ms. Barr has supported Mr. Trump, as did her character on the reboot of her sitcom. The backlash on Twitter and the cancellation move by ABC was fast and furious.

On Wednesday, CNN political commentator Symone Sanders appeared on CNN's "The Lead" and discussed President Donald Trump's decision to revoke former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) director John Brennan's security clearance. Sanders said the president sent White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders "out there today to basically poop on the people from the press secretary podium." Sanders said, "You know, I think someone wants to muck up the news cycle, Jake. Look, I definitely—I think this is ridiculous. This is nothing short of extraordinary, and we should all be scared about the state of our democracy. The president sent his White House press secretary out there today to basically poop on the people from the press secretary podium." She added, "Not only threaten, like they didn't make a threat, it was a promise. They are snatching John Brennan's national security clearance. John Brennan was in the Situation Room when American heroes took out Bin Laden. Like what is happening here?"

The Air Force suspended 92 officers at Malmstrom Air Force Base on Thursday. The officers are nearly half of the nuclear launch crew there. The Air Force acknowledged a "systemic problem" in the culture of the team entrusted to launch intercontinental ballistic missiles. Air Force Secretary Deborah Lee James said a "climate of fear" in the ballistic missile force might have encouraged launch officers to share answers to monthly proficiency tests. She said the nation's nuclear arsenal remained safe. For now, the 92 officers who have been suspended and decertified are barred from the underground missile capsules from which ICBMs are launched. The remaining launch crew members at the Montana base — just under 100 — will now perform extra duty on 24-hour standby, Defense Department officials said, and will spend at least 10 days a month in the missile capsules, up from eight. "This situation remains completely unacceptable," James said in her second news conference in two weeks to discuss the case.

The director of the Defense Intelligence Agency, Lt. Gen. Michael T. Flynn of the Army, and his civilian deputy, David R. Shedd, will retire by early fall, the agency said in an email to its employees on Wednesday. The two men are stepping down at a time when the Defense Intelligence Agency is shifting its priorities from providing intelligence to troops in Iraq and Afghanistan to working more closely with the C.I.A. to gather and distribute information on global issues like the proliferation of weapons and rising powers like China. In a statement, the Pentagon spokesman, Rear Adm. John Kirby, said that Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel "appreciates the service of these two dedicated and professional leaders," and that the retirements had been planned "for some time." Two senior American officials said tensions had flared between General Flynn and some of his Pentagon colleagues who balked at changes he wanted to make, including cuts to what he viewed as outdated intelligence programs in favor of devoting shrinking resources to newer threats, including in the digital realm.

Six weeks before the special election, a WBUR poll of 497 likely voters found Democrat Rep. Ed Markey at 41 percent and former Navy Seal Gabriel Gomez at 35 percent. The race is competitive in Massachusetts. Steve Koczela, president of the MassINC Polling Group, told WBUR: "Either way you look at it — with leaners or without leaners — you've got a race within single digits coming out of the primary. You've got a competitive race." Markey and Gomez, who has never held elected office, are running for the seat that former Sen. John Kerry, a Democrat, vacated to become secretary of state. Gov. Deval Patrick of Massachusetts appointed William Cowan, a former top aide to Kerry, earlier this year to fill the seat. Patrick also set up a June 25 special election.

Former Florida Gov. Charlie Crist (D), a former Republican, told Fusion's Jorge Ramos that racism is a "big reason" why he left the GOP. Crist said the GOP is now seen as "anti-women, anti-minority, anti-women, anti-gay, anti-education, anti-environment," saying he left the Republican Party because leadership "went off a cliff." When Ramos suggested "the moment" Crist decided to leave the Republican party was when he realized he would lose to now-Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) in the 2010 Senate race, Crist denied the claim and blamed the GOP's attitude toward President Barack Obama instead. "I couldn't be consistent with myself, and my core beliefs, and stay with a party that was so unfriendly toward the African-American president. I'll just go there," Crist said, saying anti-Obama "activists" were "intolerable." "I couldn't take it anymore," Crist added.

Australian police monitoring social media say the gunman holding hostages inside a Sydney cafe is demanding a telephone audience with Prime Minister Tony Abbott. Deputy Police Commissioner Catherine Burn said the demands are forming part of the tactical response. Burn declined to confirm or comment further on the demands or on another claim by two female hostages who called authorities to warn the gunman that two other bombs were planted at different sites in the city, Network 10 reported. Abbott has publicly announced the hostage situation may be politically motivated but has not labeled it a terrorist assault. Witnesses at the scene reported seeing a black flag with white Arabic writing flown inside, the same flag that Islamic terrorists use to promote their terrorist messages. New South Wales State Police Commissioner Andrew Scipione said, "We have not yet confirmed it is a terrorism-related event."

The U.S. House of Representatives approved a new North American trade deal on Thursday that includes labor and automotive content rules but leaves $1.2 trillion in annual U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade flows largely unchanged. The House passed legislation to implement the U.S.-Mexico Canada Agreement 385-41, with 38 Democrats, two Republicans and one independent member voting no. The bipartisan vote contrasted sharply with Wednesday night's Democrat-only vote to impeach U.S. President Donald Trump. The House vote sends the measure to the Senate, but it is unclear when the Republican-controlled chamber will take it up. Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell has said that consideration of the measure would likely follow an impeachment trial in the Senate, expected in January. The USMCA trade pact, first agreed upon in September 2018, will replace the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement. Trump has said for years to quit or renegotiate NAFTA, which he blames for the loss of millions of U.S. factory jobs to Mexico.

Former first lady Barbara Bush, 84, was hospitalized Saturday in Houston to undergo routine tests but doctors do not suspect anything serious, a family spokeswoman said. Bush was being treated at Methodist Hospital and should be released in a day or two, spokeswoman Jean Becker said late Saturday. "She hasn't been feeling well for about a week, and the doctors thought she should come in and undergo a battery of tests," Becker said. "It's not serious. She just hasn't been feeling herself and they're just trying to figure out why." Becker declined to provide details, but said former President George H.W. Bush drove his wife to the hospital Saturday morning after consulting with her doctors. A hospital spokeswoman declined comment, saying information was only being released through the family. Mrs. Bush was hospitalized for nine days after undergoing heart surgery in March 2009, for a severe narrowing of the main heart valve. Doctors at the time said the condition was common among people her age. She also was hospitalized in November 2008, when she underwent surgery for a perforated ulcer. Doctors said the two ailments were unrelated.

Seven months have passed since Bob Filner left Washington for San Diego. Filner, a member of Congress, left Washington to become mayor. The move followed a period of rapid change in City Hall that had been ruled by Republicans for close to 20 years. On Tuesday, Filner faced sexual harassment charges by employees and constituents, calls from his own supporters to step down, and the departure of some top staff members from City Hall. His former fiancée urged him to quit, detailing what she said was sexually inappropriate behavior by the mayor when they were dating. She announced last week that she had ended their engagement. San Diego has been introduced to terms such as the "Filner headlock," a description of how the mayor allegedly handled women he was trying to embrace.

John Dean, who served as White House counsel to President Richard M. Nixon, issued a warning for former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani, personal attorney for President Donald Trump. Dean said Giuliani crossed a line. Dean, who ultimately turned on Nixon and helped bring him down, said Giuliani was no longer a lawyer but a co-conspirator. Dean hinted Giuliani could face legal trouble. Giuliani has made headlines in recent days over a series of media appearances in which he alternately denied and admitted asking Ukraine to investigate former Vice President Joe Biden on behalf of Trump. In a White House summary of a conversation released on Wednesday, Trump pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to work with Giuliani on those investigations. Earlier this week, Giuliani claimed the State Department called and asked for his help with Ukraine. The State Department denied that, and described Giuliani as a "private citizen" who does not speak on behalf of the U.S. government.

Doug Ducey criticized Fox News for calling Arizona for Joe Biden. Ducey said, "Election Day votes are not fully reported, and we haven't even started to count early ballots dropped off at the polls." He added, "In AZ, we protected Election Day. Let's count the votes—all the votes—before making declarations." Miller tweeted, "We believe over 2/3 of those outstanding Election Day voters are going to be for Trump. Can't believe Fox was so anxious to pull the trigger here after taking so long to call Florida. Wow." Fox defended the decision and refuted rumors that the network had retracted its Arizona projection. Anchor Bret Baier said, "We do not retract that."

An independent inquiry into the attack on the United States diplomatic mission in Libya that killed four Americans on Sept. 11 criticized the State Department for a lack of seasoned security personnel and for relying on untested local militias to safeguard the compound. The investigation into the attack on the diplomatic mission and the C.I.A. annex in Benghazi that resulted in the deaths of Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans also faulted State Department officials in Washington for ignoring requests from the American Embassy in Tripoli for more guards for the mission and for failing to make sufficient safety upgrades. The panel also said American intelligence officials relied too much on specific warnings of imminent attacks, which they did not have in the case of Benghazi, rather than basing assessments more broadly on a deteriorating security environment. By this spring, Benghazi, a hotbed of militant activity in eastern Libya, had experienced a string of assassinations, an attack on a British envoy's motorcade and the explosion of a bomb outside the American Mission.

Rachel Maddow criticized Republican presidential candidate Carly Fiorina on her show Monday night. Fiorina, who announced her candidacy on "Good Morning America," told host George Stephanopoulos that she would make a good commander-in-chief because she "understand[s] technology, which is a tool to reimagine government and re-engage citizens in the process of government." Maddow noted that the article lists more than 30,000 sad faces, one for each person laid off during Fiorina's tenure at Hewlett-Packard. Fiorina received a $21 million severance package when she was removed. Maddow said, "It has been said once before in her political career. It will be said again: Carly will now disappear."

President Donald Trump spoke to reporters on Monday after meeting with Georgia officials to survey damage from Hurricane Michael. He said, "We have the worst immigration laws and the dumbest immigration laws in the history of the world." Reporters questioned the president about family separation policies for illegal immigrants caught at the border. "There's no country in the world that has such stupid laws as we do," he replied. Trump said the laws allow illegals to go through a court process, citing the practice of "catch and release." "They put one foot on our land and we have to bring them through a long court process," Trump said. Trump said he would continue working to change the laws but blamed Democrats for blocking any reforms. "We have the dumbest laws in history, and it's because of the Democrats," he said, "because they want to have these laws that way."

Obama administration officials are meeting this week to decide whether it is time for the United States to arm rebels in Syria with lethal weapons. According to a Fox News report, part and parcel to this is a parallel question of whether "opposition forces can be trusted" once weaponized. Throughout the Syrian conflict, the administration has wanted to arm the rebels but has feared seeing those weapons fall into the hands of "Al Qaeda-linked fighters or other extremists" fighting against Bashar al-Assad. Because of this, the Free Syrian Army stands the best chance of receiving arms from the U.S. This military group claims "no political or religious agenda" —simply the overthrow of Assad. Assad's forces have recently received a boost from Hezbollah's support of Syrian forces, and that is certainly pressuring the administration as they weigh whether to arm opposition forces now or to wait. Best guesses appear to support the theory that the Obama administration is close to saying "yes" to weapons for small groups of opposition forces that are least likely to be Al Qaeda-linked.

Corey Lewandowski, former campaign manager for presumptive Republican nominee Donald Trump, said Monday afternoon that he has no professional regrets about his role in the Trump campaign. "I have no regrets when it comes to this campaign," Lewandowski said. "My biggest regret in the campaign is not being able to have my family more involved." Lewandowski did not disclose any reason behind his firing. "I think what's fair to say is anybody that knows me...knows that I'm a very straight shooter," he told CNN's Dana Bash on Monday afternoon following the announcement of his removal. "I tell people the way it is," he added. "I'm not smart enough to lie," he added. Lewandowski said his job was to give his best advice and opinion, saying, "That's my duty and my obligation to anybody."

On Sunday, residents of Yarnell, Ariz., were told they could return home after a deadly wildfire engulfed their town for nine days. On Tuesday in Prescott, the neighboring town, residents and family mourned 19 members of their firefighting force that would not be coming home. At a memorial service for the Granite Mountain Hotshots who died in last week's fire, Vice President Joe Biden joined Arizona Gov. Jan Brewer, Sen. John McCain and Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano to speak to 1,000 of the Hotshots' family members and alumni. Biden quoted Psalm 122:1 before recalling his own family tragedy. Weeks after he was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1972, Biden's wife and one-year-old daughter were killed in a car accident in Hockessin, Del. His two sons survived, rescued by firefighters. "I didn't have the privilege of knowing any one of these heroes personally," he said of the Hotshots. "But I know them... I know them because they saved the life of my two sons," he said.

New Jersey state Sen. Donald Norcross (D) announced Tuesday afternoon that he will run for the seat of retiring Rep. Robert Andrews (D-N.J.), hours after Andrews said he will resign from Congress. In a statement, Norcross said: "I am running for Congress because South Jersey needs someone who is going to stand up for us in Washington, D.C., as Rob Andrews has done for more than two decades. I have spent my career fighting for middle-class families, senior citizens and workers." Norcross, brother of longtime South Jersey power-broker George Norcross, is a heavy favorite to succeed Andrews. He also received early backing Tuesday from state Senate President Stephen Sweeney, Camden Mayor Dana Redd and Andrews himself. At his retirement news conference, Andrews said he hoped Norcross would run. The seat leans Democratic, meaning the Democratic primary should determine the winner.

Rick Gates, the former right-hand man to Paul Manafort, President Trump's campaign chairman, is being cross-examined by defense lawyers in Manafort's trial on bank and tax fraud charges in Alexandria, Va. As defense lawyers attacked his credibility, Gates admitted to having an affair about a decade ago, but he denied using company money for his trysts. Prosecutors led him through a clinical examination of his and Manafort's business dealings, including how he hid income to avoid taxes. It is unclear whether Manafort will take the stand in his own defense. His lawyers would not say. The prosecutors said they expect to wind up their case this week. Kevin Downing, the lead defense lawyer, began cross-examination Tuesday by asking Gates's credibility, demanding an exact accounting of when he lied to the government and pleaded guilty to the charge of doing so. Gates did not articulate that timeline, prompting Judge T. S. Ellis III to intervene.

At a candidate forum in late January, three likely Republican presidential contenders — Senators Ted Cruz, Marco Rubio and Rand Paul — all made a statement: they considered "the increasing gap between rich and poor" to be a problem. On the question of whether the government should intervene to solve it, Cruz and Rubio rejected that approach. Rubio appeared to agree with them. When "government takes over the economy," Cruz said, "it freezes everything in place. And it exacerbates income inequality." He proposed lowering taxes and loosening regulations instead. A Pew Research Center poll from January 2014 surveyed about 1,500 adults. According to the poll, 69 percent of Americans consider inequality a problem, and 69 percent of Republicans say the government should act "to reduce the gap between the rich and everyone else."

The Washington Post printed a story on Nov. 1 alleging that U.S. Sen. Robert Menendez (D-N.J.) engaged with Dominican prostitutes. The Daily Caller cited conflicting evidence and stated it would continue investigating. The Caller stated it is actively pursuing the story, has investigators on the ground in the Dominican Republic, and will continue to report new facts as they emerge, whether or not they support its earlier reporting. An investigation by the Dominican National Police charged that three women who filmed a videotape alleging that Menendez had engaged prostitutes were a sponsored affair. The participants received several hundred dollars apiece for their participation. The Daily Caller also stated it will continue to investigate the case. TheDC has not independently verified the identities of the women involved in the Dominican National Police investigation but will continue to investigate the case. The article noted that "investigating the case" beats "publishing a retraction and apology."

President Obama addressed the death of Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia after wrapping up his golf game in California this afternoon. Obama said, "Tonight we honor his extraordinary service to our nation and remember one of the towering legal figures of our time," describing him as a "brilliant legal mind with a pugnacious style, incisive wit, and colorful opinions." The president made his statement at Rancho Mirage, California. Obama said he would nominate a replacement to the Supreme Court and expected the Senate to confirm his choice. "I plan to fulfill my constitutional responsibilities to nominate a successor in due time," he said. "There will plenty of time for me to do so and for the Senate to fulfill its responsibility to give that person a fair hearing and a timely vote." Obama said he took his constitutional responsibilities "seriously." "They're bigger than any one party," he added. "They're about our democracy."

President Donald Trump criticized a New York Times op-ed by former Supreme Court Justice John Paul Stevens. In all caps, Trump wrote: "THE SECOND AMENDMENT WILL NEVER BE REPEALED!" He added: "As much as Democrats would like to see this happen, and despite the words yesterday of former Supreme Court Justice Stevens, NO WAY." Stevens wrote that overturning the Second Amendment "would be simple and would do more to weaken the N.R.A.'s ability to stymie legislative debate and block constructive gun control legislation than any other available option." He also wrote: "We need more Republicans in 2018 and must ALWAYS hold the Supreme Court!"

Before President Obama left the White House on Tuesday morning to fly to an event in Albany, several aides intercepted him in the Oval Office. Within minutes, the president would endorse same-sex marriage on Wednesday. Several aides described the decision as quick and the subsequent announcement in a scheduled network television interview. The announcement followed 48 hours of speculation after Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. endorsed same-sex unions in a Sunday talk show interview. Advisers said Obama had intended since early this year to define his position before Democrats nominate him for re-election in September. Many of the president's allies believed he would not do so, citing his strong support from gay voters for ending a ban on openly gay people in the military and for disavowing a federal law defining marriage as between a man and a woman.

Representative Chris Cannon, a member of Congress from Utah's Third District, lost his bid for a seventh term on Tuesday in a Republican primary focused on whether he was conservative enough for the district. The primary was held by Jason Chaffetz, a first-time candidate. Chaffetz served as chief of staff to Governor Jon Huntsman Jr. Cannon, 57, had hoped that his name recognition, a large amount of campaign cash and a pool of more moderate voters would propel him again to the Republican nomination. An endorsement from President Bush, who remains popular in the district, had also been expected to help, as it did in 2006. Chaffetz carried the district, which covers all or parts of seven counties in central and western Utah, including southern suburbs of Salt Lake City. With almost 99 percent of ballots counted, Chaffetz had nearly 60 percent of the votes, leading Cannon by 27,266 to 18,208.

A Washington Post poll conducted by telephone April 29-May 2, 2013, asked a random sample of 1,000 adults in the Commonwealth of Virginia, including users of both conventional and cellular phones, to select which candidate would vote. The poll included a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Interactive results by political and demographic groups were available, including Democrats, ages 18-39. The Washington Post reported that the sample included a sample of 887 registered voters and 663 likely gubernatorial election voters. Sampling, data collection and tabulation were performed by Abt-SRBI of New York. The results from the full survey were produced for the Washington Post by Capital Insight.

A New York federal appeals court ordered the US government to make public secret papers justifying drone attacks against suspected terrorists, including American citizens. The case was brought by The New York Times and two of its journalists in a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) case supported by the American Civil Liberties Union. The request followed drone attacks in Yemen that killed Anwar al-Awlaki and Samir Khan in September 2011 and al-Awlaki's teenage son, Abdul Rahman, in October 2011. All three victims were United States citizens by birth or naturalization. Judges based their decision on the fact that the information had already been the subject of numerous public statements and speeches, particularly by President Barack Obama, Attorney General Eric Holder and CIA chief John Brennan. Judge Jon Newman wrote, "Whatever protection the legal analysis might once have had has been lost by virtue of public statements of public officials at the highest levels and official disclosure of the DOJ White paper." The decision reverses a judgment of January 2013, which had sided with the US government.

House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) has had conversations with top Wall Street executives, according to people familiar with the matter. The conversations asked how close Congress could push to the debt limit deadline without sending interest rates soaring and causing stock prices to go lower, people familiar with the matter said. Boehner spokesman Michael Steel said Tuesday night that he was not aware of any such conversations. Republicans are making a long list of demands in exchange for raising the debt limit. There is not a chance they will block an increase in the debt limit. They might demand a bipartisan vote, and in divided government, that is both reasonable and with precedent. Democrats need to make any concessions beyond being willing to join the GOP in voting for the debt limit increase.

Former CIA Director and deputy director for the CIA, Morell, in an op ed published in the New York Times endorsed Secretary Clinton. Morell described the Secretary's actions while in charge of the State Department as: "I also saw the secretary's commitment to our nation's security; her belief that America is an exceptional nation that must lead in the world for the country to remain secure and prosperous; her understanding that diplomacy can be effective only if the country is perceived as willing and able to use force if necessary; and, most important, her capacity to make the most difficult decision of all — whether to put young American women and men in harm's way." Morell also offered a description of what he called the Great Orange Menace. The author described the description as chilling: "In the intelligence business, we would say that Mr. Putin had recruited Mr. Trump as an unwitting agent of the Russian Federation." Comments on the story are closed.

Gallup reported that a quarter of American adults view both Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton unfavorably. The figure is more than twice as high as those who disliked both Mitt Romney and Barack Obama in 2012. In 2012, 4 percent of Americans viewed both Trump and Clinton favorably. Gallup estimated that a large number of people view both Trump and Clinton unfavorably. By Gallup's estimate, a full one-quarter of American adults view both Trump and Clinton unfavorably, a figure more than twice as high as those who disliked both Mitt Romney and Barack Obama in 2012.

President Obama took full control of the health care negotiations during a 72-hour period during which he acted as mediator between the House and Senate. The talks have turned the White House into a de facto Congressional conference. On Wednesday, Obama spent more than six hours with Democratic leaders. He continued to participate in health care talks to coordinate a response to the earthquake in Haiti. On Thursday, Obama spent much of the evening addressing House Democrats and attending his daughter Malia's band recital, where she plays flute. He returned to the negotiating table until 1 a.m., shortly before the group recessed for the night. On Friday afternoon, Obama remained in the Cabinet Room from 1 p.m. to 3:45 p.m., at which point the White House announced that Obama was done holding or attending health care meetings, at least for now. Officials are waiting for cost analysis from the Congressional Budget Office.

Rep. Ted Lieu and Rep. Don Beyer Jr. have referred Jared Kushner to the Department of Justice for criminal investigation. The referral follows reports that Donald Trump ordered Kushner to receive top-secret security clearance despite recommendations from the White House counsel and the CIA not to give him access to sensitive government secrets. The two congressmen cited Kushner's statements on security clearance forms and in public interviews as reasons for the referral. They called for an immediate investigation to determine whether Kushner is criminally liable for his false statements. In a letter, which can be read in full below, Rep. Lieu and Rep. Beyer detailed inconsistencies in Kushner's responses on the SF-86 form he had to fill out while seeking clearance. Kushner repeatedly failed to detail contacts he had with foreign officials, including meetings with Russian officials. The pair noted this is a violation of federal law and punishable by up to five years in prison. Rep. Lieu and Rep. Beyer further contend this investigation is critical because it is a matter of national security.

A Wall Street Journal/NBC poll found that Hillary Clinton, the likely Democratic presidential nominee, has not addressed the controversy over her private email server and the fundraising controversy surrounding the Clinton Foundation in an interview or with the public. The poll also found that the percentage of people who view Clinton negatively has increased six percent since the previous month's poll. Last month, roughly 36 percent of individuals surveyed said they viewed Clinton negatively, but now that number is 42 percent. The Wall Street Journal reports that 25 percent of voters say they think Clinton is honest, down more than 10 percent from a poll last summer. It has been 24 days, more than three weeks, since Clinton announced her bid for president. She has not spoken to national media about her campaign or to address the controversies she is facing. Breitbart News previously reported this is a record for presidential candidates in recent history.

Republican presidential candidate Ben Carson canceled the remainder of his campaign events Tuesday after a fatal car crash involving staff and volunteers. According to the campaign, a van carrying three volunteers and a campaign staff member slid on an icy Iowa road and flipped on its side near Atlantic, Iowa. It was then hit by another vehicle. One volunteer, 25-year-old Braden Joplin, was transported to the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Obama, Neb. where he died Tuesday around 4:30 p.m., according to a statement from the campaign. "Carson plans to meet with Joplin's family members once he arrives in Omaha later this evening to offer his condolences," the campaign said. Three of the other passengers in the van are being examined at Cass County Memorial Hospital in Atlantic, Iowa, Carson's campaign said in a written statement. The accident occurred less than two weeks before the Iowa caucuses. Carson is polling fourth behind Donald Trump, Texas Sen. Ted Cruz and Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, according to polling data from RealClearPolitics.

Democrats have frequently cast President Trump as trapped in his own Watergate. On Wednesday, Trump criticized Carl Bernstein on Twitter. Trump criticized Bernstein and CNN, for which Bernstein co-wrote the Trump Tower story. CNN has repudiated one of its own sources. Last month, CNN reported based on anonymous sources that Trump lawyer Michael Cohen was willing to testify that Trump lawyer Michael Cohen knew in advance that Donald Trump Jr. was going to meet with Russians to get dirt on Hillary Clinton. The president and his son both vehemently deny this claim. In the past week, one of the sources, Cohen lawyer Lanny Davis, admitted that he did not know that this was true. Davis told federal prosecutors under oath as part of a plea deal that he did not know that either. In addition, Davis was identified by name in CNN's story as having no comment on the report.

On Thursday, President-elect Donald Trump's senior adviser Kellyanne Conway appeared on Fox News Channel's "Fox & Friends." Conway said White House press secretary Josh Earnest's claim at the daily press briefing that Trump knew about Russia hacking the 2016 presidential election was "incredibly irresponsible." On Wednesday, Earnest said Trump was "obviously aware" of the Russian interference when referencing Trump's joke during a campaign rally inviting Russian hackers to find Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton's missing emails. Conway said, "That is just remarkable. That is breathtaking. I guess he's auditioning to be a political pundit after his job is over soon. That is incredibly disappointing to hear from the podium of the White House press secretary. Because he basically — he essentially stated that the president-elect had knowledge of this, maybe even fanned the flames. It's incredibly irresponsible and I wonder if his boss, president Obama agrees."

On Wednesday at American University in Washington, D.C., President Barack Obama spoke about the Iran nuclear deal. He declared hardliners chanting "death to America" as the ones opposed to that deal and said they were "making common cause" with Republicans. Obama said, "I recognize that resorting to force may be tempting in the face of the rhetoric and behavior that emanates from parts of Iran. It is offensive. It is incendiary. We do take it seriously. But superpowers should not act impulsively in response to taunts, or even provocations that can be addressed short of war. Just because Iranian hard-liners chant 'death to America' does not mean that that's what all Iranians believe. In fact, it's those hard-liners who are most comfortable with the status quo. It's those hard-liners chanting 'death to America' who have been most opposed to the deal. They're making common cause with the Republican caucus."

Fox News star Kimberly Guilfoyle is leaving the network to join the America First Action Super PAC that supports President Donald Trump for president. A source close to Guilfoyle confirmed reports to Breitbart News. Guilfoyle has worked for Fox News for 12 years and is a co-host of The Five. A spokesperson for Fox News confirmed in a statement to Breitbart News that Fox News has parted ways with Kimberly Guilfoyle. Guilfoyle is currently dating Donald Trump Jr. after his wife Vanessa filed for divorce in March. In a recent interview on Breitbart News Daily, she described Trump Jr. as "number one up-and-coming political figure on the right." She said: "I've seen him at these political rallies, and I went to Montana with him, and I've known him for over a decade and saw him at the convention speech. He commands the room. He's a compelling political figure."

David Wildstein, the former Port Authority of New York and New Jersey executive at the center of the New Jersey bridge scandal, does not want to testify before state lawmakers on Thursday. Wildstein is going to court to avoid it. According to the Record, Wildstein's lawsuit argues that the subpoena served to him is invalid for a number of reasons, including Wisniewski's signature on the subpoena and Wisniewski's ability to issue a subpoena for investigative purposes. The last thing Christie needs right now is Wildstein under oath tomorrow.

President Hamid Karzai appeared before thousands of Afghan leaders on Thursday in Kabul, Afghanistan. He had reached an agreement with American leaders on a security deal that would commit the two countries to a lasting military alliance. He convened the assembly that would decide the deal's fate. In a speech described as a loya jirga, Karzai told the gathering that even if the United States approved the deal, he would wait until after the April presidential elections to sign it. The declaration surprised both American and Afghan officials. It put at risk an American deadline to have an agreement signed this year. Karzai intended for the United States to continue working through him until the end of the year.

Twitter blocked President Trump from Twitter for at least a few hours until tomorrow morning. The company said three tweets from Trump have been removed, and his account will be locked for 12 hours following the removal of these Tweets. If the Tweets are not removed, the account will remain locked. The tweet prompted discussion about whether Trump would comply or dare to permanently suspend him. The article also asked what could be done to stop the insurrection and asked what would happen if Trump cannot be removed. The article noted that there is near-universal condemnation of domestic terrorists and their enablers in right-wing media, Congress and the White House. It asked whether even if Trump cannot be removed, he could be neutralized until Jan 20. It also asked whether the republican party could be put on the defensive and wound them further for enabling the insurrection and for attacking America.

President Donald Trump said gun control "had little to do" with the shooting at a Pittsburgh synagogue on Saturday that killed 11 people. He said the death toll would have been much lower had the synagogue hired an armed guard. Trump told reporters that if the Tree of Life synagogue had an "armed guard inside ... they would have been able to stop them," referring to suspected gunman Robert Bowers. Police said the gunman was armed with an assault rifle and handguns. Twitter responses criticized Trump for blaming the synagogue for failing to have a guard and noted that four of the six people wounded in the attack were police officers, all armed. They criticized him for his refusal to consider how gun laws affect gun violence in America, and for his apparent aim to put even more firearms in people's hands. The article reported that what drove Twitter users particularly bonkers was the idea of armed guards in places of worship.

Albuquerque voters on Tuesday defeated a ballot question that sought to ban abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy. The referendum was the first of its kind in the country for a municipality. Organizers on both sides used record turnout and aggressive tactics to drive voters to the polls. Political strategists assessed the outcome. Hispanics account for nearly half of the residents in Albuquerque and New Mexico and are one of the fastest-growing populations in the country. Sam Bregman, chairman of the New Mexico Democratic Party, which campaigned against the ban, said in an interview: "This was a clear counterpunch to the Republicans and right-wingers who came from out of state to push their agenda on us."

Michigan lawmakers are considering hiring a state Title IX ombudsman and requiring minor patients to be advised of their rights amid criticism of how Michigan State University handled complaints against former sports doctor Larry Nassar. The proposals were among a number outlined Monday by Democrats in the Legislature, where majority Republicans also have introduced or are working on bills after more than 200 women and girls said in court that Nassar had sexually assaulted them with his ungloved hands under the guise of medical treatment. The ombudsman would work in the Michigan Department of Civil Rights and be "dedicated to listening and believing victims," said Rep. Erika Geiss, a Democrat from Taylor. Geiss said just one in five female victims of sexual assault ages 18 to 24 report it to law enforcement, some due to fear of retaliation. The ombudsman would ensure that survivors are given needed help and support, particularly after the Trump administration scrapped Obama-era guidance on investigating campus sexual assaults in favor of instructions that allow universities to require higher standards of evidence.

President Donald Trump visited Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland, on Saturday. He said he wanted to get a three-month head start on his annual physical, which is due in February. Stephen Colbert's "Late Show" team speculated on a different reason for the visit, citing an issue with his "quid pro hole." Trump's medical visit was also the subject of speculation and remarks by Trevor Noah on "The Daily Show." Noah said, "That's not a thing. It's not like, 'Yeah, today we can just cup the balls and then in March I'll come back and cough.'" Noah also said, "It might be tough for any doctor to properly examine Trump."
