Hillary Clinton reacted to Donald Trump's press conference with military veterans on Friday, calling his actions "disgraceful." In a statement, Clinton said: "Trump's actions today were disgraceful. After five years of pushing a racist conspiracy theory into the mainstream, it was appalling to watch Trump appoint himself the judge of whether the President of the United States is American." The Trump campaign said the Republican presidential nominee would address questions about the President Obama "birther" storyline at the campaign event, but he waited until veterans supporters finished speaking before making a statement. Trump said: "President Barack Obama was born in the United States, period. Now we all want to get back to making America strong and great again." Clinton said: "This sickening display shows more than ever why Donald Trump is totally unfit be president."

President Bush spent Tuesday evening watching election returns at the White House. On Wednesday, November 3, Bush spent the evening watching election returns. In the early hours of Wednesday, Senator John Kerry refused to concede Ohio. At 12:45 a.m., after Fox News and then NBC called Ohio for Bush, senior staff members watching election returns in the Roosevelt Room hurried to the White House residence. They were there to finish the president's victory speech and prepare for his arrival at an election night party at the Ronald Reagan building on Pennsylvania Avenue. Senator John Edwards, the Democratic vice-presidential nominee, made a public appearance in Boston saying the Democrats would fight on. Senior staff and the president were left in the White House residence at 2:45 a.m. It had been a see-saw day and night since early Tuesday, when surveys of voters leaving polling sites had showed Senator John Kerry beating Mr. Bush nationally and in crucial swing states.

J.D. Scholten, a Democrat who nearly defeated Rep. Steve King (R-Iowa) in 2018, announced Monday that he will seek to challenge King once again. Scholten, a former baseball player, launched his run Monday with a video narrated by "Field of Dreams" star Kevin Costner. Last fall, Scholten lost to King by 3% of the vote, the closest margin for any of the Iowa congressman's challengers during his nine terms in Congress. King has a history of promoting racist and white nationalist rhetoric. In January, after a New York Times interview in which he said he condoned white supremacy, GOP leaders removed him from congressional committees. Scholten is the first Democrat so far to announce a run in the race against King, who represents Iowa's fourth congressional district. Several Republicans have announced primary challenges against King.

On Sunday, Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) appeared on CNN's State of the Union and called President Obama's Friday comments on Trayvon Martin and race "very impressive." McCain said, "I think we should continue to make progress," but added that "we still have a long way to go," even as he declined to "second guess" the verdict in the George Zimmerman case. McCain stated that "we were probably too optimistic" about race relations in the aftermath of the election of the country's first black president. "I think old prejudices die hard," McCain said. "We have made significant progress, but I think recent events highlight the differences that remain." McCain also said he believed that "Stand Your Ground" laws should be reconsidered in light of the Martin case, despite the fact that "Stand Your Ground" was never invoked by Zimmerman and he was acquitted on grounds of self-defense.

The foreign ministers of the European Union approved an arms embargo against Venezuela on Monday as part of what they called "restrictive measures" to pressure the administration of President Nicolás Maduro to strengthen the rule of law and democracy. The ministers also established the legal framework for sanctions, including travel bans and the freezing of assets, against government officials. The Trump administration has taken action against dozens of Venezuelan government officials, including Mr. Maduro. The ministers did not name specific officials who might be subject to such penalties. They said they still hoped Venezuela could find a "peaceful negotiated way" out of its economic and political crises. "The primary responsibility for ending the crisis in Venezuela lies in the country," the ministers said in a statement. "The E.U. calls upon the government to urgently restore democratic legitimacy, including through free and fair elections, and on the opposition to continue engaging in a united manner towards a negotiated solution to the current tensions, in the interest of the country."

Charles Krauthammer appeared Tuesday on "Special Report with Bret Baier" and asked viewers who would step out now and defend the president in denials about President Trump. Krauthammer said that when it comes to breaking allegations about President Trump by the New York Times, "I think what is really stunning is that nobody, not even from the White House, has come out under their own name in defense of the president here." He continued: "Who is going to step out now and defend the president in these denials?" Late Tuesday, the New York Times published a story reporting that Trump asked then FBI Director James Comey to end a federal investigation into former national security advisor Michael Flynn in a February Oval Office meeting. Comey reportedly detailed the meeting in a memo, writing that Trump told him "I hope you can let this go." The White House denied the report.

Israel said on Tuesday it would name a new community on the Golan Heights after U.S. President Donald Trump as an expression of gratitude for his recognition of its claim of sovereignty over the strategic plateau. Israel captured the Golan from Syria in a 1967 war and annexed it, a move not recognized internationally. The United States broke with other world powers last month when Trump signed a decree recognizing Israeli sovereignty there. "All Israelis were deeply moved when President Trump made his historic decision," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video statement on the Golan. He added that, after the Jewish Passover festival, he would "bring to the government a resolution calling for a new community on the Golan Heights named after President Donald J. Trump." Trump's Golan move followed his decision in December 2017 to recognize Jerusalem as the Israeli capital, breaking with decades of U.S. policy over the status of a city contested by the Palestinians.

Pelosi named six Democrats to a Republican Select Committee on Women's Health. "I am proud to name six strong champions of women, families and facts to stand up against the latest Republican assault on women's health," Pelosi said. "Hard-working families deserve better than a taxpayer-funded Republican Select Committee fixated on dismantling women's health. As Republicans try to take affordable family planning and lifesaving preventive care away from millions of American women, Democrats will be in the room to fight for the truth." The Democrats on the panel will be Reps. Jan Schakowsky of Illinois, Jerrold Nadler of New York, Diana DeGette of Colorado, Jackie Speier of California, Suzan DelBene of Washington, and Bonnie Watson Coleman of New Jersey. Republicans made a point of including four women among their eight members of the panel. Democrats have women as five out of six members.

President Donald Trump posted two tweets early Wednesday morning criticizing special counsel Robert Mueller's Russia probe. In the posts, Trump quoted an op-ed piece by Harvard law professor Alan Dershowitz, who claimed Trump was "right in saying that a special counsel should never have been appointed." Trump deleted the message and posted again. In the first tweet, Trump spelled "whether" wrong, used the word "the" twice in a row, and repeatedly referred to the special counsel as "special council." The second tweet, with the "special counsel" spelling wrong, also showed the "special counsel" spelling wrong. Dictionary.com explained the nature of the grammatical error. Other tweeters also criticized the president, noting the term "Special Council" trended worldwide.

A Washington Post-Schar School poll conducted by telephone November 27-30, 2017, asked a random sample of 1,304 adults in Alabama, including landline and cell phone respondents, which candidate would they vote for? The poll asked which candidate they would vote for. The sample included 1,110 registered voters and 739 likely voters. Sampling, data collection, and tabulation were performed by Abt Associates of Cambridge, Mass. The sample was sampled by telephone. The margin of error was 3.5 points among the sample of 1,110 registered voters and 4.5 points among the sample of 739 likely voters. Sampling, data collection, and tabulation were performed by Abt Associates of Cambridge, Mass.

President Obama will deliver a speech Thursday urging Congress to pass a comprehensive immigration reform bill, the White House said Wednesday night. After the budget crisis ended last week, Obama called on Congress to pass an immigration reform bill, saying it was one of his top priorities moving forward. The Senate passed a bipartisan bill on immigration earlier this year, but it has stalled since being handed to the House. Most House Republicans prefer a piece-by-piece approach. House Speaker John Boehner expressed optimism on Wednesday about House action by year's end on efforts to overhaul immigration. "I still think immigration reform is an important subject that needs to be addressed. And I'm hopeful," Boehner told reporters at a Capitol Hill news conference when asked if the House can act in the remaining weeks. The House has five legislative weeks left, though lawmakers indicated that could change. Business groups such as the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, labor unions and religious organizations including U.S. Catholic bishops and evangelicals are pressing for immigration legislation. Many of their members plan a lobbying effort on Capitol Hill next week.

Iran's official IRNA news agency reported Tuesday that Kavous Seyed-Emami, a dual Iranian and Canadian citizen, killed himself in custody. The report said Seyed-Emami was in custody for passing information on the country's missile bases to the CIA and Mossad and planning to create environmental crisis. IRNA did not elaborate. Tehran prosecutor Abbas Jafari Dolatabdi said Seyed-Emami and a network of people installed cameras in strategic areas of the country pretending to observe environmental issues but, in fact, it was for monitoring the country's missile activities and they were sending images and information to foreigners. Dolatabdi said Seyed-Emami hosted one of two U.S. intelligence officers during their visit to Iran. He did not elaborate. On Monday, Iran said Seyed-Emami took his own life.

According to the Russian newspaper Kommersant, the Russians are considering granting political asylum to Edward Snowden, the NSA whistleblower and whistleblower. Snowden, a government contractor, revealed the existence of a National Security Agency surveillance operation last week. Kommersant quoted President Vladimir Putin's press secretary as saying, "If we receive such a request, we will consider it." Snowden was previously staying in Hong Kong, where he fled to on May 20, but has since changed his location. Yesterday, Regina Ip, Hong Kong's top official overseeing security, said it would be in Snowden's "best interest to leave Hong Kong." China has an extradition treaty with the United States. Ip said, "He won't find Hong Kong a safe harbor. Those agreements have been in force for more than 10 years. If the US submits a request, we would act in accordance with the law." The US is preparing charges against Snowden and will most likely try to have him extradited once those are filed.

At Business Insider, Michelle Mark covered Donald Trump's response to Hillary Clinton's foreign policy speech. Trump's criticism followed a foreign policy speech Clinton gave earlier that day, during which she denounced Trump's policy proposals as "as a series of bizarre rants, personal feuds, and outright lies" and declared that electing him would be a "historic mistake." Trump did not detail the arguments Clinton made in her speech, describing it as "phony" and a "Donald Trump hit job." He also criticized her for the email matter that has affected her campaign for more than a year. Clinton has long sought to address concerns that her private email account posed security risks to government business and classified material. Last Wednesday, the State Department released a report stating she "did not comply" with the department's policies regarding her email.

In an interview that aired on Monday, Ramos mentioned a speech Cruz's father, Rafael, made in which he compared President Barack Obama to Fidel Castro. Cruz told Ramos his father was referring to a statement Obama made at the State of the Union where Obama said "if Congress doesn't act to enact his agenda that he will do it anyway on his own." When Ramos asked whether he felt Obama was a dictator like Castro, Cruz said there were differences but said he was concerned about the "explosion of power in the federal government" under Obama. Cruz specifically cited the NSA surveillance program scandal and Obama's expansion of "presidential power in a way that is contrary to the constitution." When Ramos asked Cruz if he thought Obama was abusing his power, Cruz said Obama "absolutely" was. "I think he has absolutely been abusing his power and when you have a president who says 'regardless of whether Congress acts I'm going to force my agenda on the American people,' that's wrong, that's not consistent with our constitutional protections," Cruz said.

Former Sen. Bob Dole (R-Kan.) lifted out of his wheelchair Tuesday to give a final salute to former President George H.W. Bush. Dole, a former political rival of Bush, paid tribute to the 41st president earlier this week, describing his fellow World War II veteran as a "cherished servant leader" who "answered the call to serve whenever the nation needed him." Bush's spokesman, Jim McGrath, described the salute as "a last, powerful gesture of respect from one member of the Greatest Generation, Senator Dole, to another." Dole, 95, told CNN that under Bush's presidency, "three-fourths of Congress were veterans and we would stick together and work across the aisle." He added, "And President Bush was a bipartisan president. So we got quite a lot done."

Legislation to avert furloughs at the Federal Aviation Administration has been delayed because of a typo in the bill, according to ABC News and CNN. The Reducing Flight Delays Act Of 2013, which would authorize the FAA to use $253 million to fund air traffic controllers, lacks an "s" in the word account. With lawmakers in recess, the bill will receive a procedural correction and be sent to the president's desk for signing Tuesday, according to ABC. The typo occurred before members of Congress left for recess. The Senate passed the bill without a roll-call vote Thursday evening, and the House passed it by a 361-41 margin Friday morning. The FAA announced it was suspending employee furloughs on Saturday and said the nation's air traffic system would be normal by Sunday evening. Beyond the FAA and travelers dependent on it, those dependent on Meals on Wheels programs, Medicare's prescription drug program, and Head Start programs have not been spared from the impact of sequestration cuts.

Sen. Kamala Harris (D-CA) said in an interview with The Des Moines Register on Sunday that 2020 presidential candidates should state President Donald Trump did not "pull the trigger" at the mass shooting at a Walmart store in El Paso, Texas, but that Trump had been tweeting out the ammunition. Harris said, "I, as a prosecutor, I prosecuted hate crimes. As the Attorney General of California, where I ran the second largest Department Justice in the United States, I on an annual basis published the Hate Crime Report. So I will tell you this stuff is not new in our country. It certainly predates the election of Donald Trump, but it has also increased under Donald Trump. He has been fueling the flames of hate. I said recently on the issue of El Paso, you know, no, when people ask me is he responsible for these killings? Well no he obviously didn't pull the trigger but he sure been tweeting out the ammunition."

The United Nations Security Council ordered new economic sanctions against North Korea on Thursday for its third nuclear test last month. The council unanimously approved a resolution that the United States negotiated with China. In response, North Korea said Friday that it was nullifying all agreements of nonaggression and denuclearization with South Korea and was cutting off the North-South hot line. It was unclear how North Korea's leader, Kim Jong-un, would react to the rebuke. His government has threatened to terminate the 60-year-old armistice that brought a halt to the Korean War and that has kept a cold peace on the peninsula since, and South Korean officials said they were on the alert for any possible attack by the North. Any military action, or response, could end up involving the American forces that have remained in South Korea as it has turned from war-ravaged ruin into one of the most advanced industrialized powerhouses.

Former Trump aide Omarosa Manigault-Newman made a public departure from the White House. Her book, "The Predator in Chief," was released. In an appearance on ABC's The View, she acknowledged being a "co-conspirator" in the 2016 election win. She also said Hillary Clinton was robbed to applause from the audience. The article noted that former Trump supporters are now lamenting their role in making the Predator in Chief possible. The article stated that Omarosa Manigault-Newman has publicly acknowledged her role in the 2016 election and Trump administration. The article also stated it does not know whether she is sincere about all of this and that she believes her role in the 2016 election and Trump administration will haunt her for the rest of her life.

The White House announced Tuesday that it was canceling all public tours of the president's home because of sequester spending cuts. In an email, the White House said: "Due to staffing reductions resulting from sequestration, we regret to inform you that White House Tours will be canceled effective Saturday, March 9, 2013 until further notice. Unfortunately, we will not be able to reschedule affected tours." The announcement comes as both the White House and Congress try to find cuts to their own budgets as part of $85 billion in cuts to the entire government. As President Obama was returning from visiting wounded veterans at Walter Reed Medical Center, a reporter shouted a question about the decision to cancel the tours as Mr. Obama was walking from Marine One to the Oval Office. He smiled and waved. At the Capitol, staffers who use the building's West Front entrance that looks out on the National Mall were told Tuesday that door would be closed as of next week in order to save money.

President Obama is set to announce executive orders on immigration. The White House is set to broadcast live video of the announcement. Markos previewed the orders. President Donald Trump tweeted on Thursday morning that it was "so wonderful" to greet some of those injured by a heavily armed gunman who opened fire on the crowd at Sunday's Route 91 Harvest Festival. Nearly 60 people were killed and more than 500 were hurt. Trump visited Las Vegas on Wednesday and met with police officers and doctors who responded to the attack. He said the trip was something he "will never forget." Trump's use of "wonderful" did not go down well on Twitter. Many people called him out for "making a tragedy sound like good news." The president's description followed Elaine Duke, the acting secretary of homeland security, who called the federal response to Hurricane Maria tearing into Puerto Rico a "good news story."

President Donald Trump's economic adviser Gary Cohn is planning a meeting next week at the United Nations to discuss climate change, according to a New York Times report. The breakfast will include climate and energy ministers from around the world, according to the Times. The Times cited an invitation describing the event as "an opportunity for key ministers with responsibility for these issues to engage in an informal exchange of views and discuss how we can move forward most productively." Cohn advocated for the Trump administration staying in the Paris Climate Agreement, describing the president in May as "evolving" on the issue. "His views are evolving, which is exactly what they should be," Cohn told reporters during a press briefing in Sicily at the G7 summit. Trump announced his decision to withdraw from the Paris agreement. "I was elected to represent the citizens of Pittsburgh, not Paris," Trump said during a speech at the White House explaining his decision.

A YouGov poll shows that Republican primary voters believe Donald Trump is a bold and strong Washington outsider. Of Marco Rubio, Donald Trump, and Ted Cruz, Trump led categories in which respondents weighed various qualities. Seventy-five percent said Trump was bold, 62 percent said he was strong, and 64 percent said he was a Washington outsider. Compare that with 23 percent who felt Rubio was bold, 29 percent who thought he was strong, and five percent who believed he was a Washington outsider. The only categories Rubio led were "typical politician" and "establishment candidate." Cruz earned the most points for being a true conservative with a 54 percent rating. He also received the highest rating for being religious and for being partisan. His honesty rating was 42 percent. When asked a choice between Trump, Rubio, and Cruz, the support split as follows:

The Obama administration did not comment Monday on claims that a German intelligence employee arrested last week was spying for the U.S. The man was taken in custody amid allegations he passed documents on to a foreign nation, rumored to be the U.S. Chancellor Angela Merkel, an outspoken critic of U.S. surveillance and intelligence-gathering efforts, said the incident, if true, would amount to a "clear contradiction" of trust between the two countries. White House press secretary Josh Earnest declined to comment on the specifics of the case but said the U.S. and Germany remain close-knit partners. "We're going to work with the Germans to resolve this situation appropriately," he told reporters. "We highly value the close working relationship we have with the Germans on a wide range of issues but particularly on security and intelligence matters. ... As of right now, I'm not in a position to comment any further on this matter."

Former Senate Democratic leader Harry Reid, 78, had surgery on Monday to treat pancreatic cancer at Johns Hopkins Cancer Center. Reid is slated for chemotherapy treatment following the surgery. A family statement read: "His doctors caught the problem early during a routine screening and his surgeons are confident that the surgery was a success and the prognosis for his recovery is good." Reid's family said he is in "good spirits" after the surgery and feels grateful to his team of doctors. The news of Reid's diagnosis and surgery was first reported by KLAS-TV reporter George Knapp on Twitter and confirmed by an unnamed source to The Nevada Independent. A previous version of the article stated that Reid served in Congress from 1982 to 2016. In fact, Reid began his first term in 1983 and finished his final term in 2017.

President Donald Trump has said he did not know anything about his attorney Michael Cohen's $130,000 hush money payment to Stormy Daniels. Rudy Giuliani and the President have provided a new explanation. China has allegedly been aiming lasers at US military aircraft in Djibouti, injuring American pilots. Trump and his allies are suggesting that North Korea will release three detained Americans today. Their status remains unclear. Sexual harassment allegations against longtime television host Charlie Rose go back as early as 1986 and as recently as April 2017, the Washington Post finds. Bill Cosby and director Roman Polanski have been expelled from one of Hollywood's most important organizations. Adidas said it has not considered breaking ties with Kanye West despite recent backlash over the rapper's description of slavery as a choice. The article also included the phrase "We've been living a lie! Swedish meatballs are actually from a different country."

Deroy Murdock wrote that not even the "paper of record" could resist the left's claim that Donald J. Trump is America's "racist-in-chief." After deadly mass shootings in El Paso and Dayton last weekend, Democrats and other Trump haters demanded that the president denounce white nationalism, which they said propelled the alleged Texas gunman. President Trump said Monday: "The shooter in El Paso posted a manifesto online consumed by racist hate. In one voice, our nation must condemn racism, bigotry, and white supremacy. These sinister ideologies must be defeated. Hate has no place in America. Hatred warps the mind, ravages the heart, and devours the soul." The Old Gray Lady's page-one online headline reflected these remarks: "TRUMP URGES UNITY VS. RACISM." The article stated that those words enraged Democrats and disproved the leftist lie that Trump is a divisive bigot.

President Trump's proposal to add $54 billion to the Pentagon budget next year would represent a 10 percent increase for a department that receives more of taxpayers' money than any other part of government. The outgoing Obama administration had forecast a $35 billion increase for the Defense Department in fiscal year 2018, so Mr. Trump's share of the proposed increase over and above that figure is $19 billion, according to budget analysts. The proposed Pentagon increase has drawn criticism from military spending hawks. White House officials said Mr. Trump will call for a significant cut in foreign aid, including programs that military officials say contribute to global stability and are seen as important in helping avoid future conflicts. Senior administration officials acknowledged on Monday that there were few specifics attached to the bigger budget number proposed for the Pentagon, so it is not yet possible to assess how many more troops, warships or jet-fighters the Pentagon will be able to field with the $54 billion.

On Wednesday's broadcast of MSNBC's "Andrea Mitchell Reports," Senator Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) stated that Paul Manafort caught a break in the overall sentence he received. Blumenthal further stated that Judge Amy Berman Jackson did not commit a "miscarriage of justice" like Judge T.S. Ellis did, but that Jackson could have been harder on Manafort. Blumenthal said, "Looking at the totality of what he did, and the totality of the sentences, both last week and now, Paul Manafort caught a break. This overall sentence is exceedingly lenient, probably excessively so, in my view." He added, "[T]he miscarriage of justice, as I've called it repeatedly, really occurred in the Eastern District of Virginia, not today in her courtroom. She did her best to be fair and factual. ... But, she could have been tougher, and she tried to be balanced and fair."

Former Republican presidential candidate George Pataki endorsed Marco Rubio for the party's presidential nomination on Tuesday. In an interview on Fox News, Pataki said he believed Rubio had a broad-based campaign and the ability to unite Americans. Pataki, a former New York governor who suspended his own presidential bid in late December, said Rubio's experience in Congress will help him lead the military and stand up to threats from abroad. "I have no doubt that Marco Rubio is ready today to lead this country, to serve and lead as our president, and to bring us together," he said. Pataki, 70, said he plans to campaign for the 44-year-old senator from Florida. "He's someone who understands not just New England or the Northeast; he understands this country," Pataki said. "I think he has the staying power and the vision to win not just the nomination, but most importantly, you have got to win the election," he said. "And I think he will."

On MONDAY, President Trump nominated Judge Brett M. Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court. The pick was viewed as having conservative bona fides. By Tuesday, critics questioned whether one aspect of Kavanaugh's legal history made him especially appealing to the president. Pointing to an article Kavanaugh published in 2009 in the Minnesota Law Review, some in the media suggested that the nominee thinks a president cannot be indicted. The Washington Post's Fact Checker reported that the text on Kavanaugh's legal paper trail is not quite so black and white. Political cartoonists including Philly.com's Signe Wilkinson are rendering judgment of Trump's high court nomination. Steve Sacks of the Minneapolis Star Tribune, DAVID FITZSIMMONS of the Arizona Daily Star, RANDALL ENOS of Cagle Cartoons, JACK OHMAN of the Sacramento Bee, and TOM TOLES of The Washington Post are also making cartoons.

Edward Snowden, 29, was fired Tuesday by Booz Allen Hamilton, where he had worked as a contract employee, the company confirmed in a statement. Booz Allen is a consulting firm that receives nearly all of its funding from the federal government. The company released a statement on Snowden's firing Tuesday: "Booz Allen can confirm that Edward Snowden, 29, was an employee of our firm for less than 3 months, assigned to a team in Hawaii. Snowden, who had a salary at the rate of $122,000, was terminated June 10, 2013 for violations of the firm's code of ethics and firm policy. News reports that this individual has claimed to have leaked classified information are shocking, and if accurate, this action represents a grave violation of the code of conduct and core values of our firm. We will work closely with our clients and authorities in their investigation of this matter." Snowden claimed he made roughly $200,000, according to The Guardian.

Steve Kroft told Piers Morgan Monday night that President Obama keeps coming back to "60 Minutes" because "we're not going to go out of our way to make him look bad or stupid." The comments followed criticism that Kroft gave a softball interview instead of asking hard-hitting questions following Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's Benghazi hearings. "We have a format that suits him. It's long. We can do 12 minutes or 24 minutes," Kroft said. "We do a good job of editing." Adding that he has covered President Obama since his candidacy, Kroft noted it is a "question of fairness." Mr. Obama "knows that we're not going to play 'gotcha' with him." Mr. Morgan commented on the "remarkable bonhomie and long-lasting friendship" between the president and Mrs. Clinton, and Mr. Kroft described the interactions between the two as revealing of the positive nature of their relationship.

Pataki, a former New York governor who suspended his own presidential bid in late December, said Rubio's experience in Congress will help him lead the military and stand up to threats from abroad. President Barack Obama said he hoped that President-elect Donald Trump would consider helping illegal immigrants brought to the United States as children who were granted amnesty by his 2012 executive order. "I will urge the president-elect and the incoming administration to think long and hard before they are endangering the status of what for all practical purposes are American kids," Obama said. Obama's DACA and DAPA executive orders were criticized for lacking permanent protection for children of illegal immigrants and their parents. Activists were hopeful that Obama would be succeeded by a Democrat or a Republican more sympathetic to their plight. Obama defended them, asserting that they belonged in the country. "By definition, if they're part of this program, they are solid, wonderful young people of good character," Obama said. He suggested that the majority of Americans still supported his decision. "It is my strong belief that the majority of the American people would not want to see suddenly those kids have to start hiding again," he said.

Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump said Monday that life has not always been easy for him, and that he was given a "small loan" of about $1 million to start his business with. "My whole life really has been a 'no,' and I've fought through it," Mr. Trumpsaid at a town-hall meeting sponsored by NBC's "Today Show." "It's not been easy for me. ... I started off in Brooklyn. My father gave me a small loan of a $1 million ... and I had to pay him back, I had to pay him back with interest." Mr. Trump said he went to Manhattan with the money and started buying properties and "did great," despite being told by many, including his father, that straying from Brooklyn and Queens real-estate may not lead to success.

President Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro met and shook hands at the Palace of the Revolution today in Cuba. Obama arrived with the U.S. delegation and shook hands with Castro for about 30 seconds in front of the cameras. The two leaders spoke pleasantries for a few moments in front of the press. "We had a great tour yesterday," Obama told Castro, referring to the First Family's sightseeing trip in Havana on Sunday. "Enjoyed it." "And we had a great dinner," he added. Susan Rice was also present as well as Secretary of State John Kerry, Secretary of Agriculture Tom Vilsack and Secretary of Commerce Penny Pritzker who also shook hands with Castro. Both leaders listened as the national anthems of Cuba and the United States were played and reviewed the Cuban troops. The leaders expect to meet and deliver statements to the press later this afternoon. It is unlikely that the press will be allowed to ask questions.

The White House announced Monday that it is putting the same minds that rescued HealthCare.gov to work on other government technology headaches with the launch of a "U.S. Digital Service." The team will be led by Mikey Dickerson, a former Google engineer widely credited with playing a central role in salvaging the HealthCare.gov site after its launch. The idea behind the USDS is to institutionalize the approach that saved the health care site and apply it to the work of the government before disaster strikes. The launch comes after months of discussion. In testimony before the Senate's Homeland Security Committee in May, U.S. Chief Information Officer Steve Van Roekel said the new team would have "centralized, world-class capability" and be "made up of our country's brightest digital talent." "Think of this as [a team of] management consultants that helps you understand your gaps," said Van Roekel.

A new NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll found Barbara Bush and Hillary Clinton tied for first place among first ladies from the past 25 years. Bush received 27 percent support, Clinton 27 percent, and former first lady Michelle Obama received 24 percent, and former first lady Laura Bush received 17 percent. The results were divided by political and demographic subgroups. Among Democrats, Bush favored Obama to Clinton by a 3-point margin. Among Republicans, Barbara Bush favored her daughter-in-law by 9 points. Obama was the favorite of 58 percent of African-Americans surveyed, while Clinton was the favorite of 30 percent of those respondents. Among Latinos surveyed, 45 percent of whom preferred Clinton and 29 percent preferred Obama. Among whites, Bush was the favorite with 33 percent, followed by Clinton with 24 percent. The NBC/WSJ poll was conducted April 23-27 among 1,000 adults, including 300 cell-phone-only respondents.

Department of Homeland Security officials decided in recent months not to grant an application for American citizenship by Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of two brothers suspected in the Boston Marathon bombings, after a routine background check revealed that he had been interviewed in 2011 by the F.B.I., federal officials said on Saturday. Mr. Tsarnaev died early Friday after a shootout with police, and officials said that at the time of his death, his application for citizenship was still under review and was being investigated by federal law enforcement officials. It had been previously reported that Mr. Tsarnaev's application might have been held up because of a domestic abuse episode. The officials said that it was the record of the F.B.I. interview that threw up red flags and halted, at least temporarily, Mr. Tsarnaev's citizenship application. Federal law enforcement officials reported on Friday that the F.B.I. interviewed Mr. Tsarnaev in January 2011 at the request of the Russian government, which suspected that he had ties to Chechen terrorists.

A roundup of results from Tuesday's primary contests in New Hampshire included U.S. Sen. Scott Brown, a former Massachusetts senator, winning the Republican primary in his bid to return to the Senate. Brown defeated former U.S. Sen. Bob Smith and former state Sen. Jim Rubens. Brown faces first-term incumbent Democrat Jeanne Shaheen in November. Former U.S. Rep. Frank Guinta defeated businessman Dan Innis and two others in the race for the GOP's nomination in the 1st Congressional District. He will face incumbent Democrat Carol Shea-Porter in another rematch between the two political foes. State Rep. Marilinda Garcia topped former state Sen. Gary Lambert and former state Rep. Jim Lawrence in the race to take on incumbent Democrat Annie Kuster in the 2nd Congressional District.

President Obama went to Fort Bliss on Tuesday before his Oval Office speech on Iraq. He thanked those Americans who most shouldered the burdens of a war. The conflict has been one of the few rays of light in the conflict since Vietnam, when soldiers were scorned for decisions made by politicians. President George W. Bush tried to make Iraq an invisible, seemingly cost-free war. He refused to attend soldiers' funerals and hid their returning coffins from the public. Obama, who has improved veterans' health care and made the Pentagon budget more rational, paid tribute to them. "At every turn, America's men and women in uniform have served with courage and resolve," he said on Tuesday night. He added: "There were patriots who supported this war, and patriots who opposed it. And all of us are united in appreciation for our servicemen and women, and our hope for Iraq's future."

A proposal to name a new community in the Golan Heights after President Donald Trump will go before the Israeli government on Sunday. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu recently suggested he wanted to name a new community after Trump because of his recognition of Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights. The community would be called Ramat Trump, or Trump Heights. The Government Naming Committee in their introduction of the proposal said: "The initiative to establish a new community in the Golan Heights, named after President Donald Trump, is an expression of gratitude for his actions for the good of the State of Israel as a whole and the Golan Heights in particular." The committee continued: "There is importance in advancing the aforementioned decision at this time in order to strengthen the political ties between the State of Israel and the United States." In March, Trump signed a proclamation recognizing Israel's sovereignty over the disputed Golan Heights, reversing years of U.S. policy on the matter.

Former Navy Secretary Richard Spencer discussed President Trump's intervention in the review of Navy SEAL Eddie Gallagher's Trident on Tuesday. Defense Secretary Mark Esper asked Spencer to resign on Sunday for going behind his back in removing Gallagher's pin. In an interview with CBS News' "This Morning," Spencer defended his actions, saying it was an effort to maintain "good order and discipline" among the troops. "The special operating community has been put under amazing pressure to do amazing things, and they're amazing performing people," Spencer outlined. "But there's ramifications that happen with that. And we have to build a system around it that has discipline, people look up to us and go, 'Yes, they actually stick by what they say, and they take the higher ground.' He added, '[A]n action like this erodes that.'"

Congressman Joe Sestak, a Pennsylvania Democrat, spoke to reporters on Friday about the White House memo revealing former President Bill Clinton as the individual who asked him to drop out of the Pennsylvania Senatorial primary in exchange for a job. When asked if he ever thought what was happening could have risen to the level of a misdemeanor or felony, Sestak said, "If I ever thought anything had been wrong about this, I would have reported it." Congressman Darrell Issa, a California Republican and ranking member on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, stood on the Capitol steps behind Sestak and watched the Pennsylvania Congressman's presser. Issa has been investigating the bribery allegations between the White House and Sestak for a number of months. Following Rep. Sestak's press conference, Rep. Issa appeared before reporters and made sure he had the last word before the Memorial day recess.

More Republican senators have declined to support Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell's efforts to gain support for a plan that would allow Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to fund Obamacare using a procedural maneuver in the Senate that Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) is challenging. Sen. David Vitter (R-LA) has endorsed Cruz's strategy. The endorsement comes after Breitbart News reported that McConnell and Sen. John Cornyn, Cruz's Texas colleague, are withholding votes against Cruz. Vitter said in a statement provided to Breitbart News: "Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid has indicated one of his first amendments after that will be to gut the provision in the bill that defunds Obamacare. I'll continue to fight President Obama & Senate Majority Leader Reid's efforts to fund Obamacare." Vitter's spokesman added that he will vote "no" on cloture.

John W. Hinckley Jr., who tried to assassinate President Ronald Reagan in 1981, will be allowed to live permanently with his elderly mother in Williamsburg, Va., leaving the psychiatric hospital where he has been imprisoned for several decades, a federal judge ruled on Wednesday. Judge Paul L. Friedman of the United States District Court for the District of Columbia wrote in his opinion that Mr. Hinckley, 61, no longer posed a danger to himself or others. The release should begin no sooner than Aug. 5, the judge said. Although Mr. Hinckley has been living part time in Williamsburg for years, family and friends of Reagan said they were outraged that he would be allowed to reside there permanently. "I think it's terribly sad and wrong," Patti Davis, one of Reagan's daughters, said in a telephone interview. In a blog post on her website, Ms. Davis wrote that she had long been haunted by the shooting.

Hillary Clinton's campaign emailed supporters Wednesday saying the campaign set a new fundraising record. Campaign Manager Robby Mook wrote: "In the first quarter of this campaign, we raised more than $45 million — a new record for this early in a campaign." Mook said people had doubted whether Clinton could get grassroots supporters, but the hundreds of thousands of donations proved critics wrong. Mook said: "We're still running the numbers, and we'll be in touch again soon to tell you a little more about the incredible group of people who've chipped in to support this campaign. Stay tuned for that." Mook requested even more donations to Clinton's campaign. He said some Republican candidates are rumored to have raised roughly $100 million dollars, "every penny of which they'll use to tear down our campaign and strengthen theirs. So we need to keep working."

White House Counselor to the President Kellyanne Conway posted on Twitter on Tuesday night after Republican Karen Handel defeated her challenger Jon Ossoff. She wrote, "Laughing my #Ossoff." Conway also criticized pundits who predicted a loss for President Trump and Republicans in Georgia. She wrote, "Thanks to everyone who breathlessly and snarkily proclaimed GA06 as a 'referendum on POTUS.' You were right." Conway thanked Handel for "being a grownup" and "running on the issues" while actually living in the district she was running to represent. She wrote, "Welcome to Congress," and highlighted Handel's call to "lift up this nation so that we can find a more civil way to deal with our disagreements."

President Donald Trump ordered a new round of economic sanctions on Iran on Monday in response to heightened tensions with the nation. "We do not seek conflict with Iran or any other country," Trump said to reporters in the Oval Office at the signing ceremony. "I can only tell you we cannot ever let Iran have a nuclear weapon." The sanctions are expected to target Iran's supreme leader as part of the response to the country shooting down an American surveillance drone in international waters. Despite ordering a military strike on Iranian targets in response to the attack, Trump called it back. The president warned Iran not to expect similar military restraint in the future. "I think a lot of restraint has been shown by us, but that doesn't mean we're going to show it in the future," Trump said. He added that he respected the Iranian people, despite what he called a dangerous governing regime. "I know many Iranians living in New York, and they're fantastic people," Trump stated.

Republican presidential candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) said that if the Republican establishment has a brokered convention to "steal the nomination from the people," it would "cause a revolt." Cruz told reporters in Orono, Maine, according to the Washington Times: "If the Washington deal-makers try to steal the nomination from the people, I think it would be a disaster. It would cause a revolt." He added: "Instead, the answer is real simple. We've got to win this nomination. I'm the only candidate who has the delegate count, who has the state wins, who is in a position to beat Donald Trump. And if you want to beat Donald Trump, the way to do it is to come together behind this campaign. But Donald Trump embodies that Washington corruption that we are angry about. The answer to that corruption is not go with someone who has been funding liberal Democrats for decades, who has been enmeshed in that corruption."

In an interview with Fox News Channel's Sean Hannity, his first since former special counsel Robert Mueller testified before the House Intelligence and Judiciary Committees, President Donald Trump criticized the Mueller investigation. Hannity asked Trump about the importance of determining the origins of the special counsel probe. Trump argued this should not be allowed to happen to another president and likened it to "treason." "This should never happen to another president of the United States again," Trump said on Thursday's broadcast of Fox News Channel's "Hannity." "This is an absolute catastrophe for our country. This was a fake witch hunt, and it should never be allowed to happen to another president again. This was treason. This was high crimes. This was everything as bad a definition as you want to come up with. This should never be allowed to happen to our country again."

Chelsea Clinton said in an interview Monday that she is deliberately moving from living a private life to a public one. Clinton said she is not looking to run for office today but that she would consider it if the country went off on the wrong track. "I had very much led a deliberately private life for a long time," the former first daughter, 33, said, "and now I'm attempting to lead a purposely public life." Clinton spoke to CNN while doing humanitarian work in Rwanda. Asked about an imminent political plans, Clinton said it could be in her future. "Not now," Clinton said. "I'm also grateful to live in a city and a state and a country where I really believe in my elected officials, and their ethos and their competencies. Someday, if either of those weren't true, and I thought I could make more of a difference in the public sector, or if I didn't like how my city or state or country were being run, I'd have to ask and answer that question."

Former House Majority Leader Dick Armey endorsed Midland University President Ben Sasse for the U.S. Senate in Nebraska. The endorsement followed FreedomWorks' endorsement of former State Treasurer Shane Osborn days earlier. FreedomWorks had previously endorsed Osborn, a former member of the Senate Conservatives Fund and the Club for Growth. Armey is former chairman of FreedomWorks, which he left last year after a dispute. The former House majority leader assisted Republicans in taking control of the House in the 1990s, helping write the conservative Contract with America before retiring in 2002. He then became involved with the tea party movement, becoming co-chairman of Citizens for a Sound Economy, which merged with Empower America to become FreedomWorks in 2004. In his endorsement, Armey criticized Osborn, saying, "We don't need career politicians running because this is just the next rung on the ladder for them."

Vice President Joe Biden spoke at a Black History Month event in Washington on Tuesday. He told about 150 attendees, "I may be a white boy, but I can jump." Biden hosted the reception at the Naval Observatory with his wife, Dr. Jill Biden. He said he wanted to team up with former NBA player and Sacramento Mayor Kevin Johnson to take on President Obama, according to The Washington Post. "I told the president, next game, I've got him," Biden said. Biden expressed disappointment with Voter ID laws passed in Southern states, including North Carolina, Alabama and Texas, saying such laws are evidence of "zealotry" and "hatred," according to a White House pool report. "These guys never go away. Hatred never, never goes away," Biden said. "The zealotry of those who wish to limit the franchise cannot be smothered by reason."

Last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that, despite their frosty relationship and the worst U.S.-Russian relations since the Cold War, President Obama would rescue him if he were drowning. On Friday, Obama said he would rescue Putin. "I'd absolutely save Mr. Putin if he were drowning. I'd like to think if anyone was out there drowning, I'd save them," Obama told reporters after being asked, according to Juliet Eilperin, who is traveling with the president in Seoul. Obama grew up in Hawaii. "I used to be a pretty good swimmer," Obama said. "I grew up in Hawaii." Obama cautioned that he is "a little out of practice."

Khalid Shaikh Mohammed, a self-described architect of the Sept. 11 attacks, said that a former top associate of Osama bin Laden who is on trial in Manhattan had no role in military operations for Al Qaeda and was enlisted to make speeches because he was "an eloquent, spellbinding speaker." Mr. Mohammed's assertions are contained in a newly filed statement in Federal District Court in Manhattan, where the former associate, Sulaiman Abu Ghaith, is being tried on charges that he conspired to kill Americans and provided support to Al Qaeda. Lawyers for Mr. Abu Ghaith have sought to obtain testimony from Mr. Mohammed, who is detained at the United States naval base at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. They have indicated that Mr. Mohammed's knowledge of Qaeda operations is unsurpassed and that his testimony "may very well exculpate" Mr. Abu Ghaith.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump posted a video on Instagram criticizing fellow GOP presidential candidate former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush for saying illegal immigration is an "act of love." Bush stated, "Yeah, they broke the law, but it's not a felony. It's an act of love." The video featured three mug shots of illegal immigrants who all committed violent crimes during their stay in the United States. The phrase "Love? Forget love, it's time to get tough!" appeared on the screen following Bush's statement. Trump previously said he would be influenced by Bush's wife, who is from Mexico. Trump told CNN, "I mean, look, I would say that he would. If my wife were from Mexico, I think I would have a soft spot for people from Mexico."

President Donald Trump signed a six-month waiver to delay the relocation of the U.S. embassy in Israel to Jerusalem. The White House issued a statement saying Trump was still committed to the promise but made the decision to delay the move for the sake of peace negotiations between Israel and Palestine. The statement read: "As he has repeatedly stated his intention to move the embassy, the question is not if that move happens, but only when." The statement followed the precedent set by former presidents Clinton, Bush, and Obama who all signed a six-month waiver of the 1995 law. The statement said: "As he has repeatedly stated his intention to move the embassy, the question is not if that move happens, but only when." The statement also said: "[N]o one should consider this step to be in any way a retreat from the President's strong support for Israel and for the United States-Israel alliance."

Last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that, despite their frosty relationship and the worst U.S.-Russian relations since the Cold War, President Obama would rescue him if he were drowning. On Friday, Obama said he would rescue Putin. "I'd absolutely save Mr. Putin if he were drowning. I'd like to think if anyone was out there drowning, I'd save them," Obama told reporters after being asked, according to Juliet Eilperin, who is traveling with the president in Seoul. Obama grew up in Hawaii. "I used to be a pretty good swimmer," Obama said. "I grew up in Hawaii." Obama cautioned that he is "a little out of practice."

On Friday, nearly six months after his escape, Joaquín Guzmán Loera, the Mexican drug lord known as El Chapo, was captured again after a gun battle near the coast in his home state of Sinaloa, Mexican officials said. President Enrique Peña Nieto announced the arrest. The arrest ended a manhunt by the government involving every law enforcement agency in the country and help from the United States. The marines captured the fugitive in an early morning raid that left five people dead, the Mexican authorities said. An American official described the raid as "a Mexican op, planned and executed by Mexico."

Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid introduced an amendment Thursday that would ban gun ownership by people convicted of misdemeanors under the Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances Act, a 1994 law intended to prevent violence and harassment at abortion clinics. Reid called gun violence "a cancer on this nation" and said the amendment is a response to last week's shooting at a Planned Parenthood clinic in Colorado, where three people were killed and nine were injured. Reid castigated his colleagues from the Senate floor Thursday morning, saying they are "complicit through our inaction. And if we continue to fail to act we'll be complicit today and every day into the future." The Senate will begin voting on amendments to the repeal bill this afternoon.

President Donald Trump responded to rapper Kanye West on Twitter. West wrote: "You don't have to agree with Trump but the mob can't make me not love him. We are both dragon energy. He is my brother. I love everyone. I don't agree with everything anyone does. That's what makes us individuals. And we have the right to independent thought." West had received criticism on Twitter for positive statements about the president. Trump responded on Twitter shortly after Breitbart News asked Press Secretary Sarah Sanders at the White House press briefing whether the president had communicated recently with West. In response, West posted a picture of a Trump MAGA campaign hat autographed by the president and a screen image of the president's tweet.

The Nimitz, the guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton and other 5th Fleet personnel continued their search on Monday, Rebarich said. She declined to identify the missing sailor, citing Navy policy. The Nimitz, whose homeport is Bremerton, Washington, has been in the Arabian Sea since late July. It replaced the aircraft carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower, which had spent months in the Arabian Sea on its deployment that saw the carrier break the Navy's previous at-sea record. Navy officials have limited port calls due to the ongoing coronavirus pandemic. The Nimitz's arrival in the Mideast saw Iran conduct a live-fire drill targeting a mockup aircraft carrier resembling it. The drill underlined the lingering threat of military conflict between Iran and the U.S. after a series of incidents last year led to an American drone strike that killed a top Iranian general in Baghdad. Tehran responded to that strike by firing ballistic missiles that wounded dozens of American forces in Iraq.

Melania Trump's website was removed from Philadelphia. For months, reporters had noted that Ms. Trump, who grew up in the Slovenian town of Sevnica, did not obtain an undergraduate degree in architecture from the University of Ljubljana, as her professional website claimed she did. Instead, she left after her first year to pursue a modeling career in Milan. As recently as a week ago, Ms. Trump's website stated that she had obtained a degree before going on to become a philanthropist and skin care entrepreneur. On Wednesday, The Huffington Post noticed that the site had been entirely scrubbed of its content. People clicking on its address are now redirected to the Trump Organization's website. In a Twitter post, Ms. Trump said the website had been removed "because it does not accurately reflect my current business and professional interests."

White House chief of staff Gen. John Kelly defended Robert E. Lee and Christopher Columbus during an interview with Fox News host Laura Ingraham. Kelly said it was a "mistake" to judge historical figures by modern standards. "It's inconceivable to me that you would take what we think now and apply it back then – I just think it's very very dangerous," he said. "It shows you how much a lack of an appreciation of history and what history is." Kelly made the comments during an interview with Ingraham about the controversy over monuments of historical figures. Kelly said that Lee was an "honorable man" who chose to fight for his state, pointing out that the loyalty to one's state was more important to Americans in that era. "The lack of an ability to compromise led to the Civil War and men and women of good faith on both sides made their stand where their conscience had them make their stand," he said.

Amy Coney Barrett's children were not wearing masks at the Rose Garden event announcing her nomination to the Supreme Court. The event turned into a superspreader event. One teachers and two high school students tested positive for coronavirus at Trinity School, a private school attended by Barrett's children. Two of Barrett's children are high school age. An aide at the school told The New York Times that at least one of Barrett's children attended school in person in the week following the White House event. It is not known whether the White House event led to COVID-19 cases at Barrett's children's school. The White House event led to COVID-19 cases at Barrett's children's school.

Rahm Emanuel, President-elect Obama's chief of staff, had direct discussions with Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich about Obama's vacant Senate seat, the Chicago Sun-Times reported. Sources with knowledge of the conversations told the Sun-Times that Emanuel spoke with the governor and pushed for the appointment of Valerie Jarrett in the days after the presidential election and asked that it be done by a certain date. The sources said Blagojevich told aides about conversations with Emanuel and sometimes gave them directions afterward. Some conversations between Blagojevich and Emanuel were likely caught on tape, the sources said. An Obama source strongly denied Emanuel spoke with the governor directly about the seat, the Sun-Times reported. Sources did not indicate that a deal was brokered in the conversations between Emanuel and Blagojevich. Blagojevich was arrested on corruption charges involving an alleged scheme to sell or trade Obama's vacant Senate seat.

The White House told Ukraine's President Viktor Yanukovich to withdraw security in Kiev as protests worsen and the death toll rises. White House spokesman Jay Carney said in a statement: "We are outraged by images of Ukrainian security forces firing automatic weapons on their own people." Carney said Yanukovich should immediately withdraw his security forces from downtown Kiev, stating that he respects the right of peaceful protest and urges protesters to express themselves peacefully. The violence caused the US State Department to issue a travel alert to Ukraine and place visa bans on 20 Ukrainian officials. Protesters have been in Independence Square since late November when Yanukovich turned down a European Union trade deal in favor of a $15 billion bailout from Russia. The violence escalated on Tuesday after 25 people were killed. The total death tolls between Tuesday and Thursday vary between outlets. Reuters reported 50, but Thursday morning CNN reported more than 100 were killed. Yanukovich announced a truce between him and opposition leaders Wednesday night, but it failed as protesters thought it was a stunt.

High-level talks on Ukraine are set to begin in Geneva on Thursday. American officials said on Wednesday that the meeting is a test of Russia's intentions in the region before the United States and European nations decide whether to impose additional economic sanctions on Moscow. A senior State Department official said the idea is that Russia would stop aiding and abetting and supporting separatists and pull its troops back from the border. The official said Western charges that Russia is behind the separatist protests in eastern Ukraine. The official said if Russia does not take this opportunity to de-escalate, the costs are going to go up. Secretary of State John Kerry will participate in the four-way meeting, which is to be held in a luxury hotel here, along with the Russian foreign minister, Sergey V. Lavrov; Ukraine's acting foreign minister, Andrii Deshchytsia; and Catherine Ashton, the top foreign policy official for the European Union.

On November 4, Vice President Joe Biden suggested Kansas Senate candidate Greg Orman (I) will caucus with Democrats if he defeats Republican incumbent Pat Roberts. Fox News's James Rosen relayed the news during the Election Day airing of The Real Story w/ Gretchen Carlson. Rosen said: "This is a late breaking development involving the White House that is threatening to shake up this very close race in its final hours, with Vice President Joe Biden telling WPLR Radio in Connecticut that Greg Orman 'will be with us.' Rosen pointed out that Orman is "a pro-choice, self-made multi-millionaire businessman running his first political race, and he has been coy about which party he would caucus with in the Senate, if elected." Biden suggested he will caucus with Democrats. The Roberts campaign responded to Biden's statement by stating: "Orman is a Democrat masquerading as an Independent."

Donald Trump sat down with The New York Times on Thursday. The interview took place during a break from his golf schedule. Trump discussed the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. He stated there was no collusion. Trump added that even if there was, "collusion is not a crime." The article noted that Robert Mueller can pack up his tent and go home. It also raised the question of investigations and laws, asking whether Trump has an absolute right to do what he wants with the Justice Department. Trump said Democrats agree there was no collusion and "walk around blinking at each other." The article also included the phrase "Botton line? Trump is nuts."

The White House responded to a book by journalist Michael Wolff. Former White House press secretary Sean Spicer discussed his time at the White House. CNN's Jake Tapper criticized President Donald Trump's claims after White House press secretary Sarah Sanders said people are "not entitled to their own facts" following the book. During winter weather, a Pennsylvania man used a lawnmower and a cardboard box to clear his snow-covered driveway. Late-night talk-show host Jimmy Kimmel criticized Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un over their war of words about nuclear prowess. Paris Hilton shared a video on social media showing her engagement to actor Chris Zylka, with a reported $2 million diamond ring. Spicer told S.E.C. that he knows he made mistakes during his time as Trump's spokesman.

A letter to the editor responded to a New York Times article dated May 5 titled "Trump Says Kentucky Derby Ruling Was 'Not a Good One'." The letter stated that stewards of the Kentucky Derby reviewed evidence and determined that the horse that placed first had competed unfairly and should be disqualified. The letter writer stated that President Trump objected to this. The writer described Trump's objection as a concise reflection of his worldview: that in a horse race, an election, or the presidency, rules and fairness do not matter as long as you win, clear evidence of malfeasance, whether in a video replay or in a special counsel's report, be damned. The writer stated that the Kentucky Derby is a longstanding American tradition whose stewards took seriously their responsibility to ensure a just outcome. The writer wished members of Congress, who are supposed to be the stewards of our democracy, could act as decisively as the stewards of the Derby.

The nonpartisan Commission on Presidential Debates announced Monday that it will implement new rules for Thursday's debate. The 90-minute debate will be divided into six 15-minute segments, with each candidate granted two minutes to deliver uninterrupted remarks before proceeding to an open debate. The open discussion portion of the debate will not feature a mute button, but interruptions by either candidate will count toward their time in the second and final debate on Thursday. The commission announced the rule changes three weeks after a contentious opening between the two presidential contenders that featured frequent interruptions, most by Trump. The commission faced pressure from the Trump campaign to avoid changing the rules, while Biden's team was hoping for a more ordered debate. In a statement, the commission said it "had determined that it is appropriate to adopt measures intended to promote adherence to agreed upon rules and inappropriate to make changes to those rules."

Sen. John McCain, the Arizona Republican who lost his bid for the White House to President Obama, criticized the new commander-in-chief for allowing what he said were over 9,000 earmarks into the $787 billion stimulus bill. McCain spoke to CBS News' Katie Couric on her webcast after Obama's speech to Congress. He criticized Democratic leadership for allowing what he said were over 9,000 earmarks into an omnibus, or catch all, spending bill over more than $400 billion that is set for a vote this week in the House. McCain also questioned Obama's claim that he had passed a stimulus that contained no pork, calling it technically true but false in reality. "In actuality it had billion[s] of dollars of earmarks in it," McCain said. McCain also expressed doubt about Obama's ability to "increase all these spending programs" and still cut the deficit by 2013, which the president has promised to do by half.

Russian President Vladimir Putin sent a New Year telegram to U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday. The Kremlin announced the message. In the telegram, Putin wrote that constructive dialogue between the two nations is essential for global stability. He wrote that the two nations could develop a "pragmatic cooperation aimed at long-term perspective" on the basis of "equality and mutual respect." Putin noted that "the development [of] a constructive Russian-U.S. dialogue is particularly important for strengthening strategic stability in the world and finding the optimal answers to global threats and challenges." Ties between Moscow and Washington declined following Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the allegations of its meddling in the U.S. presidential election last year. In an interview with The New York Times on Thursday, Trump denied Russia colluded in the 2016 presidential adding "even if there was, it's not a crime." The Associated Press contributed to this report.

During an MSNBC interview with Andrea Mitchell, former National Security Adviser Susan Rice said that the investigations into Russia's influence in the 2016 elections "are very important and very serious." Rice rejected any suggestion that the Obama White House surveilled either Trump or his team. "The notion, which some people are trying to suggest, that by asking for the identity of the American person is the same is leaking it — that's completely false," Rice said. "There is no equivalence between so-called unmasking and leaking." Rice also said that the sitting president has no personal authority to order surveillance of any American, rendering Trump's claims implausible. Her appearance drew immediate criticism from the White House. "Yes, that's the official White House director of social media. Just so you have yet another comparison between the members of any previous White House and this ... attempt," Rice said. Comments on the story are closed.

A letter to the editor responded to the "Syria and the Arab League" (editorial, Nov. 9). The letter stated that the world community can and should do more to end President Bashar al-Assad's violence against civilians in Syria. The letter stated that corporations that choose to do business with Syria must also recognize and stop their contribution to Mr. Assad's campaign of violence. The letter stated that oil companies that fuel nearly 30 percent of Syria's economy should cease operations, and that banks that enable financial transactions with the regime should freeze accounts. The letter also stated that any company that provides direct support to Mr. Assad's regime, including Area SpA, the Italian company building a surveillance system for Syria, must be vilified. The letter stated that Governments can refuse to do business with any company aiding and abetting mass atrocities, which the letter described as the aim of the Syria Sanctions Act, introduced by Senator Kirsten E. Gillibrand of New York. The letter added that companies themselves know whether they are profiting from bloodshed and violence; they need to value human lives above their own profits.

President Obama pledged to use the remainder of his presidency to address income inequality, which he called "the defining challenge of our time." This holiday weekend, Mr. Obama marked the birthday of the civil rights leader the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. with a visit to the D.C. Central Kitchen, where he, Michelle Obama and their daughters, Malia and Sasha, donned aprons and prepared burritos for distribution to local homeless shelters. On Saturday, the Obamas marked Mrs. Obama's 50th birthday with a party at the White House, with music by Beyoncé. Guests included Stevie Wonder, who also sang, Paul McCartney and Samuel L. Jackson. Those who brought cellphones were asked to check them at the door, presumably to prevent photographs on Twitter, Instagram and Facebook.

On Friday, President Obama spoke about race relations in America, saying "Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago." His extensive and personal comments called on Americans to "do some soul-searching." Obama's speech about race relations in America on July 19, 2013, said, "The African American community is looking at this issue through a set of experiences and a history that doesn't go away." During the 2008 campaign, then-senator Obama urged America to "move beyond our racial wounds" in his 'A More Perfect Union' speech. "Race is an issue that I believe this nation cannot afford to ignore right now," he said to the Philadelphia audience. In 2009, when asked about the arrest of Harvard scholar Henry Louis Gates, Obama said, "It's a sign of how race remains a factor in this society."

Trevor Noah criticized President Donald Trump's tweeted threats to fire missiles at Syria in retaliation for its domestic chemical attack. Noah, host of "The Daily Show," said on Wednesday that the president's choice of words appeared to be a matchmaker rather than a world leader. Trump responded to Russia's warning that it would shoot down any U.S. missiles by tweeting: "Get ready Russia because they will be coming nice and new and 'smart.' " Noah said: "It sounds like he's trying to fix them up with the missiles. It's like he's saying to the Russians, 'I know you don't like blind dates but these missiles they're really nice, really smart. Just come, no pressure. It's just a launch.'"
