Baltimore Mayor Catherine Pugh announced Tuesday she has accepted the resignation of police commissioner Darryl De Sousa. De Sousa, a salaried employee of the Baltimore Police Department, faces three misdemeanor counts of failing to file a federal return for tax years 2013, 2014, and 2015. The U.S. attorney's office alleged that De Sousa willfully failed to file a federal return for tax years 2013, 2014, and 2015. He was a salaried employee of the Baltimore Police Department in each of those years. De Sousa faces up to one year in prison and a $25,000 fine for each of the three misdemeanor counts. De Sousa's attorney, Steven Silverman, said federal prosecutors did not give his client a chance to offer an explanation or to file late tax returns before bringing criminal charges.

On Tuesday, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-CT) held a press conference on the steps of the Supreme Court. Blumenthal said President Donald Trump's Supreme Court nominee Judge Brett Kavanaugh must agree to recuse himself from cases involving "Trump's personal financial dealings" and special counsel Robert Mueller's probe. Blumenthal said, "I'm a no on this nominee. My colleagues should be a no on this nominee unless Judge Kavanaugh specifically commits that he will recuse himself on any issues that involve President Trump's personal financial dealings or the special counsel." He added, "He would be the swing vote. Judge Kavanaugh, if he is a justice, would be the swing vote in deciding whether he can pardon himself—get out of jail free pass. That's the accountability that will be lost if Judge Kavanaugh is confirmed. Likewise, whether he can be called before a grand jury—whether he can be indicted while he is still president."

U.S. Sen. Mark Kirk underwent surgery today at Northwestern Memorial Hospital after suffering a stroke, his office said. On Saturday, Kirk checked himself into Lake Forest Hospital, where doctors discovered a carotid artery dissection in the right side of his neck. He was transferred to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in Chicago, where further tests revealed that he had suffered an ischemic stroke. Early this morning, the senator underwent surgery to relieve swelling around his brain stemming from the stroke. The surgery was successful. Doctors are very confident in the Senator's recovery over the weeks ahead. The office released no other details. Kirk, 52, captured President Barack Obama's old U.S. Senate seat in a close 2010 election against Democrat Alexi Giannoulias.

Eric Cantor's primary defeat against David Brat on Tuesday means that House Republicans will lose one of their best fund-raisers and a crucial link to some major donors the party is otherwise not close to. Mr. Cantor's leadership PAC, which he uses to distribute campaign money to his House colleagues and to Republican candidates, has raised more money since the beginning of 2013 than any other run by a member of Congress. It brought in more than $3.5 million from last year until April 30. Figures for May will be available by June 20. Even as he raised millions for his own race, Mr. Cantor pushed hundreds of thousands of dollars to his colleagues and to his local party. Part of his fund-raising success is due to his position as majority leader, and his successor will have similar sway. But Mr. Cantor has also shown an ability to raise money from donors some Republicans struggle to attract — and that will be harder for the party to replace.

During his first State of the Union address Tuesday, President Donald Trump mentioned the words "immigrants" and "immigration" more than any other president in the last 100 years since President Woodrow Wilson started delivering the State of the Union as a speech instead of a written report. The article noted that words and phrases were used in this year's State of the Union speech and in speeches and annual addresses past. It also noted that every square represents one instance and the quote from that speech can be accessed by hovering over a square. The analysis includes annual addresses to Congress and State of the Union addresses. It includes written addresses where oral addresses are not available (1919, 1920, 1924, 1932, 1946). The 1946 address was a lengthy written address, which may skew some results.

Republican presidential candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) said on Mike Gallagher's radio program that he will not punish a staffer who spread a report that Ben Carson was dropping out of the race. Cruz said he does not make it a practice of disciplining people for passing on public news reports. Cruz reiterated that his political staff circulated a CNN report on Monday night during the caucus indicating Carson was returning to Florida instead of going to New Hampshire or South Carolina, the next primary states. The Texas senator said that his aides did not circulate a follow-up report clarifying that Carson was simply returning home to Florida for a brief break from the campaign trail but was in fact continuing on with his presidential campaign. Cruz said Wednesday that the news turned out to be accurate — he did indeed return to Florida. He apologized to Carson if his staff passing on the news report caused Carson "discomfort."

President Trump said the jacket first lady Melania Trump wore while boarding a plane to Texas to visit illegal-immigrant detention camps was a gibe at the media. The jacket had graffiti-like lettering spelling out "I really don't care, do u." Media types called the jacket insensitive in light of their insistence that the Trump administration was torturing children. Trump tweeted Thursday evening: "I REALLY DON'T CARE, DO U? The Fake News Media. Melania has learned how dishonest they are, and she truly no longer cares!" The president tweeted: "I REALLY DON'T CARE, DO U? The Fake News Media. Melania has learned how dishonest they are, and she truly no longer cares!"

The author wrote for the first time that they had written President Obama at the White House. The author wrote: "Thank you for your diligent work of behalf of the American people over the last six years. In the next two, you will have challenges keeping Congress from impeding your, and our, agenda to make the USA a better place. I think you are a truly great president, and although I do think you could have done more, sooner, I'll not quibble. I write this to offer my support of $50 to buy ink for your veto pen that I hope you use aggressively over the next two years. Where can I send my $50? I would be proud knowing the very ink flowing from your pen was paid for by me and other supporters in our joint effort to stop the spread of injustice, intolerance, ignorance, and ineptitude. I voted for you twice and would again. I am a firefighter in Austin, Texas and wish you the best in keeping down the flames of hate. Thank you for your wisdom and service."

Gary D. Cohn, the chief White House economic adviser, is convening senior climate and energy ministers from about a dozen nations in New York next Monday, the White House confirmed Tuesday. The breakfast will be held against a backdrop of devastation in the United States and the Caribbean from two hurricanes that scientists say may have been made more ferocious by warming trends. The Trump administration has declared it will withdraw from the global Paris agreement while also telling nations it remains open to continued discussions. Invitations were sent to officials from the world's largest economies. The event is billed as "an opportunity for key ministers with responsibility for these issues to engage in an informal exchange of views and discuss how we can move forward most productively," according to the invitation. The note says the group will be kept small and include ministerial-level officials only.

Donald Trump held a cabinet meeting. As reporters were being ushered out of the room, Trump declared to all in attendance that "there has never been a president as tough on Russia as I have been." The article reported that worldwide laughter was heard as the words were spoken. The article also stated that if Trump does not believe the Russians are engaged in cyber warfare and are actively working to interfere in the 2018 elections, it seems clear he is not doing anything to stop them. The article also stated that National intelligence officials should be walking out the door today, demanding Trump's resignation.

The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on two high-profile gay marriage cases this week. The Court has written and talked about what the Court said. A Pew Research Center chart shows the results. The chart was produced from a question asking respondents to name the Chief Justice of the United States from a handful of options. Less than three in ten respondents were able to name John Roberts as the current Chief Justice. More than half did not know who it was. Nearly one in five people named Thurgood Marshall, who was deceased and never Chief Justice, while four percent chose Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, who is not on the Supreme Court.

A CBS/NYT poll conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday found that a plurality of Americans approve of President Obama's response to Ferguson, while 34 percent are dissatisfied and 25 percent have an opinion. African-Americans were more likely to approve of the president than whites, whose attitudes split along party lines. Missouri Gov. Jay Nixon received less favorable reviews overall. Among blacks nationally, a quarter of blacks were satisfied with Nixon's actions, while nearly half said Nixon's performance in the aftermath of the shooting was not satisfactory. Among whites, a third were satisfied and a third dissatisfied. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percent among whites and ±8 percent among African-Americans.

A video surfaced Wednesday of President Trump's visit to the University Medical Center of El Paso following a mass shooting. The video shows Trump conversing with doctors and others at the hospital. The video shows Trump discussing crowd sizes at political rallies held in February, including one held by O'Rourke. Trump says of the February rally: "That was some crowd. We had twice the number outside. And then you had this crazy Beto. Beto had like 400 people in a parking lot, and they said his crowd was wonderful." Trump expressed frustration to aides on Air Force One that news cameras were not with him in the hospital on Wednesday and that coverage of the trip was being dominated by his opponents.

Republican presidential candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) released an advertisement in South Carolina stating, "When it comes to appointing a Supreme Court justice, "We cannot trust Donald Trump." The ad states, "Life, marriage, religious liberty, the Second Amendment. We're just one Supreme Court justice away from losing them all." The advertisement also references Donald Trump on the issue of abortion. The advertisement plays a 1999 interview in which NBC anchor Time Russert asked Trump whether a hypothetical President Trump would "ban partial-birth abortions." Trump responded, "Well, look, I'm very pro-choice. But you would not ban it?" Russert asked again. Trump said, "No, I am pro-choice in every respect." The ad ends with: "We cannot trust Donald Trump with these serious decisions."

Bill Maher criticized President Donald Trump's close relationship with Fox News host Sean Hannity on Friday's broadcast of "Real Time." Maher discussed the courtroom revelation that Hannity was the mystery client of Trump's personal attorney Michael Cohen. Maher acknowledged that he "got" that Hannity "obviously carries Trump's water every day on the air." Maher also addressed the revelation that Hannity reportedly talks with the president every day. "I mean, this is such a violation of what the Fourth Estate is supposed to be. It's not supposed to be a branch of the First Estate," Maher said. "Can you imagine if they found out that (former President Barack) Obama was talking to Rachel Maddow every day?"

Fox News co-moderator Megyn Kelly asked former Florida governor Jeb Bush a question about "your brother's war" at the Republican presidential debate in Cleveland on Thursday evening. Bush had already fielded one question from co-moderator Bret Baier about George W. Bush, and whether he was his "own man." Kelly also asked frontrunner Donald Trump about his past statements about women. Bush described the Iraq War as "your brother's war." Bush had already answered one question about his brother. Co-moderator Chris Wallace also asked Bush a question in which he referred to "your father and your brother."

North Korea denied reports it had cooperated with Syria on chemical weapons, state media reported late Thursday. KCNA, the Korean Central News Agency, cited a KCNA news agency spokesman as saying the United States made a "nonsensical argument" that it helped Syria produce chemical weapons. KCNA quoted the spokesman as saying: "As we have clearly said several times, our republic does not develop, produce and stockpile chemical weapons and opposes chemical weapons themselves." Robert Wood, U.S. disarmament ambassador to the Conference on Disarmament, said on Wednesday that there has been a history of a relationship between the two countries with regard to missile activity, chemical weapons components. Two North Korean shipments to a Syrian government agency responsible for the country's chemical weapons program were intercepted in the past six months, according to a confidential UN report on North Korea sanctions violations.

Top U.S. diplomat Rex Tillerson and Turkey's Tayyip Erdogan had a "productive and open" talk on Thursday about improving ties strained recently over their policies on Syria, in a meeting following weeks of escalating anti-American rhetoric from Ankara. Tillerson arrived in Turkey on Thursday for two days of what officials said would likely be uncomfortable discussions between the allies. The two sides have relations frayed over a number of issues, particularly U.S. support for the Syrian Kurdish YPG militia, which Turkey considers terrorists. Turkey launched an air and ground assault last month in Syria's northwest Afrin region to drive the YPG from the area south of its border. Ankara considers the YPG to be an arm of the PKK, a banned group that has waged a decades-long insurgency in Turkey. The militia is the main ground element of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), which the United States has armed, trained and aided with air support and special forces to fight Islamic State.

Fox News co-moderator Megyn Kelly asked former Florida governor Jeb Bush a question about "your brother's war" at the Republican presidential debate in Cleveland on Thursday evening. Bush had already fielded one question from co-moderator Bret Baier about George W. Bush, and whether he was his "own man." Kelly also asked frontrunner Donald Trump about his past statements about women. Bush described the Iraq War as "your brother's war." Bush had already answered one question about his brother. Co-moderator Chris Wallace also asked Bush a question in which he referred to "your father and your brother."

President Barack Obama signed into law Friday a final bill authored by former Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, who was wounded in an Arizona shooting a year ago. Giffords participated in the signing ceremony at the White House. She resigned from Congress last month as she continues to recover from a gunshot wound to the head. The legislation increases the penalties for using ultra-light aircraft when smuggling drugs into the country. The small, single-seat planes are an increasingly favored tool that smugglers use to fly at night and then release their haul without detection. Obama said he told Giffords that he expected to see more of her in the months and years to come. "I'm confident that, while this legislation may have been her last act as a congresswoman, it will not be her last act of public service," Obama said in a statement released by the White House. Giffords stepped down on the day the House passed her bill by a vote of 428-0.

The New York Post reported that Jeffrey Corzine, the son of former New Jersey Gov. Jon Corzine, was found dead from an apparent suicide in a Mexico City hotel on Thursday. Corzine was 31 years old. He was the youngest of Corzine's three children with his ex-wife Joanne. Sources told The Post that the son of former New Jersey Gov. Jon Corzine killed himself in a Mexico City hotel. The Post also reported that Jeffrey Corzine was described as depressed and had been drinking heavily recently. According to previous statements from his family, he was thought to have been "clean" and "doing well" until now. Sources said the younger Corzine had a history of substance-abuse problems and had been in and out of rehab. But he had been living in California and working as a drug counselor, and had appeared to have turned his life around, one source said.

President Obama and Hillary Clinton conducted a joint "60 Minutes" interview on Sunday. During the interview, Obama praised each other. Interviewer Steve Kroft noted that the interview was unorthodox and wondered whether it had any implications for the 2016 elections. Kroft asked Clinton, "I have to ask you, what's the date of expiration on this endorsement?" Clinton said, "Oh, Steve," and "Everyone in this town is talking about it!" Clinton laughed. Obama said, "Steve, you guys in the press are incorrigible. I literally got inaugurated four days ago, and you're talking about elections four years from now!" Clinton added, "As you know, Steve, I am still secretary of state. So I'm out of politics. And I'm forbidden from even hearing these questions."

On Tuesday, former President Bill Clinton appeared on CBS's "The Late Show" and addressed an earlier appearance on NBC's "Today." In the interview, Clinton said he did not owe former White House intern Monica Lewinsky an apology for inappropriate sexual conduct. Clinton said: "When I saw the interview, I thought that — because they had to, you know, distill it. It looked like I was saying that I didn't apologize and I had no intention to. And I was mad at me." He continued: "It wasn't my finest hour. I meant it then; I mean it now. I've had to live with the consequences every day since." Clinton added: "I still believe this #MeToo movement is long overdue, necessary, and should be supported."

On Sunday, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appeared on CBS' "Face The Nation." He said he was "baffled" by the White House's criticisms of Israeli settlements because "ethnic purification" goes "against the American values." Last week, after a Jewish group announced settlers were moving into several apartment buildings purchased in a predominantly Arab neighborhood in Jerusalem, the White House criticized Israel, saying the move is "poisoning" the peace process. Netanyahu said that putting any restrictions on where Jews could live is "against the American values. And it doesn't bode well for peace." He said not allowing Jews and Arabs to live together is promoting "ethnic purification." "The idea that we'd have this ethnic purification as a condition for peace, I think it's anti-peace," he added.

On Saturday, Donald Trump criticized Fox News on Twitter regarding Sunday interviews with former FBI Director James Comey and Rep. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.). Both men are being interviewed by Chris Wallace on "Fox News Sunday." Trump wrote that Fox News was trying "sooo hard to be politically correct." He added that "only pro Trump Fox shows do well," and that "Rest are nothing." Trump also asked, "How's Shep doing?" — referring to former Fox News host Shepard Smith, who frequently criticized Trump and left the network in October. Trump also criticized MSNBC, calling it "Commiecast" MSNBC. Twitter users responded with criticism of the Fox News interview.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR) denounced the Iranian nuclear deal, which President Obama praised early Tuesday morning, calling it a mistake. In an interview on MSNBC's Morning Joe, Cotton said, "This proposed deal is a terrible dangerous mistake that's going to pave the path for Iran to get a nuclear weapon while giving them tens of billions of dollars of sanctions relief." Cotton, a freshman senator, has made his opposition to the deal the center of his political career. He described Iran as an "outlaw, terrorist sponsoring, anti-American regime" and criticized the deal for leaving its nuclear program intact. Cotton said he believed Congress would oppose the deal once the full details of the deal were released, citing provisions such as lifting the arms embargo on Iran and the weakness of requirements of nuclear inspections. "The American people will repudiate this and I believe Congress will kill the deal," he stated.

A letter to the editor responded to a May 30 news article titled "White House Asked Navy to Hide McCain Warship." The writer stated that President Trump's denial that he was aware of the White House's request that the Navy hide the destroyer John S. McCain during his trip to Japan raises two possibilities. The writer said this would not be in the least surprising, both because Mr. Trump lies continually and because there is no act of shabby vindictiveness to which he will not stoop. The writer also said this is one of the vanishingly rare cases in which he is telling the truth. The writer said this in turn would mean that although he does not have a grip on what is happening in his own White House, he has created a climate of appalling small-mindedness and of indifference to the political neutrality of the armed forces. The writer said neither possibility suits the dignity of a proud democracy. The writer is a retired United States Air Force colonel.

President Obama summoned the heads of some of the nation's largest financial institutions to the White House on Friday and urged them to accept responsibility for their industry's excesses. The 13 chief executives emerged from the 90-minute meeting pledging to cooperate with the administration's efforts to shore up the banking industry and the broader economy. Administration officials and the bankers presented a unified message to the nation: We're all in this together. The White House had asked the banks on Thursday to provide broad, public endorsements of the administration's financial recovery program, according to bank officials. With the White House in the background, one executive after another offered support for the president's efforts in several television interviews coordinated by the administration.

An Army sergeant who served as a sexual assault prevention and response coordinator at Fort Hood, Tex., is under investigation for allegations of pandering, abusive sexual contact, assault and maltreatment of subordinates, Pentagon officials said late Tuesday. The inquiry comes as the White House, the Pentagon and the armed services are working to address the problem of sexual assault in the military. The Pentagon released a survey last week estimating that 26,000 people in the armed forces were sexually assaulted last year, up from 19,000 in 2010. A separate report recorded 3,374 sexual assault reports last year, a lower number than the survey, suggesting many victims are not reporting the crimes. The noncommissioned officer under investigation had been working as an equal opportunity adviser and sexual harassment/assault response and prevention program coordinator with a battalion of troops — about 2,000 soldiers — assigned to the Army's III Corps at Fort Hood when the allegations surfaced, the Pentagon said in a statement.

Iran's official IRNA news agency reported Tuesday that Kavous Seyed-Emami, a dual Iranian and Canadian citizen, killed himself in custody. The report said Seyed-Emami was in custody for passing information on the country's missile bases to the CIA and Mossad and planning to create environmental crisis. IRNA did not elaborate. Tehran prosecutor Abbas Jafari Dolatabdi said Seyed-Emami and a network of people installed cameras in strategic areas of the country pretending to observe environmental issues but, in fact, it was for monitoring the country's missile activities and they were sending images and information to foreigners. Dolatabdi said Seyed-Emami hosted one of two U.S. intelligence officers during their visit to Iran. He did not elaborate. On Monday, Iran said Seyed-Emami took his own life.

Donald Trump appeared in a Wednesday interview with the conservative outlet the Daily Caller. In 2017, Trump told NBC's Lester Holt that "this Russia thing" was on his mind when he fired then-FBI Director James Comey. Trump associated the Russia probe with his appointment of acting Attorney General Matthew Whitaker. "I knew him only as he pertained, you know, as he was with Jeff Sessions," Trump said in response to his "thinking" about the attorney general position. "And, you know, look, as far as I'm concerned this is an investigation that should have never been brought. It should have never been had. It's something that should have never been brought. It's an illegal investigation."

Michelle Obama said her daughters, Sasha, 9, and Malia, 12, do not use Facebook. During an interview on NBC's "Today Show" on Wednesday, she said she is "not a big fan of young kids having Facebook." She added that Facebook is "not something they need." "It depends on when we leave and how old they are," she said. The question asked whether the girls would join the social networking site after the Obamas left the White House. Facebook's rules do not permit users under 13 years of age to use the site.

Donald Trump Jr. said that if his father loses to Hillary Clinton in Tuesday's presidential election, the Republican nominee would concede defeat if the process is "legit and fair." On MSNBC's "Morning Joe," when asked if his father would concede defeat in the event of a "clear cut" win for Mrs. Clinton, Donald Trump Jr. said, "Of course — all we've wanted is a fair fight." He added, "If he loses and it's legit and fair, and there's not obvious stuff out there — without question, yes." During the third presidential debate, Donald Trump Jr. said he would keep people in suspense about whether he would accept the results of the election. He later said he would accept the results if he won.

On Thursday, a fourth night of protests occurred following the death of 16-year-old Kimani Gray, who was shot and killed by NYPD officers outside his best friend's house in East Flatbush, Brooklyn. Police maintain Gray was armed and pointed a weapon at officers. Demonstrators have since been arrested, and a police officer suffered a wound to his face after being hit by an object. Mayor Michael Bloomberg said a "full and fair" investigation into the shooting would be conducted and urged community members to abstain from violence. "I understand that there's anger in the community, but the way to get answers is not through violence or law-breaking," Bloomberg said. "We cannot tolerate that, and we will not tolerate that." HuffPost Live examined Gray's death to ask whether NYPD officers are disconnected with the communities they serve to protect.

David Friedman, the acting administrator of the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, testifies on Tuesday before a House subcommittee looking into the ignition problem of Chevrolet Cobalts and other cars. In written testimony filed in advance, Friedman argues that General Motors had critical information that would have helped identify the defect. Formal written testimony is usually not read in its entirety at a hearing but becomes part of the official record and gives strong indications about the tack witnesses will take in the question-and-answer session that follows. Friedman is scheduled to testify before the House Energy and Commerce subcommittee on oversight and investigations. The other witness is Mary T. Barra, the chief executive of General Motors. Barra is expected to apologize but not provide answers to why G.M. did not act for more than a decade to fix the problem.

Robert M. Gates wrote in his early biography of his tenure as defense secretary that Hillary Rodham Clinton performed better than President Obama or Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. Gates wrote that Obama could be cynical and controlling, and that Biden had an unerring capacity to be wrong on big issues. In Gates's assessment, Clinton was described as smart, idealistic but pragmatic, tough-minded, indefatigable, a very valuable colleague, and a superb representative of the United States all over the world. Gates also wrote that Clinton was described as smart, idealistic but pragmatic, tough-minded, indefatigable, and a superb representative of the United States all over the world. Gates's assessment differs from his earlier assessment of Clinton as secretary of state, which drew attention to her statement that she opposed the Iraq troop "surge" for political reasons during the 2008 Democratic primaries.

Republican presidential candidate Dr. Ben Carson cancelled all remaining campaign events and traveled to Omaha, Nebraska, to assist campaign staff involved in a car accident on Tuesday. A press release from the Carson campaign stated that a van transporting three campaign volunteers and a campaign employee hit a patch of ice and flipped on its side, striking another vehicle. Three passengers, including the campaign staffer driving, were checked out at Cass County Memorial Hospital in Atlantic, Iowa. One volunteer was transported to the trauma center at the University of Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha, Nebraska. The campaign said Carson spoke with the attending physician and family of the volunteer being transported to Omaha. The press release also stated that Carson had cancelled all remaining campaign events and would be traveling to Omaha this afternoon to be with the family during this difficult time.

In January 1998, as the White House was affected by the Monica Lewinsky scandal, aides offered advice to President Bill Clinton's speechwriting team on how to use the State of the Union address that month to rebuild public confidence in the president. Minyon Moore, the president's public liaison, wrote in a memo: "Please recognize, I am in no way suggesting that he use his speech to discuss our current situation head-on. I am simply stating that we cannot take his supporters for granted, nor his detractors, and they need to be reassured on several fronts." Moore suggested that Mr. Clinton invoke God "as the underpinning for his policy and thought process." Her memo was among the roughly 2,500 pages of documents from the Clinton White House years that were made public on Friday by the National Archives. More of the 30,000 documents will be released over the next several weeks.

President Trump said Wednesday that a New York Times report showing he lost more than $1 billion from 1985 to 1994 does not accurately depict real estate practices during that time frame. Trump tweeted: "Real estate developers in the 1980's & 1990's, more than 30 years ago, were entitled to massive write offs and depreciation which would, if one was actively building, show losses and tax losses in almost all cases. Much was non monetary. Sometimes considered 'tax shelter,' you would get it by building, or even buying." He added: "You always wanted to show losses for tax purposes….almost all real estate developers did - and often re-negotiate with banks, it was sport. Additionally, the very old information put out is a highly inaccurate Fake News hit job."

The author wrote that when Trump is not doing his best to scare the bejesus out of voters by threatening them with graphic visions of hordes of invading brown-skinned rapists, robbers, and murderers rampaging through their homes, Trump claims that he is solely responsible for the current strength of the economy. The author suggested a non-tribal, non-prevaricating look at the economy to determine whether Trump is the real deal or just another con-man. The author wrote that the author cannot judge Trump's economy by his claims about the stock market or economic statistics or even the unemployment rate. The author said to look at the living standards of average working Americans like them and see the economy is worse, not better, under Trump. The author asked whether the living standard is better or worse than it was on January 20, 2017.

Melania Trump broke ground on the White House tennis pavilion on Tuesday. The pavilion will be funded by private donations. The White House said the project is driven by Mrs. Trump's respect for classical architecture and her passion to provide a functional recreational area for all First Families. The White House said the pavilion utilizes the historic Children's Garden, compliments the architecture of the Executive Mansion, and draws on inspiration from both the East and West wings. Mrs. Trump said: "As we break ground on the new tennis pavilion, it is a great honor to share this moment alongside the many talented individuals and craftsmen involved in bringing it to fruition." She added: "Architectural inspiration for the pavilion is drawn from the White House, with the end goal of the new structure on the south lawn complementing and contributing to the People's house. It is my hope that this private space will function as a place to gather and spend leisure time for First Families."

The U.S. State Department has chartered two flights to evacuate passengers aboard the Diamond Princess cruise ship, currently docked in Yokahama, located about 20 miles south of Tokyo. One flight will land at Travis Air Force Base in northern California while the other will be taken to Lackland Air Force Base in San Antonio, Texas. The United States Department of Defense officials confirmed the flights. The passengers will be subjected to a mandatory 14-day quarantine period managed by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control after arrival. Should any of the evacuees test positive or become symptomatic with the coronavirus, they will be transferred to a "suitable" off base medical facility, Department of Defense officials said.

Sen. Pat Roberts apologized Thursday after receiving backlash for a joke he made about mammograms while discussing the Republicans' plan to repeal and replace Obamacare. A Talking Points Memo reporter asked the Kansas Republican if he supports a potential change in the GOP's plan that would scrap Obamacare's Essential Health Benefits rule, which requires insurers to cover "essential" health services like maternity care and mammograms. He said in a statement that he knows "several individuals whose lives have been saved by mammograms" and understands their importance, CNN reported. Before he issued his apology Thursday, Roberts told CNN that he does not think all benefits declared "essential" are really necessary, and that people should be able to choose plans that cater to what they think is essential. Asked whether mammograms should be covered, Roberts suggested he would not need them because he is a man, CNN reported.

The White House said there are two words President Barack Obama will not say Tuesday night in his speech about the end of the U.S. combat role in Iraq: "Mission accomplished." Seven years ago, President George W. Bush stood on an aircraft carrier to declare an end to major combat operations in Iraq. A banner proclaiming "Mission Accomplished" flew nearby. The Bush White House expressed regret about that sign as the war dragged on and U.S. deaths mounted. "You won't hear those words coming from us," Obama spokesman Robert Gibbs said. Instead, Gibbs said, Obama will talk about what is involved in the U.S. troop drawdown and the changing mission in Iraq. Gibbs said Obama plans to call Bush on Tuesday before delivering his Oval Office address, though he would not say what Obama's message to his predecessor would be. Obama also called Bush last year before delivering a speech laying out the Iraq withdrawal timeline.

Puerto Rico's Department of Education said Wednesday that a U.S. judge issued an arrest warrant for the agency's boss but later withdrew it after officials pledged to submit documents related to a federal investigation. The department said the unidentified documents sought by the court are from 2011 to 2013, before Julia Keleher was appointed education secretary in December 2016. The documents are being sought as part of an investigation into a school tutoring program, officials said. The department's statement contradicted an earlier interview published by the newspaper Primera Hora that quoted Pedro Fortier of the U.S. Marshals Service as saying an arrest warrant was not issued. Fortier did not return messages for comment. Lymarie Llovet, a spokeswoman for the U.S. Attorney's office, also said an arrest warrant was issued. She added that the documents in the case are sealed and that she had no further details.

The Obamas welcomed a new member to the first family, a 14-month-old female Portuguese Water dog called Sunny. In an interview with CNN's Chris Cuomo on Friday, President Obama revealed details about the new puppy. "Bo was getting lonely," the president said when asked why they got Sunny. "[He] was getting a little down in the dumps inside the house." With Sunny around, the 4-year-old Bo has a playmate. Sunny (left) hangs out with Bo Obama. First Lady Michelle Obama is in "full parenting mode," the president said, especially because little Sunny has already had a few accidents in the White House. The president did not seem concerned. "We live in rental housing. We didn't have to put down a deposit," he said. "But we are making sure that it gets cleaned up for the next occupant."

The Federal Communications Commission will double the amount of money it devotes to adding high-speed Internet connections in schools and libraries over the next two years, officials said Saturday. The increase is in an effort to meet President Obama's promise to provide broadband service for an estimated 20 million American students in 15,000 schools. Financing for the new spending will come from restructuring the $2.4 billion E-Rate program, which provides money for "advanced telecommunications and information services" using the proceeds of fees paid by telecommunications users. The proportion that goes to broadband service in schools and libraries will increase to $2 billion a year from $1 billion. Mr. Obama referred to the changes during his State of the Union address last week. The changes will not require any additional taxes or assessments, according to an F.C.C. official who spoke on the condition of anonymity because a formal announcement was being planned for this week.

Sixty years after the Supreme Court outlawed "separate but equal" schools for blacks and whites, civil rights advocates say American schools are becoming increasingly segregated. Michelle Obama, the first lady, spoke Friday in Topeka, Kan., to 1,200 graduating high school seniors. She said, "Today, by some measures, our schools are as segregated as they were back when Dr. King gave his final speech." The speech was part commencement address, part policy pronouncement and part journey into her own past. Obama said that Brown's advances were being reversed. She said, "Many districts in this country have actually pulled back on efforts to integrate their schools, and many communities have become less diverse," leading to schools that are less diverse.

A blaze damaged the William J Clinton Birthplace, a National Historic Site in Hope, Arkansas, early Christmas morning. Authorities said the fire began at about 3.20 a.m. The cause was suspected to be arson. The Hope Fire Department Chief Dale Glanton said the building does not appear to have been set on fire by accident. As of this writing, no area churches or their nativity scenes were set ablaze, lending to the appearance of graffiti at the scene.

Former CIA director John Brennan posted on social media on Friday that his presidency is "collapsing." Brennan wrote: "Your kakistocracy is collapsing after its lamentable journey. As the greatest Nation history has known, we have the opportunity to emerge from this nightmare stronger & more committed to ensuring a better life for all Americans, including those you have so tragically deceived." Brennan defined a system of government run by the worst, least qualified, or most unscrupulous citizens. He was responding to Trump's criticisms of former FBI Director James Comey on Twitter, describing Comey as an "untruthful slime ball who was, as time has proven, a terrible Director of the FBI." Comey is out with a new book that is highly critical of the president, who fired the FBI director a year ago.

A special agent with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Homeland Security Investigations unit, Kelton Harrison, was shot and wounded early Tuesday while on surveillance in northern Hidalgo County, Texas, officials said. ICE spokeswoman Nina Pruneda said in a statement that Harrison was listed in stable condition by mid-afternoon after being taken to a local hospital where he underwent surgery for a gunshot wound. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the special agent and his family," she added. The shooting happened early in a brushy area just outside Hargill, Texas, ICE said. The FBI field office in San Antonio said Tuesday it was involved in an investigation that the agency called an "AFO" or assault upon a federal officer. A spokesman for the FBI, Erik Vasys, would not offer any more details. The Texas Department of Public Safety, the Texas Rangers and the Hidalgo County Sheriff's Office were also assisting the case, ICE said.

President Donald Trump posted on Twitter early Saturday that there was "great support coming from all sides" for border security and his promised U.S.-Mexico border wall. The Associated Press reported that this was not the case. Trump is refusing to end the partial government shutdown unless Democrats grant him federal funding for the wall that he originally told voters Mexico would pay for. Democratic lawmakers, including House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, have said they do not endorse the wall idea. Talks between Trump's White House and congressional staffers are set to continue Saturday as they attempt to negotiate an end to the shutdown, the Associated Press reported. Trump followed up with another tweet in which he suggested how Democrats "could solve the Shutdown problem in a very short period of time." He wrote: "All they have to do is approve REAL Border Security (including a Wall), this would be so easy to do!"

Rep. Raul Labrador (R-ID) has officially entered the race for House Majority Leader and will face Rep. Kevin McCarthy (R-CA) for the chance to succeed Rep. Eric Cantor (R-VA), who lost his congressional primary this week and will step down by the end of July. Labrador's entry, reported by Politico, comes after Rep. Pete Sessions (R-TX) withdrew from the race, citing the need to avoid "division" in the Republican Party. House Conservatives had hoped to contest a major leadership office, especially after Cantor's defeat by conservative Dave Brat, and after leadership elections in 2011 and 2013 did not elevate any Tea Party members to senior positions in the caucus. Labrador, who is Latino, is also an opponent of comprehensive immigration reform as passed by the Senate, which was a key issue in Cantor's primary, and withdrew from bipartisan talks last year.

David Axelrod, a former top adviser to President Obama, said Sunday that it was a "mistake" for Obama to say in a speech last week that his policies are effectively on the ballot in the midterm elections this fall. "I wouldn't put that line there," Axelrod said on NBC's "Meet The Press." In a Thursday speech, Obama said: "I am not on the ballot this fall. Michelle's pretty happy about that. But make no mistake: These policies are on the ballot. Every single one of them." Republicans began running attack ads using the words to tie Democratic congressional candidates to the president, who polls show is unpopular. Axelrod added, "Understand, if you read the speech, the context of the line was the things he's pushing forward — minimum wage, pay equity, infrastructure — and he said these are on the ballot." But Axelrod concluded, "It was a mistake."

Former President Jimmy Carter announced Sunday that his most recent scan shows he is cancer free. Carter, 91, made the announcement near the beginning of Sunday School class he was teaching at Maranatha Baptist Church in Plains, according to Jill Stuckey, a close friend and fellow church member. Stuckey said by phone from Maranatha, where Carter was teaching to about 350 people, many of them visitors, that the church erupted in applause. In August, Carter said doctors had found four small melanoma lesions on his brain. The discovery followed the removal of a lesion on his liver that took about ten percent of the organ. He said he would receive four drug treatments, along with radiation therapy, and that he would cut back significantly on his schedule.

On Wednesday, on the Senate floor, Judiciary Committee member Sen. Jeff Flake (R-AZ) said he will oppose advancing any of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations out of committee until legislation protecting Department of Justice special counsel Robert Mueller receives a full Senate vote. Flake expressed concern for Mueller's Russian investigation after the appointment of Matthew Whitaker as acting Attorney General. After Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) blocked a full vote, Flake said, "One further note on this unanimous consent that has just failed today. Senator Coons and I are prepared to make it again and again until there is a vote on this vital bipartisan legislation on the Senate floor. I have informed the majority leader that I will not vote to advance any of the 21 judicial nominees pending in the Judiciary Committee or vote to confirm the 32 judges awaiting confirmation on the Senate floor until S. 2644 is brought to the full Senate for a vote."

On Thursday, Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-FL) appeared on CNN's "Newsroom" and said Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump's attorney, had "lost his way, has lost his mind, and has run amuck." She said Giuliani was going around lawful policies and procedures as it relates to foreign policy, undermining the President's own staff, and trying to attempt to get the president of Ukraine to invest in a foreign policy initiative. She described the involvement as outrageous and borders on treason. She added that if Giuliani thinks he should be praised for that type of activity, she thinks history will shine a light and reflect quite differently.

Republican candidate Scott Brown spoke at a campaign rally in Boston on the eve of the special election to fill the Senate seat left vacant by the death of Edward M. Kennedy. Brown stated, "With your help, our dream of depriving millions of health care is within reach." He then said, "Let's send a message, Massachusetts!" and added, "Let's tell people across the country that if they want health coverage, they are shit out of luck!" An aide to Brown said internal polling indicates the Republican's anti-healthcare message may be catching on: "Right now, Scott is showing a double-digit lead among people who describe themselves as douchebags." The Huffington Post's Roy Sekoff appeared on The Ed Show Tuesday evening to weigh in on the Massachusetts Senate race between Democrat Martha Coakley and Republican Roy Sekoff.

President Donald Trump announced Wednesday the United States would temporarily close the border with Canada to non-essential traffic amid the coronavirus crisis. "We will be, by mutual consent, temporarily closing our Northern Border with Canada to non-essential traffic," Trump wrote on Twitter. "Trade will not be affected. Details to follow!" Trump announced the border closure after CNN reported details of the discussions between the two countries. On Tuesday, Trump said he did not want to say he was considering closing the borders between Canada and Mexico. "We are discussing things with Canada and we're discussing things with Mexico, quite honestly, and again, the relationship is outstanding with both, outstanding," he said. Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is following the lead of other countries by restricting entry during the coronavirus crisis. On Monday, he announced that Canada would close the country's borders to foreigners, with the exception of American citizens.

On Friday, the White House disclosed a series of e-mails that it said showed the White House was more deeply involved in revising talking points about the attack on the American diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya. The administration turned over the emails to Congress. The emails show the White House coordinating an intensive process with the State Department, the CIA, the F.B.I. and other agencies to obtain the final version of the talking points, which Rice used by the ambassador to the United Nations in television appearances after the attack. The State Department pushed to remove references to Al Qaeda and Ansar al-Sharia, the Libyan militant group suspected of carrying out the attack, as well as warnings about other potential terrorist threats from the CIA, which drafted the initial talking points.

President Obama announced this morning that he would assign the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations Susan Rice to the role of national security advisor, a position left open when Tom Donilon resigned from the post. In her new role, Rice will work directly with President Obama from the White House as his senior advisor on national security matters, and operates from the White House's "Situation Room" during times of crisis. Rice's name was floated last year as a possible lead contender to become secretary of state when Hillary Clinton retired from the role. Republicans in the Senate vowed not to confirm her for that position, citing perceived missteps in the Benghazi flap, while other conservatives said that Susan Rice was a "black radical." Environmentalists also disapproved of Rice for State and accused her of being invested in creating the Keystone XL oil tar sands pipeline, which they strongly oppose. She has also been accused of enabling massive violence throughout Africa.

David Axelrod, a former top adviser to President Obama, said Sunday that it was a "mistake" for Obama to say in a speech last week that his policies are effectively on the ballot in the midterm elections this fall. "I wouldn't put that line there," Axelrod said on NBC's "Meet The Press." In a Thursday speech, Obama said: "I am not on the ballot this fall. Michelle's pretty happy about that. But make no mistake: These policies are on the ballot. Every single one of them." Republicans began running attack ads using the words to tie Democratic congressional candidates to the president, who polls show is unpopular. Axelrod added, "Understand, if you read the speech, the context of the line was the things he's pushing forward — minimum wage, pay equity, infrastructure — and he said these are on the ballot." But Axelrod concluded, "It was a mistake."

The United States and China introduced a resolution on Tuesday to expand sanctions on North Korea for its nuclear and ballistic missile activities. The resolution would target North Korean bankers and overseas cash couriers, tighten inspections of suspect ship and air cargo, and subject the country's diplomats to invasive scrutiny and increased risk of expulsion. The measure was drafted in response to the third North Korean underground nuclear test three weeks ago. China participated in drafting the language. It would be the fourth Security Council sanctions resolution on North Korea. North Korea has defied previous measures with increasing belligerence. A vote was expected on Thursday. North Korea vowed to scrap the 1953 armistice that halted the Korean War and threatened to attack the United States with what the North Korean government news agency called an arsenal of diverse "lighter and smaller nukes."

Rep. Raul Labrador (R-ID) has officially entered the race for House Majority Leader and will face Rep. Kevin McCarthy (R-CA) for the chance to succeed Rep. Eric Cantor (R-VA), who lost his congressional primary this week and will step down by the end of July. Labrador's entry, reported by Politico, comes after Rep. Pete Sessions (R-TX) withdrew from the race, citing the need to avoid "division" in the Republican Party. House Conservatives had hoped to contest a major leadership office, especially after Cantor's defeat by conservative Dave Brat, and after leadership elections in 2011 and 2013 did not elevate any Tea Party members to senior positions in the caucus. Labrador, who is Latino, is also an opponent of comprehensive immigration reform as passed by the Senate, which was a key issue in Cantor's primary, and withdrew from bipartisan talks last year.

CNN host Jake Tapper was on vacation Monday when a segment led by guest host Jim Sciutto addressed Donald Trump's transition into the White House and whether the president-elect needs to distance himself from what the program called the racist and Nazi-sympathizing "alt-right." A chyron appeared at the bottom of the screen characterizing recent comments made by white nationalist Richard Spencer. Tapper responded on Twitter, saying he was "furious" and that the chyron was "unacceptable," as it would imply the worst about the segment. Scuitto also tweeted that he was upset over the chyron after the show. A CNN spokesperson told The Huffington Post, "It was poor judgment, and we very much regret it and apologize."

During a Tuesday press conference, South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham called Republican frontrunner Donald Trump a "jackass." Trump read out Graham's private cell phone number. Graham told CBS This Morning: "I don't care if he drops out. Stay in the race, just stop being a jackass." He added: "The world is falling apart. We're becoming Greece. The Ayatollah's on the verge of having a nuclear weapon, and you're slandering everybody and anybody to stay in the news. You know, run for president, but don't be the world's biggest jackass." Trump read out Graham's phone number live during the press conference.

On June 9 Virginia state senator Phillip Pucket (D-Russel) resigned his seat. The resignation gave Republicans control of the legislative body and gave him the opportunity for a position on the state tobacco commission and his daughter the chance for a judgeship. Slate reported the resignation effectively ends Governor Terry McAuliffe's (D) plan to expand Medicaid under Obamacare. The Senate was split between 20 Democrats and 20 Republicans prior to June 9. According to The Washington Post, Democrats said Republicans were trying to buy the senate with job offers in order to thwart what McAuliffe said would be an expansion of healthcare coverage to 400,000 low income Virginians. Delegate Scott A. Surovell (D-Fairfax) said he was astounded that the Republicans "will do anything and everything to prevent low-income Virginians from getting health care." He referred to Republicans as "bullies" and said he hopes McAuliffe will continue standing up to them.

Energy Secretary Rick Perry is working his way to the White House exit according to two people familiar with his plans who spoke to Bloomberg. One person told Bloomberg that Perry "hasn't fully made up his mind." Another said his "exit isn't imminent." Perry spokeswoman Shaylyn Hunes said "He is happy where he is serving President Trump and leading the Department of Energy." Other sources insist he is greasing the skids for his departure, including preparing his deputy, Dan Brouillette, to take over, according to Bloomberg's sources. Perry's motivation for seeking to leave before the end of Trump's first term is a desire to build his income before retiring, two people said.

Former Michigan congressman and chairman of the House Intelligence Committee Pete Hoekstra spoke with Breitbart News Daily SiriusXM host Alex Marlow on Wednesday regarding FBI Director James Comey and NSA Director Adm. Michael Rogers' testimony before the House Intelligence Committee. Hoekstra said, "I found it very interesting as some have described it, that we now have Comey rules, that he arbitrarily decides what investigations can be made public and which ones cannot be made public." He called it "amazing," adding, "the leaks thing is the one area where we know that crimes have been committed, felonies have been committed, and he can't commit to say that there's actually investigations going on in that area." Breitbart News Daily airs on SiriusXM Patriot 125 weekdays from 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 a.m. Eastern.

President Obama tweeted support for a high school student arrested in Irving, Texas, after the student brought a homemade clock to school. The student, Ahmen Mohamed, was called to the principal's office after a teacher reported it. Police arrested him, put him in handcuffs, and took his fingerprints. Obama asked, "Cool clock, Ahmed. Want to bring it to the White House? We should inspire more kids like you to like science. It's what makes America great." The school suspended Mohamed for three days. Irving Police Chief Larry Boyd defended the decision to arrest Mohamed on the grounds that it was "a hoax bomb" but said that it was a "naive accident." "We are confident it's not an explosive device," he said according to the Dallas Morning News, confirming that all charges were dropped.

A letter to the editor responded to a May 17 news article titled "Trump Rants on Unauthorized Migrants: 'These Aren't People, These Are Animals'." The letter stated that the article listed "Animals," "losers," "crazy," and "psycho." The letter stated that nothing President Trump says is a surprise anymore, but it continues to draw attention. The letter also noted funding cuts in education, infrastructure, conservation, and early childhood programs, and that list also goes on. The letter writer stated that in addition to continuing to undermine what is left of civil to one another, Trump seems to be very adept at directing the focus of Americans, both Democrats and Republicans, away from the real priorities and toward the daily drama of his life. The letter writer, John N. CORBIN, wrote from CARY, N.C.

In Massachusetts, the race for the late Senator Edward M. Kennedy's senate seat is breaking in favor of Republicans on the eve of the election. Democrat Martha Coakley is trailing Republican Scott Brown. Coakley relied on the endorsement of President Obama this weekend to try to catch Brown. The endorsement did not appear sufficient to keep the seat for Democrats. The momentum is with Brown heading into the home stretch. The energy and enthusiasm is with Brown as independents are breaking 2-1 for the Republican and Democrats appear to be giving up 20% of their own votes to Brown. The election landscape this year reflects voters' dissatisfaction with spending by Congress. Such spending is epitomized by the health care bill Congress is trying to push through before seating Brown if he is elected. Doug Schoen is a Fox News contributor, pollster and author of "The Political Fix."

Pennsylvania State Police say Sunday that 20-year-old Andrew Joseph Todd of Mount Bethel, Pennsylvania, was shot and killed by police after he refused officers' orders to drop his weapon inside the Walmart late Saturday. Police were dispatched to the store shortly after 10 p.m. Saturday on reports of an armed man threatening and pointing a weapon at customers. Officials say about 100 people were in the store at the time. State police say officers ordered Todd to drop his weapon. He refused and continued to point it at officers. Police then fired at Todd, striking him in the upper chest. Todd was transported to Pocono Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead by the Monroe County coroner. State police say no customers or officers were injured. The Pocono Record reports Todd was carrying two guns and a machete.

Former New York Gov. George Pataki endorsed Marco Rubio for president on Tuesday. In an interview with Fox News, the former Republican governor said Rubio could bring Americans together. "In my mind there's one person who stands out, and that is Senator Marco Rubio," Pataki said. "Senator Rubio has the leadership, he has the vision, he has the intelligence from Congress to understand what it takes to defend us from radical Islam. I'm proud to endorse Senator Rubio." The endorsement came after another former presidential candidate, former Texas Gov. Rick Perry, endorsed Texas Sen. Ted Cruz in the race. Pataki dropped out of the race last month after failing to gain traction in the GOP primary. His Rubio endorsement comes less than a week before the Iowa caucuses; polls in the state show Rubio in third place, behind Donald Trump and Cruz.

On Monday, ABC's "The View" featured former Trump aide Omarosa Manigault Newman. Co-host Joy Behar asked Manigault Newman, "Do you have the N-word on tape?" Manigault Newman said, "I don't hold the tape. I've heard the tape. They've been talking about releasing it, releasing it. You know, I'm suspecting they're going to release it around the midterms." Behar said, "That won't hurt him. That will not hurt him." Manigault Newman agreed, saying, "The Trump world cult will probably applaud when they hear him say it because they're desensitized to his racist ways."

An envelope containing the lethal compound ricin was intercepted earlier this week before it reached the White House, law enforcement officials said Saturday, according to several news outlets, including The Associated Press. The FBI, Secret Service and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are reportedly investigating the package's source. Ricin is a highly toxic substance found in castor beans. As little as one milligram of it can kill an adult, according to a Cornell University fact sheet about the compound. There is no known antidote. It is unclear whether the package, which investigators believe was sent from Canada, was intercepted before reaching the White House mailroom, The New York Times reported. The White House mailroom is located at a remote site elsewhere in Washington. Packages containing ricin have been intercepted en route to other political figures, including former President Barack Obama and former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg.

Cambridge Analytica secured a $15 million investment from Robert Mercer, a wealthy Republican donor, and recruited Stephen K. Bannon, a political adviser. The firm did not have the data to make its new products work. The firm had secured the investment from Mercer and had wooed Bannon with the promise of tools that could identify the personalities of American voters and influence their behavior. It did not have the data to make its new products work.

A special Minnesota panel of three judges from three separate courts ruled that Al Franken, a Democrat, won the most votes in his 2008 Senate race against incumbent Republican Norm Coleman. The ruling on Monday is not expected to be the final decision in the case because Coleman previously announced plans to appeal to the State Supreme Court, which has 10 days to do so. That appeal could mean a delay of several more weeks in seating Minnesota's second senator. After a statewide recount and a seven-week trial, Franken is 312 votes ahead. He gained more votes from the election challenge than Coleman, the candidate who filed it. The state law under which Franken sued required three judges to determine who got the most votes and is therefore entitled to an election certificate. That certificate is being held up pending appeal.

The U.S. Senate voted 49-49 Wednesday to confirm Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback's nomination for an ambassador's post. Vice President Mike Pence broke the tie in Brownback's favor. The vote ended debate on Brownback's nomination by President Donald Trump to be U.S. ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom. The action starts a 30-hour clock on holding a final vote, though it could come sooner. Trump first nominated Brownback for the ambassador's post in July. Democrats and LGBT groups opposed his appointment. In 2015, Brownback rescinded an executive order from a previous Democratic governor banning discrimination in state hiring and employment against LGBT individuals. Brownback would resign as governor if confirmed. Republican Lt. Gov. Jeff Colyer would be elevated to governor.

The Pentagon will review new Army hairstyle regulations after lawmakers criticized them as discriminatory toward women of color. Pentagon spokesman Rear Adm. John Kirby said Tuesday that Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel directed his deputy secretary to work with service chiefs to address the concerns about the new standards. The standards include bans on most twists, dreadlocks and large cornrows, all styles used predominantly by black women with natural hairstyles. Sixteen female members of the Congressional Black Caucus sent a letter to the Pentagon earlier this month stating the changes unfairly restrict the hairstyles of women of color. The letter stated: "Though we understand the intent of the updated regulation is to ensure uniformity in our military, it is seen as discriminatory rules targeting soldiers who are women of color with little regard to what is needed to maintain their natural hair." Kirby added that after the reviews are complete, Hagel will make "whatever appropriate adjustments to DOD policy are necessary."

Bill Gates, the billionaire co-founder of Microsoft, announced on Monday the start of a billion-dollar investment fund to invest in transformative energy research and development to reduce emissions that cause climate change. The work would supplement and build on basic research already underway at government labs that may be threatened by the incoming administration. President-elect Donald J. Trump has expressed skepticism about climate change and appointed fossil fuel advocates to his cabinet. Gates said he expected the president-elect to recognize that government funding of basic research would eventually be good for business, jobs, infrastructure and other economic elements that Trump campaigned on. "It's a good deal," Gates said.

Former U.S. President Bill Clinton spoke at the Clinton Global Initiative annual meeting Wednesday in New York. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin can be trusted and has never broken his word on a personal agreement between them. "He kept his word in all the deals we made," Clinton said. He also praised his daughter Chelsea, stating she would make a good POTUS list. Clinton said he believes his daughter Chelsea would be a better president than his wife, Hillary, "over the long run." "Day after tomorrow, my wife because she's had more experience. Over the long run, Chelsea. She knows more than we do about everything," Clinton said. "I feel like I'm going to school every day when we have conversations."

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, a self-described mastermind of the Sept. 11 attacks, said in a statement filed in Manhattan federal court late Sunday that Sulaiman Abu Ghaith, a former spokesman of Osama bin Laden, had no role in planning military operations for al-Qaida. Mohammed said Abu Ghaith served as an al-Qaida spokesman because he was "an eloquent, spellbinding speaker." He added that Abu Gaith "had nothing to do with military operations." Abu Gaith is a son-in-law of bin Laden. He is charged with conspiring to kill Americans. Mohammed is in a detention facility in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. Abu Gaith's lawyers hope to use his testimony at the trial. They would need U.S. District Judge Lewis A. Kaplan's approval to introduce the information.

United Nations experts contend that North Korea has been shipping supplies to the Syrian government that could be used in the production of chemical weapons. The evidence of a North Korean connection comes as the United States and other countries have accused the Syrian government of using chemical weapons on civilians, including recent attacks on civilians in the Damascus suburb of eastern Ghouta using what appears to have been chlorine gas. The supplies from North Korea include acid-resistant tiles, valves and thermometers, according to a report by United Nations investigators. North Korean missile technicians have also been spotted working at known chemical weapons and missile facilities inside Syria, according to the report, which was written by a panel of experts who looked at North Korea's compliance with United Nations sanctions. The report highlights the potential danger posed by any such trade between Syria and North Korea, which could allow Syria to maintain its chemical weapons while also providing North Korea with cash for its nuclear and missile programs.

House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) presided over his first Capitol Christmas tree lighting ceremony on Wednesday. He held a moment of silence for the victims of the mass shooting in San Bernardino, California, and asked for prayers. "We are all thinking about the current and ongoing tragedy in California today," he said. "Please keep the victims and families in your prayers right now." A day earlier, Ryan had urged Congress to prioritize mental health reform in response to last week's mass shooting at a Planned Parenthood clinic in Colorado. He did not mention steps related to gun control, such as mandating background checks and closing loopholes that make it easy to buy guns. "I'm sure that members of both parties have lots of ideas in this area, but we should make this a priority to prevent the violence to protect our citizens," he said, calling mental illness a "common denominator" in gun violence.

On Wednesday, "Late Night" host Seth Meyers criticized Steve Bannon after Republican candidate Roy Moore lost Alabama's Senate race. Meyers said Bannon made mistake after mistake regarding Bannon's role in Moore's support. Before the special election on Tuesday, Bannon appeared at a Moore rally and criticized MSNBC host Joe Scarborough for not entering prestigious universities like Bannon did. Meyers noted that Scarborough, a former congressman from Florida, is an alumnus of the University of Alabama. Meyers asked, "How stupid do you have to be to insult the University of Alabama in Alabama?" He added, "Who do you think they're going to support? 'Roll Tide' or someone who looks like he literally rolled up in the tide?" A video of the segment was posted.

A Quinnipiac University poll released Thursday shows President Barack Obama and presumptive Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney tied in Ohio, a swing state. The poll shows Obama with a 45-44 edge. When voters are asked whether they would vote for an Obama-Biden ticket or a ticket with Romney and Sen. Rob Portman (R-Ohio), who many speculate will be Romney's vice presidential nominee, the two are tied at 45-45. In a poll on Feb. 15, the firm had Obama up 46-44 over Romney, and with the addition of vice presidents, he was up 47-43. Other recent polls in Ohio have shown Obama with a slightly larger edge. The state has voted for the winner in every presidential election since 1960. There remains a gender gap in Ohio polling, with men voting 50-40 for Romney and women voting 49-38 for Obama.

The Senate on Thursday confirmed the nomination of Sylvia Mathews Burwell to be secretary of health and human services. Burwell will be responsible for delivering health insurance to more than one-third of all Americans. The vote was 78 to 17. All the no votes were cast by Republicans. 24 Republicans joined 52 Democrats and two independents in voting for confirmation. Burwell, 48, has been director of the White House Office of Management and Budget since April of last year. White House officials said President Obama selected her because he wanted a proven manager to carry out the health care law, which got off to a rocky start under Kathleen Sebelius as health secretary. Senator Tim Kaine, Democrat of Virginia, supported Burwell, saying Thursday that she had brought "a more businesslike approach" to the White House budget office and that she would do the same at the Department of Health and Human Services.

Trump has expressed skepticism about climate change and appointed fossil fuel advocates to his cabinet. At the Ligueros Club in Cartagena, Colombia, prostitutes dressed in lingerie wait for a bell to ring signaling the arrival of men on the prowl. American investigators are seeking to determine the late-night activities of a group of Secret Service agents and military personnel assigned to President Obama's recent visit to Colombia. American security officials say they have begun searching for as many as 21 women believed to include prostitutes and to have spent the night with the security officers. After uncovering evidence of misconduct, investigators for the Secret Service are seeking to interview women who are said to have accompanied 11 agents, including snipers and explosives experts, to their hotel rooms after a night of heavy drinking, said Representative Peter T. King, the chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security.

A federal appeals panel in Manhattan ordered the release on Monday of key portions of a classified Justice Department memorandum that provided legal justification for the targeted killing of Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen. Intelligence officials contend al-Awlaki joined Al Qaeda and died in a 2011 drone strike in Yemen. The unanimous three-judge panel, reversing a lower court decision, said the government had waived its right to keep the analysis secret in light of numerous public statements by administration officials and the Justice Department's release of a "white paper" offering a detailed analysis of why targeted killings were legal. Judge Jon O. Newman wrote for the panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit that whatever protection the legal analysis might once have had has been lost by virtue of public statements of public officials at the highest levels and official disclosure of the D.O.J. White Paper.

Almost a decade ago, an Arab diplomat likened the relationship between the United States and Saudi Arabia to a Catholic marriage "where you can have no divorce." The Obama administration began assessing the newly reconstituted House of Saud after the death of King Abdullah on Friday. The relationship between the United States and Saudi Arabia, described as the most important Arab ally, has been characterized as critical and tumultuous. Saudi Arabia's new king, Salman, 79, inherits policies put in place by his older brother, the more assertive brother, and conflicts that have occurred in recent years. On issues from Iran to the Arab Spring, from Syria to domestic issues within Saudi Arabia like the recent flogging of a journalist, there have been significant differences between American officials and the Saudi royal family.

At an event at George Washington University today, Nancy Pelosi praised Bernie Sanders and said he could win the nomination. Pelosi said, "It would be fabulous to have a woman president. You can't ask somebody to vote for somebody because of their gender." Pelosi said she voted with Sanders against DOMA in 1996. She said, "[Hillary Clinton] is a very qualified person who happens to be a woman, but I haven't endorsed anybody yet." Pelosi said, "Bernie Sanders was my colleague in the House. We voted against DOMA, you know, against all of those things people are subjecting to scrutiny now. He's fabulous, and he has a very important tonic for the country and for the Democratic Party because he has ideas." She added, "He might win the nomination," and "I don't know that because in terms of the demographics of how popular she is in the minority community."

Rick Santorum endorsed Marco Rubio for president on Wednesday evening, hours after it was widely reported that Rubio would drop out of the race. The former U.S. senator from Pennsylvania won the Iowa caucuses in 2012. Santorum made his endorsement in an appearance on Fox News Channel's "On the Record" show, where he also formally announced the suspension of his campaign. Show host Greta Van Susteren tweeted several statements about Rubio attributed to Santorum. Santorum's effort to repeat his 2012 run stalled and never reached the low single-digits in polling. According to Van Susteren's Twitter account, Santorum said, "I don't endorse lightly," becoming the first of the four Iowa presidential dropouts to formally endorse a former rival.

During an interview with ABC's George Stephanopoulos, former FBI Director James Comey's wife, Patrice, said she supported Hillary Clinton and was "devastated" when Donald Trump won. "I wanted a woman president really badly, and I supported Hillary Clinton," Patrice Comey told Stephanopoulos. "A lot of my friends worked for her. And I was devastated when she lost." James Comey said his wife and girls participated in the Women's March on the day after Trump's inauguration. "My wife and girls marched in the Women's March, the day after President Trump's inauguration," he said. "At least my four daughters — probably all five of my kids, wanted Hillary Clinton to be the first woman president. I know my amazing spouse did."

United States Customs and Border Protection officers used tear gas on Sunday to deter hundreds of migrants attempting to cross the border into the United States. Migrants tried to enter at three locations near the border crossing in Tijuana, Mexico. A number of migrants tried to cross into the United States at the Tijuana River and were met with a law enforcement blockade with barbed wire and tear gas. In a widely viewed photograph, a woman can be seen pulling her family away from tear gas fired by Customs and Border Protection officers. Others crossed the Tijuana River on their way to El Chaparral, a port of entry on the Mexico side of the border, to evade the police blockade. Migrants also met tear gas and law enforcement officials at a set of train tracks near the San Ysidro crossing. The United States shut down the crossing in both directions in response to the migrants' attempt to cross.
