The Senate voted Monday to approve Seema Verma as administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. The vote was 55-43. Verma's confirmation comes as congressional Republicans advance their efforts this week to repeal and replace Obamacare, an overhaul that would entail great involvement from CMS. The health care bill making its way through the House currently plans to eliminate Medicaid expansion after 2020. Verma has been working on health care policy for more than a decade and developed an alternative Medicaid plan in Indiana under former Republican Gov. Mitch Daniels. When Obamacare became law, Verma helped Pence, then the Indiana governor, tweak the Healthy Indiana Plan, sell it to the Obama administration as the vehicle for Medicaid expansion, and then dramatically scale it upward. It became a program Pence championed as a conservative alternative to Obamacare's main vehicle for expanded coverage.

Sen. Ben Sasse, R-Neb., criticized Sen. Jeff Flake for sending a $100 check to Democrat Doug Jones to assist in the contest for Alabama's vacant U.S. Senate against Republican Roy Moore. Sasse tweeted Tuesday: "This donation is a bad idea. It's possible to be against BOTH partial birth abortion AND child molestation. Happily, most Americans are." Moore faces several accusations of sexual impropriety with teenage girls when he was in his 30s. He denies the allegations. When a Twitter user asked for Sasse's solution to the tough choice Alabamians face in the Dec. 12 special election, the Nebraska senator replied: "Have said from day one I wouldn't vote for either of them. If you don't reject 2 bad choices now, you won't get better choices in the future."

President Obama intends to use his State of the Union address to put a difficult year behind him and reassert command before the capital is consumed with election-year politics. After five years in office, Mr. Obama has, by his own account, come to feel acutely the limits on his power and the shrinking horizons before him. His nationally televised speech to Congress on Tuesday is a critical opportunity to drive an agenda that may yet shape his legacy. But perhaps more so than in any of his previous congressional addresses, Mr. Obama realizes that he has little chance of major legislative victories this year, with the possible exception of an overhaul of immigration law that Republicans are also making a priority. As a result, aides said, he will present a blueprint for "a year of action" on issues like income inequality and the environment that bypasses Congress and exercises his authority to the maximum extent.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday rejected a key aspect of President Obama's Middle East policy speech, saying a return to his country's 1967 borders would spell disaster for the Jewish state. In a statement released late Thursday, Netanyahu called the 1967 lines "indefensible." The statement could set the stage for a meeting Friday when Netanyahu goes to the White House. In his speech, Obama said a future Palestinian state must be based in territories captured by Israel in the 1967 Mideast war, with minor adjustments reached through negotiations. Netanyahu said such a withdrawal would jeopardize Israel's security and leave major West Bank settlements outside Israeli borders.

Jeb Bush, a Republican presidential candidate, asked a party donor recently, according to accounts provided by several sources close to Bush, "Seriously, what's this guy's problem?" Bush described Donald Trump, a real estate developer, as "a buffoon," "clown," and "asshole." Bush described Trump as "a publicity-seeking real estate developer" and "a liar," "clown," and "asshole." Bush also referenced Trump standing next to Bush at the debate and calling him an asshole. Bush said he was making sure to check the footage, noting he likes to keep close track of what people say about him.

The American Health Care Act, which was narrowly passed in the House last week, would worsen Obamacare's problems rather than fix them, according to a Congressional Budget Office analysis of a previous iteration of the legislation. The bill would end Obamacare's individual mandate and impose a fee on those who go without coverage and want to re-enter the insurance market, creating an incentive for relatively healthy people to remain uncovered. As a result, instability in Obamacare's exchanges as insurers scale back around the country would only be increased. It is unclear what health policy problem this bill would solve. The author wrote that even for an opponent of Obamacare, it is difficult to understand why House Republicans chose this path to revamping the nation's health care system.

Sen. Ben Sasse, R-Neb., criticized Sen. Jeff Flake for sending a $100 check to Democrat Doug Jones to assist in the contest for Alabama's vacant U.S. Senate against Republican Roy Moore. Sasse tweeted Tuesday: "This donation is a bad idea. It's possible to be against BOTH partial birth abortion AND child molestation. Happily, most Americans are." Moore faces several accusations of sexual impropriety with teenage girls when he was in his 30s. He denies the allegations. When a Twitter user asked for Sasse's solution to the tough choice Alabamians face in the Dec. 12 special election, the Nebraska senator replied: "Have said from day one I wouldn't vote for either of them. If you don't reject 2 bad choices now, you won't get better choices in the future."

President Obama will hold a series of interviews with weathermen from across the nation on Tuesday. The White House released a "National Climate Assessment" on Monday. The report predicts floods, droughts, superstorms and other near-apocalyptic scenarios. Obama will record the interviews on Tuesday afternoon for a program called "Weather from the White House." The White House did not specifically specify which topics would be the focus of the interviews. NBC meteorologist Al Roker tweeted on Monday: "I'm going to the White House to interview President Obama about the National Climate Assessment report coming out." The White House also said anchors will be granted special "behind-the-scenes access" to the president and his top advisers throughout the day.

University Medical Center in Tucson fired three employees for accessing private patient medical records in violation of hospital policy, FoxNews.com confirmed. The hospital would not reveal the number or identities of patients who had their records accessed or whether any were victims of the shooting that left six people dead and 14 others wounded. Hospital spokeswoman Loretta McKenzie told FoxNews.com that the patients had been notified. In addition to the three clerical staff fired by the hospital, a contracted nurse was terminated. Giffords remained in critical condition after she was shot once in the head. She is expected to live and has been making progress, including making small movements on her own, tugging at her hospital gown and touching her wounds, one of her doctors said Wednesday. Her long-term outlook remains unclear.

Conservative members of the House rebelled against their leadership on Thursday to scuttle an emergency spending measure that addressed the migrant crisis at the southern border. The vote occurred as lawmakers prepared to leave for a five-week recess. The situation occurred as lawmakers prepared to leave for recess. The failure of the Republican border bill, coupled with the Senate's inability to bring a Democratic alternative to a vote, contributed to the situation. The prospects of a broad immigration overhaul, which at the beginning of the 113th Congress held great bipartisan promise, have ground to a halt. The struggle to deal with immigration became more urgent with the flood of tens of thousands of children at the border. Congressional infighting, driven by more conservative Republicans who balked at further government spending, contributed to President Obama's approach on deporting the migrants.

Four years ago, President Obama beat Mitt Romney 51.5% to 46% in Colorado. Nine months ago, Clinton was tied or beating every Republican in Colorado. According to the latest Quinnipiac poll, to0day, every major Republican beats Clinton by double digits. In this swing state, Rubio leads Clinton 52 to 36 percent; Carson leads Clinton 52 to 38 percent; Cruz tops Clinton 51 to 38 percent. In their respective primaries, Carson leads the Republicans with 25% support; Rubio is in second place at 19%. Trump is in third place at 17%. In this same poll, in March, Clinton was polling in the mod-forties and statistically tied with her Republican opponents.

Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) said Tuesday that he is considering running for another term in 2016, when he would be 80 years old. "I'm seriously thinking about maybe giving another opportunity for you to vote for or against me in a few years from now," McCain said on KFYI-AM in Phoenix. "I'm seriously giving that a lot of thought." Host Barry Young asked if he was saying he might run again. McCain said: "That would not be wrong." The New York Times's Mark Leibovich, who is in Arizona following McCain, first tweeted the news. McCain, the 2008 GOP presidential nominee, is in his fifth term. He has never taken less than 56 percent of the vote and easily dispatched a primary challenge in 2010 from former congressman J.D. Hayworth. If he runs again, McCain will likely find himself targeted by tea party groups.

Many Twitter users reacted to Democrat Joe Biden's win over President Donald Trump. The race was not called until Saturday. Many users used the phrase "You're fired" to describe Biden's win in Pennsylvania. George Takei tweeted the phrase and said in another tweet he had wanted to say it since before Trump became president. Some users posted the phrase on Twitter. The phrase was widely used by Trump during his days on "The Apprentice." George Takei tweeted the phrase and said in another tweet he had wanted to say it since before Trump became president. Some users felt that one person above all deserved to post a "You're fired" tweet to Trump.

U.S. Rep. Xochitl Torres Small of New Mexico announced Wednesday she will not seek the Democratic nomination for an open U.S. Senate seat in the state's 2nd Congressional District. Torres Small announced she will not run to replace retiring U.S. Sen. Tom Udall and will focus on the district. U.S. Rep. Ben Ray Lujan, the No. 4 ranked Democrat in Congress, said Monday he will run for the state's open U.S. Senate seat in 2020. Lujan is the first politician to declare his candidacy for the Senate seat. Democrats hope to keep their hold on the seat held by Udall, who announced last week that he will not seek a third term. Torres Small, a freshman, won the district in November.

Rep. Heath Shuler (N.C.) formally launched his bid Monday to oust Speaker Nancy Pelosi (Calif.) as leader of House Democrats, beginning to ask lawmakers to support his more centrist campaign to be minority leader. "I'll be running," Shuler said after votes Monday. "I'll be running," Shuler said. Shuler hails from the Blue Dog Coalition, whose Democratic ranks were roughly halved by midterm elections two weeks ago. Many consider his effort a protest candidacy that will give the remaining moderate Democrats an alternative to voting for Pelosi. Pelosi's popularity plummeted during the fall elections amid thousands of campaign commercials that portrayed her in a negative light. The leadership elections for House Democrats are Wednesday morning, and the caucus expects to ratify the same slate of current leaders who oversaw its ranks for the past five years after Pelosi negotiated a deal to keep all her lieutenants at the leadership table.

Jim Gandy, chief meteorologist on WLTX in Columbia, S.C., makes a point of incorporating links between bad weather and climate change into his daily broadcasts. In an interview, Gandy said: "In Columbia, the only thing that separates us from hell in the summertime is a screen door. And all of the climate models indicate that it's going to get worse if we don't do something about it." On Tuesday, Gandy was among eight weather broadcasters invited to interview President Obama and spend the day at the White House. The guests included Al Roker of the "Today" show and local weathermen and women from Chicago, Miami, Seattle and other cities. The administration said the guests were there to spread the word contained in a new report, the National Climate Assessment, that the warming climate is causing sweeping change across the United States.

CBS News correspondent Weijia Jiang was among the reporters outside the White House on Friday morning attempting to get in a question with President Donald Trump. Trump singled her out and told her to be "quiet" at least five times, according to her count. Pressed further on the specifics of the North Korean agreement, the president turned to someone nearby, then pointed back at Jiang. Shaking his head dismissively, he said, "She's so... she's so obnoxious." Trump added another "quiet" just before he called her "obnoxious."

North Korea on Thursday demanded the end of U.N. sanctions as a condition for talks to continue with world leaders. A spokesman for the Policy Department of the National Defense Commission said the U.S.-South Korean military drills must end, as CBS News reported. "Dialogue can never go with war actions," the statement read, as CBS reported. Other conditions, CBS reported: North Korea demanded the United States withdraw all nuclear weapon assets from the South. And South Korea must put a stop to all rhetoric critical of the North. South Korea immediately dismissed the demands. "We again strongly urge North Korea to stop this kind of insistence that we cannot totally understand and go down the path of a wise choice," a spokesman for the South Korean Foreign Ministry said in the CBS report. North Korea has been threatening to attack South Korea, Japan and the United States for weeks.

On Sunday, ABC's "This Week" discussed former CIA Director Mike Morell's op-ed criticizing Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump and endorsing Hillary Clinton. Morell said he would trust Clinton with "the crown jewels" of the U.S. government. When asked why America should trust her to be commander-in-chief, Morell said, "I think there's a bigger issue here, right? I worked with her for four years. Very closely when she was secretary of state. I was at the CIA. I provided her personally provided her some of the most sensitive information that the Central Intelligence Agency has. She never misused it. Always protected it. I would trust her with the crown jewels of the United States government. And more importantly, I would trust her with the future security of the country and the future security of my kids."

The United States is providing nearly $25 million in additional humanitarian aid to the Philippines following Typhoon Haiyan last month. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry flew to central Tacloban city on Wednesday and announced the additional food aid, shelter materials, water and other supplies for typhoon-lashed families after surveying battered villages and consoling survivors. The U.S. assistance package has reached $86 million with the new aid to one of its closest Asian allies. Washington's emergency aid is helping 3 million people in the hardest-hit regions, where the U.S. military has transported more than 2,495 tons of relief supplies and evacuated more than 21,000 survivors. Haiyan left more than 6,000 people dead and nearly 1,800 others missing.

Melania Trump's professional website has disappeared from the internet, as her educational background has come under scrutiny. Her site, which at one time featured her biography, now redirects users to a website for husband Donald Trump's business, the Trump Organization, The Huffington Post reported. The disappearance of the website comes amid speculation over whether the former model and potential First Lady received her undergraduate degree in design and architecture from the University of Ljubljana in her native Slovenia. Melania Trump's online biography claimed that she had received the college degree, but an unauthorized book about her life called "Melania Trump: The Inside Story" alleged that she ditched school after one year to pursue a career in modeling. According to the Huffington Post, older versions of Melania Trump's website in online archives, including one from 2012, claimed that she earned a degree in architecture and design from the university.

Caroline Kennedy, the daughter of President John F. Kennedy, is likely to be the next United States ambassador to Japan, according to people familiar with the appointment process. The vetting of Ms. Kennedy by the White House is almost complete, and an appointment could be announced in the coming weeks, along with the names of several other choices for important diplomatic posts. Ms. Kennedy, 55, was an early supporter of President Obama in the 2008 presidential election and offered forceful backing as he battled Hillary Rodham Clinton for the Democratic nomination. She also served as a co-chairwoman of Mr. Obama's 2012 re-election campaign. The diplomatic assignment would vault Ms. Kennedy, a lawyer and the author of 10 books, into the kind of public life that her family has embraced for several generations, including in the diplomatic corps. Ms. Kennedy's grandfather Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. served as ambassador to Britain from 1938 to 1940.

A WBUR poll released late Wednesday showed Harvard professor Elizabeth Warren leading Massachusetts Sen. Scott Brown 45 to 40 percent, with 12 percent of respondents undecided. Earlier this week, three other polls also gave Warren a lead. A Suffolk University/WHDH News 7 poll showed her ahead by 4 percent, a Public Policy Polling Survey had her up by 2 percent, and a poll commissioned by MassLive.com/The Republican showed a 6-point lead. The two will face off Thursday night in the first of three debates scheduled to take place before the November election. The WBUR poll was conducted Sept. 15-17 among 507 likely Massachusetts voters and has a 4.4 percent margin of error.

With Israel and the U.N. warning the U.S. that Iran cannot be trusted outside of an agreement "to halt uranium enrichment," Obama and his national security team counter that assessment. The administration is also working to avoid congressional opposition. According to the AP, prior to talks now underway, Secretary of State John Kerry and National Security Adviser Susan Rice personally appealed to Senators in a White House meeting to hold off on seeking additional sanctions in order to give Iran time to demonstrate its seriousness in addressing concerns it is trying to develop nuclear weapons. Republican Senators are working to "keep penalties in place, and toughen them, unless Iran freezes its nuclear program completely." Israel continues to stand by U.N. Security Council demands that Iran halt uranium enrichment as a prerequisite for serious talks or relief from sanctions.

House Speaker John Boehner said Tuesday that the Obama administration is not helping Congress get to the truth over the IRS' close scrutiny of conservative groups and the agency's recent revelation that it lost emails related to that probe. Boehner told reporters that when the president made remarks about the IRS scandal almost a year ago, he said he would fully cooperate with the administration. He said the administration has not only not fully cooperated, but has not done a damn thing to help get to the truth of what really happened. The IRS said it lost some emails by Lois Lerner, who headed the division that processes applications for tax-exempt status. The agency attributed the loss to Lerner's computer crashing. Republicans have said they do not believe the explanation. Boehner said, "Listen, I grew up in a bar. This doesn't pass the straight-face test."

The author wrote that Democrats have an opportunity to go a few different directions with the conclusion of Mueller's investigation and Barr's subsequent letter to congress. The author wrote that Democrats should praise Mueller for the job he has done but stress that the Special Counsel was appointed by Trump's own Justice Department to investigate President Donald Trump. The author wrote that Democrats should demand the report be made public in its entirety without delay and criticize Barr's unilateral decision not to pursue obstruction charges against the President. The author wrote that now the investigation is over, Democrats should focus on continuing to do the job the American people overwhelming elected them to do. The author wrote that Democrats should continue to investigate Trump, his family and his administration, but more low key. The author wrote that Trump will bluster and brag about "no collusion," and that another shiny object will come along soon enough to distract him. The author wrote that Trump is vulnerable and beatable in the 2020 election and that Democrats should focus on that.

On this week's broadcast of "Fox News Sunday," Rep. Adam Schiff (D-CA) reacted to Justice Department Inspector General Michael Horowitz's report on the FBI's Russia probe. Schiff said that had he known two years ago that the FBI was abusing the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), he would have called them out. Schiff said, "I'm certainly willing to admit that the inspector general found serious abuses of FISA that I was unaware of. Had I known of them, Chris, yes, I would have called out the FBI at the same time. But I think it's only fair to judge what we know at the time, not what would be revealed two years later, but yes, there were very serious abuses of the FISA process, they need to be corrected, we need to make sure they never happen again."

President Obama addressed the Senate Republican open letter to Iran. In an upcoming interview with Vice News, Obama said: "I'm embarrassed for them. For them to address a letter to the ayatollah, who they claim is our mortal enemy, and their basic argument to them is 'don't deal with our president 'cause you can't trust him to follow through on an agreement.' That's close to unprecedented."

Federal investigators on Wednesday said the chemicals stored in a CSX train that exploded and caught fire outside Baltimore are not a risk to nearby residents. Late Tuesday evening, firefighters responded to a fire and explosion at a derailed train site in Rosedale, Md., just outside Baltimore. They controlled the blaze shortly before midnight. At least one of the trains that had caught fire had been used to transport hazardous materials, and investigators were initially concerned about the risk to nearby residents, The Associated Press reported. They ruled within hours that the chemicals are not hazardous, AP said. Federal authorities are still looking for the reasons behind the fire. National Transportation Safety Board Director Robert Sumwalt said a truck crossed the train tracks and collided with the derailed trains, but it still is not known why the driver was there. The driver, John Alban Jr., 50, was seriously injured in the crash and is still in the hospital recovering, AP reported.

On Thursday, Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-HI) appeared on CNN's "New Day" and commented on the news that Iran shot down an American drone in international waters. Hirono defended Iran's viewpoint, saying "there is a mistrust of the United States" since President Donald Trump pulled the country out of the Iran nuclear deal. "I think their perspective is 'how are we supposed to believe that the United States is going to keep its word?'" Hirono said. She added, "We need to create, I think, an environment where both sides, particularly at this point the Iranians believe that it is time to come to the negotiation table. Apparently, it's not that time yet. So, miscalculations can happen."

New Jersey Democratic Rep. Rob Andrews said Tuesday he is leaving Congress in two weeks. Andrews, who has held the Democratic-leaning, suburban Philadelphia seat since 1990, will leave office February 18 to join a law firm with offices in Washington. He said the job just opened and he "had to make a decision this weekend." Andrews is the third congressional Democrat to resign in the past several weeks, starting with Rep. George Miller in January and Rep. Henry Waxman last week. Both are from California. Andrews, 56, had been the subject of a House Ethics Committee investigation related to whether he used campaign money for trips to California, where his daughter had a fledgling singing and acting career. His departure will end the investigations. The seat will be open until the general election in November. Miller's departure had put Andrews in line to be the top Democrat on the House Education and Workforce Committee.

Kevin Nicholson, a Republican candidate, said his family has a lot of love and support from other relatives and he remains confident in his political views. He was not always a conservative but said his opinions changed after serving in the Marine Corps. "If you want to have your illusions ripped away as a young person, go to war, and you're going to learn a lot about yourself and a lot about the world," Nicholson said. The race is set to be one of the most expensive this cycle with Richard Uihlein giving $3.5 million to the Solutions for Wisconsin super PAC that endorsed Nicholson. Baldwin also has a war chest, raising $2.8 million in the last quarter of 2017, according to ABC News. President Trump won the blue-leaning state in a surprising victory in 2016, making it a top target for Republicans this year.

President Donald Trump on Friday defended former aide Rob Porter, wishing him well in his future endeavors without mentioning the two ex-wives who have accused Porter of physical and emotional abuse. Trump's comments came during a national conversation about the mistreatment of women. They came amid White House finger-pointing about who knew what and when about the severity of the spousal abuse allegations. Trump said Porter resigned when the abuse allegations became public this week and had "worked hard" at the White House and wished him well. "It's a, obviously, tough time for him. He did a very good job when he was in the White House. And we hope he has a wonderful career," Trump said in his first comments on the allegations against the onetime West Wing star. "He said very strongly yesterday that he's innocent," Trump added.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel is the homeland "only of the Jewish people" on Sunday. Netanyahu addressed a "slightly confused people" after an Israeli celebrity defended the rights of Israel's Arab population. Arabs comprise about 20 percent of Israel's 9 million residents. They have full citizenship rights but have faced decades of discrimination. On Saturday, actress Rotem Sela criticized Netanyahu's frequent talking point that his political rival will form a government with Arab political parties. "When the hell will someone in this government tell the public that Israel is a country of all its citizens," Sela wrote on Instagram. Netanyahu responded: "Israel 'is the national state, not of all its citizens, but only of the Jewish people.'"

The Senate on Wednesday unanimously approved sanctions intended to limit Pyongyang's ability to finance warheads and missiles. The legislation targets those who knowingly do business with North Korea to benefit its nuclear weapons program and authorizes $50 million to broadcast messages directly to people in the isolated nation. Senator Cory Gardner, a first-term Republican from Colorado and a co-sponsor of the bill, said the measure mandates the sanctions rather than leaving them up to President Obama's discretion and imposes the first punitive measures in response to a violation of the nation's cybersecurity infrastructure. Gardner said the measure is the first of its kind and that he believes it will be a model for sanctions against other cyber-perpetrators around the globe.

President Trump tweeted Friday that he would nominate Texas Rep. John Ratcliffe as director of national intelligence. Ratcliffe, a Republican, had previously been nominated for DNI earlier in the year. The nomination was later withdrawn. Trump tweeted: "I am pleased to announce the nomination of @RepRatcliffe (Congressman John Ratcliffe) to be Director of National Intelligence (DNI). Would have completed process earlier, but John wanted to wait until after IG Report was finished. John is an outstanding man of great talent!" The New York Democrat said: "At a time when the Russians are interfering in our elections, we need a nonpartisan leader at the helm of the Intelligence Community who sees the world objectively and speaks truth to power, and unfortunately neither Acting Director Grenell nor Rep. Ratcliffe comes even close to that."

Former Vice President Joe Biden said in a video released by his campaign that he would not accept damaging information about an opponent if a foreign entity offered it. "I won't be part of any attempt to undermine our democracy or public confidence in our institutions," Biden stated. Biden repeatedly stated that several world leaders begged him to run for president against Trump. The campaign video features Trump's interview with ABC News in which he said he would probably both accept the information and turn it over to the FBI. Biden expressed concern about Trump's answer, speaking directly to the camera while at a desk. "Donald Trump doesn't think it matters if candidates accept damaging intel on their opponent from a foreign government. He's dead wrong," Biden said. Biden also said the pledge requires candidates to "use no disinformation in their campaigns or tolerate outside interference."

On Tuesday, Rep. John Lewis (D-GA) appeared on MSNBC's "Andrea Mitchell Reports" and called for impeachment proceedings to begin against President Donald Trump. Lewis said, "We tried every other path and used any other tool. We will any find the truth unless we use the power given to the House of Representatives and the House alone, to begin an official investigation as dictated by the Constitution." He added, "The future of our democracy is at stake. There comes a time when you have to be moved by the spirit of history to take action to protect the integrity of our nation. I believe, I truly believe, the time to begin impeachment proceedings against this president has come. To delay or to do otherwise would betray the foundation of our democracy."

Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder (R) will endorse Mitt Romney for president at a luncheon on Thursday, according to two sources with knowledge of his decision. MIRS news reported Wednesday evening that the two men will appear together at a luncheon Thursday for a "major announcement." A source confirmed that Snyder will be endorsing the former Massachusetts governor. Snyder is the early favorite in the Michigan Republican primary but may face a tough race against former Pennsylvania senator Rick Santorum. Snyder is in his first term. He won an open seat race in 2010 but has encountered some tough early sledding, and his approval rating has suffered some because of it. Snyder made his endorsement official in a Detroit News editorial published Thursday. "Mitt understands the challenges confronting Michigan as few Americans do," Snyder wrote. "I hope all Michiganians will join me in supporting the candidacy of this favorite son of our great state."

Former White House phsyician Dr. Connie Mariano said former White House phsyician Dr. Chris Christie called her and yelled at her. Mariano said Christie told her to "shut up," saying she worried his weight would lead to a heart attack or stroke in office. Mariano said Christie told her to "shut up," even though he had made his weight a public issue by eating donuts on David Letterman's show. Mariano said, "It was essentially the tone of the press conference only louder. It was hard to get anything across." Mariano told 3TV, "I don't think he realized who he was talking to," adding that it is common for medical experts to weigh in on the health concerns of potential presidential candidates. "I think I'm qualified to make a comment." Mariano said she had previously supported Christie.

A plagiarism scandal caused Democrat John Walsh to drop out of his bid to retain his U.S. Senate seat in Montana. Democrats have started an online petition to draft Academy Award-winning actor Jeff Bridges. "He has great recognition! Charisma! Brains!" Pratt writes on the petition, adding that Bridges is known internationally but is also highly accessible. Bridges first bought a house in Montana four decades ago. Republican Rep. Steve Daines was almost certainly going to take the seat before the scandal, but is now 10 points up. Bridges owns a home in Montana and has donated to Democrats but has never shown any kind of interest in electoral politics.

A Missouri state senator was arrested on Monday night outside the police department of Ferguson, Missouri, authorities said. The arrest occurred during protests following the fatal police shooting of an unarmed black teenager, 18-year-old Michael Brown, by white police officer Darren Wilson on August 9. St. Louis County Police spokesman Brian Schellman said State Senator Jamilah Nasheed was taken into custody by Ferguson police officers. Further details were not immediately available. CNN footage broadcast by television station KSDK showed Nasheed shouting "No Justice" and "No peace" from several protesters as she was handcuffed along with another man. KDSK reported that Nasheed was arrested after standing in the street and blocking traffic, then failing to move despite repeated warnings from police. Demonstrations have occurred in the St. Louis area almost daily since the Aug. 9 shooting.

Sam Stein appeared on "The Ed Show" with Republican strategist Ron Christie on Monday. During the program, host Ed Schultz raised questions about possible bad blood between Democratic Senate nominee Joe Sestak and the White House, with Stein and Christie finding common ground on the need for more disclosure. The conversation moved to Connecticut Senate candidate Richard Blumenthal apologizing for misstatements about his service during and not in the Vietnam War. The segment also included a segment featuring Michael Steele discussing questions about Rand Paul's comments about the Civil Rights Act. Schultz concluded with a clip of Steele acknowledging that Barack Obama was born in the United States.

Six additional Internal Revenue Service workers lost emails sought by congressional investigators when their computers crashed, investigators announced Tuesday. The information raises Republican suspicions that the employees may have been trying to cover up political targeting of Tea Party organizations. The revelation follows the news last week that Lois Lerner, the former chief of the I.R.S. division that grants tax-exempt status to organizations, had also lost two years' worth of files when her computer crashed in mid-2011. The investigators said the growing number of disappearing records has heightened Republican concerns that the tax agency conducted politically motivated reviews. "Plotlines in Hollywood are more believable than what we are getting from this White House and the I.R.S.," said the investigators, Representative Dave Camp, Republican of Michigan, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, and Representative Charles Boustany Jr., Republican of Louisiana, chairman of the Ways and Means oversight subcommittee.

The Senate unanimously confirmed Lt. Gen. Paul Nakasone to lead the National Security Agency and U.S. Cyber Command on Tuesday. Nakasone was President Donald Trump's nominee to replace Navy Adm. Mike Rogers, who announced his retirement from the dual role in February. The Senate used a process called "hotline" for Nakasone's confirmation, which speeds up the voting process for a nominee considered non-controversial. Prior to taking over as director of the NSA and Cyber Command, Nakasone was head of U.S. Army Cyber Command. He previously served in positions at the NSA and Cyber Command. Democrats and Republicans praised his experience in the field, The Hill reported. His new job will come with a fourth star, a promotion after the Trump administration put Cyber Command on the same level as Central Command.

President Donald Trump criticized Fox News on Tuesday on Twitter. He criticized an interview that Fox News anchor Martha MacCallum conducted with Rep. Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.), who quit the 2020 race earlier this month. Swalwell sits on both the House Judiciary and Intelligence Committees that will hear former special counsel Robert Mueller's testimony on Wednesday. Trump followed up his tweet three minutes later with another praising of Sean Hannity. The Fox primetime host joined Trump on stage at a political rally before the 2018 midterms and has vowed to stump for Trump during his 2020 reelection campaign. Last month, Trump criticized Fox News after it released a poll that showed him trailing many of his potential 2020 Democratic rivals. In May, he criticized the network for covering the Democrats.

David Hogg said he will work in an advisory role for the company to focus on school as this is happening. He outlined the company's brand identity. "Union made in America to create good jobs that support American families. Have an emphasis on supporting progressive causes. Not attempt a white supremacist overthrow of the United States government. So you can sleep at night," he wrote. "We will have the name announced soon but we need to get through the legal process of trademarking as so on," Hogg wrote in one of several tweets Thursday on the venture. He acknowledged the venture is aimed at ruining MyPillow and Mr. Lindell. "Mike isn't going to know what hit him — this pillow fight is just getting started," he said.

A gun accidentally went off inside a kindergartner's backpack at a school in Memphis, the Shelby County Board of Education said Thursday. No one was injured. In a statement, the board said the child had brought a firearm to school and it discharged while students were waiting for the opening bell in the cafeteria. School staff took possession of the backpack and local law enforcement responded. The situation is under investigation and classes continued as scheduled. The board said there is no evidence at this time of harmful intent; however, weapons of any kind are prohibited on campuses, and this student will be disciplined in accordance with the state's zero tolerance policy. The board said the safety of students and staff is of the utmost importance, staff is trained to handle emergency situations, and all students were kept safe and calm while this matter was handled. If the kindergartner is found guilty of an offense, he faces a 180-day suspension.

Senate negotiators resumed negotiations on immigration on Tuesday after Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York withdrew an offer to fully fund President Trump's proposed wall at the Mexican border. "The wall offer's off the table," Schumer told reporters at the Capitol a day after senators reached an impasse to end a three-day government shutdown. Schumer's decision to renege, made on Sunday but revealed publicly on Tuesday, marked another turn in the debate over how to shield from deportation hundreds of thousands of young immigrants brought to the country illegally as children. As part of a deal to end the shutdown, Senator Mitch McConnell, the majority leader, promised what he called a "fair and open" immigration debate on the Senate floor.

Former Democratic presidential candidate George McGovern, 90, was on life support and "no longer responsive" on Wednesday, two days after he was admitted to a hospice, his family said. The family said in a statement issued Wednesday afternoon that the 90-year-old former U.S. senator from South Dakota suffers from a variety of ailments "that have worsened over recent months" due to age. McGovern is best known for his 1972 run to unseat Richard Nixon on a platform that included ending the war in Vietnam. He lost 49 of the 50 states to the Republican incumbent, who resigned in the Watergate scandal less than two years later. McGovern won a seat in the House of Representatives in 1956 and was elected to the Senate in 1962. He returned to the Senate after his presidential campaign, but lost the seat in the Republican wave that accompanied Ronald Reagan's election to the White House in 1980.

Former New York Gov. George Pataki, a former 2016 GOP presidential candidate, endorsed Sen. Marco Rubio (R-TX) on Tuesday during an interview on Fox News's America's Newsroom. Pataki said Rubio "has the leadership, he has the vision" to be President of the United States, as well as the ability "to understand what it takes to defend us from radical Islam." Pataki said Rubio's experience in the U.S. Senate as being able to lead and "bring us together." "I'm going to do everything I can to help Senator Rubio," Pataki told Fox News's Martha MacCallum. When asked about fellow GOP candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), Pataki said Cruz is "a valuable asset...in the U.S. Senate."

The FBI said early Sunday that a suspect killed by Phoenix police in a bank robbery attempt is believed to be the same man accused in the shooting death of one Mississippi police officer and the wounding of another. The statement came hours after Phoenix police shot and killed the man minutes after Saturday's bank robbery attempt. The FBI said in an email statement: "We believe that this suspect is the same individual who is responsible for the attempted bank robbery in Atlanta, the robbery of the BancorpSouth in Tupelo, (Miss.) the shooting of Officer Joseph Maher, and the murder of Officer Gale Stauffer." Phoenix police had no immediate comment when contacted early Sunday. The slain suspect's name has not been released. The officers were shot Monday. Stauffer died and was buried Friday. Maher reportedly was able to walk with some aid on Friday.

President-elect Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood took an oath of office a day early on Friday in a televised speech to tens of thousands of supporters in Tahrir Square. Morsi made a promise during the speech to work for the release of Sheik Omar Abdel Rahman, an Egyptian-born militant Islamist convicted after the 1993 World Trade Center attack of plotting to bomb several New York City landmarks. Morsi referred briefly to Abdel Rahman in the context of a vow to free Egyptian civilians imprisoned in Egypt after military trials under the rule of the generals. "I see signs for Omar Abdel Rahman and detainees' pictures," he said. "It is my duty and I will make all efforts to have them free, including Omar Abdel Rahman."

In March, Hillary Clinton compared Russian President Vladimir Putin's aggression towards Ukraine to that of Adolf Hitler before World War II. Putin responded on Tuesday. Putin said: "It's better not to argue with women. But Ms. Clinton has never been too subtle in her statements. When people push boundaries too far, it's not because they are strong, but because they are weak. But maybe weakness is not the worst quality for a woman." Clinton is not the only one who made the remarks. In Canada, a Jewish woman told Prince Charles how she fled Poland during World War II when he told her, "Putin is doing just about the same as Hitler." Putin was referencing Russia's hostility and annexing of Crimea from Ukraine. Putin said these remarks were not "royal behavior."

Former Vice President Joe Biden spoke at a fundraiser in Philadelphia on Thursday evening. Video of his remarks obtained by The Associated Press from attendees was obtained by The Associated Press. Biden announced earlier that day that he was running for president. He said President Donald Trump's "moral equivalence" between white supremacists and counterprotesters was a major motivating factor. Biden made frequent mention of Trump at the fundraiser, saying, "Every nation is held up by an invisible moral fabric, and it's being shredded, and our kids are listening." He said he hopes in a few years people will realize that the Trump era was "an aberration in American history" "because this is not who we are."

Republican Rep. Jason Chaffetz of Utah said in an Instagram post Wednesday he needs immediate foot surgery and will be out of Washington for three to four weeks, missing a key vote on a spending bill to keep the government open. Chaffetz chairs the House Oversight Committee. He announced last week he will not seek re-election. He said in the post that he needs surgery to remove screws and pins from a foot he shattered 12 years ago. X-ray images showed the 14 screws and a metal plate in his foot. He said he injured his foot during a fall from a ladder at his home. He said he was "sorry to miss the important work we are doing in Washington ... but medical emergencies are never convenient." Chaffetz, 50, has not announced his future plans, although he says he is considering private sector jobs. He is a possible candidate for Utah governor in 2020.

Twitter (TWTR) was offline for about an hour on Thursday afternoon. The company said some people may now be able to access the site again. Twitter said in a statement Thursday afternoon that it was "currently investigating issues people are having accessing Twitter." Users can continue to monitor the site's status at status.twitterstat.us. It is unclear at this time how extensive the outage was or its exact length. "The outage was due to an internal configuration change, which we're now fixing," Twitter said in an update it posted to the status monitoring site. The outage coincided with the start of the White House's Presidential Social Media Summit. Twitter, along with Facebook (FB), was not invited to the summit, while a number of right-wing extremists were.

President Trump said on Saturday that he does not think North Korean leader Kim Jong Un will retaliate in a manner that disrupts the U.S. campaign season. Trump told White House reporters as he left for events in Florida: "We'll see about North Korea. I'd be surprised if North Korea acted hostilely." He added: "I have a very good relationship with Kim Jong Un. I think we both want to keep it that way. He knows I have an election coming up. I don't think he wants to interfere with that." Trump has had a personal relationship with Kim Jong Un. He met Kim last summer at the demilitarized zone that divides the Korean peninsula.

The White House said President Barack Obama and Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton will give their first joint interview to the television news show "60 Minutes" on Sunday. Clinton is soon to leave her post as secretary of state and is being mentioned as a possible presidential candidate for 2016. Obama and Clinton competed for the Democratic nomination for president in 2008. Their relationship has been watched closely ever since. It is not clear what questions the two will face in their joint interview.

Kansas Gov. Jeff Colyer's campaign has established a "voting integrity" telephone hotline for his close Republican primary race with Secretary of State Kris Kobach. Colyer's campaign announced the hotline Thursday. Spokesman Kendall Marr said it had received "countless" reports of voters experiencing issues at the polls. Kobach is the state's chief elections officers and told reporters Wednesday that he knew of no reports of irregularities outside of a long delay in the reporting of results from the state's most populous county because of issues with its new machines. Colyer's campaign announced the hotline as election officials confirmed that a mistake shorted Colyer's vote total for another county in the state's results by 100 votes.

Pfc. Bradley Manning on Thursday admitted in open court to providing vast archives of military and diplomatic files to the antisecrecy group WikiLeaks. He said he released the information to help enlighten the public about "what happens and why it happens" and to "spark a debate about foreign policy." Appearing before a military judge for more than an hour, Private Manning read a statement recounting how he joined the military, became an intelligence analyst in Iraq, decided that certain files should become known to the American public to prompt a wider debate about foreign policy, downloaded them from a secure computer network and then uploaded them to WikiLeaks. "No one associated with WLO" — an abbreviation he used to refer to the WikiLeaks organization — "pressured me into sending any more information," Private Manning said. "I take full responsibility."

Anthony Weiner, a sitting Congressman and Democrat rising star, joined Business Insider. In May 2011, Breitbart News reported that Weiner had tweeted a picture of his crotch to a young woman who was not his wife. Weiner initially claimed his Twitter feed had been hacked. He then accused Breitbart News founder Andrew Breitbart of lying. Weiner subsequently admitted he had lied about everything and resigned his Congressional seat. During the 2013 New York City mayoral race, Weiner gained name recognition and the help of left-wing outlets like the New York Times and Buzzfeed Politics. Early polls showed him leading the pack. A new revelation that Weiner had sexted with yet another woman destroyed that campaign.

Ruth Bader Ginsburg was hospitalized for heart surgery. The coronary blockage was discovered after Justice Ginsburg experienced discomfort during routine exercise last night and was taken to the hospital, the court said in a statement. She is resting comfortably and is expected to be discharged in the next 48 hours. Ginsburg has previously addressed speculation about her possible retirement. In an interview with Elle Magazine earlier this year, she said that if she stepped down this year, President Obama could not appoint anyone she would like to see on the court. She said: "[The Senate Democrats] took off the filibuster for lower federal court appointments, but it remains for this court. So anybody who thinks that if I step down, Obama could appoint someone like me, they're misguided. As long as I can do the job full steam ... I think I'll recognize when the time comes that I can't any longer. But now I can."

The author wrote that President Trump is scary in many ways but perhaps the most frightening nightmare is of him blundering into a new Korean war. The author wrote that this would begin because the present approach of leaning on China to pressure North Korea will likely fail. The author wrote that Trump will grow angry at public snickering at the emptiness of his threats. At some point, U.S. intelligence will see a North Korean missile prepared for a test launch. The author wrote that it may be tempting for a deeply frustrated president to show his muscle. The author described a scenario in Foreign Affairs in an essay by Philip Gordon imagining how Trump might drift into war by accident. The author wrote: "He could do nothing, but that would mean losing face and emboldening North Korea. Or he could destroy the test missile on its launchpad with a barrage of cruise missiles, blocking Pyongyang's path to a nuclear deterrent, enforcing his red line, and sending a clear message to the rest of the world."

The U.S. Department of Justice is talking with beer makers Anheuser-Busch InBev and Grupo Modelo about potentially resolving a legal challenge to their $20.1 billion deal. The beer companies and the government are asking the court for a stay of all litigation proceedings until March 19. There is no guarantee a resolution will be found. The Justice Department in January sued to block the combination, saying having one company controlling nearly half of all U.S. beer sales would stifle competition. The beer makers recently revised the terms of the acquisition, which would give more control of Modelo's U.S. beer brands to a wine company, Constellation Brands Inc., in a side deal. The government is weighing whether the revised terms of the deal resolve its concerns about market competition.

The Navy is searching for a sailor who went missing from the USS Nimitz in the Arabian Sea late Sunday, military officials said. Details of the incident are murky. The Navy said the Nimitz reported a "man overboard" just before 7 p.m. local time after conducting a thorough search of the ship. The aircraft carrier USS Nimitz (CVN 68) and guided-missile cruiser USS Princeton (CG 59) are conducting search & rescue operations in the North Arabian Sea following reports of a missing U.S. Navy Sailor, Sept 6, the Navy's Fifth Fleet said in a Twitter post. The Sailor has been listed as Duty Status Whereabouts Unknown on board aircraft carrier USS Nimitz. The Sailor's name is being held in accordance with U.S. Navy policy.

Sulaiman Abu Ghaith, a close associate of Osama bin Laden, told authorities after his arrest last year that the Sept. 11 terror attacks were a surprise to him, but that he had heard around Qaeda training camps in Afghanistan "that something big was going to happen," a federal agent testified on Thursday. The agent's testimony came in the trial of Abu Ghaith, 48, who later married Bin Laden's daughter and now faces charges that include conspiring to kill Americans and providing material support to terrorists. A prosecutor had told the jury that it would hear about Abu Ghaith's "confession," and that he had agreed, at Bin Laden's request, to make motivational speeches in Al Qaeda's training camps and, after Sept. 11, to make proclamations on behalf of the group.

U.S. District Judge Paul Oetken issued a Friday order allowing Lev Parnas, an associate of Rudy Giuliani, to begin sharing information with the House Intelligence Committee. Parnas, who is charged with violating federal campaign finance laws, had sought permission from the courts earlier this week to begin turning over evidence to Congress that had been seized during the FBI's investigation into him. The House Intelligence panel subpoenaed the materials, which include documents and the contents of a seized iPhone, in October. The information could still prove relevant to the impeachment investigation of Trump since Parnas was in regular contact with Giuliani, Trump's associate on the Ukraine scheme for which he has been impeached.

On Friday, Kellyanne Conway, the campaign manager for Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump, appeared on ABC's "Good Morning America." She told co-host David Muir that Trump's line from a night earlier at a rally in Charlotte, North Carolina, about his regret for some of his past remarks was "all him." Conway said that should incentive for those criticizing him to "some recognition and some forgiveness." She said: "He was talking about anyone who feels offended by anything he said, and that's all him. You know, he took extra time yesterday going over that speech with a pen, so that was a decision he made. Those are his words. And I hope that everybody who has criticized him at some point, David, for being insensitive or for mocking someone at least shows some recognition and some forgiveness."

A new Pew Research Center poll shows 40 percent of Americans say the Obama administration has been dishonest about the deaths of four Americans in Benghazi, Libya. Thirty-seven percent say it has been honest. Twenty-three percent say they do not know. Among Republicans, 70 percent say the administration has been dishonest. Among independents, 48 percent say the administration has been dishonest, while 30 percent say it has been honest. In the same poll, 36 percent said Republicans have gone too far in their hearings on the matter, while 34 percent say the Republicans have handled the matter appropriately. Independents are evenly split. Fifty-eight percent of independents say they are not following the issue closely or at all.

Joe Biden spoke at a Black History Month event on Tuesday. He discussed his basketball skills. At one point, he commented that he wanted to team up with former NBA player and Sacramento Mayor Kevin Johnson to challenge President Obama. "I told the president, next game, I've got him," Biden said. "I may be a white boy, but I can jump." Biden also commented on Voter ID bills passed in Southern states including Alabama, Texas and North Carolina. He said such bills prove that racial hatred still exists. Opponents say such bills are aimed at discouraging black voters from showing up to the polls. "These guys never go away. Hatred never, never goes away," Biden said. "The zealotry of those who wish to limit the franchise cannot be smothered by reason."

During Saturday night's Republican debate, Cruz began by saying, "Ben, I'm sorry," and then attributed the episode to CNN reporters. Cruz recalled that the network's political anchors, Jake Tapper and Dana Bash, reported the incident on television. Cruz said CNN's political anchors, Wolf Blitzer and Jake Tapper, said the episode was highly unusual and highly significant. The article reported that CNN reporters reported the episode on television. Comments on the story were closed.

Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday in the last of three hearings on a bipartisan immigration proposal that legislation to overhaul the nation's immigration laws would further strengthen the country's security system to guard against cases like the Boston Marathon bombings. The Boston bombings occurred in 2002, the two suspects in the case entering the country legally under an asylum petition by their father. The shadow of the bombings has shadowed the hearings. Some Republican senators and conservative commentators have urged caution on any new legislation until questions surrounding the bombings have been answered. Senator Lindsey Graham, Republican of South Carolina and a member of the bipartisan group of eight senators who wrote the legislation, has floated the idea of an amendment that would require immigrants, including refugees and asylum seekers, who are deemed potentially "high risk" to undergo a more comprehensive background check.

Secretary of State John Kerry criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel on Wednesday, saying the Israeli government was undermining any hope of a two-state solution to the Middle East conflict with the Palestinians. Kerry spoke with a clarity and harshness rarely heard from American diplomats when discussing one of their closest and strongest allies. With only 23 days remaining in his four-year tenure as secretary of state, during which he made the search for peace in the Middle East one of his driving missions, Kerry said the Israeli government was undermining any hope of a two-state solution to the conflict with the Palestinians. Kerry said the American vote last week in the United Nations allowing condemnation of Israel for settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem was driven by a desire to save Israel from "the most extreme elements" in its own government. "The status quo is leading toward one state and perpetual occupation," Kerry said, his voice animated.

The National Archives plans on Friday to release 2,500 more pages of documents from former President Bill Clinton's White House. Documents released since February have covered the Clinton administration's health care overhaul plan, Republicans' sweeping victories during the 1994 midterm elections, and other topics. The records set for release Friday are the third batch to come from the Clinton Presidential Library in Little Rock, Ark. The records have shed more light on former first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton's role within the administration and her aides' attempts to shape her public image. The records are being scrutinized by reporters and others as the former secretary of state and U.S. senator contemplates a second presidential campaign. About 8,000 pages of records have been released so far, part of roughly 30,000 pages expected to be released by the National Archives in the coming weeks.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, a Nevada Democrat, filed cloture to bring his debt ceiling bill to the Senate floor for a vote. The Democratic leader failed to secure the 60 votes needed to proceed. The cloture vote was blocked by the GOP, 50 to 49. Senator Scott Brown of Massachusetts voted with the Democratic majority for cloture. Two Democrats voted with the minority — Joe Manchin of West Virginia and Ben Nelson of Nebraska. Independent Bernie Sanders, who caucuses with Democrats, also voted against the Reid bill. Senate Democratic leaders gathered in House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi's office after the cloture vote to discuss their next steps in the debt ceiling debate. Senator Reid told me as he entered Rep. Pelosi's office that he remains confident a resolution would happen by the August 2 due date.

Voters in Colorado and Washington voted to legalize marijuana on Tuesday, while voters in Oregon voted against a similar initiative. Measure 80 failed in Oregon, largely because female voters opposed the initiative. Washington state voters legalized recreational use of marijuana. In Colorado, voters approved an initiative that would make it legal for those over 21 years of age to possess one ounce of marijuana. Colorado Governor John Hickenlooper (D) said while "voters have spoken and we have to respect their will," federal law still says marijuana is an illegal drug. "This will be a complicated process, but we intend to follow through," Hickenlooper stated. "That said, federal law still says marijuana is an illegal drug so don't break out the Cheetos or gold fish too quickly." Many Colorado residents expressed concerns that this initiative would turn Colorado into a magnet state for marijuana dealers.

The Taliban claimed the capture occurred in December during a night raid in Afghanistan. The International Assistance Security Force, led by the United States, issued confirmation of the capture. An official said the dog was British, not American, Fox News said. The IASF said, "We can confirm that a military working dog went missing following an ISAF mission in December 2013. It is ISAF policy to defer identification to the appropriate national authorities." The video shows a Taliban militant with long hair parading the dog before the camera. In addition to the dog, the Taliban displayed various weaponry members said were confiscated during the same raid, AP reported. Working dogs in Afghanistan are frequently used by ISAF forces, particularly German Shepherds, Labradors and Spaniels.

President Trump's physician, Dr. Sean Conley, said Monday night that Mr. Trump's unannounced checkup at Walter Reed National Medical Center last weekend was "routine" and that the president did not have any "acute" health issues such as chest pains. Addressing speculation about the president's checkup, Dr. Conley said his visit Saturday to Walter Reed National Medical Center was "a routine, planned interim checkup as part of the regular primary preventative care he receives throughout the year." In a letter released by the White House, the doctor said: "The president has not had any chest pain, nor was he evaluated or treated for any urgent or acute issues. Specifically, he did not undergo any specialized cardiac or neurologic evaluations."

At 10:45 ET, police in Pittsburgh reported an active shooter near the Tree of Life Congregation Synagogue in Pittsburgh, Pa. Local media reports at least four dead and several reports saying 7 or more. The Squirrel Hill area is one of Pittsburgh's largest Jewish neighborhoods and Tree of Life Synagogue is one of the largest congregations. More details are available. Police are telling those in the area to shelter in place. Reports indicate the suspect in the shooting has surrendered. If you are in the area, do not take this as an all clear signal. More information is developing. ABC News reported that police in New York City are deploying protection to synagogues and Jewish locations throughout New York City. ABC News characterized the deployment as a precaution and not a response to a known threat.

The newly appointed prime minister of the Palestinian Authority, Rami Hamdallah, submitted his resignation on Thursday after two weeks in office. Hamdallah was the newly appointed prime minister of the Palestinian Authority. It was not immediately clear if the president of the West Bank-based authority, Mahmoud Abbas, would accept the resignation. Analysts said the matter was primarily a domestic matter that would not directly impinge on Abbas's ability to make decisions regarding Secretary of State John Kerry's peace mission. Analysts also said that the image of chronic political instability could undercut crucial international support for the Palestinians, both financial and political, at a time when they are supposed to be pushing for statehood. Palestinians said they viewed the political drama as another setback for Abbas and his Fatah Party.
