An official said the dog was British, not American, Fox News said. The IASF said, "We can confirm that a military working dog went missing following an ISAF mission in December 2013. It is ISAF policy to defer identification to the appropriate national authorities." The video shows a Taliban militant with long hair parading the dog before the camera. In addition to the dog, the Taliban displayed various weaponry members said were confiscated during the same raid, AP reported. Working dogs in Afghanistan are frequently used by ISAF forces, particularly German Shepherds, Labradors and Spaniels.

Former Vice President Dick Cheney said Tuesday in an interview on CNN's "Anderson Cooper 360" that he has no regrets over his administration's decision to invade Iraq and topple Saddam Hussein. Cheney said, "It was the right thing to do then. I believed it then and I believe it now." He added, "No apologies." The Iraq War became an issue in the presidential campaign earlier this year when former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush, brother of Cheney's former boss, George W. Bush, struggled to elucidate his position on the mission. After a week of incomplete answers, Jeb Bush said that "knowing what we know now, ...I would not have engaged. I would not have gone into Iraq." Later in August, the former Florida governor appeared to backtrack on that statement when he said that taking out Hussein "turned out to be a pretty good deal."

In the race to be Virginia's next governor, Democrat Terry McAuliffe has opened up a 5-point lead over his Republican opponent, according to a Quinnipiac University poll released Thursday morning. Republican Ken Cuccinelli, the state's sitting attorney general, received 38 percent to McAuliffe's 43 percent. The survey shows the race is still tight. McAuliffe, former head of the Democratic National Committee and an unsuccessful 2009 candidate for governor, has gained on Cuccinelli. A March 27 survey showed the Republican with a 2-point lead, Quinnipiac said. Peter Brown, assistant director of the Quinnipiac University Polling Institute, said: "The 17 percent of voters who say they are undecided will determine the Commonwealth's next governor. At this point, neither man seems to have much of an edge."

Democratic House Minority Leader Rep. Nancy Pelosi praised Bernie Sanders for voting against the Clinton administration's Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), which defined marriage as one man and one woman. "Bernie Sanders was my colleague in the House," Pelosi said at a forum at George Washington University, noting that she has yet to endorse anyone in the Democratic race. "We voted against DOMA, you know, against all of those things people are subjecting to scrutiny now. He's fabulous, and he has a very important tonic for the country and for the Democratic Party because he has ideas." Hillary Clinton has been criticized for her previous support for her husband's DOMA law. In a 2004 floor speech, then-senator Hillary Clinton defended the heterosexual definition of the "sacred bond" of marriage in a 2004 floor speech.

CNN and host Jake Tapper apologized for an on-screen banner that appeared during his show on Monday. Tapper said the on-screen text was "unacceptable" and "horrified." He posted several Twitter posts explaining that, despite his absence, he was "furious" and his "staff has heard from me." The phrase appeared during a discussion among Jim Sciutto, subbing for Tapper on "The Lead," and two journalists about President-elect Donald Trump's support from the alt-right. The segment focused on white nationalist leader Richard Spencer, whose anti-Semitic declarations Sciutto characterized as "hate-filled garbage." The on-screen phrase during the segment stated, "Alt-Right Founder Questions if Jews are People." CNN issued a statement calling that caption "poor judgment and we very much regret it and apologize."

President Trump criticized former President Barack Obama on Sunday, calling him "grossly incompetent." Returning to the White House from a weekend at Camp David, Trump was asked by reporters about Obama's criticism that his administration has shown a lack of leadership during the coronavirus pandemic. "Look, he was an incompetent president," Trump said. "That's all I can say. Grossly incompetent." During online remarks Saturday for an event honoring students graduating from Historically Black Colleges and Universities, Obama said, "More than anything, this pandemic has fully, finally torn back the curtain on the idea that so many of the folks in charge know what they're doing. A lot of them aren't even pretending to be in charge."

The Republican National Committee unveiled a series of online postcards mocking President Obama's upcoming vacation at Martha's Vineyard. One postcard states: "I'd say after 40 fundraisers, I've earned a vacation." Other postcards show Obama riding a bicycle. One includes Obama holding a bodyboard stating: "Finding a wave in Martha's Vineyard is almost as hard as finding a job" and the president bowling with the caption, "I hope I bowl higher than my approval rating." The RNC believes Obama should remain in Washington to focus on repairing the struggling economy. White House Press Secretary Jay Carney defended Obama's vacation last week when he said "there is no such thing as a presidential vacation" and that Obama would continue to be briefed on the economy. President Obama announced Wednesday he would unveil his plan on the economy and job creation in early September. The president leaves the White House Thursday afternoon and returns from his vacation August 27.

Secretary of State John Kerry visited Kiev on Tuesday with an offer of $1 billion in an American loan guarantee and pledges of technical assistance. Kerry stopped first at improvised memorials where protesters were killed last month as they voiced opposition to what was then Ukraine's pro-Kremlin government. He placed a lighted candle at one of the shrines, which were draped with flowers and photographs of some of the victims; met with religious leaders; and listened to Ukrainians who beseeched him for help. "We hope Russian troops will leave Crimea, and we also hope for your assistance," a Ukrainian woman told Kerry as he walked along Instytutska Street.

Bob Beauprez, a buffalo rancher and a former congressman and community banker, defeated three rivals in a Republican primary election on Tuesday to become his party's choice to take on Colorado's governor in November, The Associated Press reported. With about 73 percent of the vote counted, Beauprez had 31 percent. His closest competitor, Tom Tancredo, also a former congressman, had 26 percent. Beauprez also beat Scott Gessler, the secretary of state, and Mike Kopp, an Army veteran and a former state senator. Tancredo had built a national profile for comments he made opposing illegal immigration.

U.S. officials and their Afghan counterparts have reached a tentative security agreement. The agreement includes a letter from President Obama to Afghan President Hamid Karzai. The New York Times reported the idea of the letter was originally proposed to Karzai by Secretary of State John Kerry. With the letter, the Afghan government agrees to allow the U.S. to conduct "raids on Afghan homes in certain circumstances, which had been an area of disagreement." Another area of disagreement concerns a provision that says "U.S. forces staying in Afghanistan beyond 2014 cannot be tried in local courts for any crimes they commit." If the tentative agreement is accepted by all parties involved, U.S. troops will have sole control over Bagram Air Field, north of Kabul, but will share facilities on eight Afghan-run bases throughout the country.

White House press secretary Jay Carney said Wednesday that the president does not have an opinion on the announcement that the U.S. Postal Service will stop delivering mail on Saturdays. Carney added that the Republican-controlled House had not passed legislation designed to help the USPS. Carney said the White House put forward a series of proposals for reform of the postal service that would put it on much more firm financial ground and it passed the Senate. He said the House failed to take it up. Carney said it would be the preference that that comprehensive package of reforms be implemented for the sake of a stronger future postal service. Carney said the USPS is an independent agency and that the White House only learned of the change, which takes effect in August, on Tuesday. Polling in recent years shows that a majority of Americans support halting Saturday mail delivery to help the Postal Service deal with its financial problems.

New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio said Monday that everyone must follow laws but he will not second-guess his drivers' judgment after video footage showed his official vehicle breaking several traffic laws as he sat in the front seat. De Blasio said, "no one is above the law." He said he will not second-guess the police officers who drive him or question their security protocols. The mayor also said he does not believe the video undermines his recently launched traffic safety campaign. WCBS-TV reported that the mayor's two-SUV caravan was speeding and running stop signs Thursday. De Blasio did not answer questions Friday about the incident. He deferred to Police Commissioner William Bratton, who said he was not "overly concerned" by the footage. De Blasio did not have any public events over the weekend.

Secret Service agent Timothy McCarthy, who took a bullet during the attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan, said he hopes a federal judge is right that John Hinckley is no longer a threat and can be released to live with his mother. McCarthy, now the police chief of the Chicago suburb of Orland Park, said he is a bit perturbed he did not receive a notification of the judge's decision to allow Hinckley to go free. McCarthy noted he has never been asked for an opinion on whether Hinckley should be released. During the March 30, 1981 assassination attempt, the then 32-year-old McCarthy was shot in the right chest. He said he spent a little more than three months recuperating before returning to the president's security detail.

President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. was "cocked and loaded" to retaliate against Iran for downing an American drone. He canceled the missile strikes 10 minutes before they were scheduled to be executed after being told some 150 people could die. Trump tweeted Friday that the U.S. will never allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon. He said he is in no hurry to respond to the downing of the U.S. surveillance drone over the Strait of Hormuz. His statement was the latest indication that he does not want to escalate the clash with Tehran, but he did not rule out a future U.S. strike. He said U.S. economic sanctions are crippling the Iranian economy and more are being added. Iran claimed Friday it had issued several warnings before shooting down the drone over what it said was Iranian territory.

Michael Vines, a man with a gun face tattoo, was arrested for unlawful possession of a firearm after a car accident. According to the Greenville Police Department, Vines was involved in a car accident and allegedly tossed a loaded .38-caliber revolver into the grass. According to police, Vines is federally prohibited from possessing a firearm. Vines has a large tattoo of a gun across his forehead. Firefighters on the scene witnessed Vines allegedly tossing the gun away and alerted police. Vines was charged with driving with a suspended license, driving too fast for conditions and unlawful possession of a firearm. The Greenville police said the real weapon was placed in property and evidence. The car accident occurred southwest of downtown Greenville, South Carolina.

President Obama said during a press conference Friday that he would save Russian President Vladimir Putin if he were drowning. ABC News reporter Jonathan Karl asked Obama the question during a press conference in South Korea. Obama replied, "I absolutely would save Mr. Putin if he were drowning." He added, "I'd like to think that if anybody's out there drowning, I'm going to save them." Obama said he was a good swimmer while growing up in Hawaii but was a little out of practice. Putin was asked a similar question during a question-and-answer event in Russia last week. Putin replied, "I don't think I have a close personal relationship with Obama. I think Obama is a courageous and good person, and he would for sure save me."

On Thursday, members of Congress departed for their five-week August recess. They did not consider a five-year farm measure. House Republican leaders worked through a short-term $383 million package of loans and grants for livestock producers and a limited number of farmers. The measure passed 223 to 197. Democrats objected to the handling of the farm legislation. Some Republicans also objected to the costs. The Senate had already passed a bipartisan five-year bill. Democrats in the Senate refused to take up the House measure, saying they were disappointed that House Republican leaders did not consider the broader legislation in time.

South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford spoke to The Associated Press on Sunday outside his coastal home on Sullivans Island. He said he considered resigning as his extramarital affair became public but vowed to remain in office. Wearing khaki shorts and a t-shirt, Sanford talked of his faith in God and said leaving office would be the easy way out. The governor admitted last week to a yearlong affair with a woman in Argentina. He and his wife said they will try to reconcile. Some lawmakers are calling for him to resign because he used public money to see the mistress during one trip and because he was out of touch with his staff during his recent weeklong tryst. Sanford said he did not use public money for the recent trip.

On Thursday, MSNBC host Chris Matthews will interview President Obama at American University in Washington, D.C. Obama will answer questions from the student audience, as well as some online. Obama recently held an off-the-record meeting with several MSNBC hosts at the White House following the rollout of HealthCare.gov, an interim nuclear deal with Iran, renewed calls for immigration reform, and new budget negotiations on the horizon. MSNBC's website stated that Obama's interview with Matthews follows the rollout of HealthCare.gov, an interim nuclear deal with Iran, renewed calls for immigration reform, and new budget negotiations on the horizon. Matthews will also discuss a number of topics with Obama, including voter suppression, healthcare, political gridlock in D.C., growing dissatisfaction with the government, and more.

A Twitter account identified as @iamthespookster showed tweets criticizing the 2016 election of President Trump. The account, which was operated by a 21-year-old man identified as the gunman who killed nine people, including his sister, outside a Dayton, Ohio, bar over the weekend, showed left-leaning tweets lamenting the 2016 election of President Trump. The account also appeared to support Democratic presidential contender Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, according to The Associated Press. The account did not bear the killer's name but displayed selfies that resembled known photos of him. Twitter removed the account late Sunday, fueling speculation that it belonged to the gunman. The account was not associated with the suspect. The account was not associated with the suspect.

Iran's foreign minister, Mohammad Javad Zarif, wrote on Twitter late Friday that the U.S. move to call an emergency U.N. Security Council meeting on protests in the country marks another foreign policy "blunder" for the Trump administration. Zarif wrote that the Security Council "rebuffed the U.S.' naked attempt to hijack its mandate." He wrote that the majority emphasized the need to fully implement the nuclear deal and to refrain from interfering in the affairs of other countries. Zarif wrote: "Another FP (foreign policy) blunder for the Trump administration." U.S. President Donald Trump has voiced encouragement for anti-government demonstrations that have broken out in Iran. The U.S. called the U.N. meeting on Friday, portraying the protests that began last week as a human rights issue that could spill over into an international problem.

I think Obama is a courageous and good person, and he would for sure save me."

The poll, conducted April 23-27, involved 1,000 adults around the nation who were polled by telephone. Barbara Bush received 45 percent of the vote, Hillary Clinton received 24 percent, and Barbara Bush received 28 percent. Among blacks, 58 percent favored Obama, and Clinton received 30 percent. Among Hispanics and Latinos, Clinton received 45 percent, compared to Obama's 29 percent. Among whites, Clinton received 24 percent of the white vote. Among Hispanics and Latinos, Clinton received 45 percent, compared to Obama's 29 percent. The poll has a sampling error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

Florida Gov. Rick Scott (R) postponed a strategy meeting he had scheduled with Donald Trump in New York on Monday to monitor a storm approaching his state. Melissa Sellers, a spokesperson for Scott's political organization, said Sunday that the governor plans to stay in Florida. On Sunday, the National Hurricane Center issued a Tropical Storm Warning for parts of the Florida Gulf Coast. Sellers told The Washington Post last week that Scott intended to meet with Trump to talk about general election strategy in Florida, which is seen as a key battleground. Scott has said he is not interested in being Trump's vice presidential running mate. Sellers said that as of now, there is no date set for a re-scheduled meeting. Trump spokeswoman Hope Hicks said, "We should have a new date in the next few days."

Donald Trump shared a 30-second video on Twitter on Friday that was reportedly created by a pro-Trump meme maker. The clip was based on a Time magazine cover and accompanying video from 2018 that argued that "Trumpism will outlast Trump." It ended with Trump standing behind a lectern bearing the sign "Trump 4Eva." Time tweeted its original version of the clip to the president. The clip was posted amid escalating U.S. tensions with Iran and a new rape allegation against Trump, which the president has denied. An earlier version of the story referred to the video as "doctored." The video is a different video from Time's, but made to look similar.

Paul Ryan told the Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel that he has no complaints regarding the way Mitt Romney has deployed his running mate. Ryan said the campaign has asked him to stop something or do something differently or not do anything. Last week, Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker (R) suggested the Romney campaign was restraining Ryan. Ryan responded that the Romney campaign needs to be more bold. He said: "A, we still have a ways to go. We still have a lot left that we're planning on doing. B, I think that's just what conservatives do by nature. I think that's just the nature of conservative punditry is to do that — to kind of complain — about any imperfection they might see."

President Trump's campaign arm launched a new ad Monday celebrating Trump's first 100 days in office, highlighting his achievements in office, and dismissing negative media coverage. The $1.5 million ad buy, featuring a TV ad and a series of targeted digital ads, comes as the Trump administration seeks to counter criticism that the president's first days in office have not been as productive or as successful as had been hoped. A voiceover says, "America has rarely seen such success," but later adds, "You wouldn't know it from watching the news." The ad highlights the confirmation of Justice Neil Gorsuch to the Supreme Court, greater energy independence, de-regulation, and Trump's plan to cut taxes as examples of Trump's 100 day success. The narrator says, "America is winning again and President Trump is making America great again."

President Donald Trump held a rally in Louisville, Kentucky, on Monday. According to reports, Trump raised free agent quarterback Colin Kaepernick's inability to land a job with a team. Trump previously called Kaepernick disrespectful for taking a knee during the national anthem to protest racial injustice before games last season. Trump referenced a Bleacher Report story in which an unidentified team general manager estimated that 10 percent of teams were reluctant to sign Kaepernick over fears Trump would tweet about them. Trump said: "There was an article today … that NFL owners don't want to pick him up because they don't want to get a nasty tweet from Donald Trump. Do you believe that?"

Reporters and some Republicans gush about Obama's economic policies in private, Obama told the Hill following his economic speech in Illinois. Republicans publicly criticized the president for giving an address that offered the same failed ideas. Obama said they and the media often praise his ideas. "It's interesting, in the run-up to this speech, a lot of reporters say that, well, Mr. President, these are all good ideas, but some of you've said before; some of them sound great, but you can't get those through Congress. Republicans won't agree with you," Obama said. Obama argued some Republicans privately agree with a lot of his ideas. "I know because they've said so. But they worry they'll face swift political retaliation for cooperating with me," he said.

Sen. Dick Durbin called on the U.S. Department of Justice to investigate the death of Sandra Bland, a suburban Chicago woman who was found hanged to death in a Texas jail cell earlier this month. Durbin wrote a letter to Attorney General Loretta Lynch urging the investigation into "the arrest, incarceration, and death of Sandra Bland, a constituent of mine from Naperville, Illinois." The letter was dated Jul 25, 2015 at 9:21 PM PT.

Republican leaders are signaling that they believe the coming elections are more than a referendum on the administration's economic policies. They are also trying to make the fall campaign about the president himself and the kind of societal change he actually represents. The Republican Senate primary in Delaware this week was the latest in a series of conservative insurgents to challenge the party establishment. Such primaries have threatened to reopen longstanding rifts within the party. The increased focus on Mr. Obama's personal history is probably less about persuading the electorate as a whole than it is about unifying the disparate strands of the conservative base.

The letter was dated Jul 25, 2015 at 9:21 PM PT.

An Illinois judge on Tuesday dismissed a lawsuit that challenged the eligibility of Republican presidential candidate Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX). The lawsuit was filed by Lawrence Joyce, a lawyer who challenged Cruz's eligibility to be president because he was born in Canada to an American mother. Joyce told USA Today: "What I fear is that Ted Cruz becomes the nominee, come September, Congressman Alan Grayson of Florida will go forward with his threats and probably several other Democrats will file suit to prevent Ted Cruz from being on the ballot." In a radio interview in November, Grayson said: "I'm waiting for the moment that he gets the nomination, and then I will file that beautiful lawsuit saying that he's unqualified for the job because he's ineligible. Call me crazy, but I think the president of America should be an American."

Rep. Michele Bachmann, a Minnesota Republican, said on Wednesday that President Obama has failed to demonstrate a vital U.S. national security interest for going into Libya. Bachmann said, "I would not have gone" into the North African country where Col. Moammar Gadhafi is fighting to cling to power against a resistance force. She is considering whether to seek her party's 2012 presidential nomination. She told NBC's "Today" show she does not support intervening regularly in humanitarian crises. She said the "Obama Doctrine" would provide a rationale for the United States "to enter into one country after another." Bachmann said she opposes giving military assistance to the rebels fighting Col. Gadhafi, saying she fears there are al Qaeda elements among their numbers.

White House Press Secretary Jay Carney said Wednesday he had no idea whether singer Beyonce lip-synced during President Obama's second inauguration. Carney said, "As powerful as this office is, we don't control the weather," and noted that pre-recordings were made as a precaution, just as they were for the 2009 inauguration. In response to several more questions on the issue, Carney said, "I'm glad you guys are focused on the important issues of the day here." A spokesman for the Marine Corps band said that the music accompanying Beyonce was pre-recorded. Carney could not say whether Beyonce was lip-syncing or actually singing, referring reporters to the Presidential Inaugural Committee and the singer herself.

Thousands of Australians used the hashtag #illridewithyou on Twitter to support the Muslim community after an Islamic State sympathizer took several people hostage at a Sydney chocolate shop on Tuesday. Police stormed the downtown Lindt chocolate cafe, where a gunman had been holding an unknown number of people hostage for more than 16 hours. An Islamic State flag was reportedly raised in the shop's window during the crisis, which prompted fears among Sydney's Muslim community. More than 40 Muslim groups condemned the siege, saying in a statement that they rejected "any attempt to take the innocent life of any human being or to instil fear and terror into their hearts," Agence France-Presse reported. An Australian woman started the #illridewithyou campaign to show solidarity with Muslims who might feel targeted on public transportation.

President Donald Trump's reelection campaign removed an advertisement on Monday that promoted the Trump administration's first 100 days. The 30-second video was deleted and replaced with an advertisement titled "America has rarely seen such success." The original video was deleted and replaced with an advertisement promoting the administration's accomplishments at Mar-a-Lago. The advertisement, which promoted the administration's accomplishments during its first 100 days, featured a b-roll showing the president shaking hands with National Security Advisor Lieutenant General H.R. McMaster just after he accepted the job at Mar-a-Lago. McMaster was wearing his Army uniform. The advertisement may have violated Defense Department rules barring active-duty members of the military from participating in political advocacy in uniform.

A text of President Obama's speech on Thursday on national security issues was released by the White House. The text read: "Good morning, everybody. Please be seated. Thank you all for being here. Let me just acknowledge the presence of some of my outstanding Cabinet members and advisors. We've got our Secretary of State, Hillary Clinton. We have our CIA Director Leon Panetta. We have our Secretary of Defense William Gates (sic); Secretary Napolitano of Department of Homeland Security; Attorney General Eric Holder; my National Security Advisor Jim Jones. And I want to especially thank our Acting Archivist of the United States, Adrienne Thomas. I also want to acknowledge several members of the House who have great interest in intelligence matters. I want to thank Congressman Reyes, Congressman Hoekstra, Congressman King, as well as Congressman Thompson, for being here today. Thank you so much."

The Obama administration opened its appellate defense of the 2010 health care act on Tuesday before three randomly selected judges who each had been appointed by Democratic presidents, including two named by President Obama himself. The 14 members of the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, the first appellate court to review the law, are evenly divided as appointees of Democratic and Republican presidents. The odds of drawing three Democratic appointees in the computerized lottery are roughly 10 to 1. Lawyers do not learn the makeup of the panel until the day of the hearing. In five decisions in lower courts, three Democratic-appointed judges upheld the Affordable Care Act while two Republican-appointed judges ruled that its central provision — the requirement that most Americans obtain health insurance — is unconstitutional.

White House Press Secretary Jay Carney said Wednesday he had no idea whether singer Beyonce lip-synced when she sang the national anthem at President Obama's second inauguration. Carney said, "As powerful as this office is, we don't control the weather," and noted that pre-recordings were made as a precaution, just as they were for the 2009 inauguration. In response to several more questions on the issue, Carney said, "I'm glad you guys are focused on the important issues of the day here." A spokesman for the Marine Corps band said that the music accompanying Beyonce was pre-recorded. Carney could not say whether Beyonce was lip-syncing or actually singing, referring reporters to the Presidential Inaugural Committee and the singer herself.

Hawaii filed an amended federal lawsuit Tuesday night challenging President Donald Trump's revised travel ban. The state filed the suit with updates on its existing challenge to the previous order. The lawsuit states the order will harm the Muslim population of Hawaii. The new order, announced Monday, bars new visas for people from six Muslim-majority countries and temporarily shuts down America's refugee program, affecting would-be visitors and immigrants from Iran, Syria, Somalia, Sudan, Yemen and Libya. Hawaii's lawsuit says it is suing to protect its residents, businesses and schools, as well as its sovereignty against illegal actions of President Donald J. Trump and the federal government. Hawaii's lawsuit had been on hold while a nationwide injunction on the initial ban remained in place.

Turkey's foreign minister Mevlut Cavusoglu said U.S. forces in Syria are stalling the fight against Islamic State militants as an excuse not to cut ties with Syrian Kurdish fighters as Ankara had demanded. Cavusoglu said U.S. forces are leaving "pockets" with IS militants intact to justify continued cooperation with the Kurdish militia. Cavusoglu said ties with the U.S. are "at a critical stage" and that Washington needs to take "concrete steps" to regain Turkey's trust. Ankara is concerned over Washington's support for the Syrian Kurdish People's Protection Units, or YPG, the top U.S. ally in the anti-IS fight. Turkey considers the YPG a "terrorist" group linked to Kurdish insurgents within Turkey. U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson is due in Ankara later this week.

A Quinnipiac University poll released Thursday shows President Obama and presumptive Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney tied in Ohio. The poll shows Obama at 45 percent and Romney at 44 percent. The poll has a margin of error of 3 percentage points. The same poll on Feb. 15 showed Obama leading Romney 46 percent to 44 percent in Ohio. The latest poll found Portman would not move the needle in Ohio as Romney's running mate, showing a 45-45 tie between the tickets with the senator included. Fifty-nine percent of Ohioans said they do not know enough about Portman to form an opinion. Republicans have never won the White House without capturing Ohio.

In a closed-door meeting Wednesday, House Speaker John Boehner (R-OH) said, "people say a lot of things about [me], but he just lets 'that s–t roll off [my] back.'" According to The Hill, Boehner was meeting with GOP lawmakers when he said these things. He reportedly explained that he knew GOP lawmakers were among the critics. Thus, he said, those criticizing him included "people outside this room [and] people inside this room." Conservative Republicans do not think Boehner has fought hard enough for fiscal constraint, while Democrats say he is too closely aligned with the Tea Party. Boehner said he puts both sets of criticism behind him and that he did not take the position of Speaker to get a "big office," but to get things done.

The U.S. ambassador to Israel did not attend Wednesday's arrival of Secretary of State Mike Pompeo in Israel as he was feeling unwell and had been advised to keep away, the U.S. State Department said. Pompeo landed at Ben Gurion Airport for a one-day visit during which he will meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his designated coalition partner, Benny Gantz. A State Department spokeswoman said the envoy, David Friedman, tested negative for the coronavirus. Friedman experienced "mild upper respiratory symptoms" and was asked by medical staff to avoid proximity to Pompeo, media added, quoting a statement from the U.S. embassy in Israel. Pompeo said on Twitter after his arrival that topics to feature in talks will be the virus pandemic outbreak and regional tensions with Iran.

The body of Boston bombing suspect Tamerlan Tsarnaev was reportedly buried in a Muslim cemetery in Doswell, a small town in central Virginia, about 15 miles from Richmond. Al-Barzakh Cemetery in Doswell, the first Muslim resting place in the region, has interred Tsarnaev's remains, according to the Boston Globe. Tsarnaev, 26, died during a shootout with police in Watertown, Mass. His brother, Dzhokhar, 19, is recovering from gunshot wounds at Fort Devens. The interment came after a Virginia woman saw protests outside a Worcester, Mass., funeral home that was storing Tsarnaev's body. Nobody wanted him buried locally, and she decided to help. The woman contacted the Islamic Society of Greater Richmond and asked if members could help find a burial ground for the body. Society members found the Doswell cemetery and moved Tsarnaev on Wednesday evening, the Globe reported.

Former President Bill Clinton addressed corporate inversions during an event at the Clinton Global Initiative. He said the United States is now the only O.E.C.D. country that also taxes overseas earnings. Steel said the companies were exploiting a "loophole." President Obama said the companies were exploiting a "loophole." The Treasury Department announced new rules this week designed to reduce the benefits available through inversion. Corporate inversions became news this summer after a few high-profile companies including Burger King announced plans to merge with foreign companies, including with a Canadian chain called Tim Hortons. Inversion does not allow the companies to escape taxes on money earned within the United States but does allow them to avoid U.S. taxes on money earned abroad.

The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits fell last week and a gauge of factory activity hit an eight-month high in early November, the Labor Department said. Other data released on Thursday showed that wholesale prices fell for a second month in October, the latest sign of a lack of inflation pressure, giving the Federal Reserve some leeway as it considers when to begin tapering its bond-buying program. Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 21,000 to a seasonally adjusted 323,000, the Labor Department said. Economists had forecast a drop in the newly jobless to 335,000, and some said that the Veterans Day holiday last week could have contributed to some of the decline. The department said no special factors affected the data, which covered the survey period for the government's report on employment in November.

Sen. Marco Rubio's 12-year-old daughter, Amanda, was released from Miami Children's Hospital Sunday evening after a golf cart accident Saturday. Rubio spokesman Alex Conant said in a statement that Amanda is recuperating from a concussion and should improve in the coming days. Conant said her prognosis is good and she is expected to make a full recovery. The accident occurred in a private gated community. Amanda, the eldest of Rubio's four children, was a passenger in the golf cart. Conant added that Senator Rubio and Mrs. Rubio are grateful for the many messages of support and prayers for their daughter and grateful to the Miami Dade Fire Department and the staff at the Pediatric Trauma Center at Miami Children's Hospital for their excellent care.

Congress gave final approval Thursday to a $1.1 trillion spending bill that reduces the budget cuts known at the sequester and guarantees that the nation will not endure another government shutdown until at least Oct. 1. After three years of budget battles, the bipartisan agreement to fund federal agencies through the rest of the fiscal year passed with little fanfare. The Senate voted 72 to 26 to approve the measure Thursday evening. Republicans persuaded Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Tex.) to drop a last-minute push to force another showdown over the Affordable Care Act, reprising the fight that closed the government for 16 days last fall. The House overwhelmingly approved the spending bill earlier this week. The White House signaled that President Obama would sign it by Saturday, in time to prevent museums, agency offices and national parks from locking their gates when the current temporary funding measures expires.

A spokeswoman for Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau confirmed Monday that the prime minister will not travel to Havana for the funeral of Cuban leader Fidel Castro. On Saturday, Trudeau described Castro as a "legendary revolutionary and orator" and "a remarkable leader" in a statement. The statement drew criticism on Twitter from Republican U.S. senators Marco Rubio of Florida and Ted Cruz of Texas, both Cuban-Americans. Rubio called Trudeau's remarks "shameful" and Cruz called them "disgraceful." Castro attended the funeral of Trudeau's father, former Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau, in Montreal in 2000. Governor General David Johnston, Queen Elizabeth's II representative as Canada's head of state, will attend Castro's funeral.

Baltimore Mayor Catherine Pugh has asked the Board of Ethics to grant her an exemption from city ethics rules requiring officials to obtain approvals before soliciting private funds for community programs and events. The Baltimore Sun reports City Solicitor Andre Davis has asked the board to grant Pugh the exemption so she does not have to make requests to the ethics and spending board each time she raises private funds for the Baltimore City Foundation. The rules are meant to avoid conflicts of interest. Calling Baltimore "a poor city," Davis questioned the constraints on the mayor's ability to solicit monetary assistance. He said the five-member board has yet to make a decision. Ethics board member Stephan Fogleman says he has questions about the request. Referencing former Mayor Sheila Dixon's theft conviction, he stressed the need for transparency in city affairs.

The campaign of presumptive 2016 Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump sent an emergency email Saturday morning with a goal of raising $100,000 by the end of the day, with a campaign expected to cost in the hundreds of millions. The Clinton campaign launched a multi-million dollar ad blitz at Trump following his comments on the Orlando shooting. The Trump campaign appealed to Republican donors while the party appears to be shunning him. Comments on the story are closed.

Police in the Dominican Republic said they determined that three women who said they had sex with a U.S. senator for money were paid to make false claims by an attorney in the Caribbean country. Police spokesman Maximo Baez said officers traced the payments to attorney Melanio Figueroa. Baez said two women received about $425 each and the other was paid about $300 to falsely state on camera that they had sex with U.S. Sen. Robert Menendez of New Jersey. Baez said at a news conference Monday that authorities were seeking to interrogate Figueroa about the payments. Figueroa did not respond to messages left at his office. The women's videotaped statements were published on a conservative U.S. website. Menendez denied the allegations.

President Obama woke up in Havana on Tuesday to news that explosives had ripped through an airport and a subway in Brussels. He began a foreign trip overshadowed by violence elsewhere in the world. He held a morning briefing on the terrorist attacks with officials in Washington inside a specially equipped secure communications room. An expression of condolence and support for the Belgian people was inserted at the last minute into his speech to the Cuban people. "We stand in solidarity with them in condemning these outrageous attacks against innocent people," Obama declared in the Gran Teatro de la Habana. "We will do whatever is necessary to support our friend and ally Belgium in bringing to justice those who are responsible."

President Obama is considering speeding up the withdrawal of United States forces from Afghanistan and to a "zero option" that would leave no American troops there after next year, according to American and European officials. Mr. Obama is committed to ending America's military involvement in Afghanistan by the end of 2014, and Obama administration officials have been negotiating with Afghan officials about leaving a small "residual force" behind. Mr. Karzai has been declining to begin peace talks with the Taliban in Qatar. Mr. Karzai repudiated the talks and ended negotiations with the United States over the long-term security deal needed to keep American forces in Afghanistan after 2014.

A top Democrat in New Jersey's Legislature, Assemblyman John Wisniewski, said Sunday it is "far too early" to conclude whether Gov. Chris Christie knew about toll-lane closings that caused traffic problems near the George Washington Bridge and sparked a political scandal that could roil the 2016 presidential race. "We haven't had a chance to talk to some of the key players," Wisniewski, a Democrat who is leading legislative probes into the issue, told ABC's This Week with George Stephanopoulous. His comments came on the heels of an internal review that cleared Mr. Christie of wrongdoing and placed blame on top deputies in his office and at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey for the lane closings in Fort Lee, N.J., for several days in September.

Mr. Obama is committed to ending America's military involvement in Afghanistan by the end of 2014, and Obama administration officials have been negotiating with Afghan officials about leaving a small "residual force" behind. Mr. Karzai has been declining to begin peace talks with the Taliban in Qatar. Mr. Karzai repudiated the talks and ended negotiations with the United States over the long-term security deal needed to keep American forces in Afghanistan after 2014.

Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) appeared on CBS's Face the Nation and asked for Vice President Joe Biden to assist broker a deal over the government shutdown. McCain said, "maybe we need to get Joe Biden out of the witness protection program." He added, "I'm glad that negotiations are going on. I'm disappointed that twice…we were close to a deal and the Democrats moved the goalposts, in light of the polling data." McCain criticized President Obama for not being as active as President Clinton was during the 1995 shutdown, stating he was "disappointed" in Obama. McCain said Democrats needed to be "magnanimous and get things done... I know what it's like to be in the majority and in the minority, and it won't be forgotten."

Fox News' Major Garrett reported that President Obama's meeting on comprehensive energy legislation with bipartisan members of Congress originally scheduled for Wednesday has been cancelled. A White House official said the meeting was postponed due to scheduling conflicts. Hill sources told Fox the reason for the scheduling slide was to allow the president to focus on his meeting with Gen. Stanley McChrystal, who faces criticism for remarks he made in a series of interviews with Rolling Stone magazine. The White House and Congressional Democrats have been trying to use the Gulf Coast oil spill as an impetus to pass an energy bill that transitions America away from its dependence on fossil fuels, increases the use of renewable energy sources, and places a price on carbon pollution. Republicans say the Democrats' legislation amounts to an energy tax. A White House official told Fox the meeting will be rescheduled for next week.

Iran has extended its influence around the region by supporting Shiite opposition groups and conducting military operations in a handful of countries. Saudi Arabia is leading a coalition of Arab countries in military operations against the Houthi movement in Yemen. The formation of the coalition led to the creation, announced March 29 at an Arab summit in Egypt, of a unified Arab military force to counter Iranian influence and Islamic extremism. The United States and Iran both have military operations against the Islamic State in Iraq, though American officials insist they are not cooperating with Iran. Jordan has conducted airstrikes as part of an American-led operation, which includes many other Western countries as well.

Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Lindsey Graham said Sunday on "Fox News Sunday" that the idea of Senate Republicans voting to dismiss immediately the House impeachment articles was "dead for practical purposes," stating that the GOP majority lacked the votes. "That's dead for practical purposes," Graham said. "There are a lot of senators who I think will wind up acquitting the president, but believe that we need to hear the House's case, the president's answer to the House's case, and ask questions, and that's when the witness requests will be." His response ended speculation that Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell would hold a vote Tuesday to sink the trial without hearing the House impeachment managers make their case or the president's legal team respond.

Seth Meyers said on Monday's broadcast of "Late Night" that he knows what may have happened to the notes that President Donald Trump reportedly seized from his own interpreter following his 2017 meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Meyers said: "Now we don't know what Trump did with those notes, but we do know that in her tell-all book former Trump aide Omarosa said she saw Trump trying to destroy evidence by eating a piece of paper in the Oval Office." White House aides later denied Omarosa Manigault Newman's claims. Meyers continued: "We for real have a president who might one day say, 'If you want my notes you will need a search warrant for my belly.'"

A witness to the attacks at the Westgate shopping mall in Kenya's capital, Elijah Kamau, said Saturday that gunmen with AK-47s and grenades made a statement about Muslims as they began their attack at the mall around midday. Gunmen threw grenades and opened fire during the attack. Associated Press reporters at the scene said they saw about 10 dead bodies and dozens wounded more than two hours after the attack began. Officials did not yet give an official death toll. In late 2011, al-Shabab vowed in late 2011 to carry out a large-scale attack in Nairobi in retaliation for Kenya's sending of troops into Somalia to fight the Islamic insurgents.

Former Minnesota Governor Tim Pawlenty said Saturday on "America's News Headquarters" that his regrets related to "tactical decisions." Pawlenty said, "We took it as far as I could with my race and our resources. We didn't get it done, obviously." The former presidential candidate ended his campaign last August after finishing third in the Iowa straw polls. Shortly after that third place finish, Pawlenty endorsed Governor Mitt Romney. Pawlenty made earlier criticisms of Romney's healthcare law during an appearance on "Fox News Sunday" last June. Pawlenty told Chris Wallace, "President Obama said that he designed Obamacare after Romneycare and basically made it Obamneycare." Pawlenty now actively campaigns for Romney. He says Romney is the most capable, knowledgeable, and electable candidate.

The resignation of a Democratic state senator in Virginia, Phillip P. Puckett, occurred on Monday. The resignation set off charges that the deal was unseemly and threatened Gov. Terry McAuliffe's chances of expanding Medicaid under the president's health care law. Puckett served 16 years in the Senate. Democrats said Republicans orchestrated the resignation by promising him a plum position and speeding the appointment of his daughter to a state judgeship. Over the weekend, reports that Puckett was resigning to take a job on the Virginia tobacco commission angered his fellow Democrats, who saw the hand of Republican officials controlling the commission.

The U.S. Treasury Department will begin taking steps this week to delay hitting the government's $16.4 trillion borrowing limit. Without those steps, the debt limit would be hit on Dec. 31. Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner wrote in a letter to congressional leaders that the department will take several accounting measures to save approximately $200 billion beginning next year. The government borrows about $100 billion a month, so that would keep the government from reaching the limit for two months. Geithner said it is harder to predict how long the delay will last because ongoing negotiations over tax and budget policies make it hard to forecast what tax revenue and government spending will be next year. The debt limit is the amount the government can borrow to help finance its operations.

President Obama and Judge Sonia Sotomayor released remarks on her selection for the Supreme Court on Tuesday, as released by the White House. Obama said: "Of the many responsibilities granted to a President by our Constitution, few are more serious or more consequential than selecting a Supreme Court justice. The members of our highest court are granted life tenure, often serving long after the Presidents who appointed them. And they are charged with the vital task of applying principles put to paper more than 20 [sic] centuries ago to some of the most difficult questions of our time. So I don't take this decision lightly. I've made it only after deep reflection and careful deliberation. While there are many qualities that I admire in judges across the spectrum of judicial philosophy, and that I seek in my own nominee, there are few that stand out that I just want to mention."

U.S. Attorney General Loretta Lynch said one of her top priorities remains alleviating an "epidemic of distrust" between minority communities and law enforcement. Lynch discussed tensions between minority communities and police agencies during a speech Monday in Houston at the national convention of Delta Sigma Theta Sorority, Inc., the country's largest African-American women's organization. Lynch did not mention specific incidents related to this tension, including the in-custody death in Waller County, Texas, of Sandra Bland, a black woman who authorities say hanged herself earlier this month in her cell after a traffic-stop confrontation with a white officer. Lynch said she is determined to take on the tension between minorities and law enforcement as well as other issues "not only to build a stronger nation, but to empower its people."

Jennifer Willoughby and Colbie Holderness spoke out about their experiences with Rob Porter, their ex-husband. Porter had since become a top White House aide. On Friday, President Donald Trump said Porter "did a great job while he was at the White House. And we hope he has a wonderful career," adding that the aide had maintained his innocence. On Saturday, Trump tweeted that "lives are being shattered and destroyed by a mere allegation." Porter's resignation was announced Wednesday, hours after a photograph was published of Holderness with a black eye allegedly inflicted by Porter. Trump's staff secretary called the allegations from his former spouses "outrageous" and "simply false."

Florida's primary began with a lion's share of the vote. Former Massachusetts governor Mitt Romney appeared headed to a clear victory over former House Speaker Newt Gingrich on Tuesday. Pollster.com aggregated all polling data available on the Florida primary. The chart shows relative momentum of each candidate heading into tomorrow's vote. Romney has risen rapidly since losing in South Carolina on Jan. 21; Gingrich has dropped precipitously. The chart poses two questions: whether Romney's large lead in the Florida polling makes a double-digit victory a necessity for his campaign to end the race between now and the end of February, or whether a Romney win in Florida — of any size — is enough.

Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain acknowledged slipping from the top tier of candidates while addressing accusations of sexual harassment and confusion about his policy stands. "Obviously false accusations and confusion about some of my positions has contributed" to the downturn in polls, he said. The Georgia businessman said his campaign is sound and that supporters remain onboard what he called the "Cain train." Cain denied the accusations and said "nothing has gone wrong" in terms of the campaign's mechanics. He told CNN's "State of the Union" that some people "are heavily influenced by perception more so than reality." Cain also said he supports "targeted identification" in identifying potential terrorists. He did not see that as racial profiling and said "if you take a look at the people who have tried to kill us, it would be easy to figure out exactly what that identification profile looks like."

On Wednesday night, the official MSNBC Twitter account posted a tweet celebrating General Mills' decision to air a biracial commercial touting Cheerios during this Sunday's Super Bowl. The tweet included the phrase "the rightwing" and suggested "the rightwing" was racist. The commercial titled "Gracie" is part two of last year's "Just Checking" commercial for Cheerios. The father uses Cheerios to explain to "Gracie" she will soon have a younger sibling. Last month, MSNBC host Melissa Harris Perry criticized former Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney and his adopted biracial grandson, which led her to later issue an apology.

Gov. Mike Pence of Indiana said he would support legislation to "clarify the intent" of a new state law that has drawn widespread criticism over concerns that it could allow discrimination against gay people. In an interview on Saturday with The Indianapolis Star, the Republican governor said he had been in discussions with legislative leaders over the weekend. He expected that a clarification bill would be introduced this week to the religious objections law he signed on Thursday. Pence declined to provide details but told the newspaper that making gay and lesbian Indiana residents a protected legal class was "not on my agenda." He has disputed claims that the law allows state-sanctioned anti-gay discrimination, as some Indiana businesses, convention organizers and others have argued, and said that he did not anticipate "the hostility that's been directed at our state."

South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley (R-S.C.) will announce Monday that she is appointing Rep. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) to replace outgoing Sen. Jim DeMint (R-S.C.) in Congress, the New York Times reports. DeMint, who was elected to a second term in 2010, announced earlier this month that he will leave Congress in January to become president of the Heritage Foundation, a DC-based think tank. Scott has represented South Carolina's 1st congressional district since 2011. If appointed, he will become the state's first African American senator since the 19th century. He will also be the first black Republican in the Senate since Edward Brooke left his Massachusetts seat in 1979. DeMint's replacement will hold the seat until a special election is held in 2014.

White House counselor Kellyanne Conway said Monday that President Donald Trump withheld details of a conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2017 because of concern about leaking. Conway said on "Fox & Friends" that there was "great concern" of the leaking at the time. "That was a time when there were tremendous leaks, including from when the president would have meetings in the Oval Office. And I can recall early on two calls with foreign leaders, I believe Mexico and Australia, the contents of which leaked almost immediately. So there was great suspicion that some people, obviously were leaking this," Conway said. Conway also noted that the president has been tough on Russia with expulsions and sanctions as proof of Trump not colluding with Russia, something of which she said there is still no evidence.

Tim Pawlenty is running for vice president again, this time to be Mitt Romney's running mate. Pawlenty is trying to prove his loyalty and his effectiveness by doing Romney's dirty work. Some believe Rick Santorum is poised to do well in Pawlenty's home state of Minnesota, and the Romney team has sent the former governor on a seek-and-destroy mission. Pawlenty, who in his brief run for the nomination was reluctant to attack, has developed a taste for the jugular, calling Santorum unqualified to be president. Pawlenty is walking a fine line in his try-out for a spot on the ticket. Presidential nominees often need and want an attack dog. If the dog snarls and bites too much, it will stay in the pound.

President Obama will soon release a new budget. Progressives are angry over proposed cuts to Social Security; conservatives are denouncing the call for more revenues. House Republicans will block anything Mr. Obama proposes. The budget is best seen not as policy but as positioning, an attempt to gain praise from "centrist" pundits. The real policy action is in the states, where the question is, How many Americans will be denied essential health care in the name of freedom? I'm referring, of course, to the question of how many Republican governors will reject the Medicaid expansion that is a key part of Obamacare. In reality, nothing. But when it comes to politics, it's a different story.

New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie said Monday on Townsquare Media's monthly call-in program that he would not sign the version of an immigrant tuition bill passed by the state Senate. Christie said the Senate bill grants richer benefits than the federal Dream Act and could make New Jersey a magnet for students in the country illegally who want to go to college. The Senate bill allows state residents who were brought to the United States illegally as children to pay the cheaper in-state rate for college and allows them to apply for financial aid. The version of the bill that passed the Assembly does not address financial aid. Christie, a possible 2016 presidential candidate, said he hopes to reach a compromise with the Legislature during the lame-duck session. Latino groups who endorsed Christie's re-election widely support the in-state tuition measure.

Ciamak Morsadegh, director of the Dr. Sapir Hospital and Charity Center in Tehran, sat in his office and lit another cigarette. He recounted his wife's departure from Iran after he insisted on staying. Morsadegh said that unlike thousands of other Jews, he has never thought about leaving the Islamic Republic, citing the reason that Iran is his home. "I speak English, I pray in Hebrew, but I think in Persian," Morsadegh said. "I am Iranian. Iranian-Jewish." Last week, the government of President Hassan Rouhani donated $400,000 to the Dr. Sapir Hospital. Morsadegh was not among the donors.

On Wednesday night, rumors surfaced that Rep. Renee Ellmers (R-N.C.) was romantically involved with Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.), and that could be at least part of the reason McCarthy backed away from running for speaker of the House. McCarthy denied this, and Ellmers reportedly has declined to speak to the press. The press went looking for her. One reporter found Rep. Ann Wagner (R-Mo.). Wagner took it well when she was asked about emails linking her with McCarthy.

On Friday, President Obama addressed the Trayvon Martin-George Zimmerman case during a press briefing. He said: "You know, when Trayvon Martin was first shot I said that this could have been my son. Another way of saying that is Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago." Obama said: "You know, when Trayvon Martin was first shot I said that this could have been my son. Another way of saying that is Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago." The article reported that Obama's statement made the tragedy personal.

On Sunday's broadcast of NBC's "Meet the Press," House Intelligence Committee chairman Rep. Adam Schiff (D-CA) said Congress would get access to President Donald Trump's calls with Russian President Vladimir Putin and other world leaders. Schiff said, "The paramount need here is to protect the national security of the United States and see whether in the conversations with other world leaders and in particular with Putin that the president was also undermining our security in a way that he thought would personally benefit his campaign." He added, "If those conversations with Putin or with other world leaders are sequestered in that same electronic file that is meant for covert action, not meant for this, if there's an effort to hide those and cover those up, yes we're determined to find out."

Congress approved $6 billion in spending cuts as part of legislation to keep the government running for three more weeks and give President Obama and congressional leaders time to negotiate a package of reductions demanded by Republicans. The bill passed the Senate by an 87-13 vote. The White House and Capitol Hill Republicans remain far apart on larger legislation to cover the day-to-day operations of the government until the 2012 fiscal year begins in October. Government agencies have generally been operating at last year's levels for almost half of the budget year. Thursday's measure combined with $4 billion in cuts from a two-week extension passed earlier this month means that Congress has cut $10 billion since Republicans took over the House in January.

Florida Governor Rick Scott (R) said Friday that it is time to destroy ISIS, not the Second Amendment, when asked about President Barack Obama's renewed demands for more gun control. "The Second Amendment didn't kill anybody. Let's have a conversation about how we destroy ISIS," he said, according to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution. "This is ISIS. This is evil. This is radical Islam. When are we going to say to ourselves as a country, 'Let's focus on destroying ISIS'?" "The Second Amendment's been around for 200 years," he added. ISIS is the name of the Islamic army based in northern Syria. The Orlando murderer claimed he murdered the 49 people at the Pulse nightclub out of loyalty to ISIS.

George Mason University recently renamed its law school after the late Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia. The school first announced it would change the name to The Antonin Scalia School of Law, or ASSoL, after receiving an anonymous $30 million donation on March 31. Observers commented on the acronym's similarity to a vulgarity, with many tweeting not a fan of the conservative justice. The school acknowledged the issue in a letter to its students and alumni, writing, "The name initially announced -- The Antonin Scalia School of Law -- has caused some acronym controversy on social media. The Antonin Scalia Law School is a logical substitute." The name change will go into effect July 1, pending final approval by the State Council of Higher Education for Virginia.

Hours after former Navy SEAL Chris Kyle was shot to death at a gun range last weekend in Texas, former Texas Rep. Ron Paul issued a Facebook statement to clarify his earlier remarks. Paul had earlier tweeted, "Chris Kyle's death seems to confirm that 'he who lives by the sword dies by the sword.' Treating PTSD at a firing range doesn't make sense." In a Facebook post meant to clarify the tweet, Paul wrote, "As a veteran, I certainly recognize that this weekend's violence and killing of Chris Kyle were a tragic and sad event." He also wrote, "My condolences and prayers go out to Mr. Kyle's family. Unconstitutional and unnecessary wars have endless unintended consequences. A policy of non-violence, as Christ preached, would have prevented this and similar tragedies."
