Rep. Heath Shuler, D-N.C., refused to commit to a challenge against Nancy Pelosi for Democratic House leader in the next Congress. He was repeatedly pressed on CNN's State of the Union about his plans and did not make an announcement. Shuler said it is "unacceptable" for Pelosi to remain leader of the Democrats and "not get us where we need to go as a party." Shuler said he hopes Pelosi will step aside, she says she's not going anywhere) and that if she doesn't he WILL challenge her. He said if Pelosi does step down he wants Steny Hoyer and James Clyburn to be the party's leaders. "I don't see that happening if she's at the top of the leadership," Shuler said about Democrats chances of regaining the House majority in 2012.

A freshman House Republican, Rep. Joe Walsh of Illinois, said he will not vote for the deficit-reduction proposal pushed by Speaker John Boehner. Walsh called the proposal "a step in the right direction." He said he does not think the Boehner proposal or a rival plan offered by Senate Democratic Leader Harry Reid are sufficient. Asked if he could vote later Thursday in the House for the Boehner program, Walsh replied, "Right now, I can't." The tea party-backed lawmaker said he is still thinking about it. Walsh said lawmakers are "obsessed" with the Aug. 2 default deadline. He said chances of getting deficit-reduction right would be better if Congress were not wedded to the default deadline, saying "we've got plenty of revenues in August to service our debt."

President Obama placed a call to Chancellor Angela Merkel of Germany last Thursday. The call was intended to consult with a close ally and to mobilize Europeans to put more pressure on Russia to end its covert incursions in Ukraine. A day earlier, a young German intelligence operative had been arrested and had admitted that he had been passing secrets to the Central Intelligence Agency. Merkel did not raise the issue during the call. White House officials said the president was kept in the dark about the spying operation. They questioned who in the C.I.A.'s chain of command was aware of the case and why that information did not reach the Oval Office before the call.

Charles Krauthammer said Wednesday on "Special Report with Bret Baier" that Jeb Bush's attacks on Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump at Tuesday's GOP debate in Las Vegas will not help his campaign. Krauthammer, a syndicated columnist and Fox News contributor, said: "I think that ship has sailed. I'm happy to see Jeb stand up and get tough. I think he's had a really tough campaign. I don't think it's going to move the needle one iota." Bush criticized Trump last night, calling Trump a "chaos candidate" who "will be a chaos president." He added: "The problem is this: had [Jeb] done that in the first debate, or the second, at a time when Trump was rising...I think it might have had an effect."

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Tuesday in a video message produced on a sunny hilltop in the Golan Heights that all Israelis were deeply moved when President Trump made his historic decision to recognize Israel's sovereignty over the Golan Heights. Netanyahu said he intends to bring to the government resolution calling for a new community in the Golan Heights named after President Donald J. Trump. Trump officially recognized Israel's sovereignty over the Syrian territory on March 25. The Golan Heights is a 690-square mile region Israel annexed following the 1967 Six-Day War with Syria. It is home to some 20,000 Israelis.

Secretary of State John Kerry called Saturday's attack on a shopping mall in Kenya's capital "an enormous offense against everybody's sense of right and wrong." Kerry, who is in New York for meetings at the United Nations, described the attackers as "ruthless and completely reckless terrorists." He spoke Sunday with Somalia's foreign minister and U.N. ambassador. The Somalia-based, al-Qaida-linked group al-Shabab claimed responsibility for the attack on the Westgate Mall in Nairobi. State Department spokeswoman Marie Harf said U.S. law enforcement, military and civilian personnel in Nairobi are providing advice and assistance to the Kenyan authorities. Harf said five Americans were among the scores of people injured in the attack by Islamic extremists, but the U.S. has no reports of any American deaths.

San Antonio Mayor Julián Castro is nominated by President Obama on Friday as secretary of housing and urban development, replacing Shaun Donovan, who will become the president's new budget chief. Both nominations require confirmation by the Senate. Obama said of Castro: "He's become a leader in housing and economic development. He has done a fantastic job in San Antonio. He has done a fantastic job in San Antonio." Castro's political options in Texas have been limited by the state's conservative politics. He rarely has a high profile in Washington, and his nomination will allow him to reach a wider audience there.

Palestinian factions in the West Bank are calling for "A Day of Rage" to coincide with US President Donald Trump's visit to Bethlehem on Tuesday, where he is expected to meet with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. Trump, who is currently in Saudi Arabia for his first international trip since taking office in January, will arrive in Israel on Monday and meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, where the two are expected to discuss prospects for peace negotiations and security issues. One Palestinian organization, called the Islamic and National Forces, initiated the "Rage Day" call in a statement in conjunction with other West Bank factions, saying that they want to send a message to the American president that "the Palestinian people insist on their right to self-determination and national independence with east Jerusalem as its sovereign capital."

Twitter experienced an outage Thursday as users were unable to access the platform for over an hour. A message appeared on the company's status page stating: "We are currently investigating issues people are having accessing Twitter. We will keep you updated on whats happening." Twitter later said an internal configuration change was responsible for the disruption. Down Detector, a website that tracks outages, reported the outage began just after 2:45 p.m. ET. The disruption affected Twitter's mobile and web-based platforms. A message appeared when users tried accessing the site. The site came back online around 3:50 p.m. The outage occurred as President Trump was hosting a social media summit with right-wing personalities and tech industry critics who have accused Twitter and other websites of having an anti-conservative bias.

Ben S. Bernanke, chairman of the Federal Reserve, and most other Fed officials signaled Wednesday that they remained cautious about easing back too quickly on efforts to stimulate the economy. Some Fed policy makers suggested that the central bank could begin reducing its monthly purchases of government bonds as early as next month. Most still want continued evidence of an upswing in the job market and a decline in unemployment first, according to minutes of the most recent meeting of the Fed's policy arm released Wednesday afternoon. Confusion on Wall Street over the Fed's intentions led to a topsy-turvy day in the stock market. The major indicators were up in the morning after Mr. Bernanke testified to a Congressional committee but then fell sharply after the meeting minutes were disclosed.

Donald Trump will nominate Steve Mnuchin, 53, who has ties to both Wall Street and Hollywood, to be treasury secretary, according to a report Tuesday. The 53-year-old, who also served as finance director for the presidential campaign, was at Trump Tower on Tuesday to meet with the transition team. The New York Times reported Tuesday evening that he would be the Treasury pick. Democrats reacted to the report, saying his ties to Wall Street were a betrayal of Trump's campaign promises. Democratic National Committee spokesman Adam Hodge said: "So much for draining the swamp. Nominating Steve Mnuchin to be Treasury Secretary — a billionaire hedge fund manager and Goldman Sachs alumnus who preyed on homeowners struggling during the recession — is a slap in the face to voters who hoped he would shake up Washington."

Rush Limbaugh has not been a fan of Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton. He has given his blessing to her selection as the next secretary of state. Limbaugh called it "a brilliant stroke" by President-elect Barack Obama, who opposed Clinton for the Democratic nomination. Limbaugh appeared on Barbara Walters' "10 Most Fascinating People of 2008" on ABC. Limbaugh said: "You know the old phrase, 'You keep your friends close and your enemies closer?' How can she run for president in 2012? She'd have to run against the incumbent and be critical of him _ the one who made her secretary of state." On Monday, Obama announced Clinton as his nominee for secretary of state. ABC is owned by The Walt Disney Co.

Ben S. Bernanke, chairman of the Federal Reserve, and most other Fed officials signaled Wednesday that they remained cautious about easing back too quickly on efforts to stimulate the economy. Some Fed policy makers suggested that the central bank could begin reducing its monthly purchases of government bonds as early as next month. Most still want continued evidence of an upswing in the job market and a decline in unemployment first, according to minutes of the most recent meeting of the Fed's policy arm released Wednesday afternoon. Confusion on Wall Street over the Fed's intentions led to a topsy-turvy day in the stock market. The major indicators were up in the morning after Mr. Bernanke testified to a Congressional committee but then fell sharply after the meeting minutes were disclosed.

Gov. Chris Christie on Friday announced the resignation of the chairman of the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, David Samson, the highest-ranking public official to step down during the lane closings at the George Washington Bridge. Samson, an éminence grise in New Jersey politics and an adviser to Christie, had been under fire for his role in the lane closings since January, when emails suggested he was more concerned about the political ramifications for Mr. Christie than drivers stuck in traffic. That was followed by accusations about conflicts of interest between his role at the Port Authority and his law practice. With those conflicts under investigation by federal authorities, he had declined to cooperate with an internal investigation Mr. Christie had commissioned.

White House officials are pushing to resurrect a Republican health care bill before President Trump's 100th day in office next week. Some members of the president's team have grown consumed by that deadline, concerned that appraisals of the president's tenure will be brutal and hoping that a last push on health care might bring a measure of salvation. At the same time, Trump hits his 100th day on Saturday, April 29, Republican congressional leaders face a more urgent deadline: Much of the federal government will run out of money. Reaching agreement to keep the government open past midnight on Friday will be the first priority of Republican leaders when Congress returns Monday from a two-week recess.

An American service member was killed and four others were wounded after a skirmish on Monday in Nangarhar Province in eastern Afghanistan, the Pentagon said. The episode took place in Achin, near the Pakistan border, in an area where a number of ambushes and strikes have occurred in recent months. The Pentagon did not indicate whether the episode involved the Taliban or members of the Islamic State, but both groups have been active in the area. Gen. John W. Nicholson Jr., the commander of the Afghanistan war effort, said in a statement: "We are deeply saddened by the loss of one of our own. At this very difficult time, our heartfelt sympathies go out to the families and friends of our fallen and wounded brothers." Defense Department officials said they would have more information after they have notified family members.

Over two days of questioning in Congress, Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed that he did not know key details of a 2011 consent decree with the Federal Trade Commission that requires Facebook to protect user privacy. Zuckerberg repeatedly assured lawmakers Tuesday and Wednesday that Facebook is in compliance with that agreement. He also declined factual questions about it. At one point, he told Colorado Rep. Diana DeGette that he did not know if Facebook had received a financial penalty in that settlement. It did not. At another point, he acknowledged that he was not familiar with "all of the things the FTC said." The FTC announced in March that it is investigating Facebook. Violations of the 2011 agreement could subject Facebook to fines of $41,484 per violation per user per day.

A new Iowa caucus poll shows U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont at 15 percent among Democrats, with 11 percent for Vice President Joseph Biden and 3 percent for former U.S. Sen. James Webb of Virginia and former Maryland Gov. Martin O'Malley. Another 7 percent are undecided. An August 2007 poll of Iowa put Clinton one point behind Barack Obama and tied with John Edwards. A late February Quinnipiac poll pegged Clinton at 61 percent in Iowa. A NBC News/Wall Street Journal poll showing Clinton's favorability declining but stronger than that of top Republicans and a New York Times/CBS News poll showing her favorability rising.

Palestinian factions in the West Bank are calling for "A Day of Rage" to coincide with US President Donald Trump's visit to Bethlehem on Tuesday, where he is expected to meet with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. Trump, who is currently in Saudi Arabia for his first international trip since taking office in January, will arrive in Israel on Monday and meet with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, where the two are expected to discuss prospects for peace negotiations and security issues. One Palestinian organization, called the Islamic and National Forces, initiated the "Rage Day" call in a statement in conjunction with other West Bank factions, saying that they want to send a message to the American president that "the Palestinian people insist on their right to self-determination and national independence with east Jerusalem as its sovereign capital."

Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Sen. Lindsay Graham (R-SC) said on this week's broadcast of "Fox News Sunday" that the articles of impeachment against President Trump would not be dismissed without a trial. Host Chris Wallace asked, "Have you given up on the idea that the majority will vote to dismiss case right away?" Graham said, "That's dead for practical purposes. There are a lot of senators who I think will wind up acquitting the president but believe we need to hear the House's case and the president's case in answer to the House's case." He added, "The idea of dismissing the case early on is not going to happen, We don't have the votes for that."

Hundreds gathered in Southeast Texas on Sunday for a vigil and march in memory of Sandra Bland, an Illinois woman found dead in a jail days after her arrest during a traffic stop. Houston TV station KPRC reported attendees met at a Prairie View church and marched across Prairie View A&M University, which Bland attended. Some carried signs that said "Justice for Sandra." Others called for a Justice Department investigation into her death. Authorities said Bland hanged herself, a finding her family disputes. Also on Sunday, The Houston Chronicle reported dozens protested outside a residence in Katy, west of Houston, that they believed belongs to the state trooper who arrested Bland. Protesters criticized his actions, which were captured on dashcam video, and called for him to be fired and criminally charged. The trooper is on administrative leave pending an investigation.

Lee Miringoff of the Marist College Institute for Public Opinion, a Marist poll conducted for NBC News, said: "Any way you slice the numbers, you end up with a close race. This is one that bears watching as the campaign unfolds." Republican Joni Ernst and Democrat Bruce Braley are both at 43 percent each, with 14 percent undecided. One-third of respondents said they are unsure of their opinion about the candidates or never heard of them. Ernst edges out Braley by two points in the fav/unfav rating category. Braley receives positive marks from 36 percent of voters and a negative rating of 32 percent. Ernst receives 38 percent and 33 percent, respectively.

Former Vice President Joe Biden may no longer be the Democrats' unequivocal frontrunner but still remains ahead in the polls. On Tuesday, Rosie O'Donnell told CNN's Chris Cuomo that Biden should sit out the election. O'Donnell said Biden should "be an elder statesman" and utilize his decades of experience to advise whoever ends up taking on President Donald Trump. O'Donnell said Biden's ideas and beliefs are "antiquated" and he "is not the future of the Democratic Party." She also said she has been engaged in a yearslong war of words with the current president. O'Donnell also backed Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Kamala Harris (D-Calif.).

Mexican immigration authorities initiated the deportation process for 98 Central American caravan migrants who recently entered an international port of entry in Tijuana. The migrants were arrested during a clash with U.S. authorities. The Mexican government said some migrants tried to attack police officers. In a statement, Mexico's National Migration Institute (INM) announced that 98 Central American migrants arrested during the clash are being deported. Authorities continue to investigate the incident to locate additional migrants to charge under immigration laws for eventual removal. Mexican authorities said that during the rush for the border, some migrants tried to attack and injure several police officers securing the Chaparral/San Ysidro Port of Entry. The statement by INM revealed that those actions violate various Mexican laws regarding criminal behavior by foreigners. The 98 deportations are fewer than the original 500 the Mexican government previously promised.

Kofi Annan, the special envoy and mediator who called the Geneva peace meeting, said on Friday he was optimistic the talks would yield an acceptable result despite Russian calls for changes in his settlement ideas. "I think we are going to have a good meeting" on Saturday, Annan told Reuters television in Geneva as senior officials held preparatory talks in advance of the weekend encounter of foreign ministers, including Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton. "I am optimistic." The talks would end "with an acceptable result," he said, despite news reports suggesting that differences between Russia and other Western and Arab nations at the Geneva meeting had raised new obstacles to an agreement.

President Obama commented on Bruce Jenner's transformation into Caitlyn Jenner on the cover of Vanity Fair on Monday. The official Barack Obama account tweeted, "It takes courage to share your story." Jenner came out as transgender in last month's 20/20 interview with Diane Sawyer. Jenner broke the President's record for the fastest to reach 1 million followers on Twitter on Monday. Jenner accomplished the feat in four hours, while it had previously taken Obama five. Obama also asked followers to share their stories at Obama's Organizing for Action website. Obama joins other celebrities and family members who have tweeted support for Jenner since the Vanity Fair cover hit the Internet Monday.

The jury weighing the fate of former Gov. Bob McDonnell of Virginia and his wife, Maureen, is set to deliberate Wednesday for a second day after hearing instructions from Judge James R. Spencer on Tuesday afternoon. The seven men and five women of the jury had no questions in open court during their first five and a half hours of deliberation. In instructing the jury on Tuesday morning, Judge Spencer rejected arguments defense lawyers made last week to narrowly define what must be proved to convict the McDonnells, who are accused, separately and together, of two counts of conspiracy, three counts of bribery, six counts of extortion and related secondary charges.

President Obama's speech at the Brookings Institution will not take place until 11:15am. Fox News and Fox Business are covering the details at this hour. Major Garrett reports that President Obama will announce an effort to boost the nation's infrastructure, like roads and bridges, as well as an injection of money for small businesses. FBN's Peter Barnes breaks down the numbers. His contacts tell him the goal is to appropriate $20-40 billion to increase small business lending, to come from unused TARP funds, and another $25-30 billion for tax credits for small business to hire people to create new jobs. TARP, you'll remember, was the Troubled Asset Relief Program, designed to pull the nation out of its financial woes. The program has a surplus of funds now, which the administration wants to tap into to create jobs.

Just before midnight, Mr. Alvarez conceded in a tweet reported by NBC: "I want to congratulate Kevin Faulconer. It's clear that he will be the next mayor of San Diego. I look forward to working with him." The winning candidate said, during a last-minute speech while votes were still being counted, that his leadership would bring San Diegans together, and his administration would "invest where we need the help," NBC reported. The special election was held to replace Mr. Filner, who resigned from his office in August following sexual harassment accusations. Mr. Filner was later sentenced to house arrest for felony false imprisonment and for two misdemeanor charges of battery against three different women, NBC said.

Potential jurors at Cook County Commissioner William Beavers' trial began filling out questionnaires Monday. Other members of his defense team told the judge that attorney Victor Henderson had become ill. They asked for a delay in one-on-one questioning of panelists that was supposed to start later Monday. U.S. District Judge James Zagel said they will reconvene Tuesday morning. Jury selection typically takes a day or two. Attorneys had earlier talked about being ready for openings by Tuesday. Openings may now not happen until later this week. Beavers, 77, has denied diverting money from his campaign funds without reporting it.

The U.N. Security Council is set to hold an emergency meeting about Iran on Friday afternoon. The U.S. requested the session, which is expected to be held at a later date. Members are divided in their views of the protests and could call a vote on whether to address the topic. U.S. Ambassador Nikki Haley praised the demonstrators, saying "the U.N. must speak out" on their behalf. Russia has warned against "external interference" in what it sees as Iran's internal affairs. At least 21 people have been killed and hundreds arrested in a week of anti-government protests and unrest. Thousands of people took part in pro-government rallies Wednesday and Thursday.

Senator John McCain (R-AZ) told KFYI-AM in Phoenix that he is seriously considering running for re-election in 2016. "I'm seriously thinking about maybe giving another opportunity for you to vote for or against me in a few years from now," McCain said. "I'm seriously giving that a lot of thought." Young asked again whether it would be correct to say McCain would be running for re-election and the Arizona Senator said, "that it would not be wrong." McCain would be 80 years old in 2016 when he runs for re-election. The Arizona Republican previously stated in a September Hill article that he was probably in his last term but would decide on running again in two years and did not "want to be one of these old guys that should've shoved off."

Rick Santorum, who won the state in 2012 but finished with just one percent of the vote in 2016, is ending his campaign, according to CNN. According to CNN's sources, Santorum does plan to endorse another candidate. The article notes that this makes Santorum an interesting choice. It also notes that Santorum did not just look at the situation, noting that New Hampshire is not his kind of state and he is not polling any better in South Carolina, and that he may have skewed the results. The article also suggests that the campaign may have whipped his brain into too frothy of a mixture, which it suggests is what the author suggests. Comments are closed on the story.

During a press conference on Wednesday, President Trump stated that Republicans who stayed away from him "did very poorly. I'm not sure that I should be happy or sad, but I feel just fine about it." Trump stated, "On the other hand, you had some that decided to — let's stay away, let's stay away. They did very poorly. I'm not sure that I should be happy or sad, but I feel just fine about it." He specifically cited Carlos Curbelo, Mike Coffman, and Mia Love. Trump then cited Barbara Comstock, but said he did not blame her for not embracing him. Trump also cited Peter Roskam, Erik Paulsen, Bob Hugin, and John Faso.

If Republicans in Congress and the Obama White House fail to resolve their differences in time, the federal government will begin a partial shutdown at 12:01 a.m. Tuesday, with all but essential services curtailed or closed entirely. A few weeks later, another deadline will arrive when the government bumps up against its legally authorized borrowing limit. If Congress does not vote to increase the debt limit, it could set off severe financial problems for the government as it scrambles for the cash it needs to meet its commitments. The government could be forced to scale back operations beginning on Tuesday if Congress and the administration do not agree on extending federal spending authority; about 800,000 employees would be involuntarily furloughed, while others would possibly have to work without pay.

Gallup reported that Mitt Romney held a 49-point lead over Barack Obama among national voters. The Gallup poll was in line with other polls, including Rasmussen Reports, that have shown Romney with a similar lead among national voters in the last week. Immediately after the first presidential debate, Romney gained leads in key swing states including Florida, Virginia, and Colorado. The Gallup poll was conducted after the first presidential debate. The price of gold fell about 20% so far this year while silver declined almost 30%. The adage "don't fight the Fed" was referenced as U.S. equity markets reached new highs during the same period. The article noted that all of these gains are nominal, but warned that for American policymakers and investors, nominal gains are acceptable.

President Obama will speak in primetime Thursday regarding his planned executive action on immigration reform. The major network television stations will not televise the speech. CNN's Brian Stelter reported that ABC, NBC, and CBS will not televise Obama's speech. Stelter noted that the White House did not explicitly request airtime for the address before announcing it. Univision is expected to air Obama's speech. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest said the president opted for a prime-time address to "talk to as many as Americans as possible." Earnest added that 8:00 p.m. was when people were either "sitting in front of their televisions" or "sitting in front of their tablets or their smartphones."

A chemical spill in West Virginia affected drinking water for some 300,000 people. The U.S. attorney investigating the spill is investigating the spill. Numerous businesses have sued Freedom Industries, alleging they were forced to close and lost money until the water was safe again. Company officials have repeatedly declined to comment. Court and financial documents provide a window into the firm's history. Freedom Industries traces its start back to 1992, when it was founded by Carl Kennedy II and Dennis Farrell. Kennedy later pleaded guilty to tax fraud. Prosecutors accused Kennedy of withholding more than $1 million from employees' paychecks between 2000 and 2003 and diverting some of that money for his personal use.

New York is joining California and 14 other states in a lawsuit challenging President Donald Trump's national emergency declaration. New York Attorney General Letitia James said in the lawsuit Monday that Trump is threatening public safety with his move to divert funding from military construction and other programs to pay for a U.S.-Mexico border wall. All the states involved in the lawsuit have Democratic attorneys general. Trump declared an emergency on Friday to shift billions of dollars to the wall after Congress did not approve the amount he wanted. Trump, a Republican, considers a wall a national security necessity. The lawsuit alleges he is manufacturing a crisis and that his declaration is an "unconstitutional and unlawful scheme." This year's defense budget includes $194 million for construction at military installations in New York.

President Obama said in an interview with ABC News' George Stephanopoulos on Monday that he is the "underdog" in the 2012 race. Stephanopoulos asked about a new ABC/Washington Post poll showing 55 percent of Americans believe Obama will be a one-term president. Obama responded, "absolutely." He added, "[G]iven the economy, there's no doubt that, you know, whatever happens on your watch." Obama responded quickly to that notion, saying, "I don't mind. I'm used to being an underdog. And -- and I think that, at the end of the day, though, what people are going to say is, who's got a vision for the future that can actually help ordinary families recapture that American dream?"

Herman Cain is inviting his top supporters and donors to Atlanta on Saturday for a meeting in which he will give them advance word of whether he intends to continue his campaign, sources close to the campaign said Friday. One supporter who has been summoned to the private session said he believes Cain is likely to announce he is ending his candidacy. Another who has been invited to the morning meeting said attendees have been told he has made no decision but wanted to meet with some of the supporters to express his gratitude. Several sources indicated that Cain is likely to announce his plans publicly at a news conference after the meeting. Cain had already scheduled an event on Saturday — the grand opening of his national headquarters in his hometown of Atlanta, as well as the announcement of his campaign's senior leadership team for the state of Georgia.

President Donald Trump said Monday he would not visit the Capitol Hill rotunda this week to honor the late Rep. John Lewis. "I won't be going. No," Trump told reporters when asked about whether he would make a trip to honor Lewis. Lewis's body will lie in state at Capitol Hill on Monday and Tuesday following the arrival ceremony in the Capitol Rotunda. The public viewing will take place outside the Capitol building to help prevent the spread of the coronavirus. Vice President Mike Pence and Second Lady Karen Pence are expected to pay their respects on Monday evening. Former Vice President Joe Biden will travel from Deleware to make a Monday appearance with former Second Lady Jill Biden. It is unclear whether former President Barack Obama or former First Lady Michelle Obama will pay their respects at the Capitol building.

Viewership for the second presidential debate between Donald Trump and Joe Biden fell to 63 million viewers. The first debate was canceled after Trump's coronavirus infection and replaced by dueling town halls on ABC and NBC. The viewership for both the presidential candidates together was 27.6 million. The Biden town hall reached 14.1 million people, while Trump had 13.5 million. On Thursday, the candidates debated mostly on health care, energy policy and how Trump handled the coronavirus pandemic. Both candidates also had an exchange words over the business endeavors of Biden's son. In 2016, the first debate between Trump and Hillary Clinton garnered 84 million viewers, which is the most-watched debate ever. Their final debate had slightly less than 71.6 million, which was a higher number than their second matchup.

The Chicago Tribune reported that Senator Mark Kirk (R-IL) suffered a stroke but has been successfully treated and is resting comfortably. Kirk's office released a statement. In the statement, the office said: "On Saturday, Senator Kirk checked himself into Lake Forest Hospital, where doctors discovered a carotid artery dissection in the right side of his neck." He was transferred to Northwestern Memorial Hospital in Chicago, where further tests revealed he had suffered an ischemic stroke. Early this morning, the senator underwent surgery to relieve swelling around his brain stemming from the stroke. The surgery was successful. Due to his young age, good health and the nature of the stroke, doctors are very confident in the Senator's recovery over the weeks ahead. Best wishes for a speedy recovery to Senator Kirk."

Liz Cheney, the elder daughter of former Vice President Dick Cheney, is running for Congress. Campaign officials say Cheney plans to formally announce Monday in Gillette, Wyoming. She could not immediately be reached for comment. Cheney ran a brief Senate campaign in 2013. She attempted to unseat Wyoming's senior U.S. Sen. Mike Enzi, a fellow Republican, but did not gain traction among Wyoming's political establishment. She quit her campaign seven months before the 2014 primary. This time, Cheney seeks to replace Republican Rep. Cynthia Lummis, who plans to retire at the end of her term. Cheney faces a field of eight Republican competitors, including two experienced Wyoming state legislators.

The Senate passed a resolution to overturn the Federal Communications Commission and save net neutrality. Senators Lisa Murkowski and John Kennedy joined Susan Collins and the entire Senate Democratic caucus in voting to overturn the FCC and save net neutrality. The resolution now goes to the House. Supporters will need to secure 24 votes from Republicans to pass the rollback, assuming all Democrats support. The resolution is still subject to a veto. The article notes that most House members support net neutrality, and 99 senators are on record supporting it.

Mitt Romney's presidential campaign borrowed $20 million in August to pay for its expenses before he could begin tapping general election dollars and is now $11 million in debt, a senior campaign official confirmed late Tuesday. Romney's campaign finance filings, due to be released on Wednesday, will show the campaign with $15 million in debt, the official said, although the debt currently stands at $11 million. The National Review Online first reported the campaign's debt Tuesday night. Although Romney has raised hundreds of millions of dollars in general election funds, his campaign could not legally tap those funds until after he officially was nominated at the Republican National Convention. Through the summer, he could only spend primary dollars, and once that money dried up the campaign was forced to borrow money to pay its bills.

Former Rep. Jesse L. Jackson Jr. pleaded guilty Wednesday to a conspiracy charge involving more than $750,000 in campaign funds at a hearing before a federal judge in Washington. According to a report in the Chicago Tribune, Jackson said, "I am guilty, your honor." As part of the plea agreement, Jackson could face a jail sentence of 46 to 57 months. Both sides reserved the right to argue for more jail time. His sentencing hearing is set for this summer. "I used money I shouldn't have ... for personal reasons," Jackson said, according to the Tribune. "I acknowledge that." While leaving the courtroom, Jackson also told reporters, according to the Tribune: "Tell everybody back home I'm sorry I let 'em down, OK?"

President Donald Trump on Saturday awarded a Purple Heart to an Army sergeant recently wounded in Afghanistan. The medal was the first of many Trump likely will award during his service as commander in chief of the U.S. military. "When I heard about this ... I wanted to do it myself," Trump said during a brief ceremony at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland, outside Washington. The medal went to Sgt. 1st Class Alvaro Barrientos, who was wounded in action on March 17 in Afghanistan during what is now America's longest war. The White House did not release Barrientos' hometown. "Congratulations on behalf of Melania and myself and the entire nation. Tremendous," Trump said, mentioning his wife. It was Trump's first visit as president to the military hospital.

Throughout most of 2015, the administration of Gov. Rick Snyder told residents of Flint, Mich., that their tap water was safe to drink. Emails released on Thursday indicate the state was concerned about its own employees' exposure to the city's water as early as January of last year, and arranged for purified water to be provided at a state office building there. The emails depict an exchange that month between employees of two state departments expressing concern about the water's safety within the Michigan government long before Snyder acknowledged to residents in the fall that there was a problem. The correspondence — between employees of the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality and the Michigan Department of Technology, Management and Budget — was obtained by Progress Michigan. The news was reported on Thursday by The Detroit Free Press.

Nordstrom shares fell after President Donald Trump tweeted that the department store chain had treated his daughter "so unfairly." The company announced last week it would stop selling Ivanka Trump's clothing and accessory line, saying that was based on the sales performance of the first daughter's brand. The tweet said: "My daughter Ivanka has been treated so unfairly by @Nordstrom. She is a great person — always pushing me to do the right thing! Terrible!" It was re-tweeted more than 4,000 times in less than 30 minutes. Shares in Seattle-based Nordstrom traded around $42.70 before the tweet, then fell to $42.48 afterward at around 10:50 a.m. Trump's tweets have in the past also affected shares in U.S. automakers Boeing and Carrier.

Dean Heller, a Nevada Republican, said he would uphold gun rights after the shooting in Las Vegas on Sunday night. "You show me the law that would stop that, not only will I support it, I will be an advocate for that law," he said. The shooting left 58 people dead and 489 injured. Stephen Paddock had a cache of 23 guns in his room at the Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino. Police found another 19 at his Mesquite, Nevada, home and seven at a Reno property. Heller also revealed more details about the gunman, saying he was on "depressants" and that police believe others may have been involved in planning the event. The Nevada senator thanked President Trump and First Lady Melania Trump for their visit and said he was touched by how the president took the time to speak with survivors of the event.

U.S. Sen. Rand Paul's attorneys said in a court filing that he plans to undergo hernia surgery in Canada because of injuries he suffered when a neighbor attacked Paul while he was doing yard work at his Kentucky home. The filing in Paul's lawsuit against Rene Boucher says the senator will travel to Ontario, Canada, for outpatient surgery scheduled later this month. The document says the surgery is related to the 2017 attack. Boucher pleaded guilty to assaulting a member of Congress and was sentenced to 30 days in prison. Federal prosecutors are appealing the sentence. A Paul spokeswoman did not immediately explain why Paul is having the surgery in Canada, where medical care is publicly funded and universally provided. Paul has advocated for private-market approaches for U.S. health care problems.

House Majority Leader Eric Cantor, a Virginia Republican, criticized the new nuclear deal with Iran, saying he believes it "bodes very, very ominously for the region and U.S. security." The Virginia Republican called the arrangement "dangerous" and said it brings Iran "closer to becoming a nuclear power." The accommodation announced Sunday gives Tehran six months to increase access to its nuclear sites in exchange for keeping the central elements of its uranium program. Cantor told "CBS This Morning" Monday that the terms are softer than those already in several U.N. resolutions. In a twist on a famous Ronald Reagan statement about arms control, Cantor said the attitude toward Iran should be "mistrust and verify." Reagan famously said he favored arms pacts with the Soviet Union if there was a "trust-but-verify" standard.

President Barack Obama's nominee for health secretary, Sylvia Mathews Burwell, made her first appearance before a Senate committee on Thursday. Burwell is described as highly qualified to assume leadership of the president's health law. Senator John McCain (R-Ariz.) praised Burwell as he introduced her to the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. McCain praised Burwell for agreeing to lead HHS, describing the job as "taking over the Titanic after it hit the iceberg." Senior committee Republican Sen. Lamar Alexander criticized the Affordable Care Act, but also cited Burwell's reputation for competence. The comments indicated Burwell could be headed for a smooth confirmation even while she is called upon to defend the health law.

According to a report in the Chicago Tribune, Jackson said, "I am guilty, your honor." As part of the plea agreement, Jackson could face a jail sentence of 46 to 57 months. Both sides reserved the right to argue for more jail time. His sentencing hearing is set for this summer. "I used money I shouldn't have ... for personal reasons," Jackson said, according to the Tribune. "I acknowledge that." While leaving the courtroom, Jackson also told reporters, according to the Tribune: "Tell everybody back home I'm sorry I let 'em down, OK?"

An Air Force officer who led the branch's Sexual Assault Prevention and Response unit has been charged with misdemeanor sexual battery after an alleged assault about 12:30 a.m. Sunday in the Crystal City section of the county. Arlington County Police said Monday that Lt. Col. Jeffrey Krusinski of Arlington, 41, of Arlington, was charged with misdemeanor sexual battery after an alleged assault about 12:30 a.m. Sunday in the Crystal City section of the county. A police report said Krusinski was drunk and grabbed a woman's breast and buttocks. Police said the woman fought him off and called police. Police spokesman Dustin Sternbeck said Krusinski did not know the woman involved. An arraignment is scheduled for Thursday. Air Force spokeswoman Natasha Waggoner said Krusinski was removed from his position after the Air Force learned of his arrest.

MSNBC retracted a tweet on Wednesday night that it described as offensive. The tweet referenced a 2013 Cheerios advertisement featuring an interracial family. Cheerios released a similar advertisement. MSNBC sent a response: "Maybe the rightwing will hate it, but everyone else will go awww: the adorable new #Cheerios ad w/ biracial family." The tweet referenced a 2013 Cheerios advertisement featuring an interracial family. MSNBC subsequently deleted the tweet. The apology stated: "We deeply regret it. It does not reflect the position of msnbc. We are deleting the earlier offensive tweet. It does not reflect msnbc's position and we apologize."

Supporters and campaign staff for presidential candidates Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump watched election results roll in minutes from each other in Manhattan. As of 10PM Eastern time, The New York Times live presidential forecast projected a 72 percent chance of a Donald Trump win. This number differed significantly from the initial projections before polls closed, predicting an 85 percent chance that Hillary Clinton would be the United States' next president. The projection changes centered largely on battleground states of Michigan, Florida, Ohio, and Virginia. At the Jacob Javits Center, the Democratic headquarters, Clinton supporters appeared tense and dismayed. Meanwhile, some Manhattan blocks away at the New York Hilton Midtown, photos from inside Donald Trump's election night party indicated the mood changed from cautious to increasingly optimistic.

On Tuesday, Democrat Steve Stern won New York's 10th Assembly District by 59-41 percent, marking the 40th election of the cycle. Stern, an attorney and former Suffolk County legislator, had represented the district in the state Assembly for over three decades. Hillary Clinton won the Suffolk-area seat 52-45, and Barack Obama carried it 51-48 in 2012. The flip indicates the seat's shift toward Democrats is progressing. Daily Kos Special Elections Results tracker tracks this and every other legislative special election flip of the cycle. Republicans used this tactic in last year's race for governor in Virginia.

A picture taken by German government photographer Jesco Denzel shows U.S. President Donald Trump and German Chancellor Angela Merkel with hands firmly planted on a table facing Trump, who is seated with his arms folded and eyes closed. The photograph was tweeted by Merkel spokesman Steffen Seibert. The White House issued a photo showing Trump speaking as Merkel, Abe, and Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau listened.

Former Pennsylvania Governor Tom Ridge appeared on MSNBC's "Hardball" Thursday evening to discuss his decision not to run for the Senate in 2010. He declined to say whether he would vote for the likely Republican nominee, Pat Toomey, against Arlen Specter. "It's called secret ballot," Ridge said. Ridge, a pro-choice moderate like Specter, had faced criticism for his party. "We have to reshape our message, reduce the decibel level -- we're too doggone shrill -- and be less judgmental about the people in the party that may disagree with us," Ridge said. He reiterated the point later: "Our message became shrill. We became very divided over these social issues, and at some point in time, we'll have to be a lot less judgmental."

Former First Lady Barbara Bush, the mother of potential 2016 presidential candidate and former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush, spoke with CSPAN about political dynasties. She said she hoped her son would not run for president because "there are other families. I refuse to accept that this great country isn't raising other wonderful people." She added that she believed Jeb was the best qualified for the job. Jeb Bush may be considering a run for president more after Republican New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie's "Bridgegate" scandal. Bush posted on Twitter: "What date is Mother's Day this year? Asking for a friend."

A Quinnipiac University poll released Tuesday shows the race for U.S. Senate in New Jersey has tightened. The poll shows 53 percent support Democratic Newark Mayor Booker, while 41 percent support former Bogota Mayor Mark "Steve" Lonegan. The special election is scheduled for Oct. 16. A poll of registered votes in August showed Booker with a 25-percentage-point lead over the Republican. Booker receives the majority of his backing from women, who support him 60-34. Men and independents are split. Pollster Maurice Carroll says the results could be driven by bad news about Newark crime and publicity about Booker's business ventures. The telephone survey of 948 likely voters was conducted from Sept. 19-22 and has an error margin of plus or minus 3.2 percentage points.

Rep. Peter King, a New York Republican, said Wednesday that the Republican Party must distance itself from Steve Bannon after losing the Alabama Senate seat to Democrat Doug Jones. King tweeted: "After Alabama disaster GOP must do right thing and DUMP Steve Bannon. His act is tired, inane and morally vacuous. If we are to Make America Great Again for all Americans, Bannon must go! And go NOW!!" Bannon, who was President Trump's former White House chief strategist, was one of the first people to back Republican candidate Roy Moore in the race and continued to sustain his campaign even after allegations of sexual misconduct became public. Moore was accused by multiple women of trying to pursue physical relationships with them when they were teens and he was an adult.

A new poll from Ipsos shows that 43 percent of Republicans hold a flatly unconstitutional view that the president should be able to shut down media outlets he does not like. Thirty-five percent disagree with the statement that "the president should have the authority to close news outlets engaged in bad behavior." Forty-three percent of Republicans think Trump has the right to demand their first-born. Forty-five percent of Republicans think he should be able to shut down media outlets.

Memphis police said no charges will be filed against a 5-year-old kindergartener after a gun discharged inside the child's backpack in a school cafeteria. Police spokeswoman Karen Rudolph said the 5-year-old student and the child's mother were released from custody Thursday night, hours after the kindergartner was detained by police at Westside Elementary School. Officials said the child was waiting for the opening bell in the cafeteria when the gun went off. No one was hurt, and security officers took control of the backpack. Investigators determined the child obtained the gun from a closet at home and placed it in the backpack. Rudolph said Friday that the information was presented to the attorney general's office, which decided not to file charges. Police are not releasing the identity of the child and mother.

Republican Sen. Rand Paul said he is filing a class-action lawsuit against the Obama administration over the data-collection policies of the National Security Agency. On his website, Paul urged Americans to join the lawsuit, stating it is intended to stop Barack Obama's NSA from snooping on the American people. In an interview airing Friday night on Fox News, the Kentucky Republican told host Sean Hannity that he believes everyone in the U.S. with a cellphone would be eligible to join the class-action suit. Paul said that people who want to join the suit are telling the government that it cannot have access to emails and phone records without permission or without a specific warrant. Paul said the lead lawyer in the suit is Virginia's former attorney general, Ken Cuccinelli.

During a town hall on guns with President Obama, CNN showed a clip of Obama crying at the White House and asked for a reaction. While the clip played, the CNN cameras showed Obama's reaction to video. CNN's Anderson Cooper described the moment as an "obviously emotional ceremony" and said people who watched were "surprised by that." Obama said, "I was, too, actually," and noted that he visited the families who lost children at Newtown Elementary and it was "still very raw." "It's the only time I've ever seen Secret Service cry on duty," Obama explained. Obama recalled the details of the event to emphasize that more needed to be done on gun control.

Republican nominee Donald Trump responded to Speaker of the House Paul Ryan's statement earlier Thursday that he is "not ready" to support Trump. In an emailed statement, Trump said: "I am not ready to support Speaker Ryan's agenda. Perhaps in the future we can work together and come to an agreement about what is best for the American people. They have been treated so badly for so long that it is about time for politicians to put them first!" Trump's comment mirrored Ryan's earlier statement. Earlier on Thursday, Ryan made a CNN appearance about whether he will support Trump.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi announced at an evening news conference that the House is moving forward with an official impeachment inquiry of Donald Trump. The inquiry is expected to focus on Donald Trump's efforts to pressure the Ukrainian government into opening an investigation into one of his potential 2020 election opponents. Pelosi said, "I can say with authority, the Trump administration's actions undermine our national security and intelligence." She noted the administration's refusal to turn over to Congress the contents of an "urgent" whistleblower report, as required by law, and demanded that the report be released by Thursday. Pelosi said Trump's Director of National Intelligence "will have to choose whether to break the law or honor his responsibility to the Constitution."

The New York City Council passed expanded paid sick days legislation. The bill has the support of Mayor Bill de Blasio, a Democrat, and will give the right to have paid sick days to 355,000 workers. The bill will be the first that de Blasio, a Democrat, signs into law. He said Wednesday that the council "made history" with the legislation. Combined with previous legislation, more than a half-million New Yorkers will now be entitled to take up to five sick days without fear of losing their job. The bill passed in a 46-5 vote. It is the first major piece of legislation enacted by the council led by speaker Melissa Mark-Viverito. Some small business owners have voiced concerns that the legislation creates a financial burden.

A letter to the editor stated that Hillary Clinton and President Obama are examples of politicians who lie to the majority of voters to get elected and revert to their core ideology to govern. The letter stated that Clinton was inept as secretary of state and would do little to nothing to resolve Mr. Obama's foreign-policy disaster. It noted that she particularly did Mr. Obama's bidding when she pushed the "reset button" with Russia and when she exacerbated matters in Libya by mishandling the Benghazi terrorist attacks that killed four Americans, including our ambassador. The letter also stated that Mrs. Clinton's recent criticism of the president's foreign policy is hypocritically political at the height of the Islamic State crisis in Iraq. The letter stated that if elected president, Mrs. Clinton would still embrace Obamacare, as evidenced by her failed attempt at national health care during the Clinton administration.

Secret Service agent Timothy McCarthy and District of Columbia police officer Thomas Delahanty each took a bullet to protect President Ronald Reagan. McCarthy retired from the force after the shooting and lives in a Pittsburgh suburb. Delahanty retired on disability. McCarthy told The Associated Press he respects the judge's decision to release Hinckley from a psychiatric hospital to live with his mother. He says what Hinckley did is "unforgivable." Delahanty told AP he is "not too enthused" about Hinckley's release.

House Speaker Nancy Pelosi on Monday called for Labor Secretary Alex Acosta's resignation after details of the deal he struck as a U.S. attorney with Jeffrey Epstein resurfaced following the financier's latest arrest. Pelosi said Acosta made an "unconscionable" deal with Epstein and alleged that President Trump was aware of this deal when he appointed him to the cabinet. She tweeted: "@SecretaryAcosta must step down. As US Attorney, he engaged in an unconscionable agreement w/ Jeffrey Epstein kept secret from courageous, young victims preventing them from seeking justice. This was known by [Mr. Trump] when he appointed him to the cabinet. #AcostaResign."

Baptist minister Mark Walker (R) won the Republican runoff for U.S. House in North Carolina's 6th Congressional District on Tuesday. With nearly six out of 10 precincts reporting, the Associated Press called the race for Walker, who led Rockingham County District Attorney Phil Berger Jr., 57 percent to 44 percent. Rep. Howard Coble (R), 83, is retiring at the end of this term. Coble endorsed Berger in the runoff and campaigned for him. Walker will be a heavy favorite in November. In the 5th District Democratic primary runoff, software developer Joshua Brannon defeated Gardenia Henley. Brannon will be a clear underdog against Rep. Virginia Foxx (R) in November.

An aide to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas said Thursday that gaps between Israeli and Palestinian negotiators have widened since talks began seven months ago. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry wants both sides to agree to a framework for a peace deal — effectively ground rules for future negotiations — by April 29. Mohammed Ishtayeh, an Abbas aide and former negotiator, said the U.S. might seek an extension but that he doubts this will happen because of lack of common ground. Ishtayeh said a key obstacle is Israel's demand that the Palestinians accept it as a Jewish state. He said Abbas cannot do so "under any circumstance" because it would restrict rights of Palestinian refugees and Israeli Arabs. Abbas is meeting March 17 with U.S. President Barack Obama.

Republican nominee Donald Trump responded to Speaker of the House Paul Ryan's statement earlier Thursday that he is "not ready" to support Trump. In an emailed statement, Trump said: "I am not ready to support Speaker Ryan's agenda. Perhaps in the future we can work together and come to an agreement about what is best for the American people. They have been treated so badly for so long that it is about time for politicians to put them first!" Trump's comment mirrored Ryan's earlier statement. Earlier on Thursday, Ryan made a CNN appearance about whether he will support Trump.

Republican candidate Donald Trump spoke at a rally in Pennsylvania on Wednesday. He made a reference to former Penn State coach Joe Paterno. Trump said, "I know a lot about Pennsylvania, and it's great. How's Joe Paterno. We're gonna bring that back? Right?...How 'bout that whole deal?" Paterno died in 2012. He was criticized for his handling of former Penn State coach Jerry Sandusky, who was later convicted of child sex abuse. Sandusky was sentenced to 30-60 years in prison, and Paterno was fired in 2011. Paterno died two months after being fired. The Trump campaign clarified the comments, saying he was referencing the bronze statue of Paterno that was torn down in 2012 amid the controversy.

Tea party groups are offering a split verdict in the Nebraska Senate race. FreedomWorks announced it is backing former state treasurer Shane Osborn in the Republican primary. The Club for Growth and Senate Conservatives Fund previously announced they will back Midland University President Ben Sasse. These groups have often been on the same page in certain races — they have all endorsed Sen. Thad Cochran's (R-Miss.) primary opponent, Chris McDaniel, but there are also times when they do not join forces. The groups backing Sasse have spent more money on GOP primaries in recent years. The Republican primary in Nebraska is very likely to determine the successor to retiring Sen. Mike Johnanns (R-Neb.). The seat is not a top target for Democrats. Other GOP candidates include attorney Bart McLeay.

Fox News host Kimberly Guilfoyle has been close to the Trump family. She is currently dating Donald Trump, Jr., whose wife Vanessa Trump filed for divorce in early April. When not behind the Fox News desk, she has been jet-setting around with junior staff and Secret Service protection. The article questioned whether Fox News had an obligation to disclose how close she is to the Trump family and whether she had an obligation to refrain from what it described as obvious propaganda designed to bolster people she is in bed with. It also noted that former Fox News President Bill Shine left to join the White House communications team, and that Fox News host Sean Hannity has nightly calls and dinners with Donald Trump.

Mitt Romney is seen by more voters in three battleground states as a strong leader after his debate performance last week, but perceptions that the economy is improving remain a headwind for President Obama as the 2012 campaign enters its final weeks. The latest Quinnipiac University/New York Times/CBS News poll of likely voters in the three states, Colorado, Virginia and Wisconsin, found no sharp movement after the debate and the news last Friday that the unemployment rate in September had dropped below 8 percent for the first time since Mr. Obama took office. The poll suggested that Mr. Romney had gained strength in a number of ways since last month and that Mr. Obama's best defense is the somewhat brighter economic outlook and the fact that voters continue to relate to him more than they do to his opponent.

Bitecofer traveled to Los Angeles for an appearance on "Cape Up" before departing for the campaign. Before the appearance, she said former vice president Joe Biden will be the Democratic presidential nominee. She also said Democrats will win back the White House. Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Cory Gardner (R-Colo.) and Doug Jones (D-Ala.) are both seeking reelection this November.

On Monday, the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Republican Trump administration's request to undo a Hawaii federal judge's decision that blocked the temporary travel ban in a dispute headed to the U.S. Supreme Court. The three-judge panel said Trump's March 6 order violated existing immigration law but did not address whether it was unconstitutional discrimination against Muslims. The 90-day ban targets travelers from Libya, Iran, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.

The U.S. Senate is moving toward a vote on Kansas Gov. Sam Brownback's nomination for an ambassador's post. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell filed a motion Monday to cut off debate on President Donald Trump's nomination of the conservative Republican governor to serve as U.S. ambassador-at-large for international religious freedom. McConnell communications director David Popp said in an email that a vote on the motion would occur Friday unless minority Democrats agree to have a vote sooner. Ending debate would clear the way for a second vote on Brownback's nomination. Trump first nominated Brownback for the ambassador's post in July, but his appointment has faced opposition from Democrats and LGBT groups. Brownback would resign if confirmed. Fellow Republican Lt. Gov. Jeff Colyer would be elevated to governor.

A Southern California man was arrested after authorities said he sent an email threatening to kill Sen. Dianne Feinstein. Authorities said Craig Shaver of Lancaster sent a Sept. 30 email threatening to kill the senator. Other details were not disclosed. Prosecutors said Thursday that Shaver, who has a 1991 grand theft conviction, attempted a criminal threat and accused him of being a felon in illegal possession of a revolver. He could face more than three years in prison if convicted. It was not clear whether Shaver has an attorney. Feinstein is the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee. She has received threats and abuse because some Republicans accuse her of trying to thwart the appointment of Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court. A call to a Feinstein spokesman was not immediately returned.

The Nielsen ratings company reported Wednesday that 33.5 million people watched President Barack Obama's fifth State of the Union address on Tuesday night, the smallest audience for the annual speech since Bill Clinton's last address in 2000. The figure was down from 37.8 million people who watched his first address in 2009. Sixteen networks aired the speech Tuesday night. NBC had 6.5 million viewers. ABC had 5.5 million viewers for the speech. The speech drew 3.7 million viewers on Fox News Channel, 3.6 million on CNN and 3 million on MSNBC.

House Republicans are discussing the possibility of a short-term increase in the debt ceiling, Fox News has learned. Lawmakers are going through various scenarios at their annual retreat in Williamsburg, Va. One senior leadership aide said many at the retreat want a debate over a long-term extension of the debt ceiling to be delayed. The aide said they think "the House and Senate should first move budgets and debate about how to responsibly address the debt crisis." The first step could include passing some new spending cuts. President Obama, still considering the 2011 debt ceiling fight, has urged Republicans not to use the debt ceiling to extract concessions like spending cuts. Republicans see the debt ceiling as important leverage to pass deficit-reduction measures.

On Monday, the San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the Republican Trump administration's request to undo a Hawaii federal judge's decision that blocked the temporary travel ban in a dispute headed to the U.S. Supreme Court. The three-judge panel said Trump's March 6 order violated existing immigration law but did not address whether it was unconstitutional discrimination against Muslims. The 90-day ban targets travelers from Libya, Iran, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.

Justice Department spokesperson Sarah Isgur Flores declined to comment when asked by ABC News whether the attorney general had threatened or offered to resign. Sessions was one of Trump's most reliable backers, shares Trump's contempt for civil rights and the rights of immigrants, and has been on the job for less than four months.

U.S. Capitol police arrested at least 80 people Thursday who were demonstrating Thursday against the proposed Republican health care bill. In a statement, police officials said they responded to 13 locations in office buildings on both sides of Congress beginning about 2 p.m. Twitter feeds showed videos and images of demonstrators who were cuffed and flanked by police as some yelled through the hallways in protest of the bill. "After officers arrived at the numerous scenes, they warned the demonstrators to cease and desist with their unlawful demonstration activities," the statement said. "Those who refused to cease and desist were placed under arrest." Officers arrested 10 men and 11 women at House Office Buildings, while 22 men and 37 women were arrested on the Senate side. Officials did not identify which Congressional offices had been targeted.

A Tennessee National Guardsman is facing prosecution in the shooting of two superiors at an armory outside Naval Support Activity Mid-South in Millington, Tennessee. The sergeant's first appearance in federal court could come Friday. Maj. Gen. Max Haston, head of the Tennessee Guard, said a major and a sergeant major were wounded in Thursday's attack at the armory just outside Naval Support Activity Mid-South in Millington. Both were expected to be out of the hospital soon. A law enforcement official briefed on the case said the sergeant, whose name was not released, had been disciplined before he opened fire. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss the case publicly. Other Guard members detained the shooter before police arrived.

Martha Raddatz visited Vice President Joe Biden at his official residence on March 26, 2012, during the Women's History Month Reception. The Daily Caller reported that Raddatz attended Obama's wedding to Julius Genachowski in 1991. The Obama campaign and media minions had previously stated that Raddatz was non-partisan. Raddatz is no longer married to Genachowski.

President Trump has won preliminary approval to register 38 new trademarks in China for industries including restaurants and advertising. The latest batch covers business interests that could add to criticism over potential conflicts. As a businessman, Mr. Trump has amassed a vast portfolio of trademarks around the world. Those trademarks, at times, clash with the vision of a populist president who has espoused an "America First" strategy. China has been among the biggest targets for his business prospects. Including the latest batch, his companies have filed for at least 130 trademarks in China since 2005 for restaurants, bars, hotels, brokerage services, advertising and management consulting. As president, Mr. Trump has criticized China for its trade practices. On the campaign trail, he threatened to impose punitive tariffs against the country.

President Donald Trump criticized CNN on Saturday at a campaign rally at Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport in Belgrade, Montana. Trump said, "Like they're doing me favors right?" He added, "CNN, doing me a favor, telling me what to say, right?" The crowd booed. Trump said, "CNN is telling me how to run the campaign, but in the meantime, I'm president and they're not." Trump added, "And their ratings aren't very good either." He said the economy was doing great, but that he wanted to talk about fixing problems that still needed to be addressed.

Worcester, Mass., police chief Gary Gemme said Wednesday the department has been reluctantly dragged into the efforts to find a burial plot for dead Boston Marathon suspect Tamerlan Tsarnaev. A deal for the state prisons department to take the body has fallen through. The deal to bury the body at a prison site was reached on Monday, then "dissolved" on Tuesday. Gemme said efforts to contact state officials since then have gone unanswered. State corrections officials did not immediately return a message. He said Worcester police are wasting precious resources providing security at the funeral parlor where the body is being kept. He said sending the body to Russia is "not an option." Gemme said: "We are not barbarians. We bury the dead."

Former Democratic presidential candidate George McGovern moved into hospice care near his home in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, on Monday. His daughter, Ann McGovern, told The Associated Press that the longtime South Dakota senator is "coming to the end of his life." Ann McGovern declined to elaborate but noted her 90-year-old father's recent health problems. She said he has moved in the Dougherty Hospice House in Sioux Falls. George McGovern lost to President Richard Nixon in a landslide in 1972. Most of his work in recent years has focused on world hunger. Last October, he was treated for exhaustion after a lecture tour. Two months later, he fell and hit his head just before a scheduled interview for a C-SPAN program about failed presidential candidates who've had a lasting impact on American politics.

Trump added, "And their ratings aren't very good either." He said the economy was doing great, but that he wanted to talk about fixing problems that still needed to be addressed.

The nonpartisan Tax Policy Center's analysis of the presidential candidates' tax proposals found that the Bush administration enacted tax cuts intended to protect current management by crippling the company if someone else takes over. The analysis concluded that the tax cuts would prevent a change in management and would make it hard for the next president to change the country's direction. The analysis cited John McCain's early opposition to the Bush tax cuts, which the analysis said were excessive and too tilted toward the rich.

President Obama is releasing his budget tomorrow. The budget would include Social Security and veterans' disability benefit cuts in the form of the chained CPI. The budget would make $1.8 trillion in deficit reductions over 10 years, replacing the $1.2 trillion sequester, with $580 billion in revenue increases. Republicans have consistently refused to accept revenue increases. Republicans have been successful in resisting revenue increases, citing the $2.3 trillion in savings negotiated in the past few years. A truly balanced budget approach would be to get that revenue increase more in line with the spending cuts. That would be the principled, and smart, policy position. It would have the added bonus of showing just how extreme Republicans are on taxes.

Evangelist Billy Graham returned to his home in North Carolina after being hospitalized for observation and lung tests. Dr. William R. Hathaway, chief medical officer at Mission Hospital in Asheville, said the 95-year-old Graham was released Thursday, and that he was alert and in good spirits during his two-day stay. Hathaway said doctors are pleased with the results of Graham's evaluation. Graham also spent two nights in the hospital for pulmonary testing last month after he had gone in for a regularly scheduled hospital visit. Graham uses a wheelchair and has been hospitalized for several health-related issues over the past few years. On Nov. 7, Graham celebrated his birthday surrounded by hundreds of guests including former vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin and real estate mogul Donald Trump.

The Senate approved the nomination of Sen. Max Baucus as the next U.S. ambassador to China on Thursday by a 96-0 vote. Baucus, 72, serves as chairman of the Senate Finance Committee. He has a background in U.S. trade policy but little expertise on military and other issues. Baucus was a leading author of President Barack Obama's health care law. He has also contributed to Republican legislation such as President George W. Bush's 2001 tax cuts. Baucus' early Senate departure could help Democrats retain his seat. Montana's Democratic governor is expected to appoint a Democrat to replace him, potentially giving that person a leg up in November's elections.

The article reported that arguments on Twitter in favor of the HHS Mandate and against Hobby Lobby and Conestoga Wood Specialties betray an extreme misunderstanding of the issues involved. The Supreme Court is deciding in the Sebelius v. Hobby Lobby and Conestoga Wood Specialties v. Sebelius cases whether the rights of business owners to operate their family companies without violating their religious convictions are Constitutionally protected. The article stated that whether a business chooses to pay for an employee's contraception needs, contraception is inexpensive and widely available. It also stated that an employee's access to the pill is not contingent upon whether or not their insurance covers it. The article characterized the arguments as purposefully deceptive and obtuse.

Vice President Joseph R. Biden Jr. spoke at the Third International Regenerative Medicine Conference at the Vatican on Tuesday. He discussed his Roman Catholic faith and curing cancer. Biden spoke about the urgent need to come up with new cures for cancer, a subject that has defined his final year in office. The conference is intended to highlight the extraordinary research advances being made with adult stem cells while largely sidestepping the issue of research using fetal tissue or embryonic stem cells. Dr. Robin Smith, president of the Stem for Life Foundation and one of the organizers of the three-day conference, said in a welcoming speech Tuesday: "Most importantly, we want everyone to understand that no one has to choose between science and faith."

First Lady Michelle Obama channeled rapper Lil Jon in a Vine posted by the White House on Tuesday night. The first lady asked, "turnip, for what?" The Vine was a response to Vine user Alphacat, who, while doing a good impression of the first lady's husband, President Barack Obama, asked how many calories Michelle Obama burned "every time you 'turn up'?" Other political figures have also used the song for their campaigns. Lil Jon recorded a video for the Rock the Vote campaign, featuring Lena Dunham, Fred Armisen and Natasha Lyonne.

Former Democratic presidential candidate George McGovern moved into hospice care near his home in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, on Monday. His daughter, Ann McGovern, told The Associated Press that the longtime South Dakota senator is "coming to the end of his life." Ann McGovern declined to elaborate but noted her 90-year-old father's recent health problems. She said he has moved in the Dougherty Hospice House in Sioux Falls. George McGovern lost to President Richard Nixon in a landslide in 1972. Most of his work in recent years has focused on world hunger. Last October, he was treated for exhaustion after a lecture tour. Two months later, he fell and hit his head just before a scheduled interview for a C-SPAN program about failed presidential candidates who've had a lasting impact on American politics.

Fox TV planned to produce an upcoming NBC miniseries based on the political life of former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. That was before the Republican National Committee said it would not let NBC handle any 2016 presidential primary debates until the network dropped the project. Fox TV is no longer involved in the project. The Hollywood Reporter reported the deal died due to internal disagreements, not political fallout. Some within Team NBC expressed relief over the news, assuming it would not damage its chances of bringing the miniseries to the public. The NBC project was first announced by entertainment chairman Bob Greenblatt at the Television Critics Association confab in July. The project has also caused internal strife at the network. NBC White House correspondent Chuck Todd and others have raised concern that the drama could damage the news division's reputation.

A chemical company controlled by Morocco's King Mohammed VI is funding a May 5-7 conference in Marrakech to be hosted by the Bill, Hillary and Chelsea Clinton Foundation's Clinton Global Initiative. Former Secretary of State and prospective 2016 Democratic presidential nominee Hillary Clinton will not attend. Phosphate exporter OCP is owned by Morocco's King Mohammed VI and is providing funding of at least $1 million for the Clinton Global Initiative Middle East and Africa Meeting that is expected to attract other prominent Middle Eastern and North African officials. Hillary Clinton announced the meeting last September. A Clinton Foundation source told Politico Wednesday that she likely will not attend. The foundation has faced criticism for accepting millions of dollars in contributions from foreign governments, corporations, and individuals. Observers and observers have raised questions about conflicts of interest.

Donald Trump told reporters on Friday that "I am a young, vibrant man." He was referencing former Vice President Joe Biden, who is a few years older than Trump. Trump was seen with Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau. Trump said, "I'm so young and vibrant that golf carts are the only vehicles where I get behind the wheel." He added, "I am a young, vibrant man. Now where's the bus back to the senior center?"

Trevor Noah criticized President Donald Trump's sons Eric and Donald Jr. on Wednesday night for their criticism of Hunter Biden's status as the son of former Vice President Joe Biden. Noah said he could understand why most people would complain about Hunter Biden receiving a leg up in life via his last name, but that what he could not understand was the Trump children doing it. On Tuesday, Trump Jr. criticized Hunter Biden for acknowledging in an interview that he would not have acquired certain roles on the boards of companies had he not been the son of former Vice President Joe Biden. On Wednesday night's "The Daily Show," Noah said of the Trump offspring: "If there was ever an example of people who got opportunities because of their names, it's these two."

President Obama issued a statement about the Republican open letter to Iran. In an interview with VICE News, Obama said he was embarrassed for the Republicans. He said: "For them to address a letter to the ayatollah — the supreme leader of Iran, who they claim is our mortal enemy — and their basic argument to them is: don't deal with our president, because you can't trust him to follow through on an agreement... That's close to unprecedented." VICE News released a "trailer" of the interview with Obama, which it conducted Thursday, but will not release the full interview until Monday. The trailer included Obama's comments on the letter.
