The memorandum instructs the secretary of state, the attorney general, the secretary of homeland security, and the director of national intelligence to implement the ban 72 hours after all applicable court injunctions are lifted or stayed.

The United States has obtained intelligence indicating Iran may be planning a retaliatory strike against the American Embassy in Baghdad if the United States launches a military strike against Syria, a senior U.S. official told CNN. The official said Iran has "a lot of Shi'a friends" in Iraq that would be willing to carry out an attack. The official was responding to a Wall Street Journal report that the United States intercepted an order from Iran to militants in Iraq to attack the embassy and other American interests in Baghdad if the United States struck Syria militarily for alleged chemical weapons use. The State Department had no comment on the report but added it had not taken any action in terms of security at U.S. diplomatic posts in Iraq.

A Fox News spokesperson said Roger Ailes had three brief conversations with Donald Trump about possibly appearing at the debate. The spokesperson said there were not multiple calls placed by Ailes to Trump. In the course of those conversations, Ailes acknowledged his concerns about a satirical observation made to quell attacks on Megyn Kelly, and prevent her from being smeared any further. Trump offered to appear at the debate upon the condition that Fox News contribute $5 million to his charities. The spokesperson explained that was not possible and they could not engage in a quid pro quo, nor could any money change hands for any reason. The spokesperson said the two goals were accomplished and they were pleased with the outcome. The spokesperson also said Fox News is proud to have Megyn Kelly on stage as a debate moderator alongside Bret Baier and Chris Wallace.

Treasury Secretary Jack Lew said Sunday on CNN's "State of the Union" that Republicans in Congress are "playing with fire" and that there is "no option" available for the president if they refuse to raise the debt ceiling. Some Republicans have suggested that once the debt ceiling is breached, President Barack Obama could take action on his own to prevent the country from entering into default, triggering cascading world financial problems. With the debt ceiling deadline set for later this month, Lew said Sunday that "there is no option preventing us from being in default if we don't have the cash to pay our bills." He said Republicans' approach to the debt ceiling is "reckless, because the reality is there are no good choices if we run out of borrowing capacity."

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee outraised its Republican counterpart in March by about $400,000. The National Republican Congressional Committee announced Sunday that it raised about $9.9 million in March and ended the month with $31.2 million in the bank. The DCCC announced last week that it brought in $10.3 million and ended March with $40.2 million in the bank. President Obama continued lending support to the DCCC last month, appearing at a Miami fundraiser. The DCCC raised more money from January through March, hauling in $23.6 million to the NRCC's $21.2 million. Neither committee is carrying any debt. House Democrats need to pick up 17 seats to win back the majority, a goal that strategists in both parties agree is all but impossible.

Donald J. Trump received more airtime than any other candidate and twice as much time as Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky. Trump had almost three times as many opportunities to speak as Paul or Gov. Chris Christie of New Jersey, through direct questions from moderators or from rebuttals to other candidates. Darker bars indicate responses that were longer than 60 seconds. The candidates in the 5 p.m. debate largely refrained from attacking each other. The participants in the later debate engaged in several heated exchanges. As in the earlier debate, President Obama and former Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton drew the most criticism from the Republicans. The thicknesses of the lines below are proportional to the number of attacks.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry arrived in Russia to meet President Vladimir Putin. Kerry lay a wreath at a World War II memorial in Sochi before meeting Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Putin. The visit was his first to Russia since May 2013. U.S. officials said Kerry planned to test Putin's willingness to push pro-Russia separatists in Ukraine to comply with a ceasefire. The officials also said Kerry would seek to gauge the status of Russia's support for Syrian President Bashar Assad, whose forces have been losing ground to rebels. After several hours in Sochi, Kerry will depart for a NATO meeting in Turkey.

Military lawyers ordered to assist Maj. Nidal Hasan as he faces the death penalty for the 2009 Fort Hood shooting are not being allowed to take over his case. The penalty phase of Hasan's trial is underway. It is his last chance to address jurors before they decide whether to sentence him to death. On Tuesday, he rested his case without calling witnesses or testifying. That prompted his standby attorneys to ask to take over. They say he is not presenting evidence that could convince jurors to sentence him to life in prison, such as good behavior in jail and his offer to plead guilty before trial. The judge, Col. Tara Osborn, denied their request. She said that while ill-advised, Hasan has the constitutional right to represent himself.

Negotiations over Iran's nuclear program entered a 13th day in Vienna on Thursday, with diplomats reconvening amid uncertainty and vague pronouncements from participants. Iran's President Hassan Rouhani said his nation is preparing for a "post-sanctions" era, suggesting a deal may be in sight to curb the Iranian nuclear program in exchange for the removal of economic sanctions. At roughly the same time, the White House issued a brief statement saying President Barack Obama had conferred with the U.S. negotiating team and provided them with "guidance" on how to proceed. The talks have been extended until Friday. The Obama administration must submit an agreement to Congress in the first few hours of Friday if it wants to avoid an extended legislative review.

A senior administration official said Thursday that the White House is examining possible aid cuts to the Palestinian Authority. The official spoke to The Times of Israel days after US President Donald Trump said the administration would review funding to the Palestinian Authority. The official said the review comes after Trump tweeted late Tuesday that he wanted to cut funding to the Palestinians "because they are no longer willing to talk peace." The administration has sent mixed signals over whether it is looking to cut all funding to the Palestinians, or just that which is funneled to the UN refugee agency UNRWA.

Keith Crisco, a Congressional candidate in the 2nd Congressional District who was in a close race with "American Idol" finalist Clay Aiken, died suddenly Monday. Crisco passed away after suffering an accident in his home. Unofficial results from the Democratic primary in the 2nd Congressional District showed Aiken leading Crisco by less than 400 votes out of more than 28,000 cast. The Associated Press reported last week that Aiken had enough votes to avoid a runoff, and the margin was too large for Crisco to request a recount. Aiken will be the Democratic candidate in NC-02 regardless of the final tally. Condolences to Crisco's family and friends were sent.

A federal judge on Monday blocked enforcement of North Dakota's recently enacted ban on most abortions, calling it "invalid and unconstitutional." The law under challenge, which was set to take effect Aug. 1, would have imposed the country's most stringent limit on abortions. With few exceptions, it would bar the procedure once a fetal heartbeat is detected, often about six weeks into pregnancy — a point when many women are not aware they are pregnant. From the moment in March when it was adopted, most legal experts said the law would not survive because it posed a direct challenge to Supreme Court guidelines, which state that a woman has a right to an abortion until the fetus is viable outside the womb. Viability must be determined by a physician and often occurs around 24 weeks into pregnancy.

House Minority Whip Eric Cantor (D-MD) responded to assertions by House Minority Whip Doug Thornell (R-VA) that Van Hollen is "fanning the flames" of threats against lawmakers. Thornell said in a statement: "Yesterday, Congressman Van Hollen called upon Republican leaders to condemn the harsh rhetoric that is fanning the flames of extremism around the country. Today, Mr. Cantor had the opportunity to join Mr. Van Hollen in calling for restraint. Instead, he chose to use his press conference to level false accusations. This is straight out of the Republicans' political playbook of deflecting responsibility and distracting attention away from a serious issue." Earlier today, Cantor said that his Richmond, VA office had been shot at Monday.

Stephen L. Holl, chief of police at the Washington Metropolitan Airports Authority, gathered his staff for the regular morning meeting on Monday. Holl opened by saying, "It wasn't our turn this time. Our turn could be next or it could be never." He added, "We believe this could happen any time." Last week at a security checkpoint at Los Angeles International Airport, a shooting left one Transportation Security Administration official dead and two others wounded. Security experts are re-examining strategy for making airports safe. They say there are no obvious solutions and that extending any security perimeter raises other problems.

A Fox News spokesperson said Roger Ailes had three brief conversations with Donald Trump about possibly appearing at the debate. The spokesperson said there were not multiple calls placed by Ailes to Trump. In the course of those conversations, Ailes acknowledged his concerns about a satirical observation made to quell attacks on Megyn Kelly, and prevent her from being smeared any further. Trump offered to appear at the debate upon the condition that Fox News contribute $5 million to his charities. The spokesperson explained that was not possible and they could not engage in a quid pro quo, nor could any money change hands for any reason. The spokesperson said the two goals were accomplished and they were pleased with the outcome. The spokesperson also said Fox News is proud to have Megyn Kelly on stage as a debate moderator alongside Bret Baier and Chris Wallace.

South Korea's military said that North Korea fired a projectile into the waters off the North's east coast. It was not immediately clear what was fired. Pyongyang has conducted a series of missile test-launches of various range in recent months. Leader Kim Jong Un is pushing for a nuclear and missile program that can deter what he calls U.S. and South Korean hostility toward the North. The launch occurred days after Seoul and Washington started joint military drills. The South's Joint Chief of Staff said in a statement that Monday's launch was made in the Tongchang-ri area in North Pyongan province. The area is the home of the North's Seohae Satellite Station, where it has conducted prohibited long-range rocket launches in recent years.

President Barack Obama is sending three White House aides to attend the funeral of Michael Brown, an 18-year-old black man whose fatal shooting by a white police officer sparked days of racial unrest in Ferguson, Missouri. Leading the group for Monday's service will be the chairman of the My Brother's Keeper Task Force, Broderick Johnson. My Brother's Keeper is an Obama initiative that aims to empower young minorities. Also attending will be the deputy director of the White House Office of Public Engagement, Marlon Marshall, and an adviser for the office, Heather Foster. The White House says Marshall is a St. Louis native and attended high school with Brown's mother. Michael Brown was unarmed when he was shot six times by Ferguson police officer Darren Wilson on Aug. 9.

Keith Crisco, a Congressional candidate in the 2nd Congressional District who was in a close race with "American Idol" finalist Clay Aiken, died suddenly Monday. Crisco passed away after suffering an accident in his home. Unofficial results from the Democratic primary in the 2nd Congressional District showed Aiken leading Crisco by less than 400 votes out of more than 28,000 cast. The Associated Press reported last week that Aiken had enough votes to avoid a runoff, and the margin was too large for Crisco to request a recount. Aiken will be the Democratic candidate in NC-02 regardless of the final tally. Condolences to Crisco's family and friends were sent.

On Friday evening, 56-year-old flight attendant Rose Hamid, a flight attendant at a Donald Trump rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina, was ejected from the venue. About halfway through the rally, Hamid said some people in the crowd turned ugly toward her, shouting "epithets." She was then escorted out by security. Trump commented on Hamid as she was being ejected. "There is hatred against us that is unbelievable. It's their hatred, it's not our hatred," Trump said. Hamid was wearing a shirt reading "I come in peace," by the way.

Florida Gov. Rick Scott canceled his trip Monday to New York to meet with presumptive GOP presidential nominee Donald Trump so he can monitor a tropical depression expected to hit the state, Fox News confirmed Sunday. Scott and Trump were purportedly going to discuss Trump's general election strategy in Florida. President Obama won the state in 2008 and 2012. A RealClearPolitics.com poll average shows Trump and Democratic presidential front-runner Hillary Clinton tied in a hypothetical matchup in the state. Scott, a former businessman like Trump, was being mentioned as a possible vice presidential pick. However, the two-term governor on Friday told CNN, which first reported the canceled meeting, that he was not interested. Scott has endorsed Trump, who in March won the Florida primary.

The Trump administration has requested the Pentagon to house up to 12,000 detained migrant family members and help prosecute them. Some lawmakers are criticizing the move. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis argues that the Defense Department is obliged to provide help. Several senators object to Mattis providing 21 military lawyers to the Justice Department. The Pentagon has received a Department of Homeland Security request to house up to 12,000 detained migrant family members, starting with shelters for 2,000 people to be available within 45 days. It also has agreed to make housing available at an air base for up to 20,000 unaccompanied migrant minors. Mattis has made improving the military's fitness for combat a top priority.

The White House declined to comment on Beyonce's lip-syncing of the national anthem. White House spokesman Jay Carney said he had "no idea" whether the pop diva sang "The Star-Spangled Banner" or not. Carney would not say whether Obama was aware of her plans to fake sing when he asked her to play such a key role in his inaugural. "I really don't think it's an important issue to address from the podium here," Carney told reporters at Wednesday's press briefing. "I'm glad you guys are focused on the important issues of the day."

President Obama is surrounding himself with firefighters and police to claim that the sequester, which he invented, will force them out of their jobs. The media is aflutter about the claim. The article identifies the emergency services as state and local governments. It asks why federal funding affects that, noting that some states and local governments spend foolishly on other things. It asks why other taxpayers should subsidize that, when essential national services, like defense, also face cuts. It also asks who proposed the sequester in the first place, in a ruse to pressure the opposition. The article describes this as "textbook demagoguery," and calls for Obama to be called out.

Former Texas Gov. Rick Perry is dropping out of the race for president, ending his second bid for the Republican nomination and becoming the first major candidate of the 2016 campaign to give up on the White House. Perry's campaign said the longest-serving governor in Texas history would tell a group of conservative activists in St. Louis on Friday night that "some things have become clear." "We have a tremendous field, the best in a generation, so I step aside knowing our party is in good hands, and as long as we listen to the grassroots, the cause of conservativism will be too," Perry planned to say according to remarks released by his campaign. Perry suspended his campaign while spending limited campaign funds and polling remained near zero.

A letter to the editor responded to a Nov. 16 news article titled "'Pink Wave' May Complicate Race for Speaker." The letter asked why Democrats internalized and parrot Republican smear campaigns against their party's accomplished women. The letter writer stated that after a critical blue wave, why squander the savvy, tenacity and expertise that Nancy Pelosi would bring to steering the Democratic agenda? The writer said Pelosi's deft skills are unquestioned. The writer said Republicans cast Pelosi as evil incarnate, as they did Hillary Clinton, precisely for fear of her effectiveness. The writer said there is nothing progressive or wise about discarding Pelosi; the writer called it downright ludicrous to sideline a most formidable and accomplished warrior, especially when the battle has just begun. The letter was from Weston, Conn.

U.S. officials said the White House is announcing an aid package to Ukraine of $1 billion in lost energy subsidies as it seeks to extract itself from Russia's influence. The announcement came as U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry landed in Kiev on Tuesday. Russian troops have overtaken the local government in Crimea, a strategic region in Ukraine's southeast. Western leaders are threatening economic sanctions as early as this week against if Moscow does not retreat. The economic package also includes training assistance to Ukraine's national bank, Finance Ministry and election observers ahead of a May 25 national vote. The U.S. officials spoke on condition of anonymity because the announcement had not yet happened.

Franklin Regional School District announced the reopening plans on its website Saturday. The district said teachers will return to work Monday and students will be able to visit the school with their families on Tuesday. Authorities said 16-year-old Alex Hribal attacked fellow students at the suburban Pittsburgh school with a pair of kitchen knives. Hribal faces four counts of attempted homicide and 21 counts of aggravated assault. Four students remain hospitalized, all in critical condition. Hospital officials said one wounded student, a 14-year-old boy, was discharged Saturday afternoon. Police said they do not yet have a motive for the rampage.

The Federal Reserve announced it will raise its benchmark interest rate on Wednesday for the first time since last December. The Fed will also publish a 2017 forecast, including its predictions for economic growth and the path of monetary policy. The Fed entered 2016 predicting it would raise rates four times, which would have amounted to a significant retreat from its stimulus campaign. Instead, the central bank has held steady because growth remained slow and there was little sign of inflation. The unemployment rate fell to 4.6 percent in November, about as low as most Fed officials would like to see.

The White House declined to comment on Beyonce's lip-syncing of the national anthem. White House spokesman Jay Carney said he had "no idea" whether the pop diva sang "The Star-Spangled Banner" or not. Carney would not say whether Obama was aware of her plans to fake sing when he asked her to play such a key role in his inaugural. "I really don't think it's an important issue to address from the podium here," Carney told reporters at Wednesday's press briefing. "I'm glad you guys are focused on the important issues of the day."

Charlotte-Mecklenburg Police said officers shot and killed a person who they said was armed and posed a threat. A statement from the department said officers were at an apartment complex on Tuesday looking for a suspect with an outstanding warrant when they encountered a person inside a car. Officials said the person exited the car with a gun, then got back in. The statement said when officers approached the car, the person got out of the car with the gun again. The officers considered the person to be a threat and fired their weapons. Emergency personnel took the person to Carolinas Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The suspect's identity has not been released. The officers have been placed on administrative leave.

A Greenville, South Carolina, man with a face tattoo of a pistol was charged with unlawful firearm possession after firefighters witnessed him throw a revolver into the grass. Fox News reported that Michael Vines was involved in an accident and allegedly threw a firearm into the grass. The Greenville Police Department reported that Vines allegedly tossed a fully-loaded S&W .38-caliber revolver into the grass after a recent car wreck near the intersection of Green Avenue and Guess Street. The GPD noted that Vines is federally prohibited from firearm possession and has a tattoo of gun on his forehead. He was charged with "driving under a suspended license, driving too fast for conditions and unlawful carrying of a firearm."

A Minnesota court confirmed that Democrat Al Franken won the most votes in his 2008 Senate race against Republican Norm Coleman. The ruling was not expected to be final because Coleman previously announced plans to appeal to the state Supreme Court, which he has 10 days to do so. That appeal could mean weeks more delay in seating Minnesota's second senator. After a statewide recount and seven-week trial, Franken stands 312 votes ahead. Franken gained more votes from the election challenge than Coleman, the candidate who brought it. The state law Coleman sued under required three judges to determine who received the most votes and is therefore entitled to an election certificate. That certificate is on hold pending appeal.

The ruling was not expected to be final because Coleman previously announced plans to appeal to the state Supreme Court, which he has 10 days to do so. Franken gained more votes from the election challenge than Coleman, the candidate who brought it. The state law Coleman sued under required three judges to determine who received the most votes and is therefore entitled to an election certificate. That certificate is on hold pending appeal.

Lawyer Thomas Goldstein, a Washington lawyer, filed a challenge Friday to the appointment of Matthew Whitaker as U.S. acting attorney general. Goldstein said the high court should rule quickly that President Donald Trump's appointment of Whitaker to temporarily lead the Justice Department is illegal. Goldstein was part of a legal team challenging Whitaker's appointment Friday in a pending Supreme Court case dealing with gun rights. The filing asks the court to name Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein as a party in the case, instead of Whitaker. There is no deadline for action by the justices. Goldstein is part of the legal team that is mounting a similar challenge in federal district court in Maryland.

U.S. President Barack Obama and Pakistani President Asif Zardari met at the White House on Friday. The White House said in a statement that their discussion focused on fighting terrorism and the importance of cooperating toward a peaceful and stable outcome in Afghanistan. The statement also said the President underscored the importance of the U.S.-Pakistan relationship and our continued support for Pakistan. Zardari is in Washington to attend a memorial service Friday for diplomat Richard Holbrooke, who was Obama's envoy in Pakistan and Afghanistan. Holbrooke died last month. U.S. Vice President Joe Biden met with Zardari on Wednesday in Islamabad during his unannounced visit to the region. Biden also met with Prime Minister Yousuf Raza Gilani and senior military officials.

Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) appeared on CBS's Face the Nation after a peace deal in which Putin-backed leader Viktor Yanukovich relinquished power halted widespread violence and unrest in Ukraine. McCain said the Ukrainian people had to determine their own future and that a partition of Ukraine was unacceptable. He said a message had to be sent to Putin. McCain said the Russian people are "tired of the crony capitalism and the kleptocracy that governs Russia today." He added, "If I were him, I would be little nervous."

When asked if he would consider running for a third term during a town-hall in Minnesota, President Obama said, "Not only the Constitution bars it, but Michelle bars it — and you can't change Michelle's mind." The remarks came on the same day the Supreme Court issued a unanimous rebuke to President Obama on Thursday, saying he had overreached in issuing recess appointments during brief breaks in the Senate's work.

The Chipotle chain voluntarily shut down 43 restaurants in Washington State and Oregon over the weekend after health authorities began investigating an E. coli outbreak. Health authorities are investigating 19 cases of illness related to the bacteria in Washington and three cases in Oregon, involving an unknown type of food. Eight people have been admitted to the hospital, officials said. No one has died. Chris Arnold, the communications director for Chipotle, said in an emailed statement on Monday: "There have been links made to six restaurants in the Seattle and Portland areas. We have closed 43 restaurants in those markets out of an abundance of caution." The Oregon Health Authority said in a statement over the weekend that the infection affected people who ate at Chipotle outlets between Oct. 14 and 23.

Police used smoke bombs to clear demonstrators blocking Interstate 94 in St. Paul during a protest sparked by recent police killings of black men in Minnesota and Louisiana. The smoke was used just after midnight when about 200 protesters were in the roadway as police in riot gear moved in. Police said several officers were injured by rocks, firecrackers and other debris thrown by protesters Saturday night. A protest leader urged the group to march to the governor's mansion, where protesters have gathered since the fatal police shooting Wednesday night of Philando Castile. The 32-year-old black man was shot during a traffic stop in suburban St. Paul. The St. Paul Police Department tweeted that arrests have been made during the protest but did not indicate how many.

James Mattis, the U.S. defense secretary, said on Tuesday that he was assured by President Trump that his job is "100 percent" safe. The interview with Trump led to speculation about the cabinet member's future. Mattis told reporters he had an in-flight conversation with Trump and was told by the president that he has his full support. In an interview that aired Sunday, Trump appeared to question Mattis' future, saying he "may leave." Trump told Lesley Stahl: "I think he's sort of a Democrat, if you want to know the truth. But Gen. Mattis is a good guy. We get along very well. He may leave. I mean, at some point, everybody leaves."

The State Department ordered nonessential U.S. diplomats to leave Lebanon due to security concerns Friday as the Obama administration and Congress debate military strikes on neighboring Syria. In a travel warning for Lebanon issued early Friday, the department said it had instructed nonessential staffers to leave Beirut and urged private American citizens to depart Lebanon. The step had been under consideration since last week when President Barack Obama said he was contemplating military action against the Syrian government for its alleged chemical weapons attack last month that the administration said killed more than 1,400 people near Damascus. The U.S. closed 19 embassies and consulates across Africa and the Middle East last month for more than a week after a terrorist threat. Hezbollah, an Assad ally that has sent fighters into Syria, is based in Lebanon.

When asked if he would consider running for a third term during a town-hall in Minnesota, President Obama said, "Not only the Constitution bars it, but Michelle bars it — and you can't change Michelle's mind." The remarks came on the same day the Supreme Court issued a unanimous rebuke to President Obama on Thursday, saying he had overreached in issuing recess appointments during brief breaks in the Senate's work.

After Hillary Clinton's loss on Tuesday, the collective devastation of her supporters and many women in general was evident. During her concession speech Wednesday morning, Clinton said to a crowd: "To all the little girls watching this, never doubt that you are powerful and valuable and deserving of every chance and opportunity in the world," and later added: "Never stop believing that fighting for what's right is worth it." On Thursday morning, Cosmopolitan created a short video of women holding up signs featuring sentiments they wish they could tell Clinton herself. The short video is described as a reminder of what Clinton — the first woman to represent a major party in the U.S. — means to so many people around the country.

President Donald Trump's latest tweets on North Korea received a muted response in South Korea. Media focused on U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson's acknowledgement that the U.S. is keeping open direct communication channels with the North. South Korea's largest daily newspaper, Chosun Ilbo, warned Monday that any U.S.-North Korea talks should not recognize the North as a nuclear state, or the South would be forced to seek nuclear arms. On Saturday, Tillerson said in Beijing that the Trump administration is probing North Korea's willingness to talk. On Sunday, Trump tweeted that he told Tillerson "he is wasting his time trying to negotiate with Little Rocket Man," referring to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

President Donald Trump posted on Twitter on Wednesday morning warning that "anonymous sources" should stop reading the story if "anonymous sources" were cited by a news organization. In two tweets, Trump wrote that "many anonymous sources don't even exist." He also criticized CNN and called the network the "enemy of the people." Fellow Twitter users criticized Trump over the time he promoted his Birther conspiracy theory by claiming an unidentified but, according to him, "extremely credible source" had called his office to say former President Barack Obama's birth certificate was a fraud.

On Tuesday's broadcast of the Fox News Channel's "Hannity," House Intelligence Committee Ranking Member Devin Nunes (R-CA) said Democrats were trying to hide impeachment proceedings by keeping them in the House Intelligence Committee. Nunes stated, "[T]his is not a real impeachment. This is like a faux impeachment. What they're doing is, by keeping this at the House Intelligence Committee, we're not built — the House Intelligence Committee is not a place to run impeachment hearings. So, what they're trying to do is they're hiding this from the American people. They don't want the normal process."

White House press secretary Sarah Sanders announced a ban on personal cellphones and devices in the West Wing. In a statement to reporters, Sanders said: "[S]tarting next week the use of all personal devices for both guests and staff will no longer be allowed in the West Wing. Staff will be able to conduct business on their government-issued devices and continue working hard on behalf of the American people." She added that the new policy demonstrated the Trump administration's commitment to security. The announcement followed leaks in the book on the Trump presidency by Michael Wolff, which described White House aides as insecure and seeking influence.

Donald Trump will visit California next week, his first visit to the Golden State as president, the White House announced on Wednesday. Sources familiar with Trump's plans say he is expected to visit California to the US-Mexico border to look at border wall prototypes in the San Diego area. One source said the President and White House have been looking to schedule a trip to the border "for a while." Trump has not visited California since he was sworn into office, though Vice President Mike Pence visited the state in October. White House press secretary Sarah Sanders confirmed Trump is traveling to California next week but did not provide more specific details. Asked why he has not visited before now, Sanders said Trump had been busy enacting elements of his agenda, such as creating jobs and growing the economy.

A patient admitted to a New York hospital this week with fever and gastrointestinal symptoms similar to Ebola tested negative for the virus, the Mount Sinai Hospital said Wednesday. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention determined the patient kept in isolation since Monday, August 4, 2014 at the hospital had tested negative for Ebola Virus Disease. The patient is in stable condition, is improving, and remains in the care of physicians and nurses. The man had recently traveled to West Africa, which is experiencing the largest outbreak of the hemorrhagic fever in history. A total of 932 people have died since March in Sierra Leone, Guinea, Liberia and Nigeria. Ebola is spread through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person.

Logan said he opposes President Obama's gun control proposals. He said he is not saying gang bangers go to gun-free zones. He said these maniac killers have gone to those zones. He said Obama wants to direct all his laws to those incidents and wants to prescribe the exact wrong solutions and play on people's emotions because he has something more in mind, not just banning assault weapons, but getting -- confiscating our weapons. Limbaugh said they have to be suspicious. Hannity asked, "Guys, we've got to go." Limbaugh said, "You're spreading paranoia, David." Limbaugh said, "I love it." Hannity said, "Good to see you both."

ABC News 10 in San Diego reported that San Diego Mayor Bob Filner will give the keynote address at a benefit for sexual assault victims. A women veterans group confirmed the appearance. Filner had been originally scheduled to attend as an award recipient. The group stripped him of the award, but he will appear and address the scandal now consuming City Hall. The National Military Women Veterans Association of America had decided to honor Filner with a lifetime achievement award for his work on behalf of women veterans, including the issue of sexual assault. The group released a statement rescinding the award, stating, "We do not tolerate sexual discrimination at any level within our society."

The New York Times reported that Ferguson, Missouri, police officer Darren Wilson told investigators that 18-year-old Michael Brown reached for the gun during a scuffle. Wilson told authorities that he was pinned in his vehicle and in fear for his life as they struggled over his gun. The Times also reported that Wilson's account to authorities did not explain why he fired at Brown multiple times after emerging from his vehicle. The account came from government officials briefed on the federal civil rights investigation into the Aug. 9 shooting. Racial unrest and weeks of protests followed Brown's death.

President Obama and first lady Michelle Obama celebrated Valentine's Day Thursday with dinner at MiniBar, a restaurant in Penn Quarter in the District. The Obamas dined at MiniBar, a Jose Andres restaurant known for difficult reservations. The menu price is $225 per person, beverages not included, and the web site describes eating there as a "once-in-a-lifetime experience that pushes the limits of what's possible with food." Pool reporters covering the Obamas' outing were stationed nearby at Austin Grill, where a burrito can be purchased for $9. During a trip to Georgia earlier in the day, Mr. Obama joked that he had to get back to Washington for "our date tonight."

On Wednesday, Democrats applauded Sen. John McCain (R-AZ) when he entered a closed-door meeting between President Barack Obama and Congressional Democrats on Capitol Hill. McCain, who has been described as Sen. Majority Leader Harry Reid's (D-NV) favorite Republican, said he had accidentally entered the wrong door. The Hill reported that Democrats in the room erupted in applause and laughter when McCain entered. Earlier this week, McCain said Fox News was "schizophrenic" and suggested he was open to supporting Hillary Clinton, whom he called a "rock star" despite her role in the Benghazi scandal, over Sen. Rand Paul (R-KY) in a potential 2016 presidential matchup.

Members of Congress are demanding answers about why security at the U.S. diplomatic mission in Libya was "grossly inadequate" when militants stormed the facility on Sept. 11, killing the ambassador and three other Americans. The House and Senate foreign affairs committees are scheduled to hold hearings on Thursday. The public testimony comes two days after an independent review panel issued a report blaming management failures at the department for inadequate security at the compound in Benghazi, a city in eastern Libya. The findings led four State Department officials to step down Wednesday. Lawmakers insist that Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton testify soon. She had been scheduled to appear Thursday but canceled because of illness.

Sen. John R. Thune (R-SD) appeared on "Fox News Sunday" and said it was in President Donald Trump's "best interest" to sign the Russia sanctions bill moving through Congress. Thune said, "I think that in the end, the administration will come to the conclusion that an overwhelming majority of congress has and that is that we need to sanction Russia for their meddling in the U.S. election. That I think will pass probably overwhelmingly again in the Senate with a veto proof majority." He added, "I think it is in his best interest for a lot of reasons to sign it, and I believe he will."

The Democratic National Committee announced that NBA veteran Jason Collins will headline its annual lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender gala. Last week, Collins became the first active player in any of four major U.S. professional sports leagues to come out as gay. President Barack Obama called the 34-year-old athlete the same day to congratulate him and tell him he was proud of his courage. The DNC also announced that first lady Michelle Obama will also attend the May 29 fundraiser in New York. Tickets start at $1,250 per person and go up to $32,400 per couple to chair the event. The DNC included a call to legalize same-sex marriage in the party's convention platform last year. Collins has played for six teams in 12 seasons and is now a free agent.

Nineteen members of the elite firefighting Hotshot crew were killed fighting a wildfire on June 30 in Yarnell, about 80 miles northwest of Phoenix, when the blaze overtook them, killing 19 members of the crew. One member who was serving as a lookout survived. The service is set for Tuesday morning in nearby Prescott Valley and is expected to draw firefighters from around the nation to pay their respects. Vice President Joe Biden and Arizona Gov. Jan Brewer are set to speak at the memorial. The blaze had burned about 13 square miles and more than 100 structures before firefighters gained control of it over the weekend.

The White House is preparing to instruct federal agencies not to renew their subscriptions to The New York Times and The Washington Post. White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham described the move as a cost-saving measure. Grisham said "not renewing subscriptions across all federal agencies will be a significant cost saving for taxpayers - hundreds of thousands of dollars." President Donald Trump has frequently criticized the two newspapers. In a Fox News interview on Monday, Trump said "we don't want" the Times in the White House anymore, and "we're going to probably terminate that and The Washington Post."

Six New Jersey residents filed a federal lawsuit in federal court Thursday against Gov. Chris Christie, the state of New Jersey, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, and others over traffic jams in Fort Lee, New Jersey. The suit appears to be the first civil claim over traffic that appear to have been caused as political punishment for the Fort Lee mayor. The plaintiffs want it certified as a class action. Lawyer Rosemarie Arnold said she filed it after learning this week that lane closures on an approach to the George Washington Bridge were "deliberate actions." She said that her clients were late for work and that one suffered a panic attack. Christie has denied involvement. His spokesman did not respond to an email seeking comment.

The Pentagon said it has no plans to coordinate with Iran on possible military action in Iraq. Pentagon press secretary Navy Rear Adm. John Kirby told reporters Monday that while there may be discussions between U.S. and Iranian officials in Vienna about security in the region, it will not include any military coordination. Secretary of State John Kerry said in an interview with Yahoo! News that Washington is "open to discussions" with Tehran if the Iranians can help end the violence and restore confidence in the Iraqi government and would not rule out military cooperation. Kirby said this does not mean the U.S. is planning to engage with Iraq on military activities inside Iraq. Kerry also said that U.S. drone strikes "may well" be an option.

CNN reported that the first charges have been filed and approved by a grand jury in Washington, D.C. Special counsel Robert Mueller is on the move. The charges are still sealed under orders from a federal judge. Plans were prepared Friday for anyone charged to be taken into custody as soon as Monday, the sources said. It is unclear what the charges are. A spokesman for the special counsel's office declined to comment. On Friday, top lawyers who are helping to lead the Mueller probe, including veteran prosecutor Andrew Weissmann, were seen entering the court room at the DC federal court where the grand jury meets to hear testimony in the Russia investigation. Reporters present saw activity at the grand jury room, but officials made no announcements.

A Southern California man was arrested after authorities said he sent an email threatening to kill U.S. Sen. Dianne Feinstein. Authorities said Craig Shaver of Lancaster sent a Sept. 30 email to the senator. Other details were not disclosed. Prosecutors said Thursday that Shaver, who has a 1991 grand theft conviction, attempted a criminal threat and accused him of being a felon in illegal possession of a revolver. He could face more than three years in prison if convicted. It was not clear whether Shaver has an attorney. Feinstein is the top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee. She has received threats and abuse because some Republicans accuse her of trying to thwart the appointment of Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.

Three Republican challengers to President Donald Trump, Bill Weld, Joe Walsh and Mark Sanford, wrote in a Washington Post opinion piece published Friday that the Republican Party has "taken a wrong turn" in letting Trump define the party. They describe the president as "a serial self-promoter who has abandoned the bedrock principles of the GOP." At least four states — South Carolina, Nevada, Arizona and Kansas — have canceled Republican primaries and caucuses next year. Weld, Walsh and Sanford are urging the party to reconsider. Trump has referred to the three challengers as "The Three Stooges." None of them is expected to generate enough support to defeat Trump.

The head of the Transportation Security Administration, John Pistole, said Friday on CBS's "The Early Show" that close-quarter body inspections are unavoidable in a time of terrorist threats. Pistole said he understands public distaste for more intense security procedures, including hand pat-downs. He called it a "challenge" for federal authorities and airport screeners. Pistole said the attempted bombing of a U.S. bound plane last Christmas and the effort to ship packages with bombs to this country on cargo planes more recently makes tougher security necessary. He said, "The bottom line is, we're trying to see that everybody can be assured with high confidence that everybody else on that flight can be properly screened."

The Democratic National Committee announced that NBA veteran Jason Collins will headline its annual lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender gala. Last week, Collins became the first active player in any of four major U.S. professional sports leagues to come out as gay. President Barack Obama called the 34-year-old athlete the same day to congratulate him and tell him he was proud of his courage. The DNC also announced that first lady Michelle Obama will also attend the May 29 fundraiser in New York. Tickets start at $1,250 per person and go up to $32,400 per couple to chair the event. The DNC included a call to legalize same-sex marriage in the party's convention platform last year. Collins has played for six teams in 12 seasons and is now a free agent.

Former first daughter Jenna Bush Hager announced Wednesday that she is pregnant with her first child, due in the spring. The 31-year-old made the announcement on NBC's "Today" show, where she is a contributing correspondent. Hager is the twin daughter of former President George W. Bush and her husband, Henry. They have been married for four years. Henry joined his wife on the "Today" set when she made the announcement. During a phone call on the show, former President Bush said he is "fired up" about becoming a grandfather, and former first lady Laura Bush said she is "thrilled." It will be the couple's first grandchild.

They describe the president as "a serial self-promoter who has abandoned the bedrock principles of the GOP." At least four states — South Carolina, Nevada, Arizona and Kansas — have canceled Republican primaries and caucuses next year. Weld, Walsh and Sanford are urging the party to reconsider. Trump has referred to the three challengers as "The Three Stooges." None of them is expected to generate enough support to defeat Trump.

Eric Trump, President Donald Trump's second-eldest son, posted on Twitter on Thursday that Rudy Giuliani, his father's personal attorney who had held a press conference the previous day to discuss Trump's election defeat, "took down the New York mob." Eric Trump added, "Hell take down these dirtbags as well..." Twitter users responded critically, warning Eric Trump to be careful about what he wishes for, noting how spelling and punctuation matters, and criticizing Giuliani's handling of a scene in the "Borat 2" movie.

MSNBC anchor Chris Matthews said on Tuesday's "Hardball" that Susan Rice's job is to watch national security. Matthews said Rice made clear what she was doing when she saw an American name appear in surveillance of a foreign agent. He asked, "What's wrong with that?" Panelist Simon Marks remarked conservatives were "looking for a piñata" to beat up. Matthews responded, "Notice it's always a female? Just a thought."

President Donald Trump paused his final campaign rally on Monday after a supporter collapsed in Missouri. During the rally, supporters sang Amazing Grace. Trump said, "Is there a doctor in the house?" while waiting for the supporter to get medical attention. The president paused for six minutes while medical staff attended to the woman. "Don't rush," he said. "That's one of our great people there ... say a little prayer." Supporters responded by singing the hymn "Amazing Grace" while medical staff took the supporter out on a stretcher. "I want to just thank everybody, that was beautiful," Trump said afterward. "Hopefully she will be ok."

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) made jokes about giving coronavirus relief payments to struggling Americans on Monday. The comments came in response to a tweet by Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), who suggested Congress prop up the faltering U.S. economy by sending every person in the country money until three months after the pandemic ends. Markey was not having it. Cruz has not responded to Markey. Other Twitter users criticized Cruz's response. Some users found Cruz's remarks odd because they seemed to suggest that soy lattes are a rich person's luxury.

No one knows whether former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush will run for president in 2016. Barbara Bush, in an interview with C-SPAN for its "First Ladies" series, said she hopes he will not. She said she "hope[d] he won't, because I think he'll get all my enemies, all his brother's, all — and there are other families. I refuse to accept that this great country isn't raising other wonderful people." Andy Marlette, an editorial cartoonist at the Pensacola News Journal, offered his take on Barbara Bush's comments on her son's candidacy. The article is available.

U.S. Defense Secretary Ash Carter said Friday at his Brussels hotel that a key Persian Gulf ally has agreed to send special forces soldiers to Syria to assist in the development of local Sunni Arab fighters focused on recapturing Raqqa, the Islamic State group's capital. Carter made the comment after meeting with his counterpart from the United Arab Emirates. Carter declined to say how many Emirati special forces would go to Syria. He said they would be part of an effort led by the United States and bolstered by Saudi special forces to train and enable local Arab fighters who are motivated to recapture Raqqa. The U.S. war plan for fighting the Islamic State in Syria and Iraq is designed to unseat the extremists in Raqqa and Mosul, which is the group's main stronghold in northern Iraq.

Former Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson won the Republican nomination for a U.S. Senate seat the party is seeking for the first time in more than five decades. Thompson, a former governor and Health and Human Services secretary under President George W. Bush, defeated three Republican rivals during Tuesday's primary. It marked Thompson's first time on the ballot since 1998. He advances to face Democrat Tammy Baldwin in the Nov. 6 election. The seat became open following the retirement of Democrat Herb Kohl. The win follows a primary in which hedge fund investor Eric Hovde invested nearly $5 million of his own money into the race. U.S. Rep. Mark Neumann and state Assembly Speaker Jeff Fitzgerald also sought the GOP nomination.

Ahmed Abu Khattala was described as open about his animosity toward the United States and his conviction that Muslims and Christians were locked in an intractable religious war. In an interview, he said: "There is always hostility between the religions. That is the nature of religions." During the assault on the American diplomatic mission in Benghazi, Libya, on the night of Sept. 11, 2012, witnesses saw Abu Khattala directing the attackers who killed Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans. Afterward, Abu Khattala offered contradictory denials of his role, sometimes saying he did not do it but strongly approved. He appeared to enjoy his notoriety.

She said she "hope[d] he won't, because I think he'll get all my enemies, all his brother's, all — and there are other families. I refuse to accept that this great country isn't raising other wonderful people." Andy Marlette, an editorial cartoonist at the Pensacola News Journal, offered his take on Barbara Bush's comments on her son's candidacy. The article is available.

Vermont U.S. Sen. Patrick Leahy said the discovery of a malware code used by Russian hackers on a Vermont utility's laptop is the latest example that state-sponsored Russian hacking is a serious threat. The Burlington Electric Department said Friday it detected the malware in a laptop not connected to its grid systems. It took immediate action to isolate the laptop and alerted federal officials. Leahy, a Democrat, said he and his staff were briefed by Vermont State Police on Friday night. He said the incident goes "beyond hackers having electronic joy rides" and that trying to potentially manipulate the electric grid and shut it down is a direct threat to Vermont.

Thompson, a former governor and Health and Human Services secretary under President George W. Bush, defeated three Republican rivals during Tuesday's primary. It marked Thompson's first time on the ballot since 1998. He advances to face Democrat Tammy Baldwin in the Nov. 6 election. The seat became open following the retirement of Democrat Herb Kohl. The win follows a primary in which hedge fund investor Eric Hovde invested nearly $5 million of his own money into the race. U.S. Rep. Mark Neumann and state Assembly Speaker Jeff Fitzgerald also sought the GOP nomination.

President Obama spoke to Prime Minister Netanyahu on Wednesday on regional security issues and Middle East peace, the White House said in a read-out of the conversation. The White House said the two leaders agreed to continue "close coordination" on a "range of security issues" but did not say whether they discussed airstrikes Israel launched on Syrian targets over the weekend. On Sunday, Israel launched an airstrike on an arms depot in the Syrian capital of Damascus that killed at least 43 Syrian soldiers. Israel reported it was worried that Iran was using Syria to try to ship some high-tech weapons to Hezbollah fighters in Lebanon who could use them to strike Tel Aviv. On Monday, White House spokesman Jay Carney defended Israel's right to "take action" to protect itself.

Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach said he will recuse himself from directing the recount of a gubernatorial primary he is a candidate in. Kobach told CNN, "I'll be happy to recuse myself." The announcement came a day after he did not recuse himself and shortly after Colyer pointed out that Kobach's office was giving local election officials incorrect information. Counting is still going on in the race, with mail-in ballots still coming and provisional votes being counted next week. Only around a hundred votes separate the two candidates, making a recount a very real possibility.
