Counting is still going on in the race, with mail-in ballots still coming and provisional votes being counted next week. Only around a hundred votes separate the two candidates, making a recount a very real possibility.

President Obama recounted his anger over the mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012. The article reports that the tears dominated the media this week. Paul Ryan, the House Speaker, told Katie Couric of the president's display of emotion: "I was affected by it, but I thought we should've had the same kind of reaction when James Foley was beheaded, when San Bernardino and Paris occurred. That's the kind of reaction I had when those occurred." Comments on the story are closed.

On Thursday in Baton Rouge, LA., President Barack Obama spoke at a town hall. He said that if climate change is not addressed, a cure for cancer would be meaningless. Obama said, "But don't think that this is not a problem for all of us. This is the main message I have. You know, we talked — that young lady was asking me about curing cancer. Well, we might cure cancer, but if temperatures have gone up two, three degrees around the planet, four degrees and oceans are rising, we got — we're going to have more problems than medical science can cure. We have got to make that investment now and we can do it. Good question."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday that the coming month will be "critical" for preventing a nuclear deal with Iran. Netanyahu said the U.S. Congress may be the body that influences the emerging deal between world powers and Iran. He said he will travel to Washington to explain why the deal is "dangerous to Israel, dangerous to the region and dangerous to the world." Netanyahu's opposition to compromising with Iran over its nuclear program has further stressed his relationship with U.S. President Barack Obama. The White House is considering ways of undercutting the upcoming visit. Several members of Congress have said they will boycott Netanyahu's address. Netanyahu has warned a bad deal with Iran will allow it to build nuclear weapons that it could use to threaten Israel.

On Sunday, California Attorney General Xavier Becerra appeared on ABC's "This Week" and said he planned to file a lawsuit challenging President Trump's declaration of a national emergency on the U.S.-Mexico border. When asked if and when a lawsuit would happen, Becerra said, "Definitely, and imminently." He added, "We are prepared. We knew something like this might happen, and with our sister state partners, we are ready to go." Becerra specified to ABC News after his interview that New Mexico, Oregon, Hawaii and Minnesota will join California in the lawsuit.

Kellyanne Conway on Wednesday became the first female to run a Republican general election presidential campaign. On ABC's Good Morning America, reporter Tom Llamas explained that overnight, Donald Trump promoted pollster Kellyanne Conway to campaign manager. On NBC's Today, Savannah Guthrie said, "with less than three months until election day, Donald Trump's campaign undergoing a major staff shake-up this morning." Hallie Jackson said, "Kellyanne Conway, who's already been a senior adviser, will now become campaign manager."

President Obama plans to return 5 percent of his salary to the Treasury in solidarity with federal workers affected by the sequester, an administration official said Wednesday. The voluntary move would be retroactive to March 1 and apply through the rest of the fiscal year, which ends in September. The White House came up with the 5 percent figure to approximate the level of spending cuts to nondefense federal agencies that took effect that day. "The president has decided that to share in the sacrifice being made by public servants across the federal government that are affected by the sequester, he will contribute a portion of his salary back to the Treasury," the official said.

China's State Administration for Industry and Commerce, under the control of the state administration, said Friday that China assesses all applications for trademarks equally, including those submitted by President Donald Trump. The agency's chief, Zhang Mao, said the process by which Trump was granted preliminary approval for 38 trademarks "strictly conforms" to regulations. Critics said foreign governments might gain leverage from Trump's global portfolio of brands. Democrats in Congress criticized Trump after The Associated Press reported Wednesday that the potentially valuable trademarks had been granted, raising questions of conflict of interest. Zhang, whose administration oversees the country's trademark office, said all domestic and foreign trademark applications are evaluated uniformly and the system is transparent. The recent provisional approval of Trump's trademarks came at a pace that some experts view as unusually quick.

Venezuelan lawmakers stripped opposition leader Juan Guaido of his immunity from prosecution on Tuesday. The move by the government-backed National Constituent Assembly paves the way for Guaido's prosecution and possibly his arrest. It is unclear whether Maduro will actively threaten Guaido, who has embarked on an international campaign to topple the president's socialist administration. Up until now, Maduro has avoided putting the 35-year-old lawmaker in jail. The United States and roughly 50 other nations have recognized Guaido as Venezuela's legitimate leader. In January, Guaido declared himself Venezuela's interim president and vowed to overthrow Maduro. Maduro blames Washington for trying to install a puppet government to seize Venezuela's vast oil reserves.

Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, rested his case during the penalty phase on Tuesday without calling any witnesses or testifying. Jurors are deciding whether to sentence him to death. Closing arguments are set for Wednesday. Hasan was convicted last week for the November 2009 shooting, which also wounded more than 30 people at the Texas military base. Hasan did not testify or call witnesses during his trial. He questioned only three of prosecutors' nearly 90 witnesses. Through media leaks and statements to the judge, Hasan said he justified the attack as a way to protect Islamic leaders from U.S. forces in Afghanistan and Iraq.

China said any change in U.S. policy favoring formal recognition of Taiwan will "seriously" damage peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and undermine relations between Beijing and Washington. The comments from the spokesman for the Cabinet's Taiwan Affairs Office on Wednesday follow President-elect Donald Trump's remarks over the weekend that he did not feel "bound by a one-China policy" unless the U.S. could gain benefits from China in trade and other areas. Under the one-China policy, the U.S. recognizes Beijing as China's government and maintains only unofficial relations with Taiwan, which broke from the Chinese mainland in 1949. Spokesman An Fengshan said breaching the one-China principle "will seriously affect peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait."

A top Syrian Kurdish official told The Associated Press Wednesday that the U.S. decision to arm Kurdish fighters with heavier weapons will help legitimize the force, which is denounced as a terrorist organization by Turkey. The Trump administration announced Tuesday it will arm the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces "as necessary" to recapture the Islamic State stronghold of Raqqa. NATO ally Turkey opposes the alliance because it regards the Kurds as an extension of the insurgency in its southeast. Ilham Ahmed, a top official in the Syrian Democratic Forces' political office, told The Associated Press the decision means the SDF is the force designated to recapture Raqqa. She said the decision is likely to be met with "aggression" from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is to visit Washington next week.

President Trump spoke to reporters after a conversation with North Korean official Kim Yong Chol on Friday. He announced that his June 12th meeting with Kim Jong-un in Singapore will take place. Trump said, "We'll be meeting on June 12th in Singapore. It went very well. It's really a get to know you kind of a situation. Mike has spent two days doing this. We've gotten to know their people very well. … And I think it'll be a process. It's not — I never said it goes in one meeting. I think it's going to be a process, but the relationships are building and that's a very positive thing."

Lawmakers on Wednesday passed bills closing most of a $3.2 billion state budget deficit, scaling back pension benefits for new government employees, and overhauling the public authority system. Financial watchdogs said lawmakers made many concessions that did little to address fundamental problems with state government. Gov. David A. Paterson was not among the participants. The Senate voted against the measures on a day when legalizing same-sex marriage, which was considered a signature issue of Paterson's, defeated in the Senate. The Senate has often struggled to vote on any subject.

Standard & Poor's placed Harley Davidson's debt on a credit watch due to cost increases from a U.S. trade dispute with the European Union. The ratings agency said the Milwaukee company's A-minus debt has negative implications because of tariffs imposed by the EU in retaliation for U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum. S&P said the tariffs could lead to profit margin deterioration and increased risks when combined with falling retail sales and shipments. This week Harley said it would move production of motorcycles bound for Europe overseas, blaming EU tariffs that it said would add $2,200 to the cost of an average bike. S&P said it will resolve the credit watch after Harley's second-quarter earnings. Messages were left Wednesday seeking comment from the company.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Monday threatened to "totally destroy and obliterate" the Turkish economy if Turkey took any action he considered off-limits following his decision to withdraw American forces from northeastern Syria. The withdrawal was announced by the White House late Sunday. A bipartisan group of lawmakers condemned the withdrawal, saying it could open the way for a Turkish strike on Kurdish-led forces long allied with Washington. Trump tweeted: "As I have stated strongly before, and just to reiterate, if Turkey does anything that I, in my great and unmatched wisdom, consider to be off limits, I will totally destroy and obliterate the Economy of Turkey (I've done before!)"

President Barack Obama told ABC in an interview that he had already decided to come out for gay marriage before Vice President Joe Biden publicly endorsed it. Obama said he was not worried about being upstaged by his vice president on the social issue. At one point, he said, "Would I have preferred to have done this my own way? .... Sure." He added, "All's well that ends well." He told ABC's Robin Roberts that he had already made a decision to take this position before Biden made his comments in response to a question asked on a nationally broadcast interview Sunday. Education Secretary Arne Duncan endorsed gay marriage on Monday, two days before Obama's statement. Obama said he did not revise his position to achieve any political advantage.

On Wednesday, President Obama fielded questions on deficit reduction negotiations and other topics at the White House. He suggested that Republicans might be procrastinators. He remarked, "Malia and Sasha generally finish their homework a day ahead of time. Malia's 13, Sasha's 10. It is impressive. They don't wait until the night before. They're not pulling all nighters. They're 13 and 10. You know, congress can do the same thing. If you know you've got to do something, just do it." Malia Obama turns 12 on Monday, July 4.

On Friday's broadcast of MSNBC's "MTP Daily," Michael Cohen legal adviser Lanny Davis did not confirm or deny BuzzFeed's reporting that President Trump ordered Cohen to lie to Congress. Davis stated that Cohen "had nothing to do with the writing of the story." Davis said, "Mr. Cohen and myself neither deny nor confirm. We're just not commenting on the story, and I'm adding today, another comment. He had nothing to do with the writing of the story. He didn't initiate the story. It was done by independent reporting. So, the story stands on its own."

White House senior advisor Dan Pfeiffer criticized House Republicans on Tuesday for embracing an immigration plan that would grant legal status for undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children but would not do the same for their parents. Pfeiffer tweeted a link to a La Opinion editorial critical of how the GOP is handling immigration reform. Brendan Buck, a spokesman for House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio), criticized Pfeiffer over the comment, saying it was "counter-productive" to immigration reform. The exchange occurred as the House Judiciary Committee prepares to convene a hearing on what to do about undocumented immigrants who were brought to the U.S. as children.

The Justice Department announced that 6,000 federal prisoners will be released over a four-day period beginning Oct. 30. The release follows a decision last year by the United States Sentencing Commission to reduce sentencing guidelines for many nonviolent drug crimes. The release is being called one of the largest discharges of inmates from federal prisons in American history. More than 2.3 million people are behind bars in America. More than 10,000 of them are released from state and federal prisons every week, and more than 650,000 are released every year.

Presidential candidate Donald Trump said in an interview broadcast Monday on ITV's Good Morning Britain that he may have a poor relationship with British Prime Minister David Cameron. Trump criticized Cameron's criticism of Trump's call for all Muslims to be temporarily banned from entering the United States. Trump also described London's new mayor, Sadiq Khan, as rude for calling him ignorant. Cameron has not retracted comments describing Trump's proposed Muslim ban as "divisive, stupid and wrong." Asked about Cameron's view, Trump said: "It looks like we are not going to have a very good relationship. Who knows, I hope to have a good relationship with him but he's not willing to address the problem either." Trump said he is "not stupid" and denied he was divisive.

On Sunday marked the 39th anniversary of Roe v. Wade, the Supreme Court decision that legalized abortion. On Monday, anti-Roe demonstrators are holding a "March for Life" in Washington. While Roe continues to protect a woman's right to terminate a pregnancy, a wave of state abortion restrictions last year reshaped the access and availability of abortion. These graphs and maps look back at how abortion rights, as well as abortion rates, have changed since the 1973 landmark decision. On Sunday, I interviewed Nancy Keenan, president of NARAL, which opposes restrictions on a woman's right to abort, and Charmaine Yoest, president of Americans United for Life, which opposes abortion rights.

On Wednesday, the House voted to extend the Bush tax cuts for all income levels. The House rejected a bill sponsored by Democrats that would deny the tax cuts to incomes above $250,000. Nineteen Democrats joined all but one Republican to extend the Bush tax cuts, which passed 256-171. The Senate bill, which would only extend the tax cuts to income below $200,000 for individuals or $250,000 for families, was defeated in the House, 170-257. President Barack Obama would veto the House bill. Details about whether to extend the Bush tax cuts will occur during the lame duck session of Congress. Democrats have publicly threatened to take the country over the fiscal cliff by allowing the tax cuts to expire.

President Barack Obama is taking a "year of action" tour to Minnesota, heading to St. Paul on Wednesday to announce a new competition encouraging investments to create jobs and restore infrastructure. Obama will speak at St. Paul's newly renovated Union Depot transportation hub. The White House did not provide further details of the competition but described it as part of the president's "year of action," a series of policy initiatives the White House is undertaking without the help of Congress. Last week, for example, Obama highlighted increased fuel efficiency standards for trucks at a Safeway distribution center in Maryland, highlighting steps the grocery store chain has taken to use less fuel in its fleet of trucks.

Jeffrey Earl Thompson, identified Monday in federal court as "Uncle Earl," was identified as the man who funneled hundreds of thousands of dollars into a campaign to get Vincent C. Gray elected mayor in 2010. Thompson's kindness and fund-raising acumen delivered to goodwill causes and organizations. Thompson was allocutioned and federal prosecutors in open court said otherwise on Monday. The justice system calls for everyone to be deemed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. Evidence indicates that Mr. Gray had firsthand knowledge of the illicit scheme, which included straw donors. Several Gray campaign aides have acknowledged their roles in the "shadow campaign."

The process of health care reform concluded on Sunday night with a victory for Americans who had been victimized or neglected by the health care system. The bill was approved by the Senate in December and by the House on Sunday. It represents a national commitment to reform the worst elements of the current system. It will provide coverage to tens of millions of uninsured Americans, prevent the worst insurance company abuses, and begin to wrestle with relentlessly rising costs while slightly reducing future deficits. Amendments approved by the House and awaiting approval in the Senate would provide additional coverage and make somewhat deeper reductions in the deficit.

The White House said President Obama and Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari discussed terrorism and Pakistan's economy in a short meeting Friday. Zardari was in Washington to attend a memorial service for Richard Holbrooke, who served as Obama's special envoy to Afghanistan and Pakistan. National Security Adviser Tom Donilon said that because Zardari is on a private visit, his meeting with Obama was not as detailed on issues of military cooperation and counterterrorism as it might otherwise have been. The White House said the two leaders will have opportunities for broader discussions later this year. Obama plans to travel to Pakistan, though a date for his visit has not been set. Donilon said the two leaders also discussed Pakistan's blasphemy laws that stipulate death for those insulting Islam.

Iowa voters prepare to caucus Monday. They will not be without information about the location of their caucus sites, what time to go, or the candidates' platforms. They have been inundated for months by retail politics and a blitz of television advertising, not to mention thousands of digital ads. On the morning of the caucuses, the Clinton campaign purchased a home page takeover of the Des Moines Register. Visitors to the website of Iowa's largest newspaper will first be greeted with a nearly full-window ad featuring Mrs. Clinton with a quote from the paper's endorsement of her last week. It links to the "find your caucus" part of her campaign's website.

The South Carolina Republican Party released the final tally of delegates won in its Jan. 21 primary. Newt Gingrich won 23 of the state's 25 delegates to the nominating convention. In the past, these contests were winner-take-all, but under new rules the delegates are split with the overall winner receiving 11 delegates and then delegates awarded for winning in each of the congressional districts. Mitt Romney's two delegates came by virtue of winning the state's 1st congressional district. The party also said that turnout set a new record, with 605,710 voters casting ballots — well in excess of the prediction, and topping 2000's record of 573,101. In 2008, 445,499 people voted in the GOP's contest.

Rep. John Murtha, D-Pa., will be buried next week in the heart of the Pennsylvania district he represented for 3 1/2 decades. His family said Tuesday that the viewing for Murtha will be Sunday and Monday at Duca's Funeral Home in Westmont, just west of Johnstown. He will be buried Tuesday in Grandview Cemetery, also in Westmont. The times of the viewing and burial will be announced later. Murtha died Monday at a hospital at age 77 after complications from gallbladder surgery. Gov. Ed Rendell must now decide when to schedule a special election to replace Murtha. In 1974, Murtha became the first Vietnam War combat veteran elected to Congress and went on to win election to 18 terms.

The House Judiciary Committee announced that its next impeachment hearing will be Monday. In a statement that followed soon after House Speaker Nancy Pelosi announced that the House will draft formal articles of impeachment against Donald Trump, the committee said the hearing's purpose will be to receive presentations from counsels to the Intelligence and Judiciary Committees. Majority and Minority counsels will present evidence. No new evidence is expected to be presented, only a summation of the evidence discovered to date by impeachment investigators. The article states that the House will send articles of impeachment to the Senate in the next few weeks, regardless of the continued—and, so far, unpunished—refusal of key Trump figures in the Ukrainian extortion scandal to comply with House demands for documents and testimony.

Fiat Chrysler said this week it would move production of its Ram heavy-duty pickup trucks from Mexico to Michigan. The move would allow the company to avoid import duties that would apply if NAFTA is rolled back. The United States and Canada are the principal markets for full-size heavy-duty pickup trucks, accounting for 90 percent of Ram sales. The plant in Mexico will be repurposed for the production of commercial vehicles to be sold outside the United States, the company said in a statement.

FreedomWorks and other activists are hosting a "Get Well Soon Mr. President" prayer rally outside the gates of Walter Reed National Military Medical Center, Gate 2, on Wisconsin Avenue in Washington, DC, at 7 p.m. Saturday. Supporters of the president began gathering early Saturday morning. The president is spending several days at the center after receiving a positive test for the coronavirus. Trump is staying in the presidential suite at the medical facility and will continue to carry out his duties, according to White House staff. Doctors said Trump does not have a fever and is not suffering from breathing difficulties. A large press presence is also camped out around the center.

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton tweeted that she agrees with Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders. She welcomed him to the race for the Democrat nomination, saying, "Focus must be on helping America's middle class." Clinton then pivoted to criticizing the GOP, tweeting, "GOP would hold them back." Sanders responded that "getting the big money out of politics" from Clinton qualifies as something of an ouch. He wrote: "Thanks @HillaryClinton. Looking forward to debating the big issues: income inequality, climate change & getting big money out of politics."

Former Texas governor Rick Perry announced he is dropping out of the race for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination. Perry served as governor of Texas from 2000 to 2014. He was the first Republican candidate in the field to exit the race. His campaign faced financial difficulties after Perry did not poll high enough to participate in the first presidential debate. The article's author, identified as ML, wrote a poll on D-Kos.

The White House says President Donald Trump will meet with Guatemalan President Jimmy Morales on Monday to discuss immigration and security issues. Guatemalans fleeing gang violence and poverty have helped fuel the surge of migrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. The White House says the leaders will discuss how Guatemala can build a stronger economic relationship with its Central American partners. Trump had said recently Guatemala would be signing an agreement that requires asylum seekers to apply for refuge in the first "safe" country they arrive in. Many in Guatemala oppose such a deal. A spokesman for Morales says the visit is not for the purpose of signing a "safe third country" deal. Trump will also welcome Prime Minister Mark Rutte of the Netherlands to the White House on Thursday.

The Democratic presidential campaigns of Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders have reached an agreement in principle to hold another presidential debate next week in New Hampshire and three more later this spring. Both campaigns say a final deal has not yet been reached and the Democratic National Committee has not signed off on the agreement. The New Hampshire debate next Thursday would give Clinton and Sanders a high-profile encounter before the nation's first presidential primary. The agreement was first reported by BuzzFeed. Clinton and Sanders are in a tight race before Monday's Iowa caucuses and Clinton trails the Vermont senator in New Hampshire. Clinton has urged the DNC to add the televised forums while Sanders has been willing to appear at the proposed debate next week in exchange for three more debates later this spring.

Chris Matthews will interview President Obama on Thursday. The exchange will take place at American University and air 7 p.m. Thursday. "Hardball" producer Michael LaRosa tweeted the news on Tuesday. Obama has largely declined interviews on MSNBC. His interview on "Morning Joe" in October was the first interview on MSNBC in a long time; months earlier, he had declined an interview with Matthews. During the Syria crisis, Obama granted interviews to six news networks, including NBC News, but did not sit down with MSNBC. Network president Phil Griffin has used MSNBC to defend against allegations that the network is in line with the Democratic party.

Mitt Romney's campaign is blocking reporters from covering Republican vice presidential candidate Paul Ryan's first meeting with donors in Las Vegas on Tuesday night. The event is expected to draw casino owner and Republican mega-donor Sheldon Adelson. The campaign said the decision to block access differs from rules previously established by the campaign. Reporters usually are allowed to cover President Barack Obama's fundraisers when they are held in public venues. A Romney aide who was not authorized to speak for the record said the event is closed to the media because it is a "finance meeting" instead of a fundraiser. The aide said fewer than 40 people were expected to attend. Ryan attended two Denver-area fundraisers on Monday night where media coverage also was prohibited.

The Senate unanimously confirmed Anthony Foxx, the mayor of Charlotte, N.C., as transportation secretary on Thursday by a 100-0 vote. Foxx, 42, was approved by a 100-0 vote. He replaces outgoing secretary Ray LaHood, who campaigned against distracted driving and led the Obama administration's efforts to boost the economy by improving the nation's infrastructure and jump-starting high-speed trains. As secretary, Foxx will oversee the agencies within the department that regulate the nation's aviation, rail, transit and highway systems, as well as auto safety. The mayor won national recognition when Charlotte hosted the Democratic National Convention last year. He calls Obama a friend and was a key surrogate in North Carolina for the president during his re-election bid last fall.

Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel summoned 15 of his top Air Force, Navy and nuclear mission leaders to the Pentagon on Wednesday to examine whether cultural problems within the nuclear force make launch officers feel more compelled to cheat on proficiency tests. The officials discussed the breadth of the problems, which include low morale, cheating and serious security lapses, and how to begin solving them. The meeting was the first for Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel. Pentagon press secretary Rear Adm. John Kirby said the officials discussed the breadth of the problems, which include low morale, cheating and serious security lapses, and how to begin solving them.

House Speaker John Boehner's office released a video Thursday morning criticizing President Obama for his unwillingness to negotiate over raising the nation's debt ceiling. The ad noted that the Obama administration negotiated a solution to Syria's chemical weapons stockpile with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The ad asks, "Why is the Obama administration willing to negotiate with Putin on Syria ... But not with Congress to address Washington's spending problem?" Obama and his top aides have repeatedly stated they want Congress to pass a clean debt limit increase. The nation will hit its borrowing capacity sometime next month. House Republican leaders on Wednesday said they will demand concessions in return for increasing the borrowing authority, including a one-year delay of Obama's signature health-care law.

President Obama released a new video on Monday urging voters to support Democratic Newark Mayor Cory Booker in his New Jersey Senate campaign. The video was posted to Booker's campaign website. In the video, Obama said New Jersey voters have "an opportunity to send a message to the entire country about what kind of leadership we expect from our representatives in Congress." The federal government shutdown enters its third week and Washington remains deadlocked over raising the nation's debt limit. Obama said, "We're better than the shutdown politics we've seen in Washington." He continued, "Cory Booker has spent his entire life bringing people with different perspectives together, regardless of party, to take on tough challenges. Take if from me: Now more than ever before, that's the kind of leader we need in the Senate."

Voters in Colorado and Washington voted to legalize marijuana on Tuesday, while voters in Oregon voted against a similar initiative. In Colorado, voters approved an initiative that would make it legal for those over 21 years of age to possess one ounce of marijuana. Colorado Governor John Hickenlooper (D) said while "voters have spoken and we have to respect their will," federal law still says marijuana is an illegal drug. "This will be a complicated process, but we intend to follow through," Hickenlooper stated. "That said, federal law still says marijuana is an illegal drug so don't break out the Cheetos or gold fish too quickly." Many Colorado residents expressed concerns that this initiative would turn Colorado into a magnet state for marijuana dealers.

The U.S. military is sending a land-based missile defense system to Guam to defend against possible North Korean ballistic missile launches, according to a Department of Defense news release. The missiles, a truck-mounted launcher, and radar and target acquisition systems will be deployed in the coming weeks. The system, called the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense System, fires missiles at enemy targets in the "terminal phase" as they approach defended territory. Guam is about 2,000 miles from North Korea. Most observers say North Korea is still years away from having the technology to deliver a nuclear warhead on a missile, but it has conventional military firepower, including medium-range ballistic missiles that can carry high explosives for hundreds of miles.

President Obama's plan to put 6,000 prisoners back on U.S. streets is already beyond the planning phase. On Tuesday, the New York Times, Washington Post, and other outlets reported that 6,000 federal drug offenders would be released early — starting at the end of this month, specifically, October 30 to November 2. The prisoners' terms are being retroactively shortened as a result of softened sentencing guidelines for drug dealers. The New York Times, Washington Post, and other outlets reported that thousands of the offenders are already out of prison.

President Barack Obama said in his weekly radio and Internet address that he is taking action on his own because Congress is doing so little for working families. Obama said the economy is improving and that decisions made now can ensure things keep improving. Obama said he has been pushing policies addressing jobs, student loans and wages. He said all of the policies would help families feel more stable, but all have been blocked by Republicans. Obama said Congress left town for their August vacation with unfinished business. He said he hopes when lawmakers get back, Washington can join together in common purpose. In the Republican address, Rep. Greg Walden of Oregon said Obama is disengaged when he should be leading. He said the midterm elections are a chance to deliver accountability.

Chris Matthews will interview President Obama on Thursday. The exchange will take place at American University and air 7 p.m. Thursday. "Hardball" producer Michael LaRosa tweeted the news on Tuesday. Obama has largely declined interviews on MSNBC. His interview on "Morning Joe" in October was the first interview on MSNBC in a long time; months earlier, he had declined an interview with Matthews. During the Syria crisis, Obama granted interviews to six news networks, including NBC News, but did not sit down with MSNBC. Network president Phil Griffin has used MSNBC to defend against allegations that the network is in line with the Democratic party.

President Barack Obama signed a second short-term spending bill to keep the government running through April 8. The measure gives lawmakers more time to agree on a package of spending cuts Republicans are demanding. Obama signed the bill Friday at the White House before traveling on a five-day tour of Latin America. Administration officials met with top aides to Republican House Speaker John Boehner and Democratic Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to discuss budget cuts that would be included in a bill to fund the government through the end of the fiscal year on Sept. 30. The House passed a bill with $61 billion in spending cuts, but it does not have enough votes to clear the Senate. Obama also has threatened to veto it.

Two Tennessee National Guard members were shot during a fight at a suburban Memphis armory on Thursday, and a third was in custody, authorities reported. The suspected gunman was subdued by others at the armory, said Rita Stanback, the police chief in the northern Memphis suburb of Millington. Each of the victims was shot once, one in the leg and one in the foot, Stanback said. A U.S. military official told CNN's Barbara Starr that a Guard member shot two others during a fight. The armory is on property leased to the Guard by the U.S. Navy, which has its personnel and recruiting commands across the road. The Navy compound was on lockdown after the shooting, and the lockdown has since been lifted, the service reported via Twitter.

Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder endorsed Mitt Romney's bid for the Republican presidential nomination in an op-ed published Thursday by The Detroit News. Snyder said Romney "has what it takes to build a foundation for America's success in this global economy." Romney is competing against Rick Santorum, who is seeking the nomination. Romney's father, George, served as Michigan's governor before losing his presidential bid in 1968. Snyder, a former venture capitalist, was elected in 2010 after campaigning as an outsider with business experience. Romney and Santorum both have campaign events Thursday in Michigan.

North Korea's supreme leader Kim Jong Un visited the hydro-meteorological service and criticized its weather forecasts. Rodong Sinmun, a state-run newspaper, reported Kim's message to his meteorologists. Kim said there are many incorrect forecasts as the meteorological observation has not been put on a modern and scientific basis. He said it is necessary to fundamentally improve the work of the Hydro-meteorological Service to scientifically clarify meteorological and climatic conditions and provide accurate data for weather forecast and meteorological and climatic information required by various fields of national economy in good time.

Britain's Foreign Office is urging U.K. nationals to immediately leave the Libyan city of Benghazi in response to an imminent threat against westerners. The Foreign Office has advised against all travel to Benghazi since September. On Thursday, it said it is aware of a "specific and imminent threat" to westerners in Benghazi, eastern Libya, and urged all British nationals still there to leave immediately. It would not comment on the nature of the threat. The warning comes a day after U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton testified to U.S. lawmakers about the handling of the Sept. 11 attack on the American mission in Benghazi. The attack killed the U.S. ambassador to Libya and three other Americans.

President Barack Obama will speak at 4 p.m. from the White House before convening a meeting with his national security team on the militant threat in Syria and Iraq. The U.S. is already launching airstrikes against Islamic State group targets in Iraq and Obama is considering similar action in Syria. The president's remarks also come amid increased tensions between Russia and Ukraine. Officials in Ukraine say two Russian military columns rolled into the southeastern part of the country after missiles were fired at a border post. The U.S. and European Union have levied economic sanctions against Russia as punishment for its provocations. The penalties appear to have had little impact on Russian President Vladimir Putin's thinking.

Senate Majority Leader Patrick Leahy, a Democrat from Vermont, fell ill and was scheduled to preside over the impeachment trial of former President Donald Trump. Leahy, a senator, was admitted to the hospital on Tuesday night after being evaluated. Leahy spokesman David Carle said he looks forward to returning to work. Carle said Patrick and Marcelle deeply appreciate the well wishes they have received. Leahy was sworn in last week as president pro tempore, becoming third in the line of succession to the president. The position traditionally goes to the senior member of the majority party. The Senate revealed this week that Leahy, not Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., will preside over the impeachment trial.

The Senate is considering legislation to impose more stringent sanctions on North Korea. The bill is scheduled for a vote on Wednesday. The consideration follows Pyongyang's satellite launch a few days ago and technical advances U.S. intelligence agencies say North Korea is making in its nuclear weapons program. The bill's backers say it targets North Korea's ability to access the money needed for developing miniaturized nuclear warheads and long-range missiles. That is according to the legislation's backers. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell says North Korea's "belligerence" can't be ignored. The House overwhelmingly approved a similar measure last month. There is strong bipartisan support in the Senate for the North Korea Sanctions and Policy Enhancement Act.

Donald J. Trump ran on a campaign promise to dismantle the Affordable Care Act. He signed an executive order urging his administration to fight it as much as possible. The order, alone, will not allow President Trump to unwind the health law known as Obamacare. Mr. Trump and Republican leaders in Congress are engaged in negotiations about legislation that might substantially undo or replace the health law. Even before the inauguration, Congress took a first step toward gutting major provisions. As that process underscores, major changes to health policy will require new legislation. The Trump executive order should be seen more as a mission statement, and less as a monarchical edict that can instantly change the law.

Mitt Romney's presidential campaign released a letter from his doctor on Friday stating that he is healthy and physically fit to meet the rigorous demands of a presidency. The letter from Romney's longtime physician stated that his heart is healthy and that he takes baby aspirin and cholesterol medicine to keep it that way. It also stated that he does not smoke or drink, or have any serious illnesses. The campaign also released a health summary for his running mate, Paul Ryan, that declares his health excellent. Ryan's doctor said he exercises vigorously, does not smoke, and uses alcohol infrequently. He pays close attention to cardiac health because of a family history of heart disease. Presidential and vice presidential candidates routinely release summaries of their medical standing. The White House releases results from President Obama's annual physical.

U.S. Secretary of State Kerry is in Jordan to meet with Jordan's King Abdullah II about Mideast peace. Kerry is hoping to broker a peace plan between Israel and Palestine authorities and wants to present a framework for an agreement by the end of April. A major part of his proposal centers on security in the Jordan Valley that runs through parts of Israel and the West Bank. Jordan has been a key part of those negotiations. Kerry was to meet privately Friday afternoon with Jordan's King Abdullah II at his private residence in the seaside resort city Aqabah. Jordan Foreign Minister Nasser Judeh flew to Aquaba with Kerry from Rome. Kerry returns to Washington on Friday.

Mitt Romney will travel to Iowa next week to campaign for U.S. Senate candidate Sen. Joni Ernst (R) days before the June 3 primary. Romney will stump for Ernst in Cedar Rapids and Davenport on May 30, her campaign said. The 2012 GOP presidential nominee endorsed Ernst, a state senator, in March. Ernst is among a crowd of Republicans vying for the GOP nomination to fill the seat of retiring Sen. Tom Harkin (D). Her main competition is businessman Mark Jacobs (R). Recent polling has shown Ernst to be the frontrunner. The winner of the GOP nomination is expected to face Rep. Bruce Braley (D) in the general election. The Des Moines Register first reported the news of Romney's planned campaign appearance.

South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford has backed out of a promise to release personal financial records to the media proving he did not use state money for trips to see his mistress. The decision came a day after Sanford said in an Associated Press interview that his mistress is his soul mate. Sanford spokesman Joel Sawyer said the governor does not want to discuss personal matters in the media anymore. Sanford is providing the records to law enforcement as part of an investigation of his travel to see the Argentine woman. Sanford agreed this week to provide the AP with proof of his payment for trips to New York and Argentina to see her. His staff first said the records might be made available Tuesday, and then the governor's spokesman said Wednesday Sanford would not release them.

Rep. Chris Gibson (R-N.Y.), one of a number of Republicans who have broken with Grover Norquist in recent days, has not renewed his anti-tax pledge. His spokeswoman explained that the Congressman signed the pledge as a candidate in 2010 for the 20th Congressional District. Regarding the pledge moving forward, the spokeswoman said the congressman does not plan to re-sign it for the 19th Congressional District, which he now represents. The pledge is made out to the taxpayers of the _____ district and to the American people. Gibson represents his old district in the lame duck session.

Conservative attorney George Conway, husband of top White House aide Kellyanne Conway, tweeted late Friday: "In light of the fact that you are a pathological liar, you should not be heard to complain about inaccurate media reports." The tweet followed Trump's latest criticism of the "fake news" media. The tweet came after special counsel Robert Mueller's office cast doubt on elements of a BuzzFeed report that alleged Trump instructed his former fixer and personal lawyer Michael Cohen to lie to Congress.

President Barack Obama announced Tuesday at a Maryland middle school that new private-business commitments will help "close the technology gap" in America's schools. The money will be used to connect more students to high-speed Internet. The White House hopes the pledges will help fulfill a goal Obama set last summer to have 99 percent of students in schools wired at high speeds within five years. The president says access to the Internet will help American children compete with students from around the world. The initiative also builds on Obama's focus for 2014 on helping more Americans join and stay in the middle class amid an economic recovery in which the benefits have come more quickly for those at the top of the income scale.

President Obama addressed criticism of his response to turmoil from Eastern Europe to the Middle East on Monday. He defended his approach to foreign policy as a slow but steady pursuit of American interests while avoiding military conflict. He criticized critics he said reflexively call for the use of force. Standing next to Philippine President Benigno S. Aquino III, Obama said his critics had failed to learn the lessons of the Iraq war. On a day in which he announced new sanctions against Russia for its continued threats to Ukraine, Obama said his foreign policy was based on a workmanlike tending to American priorities that might lack the high drama of a wartime presidency but also avoided ruinous mistakes.

Rep. Renee Ellmers, R-N.C., said Friday that she has been the victim of "completely false accusations." The statement was made in an oblique reference to ongoing rumors that she had an affair with House Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif. Reports increased yesterday when McCarthy announced the end of what was thought to be his front-runner status to be the next House speaker. In a short statement, Ellmers indicated that nothing happened between the two. "As someone who has been targeted by completely false accusations and innuendo, I have been moved by the outpouring of support and prayers from my colleagues, constituents and friends," she said. "Now I will be praying for those who find it acceptable to bear false witness."

The Council on American-Islamic Relations issued a call for an apology late Friday, hours after Rose Hamid was ejected from a Trump rally at Winthrop University in Rock Hill, South Carolina. Hamid said she was standing up in protest to a Trump statement when members of the audience pointed her out by chanting "Trump, Trump, Trump." CAIR National Executive Director Nihad Awad also called on Trump to meet with American Muslim leaders to help stem what Awad described as anti-Muslim hysteria resulting from his rhetoric and that of other GOP presidential candidates.

President Barack Obama said House Republicans are trying to pass the most extreme and unworkable version of an immigration bill even though they know the bill is not going anywhere. Republicans are pushing legislation that could clear the way for eventual deportation of more than 500,000 immigrants brought here illegally as children and address the surge of immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border. Obama said Republicans know that legislation won't succeed in the Senate. He said Republicans are not trying to solve the problem. He said they are just trying check a box before leaving town for the annual August recess. Obama said he will have to act alone to address the crisis because the government is running out of money to deal with it.

Vice President Joe Biden will deliver an address at the Vatican on Friday addressing global research partnerships and how his cancer "moonshot" project may have an international impact. Biden is due to speak at an international conference on breakthroughs in regenerative medicine hosted by the Pontifical Council for Culture and the Stem for Life Foundation. The vice president's office said the address will look at global research partnerships and describe how his cancer "moonshot" project may have an international impact. Biden is also scheduled to speak at an international conference on breakthroughs in regenerative medicine hosted by the Pontifical Council for Culture and the Stem for Life Foundation.

Joy Behar, a Current TV reporter for President Barack Obama, cozied up to Obama during today's taped edition of "The View," her other day job, posted on Twitter defending Obama against what she described as the indefensible. While the Middle East burns and Iran threatens to wipe out Israel, described as Israel's closest ally in that region, Obama did not speak with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Instead, Obama discussed important issues including his wife's nonexistent political career and being "eye candy" with the "View" crew.

The State Department announced Thursday that Laurence Pope, an Arabic-speaking 31-year foreign service officer who retired in 2000, has arrived in Tripoli to assume temporary control of the embassy in Tripoli. Pope will serve as charge d'affaires pending confirmation of the nomination of a successor to Ambassador Chris Stevens, who died in the Sept. 11 attack. Pope, a former ambassador to Chad and counter-terrorism director, would continue the work Stevens had been doing. The department said his appointment underscored a U.S. commitment to work with Libya as it transitions to democracy after decades of authoritarian rule.

President Obama praised the Arab League for suspending Syria's membership, stating the group's leadership in seeking to end attacks on peaceful protesters. Obama said the vote shows the increasing diplomatic isolation of President Bashar Assad's government, which he said engages in "callous violence." In a statement Saturday, Obama said the Assad regime has failed to keep its commitments. The president said the Arab League has shown leadership in its effort to end the 8-month-old crisis and hold the Syrian government accountable. The league voted Saturday to suspend Syria and warned that it could face sanctions if it does not end its crackdown on anti-government demonstrators. The vote was a symbolic blow to a country that prides itself on its commitment to Arab nationalism.

President Obama and outgoing Secretary of State Hillary Clinton will speak to "60 Minutes" together in their first joint interview, the White House announced Friday. Communications director Dan Pfeiffer said the interview will air Sunday. "60 Minutes" noted that it will be Obama's first interview with anyone besides Michelle Obama. Politico's Mike Allen reported that Steve Kroft, who has talked to Obama many times on "60 Minutes," will conduct the interview. The article noted that it is hard to imagine the two sitting down for a chat during the 2008 presidential campaign. Clinton recently confessed her distaste for Sunday morning shows.

Hillary Rodham Clinton said Wednesday during the Clinton Global Initiative meetings that she plans to lead an effort to evaluate the progress women have made around the globe in becoming full and equal participants in society. The former secretary of state said the work will be done by 2015, which is the 20th anniversary of her 1995 speech at a United Nations women's conference in Beijing. As first lady, Clinton declared that "women's rights are human rights." She said that despite progress, women are a "long way from the goal of full and equal participation." Clinton is a potential Democratic presidential candidate in 2016. She said the evaluation through the Clinton Foundation will assess progress by women and chart a path forward for full participation in society.

President Barack Obama is inviting lawmakers and intelligence officials to the White House to discuss National Security Agency programs. The White House says Obama will meet Wednesday with leaders from the U.S. intelligence community and with members of an oversight panel focusing on privacy and civil liberties. Obama will meet with key lawmakers Thursday. That day privacy groups will be at the White House to meet separately with administration officials. A months-long intelligence review prompted by disclosures by former NSA contractor Edward Snowden is nearing a conclusion. A review panel appointed by Obama has suggested dozens of changes. Obama is expected to announce this month which of the recommendations he will implement.

Last week's chemical spill into West Virginia's Elk River cut off water to more than 300,000 people. West Virginia has a history of regulating coal and chemical companies that form the heart of its economy. Angela Rosser, executive director of the West Virginia Rivers Coalition, said: "We can't just point a single finger at this company. We need to look at our entire system and give some serious thought to making some serious reform and valuing our natural resources over industry interests." Rosser said lawmakers have not explained why the storage facility was allowed to sit on the river and so close to a water treatment plant that is the largest in the state.

Former Florida Republican governor turned Democrat Charlie Crist filed paperwork to run for his former job with his new party, the state Division of Elections, according to the filing on its website Friday. Crist could not be immediately reached for comment but has an announcement scheduled for Monday morning in St. Petersburg. Crist has been preparing for an announcement for months, talking to Democratic groups and campaigning with Democratic candidates, including President Obama last year. He has established a website and his speeches recently criticized Republican Gov. Rick Scott. Scott's political committee has purchased anti-Crist ads to begin airing the day of the announcement. The race is expected to be one of the most expensive governor's races in the county next year.

Rocket sections are apparently being trucked into North Korea's northwest launch site. Some analysts are asking whether the preparations are a calculated bluff meant to jangle the Obama administration and influence South Korean voters ahead of presidential elections. Questions have been raised about whether North Korean scientists have corrected whatever caused the launch of its last rocket shortly after liftoff in April, and whether Pyongyang is willing to risk another failure along with U.N. condemnation and more sanctions. Before its last two launches, North Korea notified international organizations of its plans to send a satellite into orbit aboard a rocket. South Korea and analysts say North Korea has yet to provide such notification, something that usually happens weeks in advance.

A Public Policy Polling survey released Monday found that 55 percent of very conservative respondents and 41 percent of Republicans said the Benghazi attacks are "the biggest political scandal in American history." Twenty-three percent of Americans agreed with this assessment. Twenty-six percent of very liberal respondents agreed. Twenty-five percent of Democrats agreed. Among the very liberal respondents, 19 percent agreed. Among Democrats, 20 percent agreed.

Military jurors began deliberating Thursday in the case of Maj. Nidal Hasan, the soldier accused of killing 13 people during the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood. The case was given to the jury. Hasan faces numerous counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder for the attack on the Texas military base. If convicted, Hasan could face the death penalty. The jury consists of 13 members, all military officers. They heard testimony from nearly 90 witnesses, many of whom identified Hasan as the gunman who opened fire inside the Fort Hood building in November 2009. Hasan is acting as his own attorney but has put up little defense. He did not give a closing argument earlier Thursday.

President Trump spoke to reporters on Wednesday. He said he does not mind the public seeing Special Counsel Robert Mueller's report and stated, "Let people see it." When asked whether the public has the right to see the report, Trump responded, "I don't mind. I mean, frankly, I told the House, if you want, let them see it." He added, "[L]et it come out. Let people see it. That's up to the attorney general. We have a very good attorney general." Trump also stated, "I want to see the report."

In a new campaign ad, Hillary Clinton speaks directly to the camera as a soft piano soundtrack plays in the background. She says, "It's not just my name and my opponent's name on the ballot, it's about the kind of country we want for our children and our grandchildren. Is America dark and divisive or hopeful and inclusive?" Clinton acknowledges that the country has been through tough economic times but says she would work to make life better for the American people. "We won't always get it right but you can count on this," she said. "I've never quit and I never will."

North Korea on Thursday requested the withdrawal of U.N. sanctions against it and the end of joint U.S.-South Korean military exercises as conditions for any talks with Seoul and Washington. The North's National Defense Commission said in a statement carried by state-run media that the United States and South Korea "should immediately stop all their provocative acts against the DPRK and apologize for all of them," using the shortened version of North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. The United States has said recently that for it to enter talks, North Korea would have to show a serious commitment to moving away from its nuclear program, something the regime of Kim Jong Un insists it will not do.

Jackie Speier, a California Democrat, said on CNN that she trusts the tweets the president puts out when he is unsupervised. Speier said she thinks what has been seen over and over again is his intention to obstruct justice. Trump tweeted several times over the weekend about the special counsel's case into collusion claims between his campaign and Russia. Many observers interpreted the tweets as a sign that Trump was pushing to fire special counsel Robert Mueller. Speier tweeted her response over the weekend, saying that Trump was leading the country toward a "constitutional crisis." The White House has repeatedly said the president has no intention of firing Mueller.

George Mason University is changing its plan to rename its law school the Antonin Scalia School of Law to avoid an acronym. The university said last week that it planned to name the law school after the late conservative Supreme Court justice. The new name was suggested by an anonymous donor who is giving the school $20 million. The acronym was mocked on social media. On Tuesday, the proposed name was changed to the Antonin Scalia Law School. One group of state legislators wants to scrap the idea entirely. Eleven Democratic lawmakers sent a letter Tuesday to the State Council of Higher Education for Virginia, asking it to reject the renaming plan. The university has said it needs approval from the council for the new name.

China defended its handling of 38 trademarks it recently approved provisionally for President Donald Trump, saying it followed the law in processing the applications at a pace some experts view as unusually quick. Trump secured one recently after a 10-year fight that turned his way only after he declared his candidacy for the presidency. He had applied less than a year ago for the 38 trademarks that were granted preliminary approval Feb. 27 and March 6. China's foreign ministry spokesman Geng Shuang said Thursday in a regular briefing with reporters that Chinese authorities handle all trademark applications "in accordance with the law and regulation." He declined to comment on speculation about political influence on Trump's trademark approvals.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump was endorsed by several players from the University of Iowa Hawkeye football team at a rally in Iowa City, Iowa on Tuesday night. Trump said, "The next Tom Brady…and I know Tom and He's a great guy." He pointed at the University of Iowa quarterback and brought members of the Iowa football team onstage. "What a team!" Trump announced to the crowd. "They endorsed Trump," he said. "I like them." The crowd chanted, "Let's go Hawks!" The Hawkeyes played in the Rosebowl Game, where there was anti-Trump skywriting over the 2016 Rose Parade.

Caroline Kennedy, the daughter of Hillary Rodham Clinton, will seek the United States Senate seat in New York being vacated by Hillary Rodham Clinton. Ms. Kennedy ended weeks of silence with a series of phone calls to the state's leading political figures, including Gov. David A. Paterson, in which she emphatically and enthusiastically declared herself interested in the seat, according to several people who received the calls. "She told me she was interested in the position," Mr. Paterson said at a news conference outside Albany on Monday. He added, "She'd like at some point to sit down and tell me what she thinks her qualifications are."
