Sylvia Mathews Burwell's confirmation hearing Thursday to replace Health and Human Services Secretary Kathleen Sebelius was described as a referendum on the Affordable Care Act. Twitter users noted the 7-foot-tall document at the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions hearing. Republicans have used the tower to examine thousands of pages of regulations tied to the Affordable Care Act. Burwell, the White House's budget chief, received wide support during the confirmation process for her current job. She faces confirmation in the Senate with the health care overhaul as the backdrop.

President Barack Obama said in a statement that he is willing to work with Democrats and Republicans to improve his health care law but warned lawmakers not to "go backward" and repeal the measure. In a statement, Obama said Americans deserve the freedom and security of knowing insurance companies can not deny, cap or drop their coverage when they need it most. The House on Wednesday is expected to vote on repealing the health care overhaul. Democrats still have a majority in the Senate and have promised to block the effort. White House spokesman Robert Gibbs on Tuesday dismissed the vote, saying it is not "a serious legislative effort." Gibbs said Obama would likely veto the measure if it reached the White House, but he does not think it is going anywhere.

Army Private Bradley Manning, charged in the biggest leak of classified material in U.S. history, is scheduled to testify Thursday before a military judge. The judge is considering whether to accept Manning's offer to plead guilty to some charges. Manning's only public explanation for giving classified material to WikiLeaks can be found in logs of an online chat with a confidant-turned-government informant. In those chats, Manning wrote that he engineered the leak because "information should be free" and he wanted "people to see the truth." Even if a judge accepts his guilty plea, prosecutors can still pursue more serious charges against Manning. One charge is aiding the enemy, which carries a potential life sentence.

Rep. John Murtha (D-PA) died on Monday. His death was reported by various news outlets as resulting from complications following gallbladder surgery. The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported that the complications involved a mistake by Murtha's surgeons. Murtha was first hospitalized with gallbladder problems in December. He had surgery Jan. 28 at the National Naval Hospital in Bethesda, Md. He went home, but was hospitalized two days later when complications developed. According to a source close to Murtha, confirming a Politico report, doctors inadvertently cut Murtha's intestine during laparoscopic surgery, causing an infection.

White House assistant chef Sam Kass, who serves as a food policy advisor, revealed Tuesday during an interview with food reporters that he will lose several days of work as part of the sequester. Kass, who worked for the Obamas in Chicago as a private chef, joined the White House staff under Executive Chef Cristeta Comerford in 2009. He serves as a point person on healthy eating iniatives, often accompanying the first lady in public events advocating against childhood obesity. Kass said that work will not be affected.

President Barack Obama is commemorating the 60th anniversary of the Supreme Court's Brown vs. Board of Education school desegregation decision by meeting with families of the plaintiffs in the case as well as the lead attorneys and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. Obama will host the group, including lawyers Jack Greenberg and William Coleman, in the White House East Room Friday afternoon. Greenberg argued the case; Coleman was a leading legal strategist in the case. First lady Michelle Obama was observing the anniversary by traveling Friday to Topeka, Kan., site of the lawsuit that initiated the case. The first lady was to meet with high school students in a college preparatory program and later was speaking at a pre-graduation event for seniors in the Topeka Public School District.

A man wielding two handguns was shot and killed at a Walmart in Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, authorities said. Pennsylvania State Police responded to the store late Saturday night and found a man with two handguns at the scene. Stroud Area Regional Police responded. Officers told the man to drop his gun, but he refused and pointed his weapon at police, authorities said. Officers shot the man in the upper chest area. He was pronounced dead at a local hospital. No officers or anyone else at the Walmart was injured, state police said. Police have not identified the gunman, pending notification of his relatives. The Monroe County District Attorney's Office and Pennsylvania State Police are investigating the officer-involved shooting, state police said.

President Obama opened a previously scheduled speech in Cuba by addressing Tuesday's terrorist attacks in Brussels. He said the thoughts and prayers of the American people are with the people of Belgium and that the United States stands in solidarity with them in condemning the attacks against innocent people. He said the United States will do whatever is necessary to support Belgium in bringing to justice those responsible, and that this is yet another reminder that the world must unite. He said the United States must be together, regardless of nationality or race or faith, in fighting against terrorism, and that the United States can and will defeat those who threaten the safety and security of people all around the world. Obama has spoken with the prime minister of Belgium.

South Carolina removed the Confederate flag from the statehouse grounds on Friday. State officials removed the flag since the dawn of the civil rights movement. The accused shooter was a Confederate flag enthusiast. Vanderbilt University professor Carol Swain said the flag's removal would not eliminate racism, poverty, or lack of access to resources in the South. Swain said the flag's removal might make things worse given the strong feelings of some whites and blacks over Confederate imagery. She also said the lowering would not be a first step in racial reconciliation.

North Korea tested a new type of high-thrust engine to propel its rockets, according to a report by the Korean Central News Agency. Leader Kim Jong Un attended the test at the Sohae launch site, according to the report. The report added the test was intended to confirm the engine's thrust power and gauge the reliability of its control system and structural safety. The report Sunday said the test was a success. It provided little detail but indicated the engine is to be used for North Korea's space and satellite-launching program. North Korea is banned by the United Nations from conducting long-range missile tests. It claims its satellite program is for peaceful use, a claim many in the U.S. and elsewhere believe is questionable.

Blackwater Worldwide founder Erik Prince is considering a Republican primary challenge to Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, a senior member of the Senate Republican leadership team. A person familiar with Prince's thinking says he was in Wyoming this weekend to discuss a possible Senate campaign with family members. Prince has been encouraged to run by Steve Bannon, a former top strategist to President Donald Trump, according to the person who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe private deliberations. Prince's potential candidacy was first reported by The New York Times. Prince is also founder of Frontier Resource Group, a private equity firm, and is brother of Education Secretary Betsy DeVos. Security contractor Blackwater came under scrutiny after its guards were involved in the shooting deaths of 14 civilians in Baghdad in 2007.

President Barack Obama's national security adviser, James Jones, said Israel will still have a "robust" delegation at a nuclear security summit in Washington next week. Netanyahu had said he would attend the conference to underline the danger of terrorists acquiring nuclear weapons. Officials in Netanyahu's office said Netanyahu reversed his decision because some nations planned to use the conference to target Israel over its concealed nuclear weapons program. Speaking to reporters traveling with Obama, Jones said Israel did not want to be a catalyst for changing the theme of the summit.

Massachusetts Attorney General Maura Healey and New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman launched a joint investigation Saturday into Cambridge Analytica, a British data analysis firm, after reports that the firm captured information from 50 million Facebook users without their consent. Cambridge Analytica is tied to President Donald Trump's 2016 campaign. Healey said residents in her state "deserve answers immediately," from Facebook and Cambridge Analytica about what data was shared and how it was allowed to happen. Her office said it has been in touch with Facebook about the investigation.

The White House says President Barack Obama will travel to Tennessee next week to promote his proposals for boosting U.S. manufacturing and high-wage jobs. Obama will fly on Tuesday to Chattanooga, where he will visit an Amazon fulfillment center, which packs and ships products to online purchasers. The White House says Obama will discuss ideas he has presented previously to promote American competitiveness and job growth, and also some new ideas. It is the first in a series of speeches Obama will give on specific policy areas. The speeches build on Obama's visits this week to Illinois, Missouri and Florida, where he is speaking broadly about the state of the economy and the need to build a stronger middle class ahead of fiscal fights in Congress this fall.

Six New Jersey residents filed a federal lawsuit in federal court Thursday against Gov. Chris Christie, the state of New Jersey, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, and others over traffic jams in September. The suit appears to be the first civil claim over traffic jams that appear to have been caused as political punishment for the Fort Lee mayor. The plaintiffs want it certified as a class action. Lawyer Rosemarie Arnold said she filed it after learning this week that lane closures on an approach to the George Washington Bridge were "deliberate actions." She said that her clients were late for work and that one suffered a panic attack. Christie has denied involvement. His spokesman did not respond to an email seeking comment.

A man tested for Ebola at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York does not have the disease, the hospital said Wednesday afternoon. The man, who was kept in isolation since he was admitted Monday with a high fever and gastrointestinal symptoms, is in stable condition and is improving, the hospital said in a statement. The death toll from West Africa's Ebola outbreak has risen to 932 after 45 patients died from Aug 2 to Aug 4, the World Health Organization said in a statement Wednesday. The number of suspected, probable or confirmed cases rose by 108 over the same period to a total of 1,711. Most of the newly reported deaths were in Liberia while the number of cases in Nigeria climbed from 4 to 9, including one previous death.

The Romney campaign paid for a 54-second spot that opens with the president at a White House press conference. The ad shows eight people discussing staff cuts, job loss, personal bankruptcy, a two-year job hunt, no health care and a slashed pension, and other concerns. The ad closes with the statement, "No, Mr. President, we are not doing fine." Romney is using Obama's remark to portray the president as out of touch with the average American, a criticism the president's campaign has tried against Romney. The economy, with its 8.2 percent unemployment rate, is the biggest issue for voters and a weak spot for Obama.

President Barack Obama held a news conference on Wednesday about his 12-year-old daughter Malia. He said she "generally finish their homework a day ahead of time," unlike lawmakers on the hill. Politico reported that Obama had expressed fears about his daughter Malia becoming a teenager next month. On Wednesday, Obama thought she had already turned 13. At a press conference at the White House, Obama suggested that his daughters, who "generally finish their homework a day ahead of time," could serve as role models for members of Congress.

On this weekend's broadcast of "Fox News Sunday," former U.S. Rep. Mark Sanford said he will challenge President Donald Trump in the 2020 Republican primary. Sanford said, "I'm here to tell you now that I am going to get in." Wallace said, "You're going to run for president against Donald Trump in the Republican race." Sanford said, "I am." Wallace asked, "Why?" Sanford answered, "We need to have a conversation on what it means to be a Republican," and said the GOP has lost its way on the debt.

A Republican Party race for an open North Carolina congressional seat went to Mark Walker. GOP voters in the district, which runs along the Virginia border from Mount Airy to north of Raleigh, selected Baptist minister Walker of Greensboro over Phil Berger Jr. of Eden. Berger is the Rockingham County district attorney and son of state Senate leader Phil Berger. Walker won 56 percent of the vote in unofficial returns and now advances to face Democrat and retired University of North Carolina system administrator Laura Fjeld in November. The winner will replace 30-year GOP incumbent Howard Coble in the heavily Republican 6th Congressional District. Tuesday's Republican primary runoff featured Walker and Berger trading accusations of cronyism, lying, and incompetence.

Mitt Romney won the Maine Republican presidential caucuses with a narrow victory, according to an analysis by The Associated Press. The former Massachusetts governor won at least eight delegates, with six delegates left to be allocated. Texas Rep. Ron Paul won at least seven. Rick Santorum and Newt Gingrich were not included. Maine's local caucuses were the first step of a multi-step process to determine the state's delegates to the national convention. Romney would win the most delegates if the candidates maintain the same level of support throughout the process. Romney leads the overall race for delegates, with 120. Santorum has 72, Gingrich has 32 and Paul has 16. It takes 1,144 delegates to win the nomination.

A new attorney for President Donald Trump's former personal lawyer Michael Cohen, Guy Petrillo, requested access to files seized by the FBI from Cohen's home and office in April raids. Petrillo's request was revealed in a letter to a New York judge Tuesday by Cohen's other lawyers, who have already seen the files. Cohen had worked for the Trump Organization and Trump before he became ensnarled in a criminal probe. Prosecutors said after the raids that they were looking into his business dealings. Lawyers who represented Cohen in his effort to designate some raid items as protected by attorney-client privilege asked a judge for permission to turn over raid materials to Petrillo. The lawyers said prosecutors did not object.

On Monday, White House press secretary Sean Spicer appeared on "Fox & Friends." Spicer said U.S. District Court Judge James Robart issued a Friday ruling blocking President Donald Trump's executive order restricting travel from seven Muslim-majority countries. Spicer said the law is clear that the president has broad powers to keep the country safe and to limit access to people who could come into this country and do harm. Spicer said the president utilized that power in a very legal, constitutional manner to ensure that the country is safe, its people are safe, the country is safe, and institutions are safe. Spicer said it was somewhat sad to see a judge go rogue like this.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont, announced his candidacy for the Democratic primary for president. Sanders told the Associated Press that while the average person is working longer hours for lower wages, income and wealth inequality is reaching obscene levels. He is the second prominent Democrat to officially announce a campaign, following former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Sanders said he is not running to push Clinton to the left or raise awareness for liberal issues. National primary polls show him averaging 6 percent; Clinton is at 61 percent. Sanders said: "This is a rigged economy, which works for the rich and the powerful, and is not working for ordinary Americans. ... You know, this country just does not belong to a handful of billionaires."

Alabama Sen. Jeff Sessions, the senior Republican on the Senate Judiciary Committee, said he will vote against Supreme Court nominee Sonia Sotomayor. Sessions said he does not think Sotomayor has the convictions to resist judicial activism once she becomes a justice. His decision comes the day before the Judiciary panel is scheduled to vote on President Barack Obama's first high court nominee. Sotomayor is virtually certain to be confirmed by a vote of the full Senate by the end of next week, becoming the first Hispanic justice. Most conservative Republicans are lining up against Sotomayor, but a handful of GOP senators are aligning with majority Democrats to back her. Sessions announced his decision in an opinion piece in USA Today.

President Obama asked the Senate on Wednesday to confirm two Democrats whose recess appointments to the National Labor Relations Board were ruled unconstitutional by a federal appeals court last month. The two, Sharon Block, a former labor counsel to Senator Edward M. Kennedy, and Richard Griffin, former general counsel for the International Union of Operating Engineers, have been serving on the board since January 2012. The president appointed them during a Senate recess after Republicans blocked their confirmations. After a three-judge appeals panel decided three weeks ago that their recess appointments were invalid, 40 Senate Republicans issued a letter asking Block and Griffin to step down immediately from the labor board.

USA Today reported that a Sergeant First Class in charge of sexual assault prevention at Ft. Hood is being investigated for sexual assault and for running a prostitution ring. The solider, whose name is not being released, oversaw sexual assault prevention for about 800 soldiers. He has not been charged. Authorities said the investigation revolves around charges of "abusive sexual contact, pandering, assault and maltreatment of subordinates." This includes "forcing a subordinate into prostitution and sexually assaulting two others." Pentagon officials speaking anonymously said the soldier is also under investigation for running a prostitution ring. Secretary of Defense Chuck Hagel expressed frustration, anger, and disappointment over these allegations and the breakdown in discipline and standards they imply.

The official website of the White House is being used by Barack Obama to criticize Republican members of Congress for the government shutdown. A pop-up window titled "Government Shutdown" informs the viewer: "Because Congress did not fulfill its responsibility to pass a budget, much of the federal government will shut down." Underneath the window, the caption reads, "Learn more." Upon clicking that window, a window states: "Due to Congress's failure to pass legislation to fund the government, the information on this web site may not be up to date. Some submissions may not be processed, and we may not be able to respond to your inquiries."

Air Force officials said a culture of fear led launch officers to believe they had to obtain perfect test scores to be promoted. Half of the 183 launch officers at Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana have been implicated and suspended. Air Force Secretary Deborah Lee James said the scandal has not affected the safety or reliability of the military's nuclear mission. Speaking to Pentagon reporters Thursday, Air Force officials said the cheating appears confined to the Montana base, though a climate of frustration, low morale and other failures permeates the nuclear force. The cheating scandal is the latest in an array of troubles that have drawn the attention of senior defense officials.

The two, Sharon Block, a former labor counsel to Senator Edward M. Kennedy, and Richard Griffin, former general counsel for the International Union of Operating Engineers, have been serving on the board since January 2012. The president appointed them during a Senate recess after Republicans blocked their confirmations. After a three-judge appeals panel decided three weeks ago that their recess appointments were invalid, 40 Senate Republicans issued a letter asking Block and Griffin to step down immediately from the labor board.

Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, in his role as vice chair of Donald Trump's voter suppression commission, asked every state to provide him voter registration information including the last four digits of a voter's Social Security number. Kobach will apparently not give National Kobach what he wants. The article notes that not getting Social Security digits does not mean the threat from his request is gone. The article also states that Kobach is still planning to collect a lot of information and disenfranchise a lot of voters with it. The article concludes that this was nice of him to demonstrate how extreme his efforts are in this way.

Polls have closed for voters in this year's primary and judicial elections in Arkansas. Tuesday's election was the first statewide enforcement of a state law requiring voters to present identification before casting ballots. The Republican-led Legislature last year approved a voter ID law, saying Arkansas needed one to cut down on fraud. Voters without an ID could cast a provisional ballot. Party primaries for governor and two U.S. House seats were at the top of the ballot Tuesday. Neither of the Democratic and Republican candidates in a U.S. Senate race drew a primary challenger and will automatically advance to the Nov. 4 general election.

A White House official issued a statement when asked whether the sequester would affect the first lady's office budget. The official said: "The First Lady's office is part of the Executive Office of the President. To comply with the sequester, White House components will cut back on all but the most urgent supply and equipment purchases. Personnel costs will be reduced by implementing a hiring slow-down or freeze, furloughing employees or reducing salaries. The reduced staffing levels will necessarily affect the critical, day-to-day official functions of the White House - but they also have an impact on routine public functions like responding to public correspondence, updating the White House website and facilitating White House tours of both the residence and the West Wing."

American manufacturing activity reached its highest point in nearly three and a half years last month and construction spending rebounded strongly in July, according to data released on Tuesday. The data added to reports on employment and housing that have suggested growth remains sturdy, despite a slowdown in consumer spending in recent months. Dan Greenhaus, chief strategist at BTIG, an institutional brokerage firm, said: "Things continue to fall into place for our view that growth should accelerate in the year's back half." The Institute for Supply Management said its index of national factory activity rose to 59 last month, the highest reading since March 2011, from 57.1 in July.

The Secret Service issued a privacy notice warning residents of President Donald Trump's New Jersey golf course in Bedminster, N.J., about a planned test of a tethered unmanned surveillance aircraft while Trump is staying at his home on the course. Trump starts his 17-day vacation Friday. The Department of Homeland Security is conducting a privacy impact assessment to evaluate privacy risks from the drone's surveillance and image capturing capabilities as it flies 300 to 400 feet in the air. Homeland Security says a similar surveillance system was used to provide security for this year's Boston Marathon and by the military.

A House panel voted Wednesday to place a five-year moratorium on bonuses to senior executives at the Department of Veterans Affairs. The sponsor of the proposal, Rep. Jeff Miller, Republican chairman of the House Committee on Veterans' Affairs, said the legislation was in response to media reports about various executives who received performance bonuses despite significant problems that occurred during their watch, such as the increase in the number of disability claims pending longer than 125 days. The VA had already halted bonuses for those executives overseeing disability claims, but Miller's legislation approved Wednesday extends the ban to other divisions within the government's second-largest department. The VA did not respond to a request for comment, but has stated previously that bonuses have been reduced in recent years.

A United Nations Security Council meeting on Friday discussed recent protests in Iran. The United States requested a meeting on what some member states said was an internal issue for Tehran. France's ambassador to the UN, Francois Delattre, said the protests do not threaten international peace and security. Delattre said: "We must be wary of any attempts to exploit this crisis for personal ends, which would have the diametrically opposed outcome to that which is wished. However worrying the events of the last few days in Iran may be, they do not constitute per se a threat to international peace and security."

The Cook Political Report moved the Iowa Senate race between Republican Joni Ernst and Democrat Bruce Braley to the Toss Up category. With Tom Harkin retiring, Republicans appear united behind Ernst. Braley has fallen. Braley is a solid recruit, but he has taken several missteps, including insulting Sen. Chuck Grassley, who is very popular in the state. Polling shows the race tied. Republican Governor Terry Branstad will also appear on the ballot, which is thought to be a plus for Ernst. Democrats have characterized Ernst as too conservative for Iowa and have called her "the Sarah Palin of Iowa." The result has been a rise in her polling numbers.

On Wednesday's "CNN Newsroom," 2020 presidential candidate Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) stated that Alabama's abortion ban and similar efforts are "an all-out attack on women's reproductive freedom and our basic civil rights." Gillibrand said, "This Alabama effort and the effort across this country now in 29 states is an all-out attack on women's reproductive freedom and our basic civil rights. This is a plan by the Republican Party, make no mistake, to overturn Roe v. Wade and turn back the clock on women's reproductive civil and human rights."

U.S. District Judge Kimba Wood said Tuesday that attorney Guy Petrillo can access files seized by the FBI from Michael Cohen's home and office in April raids. Wood responded to a request from Cohen's other lawyers, who have already seen the files. Prosecutors said they are looking into Cohen's business dealings. Cohen worked for the Trump Organization and Trump before he became ensnarled in a criminal probe. Lawyers who represented Cohen in his effort to designate some raid items as protected by attorney-client privilege asked Wood for permission to turn over raid materials to Petrillo. The lawyers said prosecutors did not object.

Former president Bill Clinton said his wife would make a fine president, but that over the long run, he has another Clinton in mind: their daughter. "Day after tomorrow, my wife, because she's had more experience," Clinton told CNN's Piers Morgan when asked whether Hillary or Chelsea Clinton would be a better president. "Over the long run, Chelsea. She knows more than we do about everything." Bill Clinton added: "I feel like I'm going to school every day when we have conversations." There has been speculation about when Chelsea Clinton will enter politics. She has said this year that she is trending toward a more "purposely public life." Last month, over at The Fix, I ran through some of her options.

Former Texas Congressman Ron Paul posted a tweet on Feb. 2 regarding sniper Chris Kyle. Kyle, a Navy SEAL and sniper, was allegedly shot and killed by a fellow veteran at a firing range on Feb. 2. Paul cited a verse from the Gospel of Matthew 26:52. Paul served in the military as an Air Force flight surgeon and the Air Force National Guard during the 1960s. After public criticism of the tweet, Paul published a clarification on his Facebook page.

The Senate passed a spending bill to keep the government open through the end of September. The measure prevents a government shutdown but leaves in place automatic spending cuts that will lead to job furloughs for hundreds of thousands of federal workers. The vote was 73-26. The measure was sent to the House, which is expected to approve it on Thursday and send it to President Obama for his signature. The measure would fund the day-to-day operating budgets of every Cabinet agency through Sept. 30, provide another $87 billion to fund overseas military operations in Afghanistan and Iraq, and maintain a pay freeze for federal workers. The measure gives the Pentagon relief from a cash crunch in accounts for training and readiness and gives veteran health programs their scheduled increases.

Rep. Howard "Buck" McKeon, chairman of the House Armed Services Committee, has decided to retire after 11 terms. Republican officials said the 75-year-old McKeon will announce his plans on Thursday. The California Republican has represented a district north of Los Angeles that includes several major defense contractors. McKeon campaigned for Republican candidates in 2010 and gained the committee chairmanship after the GOP wave took over the committee. He has fought to protect Pentagon spending in a struggle with deficit hawks in Congress, including many in his party. The Republican officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss McKeon's plans ahead of his official announcement.

Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn, the head of the Defense Intelligence Agency, will step down at the end of summer, according to sources who spoke to Fox News. Lt. Gen. Mary Legere, currently head of Army Intelligence, is the leading candidate to replace him, subject to confirmation hearings, sources told Fox News. Flynn has been DIA chief for the past two years and has been in the Army for 33 years. While heading the DIA, Flynn reportedly worked on reforming the organization and getting more military intelligence analysts to regional command centers around the world. James Clapper, Director of National Intelligence, issued a statement Wednesday night calling Flynn a "dedicated visionary" who "pushed the intelligence enterprise to anticipate and prepare for the threat environment of the future."

On Wednesday, 'SNL' spoofed President Obama's debate performance. During his opening remarks, Obama wished the First Lady a happy anniversary. Jay Pharoah and Jason Sudeikis reprised their roles as Barack Obama and Mitt Romney, with Chris Parnell as moderator Jim Lehrer. The sketch featured Jay Pharoah and Jason Sudeikis reprising their roles as Barack Obama and Mitt Romney, with Chris Parnell as moderator Jim Lehrer. The focus of the sketch was on what went wrong with Obama. Sudeikis also performed Romney's "creepy debate stare."

President Donald Trump faces fallout from revelations in The New York Times that he suffered business losses in the 1980s and 1990s. Ten years of tax data obtained by the newspaper revealed that Trump lost $1.17 billion, which appeared to be more than nearly any other U.S. individual. The Times said his $418 million in losses by 1991 represented 1% of all losses reported by individual taxpayers that year. The news had many of the president's critics suggesting that the host of the reality TV show "The Apprentice" might have been better suited for another broadcast. The article also included the phrase "BIGGEST LOSER" and the phrase "BIGGEST LOSER."

Donald Trump posted an online campaign advertisement on Wednesday afternoon. The 15-second video juxtaposes footage of Vladimir Putin practicing martial arts with footage of an Islamic State soldier pointing a gun. The ad includes a clip of Hillary Clinton barking like a dog. The video begins: "When it comes to facing our toughest opponents... The Democrats have the perfect answer..." and plays the clip twice. The titles conclude: "We don't need to be a punchline!" The video concludes with footage of Putin laughing.

President Donald Trump praised Rep. Greg Gianforte's (R-Mont.) May 2017 attack on Guardian journalist Ben Jacobs during a rally in Missoula, Montana, on Thursday. Trump told the crowd, "Any guy that can do a body slam, he's my kind of guy." Following the 2017 attack, Gianforte pleaded guilty to misdemeanor assault. The remark was immediately condemned on Twitter, with many commenters noting it came amid tensions rising over the disappearance of Saudi journalist and Washington Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi.

The White House said President Barack Obama will sign an executive order setting the minimum wage for workers under new federal contracts at $10.10 an hour. The president will announce the increase in his State of the Union address. The increase will not affect existing federal contracts, only new ones. The current minimum wage is $7.25 an hour. Obama will renew his call for Congress to increase the national minimum wage to $10.10 and tie future increases to inflation. Increasing the wage for federal contractors does not require congressional action. The White House said those who would benefit from the executive order include federally contracted janitors and construction workers as well as workers in military bases who wash dishes, serve food and do laundry.

In a preview clip from an interview airing Sunday evening on CBS's "60 Minutes," President Donald Trump said Defense Secretary James Mattis "may leave" his administration. Trump said, "I have a very good relationship with him. I had lunch with him two days ago. I have a very good relationship with him. It could be that he is. I think he's sort of a Democrat if you want to know the truth. But General Mattis is a good guy. We get along very well. He may leave. I mean, at some point, everybody leaves. Everybody. People leave. That's Washington."

President Donald Trump faces fallout from revelations in The New York Times that he suffered business losses in the 1980s and 1990s. Ten years of tax data obtained by the newspaper revealed that Trump lost $1.17 billion, which appeared to be more than nearly any other U.S. individual. The Times said his $418 million in losses by 1991 represented 1% of all losses reported by individual taxpayers that year. The news had many of the president's critics suggesting that the host of the reality TV show "The Apprentice" might have been better suited for another broadcast. The article also included the phrase "BIGGEST LOSER" and the phrase "BIGGEST LOSER."

Sen. Marco Rubio criticized Charlie Crist during a Fox News appearance. Crist cited race-based hostility toward the president as his reason for leaving the Republican Party. Rubio said Crist was "absolutely" a phony. Rubio said, "It's ridiculous and silly." He added, "Even Democrats will be embarrassed that Charlie Crist became a Democrat." Rubio also said, "I've never met a single Republican activist involved in my campaign that has ever, in my opinion, ever been motivated by race to state their objections."

President Barack Obama's campaign said in a Tuesday statement that he is "disappointed" with North Carolina's constitutional amendment banning gay marriage. Obama campaign spokesman Cameron French said in the statement that the ban on same-sex unions is "divisive and discriminatory." French said same-sex couples deserve the same rights and legal protections as straight couples. Obama officials have been involved in a national discussion of same-sex marriage since Vice President Joe Biden said Sunday that he is "absolutely comfortable" with gay marriage. Obama has not embraced legalizing gay marriage, saying his views on the subject are "evolving." North Carolinians voted Tuesday to amend their state constitution, strengthening a state law that already outlawed same-sex unions.

Mexico's Attorney General's Office said Sunday in a statement that the government notified recaptured drug lord Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman that he is wanted in the United States, formally beginning extradition proceedings against him. The Office said Guzman was told that two arrest warrants from the U.S. are being processed. The notification was done by agents of the international police agency Interpol at the maximum security prison where Guzman is being held. Guzman was recaptured Friday, six months after breaking out of a Mexican prison. Officials have cautioned that the extradition process might take a while. Guzman's attorney Juan Pablo Badillo said the defense has filed six motions to challenge extradition requests.

The United States announced Monday it was lifting its ban on refugees from 11 countries. The ban was described as affecting refugees from 11 high-risk countries. Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen said applicants from 11 countries, unnamed but understood to include 10 Muslim-majority nations plus North Korea, would face tougher "risk-based" assessments. Nielsen said: "It's critically important that we know who is entering the United States. These additional security measures will make it harder for bad actors to exploit our refugee program, and they will ensure we take a more risk-based approach to protecting the homeland."

Eric Trump posted two hashtags on Tuesday night: #NoGoodDeedGoesUnpunished and #SnakeInTheGrass. Within minutes of the post, other Twitter users mocked him. Trump did not explicitly state what he was referring to. The post was likely referencing former White House aide Omarosa Manigault Newman, who released secretly recorded conversations from her time working in the White House while promoting her new tell-all book Unhinged. Twitter users responded critically to Trump's latest message.

The White House confirmed that President Donald Trump may allow exemptions from steel and aluminum tariffs when the president signs the new trade restrictions later this week. The position was first reported by Breitbart News. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Wednesday that the president expects to sign something by the end of the week. Sanders said there are potential carve-outs for Mexico and Canada based on national security and possibly other countries as well. She added that any exemptions would be evaluated on a case-by-case, country-by-country basis. The impact on national security would determine whether an exemption is available, she said.

Melania Trump will hear directly from teens and young adults about their experiences with electronic cigarettes and vaping. The White House said she has invited a group from the Truth Initiative to participate in a listening session on Wednesday. This will be the second time this week that the first lady has highlighted e-cigarettes and vaping among youth. Mrs. Trump used a speech Monday to call on companies to leave children out of marketing campaigns for e-cigarettes. Scheduled to join her at Wednesday's session are Health and Human Services Secretary Alex Azar and White House counselor Kellyanne Conway. The Truth Initiative is the largest nonprofit public health organization dedicated to achieving a culture where all youth and young adults reject tobacco.

Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-SC) appeared on MSNBC's "Nightly News" on Tuesday and told a reporter that President Donald Trump's budget proposal was "dead on arrival" given cuts included to the State Department. "It's dead on arrival," Graham said. "It's not going to happen. It would be a disaster. If you take soft power off the table, then you're never going to win the war. What's most disturbing about the cut in the State Department's budget is it shows a lack of understanding of what it takes to win the war."

Meals on Wheels confirmed a $50,000 donation from former San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick on Tuesday. The group that provides food for seniors in need thanked Kaepernick for his donation. The donation came a day after President Donald Trump criticized Kaepernick during a campaign-style rally in Kentucky by taking credit for the lack of suitors for the free agent. Kaepernick refused to stand for "The Star-Spangled Banner" ahead of 49ers games last season as a protest of police treatment of minorities became a topic of national debate. Meals on Wheels faces a funding cut under Trump's proposed budget. Kaepernick is also promoting a campaign to raise millions of dollars for drought relief in Somalia.

On Sunday, Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, a Republican, and Senator Tom Cotton of Arkansas, a libertarian-minded Republican, disagreed on whether Edward J. Snowden deserves a death penalty or life in prison. Paul said on the ABC News program "This Week" that he disagreed with those who argued for the most severe penalties for Snowden, a former National Security Agency contractor. Paul said, "I don't think Edward Snowden deserves a death penalty or life in prison; I think that's inappropriate, and I think that's why he fled, because that's what he faced."

President Barack Obama traveled Thursday to Cooperstown, New York, home of the Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum, to discuss steps to help spur international visits to the 50 states. In his weekly address last week, Obama said the overall U.S. economy and local businesses will benefit if it is not a hassle for people from other countries to visit the U.S. and spend money at its hotels, restaurants, tourist destinations and other businesses. From upstate New York, Obama was heading to Chicago to headline a pair of fundraisers benefiting Democratic Senate candidates.

President Donald Trump's son-in-law and senior adviser, Jared Kushner, is in Iraq. A senior administration official said Kushner is traveling in the Middle East with the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. Joseph Dunford. Other details about the trip are not being released. The official was not authorized to speak about confidential meetings by name and demanded anonymity. Kushner's West Wing portfolio includes senior positions in presidential staffing and a role as shadow diplomat advising on relations with the Middle East, Canada and Mexico. Last week he launched a task force meant to modernize government using lessons drawn from the private sector. Kushner is married to Trump's oldest daughter, Ivanka.

President Barack Obama said on Tuesday that Ahmed Abu Khatallah, the recently captured suspected ringleader of the 2012 attack on the U.S. diplomatic compound in Benghazi, Libya, would face the "full weight" of the U.S. justice system. In a statement released by the White House, Obama said he had authorized the strike in Libya in which U.S. military troops, working with law enforcement personnel, captured Khatallah on Sunday. "Since the deadly attacks on our facilities in Benghazi, I have made it a priority to find and bring to justice those responsible for the deaths of four brave Americans," Obama said.

Stephen Hawking, a British astrophysicist, told ITV's morning show Monday that he cannot fathom the popularity of Donald Trump. He said the presumptive Republican Party candidate for U.S. president "is a demagogue who seems to appeal to the lowest common denominator." Hawking also appealed to British voters to vote to keep the United Kingdom inside the European Union in a June 23 referendum. He said remaining within the EU provided essential support for British scientific research as well as its economy and security. He said: "Gone are the days we could stand on our own against the world. We need to be part of a larger group of nations, both for our security and our trade."

A U.S. military official said Thursday that a military dog seized by the Taliban in Afghanistan does not belong to U.S. forces, contrary to the Taliban's claim, but rather belongs to the British. The official declined to go on record because it is the policy of the NATO alliance that each country makes its own announcement about its situation. The Taliban distributed a video of the dog in an elaborate harness and contended in links to its Twitter account that the "mujahideen seized US dog" during an "attempted nighttime raid" by U.S. forces on December 23 in the eastern province of Laghman. International Security Assistance Force officials were not immediately available for comment.

The Washington Post reported that President Donald Trump referred to Attorney General Jeff Sessions as "Mr. Magoo." The Post cited unnamed sources and said Trump complained that he had hired the best lawyers in his life but now was stuck with Sessions, who he does not believe is loyal enough. On Wednesday, Trump renewed his criticism of Sessions, calling his actions "disgraceful." Sessions responded by saying he would work with "integrity and honor."

On Oct. 31 Politico reported that two women had filed sexual harassment claims against Republican presidential candidate Herman Cain while he was head of the National Restaurant Association in the 1990s. In the weeks that followed, more women came forward, and two went public with their accusations. Atlanta businesswoman Ginger White spoke out alleging she and Cain had an extramarital affair for 13 years. Cain has repeatedly denied the allegations. Cain has also come under criticism for referring to House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) as "Princess Nancy" during a Republican presidential debate.

The White House said Friday's public disclosure of emails related to the attack on a U.S. compound in Libya is an attempt by Republicans to "politicize" the investigation. Spokesman Jay Carney said lawmakers have known about the emails since earlier this year. Carney disputed the notion that the emails suggest the White House was more involved in the crafting of talking points about the attacks than previously indicated. The talking points suggested that the attacks on the Benghazi compound were spontaneous. It was later revealed that the attacks were planned. The emails show White House officials were aware of the concerns from other agencies, including the State Department, about mentioning that specific groups might have been behind the attacks.

House Minority Leader Kevin McCarthy, a California Republican, said Tuesday that Speaker Nancy Pelosi's announcement that the House is in the middle of an impeachment inquiry was an empty gesture. "What she said today is no different than what's been going on," McCarthy told reporters an hour after Pelosi reversed herself and said she now backs beginning the impeachment process against Mr. Trump. Pelosi said she has told six committee chairs, who are already investigating Mr. Trump, that they are now operating under the "umbrella of impeachment inquiry."

Thousands of protesters gathered in Madison in reaction to Gov. Scott Walker's (R) new budget proposal. Wisconsin faces a $137 million budget deficit. In order to close it, Walker wants to curtail the collective bargaining rights of public employee unions, effectively preventing them from negotiating benefits, hours and working conditions. They would still be able to bargain over base wages, and Walker decided to exempt firefighters and police workers from his measure. Public workers would also have to contribute more money toward pension and health insurance plans. HuffPost Eyes and Ears contributors Matt Robison and Julia Meuse took photos of the protests in Madison.

Former Florida governor and potential 2016 presidential candidate Jeb Bush told Fox News Radio's "Kilmeade & Friends" on Thursday that he does not read the New York Times. Host Brian Kilmeade asked Bush for his response to a recent NYT article about members of the Christian right seeking an alternative contender. Bush responded, "I don't read The New York Times to be honest with you, so I guess you're going to force me to do so." The Washington Post has previously stated that "it's dumb" for a politician to say they don't read the Times. New York Times reporters also pointed out that Bush's response was even better.

Tim Scott has been appointed to fill the South Carolina Senate seat being vacated by the retiring Jim DeMint. The appointment was made by Governor Haley. Radio host Amos Brown, a Republican from Indianapolis, Indiana, posted on Twitter stating that African American Tim Scott is not really a black man. Brown is a Republican. Governor Haley appointed Scott to the vacant seat. Brown used his Twitter account to claim that Scott is not really a black man. The article states that Scott is a Republican and that the hatemongers have come out in force with what it describes as racist name calling.

Kimani Gray's mother, Carol Gray, and other relatives are holding a press conference Thursday afternoon in Brooklyn. Police say 46 protesters have been arrested following a candlelight vigil on Wednesday night. Most are charged with disorderly conduct. One police officer suffered a gash in the face after being hit by an object tossed from a building. A spokesman for Gray's parents said previously that they would not speak publicly as long as there was violence. Authorities say 16-year-old Gray was shot Saturday night by two plainclothes police officers after he pointed a gun at them.

Rep. Paul D. Ryan said Sunday he would have a decision within days on whether he will seek the Senate seat from Wisconsin being vacated by retiring Sen. Herb Kohl. Ryan, a Republican who rose to national prominence from his position as chairman of the House Budget Committee, is considered a leading contender on the GOP side to replace Kohl, a Democrat who made his retirement announcement on Friday. Speaking on CNN early Sunday, Ryan said, "My family and voters are just started digesting this. I plan on making an announcement very quickly." Kohl becomes the sixth Democrat in the Senate who will forgo a bid for re-election in 2012.

Republican presidential nominee Mitt Romney said Chicago teachers are turning their backs on thousands of students and President Barack Obama is supporting the striking teachers. In a statement released Monday hours before he was set to land in Chicago for fundraisers, Romney said he is disappointed by the Chicago teachers' decision to walk out of negotiations. Romney said he sides with parents and students over unionized teachers. Thousands of teachers walked off the job in Chicago's first schools strike in 25 years. The walkout by 26,000 teachers and support staff in the nation's third-largest school district affects almost 400,000 students. Romney has been critical of public employee unions, including teachers. Romney said union interests run counter to students' education.

Pakistani intelligence officials said a suspected U.S. drone strike killed seven militants near the Afghan border on Friday night. The strike occurred in the Shawal area along the border dividing the North and South Waziristan tribal regions. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to release the information. Many Pakistanis oppose U.S. drone strikes because they say they the strikes kill large numbers of innocent civilians, something the U.S. denies, and end up breeding more extremism by those seeking retribution. The country's new Prime Minister, Nawaz Sharif, has criticized the U.S. drone program and called for an end to it.

On June 17, a white man entered a church in Charleston, South Carolina, and killed nine black people during a prayer meeting. Twenty-three days later, after a national outcry and a legislative debate, a Confederate battle flag, the one the gunman, Dylann Roof, had waved in photos before the shootings, was lowered from the grounds of the State House, where it had flown for more than 50 years. Crowds cheered and chanted as the flag was brought down and carefully folded just after 10 a.m. on Friday. Before the ceremony, reporters who were there said that though people who were both for and against the flag's removal attended the ceremony, the crowd was calm.

Friends and family members testified at the sentencing phase of Dylann Roof's death penalty trial in Charleston, South Carolina. They described personalities, future plans, and final conversations. The jury convicted Roof, 22, of hate crimes and other charges. The jury will decide whether to sentence him to life in prison or death. Roof faces murder charges in state court, where his trial had been slated to start later this month. A state judge on Thursday delayed that trial indefinitely because federal proceedings are ongoing.

President Bush will call on Congress this morning to approve offshore drilling for oil in states such as Florida and California. Bush is also considering reversing a ban on offshore exploration put into place by his father through an executive order in 1990. The White House concluded that gas prices have made offshore drilling a necessity. Bush will speak to the press in the Rose Garden at 10:35 a.m. His announcement will draw attention from Sen. John McCain and the Sen. Barack Obama. McCain, the presumptive Republican nominee from Arizona, on Tuesday advocated for offshore exploration. Obama, the presumptive Democratic nominee from Illinois, said such an action would not do anything to reduce gas prices in the short term.

Vice President Joe Biden attended worship services at Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, on Sunday, where nine people were killed during a Bible study. Biden wore a purple tie. He said it was not his first visit to the church and that he knew the Rev. Clementa Pinckney, the pastor of the church, who was killed along with eight others earlier this month. "We came back because my family and I wanted to show solidarity with the families and with the church," Biden said. Biden received a standing ovation after reading a selection of scripture.

North Korea launched four ballistic missiles from its long-range rocket launch site on Monday morning. According to the South Korean military, North Korea launched four ballistic missiles from its long-range rocket launch site. Analysts said the launches suggested North Korea could pose a more serious threat than indicated by previous tests. North Korea said on Tuesday that the tests were conducted by units "tasked to strike the bases of the U.S. imperialist aggressor forces in Japan in contingency."

Hillary Rodham Clinton plans to headline a California fundraiser for Terry McAuliffe, a longtime family friend running for governor in Virginia. The former secretary of state will attend the Beverly Hills fundraiser on Oct. 30. It will be hosted by longtime Clinton donors Haim Saban and his wife Cheryl. The former first lady has been helping McAuliffe in the final weeks before November's election. She was raising money for McAuliffe in New York on Tuesday and plans to appear at a "Women for Terry" event in Falls Church, Va., on Saturday. Democrats consider Clinton to be a strong contender for the 2016 Democratic presidential nomination should she decide to run. McAuliffe faces Republican Ken Cuccinelli in the November election.

Former United States senator Ted Stevens died Monday night in a plane crash at age 86. He helped shape modern Alaska with federal laws and billions in federal dollars. Stevens served in the Senate for 40 years, longer than any other Republican. He was known as a fierce and often hot-tempered advocate for his state. In October 2008, a federal jury in the District of Columbia found that Stevens had concealed more than $250,000 in gifts and convicted him on seven felony counts. Eight days later, he lost a bid for a seventh term to Mayor Mark Begich of Anchorage, a Democrat.

Turkey's Dogan news agency and other media reported that a court issued a temporary injunction ordering the telecommunications authority to restore access to Twitter, five days after the government blocked the social network. The telecommunications authority had accused Twitter of disobeying court orders to remove content. The ban came shortly after Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan threatened to "rip out the roots" of the social network, which has been a conduit for links to recordings suggesting government corruption. Many in Turkey circumvented the ban. Lawyers and the opposition party asked courts to overturn the Twitter ban, arguing it was illegal and unconstitutional. It was not clear when or if the telecommunications authority would follow Wednesday's court order.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel called on all sides in the conflict in Ukraine to work toward the ceasefire envisaged by the Minsk accords, saying implementation of those agreements could lead to the lifting of EU sanctions against Russia. Speaking in the Russian town of Sochi after discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Merkel said there was no need to replace the Minsk process, which is designed to bring an end to the conflict between Moscow-backed rebels in Ukraine's east and the Kiev government. "For me the aim is to reach the point in the implementation of the Minsk accords where we can lift the European Union's sanctions against Russia," Merkel said.

Reality television star Kim Kardashian traveled to the White House Wednesday afternoon to discuss prison reform with President Donald Trump. Trump tweeted about the visit about an hour after her arrival: "Great meeting with @KimKardashian today, talked about prison reform and sentencing." He shared a photograph of Kardashian at his side behind the Oval Office's Resolute Desk. According to Vanity Fair, Ivanka Trump and son-in-law Jared Kushner are set to dine with Kardashian this evening. The trio discussed prison reform and a potential pardon for Alice Johnson, a 62-year-old great-grandmother serving a life sentence without parole on drug charges.

President Donald Trump met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas during the second leg of his first foreign trip as president. Trump is pressing forward with his bid to advance the peace process. He does not expect to emerge from his two-day visit to Israel and the West Bank with a deal in hand. He is the latest president to arrive at the Middle East peace talks with a goal in mind. "During my travels I have seen many hopeful signs that lead me to believe that we can truly achieve a more hopeful future for people of this religion and for people of all faiths and all beliefs and frankly all over the world," Trump said, delivering remarks Monday evening alongside Netanyahu.

A GOP office in Hillsborough, North Carolina, was firebombed overnight, with a swastika and the words "Nazi Republicans get out of town or else" spray painted on an adjacent building, according to local officials. Local officials described the incident as despicable. Hillary Clinton responded appropriately. The NCGOP responded that at this point there is no evidence as to the perpetrators. Donald Trump weighed in. Law enforcement has no idea who was responsible for the bombing, or at least they are not yet saying. Comments are closed on this story.

Rep. Michele Bachmann (R-MN) sent a letter regarding Huma Abedin to U.S. intelligence and security agencies. Senator John McCain (R-AZ) criticized the letter. Rep. Keith Ellison (D-MN), the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Congress, also criticized the letter. Bachmann subsequently added Ellison's name to the list of U.S. officials whom she believes should be investigated for ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Ellison responded by saying Bachmann's allegations are false and that he believes she just wants attention.

On Monday, Post reporters provided updates on Jeffrey E. Thompson, D.C. businessman Jeffrey E. Thompson, and the "shadow campaign." Thompson was scheduled to appear before a judge. A local charge carries a technical five-year sentence, with guidelines ranging from probation to 12 months. A prosecutor stated that Thompson gave Thompson a $425,000 budget for a television campaign. Thompson told him he would pay it secretly through an adviser. A prosecutor also reported that on request of a Gray adviser, Thompson paid $40,000 for home improvements for a close friend of Gray. Gray thanked Thompson for the money.

Bernie Sanders' campaign said Tuesday it raised $3 million through online fundraising 24 hours after he nearly defeated Hillary Clinton in the Iowa caucuses. The campaign raised the haul after Sanders gave his speech Monday night, campaign spokesman Michael Briggs said. The campaign's online fundraising comes as Sanders and Clinton compete in New Hampshire. Sanders has largely kept pace with Clinton in the money race throughout the campaign, logging $20 million in January alone, according to his campaign. The Sanders campaign has touted its online fundraising after events like Democratic and Republican debates and taunted the Democratic National Committee in December, saying it raised $1 million following a voter database breach.

Rudolph W. Giuliani, President Trump's personal lawyer, held a press conference Thursday. During the press conference, a dark substance dripped down both sides of his face. Social media users assumed the substance was hair dye. The liquid was visible from near each of Giuliani's ears and running down his cheeks while he addressed reporters. Giuliani, the former mayor of New York City, grew wet sideburns while speaking. The substance left a dark, narrow line on the sides of his face as gravity dragged it down to his jaw.

President Obama will travel to Massachusetts on Wednesday to deliver a speech on the Affordable Care Act's benefits in the state that passed a similar law in 2006. The White House said the president will speak at Faneuil Hall in Boston, where the original "tea party" patriots fomented their rebellion against British tyranny. The White House said the president will talk about "the importance of providing all Americans with quality, affordable health insurance and the experience in Massachusetts." The state adopted its version of government-subsidized health insurance under former Gov. Mitt Romney, Mr. Obama's opponent in 2012.

On Thursday, MSNBC's "The Cycle" added political pundit Touré to its program. Touré agreed with Breitbart News' assessment of Barbara Walters' interview of potential presidential candidates Chris Christie and Hillary Clinton. Walters said, "you would never ask a man that." Touré asked why she was asking her that and whether she recognized the sexism she was activating and commenting on. Touré responded that even a broken clock is correct twice a day.

Friends of Tamerlan Tsarnaev's wife, Katherine Russell, describe the suspected Boston Marathon bomber who was killed in a Thursday evening shootout as someone who changed around 2008, believing Islam "was under attack." According to NPR's Laura Sullivan, Russell's friends said Tamerlan would party with them, but his behavior started to change in 2008; he became "very religious, and he stopped smoking, and he stopped drinking, and he stopped going out with them." Sullivan reports that Russell's friends said this is when Tamerlan started having "an extremist point of view, that he started talking about being angry with the government, and he said that he felt that Islam was under attack."

Former Vice President Joseph R. Biden said Thursday at the Democratic presidential debate in Los Angeles that he would not commit to running for a second term if he wins next November. Biden said, "No, I'm not willing to commit one way or another. Here's the deal - I'm not even elected one term yet, and let's see where we are. Let's see what happens." Moderator Tim Alberta noted that Biden would turn 82 years old at the end of his first term and be the oldest president in "American history."

Donald Trump posted on Twitter about his possible impeachment, along with calls for civil war and a demand to meet the whistleblower. Trump then tweeted a demand for House Intelligence Committee Chairman Adam Schiff to be arrested for treason. The tweet read: "Rep. Adam Schiff illegally made up a FAKE & terrible statement, pretended it to be mine as the most important part of my call to the Ukrainian President, and read it aloud to Congress and the American people. It bore NO relationship to what I said on the call. Arrest for Treason? Trump is in full-blown panic mode."

Law enforcement agents intercepted a package addressed to the White House containing the toxic poison ricin earlier this week, according to CNN and the New York Times. The package was addressed to President Donald Trump. A facility outside the White House typically screens all mail before it is delivered to the White House. An official speaking to the New York Times said the letter is believed to have been sent from Canada. An attempt to mail ricin to President Trump was also intercepted in October 2018. William Clyde Allen, a former Naval officer, was arrested by the FBI for mailing ricin filled letters to Secretary of Defense James Mattis, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. John Richardson, and FBI Director Chris Wray.

A proposal by Central American businessmen to build a natural gas pipeline from Mexico to Panama will be presented during a weekend meeting between U.S. President Barack Obama and Central American presidents. Nicaraguan businessman Jose Aguerri said Tuesday that the project would lower energy costs in the region and make its economies more competitive. Aguerri said the idea was first proposed by Nicaraguan businessmen and has since gained support across Central America's private sector. He said he hopes Obama will back the idea because the pipeline would make the region more self-sufficient. After a two-day visit to Mexico, Obama will be in Costa Rica on Friday to meet with Central American presidents.

Reclaim America, Sen. Marco Rubio's (R-FL) leadership PAC, will air a new television advertisement for Iowa GOP Senate candidate Joni Ernst, according to Terry Sullivan, the PAC's director. Sullivan told Breitbart News that Rubio, who shares a consultant, Todd Harris, endorsed Ernst on May 5. Ernst holds a lead over businessman Mark Jacobs. Her first television advertisement began with the words, "I grew up castrating hogs on an Iowa farm." Former Gov. Mitt Romney and former Gov. Sarah Palin have also backed Ernst.

President Donald Trump said he thinks former national security adviser Susan Rice committed a crime when she reportedly unmasked American citizens involved with his campaign. "I think it's going to be the biggest story," Trump said to the New York Times. "It's such an important story for our country and the world. It is one of the big stories of our time." Trump's remarks are his first public statement on the subject since reports claimed Rice was responsible. Trump did not reveal any new details to the New York Times but said he would explain himself "at the right time."

On CBS's Face The Nation on Sunday, White House chief of staff Denis McDonough said Syrian President Bashar al-Assad was a liar for denying that he used chemical weapons against his people. McDonough said Assad's statements, which were reported by CBS's Charlie Rose, who interviewed Assad in Damascus, were "misleading" and that his claim not to have authorized chemical weapons use "does appear to me to be a lie." "What we need is to communicate very clearly what is expected of him," McDonough said of Assad. Assad reportedly told Rose that there was no evidence that chemical weapons were used to attack Syrians in an interview that CBS will reportedly air on Monday.

In the final leg of New Jersey's governor's race, both candidates are casting about for ways to save the state from financial doom as they confront the economic reality that will severely restrict the winner of Tuesday's voting. The Democratic governor, Jon S. Corzine, says he may revisit his plan to lease the New Jersey Turnpike to raise cash — a proposal that he abandoned last year after intense opposition from lawmakers and voters. His Republican challenger, Christopher J. Christie, retreating from a key campaign promise, says he can no longer fully restore property tax breaks for homeowners, given the uncertainty of the state's finances.

North Korea has increased its rocket launch activities at Sohae Satellite Launching Station in North Korea, the satellite operator DigitalGlobe said Tuesday, citing recent satellite imagery of the facility. The increased activities came months after the Unha-3 rocket, launched from the same site in April, disintegrated shortly after takeoff and failed to put what North Korea claimed was a scientific satellite into orbit. The United States and its allies condemned the launching as a violation of United Nations Security Council resolutions that banned North Korea from testing technology that could be used to develop long-range ballistic missiles.

Hackers blocked access to Indiana's state government website Friday afternoon in response to the state's "religious freedom" bill being signed into law this week. Some users were unable to access the state's website, www.in.gov, the Indianapolis Star reported. Indiana Office of Technology spokesman Graig Lubsen said the website was not hacked. A denial of service attack consists of sending many traffic requests at the same time in order to overwhelm a website and have it not load. The denial of service interruption began at approximately 2:00, but the site has not been continuously down.

The U.S.-led coalition in Afghanistan formally ended its combat mission on Sunday, more than 13 years after an international alliance ousted the Taliban government for sheltering planners of the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks on American cities. At a ceremony marking the end of the mission held at ISAF headquarters in Kabul, U.S. General John Campbell, commander of the International Security Assistance Force (ISAF), said, "Today marks an end of an era and the beginning of a new one." He added, "We will continue to invest in Afghanistan's future."

According to a CBS News story, also quoted in The Hill, the Secret Service paid $35,185 to the Trump organization for golf cart rentals at Mar-a-Lago golf club in Palm Beach County, Florida. One purchase order reviewed by CBS News shows the Secret Service spent $35,185 on golf cart rentals for a President's visit there since the President's inauguration. The report also states that whatever profit Mar-a-Lago receives from the Secret Service rentals goes into the Trump trust and back into Trump's pocket. Comments on the story are closed.

Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign raised at least $45 million during its first quarter, her campaign told Bloomberg on Wednesday. The campaign reported that 91 percent of donations were of $100 or less. The campaign attributed the increase to grassroots enthusiasm. Clinton's haul from her campaign's launch in mid-April through June 30 is a record for primary money raised in a candidate's first quarter. President Barack Obama held the previous record for a campaign's first quarter, raising $41.9 million after launching his re-election bid.

President Donald Trump insisted that his reimbursement of a 2016 hush payment to porn actress Stormy Daniels had nothing to do with his election campaign. The revelation of the president's payment clashed with his past statements. White House aides were blindsided when Trump's attorney, Rudy Giuliani, said Wednesday night that the president had repaid Michael Cohen for $130,000 that was given to Daniels to keep her quiet before the 2016 election about her allegations of an affair with Trump. Giuliani's revelation contradicted Trump's past statements.

The House passed a disaster relief bill extending disaster assistance to livestock producers affected by rising feed prices caused by the drought that has affected much of the nation. The vote to revive expired disaster relief programs for cattle and sheep producers occurred one of the House's last before lawmakers left for their five-week August recess. It was uncertain whether the Senate would act on the bill before it adjourns for the summer break. Democratic opponents characterized the legislation as cover for Republicans having to explain to rural constituents why they put off action on a comprehensive five-year farm policy bill. Many crop farmers have insurance that provides some protection from the effects of the drought. Livestock producers are vulnerable to sharp increases in feed prices resulting from the dry weather.

Democrat J.D. Scholten announced Monday he is running to unseat Rep. Steve King in Iowa's 4th Congressional District. Scholten, a former professional baseball player, made the announcement in a video narrated by actor Kevin Costner. "This time, we're going to get the job done," Scholten said in a statement. "Too many Iowan families feel like they're getting kicked in the dirt, suffering from an economy and a government that just doesn't have their interests at heart."

Democratic U.S. Rep. Deb Haaland of New Mexico called for an impeachment inquiry of President Donald Trump on Wednesday. The first-term lawmaker from Albuquerque said in a statement that Trump "has proven he's unfit to serve as president" and that Congress needs to "shed light on what his administration is hiding and hold the president accountable." Haaland previously said she favored more aggressive oversight of Trump that might lead to impeachment hearings. A tally by The Associated Press indicates more than half of House Democrats support launching an impeachment inquiry.

Three potential nominees for President Obama's administration, including CNN's Dr. Sanjay Gupta, withdrew Thursday. None had been officially nominated. A White House official confirmed to The Washington Times that Dr. Gupta had been under serious consideration for surgeon general but withdrew his name. Separately Thursday, several news outlets reported that former U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission member Annette Nazareth withdrew from consideration for deputy secretary at the Treasury Department. Additionally, Caroline Atkinson withdrew her name from consideration for undersecretary of Treasury for international affairs.

Two reporters for The New York Times, David M. Halbfinger and David Kocieniewski, conducted wide-ranging interviews with the major-party candidates for governor of New Jersey, Jon S. Corzine, the Democratic incumbent, and Christopher J. Christie, his Republican challenger. The article included excerpts from the interviews. The first question asked: "Given all the factors we know, and the uncertainties, what do you really think you can get accomplished in your next term? A. The most important issue that impacts what you can get done is, are we going to get a national economic recovery that comes sooner and comes stronger to the state? I believe we've positioned ourselves for that."

After final negotiations that ran late into Thursday night, the House is expected to vote Friday on the Republican plan to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act. Lawmakers added more changes on Thursday. The biggest was a weakening of a federal requirement that health insurers provide a basic set of benefits, called essential health benefits. House Republicans had released several key changes to their plan on Monday, two weeks after its initial unveiling, in an attempt to appease both conservatives and moderates. The bill compares with the Affordable Care Act, with proposed changes to the original bill highlighted.

Hillary Clinton's presidential campaign raised at least $45 million during its first quarter, her campaign told Bloomberg on Wednesday. The campaign reported that 91 percent of donations were of $100 or less. The campaign attributed the increase to grassroots enthusiasm. Clinton's haul from her campaign's launch in mid-April through June 30 is a record for primary money raised in a candidate's first quarter. President Barack Obama held the previous record for a campaign's first quarter, raising $41.9 million after launching his re-election bid.

Just before he was fired, FBI Director Comey had asked the Justice Department for vastly increased funding and staff for the Russia Investigation. The question was raised whether Interim Director McCabe would request the same ramping up of the Russia investigation, or whether he was giving a victory to Donald Trump in his attempt to obstruct justice by not ramping up the investigation the way Comey intended. Another question was asked: without the increased funding that was requested by Comey, how many years will it take for the FBI to complete its investigation? Eight? Should the FBI ramp up the Russia Investigation the way Comey intended? Comments are closed on this story.

BP earned $17 billion last year and ended the year with more than $8 billion in cash. The company said it could pay short-term costs of the Deepwater Horizon oil well leaking millions of gallons into the Gulf of Mexico. Government, Gulf Coast residents and investors have expressed concerns about BP's ability to meet its obligations over the long term or survive the crisis intact. The ultimate cost of the disaster remains uncertain. Wall Street estimates range from $17 billion to $60 billion, including penalties, damages and cleanup costs for the Deepwater Horizon disaster.

A House stenographer stated she was working on completing the transcript. She said the author would not be mocked, would not be mocked, and would not touch her. She said the greatest deception was that the nation was not one under god, that it never was, that had it been, it would not have been, no, it would not have been Constitution would not have been written by Freemasons. She said they go against god, that you can not serve two masters, that you can not serve two masters, and that Praise be to god you are Jesus Christ. The stenographer then began speaking against the secular form of government. She was removed from the floor only after belting out her religious views.

China and the United States are introducing new sanctions against North Korea at the U.N. on March 5. The resolution tightens existing sanctions against ballistic missile and nuclear tests and also contains sanctions on "the import and export of nuclear and ballistic-missile related material." Embargoes on luxury items, arms imports and exports, and financial and travel sanctions are also included. The newest aspect of these measures is believed to broaden financial and travel sanctions. Although an oil embargo would be the most difficult punishment for North Korea to skirt, China will not support it for fear that North Korea would collapse, negatively impacting China's economy.
