President Obama said Afghanistan will no longer "be a source of terrorist attacks again," a week before the United States is set to end its combat mission in the Middle Eastern nation. "We've been in continuous war now for over 13 years. Next week we will be ending our combat mission in Afghanistan," Obama told troops in Hawaii late Thursday, celebrating Christmas. "Because of the extraordinary service of the men and women in the armed forces, Afghanistan has a chance to rebuild its own country," he said. "We are safer. It's not going to be a source of terrorist attacks again."

Former Vice President Joe Biden (D) won the state of Missouri on Tuesday evening, according to the Associated Press. Missouri is one of six states holding a Democrat primary on Tuesday, offering 68 pledged delegates. In 2016, Bernie Sanders lost the Democratic primary to Hillary Clinton by less than half of a percentage point, or 1,531 votes. The margin of Biden's victory is not yet known for Missouri's race. Michigan, which offers 125 pledged delegates, is also holding a Democratic primary on Tuesday. Final polls close at 9:00 p.m. ET.

Michael D'Antonio, author of the new book "Never Enough: Donald Trump and the Pursuit of Success" (St. Martin's Press), wrote a commentary for CNN. In the commentary, Donald Trump said, "It has not been easy for me" and that "my whole life has been a 'no' and I fought through it." He said his father's $1 million loan got him started as a developer.

Justice Clarence Thomas criticized New Jersey Democratic Sen. Cory Booker over the "Spartacus" comment he made during Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh's confirmation hearing. "Honorable – if we could use that word about more people who are in public life, people who actually ask the questions at confirmation hearings, instead of 'Spartacus,'" Thomas said during conversation with the Federalist Society's Leonard Leo last week. The conversation aired on C-SPAN Wednesday and was filmed at the inaugural Gregory S. Coleman Memorial Lecture. The audience and Thomas both laughed following the comment.

Marco Rubio has told colleagues and advisers that he is considering running for president again in 2020 or 2024. As he and his team weighed a re-election campaign, they debated how well situated he would be in once more seeking the presidency from the Senate. Rubio set the record for the most half-assed Senate term and announced he wants the job back.

A Muslim ninth grader named Ahmed Mohamed was arrested yesterday after school officials mistook his homemade clock for a bomb. After a friend posted a picture of Mohamed getting arrested, his story received nationwide attention. #IStandWithAhmed immediately started trending as support poured in from all over the country. Ahmed was invited to the White House by President Obama himself via Twitter. The Huffington Post secured the formal invitation and security briefing from the white house to Ahmed Mohamed. On the second page, the White House briefed him on the security detail. The briefing also informed him there would be an itinerary.

The number of people applying for unemployment benefits fell 21,000 to a seasonally adjusted 323,000 last week, the lowest since late September. The Labor Department reported the four-week average fell for the third straight week to 338,500. Both figures are near pre-recession levels. Applications are a proxy for layoffs. They spiked in early October because of the partial government shutdown and processing backlogs in California. First-time applications have fallen in five of the past six weeks. The decline indicates that employers are laying off fewer workers.

President Obama said former Secretary of Defense Robert Gates did an outstanding job while at the Pentagon and called him a good friend. Obama responded to Gates' book, "Duty: Memoirs of a Secretary of War," by saying that his administration's policy in Afghanistan was the right one. In the book, Gates questions Obama's commitment to his war policy and details discord among the team that made key decisions about the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Obama said that part of his job as commander in chief is to, quote, "sweat the details" on policies that send men and women into harms' way. Obama spoke Monday as he concluded a meeting with Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy.

The Senate is attempting to pass an anti-violence bill. The previous year, the Democratic-led Senate and Republican-led House passed extensions of the 1994 Violence Against Women Act. Both chambers were unable to reach a compromise. Senate advocates are seeking to address Republican losses among women voters in the November election. The bill is scheduled for a test vote on Monday. It essentially follows the measure that passed the Senate last April.

Officials in Washington and Oregon confirmed Tuesday that 37 people have taken ill with the E. Coli bacteria, up from 22 confirmed illnesses on Monday. Chipotle restaurants are a suspected source of the bacteria. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention praised the restaurant chain for closing 43 of its restaurants in the I-5 region between Portland, Ore. and Seattle, Wash. The CDC had little additional information to share about the exact cause on Tuesday. Dr. Tom Frieden, director of the CDC, said Tuesday: "We don't yet know of a vehicle, which food caused it, or even with certainty that all of the cases that are identified there are related to each other."

Sixteen states filed a lawsuit on Monday challenging President Donald Trump's national emergency declaration for the southern border. The lawsuit was filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The attorneys general from Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New York, Oregon and Virginia joined California Attorney General Xavier Becerra in the lawsuit. The attorneys general from Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon and Virginia joined California Attorney General Xavier Becerra in the lawsuit.

Sen. Bernard Sanders of Vermont said at the Democratic presidential debate in Los Angeles that while the North American trade pact the House passed Thursday is a "modest improvement" over the status quo, he would not vote for it. "It is not going to stop outsourcing. It is not going to stop corporations from moving to Mexico," Sanders said. "The word climate change, to the best of my knowledge, is not discussed in this new NAFTA agreement at all, which is an outrage." On an overwhelming bipartisan vote, the House on Thursday approved President Trump's rewrite of the North American Free Trade Agreement.

A three-judge panel refused a request by Al Franken, the Democratic Senate candidate, to block a lawsuit over a recount in his contest. Franken led Republican candidate Norm Coleman by 225 votes in the recount, and Coleman is contesting the result. The judges' decision means the trial on the lawsuit will start Monday. Mr. Coleman argues that the recount process was flawed. He says that votes were double-counted in some precincts and that more absentee ballots should be admitted.

A shouting stenographer was removed from the House floor as lawmakers voted on a deal to reopen the government and avoid a debt crisis. The stenographer began shouting as the House approved the number of votes needed to pass the bill. According to reporters, she was yelling about God and Freemasons. An official house court stenographer took to the microphone and was screaming ab God. She was saying in the hall you can't serve two masters. Public Radio International's Todd Zwillich recorded the incident.

As classes began at a high school in suburban Pittsburgh on Wednesday morning, a 16-year-old student walked through the hallway stabbing and slashing students with two large knives, authorities said. An assistant principal tackled the student and stabbed 20 students and a security guard, sending students running from the school, officials said. At least four students had serious wounds to the abdomen and torso but were expected to survive. The suspect, Alex Hribal, was treated for cuts to his hand at a hospital before he was taken into custody. He was charged as an adult on Wednesday with four counts of attempted homicide and 21 counts of aggravated assault.

President Obama is reportedly giving serious consideration to a speedy withdrawal of U.S. forces from Afghanistan, leaving no troops there after 2014, The New York Times reported. The Times reported that Obama is considering the "zero option," instead of leaving a residual force, because of his deteriorating relationship with Afghan President Hamid Karzai. The Times said Karzai was upset with American peace talks with the Taliban in Qatar. Karzai accused the U.S. government of leaving the country exposed to its enemies. A June 27 video conference between Obama and Karzai ended badly, which The Times reported contributed to the withdrawal plan.

During a speech on Tuesday, President Trump called for the death penalty for criminals who kill police officers. Trump said, "We're not going to let bad things happen to our police. So we must show appreciation, gratitude, and respect for those who police our streets and patrol our communities. In 2016, an officer was assaulted in America on an average of every ten minutes. Can you believe that? It's outrageous and it's unacceptable. We must end the attacks on our police, and we must end them right now. We believe criminals who kill our police should get the death penalty. Bring it forth."

Three new polls show a close race in Michigan. PPP's latest survey shows a small Santorum lead. A Mitchell Research poll released this morning shows Romney ahead. FiveThirtyEight's latest forecast gives Romney a 51 percent chance of victory. In recent days, Romney's super PAC has focused its ad campaign on attacks on Santorum. Ron Paul is launching a new statewide ad campaign in Michigan attacking Rick Santorum as well. Although their ads are different, the message is the same: attacking Rick Santorum's fiscal record from the right.

Mitt Romney will be talking with Benjamin Netanyahu today. President Obama spoke to the Israeli Prime Minister on the phone. Romney and Netanyahu have been friends for decades. Romney has accused Obama of ignoring the relationship between the U.S. and Israel. He has also criticized Obama for not taking a harder line on Iran. Obama has called it unacceptable for Iran to have a nuclear weapon; Romney has said that it is unacceptable for Iran to develop "nuclear capability." In one interview, Romney described his position and Obama's as the same. Netanyahu wants the U.S. to draw a "red line" that Iran cannot cross without facing an American attack.

Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) said Sunday that he wants Vice President Joe Biden to participate in the talks on raising the U.S. government's debt ceiling and ending the government shutdown. "I hope the president will become engaged. Maybe we need to get Joe Biden out of the witness protection program," McCain said on CBS's "Face the Nation." McCain noted that Biden has good relationships with many lawmakers. Biden has mostly stayed out of negotiations over ending the shutdown, reportedly at the behest of Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-Nev.).

The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals in New Orleans ruled that the State of Texas can now enforce HB 2, an omnibus anti-choice law that mandates that legal abortion facilities meet the standards of ambulatory surgical centers and that doctors who provide abortions have admitting privileges at local hospitals. The law was opposed as medically unnecessary and even dangerous by state- and national-level major medical associations. Anti-choice lawmakers said, against all evidence to the contrary, that HB 2 would increase the "health and safety" of Texans who seek legal abortion care. The law also bans abortion after 20 weeks and severely limits the provision of medication abortion.

A former adviser to Barack Obama's presidential campaign, Samantha Power, is working on the transition team for the State Department for Clinton's anticipated nomination as secretary of state. State Department officials said Friday that Power is among foreign policy experts the president-elect's office selected to help prepare for Clinton's anticipated nomination. The Obama transition team's website includes Power's name as one of 14 members of the "Agency Review Team" for the State Department. During the Democratic primary campaign, Power called Clinton "a monster" in an interview. She then resigned, calling her remarks inexcusable and contradictory to her admiration for Clinton.

President Obama visited DC Central Kitchen, a soup kitchen in Washington, DC, on Monday. He accompanied his wife, Michelle, and daughters Malia and Sasha. They joined an assembly line that was churning out burritos. Asked what the burritos were being stuffed with, Obama said it looked like lamb, along with unidentified vegetables and cheese. Obama said he came to help the facility mark its 25th anniversary on Monday. DC Central Kitchen prepares thousands of meals every day for distribution to local shelters.

Obama said he came to help the facility mark its 25th anniversary on Monday. DC Central Kitchen prepares thousands of meals every day for distribution to local shelters.

Sen. Joni Ernst, the first Republican female to address President Trump's Supreme Court nominee Judge Amy Coney Barrett at Monday's confirmation hearing, expressed excitement for another woman to serve on the high court. If confirmed, Judge Barrett would be the fifth woman ever to serve on the Supreme Court but she would be the first to be a working mother with school-age children. "As a fellow woman, a fellow mom, a fellow Midwesterner, I see you for who you are, and I am glad the American people have the opportunity to get to know Amy Coney Barrett," the Iowa Republican said.

Former pizza executive Herman Cain is reportedly expected to withdraw his name from consideration for the Federal Reserve's Board of Governors, according to an ABC News report. The report states that the decision follows lackluster support from Republican senators. President Trump announced Cain last week. Stephen Moore is a conservative economist and author who is a columnist for The Washington Times. Cain, the former CEO of Godfather Pizza, ran for the GOP presidential nomination in 2012 on a tax plan that would eliminate tax laws in favor of a 9 percent tax on sales, individual income and corporate income across the board.

The White House announced the creation of a team of digital experts tasked with upgrading the government's technology infrastructure and making its websites more consumer friendly. The move is aimed at avoiding a repeat of the website debacle that affected the rollout of President Barack Obama's signature health care legislation last year. While the administration ultimately surpassed its enrollment targets, the opening weeks of sign-ups were plagued with website troubles that raised questions about the administration's competence. The new digital team will be overseen by Mikey Dickerson, an engineer who took leave from Google to supervise fixes to the HealthCare.gov site.

The Chicago Sun-Times reported that President-elect Barack Obama's incoming chief of staff Rahm Emanuel had a deeper involvement in pressing for a U.S. Senate seat appointment than previously reported. Emanuel had direct discussions about the seat with Gov. Blagojevich, who is accused of trying to auction it to the highest bidder. Emanuel talked with the governor in the days following the Nov. 4 election and pressed early on for the appointment of Valerie Jarrett to the post, sources with knowledge of the conversations told the Sun-Times. There was no indication from sources that Emanuel brokered a deal.

Allies are growing worried about President Donald Trump's legal situation, as his lawyers offer an optimistic view. The shifting explanations for why Trump fired national security adviser Michael Flynn have revived questions about whether the president may have obstructed an ongoing investigation of potential contacts between his campaign and Russia. Pressure on the administration has mounted since Flynn last week pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI about his conversations with the Russian ambassador, with prosecutors revealing that he is now cooperating with special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation. A muddled White House response, including a presidential tweet, has left some Trump confidants worried that the president is not being well-served by his legal team.

On Wednesday broadcast of NBC's "Nightly News," 2020 Democratic presidential candidate Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) said he has no plans to slow his presidential campaign after he suffered a heart attack last week. Sanders said, "I misspoke the other day. I said a word I should not have said and media drives me a little bit nuts to make a big deal about it." He added, "We're going to get back into the groove of a very vigorous campaign, I love doing rallies and I love doing town meetings."

The Obama administration will prosecute Khalid Shaikh Mohammed and four other people accused of plotting the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks before a military commission and not a civilian court, as it had planned. Attorney General Eric H. Holder Jr. announced on Monday that he has cleared military prosecutors at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, to file war-crimes charges against the five detainees in the Sept. 11 case. Holder had decided in November 2009 to move the case to a federal civilian courtroom in New York City, but the White House abandoned that plan amid a political backlash.

A freight train derailed Tuesday afternoon just outside Baltimore in the Rosedale area, according to Baltimore area fire and police officials. The incident happened around 2 p.m., officials said. Emergency personnel were on the scene. Social media feeds from fire and police agencies reported an explosion, smoke and fire and that several buildings collapsed in the warehouse area where the train derailed. No injuries were reported. As of 3 p.m., the National Transportation Safety Board said it was watching the situation to determine whether to send investigators to the scene. The train derailed in the 7500 block of Lake Drive and exits from I-95 and I-895 to Pulaski Highway were closed.

At least seven people were killed late Friday when an American drone fired three missiles at a house in Mangroti village in the Shawal area of North Waziristan, the tribal region straddling the border with Afghanistan, according to an intelligence official. The incident occurred hours after Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif announced his cabinet. During his campaign, Sharif often criticized the United States for using drone aircraft to kill militants. The drones targeted a house in Mangroti village in the Shawal area, according to the intelligence official. The identities of the victims were not immediately known, but an intelligence official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described them as militants.

On Sunday, former White House Senior Adviser David Axelrod appeared on NBC's "Meet the Press." Axelrod said it was a "mistake" for President Barack Obama to say his polices are on the ballot this fall in a speech on Thursday. The line, "I'm not on the ballot this fall … but make no mistake, these policies are on the ballot — every single one of them," is already being used in advertisement by Republicans seeking to run against the president. In reaction, Axelrod said, "It was a mistake."

A secret intelligence court has decided to continue an order requiring Verizon Communications to turn over hundreds of millions of telephone records to the government each day in its search for foreign terror or espionage suspects. The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court order must be renewed every three months. It had been set to expire Friday. National Intelligence Director James Clapper announced the new order. The surveillance program has been under scrutiny since June, when former CIA employee and National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden leaked details of two top secret U.S. surveillance programs that critics say violate privacy rights. Snowden has been charged with espionage and is seeking asylum from several countries, including Russia.

President Trump and Republicans have promised that their plan to overhaul the federal health care law will make medical coverage much more affordable. In April, Mr. Trump tweeted that Premiums and deductibles will be "much lower." He also assured Americans that the plan to replace the Affordable Care Act would protect people with potentially expensive medical conditions. As Senate Republicans unveiled draft legislation this week, they reiterated the goal of making it easier and cheaper for consumers to buy coverage than under the current law. "This plan will improve the affordability of health insurance," the Senate majority leader, Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, wrote in an opinion piece on Friday.

The White House defended President Donald Trump's failure to acknowledge the women who accused former staff secretary Rob Porter of domestic violence. White House spokeswoman Sarah Huckabee Sanders told reporters that Trump and the entire administration take domestic violence very seriously. She said the president believes all allegations need to be investigated thoroughly. Sanders said she spoke directly with the president and he had "relayed that message directly to me." Trump posted on Twitter over the weekend that, "Peoples lives are being shattered and destroyed by a mere allegation. Some are true and some are false." He also said he wished Porter well in his future career.

On Wednesday broadcast of NBC's "Nightly News," 2020 Democratic presidential candidate Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) said he has no plans to slow his presidential campaign after he suffered a heart attack last week. Sanders said, "I misspoke the other day. I said a word I should not have said and media drives me a little bit nuts to make a big deal about it." He added, "We're going to get back into the groove of a very vigorous campaign, I love doing rallies and I love doing town meetings."

Last night, Mitt Romney answered one of our many questions on his immigration stance and said he would respect Obama's Deferred action policy if elected into office. Many of you commented on the announcement. The article asked whether this was a desperate move by Romney and his team to get more Latino votes, and whether his shift from his self-deportation comments earlier in the year showed signs of an "evolving" Romney.

On Sunday, former White House Senior Adviser David Axelrod appeared on NBC's "Meet the Press." Axelrod said it was a "mistake" for President Barack Obama to say his polices are on the ballot this fall in a speech on Thursday. The line, "I'm not on the ballot this fall … but make no mistake, these policies are on the ballot — every single one of them," is already being used in advertisement by Republicans seeking to run against the president. In reaction, Axelrod said, "It was a mistake."

Gov. Lincoln Chafee said Monday that Rhode Island will be in good shape despite changes in legislative leadership following law enforcement raids of former House Speaker Gordon Fox's home and office. The Democratic governor said he has been briefed on the investigation related to the raids but declined to comment and referred all questions to federal authorities. Fox has resigned his leadership position. The House is expected to pick a new Speaker Tuesday. Chafee said he looks forward to working with whoever succeeds Fox and said he is confident state leaders can remain focused on their work.

Federal and state investigators learned today that an additional chemical that was not previously identified was in the tank that leaked on Jan. 9 at Freedom Industries tank farm just upstream from West Virginia American Water's regional drinking water intake. The chemical, the company claims, has "low oral toxicity." Company officials told investigators that the "Crude MCHM" that spilled also contained a product called "PPH," which stands for polyglycol ethers, according to the U.S. Chemical Safety Board. The chemical is probably as safe for pregnant women as the other stuff they spilled into the Elk River.

Mitt Romney praised Poland's "economic liberty and smaller government" in a speech Tuesday in Warsaw, Poland. Romney also praised Poland's higher living standards and strong military. The comments fit into his campaign's themes of smaller government, reduced federal spending, and fewer regulations on business. Romney said Poland is thriving because it sought to "stimulate innovation, attract investment, expand trade and live within its means." He said Poland's success is a reminder that "free enterprise can propel an economy and transform a society."

President Barack Obama said the detention center at Guantanamo Bay undermines America's national security and needs to be closed. Obama said the detention center is counterproductive in the fight against terrorism because it is used as propaganda to recruit terrorists and drains military resources. The White House released Obama's plan to close the facility on Tuesday. The plan faces opposition from the GOP-led Congress. The plan calls for transferring remaining detainees to the United States and seeks up to $475 million in construction costs that would ultimately be offset by as much as $180 million per year in operating cost savings. It does not specify where in the U.S. the detainees would go.

Gov. Scott Walker said Wednesday he is optimistic that President Donald Trump's administration will be able to make "meaningful reforms" to the Medicaid program. Walker released a letter that U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price sent to governors pledging to improve the program, which is jointly funded by states and the federal government. The letter comes as Congress is considering a Republican-backed bill that would cut payments to states for Medicaid, the program that provides health care to the poor and lower-income workers.

Sen. Scott Brown (R-Mass.) leads Harvard law professor Elizabeth Warren (D) by four points in the latest Boston Herald/UMass Lowell poll. The poll, conducted four days earlier, shows the Democratic challenger ahead. Brown leads by six points with registered voters and four points with likely voters. The survey has a 5.5 point margin of error. Unlike other recent surveys, this poll finds no convention bounce for Warren. Brown's lead with independents and his support among Obama voters are both larger. A third of Brown supporters are open to changing their vote; 19 percent of Warren backers say the same.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid (D-NV) said Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) "stands for everything America doesn't" and that the Republican Party would end if the GOP nominated Cruz for president in 2016. In an interview with MSNBC's Rachel Maddow that aired on Wednesday, Reid said, "If I didn't care so much about our country, I would hope he would get the Republican nomination for president, because that would mean the end of the Republican Party." Reid then said the Republican Party "is staggering right now" and that he did not "know who they can expect to have a vote for them."

Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton addressed the New Hampshire audience. She said, "I know you have a favorite, but everyone takes a second look, maybe a third or a fourth look. And I hope you give me one of those looks over the next few days." She added, "Of course I still hope to persuade those who are looking at Senator Sanders, but I want you to know that I am truly happy that you are involved in this election and the Democratic Party." The remarks came 24 hours after Clinton and Sanders argued on the debate stage in Durham. Clinton beat Sanders by .2 percent in the Iowa caucus. The Vermont Senator currently leads Clinton by twenty points in some New Hampshire polls.

Congressional bargainers are working toward a border security deal. The White House is preparing to accept a bipartisan agreement that would give President Donald Trump a fraction of the money he has demanded for his proposed southern border wall. Participants said they expect money for physical barriers to end up well below the $5.7 billion that Trump has sought to begin construction of the wall, which has gained significant significance for him and his conservative supporters. The amount seems sure to fall much closer to $1.6 billion, the participants said, a figure that was in a bipartisan Senate bill last year. An agreement would also avert a new partial federal shutdown next weekend.

At least 80 demonstrators were arrested Monday in House and Senate office buildings on Capitol Hill, according to the U.S. Capitol Police. Most were demonstrating against proposed changes to federal health care law, which includes congressional Republicans' efforts to make changes to ObamaCare. Police officials said those arrested were first told to cease and desist their unlawful demonstration and that those who refused were arrested and charged with "crowding, obstructing or incommoding." Officials said 21 adults — 10 males and 11 females — were arrested in the House office building, and 59 adults — 22 males and 37 females — were arrested in Senate office buildings.

The official death toll from Washington's mudslide has increased to 27, with the Snohomish County medical examiner's office reporting 19 victims positively identified. That is up from 24 dead with 18 identified on Monday. Workers are working to improve the flow of the Stillaguamish River through the landslide at Oso to reduce flooding as they continue the recovery of bodies. The latest name to the list is 58-year-old Brandy L. Ward of Arlington. Like the rest she was killed by blunt force injuries in the March 22 slide.

Vietnam's foreign minister Pham Binh Minh arrived in North Korea on Tuesday ahead of a planned summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in Vietnam's capital later this month. Pham Binh Minh is expected to stay until Thursday. No further details of his schedule have been released by his North Korean hosts. Vietnam's capital, Hanoi, is scheduled to host the summit between Trump and Kim on Feb. 27-28. The two leaders held their first summit last June in Singapore. The United States is seeking a firm commitment on denuclearization from Kim.

EMILY's List announced it is spending $250,000 on a radio advertisement supporting Attorney General Martha Coakley (D). The ad is airing statewide with a concentration in the Boston market, a source said. The group said the 60-second ad highlights Coakley's record of voting with the Republican leadership 90 percent of the time and siding with special interests over Massachusetts families. The group had been expected to lose the race until last week.

The Delaware Republican Senate primary produced Christine O'Donnell, a former Opinion Blogger/Editor of The Watercooler, as the victor. The article reported that conflicts arose about whether O'Donnell could win in the November election. Conservative movement leaders expressed support for O'Donnell. Kerry Picket, a former Opinion Blogger/Editor of The Watercooler, was associate producer for the Media Research Center, a content producer for Robin Quivers of "The Howard Stern Show" on Sirius satellite radio, and a production assistant and copy writer at MTV.

Pennsylvania Governor Tom Corbett (R) announced he will not appeal yesterday's federal district court decision striking down the state's exclusion of gay couples from marriage. That makes Pennsylvania the nineteenth state where same-sex marriage will be ongoing. Corbett explained his decision. He said: "I have thoroughly reviewed Judge Jones' opinion in the Whitewood case. Given the high legal threshold set forth by Judge Jones in this case, the case is extremely unlikely to succeed on appeal. Therefore, after review of the opinion and on the advice of my Commonwealth legal team, I have decided not to appeal Judge Jones' decision."

A Wednesday afternoon lunch scheduled for 1:10 p.m. at the White House was postponed, an administration source said. The source said the meeting was canceled because of President Barack Obama's changing schedule and his expected remarks on the matter involving Gen. Stanley McChrystal. The lunch initially was intended to be a bipartisan meeting but was canceled, then rescheduled as a meeting with about half a dozen senators, but only Democratic ones, a source familiar with the schedule said. The lunch had been scheduled for 1:10 p.m.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Jan. 7 that JPMorgan Chase & Co officials will not be penalized as part of a settlement the bank is negotiating with federal authorities to resolve suspicions that it ignored signs of Bernard Madoff's Ponzi scheme, citing people close to the talks. JPMorgan was not immediately available for comment by Reuters outside regular U.S. business hours. Madoff was convicted in 2009 of defrauding thousands of investors and is serving a 150-year prison sentence. JPMorgan has been accused of ignoring warning signs that Madoff's business was a fraud, often to win more fees and commissions for services they provided.

During an online Q&A, First Lady Michelle Obama was asked by Obama impersonator Iman Crosson how many calories could be burned just by dancing. Cross asked, "On average, how many calories do you burn every time you 'turn up'?!?" In response, the First Lady posted a Vine holding a turnip and dancing to the song "Turn Down For What." The meme originated on the internet in response to the song by DJ Snake and Lil Jon. The White House Vine is approaching 6 million "loops."

Chinese state media reported that President Xi Jinping called for restraint when dealing with North Korea during a telephone call with President Donald Trump. The official broadcaster CCTV quoted Xi as telling Trump that China strongly opposed North Korea's nuclear weapons program and hoped "all parties will exercise restraint and avoid aggravating the situation" on the Korean Peninsula. The Trump administration warned that all options, including a military strike, are "on the table" ahead of a possible sixth nuclear test by Pyongyang, which could come as early as this week. The call is the second time the two leaders have spoken directly since meeting in Florida earlier this month as tensions mounted.

CNN and NBC News reported Monday that special counsel Robert Mueller told Attorney General William Barr some three weeks ago that his report would not be conclusive on the question of whether Donald Trump obstructed justice. CNN correspondent Laura Jarrett also reported that a definitive answer on obstruction was "not expected." That means Barr and Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein, who oversaw most of the Russia investigation, had three weeks to plan for the summary they wrote in which they decided to unilaterally exonerate Trump, even though Mueller did not. It is unclear whether they had access to the full range of evidence Mueller laid out in his report.

U.S. Sen. Mark Kirk said in a Chicago Sun-Times column posted Monday that he "looks forward" to President Barack Obama nominating a replacement for Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia. Kirk said the constitution gives the president, Republican or Democrat, the right to send a nominee to the Senate. He said he swore an oath to uphold the constitution, "not to a party or any one individual." Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and other Republicans said the next president should choose Scalia's successor.

President Obama said Thursday that he was not planning to significantly expand the war against the Islamic extremist movement anytime soon. His remarks followed days of debate inside the top levels of his national security bureaucracy about how, where, and whether to strike ISIS in Syria. Those deliberations included an intelligence assessment of America's potential allies in Syria. The deliberations did not produce a consensus battle plan. Obama, who has long been reluctant to enter into the Syrian conflict, told reporters Thursday that "we don't have a strategy yet" for confronting ISIS on a regional level.

Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner said Wednesday that he does not plan to serve in the next Obama administration if President Barack Obama wins a second term in November. Geithner said he was confident that Obama would be re-elected but added that he was also "confident that he is going to have the privilege of having another secretary of the Treasury." The comments came in an interview with Bloomberg Television.

Gallup conducted a survey of congressional leaders on September 5-8 and found Reid has the lowest approval rating among congressional leaders. The poll comes days before Reid attempts to amend the continuing resolution the House passed last week that would fund the government except for the Affordable Care Act. Reid has said he will use a 51-vote threshold to add an amendment that would fund the Affordable Care Act and send the bill back to the House. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) and other conservatives like Mike Lee (R-UT) have said Republicans need to unite to oppose a cloture vote on moving the bill forward so Reid is unable to insert funding for the Affordable Care Act.

The author wrote that they worry that if the United States does not do the Trans-Pacific Partnership, China will break the rules. The author stated that Clinton understands this. The author wrote that once the election is over and trade is addressed, people understand there are a couple of things they want to fix on it, but going forward they've got to build a global economy. The author described this as coming on top of Clinton's true colors leaking out in the Democratic Platform. The author also wrote that Clinton was not believable when she announced her opposition to the Trans-Pacific Partnership negotiated as Secretary of State. The author wrote that Sanders would have opposed the Trans-Pacific Partnership. The author concluded that fair traders are left with Donald Trump.

On October 30, Hillary Clinton, a former Secretary of State from New York, will travel to Los Angeles to raise money for Virginia gubernatorial candidate Terry McAuliffe. The event will be hosted by Haim Saban, a billionaire and former President of the Democratic National Committee. Tickets for the event are priced at $15,000 per person and $25,000 per couple. Clinton is expected to endorse McAuliffe formally this week, as is her husband, former President Bill Clinton. McAuliffe leads in polls in his race for Virginia governor over current state attorney general Ken Cuccinelli.

President Obama said Thursday that he was not planning to significantly expand the war against the Islamic extremist movement anytime soon. His remarks followed days of debate inside the top levels of his national security bureaucracy about how, where, and whether to strike ISIS in Syria. Those deliberations included an intelligence assessment of America's potential allies in Syria. The deliberations did not produce a consensus battle plan. Obama, who has long been reluctant to enter into the Syrian conflict, told reporters Thursday that "we don't have a strategy yet" for confronting ISIS on a regional level.

President Barack Obama said that in an interconnected world, outbreaks of deadly viruses like Ebola have the potential to affect every nation. Obama spoke to representatives of more than 40 countries attending a global health summit at the White House. The president said that while the U.S. is taking "an opportunity to lead" the response to the Ebola outbreak in West Africa, it must also be a global priority. Obama announced last week that the U.S. was dispatching 3,000 military personnel to the region to help contain the outbreak.

Donald Trump Jr., son of President Donald Trump, appeared on Fox News Sunday's "Sunday Morning Futures" and said he believed Democrats and the media "hate" his father more than they love America. Trump said, "They will double down. Any opportunity to hurt Trump, and that is the reality." He continued, "Democrats and media hate Trump much more than they love America because you can't dispute the numbers. You can't dispute all-time low unemployment for every group in this country, every demographic."

MSNBC reported that Donald Trump will not participate in the FOX Debate on January 28. The reason cited by Trump is Meygan Kelly, who Trump said he still hates and is a moderator of that debate. Trump said he will do a fund raiser for veterans instead. Comments on the story are closed.

On Sunday, during NBC's "Meet the Press," President Donald Trump said his administration would speak with Iranian officials without preconditions. Trump said, "I'm not looking for war, and if there is, it'll be obliteration like you've never seen before. But I'm not looking to do that. But you can't have a nuclear weapon. You want to talk good." When host Chuck Todd asked if talks would include preconditions, Trump said, "Not as far as I'm concerned. No preconditions."

On Tuesday at an event in New York City hosted by Cornell University's Institute of Politics & Global Affairs, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-CA) said President Donald Trump was "goading" Democrats to impeach him. Pelosi said, "Trump is goading us to impeach him. That's what he's doing. Every single day, he's just like taunting, taunting, taunting because he knows that it would be very divisive in the country, but he doesn't really care. He just wants to solidify his base."

MSNBC reported that Donald Trump will not participate in the FOX Debate on January 28. The reason cited by Trump is Meygan Kelly, who Trump said he still hates and is a moderator of that debate. Trump said he will do a fund raiser for veterans instead. Comments on the story are closed.

On Thursday, after the House of Representatives passed the revised version of the American Health Care Act, Planned Parenthood President Cecile Richards released a video on Twitter urging voters to call their senators to stop the bill. She described the bill as the "worst bill for women and women's health in a generation," saying, "we have got to stop it in the Senate, but it's going to take every single one of us. We have one job in this moment. Call you senators, and tell them that you oppose the American Health Care Act. This is the fight of our lives."

Twenty or 21 women were brought back to the hotel in Colombia by U.S. Secret Service agents and members of the U.S. military in an incident last week involving alleged misconduct with prostitutes, U.S. Senator Susan Collins said on Tuesday. Collins was briefed by the director of the Secret Service, Mark Sullivan, on Monday evening. "There are 11 agents involved. Twenty or 21 women foreign nationals were brought to the hotel, but allegedly Marines were involved with the rest," the Republican senator said in comments emailed to Reuters by her spokesman.

Rhode Island House Speaker Gordon Fox said in a written statement sent Saturday evening that he is resigning from his leadership post and will not run for re-election. Fox said he will not let Friday's raids distract his colleagues from addressing the challenges facing the state. He said he wants to focus on his family and dealing with the investigation. The raids were part of an investigation by the U.S. attorney's office, FBI, IRS and state police. Officials have not said whom or what they are investigating.

Twenty or 21 women foreign nationals were brought to the hotel, but allegedly Marines were involved with the rest," the Republican senator said in comments emailed to Reuters by her spokesman.

Eric Trump tweeted four words during Monday's opening night of the Democratic National Convention: "This is absolutely terrible." The tweet prompted criticism from responders, who assumed the comment was about the DNC. One person commented: "The state of the union? Yes it is. This Presidency sure is. Can't end soon enough." Other responders mocked the lineup for next week's Republican National Convention.

Melania Trump addressed a cyberbullying summit in Rockville, Maryland, on Monday. She acknowledged that social media can be "destructive and harmful when used incorrectly." She followed up with a captioned tweet: "#BeBest." Twitter users responded by highlighting the Twitter attacks her husband President Donald Trump launches at political rivals, celebrities, and anyone else who crosses him.

Republican Sen. John McCain said Tuesday in an interview with radio station KFYI-AM in Phoenix that he is considering a sixth term in 2016, the year he turns 80. McCain said he is seriously giving a lot of thought to another bid for re-election. He said he is receiving encouragement from businesses that are upset with the recent partial government shutdown. He had opposed the tea party tactic of linking gutting the health care law to keeping the government operating. McCain unsuccessfully sought the presidency in 2008 and won another Senate term in 2010. He has challenged President Barack Obama on foreign policy but has worked with Democrats on immigration legislation.

Gov. Rick Scott said Friday he has not seen the letter that had been sent to Florida Secretary of State Ken Detzner on Wednesday. A spokeswoman for Detzner said the agency was reviewing the request. The Presidential Advisory Commission on Election Integrity asked election officials across the country for voter information, including names, political party affiliation and voter history. The request included asking for the last four digits of voters' Social Security numbers. Democratic officials in some states said they will not comply with the request because it is based on false fraud accusations. Trump has claimed, without evidence, that between 3 million and 5 million people voted illegally last year.

Protesters shouting about the Keystone XL pipeline interrupted President Barack Obama's speech on health care in Massachusetts on Wednesday. Obama responded to the protesters with a joke about their timing. "This is the wrong rally!" Obama said as the protesters were escorted out. "We had the climate change rally back in the summer." A video of the incident was recorded. At 4:37 p.m., Sophie Robinson and Shea Riester were named as protesters by 350.org. "Mr. President, Reject Keystone XL! Stop Climate Change! For our generation, Stop the pipeline!" the two shouted during Obama's speech.

Hillary Rodham Clinton's coming memoir about her tenure as Secretary of State will be titled "Hard Choices," her publisher said early Friday. The title reflects the dilemma Mrs. Clinton faced at the State Department, carrying out President Obama's vision of diplomacy while bringing her own more hawkish stance to foreign policy discussions. As Mrs. Clinton emerges as a potential 2016 presidential candidate, she has been pushed to more clearly define her legacy as secretary of state. When asked recently at an event in New York what her proudest accomplishment was at the State Department, her response lacked specifics and set off criticism.

President Obama spoke Saturday before the Global Entrepreneurship Summit in Kenya, where he is conducting his first presidential visit to the country. "Entrepreneurship offers a positive alternative to the ideologies of violence and division that can all too often fill the void when young people don't see a future for themselves," Obama said. The president noted "Africa is on the move" and that it is "one of the fastest-growing regions in the world," according to Reuters. China has overtaken the U.S. as the continent's biggest trading partner. Obama pushed the Kenyan government to do more to protect businesspeople from corruption.

As Republicans prepared to campaign on a pledge to try to repeal the measure, Obama and the Democrats will work to keep voters focused on the new benefits, rather than the size, cost or complexity of the bill. Democratic strategist Chris Kofinis said the real political battle over health-care reform begins after its passage. Kofinis said Republicans cannot let Republicans seize the message advantage, as they did during last summer's "tea party" and town hall protests. Kofinis said Democrats must take the initiative and aggressively sell the reform to the American people not for a few days, or weeks, but all the way through the election.

White House spokesman Robert Gibbs said President Obama will travel to Manitowoc, Wisconsin, on Wednesday regardless of the outcome. Gibbs made the prediction this week, prompting speculation that Obama would attend the Super Bowl if the Bears win. When asked about his plans for the game, Obama laughed and said: "Oh, if the Bears are in the Super Bowl, we're going." Gibbs said that as a superstitious fan, it was too soon to be making Super Bowl plans.

President Barack Obama entered hip-hop music at the White House Correspondents' Dinner on Saturday. "How do you like my new entrance music?" Obama said, smirking. "Rush Limbaugh warned you about this. Second term, baby." Obama entered "All I Do is Win," a DJ Khaled song featuring Ludacris, who once rapped about wanting to paint the White House black. The president also joked, in reference to Limbaugh, "We're changing things" in the second term.

President Barack Obama told reporters he had "no reaction" to reports that Donald Trump would address the situation today. Obama said he was "shocked" that the media was covering the issue, adding he finds it "typical." "I was pretty confident about where I was born, I think people were as well," he said. "And my hope would be that the presidential election reflects more serious things than that."

After the primary election defeat of Representative Eric Cantor of Virginia, the race to remake the Republican leadership may shift to the right. Representative Kevin McCarthy of California appeared all but certain on Thursday night to rise from majority whip, the No. 3 job, to majority leader after Representatives Pete Sessions and Jeb Hensarling of Texas withdrew from the race to succeed Mr. Cantor. Unless a new contender emerges before the leadership vote next Thursday, the new majority leader will have a less conservative voting record than the man he is replacing.

Former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg said Tuesday in the Democratic presidential debate in Charleston, South Carolina, that he is concerned marijuana is damaging the brains of the nation's youth. Bloomberg said he supports decriminalizing the possession of marijuana but said the federal government should go slow when it comes to all-out legalization. "They haven't done enough research and the evidence so far is worrisome," Bloomberg said. "Until we know the science, it is not sensible to push ahead."

North Korea launched a rocket on Sunday that Western experts believe is part of a program to develop intercontinental ballistic missile technologies. The rocket blasted off from Tongchang-ri, the North's main satellite launch site near its northwestern border with China, a spokesman for the South Korean Defense Ministry said. President Park Geun-hye of South Korea called an emergency meeting of top national security advisers on Sunday to address the launch, her office said. South Korea, the United States and Japan also requested an emergency meeting of the United Nations Security Council.

Japan said on Saturday it was coordinating with the U.S. government for American citizens to leave the quarantined cruise ship Diamond Princess and return home on U.S.-chartered flights. The Japanese government believes the steps taken by the United States will ease Japan's burden regarding the medical response to the situation on the Diamond Princess and it appreciates these measures, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said. The United States said earlier on Saturday it would send an aircraft to Japan to bring back U.S. passengers on the Diamond Princess, where the most coronavirus infections outside China have occurred.

The U.S. government will hit the $16.4 trillion federal debt limit on Monday and turn to "extraordinary measures" to continue borrowing, the Treasury Department said Wednesday. The countdown begins until Congress passes legislation to allow more borrowing or the government defaults on its debt.

Vietnam's foreign minister Pham Binh Minh arrived in North Korea on Tuesday and is expected to remain until Thursday, according to a North Korean source. No further details of his schedule have been released by his North Korean hosts. Hanoi is scheduled to host the summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on Feb. 27-28. The two leaders held their first summit in Singapore in June last year. The United States is seeking a firm commitment on denuclearization from Kim.

The campaign of former Israeli military chief Gantz, who is a leading challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the race for re-election, said the candidate has been targeted by an Iranian hacking attack. Gantz's campaign said its opponents leaked the information to damage his political bid. The campaign said the timing of the report weeks before Israel's April 9 elections "raises important questions." A campaign official said the security breach happened several months ago, before Gantz entered politics. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to media.

The Senate Armed Services Committee will hold a confirmation hearing on the nomination of Chuck Hagel to be the next defense secretary on Jan. 31. The panel announced the hearing in a statement issued Wednesday. Committee chairman, Sen. Carl Levin of Michigan, has expressed support for Hagel, President Barack Obama's pick to replace Leon Panetta as Pentagon chief. The panel's top Republican, Sen. Jim Inhofe of Oklahoma, said in a statement late Tuesday that he would oppose the nomination. Inhofe is one of a handful of Republicans who have expressed opposition to Hagel, a Republican who served two terms as senator from Nebraska.

Prosecutors are close to resting their case against Maj. Nidal Hasan, an Army psychiatrist accused of killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others in a Fort Hood shooting. Hasan might begin presenting his defense as soon as Tuesday. The question is whether Hasan will testify on his own behalf. Hasan is acting as his own attorney. The U.S.-born Muslim began the trial by telling jurors that he was the gunman who killed and wounded the others in the 2009 shooting rampage. He also has leaked documents during the trial that seek to justify the shooting as a defending his faith.

A man helping campaign for U.S. Republican presidential candidate Ben Carson died after being injured in a car accident in Iowa on Tuesday, according to a statement from Nebraska Medical Center in Omaha, Nebraska, released by Carson's campaign. Campaign volunteer Braden Joplin, 25, died in Nebraska Medical Center after being admitted in critical condition following the accident in Atlantic, Iowa, the statement said. Carson, a retired neurosurgeon, temporarily suspended his campaign and was traveling from South Carolina to Omaha where he was planning to meet with Joplin's family members and offer his condolences.

Republican nominee Donald Trump's speech at the Republican National Convention drew at least two million more viewers than Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton's speech at the Democratic National Convention. According to Nielsen television ratings, just under 28 million viewers tuned in for Clinton's speech, while 30 million viewers tuned in for Trump's speech. Although Trump had a bigger audience than Clinton, more people watched the DNC over the RNC earlier in the week. CNN reported that the second night of the DNC had 25 percent more viewers than the second night at the RNC.

Donald Trump Jr., President Donald Trump's eldest son, posted a tweet asking people to "name a single Democrat accomplishment?" The tweet referenced the signing of a new trade agreement with China by his father. Commenters noted that the Democratic-controlled House had just impeached him over the Ukraine scandal. One commenter wrote, "I'd say that was a pretty big accomplishment." Other commenters highlighted the Democratic taking of the House in the 2018 midterms.

The Senate voted on Wednesday to save the FCC's Obama-era net neutrality rules, which are set to expire on June 11. Democrats used a legislative mechanism known as the Congressional Review Act to force a vote. Three Republican senators — Susan Collins (R-ME), John Kennedy (R-MS), and Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) — voted for the measure. The Senate's efforts to have the rules reinstated have not succeeded. The bill faces little chance of passing the Republican-controlled House. The Commission, now chaired by Ajit Pai, repealed the order in April.

The European Union banned arms sales to Venezuela and established a system for asset freezes and travel restrictions on some Venezuelan officials. EU foreign ministers announced the measures at talks in Brussels on Monday. The weapons ban would stop sales of military equipment that could be used for repression or surveillance of Venezuelans. The EU said in a statement that the measures can be reversed depending on how Maduro reacts to demands for more democracy in the South American nation. The United States last Thursday imposed financial sanctions on another 10 current and former Venezuelan officials over corruption and abuse of power allegations related to Maduro's crackdown on the opposition.

First Lady Michelle Obama retired President Barack Obama's mom jeans. The jeans will not be immortalized in Cooperstown. President Barack Obama told an audience at the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown on Thursday. "At the Hall's request, I contributed something of my own, which was the jacket I wore when I threw out the first pitch at the 2009 All-Star Game," Obama said, according to pool reports. "I hear that with all the media attention about it, there was also some interest in the jeans I wore that night. But Michelle retired those jeans quite a while back."

President Obama will make his first trip as president to Kenya and Ethiopia later this week. In 2008, the United States elected the son of a Kenyan economist to its highest office. Seven years later, the organization is seeking African participants to share their experiences and perspectives on how Mr. Obama has performed and what he should still try to accomplish. The questions include whether the president lived up to expectations and whether he has made a difference in the lives of Africans. The organization may publish a selection of the responses with upcoming coverage. The submission form is no longer accepting submissions.

Wall Street Journal columnist Peggy Noonan described President Obama's decision to go on five Sunday shows in one day as "boorish" in a Sunday show appearance with ABC News host George Stephanopoulos. Noonan, a former speechwriter, told Stephanopoulos: "He's doing it because he can. The media environment allows a modern leader to be something subtly damaging, and that is boorish. They get their face in your face every day all the time. It's boorish and it makes people not lean toward you but lean away from you, no matter what the merits of the issue."

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi has named six Democrats to a special panel formed by Republicans to investigate Planned Parenthood. Rep. Jan Schakowsky of Illinois will act as ranking member of the 13-member special committee, which will be housed within the Energy and Commerce Committee. The committee will be given broad authority to investigate alleged wrongdoing by the women's health and abortion provider, which has come under fire for supplying aborted fetal tissue to human tissue companies. The other five Democrats on the panel will include Reps. Jerry Nadler of New York, Diana DeGette of Colorado, Suzan DelBene of Washington, Jack Speier of California and Bonnie Watson of New Jersey.

American intelligence reports indicate that the forces of President Bashar al-Assad of Syria have substantially increased their air attacks, which the reports describe as exploiting an offensive advantage against Syrian rebels. Top Obama administration officials met Wednesday to review military options to help the rebels reverse their deteriorating position. The Syrian military's use of warplanes and helicopters has increased. It carried out at least 500 air-to-ground attacks against rebels and civilians in May, according to the intelligence reports, which were described by officials who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to discuss them.

BP agreed to put $20 billion into an escrow account for victims' claims. That does not include cleanup costs. A White House official said the $20 billion is not a cap, meaning if costs exceed $20 billion, they may go to BP for more. Kenneth Feinberg, the same attorney who oversaw payments to victims of the 9/11 attacks, oversaw payments to victims of the Deepwater Horizon oil leak.

Secretary of State Hillary Clinton testified before Congress on Wednesday morning. She cautioned against retreating from dangerous diplomatic posts and made an emotional display of emotion as her voice broke. She said she takes the issue of diplomat safety personally. The Post reported that Clinton is more popular than ever, and that American Foreign Service Association president Susan Johnson spoke about the dangers embassy workers face in an interview with Federal Diary columnist Joe Davidson.

President Barack Obama nominated Loretta E. Lynch to be the next attorney general. At a White House ceremony Saturday, Obama said Lynch has a fierce commitment to equal justice and a solid record as a tough, fair federal prosecutor. Obama said it is "pretty hard to be more qualified" for the job. Lynch, 55, would be the first African-American woman to serve as attorney general. She is currently the top federal prosecutor in Brooklyn, New York. Outgoing Attorney General Eric Holder also attended Saturday's announcement. Holder was the first black head of the Justice Department.

Israel aircraft bombed a target in Syria overnight Thursday, an Obama administration official said Friday night. United States officials said they were considering military options, including carrying out their own airstrikes. American officials did not provide details on the target of the Israeli strike. In late January, Israel carried out airstrikes against SA-17 antiaircraft weapons, which the Israelis feared were about to be moved to the Hezbollah Shiite militia in Lebanon. Israel has been concerned that chemical weapons and advanced arms might be transferred to Hezbollah from Syria. The Israeli military has made clear that it is prepared to take action to stop such shipments.

The Senate Judiciary Committee will begin its immigration hearings this year with testimony from Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano next week. Napolitano has overseen the administration's immigration efforts for the last four years. She is currently traveling through the Southwest, where she says the border is finally secure, and has urged lawmakers to turn their attention to legalizing illegal immigrants and overhauling the broader immigration system. Both the House and Senate are holding hearings ahead of what is expected to be a contentious legislative fight. The House Judiciary Committee held its first hearings Tuesday, with testimony from advocates and former government experts, but nobody from the Obama administration.

On Wednesday, the Obama administration announced it would withdraw from a United Nations vote on ending Jewish settlement building on occupied Palestinian territory. Secretary of State John Kerry delivered a 72-minute address from Foggy Bottom. The decision followed the administration's abstention from a United Nations vote on ending Jewish settlement building on occupied Palestinian territory. Kerry addressed Israeli leaders about the importance of peace and a two-state solution. "If the choice is one state, Israel can either be Jewish or democratic, it cannot be both, and it won't ever really be at peace," he said.

President Trump said Tuesday he would prefer to let Russia back into the G-7 group of top industrialized nations. Speaking in the Oval Office during a visit with the president of Romania, Trump said, "I think it's much more appropriate to have Russia in." Russia's participation in the Group of Eight was suspended in 2014 after its annexation of the Crimean peninsula from Ukraine. The country announced its permanent withdrawal in 2017.

Former NBA player and Celebrity Apprentice contestant Dennis Rodman tweeted to Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) that Donald Trump is "about to fire your ass." Cruz mentioned Rodman during the CNN Republican presidential debate on Thursday in Houston. Cruz said that while Cruz was busy fighting amnesty, Trump was busy "firing Dennis Rodman on Celebrity Apprentice." Rodman endorsed Trump in July, saying that Trump "has been a great friend for many years. We don't need another politician, we need a businessman like Mr. Trump!"

White House Chief of Staff John Kelly denied a report that he called President Donald Trump an "idiot." Kelly told NBC News on Monday that he always knows where he stands and that he and Trump both know the story is total BS. Kelly said he is committed to the president, his agenda, and the country. The report circulated online.

President Donald Trump tweeted several times over the weekend that he "won the election," despite the fact that he lost. Trump also made claims of voter fraud more than one week after President-elect Joe Biden was projected the winner of the 2020 election. Several world leaders congratulated Biden on his win, and several GOP lawmakers have called him the president-elect. Some Republicans have echoed Trump's rhetoric, floating the idea that Trump still has a chance at a second term in office.

International envoy Kofi Annan announced in Geneva that the United Nations Security Council will hold a conference on Syria on Saturday. Annan said the five permanent members — Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States — are invited, along with Turkey. Annan said the invitations included the U.N. secretary-general and representatives of the League of Arab States, including diplomats from Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar. The conference aims at finding ways to stop the violence in Syria.

John Kerry made his first visit to sub-Saharan Africa as secretary of state on Saturday. He urged Nigeria to uphold human rights as it steps up its fight against Islamic extremists. When asked about reports of serious human rights violations by Nigerian forces, Kerry said, "One's person's atrocity does not excuse another's." He added, "We defend the right completely of the government of Nigeria to defend itself and to fight back against terrorists." Kerry also raised the issue of human rights with the government.

The public corruption case against former Virginia Gov. Bob McDonnell and his wife, Maureen, is in the hands of a federal jury. The seven-man, five-woman jury left the courtroom to begin deliberations Tuesday after hearing nearly two hours of instructions from U.S. District Judge James Spencer. The jury heard from dozens of witnesses over a five-week trial. The McDonnells are charged with doing special favors for Jonnie R. Williams Sr., the former CEO of dietary supplements maker Star Scientific Inc., in exchange for more than $165,000 in gifts and loans.

The morning meeting concluded with the announcement that FOX had confirmed the new Supreme Court nominee. At 10:15 am, President Obama was scheduled to introduce Sonia Sotomayor. The article provided bio information, analysis of the decision, and a summary of the decision. The article reported that North Korea had conducted missile testing. Two more missiles were tested. The article asked what the United States would do about the testing and whether the UN would be able to make an impact. Peter Brooks was scheduled to join the 12 PM hour for the discussion.

President Obama signed legislation Wednesday canceling furloughs of air-traffic controllers that had resulted in airport delays. The Federal Aviation Administration said it instituted the furloughs due to automatic budget cuts that took effect March 1. The law allows the agency to transfer as much as $253 million from other accounts through September, action the agency said it did not have flexibility to do under the budget cuts.

A Bloomberg National Poll shows Hillary Clinton's favorability rating at 70 percent, down from 58 percent in December. Among Americans, 22 percent view her very unfavorably, compared to 11 percent in December. Forty-two percent of Americans say they would vote for her for president, while 33 percent say they would not. Forty-three percent of women would vote for her. Among Democrats, three-quarters would back her, while 33 percent would not. Among independent voters, 47 percent disapprove of how Clinton handled Benghazi, while 34 percent approve.

Rabbi Jeffrey Myers said on "Good Morning America" on Monday that Saturday's shooting attack on his synagogue was an "attack upon America." Myers said, "Many will just see this as an attack upon the Jewish community. It's not." Robert Gregory Bowers, arrested and accused of killing 11 individuals at the Tree of Life Synagogue, was arrested and is accused of killing six more victims, including four police officers. The suspected gunman is due in court on Monday.

Hillary Clinton raised $45 million in donations from supporters during the first quarter of her campaign, according to early numbers released by her staff. The mid-April to June 30 haul was a record for a candidate in their first quarter, surpassing the previous record held by President Obama, who raised $41.9 million in the first quarter of his re-election campaign. Ninety-one percent of all donations were $100 or less, according to Hillary for America Chairman John Podesta. Clinton said this was a number she and the campaign are "especially proud of."

President Barack Obama delivered a speech at American University in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. He was late for the speech and attributed printer toner issues to the delay. "I apologize for the slight delay; even presidents have problems with toner," he said. He then smiled as the audience laughed. Obama is delivering an Iran nuclear deal pitch at the university, one of many such events over the next several weeks to help build support in Congress for the deal.

Bob Dylan declined an invitation to meet President Obama at the White House on Wednesday. The singer-songwriter will not be among a group of U.S. Nobel Prize laureates meeting with Obama in the Oval Office. The president invited the winners to congratulate them before they travel to Sweden to receive their prizes on Dec. 10. Dylan, awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature, is not traveling to Stockholm for the ceremony.

House Speaker Rep. Paul Ryan, R-Wis., said on Thursday that the United States was too soon to say whether the mass shooting in San Bernadino, Calif., was an act of terrorism. He argued that the proper response to mass shootings is to overhaul the nation's mental health system rather than changing gun laws. "If your stomach isn't turned when you see these acts of violence on TV, there's something wrong with you," Ryan said on MSNBC's "Morning Joe" on Thursday. "The question is, can we address these issues without violating a citizen's rights?"

On NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi indicated tentative support for former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton's probable 2016 presidential run. Pelosi said she makes a habit of not endorsing people until they make a decision to run, but she thinks there are many people waiting to see if Clinton runs. She added, "I'm really excited about the prospect of a woman president of the United States. I think it would be well, especially a woman as well qualified as Hillary Clinton."

A shooting at Santa Fe High School in Santa Fe, Texas, killed at least eight people Friday morning and injured one police officer. Politicians reacted with tweets and statements offering variations of the now-standard "thoughts and prayers." Parkland school shooting survivors responded with a different tone. They responded both to the Santa Fe High School shooting and to politicians they accuse of enabling it. President Donald Trump had to say: "For the record, here's what President Donald Trump had to say."

Former Senate Majority Leader Bob Dole saluted President George H.W. Bush at the casket of the late president. Dole, a World War II veteran who represented Kansas in the U.S. Senate, arrived in the Capitol rotunda Tuesday in a wheelchair pushed by an aide. At the casket's side, the aide lifted Dole, 95, into a standing position. Once steadied, Dole saluted. Bush achieved the office that Dole sought in 1996 as the Republican presidential nominee.

The Institute for Supply Management reported its services index rose to 59.6 in August from 58.7 in July, the highest since the measure was introduced in January 2008. Fifteen of 17 industries reported growth last month. Mining and arts, entertainment and recreation contracted in August. The ISM is a trade group of purchasing managers. Its services survey covers businesses that employ 90 percent of the American workforce, including retail, construction, health care and financial services firms.

More than 100 law officers continued a nationwide manhunt for an armed bank robber suspected of shooting two Tupelo, Mississippi, police officers, one of them fatally, the FBI said Thursday. The bank robbery in Tupelo turned into a shootout Monday afternoon, and the robber or robbers escaped and remain at large, the FBI said. The FBI, local banks and business are offering a more than $150,000 reward leading to the identification and capture of the bank robber, the FBI said. The suspect was driving a gray sedan as he fled eastbound on Carnation Street in Tupelo, the FBI said.

Michigan Gov. Rick Snyder (R) live-tweeted Sunday night's Democratic presidential debate in Michigan. He defended his administration's choices that led nearly 100,000 Flint residents drinking poisonous water. Snyder tweeted that he is "taking responsibility" for the crisis and argued that the choice to use corrosive water from the Flint River was "never about money." "This was a failure of government at all levels that could be described as a massive error of bureaucracy," he tweeted.

The White House is naming Hope Hicks as communications director. Hicks, 28, is a longtime aide of President Donald Trump who served as his presidential campaign's lead spokeswoman. She has been interim communications director for the past few weeks. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said Tuesday that Hicks has been named to the job permanently. Hicks is the third White House communications director in the administration's nearly eight months. Her predecessor, Anthony Scaramucci, served in the role for less than two weeks after being removed over language he used about two then White House advisers.

A gunman holding hostages in a Sydney cafe is said to be demanding an ISIS flag and a phone call with Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott. Photographs from local media showed people, believed to be hostages, with their hands pressed against the glass of the Lindt Chocolate Cafe in Sydney's central business district. The writing on the flag in the window stoked fears that the crisis in Sydney could be linked to Islamic extremists. Australia, which is part of the international coalition fighting ISIS in the Middle East, said in September that it had foiled a plot by Islamic militants to carry out a public execution.
