Financial markets ended slightly lower Thursday, for their first loss in a week of nominal highs. The escalating conflict in Ukraine, along with disappointing earnings and profit outlooks from retailers, weighed down the market. The United States economy and labor market data also declined. Erik Davidson, deputy chief investment officer at Wells Fargo Private Bank, said the key driver was largely the Ukraine news and the uncertainty of what that means. President Petro O. Poroshenko of Ukraine said Russian forces had entered his country. He called an emergency meeting of the nation's security council.

President Obama visited activists fasting to protest House inaction on immigration legislation. On the day after Thanksgiving, the president stopped by a white tent on the National Mall where some activists have shunned all food except water for the past 18 days. A top labor organizer is among them. Obama told the activists that he appreciated their efforts. He also reiterated his view that there is still time this year for the House to pass legislation. House Speaker John Boehner has refused to schedule votes on a comprehensive immigration measure the Senate passed this summer. Boehner has opted for a piecemeal approach. Immigration advocates say that process has moved too slowly to satisfy immigration advocates.

Iranian President Hassan Rouhani said Wednesday he wants to extend health insurance coverage to 5 million of his country's uninsured. In a tweet, Rouhani referred to his plan as "RouhaniCare." The term "RouhaniCare" is a familiar label for the president. Rouhani, in contrast to his predecessor Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, has sought inroads with the West and, in particular, the United States. His English language Twitter account is often topical and plays to that Western audience. Rouhani is also in the midst of nuclear negotiations aimed at reining in his country's ability to produce a nuclear bomb.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry said "very real gaps" persist between world powers and Iraq over the contours of a nuclear agreement as a Sunday deadline for a deal approaches. Kerry cited some progress after two days of nuclear talks with Iran and its European partners in Vienna. He said much work remains. Kerry said he is returning to Washington on Tuesday to consult with President Barack Obama and Congress about the state of negotiations. He said he will also discuss the possibility of extending the talks past the deadline so negotiations can continue.

Early results from Iran's presidential election showed reformist-backed candidate Hassan Rouhani in the lead. Official figures gave him 51% of the five million ballots counted so far, ahead of second-placed Tehran mayor Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf on 17%. If Rouhani maintains that margin, he will avoid a run-off vote. Electoral officials said turnout was high among the 50 million Iranians eligible to vote on Friday for a successor to Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.

Funeral services for Rev. Clementa Pinckney are scheduled for today. The service is open to the public and thousands are expected to attend, including President Obama, who will deliver the eulogy, First Lady Michelle Obama, Vice President Joe Biden, Hillary Clinton, a congressional delegation, and many other leaders from across the country. According to aides, President Obama wrote and delivered the eulogy for Beau Biden, son of Vice President Biden. According to aides, he also wrote the eulogy for Rev. Clementa Pinckney himself.

North Korea has been open about its ultimate military goal. Kim Jong Un wants a nuclear weapon on top of an intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching the United States. The regime has recently shown significant advancements in its internationally condemned nuclear program and exchanged escalating threats with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration. Former President Barack Obama warned his successor about Kim. North Korea has become one of the Trump administration's most pressing international concerns.

A poll released Monday by Chegg, an online textbook rental and tutoring company, found that a plurality of college students think billionaire businessman Donald Trump won the first Republican presidential debate. Twenty-six percent of college or college-bound students said Trump won the debate, according to the survey. Sixteen percent said former Florida Gov. Jeb Bush won, 14 percent thought Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Fla.) won, and 10 percent went for Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.).

A super PAC supporting Ted Cruz's presidential campaign released two new ads on Wednesday. One video shows conservative firebrand Sean Hannity and pollster Frank Luntz saying Cruz had the line of the night during CNBC's debate and former Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin arguing that Cruz "schooled the media." Cruz is shown saying: "The questions that have been asked so far in this debate illustrate why the American people don't trust the media. The questions that are being asked shouldn't be trying to get people to tear into one another. ... This is not a cage match."

TSA administrator John Pistole acknowledged that new pat-downs are more invasive than what travelers were used to in the past. Pistole said he has received the new pat-down, as has Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano. Some travelers complain that the new inspections target sensitive body areas. Pistole said he understands those privacy concerns but says the government must provide the best possible security for air travelers. Pistole was testifying before a Senate committee about TSA policies and procedures. The hearing was scheduled before recent criticism of airport security pat-downs.

On Monday, Bo, President Barack Obama's family's dog, got a sister named Sunny. Sunny, who was born in Michigan in June 2012, is also a Portuguese Water Dog, which helps because Malia Obama has allergies. The White House said Sunny is the perfect little sister for Bo, full of energy and very affectionate, and the First Family picked her name because it fit her cheerful personality. In October, Michelle Obama said Bo did not have enough "doggie interaction." The Obamas reportedly first got the idea of getting a Portuguese Water Dog from the late Sen. Ted Kennedy (D-MA).

On Monday, Rep. Ted Lieu (D-CA) appeared on CNN and said President Donald Trump's tweet about a video showing him wrestling a man with a CNN logo as his face suggested violence against journalists. Lieu said, "Donald Trump has had a series of highly disturbing tweets, but his tweet yesterday morning was beyond inappropriate. It was suggesting violence against journalists, and that's going to increase the risk of harm to journalists. The president of the United States should never be inciting violence against any human being."

U.S. Representative Michele Bachmann (R-MN) announced on her Facebook page that she plans to form an exploratory committee for a presidential run in 2012. She has yet to file with the Federal Election Commission. Last week, the blog featured quotes from Bachmann. The blog also included a selection of possible running mates for her campaign. The blog invited readers to vote for a potential running mate.

Heavy rain and lightning early Wednesday morning forced dozens of Girl Scouts camping on the South Lawn of the White House to shelter inside the Eisenhower Executive Office Building. First Lady Michelle Obama hosted the scouts for a camp-out to promote her "Let's Move" campaign designed to get young people exercising more outdoors. Early in the evening, the first lady told the girls they were making history with their South Lawn sleepover, noting that no one had ever camped out in tents on the White House grounds before. The president also made an appearance and spoke to the young scouts.

President Obama spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in person but on the phone. The call followed Netanyahu's public demand for red lines on Iran during his UN speech. In the phone call, Obama reiterated his earlier position that no red lines will be set. The two leaders discussed a broad array of issues. The Obama administration stated they are in full agreement on the shared goal of preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Obama told Netanyahu there will be no red lines for you.

White House press secretary Jay Carney said press secretary Cummings had been "disrespected." Carney said Cummings is always the smartest guy in the room and that if he wants to speak, he should be allowed to speak. Cummings tried to ask a procedural question Wednesday during a hearing with former IRS official Lois Lerner when Rep. Darrell Issa, chairman of the House Oversight Committee, ended the session. Cummings shouted that he deserved the right to speak and told Issa, "you cannot run a committee like this."

Rep. Dennis Kucinich, R-Ohio, has offered an amendment to defund the Libya operation. The most recent amendment was voted down yesterday, 229-199. Several other Libya efforts failed in the House last month. The Defense Appropriations Subcommittee Chair, Bill Young, R-Fla., told Kucinich on the floor that he "is persistent" and expressed concern that Kucinich had introduced the amendment after multiple days of debate on the bill.

Kansas Sen. Pat Roberts (R) won his re-election bid, defeating Independent candidate Greg Orman in the midterm elections, according to CBS and Fox News. Roberts had been competing against Democrat Chad Taylor until September 2014, when Taylor withdrew from the race and requested his name removed from the ballot. After a dispute between Taylor and Kansas Secretary of State Kris Kobach, the state Supreme Court ordered Kansas to remove Taylor's name. Roberts was first elected to the Senate in 1996 and before that served as a member of the House of Representatives.

U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions said Tuesday at a conference in Atlanta that one of his top priorities is investigating and prosecuting sex crimes against children, even though technology has made it easier for criminals to avoid detection. Sessions, a former prosecutor, said predators have an easier path to reach children through phones and tablets. He did not address President Donald Trump's criticism of the Department of Justice's legal strategy to defend a travel ban before the Supreme Court. Trump made the comments Monday on Twitter.

U.S. President Donald Trump accused Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau on Thursday of "being so indignant," as the two leaders prepared for a Group of Seven summit in Quebec on Friday. The summit is likely to center on trade disagreements. Trump wrote on Twitter: "Prime Minister Trudeau is being so indignant, bringing up the relationship that the U.S. and Canada had over the many years and all sorts of other things ... but he doesn't bring up the fact that they charge us up to 300% on dairy — hurting our Farmers, killing our Agriculture!"

Vice President Mike Pence addressed Young America Foundation's fall college retreat on Friday. Pence said, "We're going to fight for an outcome in this election that wins us four more years." Pence made the remarks as President Donald Trump continues to refuse to concede. Trump has repeatedly pressed allegations of widespread voter fraud. His administration has said there is no evidence to support the claims.

On Tuesday night in an interview with CBS's Charlie Rose, Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg said there was "no doubt" sexism played a role in former Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton's loss. When asked if sexism played a role in 2016, Ginsburg said, "I have no doubt that it did." When asked if it was "decisive," Ginsburg added, "There are so many things that might have been decisive, but that was a major, major factor."

On Sunday morning, President Donald Trump tweeted a video showing him wrestling a CNN logo. CNN responded with a statement. The statement stated: "It is a sad day when the president of the United States encourages violence against reporters." White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the president had never done so. The statement also said: "Instead of preparing for his overseas trip, his first meeting with Vladimir Putin, North Korea and working on the health care bill he is involved in juvenile behavior far below the dignity of his office. We'll keep doing our jobs. he should start doing his."

After a week of violent unrest in the United States, peace largely prevailed on Tuesday and into the night, with clashes between police and the public seeming to subside. In major cities, including New York, Washington, Los Angeles, and Minneapolis, protesters defied curfews to express outrage over racism and police brutality following the death of yet another black man in police custody. In Washington, swarmed by a federal force, police near the White House fired pepper balls at protesters, who responded with shouts and fireworks early Wednesday.

The chairman of a Senate committee, Carl Levin of Michigan, said at a hearing Tuesday that the sexual battery arrest of the Air Force officer who led the branch's Sexual Assault Prevention and Response unit underscores how far the Defense Department has to go in addressing sexual crimes in the military. Levin said a Pentagon report to be released reportedly estimates that, on average, there are more than 70 sexual assaults involving military personnel every day. Authorities in Arlington County, Va., said Lt. Col. Jeffrey Krusinski has been charged with groping a woman in a northern Virginia parking lot on Sunday.

Twitter suspended President Trump's account, @realDonaldTrump, on Wednesday evening and threatened to permanently ban him from the platform. The suspension followed an unprecedented and ongoing violent situation in Washington, D.C. Twitter stated it required the removal of three @realDonaldTrump Tweets posted earlier that day for repeated and severe violations of its Civic Integrity Policy. Twitter stated the account would be locked for 12 hours following the removal of these Tweets. If the Tweets are not removed, the account will remain locked.

President Trump said Friday he "fell asleep" trying to watch President Obama's 2018 election takedown speech. Trump said, "He's very good, very good for sleeping." He made the remarks as he kicked off a campaign rally in North Dakota. Obama had criticized Trump, accusing him of pandering to radicals, losing control of the White House, squandering international good will, and dividing the U.S.

Two weeks ago, Hillary Clinton tweeted that "every survivor of sexual assault deserves to be heard, believed and supported." At a campaign event in New Hampshire on Thursday, a woman in the audience asked Hillary if believing all "survivors" meant believing Bill's accusers, including Juanita Broaddrick, Kathleen Willey and Paula Jones. Hillary Clinton responded: "I would say that everybody should be believed at first until they are disbelieved based on evidence."

President Obama selected Myrlie Evers-Williams, widow of slain civil rights icon Medgar Evers, to deliver the invocation at his public swearing-in later this month. The invocation is believed to be the first time a woman, and a layperson rather than a clergy member, has been chosen to deliver what may be America's most prominent public prayer. The inaugural committee announced that the benediction will be given by conservative evangelical pastor Louie Giglio, founder of the student-focused Passion Conferences, which draw tens of thousands of people to events around the world.

Norm Coleman will speak to the press at 3 p.m. CT. The Minnesota Canvassing Board certified that Al Franken is leading the Minnesota US Senate race by 225 votes. The UpTake, which has been covering the recount in Minnesota for nearly two months, will also hold a press conference at the State Office Building. The UpTake has previously refused to cover news conferences held at the Coleman campaign headquarters. The State Office Building is a public venue where the UpTake can not be refused entry.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel said Friday that meetings between U.S. and Russian presidents should become "normal" again. Merkel made the comments after President Donald Trump invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to the White House. Earlier this week, the two had a meeting in Finland. Merkel said that "in principle it's always good for everyone when there are talks, particularly when there are talks between these two countries." She added: "I think it must once again become normal for Russian and American presidents to meet."

Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney is expected to visit Virginia, North Carolina and Florida, although the schedule may change in the coming days. Romney returned from an overseas trip late Tuesday. He was spending Wednesday in meetings at his Boston campaign headquarters. Romney is scheduled to campaign in the Denver area on Thursday. Aides report that he will attend a Republican Governors Association fundraiser in Aspen later that night. A handful of governors often mentioned as possible Romney running mates are scheduled to attend. Next week's bus tour could be part of the rollout for a running mate. Republican officials are expecting that announcement any day.

On Monday, "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" reimagined the classic holiday song "The Twelve Days of Christmas" to be about special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into alleged Russian meddling in the 2016 presidential election. The song's central focus was the guilty plea from Trump's former national security adviser, Michael Flynn, for lying about his contacts with the Russian government.

President Donald Trump used the word "anonymous" during a rally in Montana on Thursday evening. On Twitter, the phrase quickly went viral. Some users interpreted the error as a new "covfefe," referring to a typo that became a social media sensation last year when Trump used it in a since-deleted tweet. Several people have already recorded the moment to music. Others laughed at the misspeak.

Former FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe faces the prospect of criminal charges after his attorneys were unable to persuade senior Justice Department officials not to pursue charges. Two people familiar with the matter said the deputy attorney general declined an appeal from McCabe's lawyers aimed at preventing a prosecution. The attorneys argued that McCabe, a frequent target of President Trump's wrath, should not face charges on accusations he lied during an internal investigation. The people were not authorized to discuss the issue by name and spoke on condition of anonymity.

CBS News reported that President Donald Trump has bolstered his White House communications staff to fight impeachment. Reporter Paula Reid cited a Senior Administration Official confirming that former Florida Attorney General Pam Bondi and former Assistant Secretary for Public Affairs Tony Sayegh were expected to join the White House team to work on "proactive impeachment messaging." The official said their roles would be temporary as special government employees. Both Sayegh and Bondi have experience defending the president on television, increasing the president's defense in the establishment media.

Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont, who was sworn in to preside over the upcoming impeachment trial, has been taken to the hospital for observation. His office issued a statement saying he was feeling unwell, had been seen by a doctor, and had been taken out of an abundance of caution for observation and evaluation. Dick Durbin spoke to Leahy's wife, who said the senator is resting comfortably and may be back tomorrow and things are going well.

Colombian police arrested a sixth suspect in the slaying of a U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent, James Watson. Metropolitan Bogota police commander Luis Edwardo Martinez announced the arrest on Wednesday. Martinez said officials believe the June 20 killing occurred during a robbery and was not related to work done by Watson, who was known as Terry. Officials say the gang attacked Watson on June 20 after he got into a taxi outside a restaurant and stabbed him to death. They say the group apparently had carried out similar robberies using taxis.

The article's headline stated "What the fight for marriage equality really means: Advancing the gay agenda." The article also included the phrase "Don't let all those so-called 'equality' people fool you ... what they're really after is to forcibly shove the gay agenda straight down the throats of all real Americans." The article's author wrote that the fight for marriage equality really means Advancing the gay agenda.

The article's headline stated that Trump wrote that Republicans need more Republicans in 2018 and must always hold the Supreme Court. The article reported that the SCOTUS judges politically far to often and is supposed to be impartial. The article reported that the president publicly supported the decision's politicization by tweet. The article stated that the second amendment would never be repealed, and that Democrats would like to see this happen despite the words of former Supreme Court Justice Stevens. The article concluded that Democrats would like to see this happen, and that Republicans need more Republicans in 2018 and must always hold the Supreme Court.

Saudi state TV reported that King Abdullah, a U.S. ally who joined Washington's fight against al-Qaida and sought to modernize the kingdom, died at age 90. The TV station said Abdullah died Friday. His expected successor is his 79-year-old half-brother, Prince Salman, who recently took on Abdullah's responsibilities. The announcement came in a statement read by a presenter on Saudi state TV, which aired video of worshippers at the Kaaba in Mecca.

President Trump delivered a prime-time address urging Americans to support his border wall plans. Opposition to the idea continued. Public opinion polls have shown public dissatisfaction with the president. A Quinnipiac University Poll released Monday found 43 percent of Americans support building a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border, the same percentage as in December, before the shutdown began.

Iranian official news agency Fars News Agency ran a piece from The Onion today as news. The piece, a parody, suggested that a Gallup poll released Monday showed the overwhelming majority of rural white Americans favored Ahmadinejad over Obama. The Onion reported that the poll found the overwhelming majority of rural white Americans said they would rather vote for Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad over U.S. President Barack Obama. Fars was reported to have been excited to run the piece as fact.

A state of emergency has been declared in Charlotte, North Carolina. Protests continue at this hour. The protests began a day earlier after Keith Lamont Scott was shot by a police officer in a north Charlotte apartment complex parking lot. Police officers on Wednesday morning repeated their account that Scott was armed with a gun and ignored their commands to drop his weapon. At the moment, things appear calm and hopefully will stay that way. Video of police firing tear gas at protesters can be viewed below the fold. Comments are closed on this story.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met with President Donald Trump on Monday before leaving for the meeting. Netanyahu said he and Trump see "eye-to-eye" on a lot of issues. Netanyahu said, "The alliance between Israel and America has always been extremely strong, it's about to get even stronger. President Trump and I see eye-to-eye on the dangers emanating from the region, but also on the opportunities. And we will talk about both as well as upgrading the relations between Israel and the United States in many many fields."

The Trump administration is considering sending checks to Americans to provide cash for the coronavirus crisis, Treasury Secretary Steve Mnuchin said at a White House briefing on Tuesday. Mnuchin said the administration has increased the amount of tax payments that can be deferred. "We're looking at sending checks to Americans immediately," Mnuchin said. "Americans need cash now ... and I mean now in the next two weeks." Mnuchin also said that individuals can defer tax payments up to $1 million and corporations can defer tax payments up to $10 million for 90 days, interest and penalty-free.

A Washington restaurant, the Bird DC, promoted a special $5 "Moscow Mueller" drink every time special counsel Robert Mueller indicts an associate of President Donald Trump. The restaurant added the hashtag "#muellertime." The drink's name is a play on the popular Moscow Mule, a beverage made with vodka, ginger beer and lime juice. Mueller is investigating potential links between Russia and Trump's presidential campaign.

The article reports that there does not appear to be anything terribly unethical about the White House offer of an unpaid advisory position to Joe Sestak if he would withdraw from the Pennsylvania Democratic primary, in which he later defeated Senator Arlen Specter. It questions why President Obama's White House would not inform the public for three months, allowing Republicans and the conservative blogosphere to hyperinflate the matter into what it turned out to be a grave scandal on Friday.

Former President Jimmy Carter appeared on HuffPost Live on Tuesday to discuss his book "A Call To Action." He criticized the Obama administration's use of drones. When asked about his stance on drone warfare, Carter said he would not rely on drone warfare, arguing that they kill innocent people and aggravate hatred toward the United States. "I believe it creates more additional terrorists, with the fervor of killing Americans, than we would be if we were not using the drones to kill people," Carter said of the policy.

Most polls show Hillary Clinton defeating Donald Trump in a presidential contest. A new survey released by Mercury Analytics, a Democrat-run firm with clients including Fox News and MSNBC, found 19 percent of likely Democratic voters said they would consider bucking their party and vote for Trump, while 14 percent of GOP voters said they might do the same for Clinton. The company also found a much higher percentage of Democrats were "100 percent sure" of voting for Trump than Republicans considering voting for Clinton.

During her weekly press briefing, California Democrat Nancy Pelosi and Minority Whip Steny Hoyer exchanged rhetorical exchanges. Pelosi said lawmakers, including Hoyer, a 19-term Maryland Democrat, were incapable of crafting sound immigration policy because of their skin color. "The five white guys I call them, you know," Pelosi said. "Are they going to open a hamburger stand next or what?"

US President Barack Obama will announce in his State of the Union address Tuesday that he will pull 34,000 US troops home from Afghanistan in the next year, a source familiar with his speech said. The move will halve the size of the current 66,000 strong US force in Afghanistan, ahead of a final withdrawal of most foreign combat troops by the end of 2014.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday will hear arguments in a case that pits religious liberty against women's rights. The issue is momentous enough. It only begins to touch on the potential consequences of the court's ruling in the case, notably for laws banning discrimination against gay men and lesbians. The question directly before the justices is whether for-profit corporations must provide insurance coverage for contraception, a requirement of the Affordable Care Act. Hobby Lobby, a chain of crafts stores, challenged the requirement, saying it conflicts with the company's religious principles.

President Donald Trump on Monday announced a new round of sanctions on Iran, including measures targeting its supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The White House transcript shows Trump said "Ayatollah Khomeini," referring to Ruhollah Khomeini, who led the country from 1979 until his death in 1989. The announcement prompted Twitter users to post Khomeini's name on Monday afternoon and evening.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) posted a picture of one of the Zodiac Killer's letters on Twitter on Wednesday. The post referenced conspiracy theories that claim Cruz is the serial killer. Cruz posted the letter in response to a post by Sen. Ben Sasse (R-NE), and his reply went viral on the social network ahead of his debate with Sen. Bernie Sanders (D-VT). Conspiracy theories and memes have often joked that Cruz is the Zodiac Killer, based on old police sketches of the serial killer who was never caught.

President Obama left for his 11-day vacation on Martha's Vineyard on Thursday afternoon along with his dog, Bo. Several stores stocked up on Obama merchandise ahead of their arrival. No word yet on whether Michelle Obama and the first daughters are already on the island. Photos of local shops preparing for the President's arrival were also available.

Rick Santorum suggested President Obama should be pro-life because he is black. Santorum said Conservatives are attempting to racialize the abortion debate because the prolife base of older white evangelical rural voters is shrinking. Santorum said the question is whether human life is a person under the constitution, and that Barack Obama says no. Santorum said it is almost remarkable for a black man to say "now we are going to decide who are people and who are not people."

On Tuesday, Jimmy Kimmel, host of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" and host, responded to a tweet by Eric Trump, President Donald Trump's son, concerning attorney George Conway, husband of White House counselor Kellyanne Conway. Kimmel asked, "The president's son, Eric Trump, is he the smart one?" He replied, "No, there are no smart ones."

Authorities reported that the number of confirmed dead from the mudslide in Washington state has increased from 18 to 21. Snohomish County Emergency Management Director Jason Biermann said Sunday that 15 victims have been identified by the Snohomish County medical examiner, and six have yet to be identified. Biermann said another four bodies were found in the debris field on Sunday. About 30 people remain missing after the mudslide in the mountainside community of Oso on March 22.

No word yet on whether Michelle Obama and the first daughters are already on the island. Photos of local shops preparing for the President's arrival were also available.

The Senate Finance Committee approved the $1.5 trillion Republican tax overhaul proposal late Thursday night after four days of markup. The vote was 14-12 along party lines. Earlier this week, Senate Republicans added a provision repealing the Affordable Care Act's individual mandate to help raise revenues for tax cuts. The bill next heads to the Senate floor, where the Senate is expected to take action sometime after the Thanksgiving break. Earlier Thursday, the House of Representatives passed its tax reform bill, which differs from the Senate version and does not include the mandate repeal provision.

China criticized the European Union's decision to stop importing oil from Iran over its nuclear program. The official Xinhua News Agency on Thursday quoted the Foreign Ministry as saying, "To blindly pressure and impose sanctions on Iran are not constructive approaches." The EU embargo announced Monday is the latest attempt to pressure Iran over a nuclear program the United States and its allies argue is aimed at developing nuclear weapons but which Iran says is for purely peaceful purposes. China said the dispute should be resolved through dialogue and consultation. China is a major buyer of Iranian crude oil.

Kimmel asked, "The president's son, Eric Trump, is he the smart one?" He replied, "No, there are no smart ones."

President Donald Trump plans to visit wounded service members at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Maryland. It will be Trump's first visit to the facility. Trump tweeted Saturday that he was looking forward to "seeing our bravest and greatest Americans." First lady Melania Trump was expected to join the president. Trump planned to meet with about a dozen service members who are receiving care at the hospital. He is also expected to award at least one Purple Heart, the U.S. military's decoration given to those wounded or killed in action.

U.N. Human Rights Commissioner Al Hussein said in a formal speech to the Human Rights Council in Geneva that in the United States, he is deeply concerned by recently adopted policies which punish children for their parents' actions. Al Hussein called on the United States to end the policy immediately and to ratify the Convention on the Rights of the Child "to ensure that the fundamental rights of all children" will be the focus of all laws. This was Al Hussein's last global update to the Human Rights Council this session.

Tom Ridge, the former governor who became the first homeland security secretary, may challenge Senator Arlen Specter next year, Republican Party leaders said. Senator John Cornyn, Republican of Texas and chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said he is considering it. Bob Asher, the state's Republican national committeeman, said he met with Ridge in recent days and urged him to run.

The House voted 228-192 to add $33.7 billion to legislation to help victims of Superstorm Sandy. The storm was one of the worst to strike the Northeast. The total was increased to $50.7 billion. The House is expected to approve the entire measure later Tuesday night. Sandy passed several states in late October. It has been blamed for 140 deaths and billions of dollars in residential and business property damage, much of it in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut.

On Monday, former Secretary of State and presumptive Democratic 2016 presidential frontrunner Hillary Clinton posted a tweet to swimmer Diana Nyad of Cuba. Nyad said: "Because it's all about Hillary." Clinton did not comment on Syria. Ben Shapiro is Editor-At-Large of Breitbart News and author of the New York Times bestseller "Bullies: How the Left's Culture of Fear and Intimidation Silences America" (Threshold Editions, January 8, 2013).

Sarah Palin gave a speech in support of John McCain's re-election campaign in Arizona. At one point, she was interrupted by a heckler. He was quickly overwhelmed by the roar of the crowd and eventually escorted from the rally. Responding to the heckler, Palin said, "Young man, stick around and listen to what we're going to say. Sir, maybe you'll learn something." An ABC station captured video of another protester being held on the ground following his ejection from the event.

Gina McCarthy, former EPA head, said on CNN that Scott Pruitt needs to be more concerned about the environment. "The only thing Scott Pruitt talks about or seems to consider is whether or not it's reducing the cost of business," McCarthy said. "His job is to protect public health and the environment in ways that continue to keep the economy moving." She said Pruitt, the current EPA administrator, needs to be more transparent in his actions at the agency. He has recently been flagged for possible violations concerning his housing in Washington where he rented from a lobbyist in the energy sector.

Republican leaders said the House will vote Thursday to block President Barack Obama from extending relief from deportation to any more immigrants brought here illegally as children. The move is aimed at winning conservatives to support an emergency spending bill for the immigration crisis on the border. House Republican leaders agreed to a second vote on a measure to prevent Obama from expanding an existing program granting work permits to immigrants brought here illegally as children. The two votes will occur as Congress wraps up its work before heading out for a five-week recess.

Attorney General Eric Holder announced Monday that Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and other accused 9/11 conspirators will face a military tribunal at Guantanamo Bay. The announcement reverses a November 2009 decision by President Obama and Holder to try the suspects in a civilian court on U.S. soil.

On Sunday, Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY) spoke on the Senate floor. He said the current government shutdown was a result of President Donald Trump being "dysfunctional." Schumer said, "Americans know why this dysfunction is occurring. Dysfunctional president. We are in a Trump Shutdown, and party leaders who won't act without him have created the chaos and the gridlock we find ourselves in today. It all really stems from the president, whose inability to clinch a deal has created the Trump Shutdown."

The Pentagon announced Wednesday that the top two officials at its Defense Intelligence Agency are retiring. The departure of Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn as director of the DIA and David Shedd as deputy director was announced by Pentagon press secretary, Navy Rear Adm. John Kirby. Kirby said the two are retiring this year, but he was not more specific about the timing and offered no reason for their decisions to leave. Kirby said the Flynn and Shedd retirements have been planned for "some time." He said replacements would be announced later.

Police said they suspect Allison Johnson of Norman was also connected to vandalism at a school and arts center in the city. Johnson was booked Thursday afternoon into the Cleveland County Detention Center on a complaint of terroristic threats. No criminal charges have been filed, and jail records do not indicate if Johnson has an attorney. The vandalism was discovered Wednesday morning on the windows and sidewalk outside the Cleveland County Democratic Party headquarters in Norman. Similar epithets were found spray-painted March 28 outside the Democratic Party headquarters in Oklahoma City and the Oklahoma City office of the Chickasaw Nation.

Porn star Stormy Daniels filed a lawsuit for defamation on Monday against President Donald Trump's personal attorney Michael Cohen. Cohen denied Daniels' claims of an affair more than a decade ago but acknowledged making a $130,000 hush agreement with her. The additional claim in the lawsuit, filed on Monday, says Cohen's denial is a defamatory statement. The complaint reads: "It was reasonably understood Mr. Cohen meant to convey that Ms. Clifford is a liar." The defamation claim begins on page 17.

Rick Gates testified Tuesday in the tax and bank fraud trial of Paul Manafort. Gates said his former boss's income streams had dried up after his friends in the Ukrainian government lost power, creating financial difficulties for the former Trump campaign chairman. "It substantially decreased in terms of income he was accustomed to receiving in prior years," Gates said. Prosecutors alleged that after Manafort's income dropped, he turned to hiding his money in overseas accounts to evade the IRS.

Michelle Obama said her daughters, Sasha, 9, and Malia, 12, do not use Facebook. During an interview on NBC's "Today Show" on Wednesday, she said she is "not a big fan of young kids having Facebook." She added that even if the girls were not living in the White House, Facebook is "not something they need." She added that maybe when they get older.

On Tuesday, House Intelligence Committee chairman Rep. Adam Schiff (D-CA) told CNN's senior congressional correspondent Manu Raju that the case for opening impeachment proceedings against President Donald Trump was getting stronger. Schiff said, "I think that that the administration is certainly pushing the Congress in that direction by obstructing everything. I expect we'll have a discussion about that today." He added, "I think The case gets stronger the more they stonewall the Congress."

The U.S. Capitol building is on lockdown with police barring people from entering. The Senate seargant at arms issued a lockdown alert for the building and visitor center, saying police activity has been reported. Capitol office buildings are open. Capitol police say they are searching for an individual but offered no details. House press gallery staff says the building is on lockdown but that the House met briefly and immediately recessed. Voting scheduled to begin at 9:15 a.m. is postponed, gallery staff said.

Secretary of State Hillary Rodham Clinton suffered a concussion early last week after fainting and striking her head, the State Department disclosed on Saturday. As a result, she will not testify as scheduled on Thursday before Congressional committees investigating the September attack on the American diplomatic outpost in Benghazi, Libya. The fainting episode occurred after Mrs. Clinton, who is being widely discussed as a possible presidential candidate in 2016, became dehydrated because of a stomach virus she contracted during a trip to Europe, according to statements released by a close adviser and her doctors.

The Supreme Court handed down a ruling Friday making gay marriage legal in all 50 states. Celebrities posted on Twitter celebrating the ruling, including President Obama's #LoveWins hashtag. Obama wrote: "Woke up to learn that love is free! Thank you to all those who fought so hard to make this historic moment happen. The Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage in all 50 states today. IT'S ABOUT. FUCKING. TIME. Very happy about the SCOTUS rulings this week! Marriage Equality, Fair Housing and Affordable Health Care!"

Harry Reid underwent surgery for cancer. Reid's family said he is in good spirits and resting with his family. They said doctors caught the tumor early during a routine screening and his prognosis is good. The former Senate Democratic leader declined to seek re-election in 2016 after more than three decades in Congress. He suffered an accident in 2015 that left him blind in one eye. Nevada's longest-serving senator helped propel the passage of President Barack Obama's signature health care law, blocked the development of a nuclear waste dump in Nevada, and built a well-organized Democratic machine in the state.

Defense Secretary Mark Esper fired Navy Secretary Richard Spencer on Sunday after Spencer proposed a secret agreement with the White House regarding Navy SEAL Eddie Gallagher, according to a senior defense official. Esper asked for Spencer's resignation after "losing trust" and "confidence in him," according to a Pentagon statement. Spencer submitted a letter to President Donald Trump on Sunday acknowledging his termination.

President Trump signed an executive order on Monday banning all refugees from entering the United States for 120 days. The order also cuts the refugee program in half, capping it at 50,000 people for the 2017 fiscal year, down from the 110,000 ceiling put in place under President Obama. The United States accepted 84,994 refugees from 78 different countries in 2016. The order also temporarily halts new visas for six countries: Iran, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.

Saudi Arabia's ambassador to the U.S., Adel Al-Jubeir, said Sunday on CBS that the fighting in Yemen is not a proxy war between Saudi Arabia and Iran. Al-Jubeir described the situation as a war of necessity and said the country had no choice but to avoid it. Houthi rebels, who are Shiite Muslims backed by Iran, have overrun parts of Yemen. Saudi Arabia, with a coalition of nine other Arab countries, has launched a military campaign against the rebels to restore stability.

Deposed FBI Director James Comey wrote a memo following a February 14 meeting with Donald Trump in which he said the President told him "I hope you can let this go" regarding fired aide Michael Flynn's role in the ongoing investigation into Russia's efforts to influence the 2016 campaign. The New York Times and CNN reported that Comey's memo as reported misrepresents the tenor of the conversation on that February day.

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg had surgery Wednesday morning to replace a stent in her right coronary artery. Ginsburg, 81, is resting comfortably and is expected to leave a Washington-area hospital within 48 hours. Court spokeswoman Kathleen Arberg said Ginsburg had the procedure at MedStar Heart & Vascular Institute at MedStar Washington Hospital Center after a coronary blockage was discovered. Ginsburg experienced some discomfort Tuesday night during routine exercise and was taken to the hospital. Ginsburg has been on the court since 1993.

On Friday in Nashua, NH at the Young America's Foundation Conference, Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), a 2016 candidate for the Republican presidential nomination, outlined his vision to repeal and replace ObamaCare. Listing three specific reforms, Cruz said, "Number one, allow people to buy insurance across state lines." He continued, "Number two, we need to expand health saving accounts," and he concluded with, "Number three, we need to de-link health insurance from employment."

Former Vice President Joe Biden appeared on ABC on Thursday night for a town hall in lieu of a debate, opposite a town hall for President Donald Trump on NBC at the same time. Biden made several statements that were considered factually challenged. He acknowledged his own crime bill was a mistake, but not at the federal level. Biden said: "Yes, it was. But here's where the mistake. The mistake came in terms of what the states did locally."

The House will proceed on August recess as planned. Unlike the Senate, most incumbents up for re-election this fall are Democrats. Majority Leader Mitch McConnell can hurt incumbents in the House. Everyone in the House is up for re-election. Republicans need to get home to campaign. The article also included a solicitation asking readers to donate $1 to elect a Democrat in each Daily Kos-targeted House district.

The Daily Beast reported that Judge Sonia Sotomayor has a wonderful poker face. The author recounted that a couple of months ago, they were on a panel discussing the nomination and confirmation of federal judges. At that time there were not yet any vacancies on the Supreme Court. At the start of her remarks, the author turned toward the judge and remarked that she hoped she would soon be addressing her not as "Judge Sotomayor" but as "Justice Sotomayor."

The House of Representatives approved a bill by unanimous consent to deny a visa for Hamid Aboutalebi. Iran has appointed Aboutalebi to be its Ambassador to the United Nations. Aboutalebi was a participant in the Iranian uprising that seized the US Embassy in Tehran in 1979 and took American hostage for 444 days. The Senate approved by unanimous consent a measure to deny a visa for Aboutalebi earlier this week. Sens. Ted Cruz (R-TX) and Chuck Schumer (D-NY) crafted the plan.

Jason Collins, an NBA player who came out last week as the first openly gay athlete in one of the four major sports, will join with first lady Michelle Obama to help Democrats raise money at their LGBT Gala later this month. Mr. Barr said Friday that he intended to provide Congress with Mr. Mueller's "principal conclusions" as early as this weekend. Congress and the public must wait at least one more day to learn the results of the most significant investigation into the president of the last 20 years.

New York lawmakers rejected a bill to legalize gay marriage in the Senate on Wednesday. The decision followed months of delays and arm twisting by lawmakers sympathetic to the bill but representing conservative districts. It followed a referendum in Maine earlier this month that struck down a gay marriage law before it took effect. Advocates said they were not surprised by the decision. Most, including Gov. David Paterson, said they at least wanted a floor debate and vote. Gay marriage is legal in Connecticut, Iowa, Massachusetts and Vermont. A New Hampshire law takes effect Jan. 1.

Martha Raddatz of ABC News moderated the first and only vice presidential debate of 2012, sponsored by the Commission on Presidential Debates. Raddatz said she was honored to moderate the debate between two men who have dedicated much of their lives to public service. The debate was divided between domestic and foreign policy issues. Raddatz said she would move back and forth between foreign and domestic since that is what a vice president or president would have to do.

Judges dismissed legal challenges that the president's campaign had launched Wednesday as the presidential election remained uncertain with votes still being tabulated in a number of battleground states. President Trump's campaign alleged late absentee ballots in one Georgia county were illegally placed alongside on-time ballots instead of set aside, as required by state law. The issue involved about 53 ballots. They called on the court to separate late-arriving ballots, but a judge dismissed the lawsuit Thursday.

Most every Hillary Clinton supporter in this country is probably stunned right now, as may be a few (or more) Donald Trump supporters. Add the optimism and expectation among the Clinton faithful to the decisive defeat handed down by Trump on Tuesday, and it made for some remarkable and poignant photography on Tuesday night and early Wednesday morning at the Jacob K. Javits Convention Center in New York City. Here are some images that tell that tale of one of the most shocking political events in history from the losing side.

Stephen Colbert criticized President Donald Trump for his personal attack on porn star Stormy Daniels, who claims to have had an affair with Trump about a decade before his election. In a tweet, Trump referred to her as "horseface" after a federal judge dismissed her defamation suit. Colbert responded that Trump's insult came "straight from the horse's ass." A clip of the segment was available.

Rep. Jason Chaffetz, a Utah Republican, said Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy was wrong to say what he did about the special committee on Benghazi. Chaffetz intends to challenge McCarthy for the speakership. The House GOP appears to believe this is the only way it can address the matter. McCarthy admitted to Sean Hannity that the committee is political and its true target is Hillary Rodham Clinton's run for the presidency.

President Barack Obama spoke Thursday from the White House press briefing room. He said there is no "elaborate strategy" to go "full scale" and defeat ISIS. He said he did not want to "put the cart before the horse," but instead the immediate goal is to keep American people and interests safe while the administration is working politically and diplomatically to "cobble together a collation" of allies to create a military, political and economic answer to ISIS.

Police officers in Charlotte, North Carolina, on Thursday morning helped local business owners clean up from damage sustained during riots on Wednesday night. Images shared on social media showed local businesses vandalized, with windows broken and merchandise looted. Demonstrators were marching over the death of Keith Lamont Scott, a black man shot and killed by a black police officer. On Thursday, police officers stood outside looted businesses with weapons drawn and helped store owners pick up debris.

White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders announced during Wednesday's press briefing that President Trump ordered former CIA Director John Brennan's security clearance to be revoked. In her opening remarks, Sanders said, "Mr. Brennan has a history that calls into question his objectivity and credibility."

President Barack Obama presented Purple Hearts to two troops wounded in service. Obama presented the honors while visiting wounded troops at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center in Bethesda, Md. That facility is where many U.S. troops injured in Iran and Afghanistan are treated. Obama visited for about an hour with 15 service members from the Army and Marines and one member of NATO forces. He also participated in a promotion ceremony for a military member. The White House did not release names or details about the wounded troops.

The Justice Department is expected to oust the head of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, according to people familiar with the matter. The operation has grown into the agency's biggest scandal in nearly two decades. Moves toward the replacement of Kenneth Melson, acting ATF director since April 2009, could begin next week, these people said. The precise sequence of events remains to be decided.

President Barack Obama made his case to the nation for taking the fight to ISIS. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry traveled through the Middle East to urge regional leaders to support America's plan to defeat the terror group. The group has seized territory stretching from northern Syria to central Iraq with alarming pace in recent months.

On Thursday, Secretary of State John Kerry appeared on CNN in an interview with Elise Labott in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Kerry said America is not at war with ISIS. He stated, "What we are doing is engaging in a very significant counter-terrorism operation. It's going to go on for some period of time. When asked about 17 members currently opposing her and if she could still win, Pelosi said, "Yes." She continued, "I have overwhelming support in my caucus to be speaker of the House." She added, "I happen to think at this point, I'm the best person for that."

Jim Carrey promoted voter registration with artwork featuring President Donald Trump. Carrey shared a painting of Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Twitter. Carrey overlaid the words "Would" and "Wouldn't" over his depictions of Trump and Putin for the image, which he posted online earlier this week. President Donald Trump visited U.S. troops stationed in Iraq on Wednesday. During the visit, he declared that "the United States cannot continue to be the policeman of the world." He defended his decision to pull U.S. troops out of neighboring Syria, saying there would be no delays. "You can't have any more time. You've had enough time," he said he had told his generals.

Sen. Charles E. Schumer (D-N.Y.) announced his support Tuesday for the nomination of former senator Chuck Hagel as Secretary of Defense. Schumer, the No. 3 Democrat and most senior Jewish senator, made the decision following a 90-minute meeting Monday in the West Wing. Schumer and White House officials kept the details of the meeting secret until the decision to announce his support.

The Federal Aviation Administration extended a temporary reprieve on Wednesday for contract weather observers whose jobs the agency had proposed eliminating starting this month. The FAA said it will defer action on its plan to shift responsibility for weather monitoring to air traffic controllers instead of contractors. The FAA said all the contracts would be extended through Sept. 30 "to allow for more stakeholder input on how to proceed going forward." More details on this development are available in an article by the Washington Post's Weather Gang.

North Korea agreed to "actively cooperate" with South Korea in talks to reduce military tensions ahead of next month's Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang. Tuesday's trip south of the border by North Korean officials marked the first in-person meeting between countries in nearly two years. The North Koreans agreed at the last minute to open the meeting in the Demilitarized Zone to the press. South Korean media reported both countries agreed to continue discussions about improving conditions along their shared border.

He will run for reelection to his current post as a Democrat in 2010. The move puts Democrats within one vote of a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate.

Former Florida Governor Jeb Bush is getting closer to making a decision about running for president. He has questioned whether he can secure the Republican nomination without pandering to the party's conservative base. The New York Times's Jonathan Martin reported that Bush is deeply conservative on some issues and that in other ways, culturally and philosophically, he is out of step with grass-roots activists who animate the party.

The Senate voted 60-40 on Thursday afternoon to end debate on the financial reform bill. The vote makes it likely the measure will pass the Senate within days. President Obama and Democratic leaders prevented major changes to the legislation sought by Republicans and liberal Democrats during four weeks of Senate debate. The vote reversed a closer vote Wednesday, in which Republicans joined forces with two liberal Democrats to stall the measure temporarily.

The White House cancelled a Friday event at which Michelle Obama was set observe Earth Day. The event, which was to be held in northwest Washington Park, was called off after rain showers and cool temperatures moved into the D.C. area. The first lady was scheduled to meet with school children and students from the White House Mentorship program and participate in a "habitat improvement project" at Fort Dupont Park. Obama was also slated to present certificates to children who took part in her "Let's Move!" initiative.

President Barack Obama will issue an order restoring U.S. funding for international family-planning groups involved with abortion on Thursday, the anniversary of Roe v. Wade. He did not make an abortion-related order on the anniversary of the Supreme Court ruling.

The first person diagnosed with the deadly Ebola virus on United States soil is now in a critical condition, health officials said Saturday, having previously described him as seriously ill. Latino organizations are coming together following Donald Trump's hosting appearance on "Saturday Night Live." Hillary Clinton won the larger portion of the delegates allocated at Saturday's Nevada State Democratic Convention. Clinton received seven delegates, while Sanders received five. As the results were announced, Sanders supporters in attendance shouted in protest, reacting to news that a number of Sanders supporters were barred from participating. One local report showed that by a slim margin, Clinton's 1,695 supporters allowed to participate outnumbered Sanders' 1,662 backers.

He added, "When the vicitims turn to us for leadership and help, we will have nothing to show but empty hands and a few empty gestures. It's despicable."

U.S. President Donald Trump said on Friday that the United States and Mexico would restrict non-essential travel across their shared border in an effort to limit the spread of the new coronavirus. During a press conference with top U.S. officials, Trump also announced that he would invoke a health-focused statute to block migrants from either border from entering the United States illegally, saying illegal immigration "threaten to create a perfect storm."

Matt Morgan, general counsel for Trump 2020, said poll workers struggled to operate the new voting machines in Maricopa County and improperly pressed and told voters to press a green button to override significant errors. Morgan said the voting machines disregarded votes cast by voters in person on Election Day in Maricopa County. The campaign wants overvoted ballots inspected. The Arizona filing comes as the president also has ongoing litigation in other battleground states, refusing to concede the election.

New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo (D) is reportedly planning a trade mission to Cuba, according to The Wall Street Journal. The Obama administration recently announced it was taking moves to normalize full relations with the Communist island. The U.S. government is making it easier for most Americans who want to go to Cuba to find a way to do so under new rules adopted on Friday. Cuomo's visit would be the first by a high-profile U.S. official since the accord was announced.

China's Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office said on Wednesday its deputy head met William Klein, the U.S. embassy's minister counselor for political affairs, and lodged representations over the new U.S. law on Hong Kong. U.S. President Donald Trump last month signed into law congressional legislation which supported Hong Kong protesters, despite objections from Beijing. Trump is seeking a deal to end a trade war.

The House approved a $50.7 billion measure for Superstorm Sandy victims by a 241-180 vote. The measure was sent to the Senate, which is expected to take it up next Tuesday. Northeast lawmakers from both parties have been pressing for the aid for more than two months. The storm is blamed for 140 deaths and struck the Atlantic coast from North Carolina to Maine with hurricane-force winds and coastal flooding. New York, New Jersey and Connecticut were the hardest hit.

Lynne Hale, a Star Wars writer and editor at large, said President Obama might have created a mash-up of Star Wars friends at Lucasfilm and Star Trek, but he might be more savvy with his knowledge of Star Wars than anyone is giving him credit for. She noted that in some Star Wars spin-off books there is a "Force Meld." She added that all of President Obama's friends at Lucasfilm would love to believe his expertise in Star Wars knowledge runs deep.

Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders criticized Republican presidential front-runner Donald Trump on Friday, accusing him of trying to divide the nation with fear. On Twitter Friday afternoon, the Vermont senator wrote: "We must bring people together to take on the powerful who've hurt the middle class. Trump is trying to play on fears and divide us up." He added: "I believe we stand together to address the real issues facing this country, not allow them to divide us by race or where we come from."

The U.S. Treasury on Friday said it would raise about $5 billion from its sale of American International Group stock. The government's stake in the company decreased to around 55 percent from 61 percent. Treasury priced its AIG offering at $30.50 per share, the same value of its May offering, and above the $28.72 price required for the government to break even on its investment in the insurer.

President Barack Obama delivered his State of the Union address to a joint session of congress on Tuesday night. The address addressed issues including the minimum wage, tax reform, manufacturing, foreign policy, and global warming. It also highlighted the imperative nature of the nation's investment in energy, education access, gun control, and immigration reform.

Stephen Hawking, a theoretical physicist, criticized Donald Trump, the likely Republican Party presidential nominee, previously joking about his intelligence. Trump said: "I'm the best baffler. People who really baffle people tell me I'm the billionaire of baffling." Comments on the story are closed.

After losing to the medical board and making little headway in the Democrat-controlled Legislature, Project Defending Life gathered enough signatures to place a late-term abortion ban on the municipal ballot. The referendum is believed to be the first such referendum of its kind in the country and is being watched as a possible new front for activism in the abortion wars that have typically been waged at the federal and state levels. On Tuesday, Albuquerque voters will decide whether to ban abortions after 20 weeks.

President Obama signed an executive action protecting up to 5 million illegal immigrants from deportation. The White House acknowledged that many of the immigrants spared from deportation under the executive action will become eligible for Social Security and Medicare benefits once they reach retirement age. The conservative backlash has been swift and will extend into a GOP Congress' deliberations in 2015 over how to limit the reach of the president's immigration blueprint.

Congressional Democrats involved in health care talks at the White House are returning to Capitol Hill for a vote on the House Floor. They are then going back to the White House for a second session of talks. Speaker Nancy Pelosi, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, and other members of the democratic leadership are meeting with President Obama to discuss health care. Sources told Major Garrett and Mike Emanuel that negotiations are intense, but that the President is open to certain changes that House Democrats have requested.

Fred Eshelman, a venture capitalist who gave $2.5 million to a non-profit called True the Vote, promised to find evidence of voter fraud that would overturn the 2020 election results and give the win to Trump. According to Eshelman, they promised to provide results or he would get his money back. They filed a few lawsuits but withdrew them.

Since Barack Obama was elected president, 10 percent of Americans believe race relations have gotten better, according to a New York Times/CBS Poll published today. The poll found 17 percent of blacks and 8 percent of whites believe race relations have improved under Obama. Thirty five percent of Americans believe that race relations have gotten worse in the Obama era, including 40 percent of whites and 21 percent of blacks. Fifty-two percent of Americans polled said that race relations have stayed about the same.

Indiana Gov. Mitch Daniels will deliver the Republican response to President Obama's State of the Union address on Tuesday. House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell made the announcement in a statement Thursday. They said Daniels has a solid record of effective governing and fiscal responsibility. Daniels is in his eighth year as governor of Indiana. He was talked about as a candidate for president until he decided against a White House run. Daniels will speak after Obama's address.

President Obama and his advisers have insisted repeatedly that the only way to avoid a default is for Congress to raise the debt ceiling. Each time the clock starts ticking for lawmakers to vote to raise it or face a default, the question arises whether there is another way out. The possibility that the U.S. could fail to make a payment on its bonds or other obligations is so unthinkable that other alternatives that would normally be unthinkable become thinkable.

Jimmy Carter told his Sunday school class that he has been declared cancer-free after several months of treatment. The former president, now age 91, underwent radiation treatment and drug treatments beginning in August for melanoma previously found in his liver which had spread to his brain. While teaching a class of about 350 people Sunday morning at Maranatha Baptist Church in the Atlanta area, Carter said a recent scan showed the cancer was gone, attendee Jill Stuckey told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution.

President Obama addressed a supporter in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, who asked whether the first lady might be persuaded to run for president someday. Obama said, "Let me tell you, there are three things that are certain in life: death, taxes, and Michelle is not running for president."

President Barack Obama attended the annual White House Correspondents' Dinner on Saturday night at the Washington Hilton hotel. Comedian Conan O'Brien hosted the event, which dates back to 1920. Celebrities at the dinner included Olivia Munn, Kerry Washington, Gerard Butler and Sophia Vergara. A video of Obama's full remarks was available. A slideshow of photos from the event was also available.

Shots fired at a security checkpoint near the White House. The suspect is apparently alive and secured, for now. The President is safe and was not at the White House at the time. No White House staff were hurt. CNN reported that the city's EMS said a patient identified as the suspect had been transported to a local hospital with critical injuries. A law enforcement official said investigators located the suspect's vehicle near the shooting area. A law enforcement official told CNN the man does not have a record with the Secret Service.

Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee announced on Friday that the state was terminating its Medicaid provider contract with Planned Parenthood. The announcement followed secretly recorded videos released by an anti-abortion group showing Planned Parenthood officials describing how they provide aborted fetus tissue for medical research. Alabama and Louisiana earlier this month announced they were ending Medicaid payments to Planned Parenthood. Planned Parenthood received more than $51,000 in Medicaid payments in Arkansas over the past fiscal year for family planning and gynecological services. None of the money went toward abortions.

White House press secretary Sean Spicer responded on Monday afternoon to a New York Times story that described President Trump watching television in a bathrobe. Former professional football player Clint Didier announced Monday that he will run for Congress in the 4th District, which is being vacated by Rep. Doc Hastings. Didier, a former professional football player who ran unsuccessfully as a Republican for the Senate in 2010, will seek the seat. Hastings announced last week he will retire at the end of the year after representing the district in eastern and central Washington for 20 years.
